units.la: GENERIS NOBILITATE, VIRTUTE ET LITERIS ORNATISSIMO adolescenti, Domino Josiæ à Wolmerchausen, amico meo honorando, Philippus Althusius U.J.D. Corbachensis salutem.
units.tr: To the young man most distinguished by nobility of birth, virtue and learning, Lord Josias von Wolmerchausen, my honoured friend: Philippus Althusius, Doctor of Both Laws, of Corbach, sends greetings.

units.la: Ibellum hunc, nobilis. Domine Josia, in lucem adspectumque hominum producere & juris publici facere, autor Joannes Althusius patruelis meus dubitauit. Ego sub nomine ipsius edere minime dubitavi: Discedit in hoc passim à communi & huc usque recepta philosophorum sententia. Litium igitur occasio & materia dari videbatur. Paradoxa quoque bonis viris sæpè suspecta & odiosa esse, memor eram. Has rationes perpedi mecum & aliis communicavi. Sed illæ neque aliis, neq; mihi satisfacere potuerunt. Quis enim unquam ob has causas philosophandi libertatem sibi, nisi homo servilis, vecordis, humilis & abiecti ingenii, adimi passus est? Plane si idem semper sentiendum & loquendum veteres Philosophi esse existimassent, nunquam profecto tam exculta philosophia artesque liberales in nostras manus peruenissent. Veritatis scis, hoc esse elogium, quod temporis sit filia. Ita enim experientia testatur, hanc incognitam quasi in profundo puteo demersam aliquādo delituisse; quæ cum tempore tamen postea ex tenebris bris emersit & innotuit. Concordia philosophicæ tranquillitatis colenda est. Fateor: sed usq; adaras: modo veritati per temporis præscriptionem non generetur prejudicium: modo libertati philosophicæ nulla vis inferatur, ejusve usus ad paucos restringatur. De qua re pluribus hîc nō dicam. Dicerem verò si opus esset. Ut igitur aliis nihil præscribo, sic nec mihi ab alio hac in re præscribi patior. Libertatem philosophicam Socraticam & Rameam amo. Αὐθάδειαν & cacoëthes scribendi & sentiendi odi. Studio veri quærendi & indagandi teneor, idque in aliis probo. Philosophicum & Christianum puto, sententiam & opinionem suam veritatis causa mutare & aliam amplecti. Si quis igitur hisce opinionibus contra-dixerit jure, tantum abest ut in jus hunc, vel ego, vel patruelis meus autor vocare, eique litem move-re velimus, ut potius gratias illi simus acturi. Quare enim non agnosceremus beneficium ejus, qui nos errore liberaret? Quare non agnosceremus veritatem o-stensam, eiq; gratularemur? cui frustra & non sine peccato bono-rumque offensione essemus contradicturi? Hæc enim tandem, omnibus etiam reclamantibus, vincet & hostes suos sub jugum mittet. Scribat igitur alius contra hæsce meditationes; sentiat judicet, quidquid velit, modo eo animo scribat, ut id quod dixi, beneficium in nos collatum & veritatem agnoscere & exosculari possipossimus. Quæ cum ita sint, & patruelis meus editionem libri hujus meo judicio&arbitrio permisset, volui eündem sub tuo nomine prodire. Scio te naturali quadam inclinatione, morū suavitate & civili conversatione, quā hīc autor præscribit, affici & plurimum delectari : contrā vero insita quadam ἀντιπαθεία inciviles, inconcinnos & insulsos homines, tanquam bovem in cornu fœnum habentem, aversari. Scio in hisce autorem ea persecutum, quæ nostris temporibus sunt adcommodata, & quæ ad honesté & secundum virtutem vivendi rationi sunt apta & idonea, & Συμβίωσιν hominum concernunt. Qua de de caussa hasce subcísivas meditationes, quas patruelis meæ in hunc, quem vides ordinem conjecit, tibi gratas fore exfti- mavi. Non dubito quin hasce ip- fe autor aliquado incudi fit red- diturus & limaturus. etsi publi- cis negotiis districtus, vix fa- tis otii ad res suas curandas ha- beat, & id ipsum quod concedi- tur otii, in juridicis studiis, in- primis Dicæologica sua, quam parturit, ipsum consume- re ego mallem. Rationem me- thodi, qua author usus est, & præ- ceptorum, non reddo. Num convenientia ista & fecundum Logicas regulas coformata sint, ex Logica examinandum relin- quo. Materia & res tota, uti vi- des, est moralis, non domi meæ vel patruelis mei nata, sed ex bo- nis authoribus, quorum nomina laudata sunt, huc translata. Sic habes editionis hujus & inscriptionis caussas, quas judicio tuo spero satisfacturas. Bené vale & vive in Christo, qui prior nos dilexit. Anno M D C I. Mense Augusto.
units.tr: Noble Lord Josias, my cousin, the author Johannes Althusius, hesitated to bring this little book out into the light and before the eyes of men, and to make it public property. I did not hesitate at all to publish it under his name. It departs in many places from the common opinion of the philosophers, which has been accepted until now, so an occasion and material for quarrels seemed to be given. I also remembered that good men often regard paradoxes with suspicion and dislike. I weighed these reasons myself and shared them with others, but they could satisfy neither others nor me. For who has ever allowed his freedom to philosophize to be taken away on these grounds, unless he was a servile, senseless, humble man of a base spirit? Clearly, if the ancient philosophers had thought that the same things must always be felt and said, philosophy and the liberal arts, so refined as they are, would never have come into our hands. You know the saying that truth is the daughter of time. Experience indeed bears witness that this truth, unknown, lay hidden for a time as if sunk in a deep well, but afterwards, with time, it emerged from the shadows and became known. The harmony of philosophical tranquillity is to be cultivated. I grant it, but only so far: provided that no prejudice is created against truth by the prescription of time, and that no violence is done to philosophical liberty or its use restricted to a few. I will say no more on this here; I would say more if it were needed. Just as I prescribe nothing to others, so I do not allow anything to be prescribed to me by another in this matter. I love Socratic and Ramean philosophical freedom. I hate self-will [αὐθάδειαν] and the itch of writing and of thinking. I am held by the zeal of seeking and investigating truth, and I approve of this in others. I think it is philosophical and Christian for a man to change his opinion and judgment for the sake of truth and to embrace another. So if anyone has justly contradicted these opinions, I, or my cousin the author, are so far from wanting to summon him to court and bring a lawsuit against him that we would rather be going to thank him. For why should we not acknowledge the kindness of one who frees us from error? Why should we not acknowledge the truth shown to us and rejoice in it, when to contradict it would be vain, and not without sin and offence to good men? For truth, at last, even with everyone protesting, will conquer and send its enemies under the yoke. Let another therefore write against these meditations; let him feel and judge whatever he likes, provided that he writes with the mind that what I have said is a kindness conferred upon us, and that we may acknowledge and embrace the truth. Since these things are so, and my cousin has left the publication of this book to my judgment and decision, I wished it to come out under your name. I know that by a certain natural inclination you are affected and greatly delighted by the sweetness of manners and the civil conversation [Συμβίωσιν] which the author prescribes here; but, on the other hand, by an innate antipathy [ἀντιπαθεία] you turn away from uncivil, awkward and dull men, as one would from an ox with hay on its horn. I know that in these pages the author has pursued matters suited to our times, and apt and fit for a way of living honourably and according to virtue, and concerning the living together of men. For this reason I thought these leisure meditations, which my cousin has put into the order you see, would be pleasing to you. I do not doubt that the author himself will at some point polish and file them into shape again, though he is occupied with public business and hardly has enough leisure to attend to his own affairs. I would rather he spent even the leisure that is granted him on his legal studies, above all on his Dicaeologica, which he is now bringing to birth. I do not give an account of the method the author has used, or of his precepts. Whether those arrangements are sound and shaped according to the rules of logic, I leave to be examined by logic. The material and the whole subject, as you see, is moral. It was not born in my house or in my cousin's, but has been transferred here from good authors, whose names have been praised. So you have the reasons for this edition and this inscription, which I hope will satisfy your judgment. Farewell, and live in Christ, who first loved us. August 1611.

units.la: JOHANNIS ALTHVSII J. C. clarissimi, CIVILIS CONVERSATIONIS LIBER PRIMVS, qui est De conuersatione communi.
units.tr: THE FIRST BOOK OF CIVIL CONVERSATION, by the most distinguished jurist Johannes Althusius, which concerns common conversation.

units.la: CAPUT I. De generalibus adfectionibus communis conuersationis.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. On the general affections of common conversation.

units.la: ONVERSATIO ciuilis est ars moribus decentibus vtendi. vel, ars mores secundum decorum & rectam rationem conformandi. Eodem sensu etiam ETHICA vocari potest, quare-nera nihil aliud, quam ars decore conuersandi cum hominibus.
units.tr: Civil conversation is the art of using decent manners, or the art of shaping manners according to propriety and right reason. In the same sense also ETHICS can be called, wherefore it is nothing other than the art of conducting oneself becomingly with people.

units.la: Mores boni secundum rectam rationem conformati & decori, sunt sermo & habitus corporis naturæ & adfectioni negotii quod agitur, & personis conueniens & adcommodatus, referes, exprimens & significans decentem, aptam & concinnam agentis & conuersantis affectione, aliarum artium praeceptis congruente. Hoc est, vt paucis dicam, mores decori sunt, qui venustatem & concinnitatem, pulchritudinem & decorum sermonis & actionum nostrarum cum symmetria & gratia in ciuili conuersatione exprimunt. Unde mores Varroni dicti a memoria, quia scilicet ex artibus perceptae virtutes sermone & actione nostra repetuntur & exprimuntur.
units.tr: Good manners, shaped according to right reason and propriety, are speech and bodily bearing that suit the nature of the business being done and the persons involved, reflecting, expressing and signifying the fitting, apt and graceful disposition of the one acting and conversing, and agreeing with the precepts of the other arts. To put it briefly, manners of propriety are those which express, in civil conversation, the charm and harmony, the beauty and decorum of our speech and actions, with symmetry and grace. Hence Varro called manners mores from memoria (memory), because the virtues learned from the arts are recalled and expressed in our speech and action.

units.la: Quando igitur quaeritur an quid recte, iure & bene fiat, hoc ex aliis artibus discendum. Sin vero quid venuste, decore, congruenter, concinne & cum gratia fiat, hoc Ethica praescribit. Fieri enim potest vt recte quidem quid facias vel loquaris, sed tamen id ipsum non rite neque decore pro rei, persona, loci, temporis aliarumque circumstantiarum dignitate, gravitate vel cotra facias. Iacob. c. 3. 13. Quis sapiens & scientia praeditus inter vos? demonstret ex bona conversatione operatio sua cum mansuetudine sapientia. Roman. c. 12. 3. 4. & c. 15. 2. Vnusquisque nostrum proximo placeat in bonum, id est, ad aedificationem, &c. 14. 19. & 1. Corinth. 13. 5. Charitas non agit indecore. & 1. Corinth. c. 11. 4. 5. & seqq. Apud vos iudicate num decorum sit. Nam recte Clemens Alexandrinus ait lib. 2. Paedagogi c. 5. Omnino quaecunque hominibus a natura insunt, illa non sunt ex illis tollenda, nec etiam tolli possunt, sed potius modus illis atque tempus opportunum adhiberi convenit. Non enim quoniam homo est animal viridendi praeditum, ideo perpetuo ridendum est, quandoquidem nec equus, cuius est proprius hinnitus, semper hinnit. Tanquam animalia ratione praedita, oportet nos temperate componere studii nostri acrimoniam & nimium intensam vehementiam moderate remittere, non autem inconcinne dissoluere, d. cap. 5.
units.tr: When, therefore, one asks whether something is done rightly, justly and well, this must be learned from the other arts. But if one asks whether something is done charmingly, becomingly, fittingly, harmoniously and with grace, Ethics prescribes this. For it can happen that you do or say something rightly, yet do not do it properly or decently, contrary to the dignity and seriousness of the matter, the person, the place, the time and the other circumstances. James 3:13: Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? Let him show out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom. Romans 12:3, 4, and 15:2: Let every one of us please his neighbour for good, that is, for edification, etc.; 14:19; and 1 Corinthians 13:5: Charity does not behave itself unseemly. And 1 Corinthians 11:4, 5 and following: Judge among yourselves whether it is comely. For Clement of Alexandria rightly says in Book 2 of the Paedagogus, chapter 5: In general, whatever is natural to men must not be removed from them, nor can it be removed, but rather a measure and a fitting time ought to be applied to it. For because man is an animal endowed with the capacity to laugh, it does not follow that he must always laugh, since the horse, whose proper sound is the neigh, does not always neigh. As animals endowed with reason, we ought to moderate the sharpness of our zeal in a temperate way, and to relax its excessive intensity in a measured way, and not to dissolve it in an unseemly manner, ibid., chapter 5.

units.la: Vnde facile contra apparet τὸ ἀνυπόθετον, & qui mores illiberales, inciuiles, indecori & improbi dici debeant, qui nimirum negotii gesti natura in aliis artibus tradita, non conueniunt, atque indicium & præsumptionem tacitam seu imaginem exhibent rerum turpium, inhonestarum & odiosarum, atque adumbrant & repræsentant res sensibus aliorum externis, nimirum visui, auditui, tactui, gustui, olfactui, vel internis scil. intellectui & voluntati inhonestas, graues, odiosas & contrarias.
units.tr: Hence it readily appears what is unconditional [τὸ ἀνυπόθετον], and which manners ought to be called illiberal, uncivil, unbecoming and base. These are the manners which, by their nature, do not agree with what the other arts teach about the matter in hand, and which show a sign and tacit presumption, or an image, of things base, dishonourable and odious. They adumbrate and represent things that are dishonourable, grave and hateful to the external senses of others, namely to sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell, or to their inner faculties, that is, to understanding and will.

units.la: Hi mores caeterarum artium liberalium præceptis contrarii accurate vitari debent, & vocantur turpes, inhonesti, illiberales, inconcinni, fœtidi, tædiosi, insuaues, agrestes, rustici, rigidi, insulsi, qui in odium & contemptum τῶν ἀπείθητων alios impellunt, iisque stomachum mouent, vt consortium horum male moratorum hominum fugiant & auersentur tanquam bouem fœnum in cornu habentem. Contra vero mores boni & ingenui aliquem ex sensibus delectant, vel saltem neque sensus neque appetitum vel imaginationem eorum quibus cum vivimus, aliqua afficiunt molestia. Ex quibus honestis & elegantibus moribus homo amabilis, gratiosus, ingenuus, φιλόφιλος, suauis & virtute praeditus esse iudicatur & bona indolis. Unde beneuolentiam eorum quibus cum viuit & conuersatur facile sibi comparat & præsumptionem interna virtutis moribus externis respondentis, cuius gratia homines adiuti & euecti ad dignitatem & amplissimorum honorum gradus, vt Galatæus ait. Ideo Cicero in epistolis ad Atticum in institutione filii fratris τὸ ἴδιος ἐπι· μελλητ​ιον, seu bonorum morum curam habendam esse censet. Nam intelligentia & prudentia infimos extollit, & deucit imprudentia summos. Proverb. c.17.2. Ecclesiast.c.7.30. Ecclesiast.c.20.12.28.
units.tr: Such manners, which are contrary to the precepts of the other liberal arts, ought to be carefully avoided. They are called shameful, dishonourable, illiberal, unbecoming, foul, tedious, unpleasant, rustic, boorish, rigid, insipid. They drive others to hatred and contempt of the disobedient [τῶν ἀπείθητων] and stir their stomachs, so that they flee and shun the company of these ill-mannered people, as one would an ox with hay on its horn. Conversely, good and well-bred manners delight one of the senses, or at least neither offend the senses, appetite or imagination of those with whom we live. From such honest and elegant manners a man is judged to be lovable, gracious, well-bred, friend-loving [φιλόφιλος], pleasant, endowed with virtue and of good disposition. Thus he easily wins the goodwill of those with whom he lives and associates, and presents an inward virtue corresponding to outward manners, by whose favour men are helped and raised to dignity and to the highest grades of honour, as Galateus says. Therefore Cicero, in his letters to Atticus, holds that in the education of his brother's son one must have care for good morals (to be his own care [τὸ ἴδιος ἐπιμελητιον]), or good manners. For intelligence and prudence raise up the lowest, and imprudence casts down the highest. Proverbs 17:2; Ecclesiasticus 7:30; Ecclesiasticus 20:12, 28.

units.la: Mores eiusmodi & decorum exprimitur sermone conuersantis, vel actione decoris.Cicer.1. De orat. Sunt quidam, ait, ita lingua haesitantes, aut ita voce absoni, aut ita vultu motuq; corporis vasti atque agrestes, vt etiamsi ingeniis atq; arte valeant, tamen in doctorum numerum venire non possint. Sunt autem quidam ita natura muneribus in iisdem rebus habiles, ita ornati, vt non nati, sed ab aliquo Deo fidei esse videantur.Coloss.c.4.v.5. Sapienter vos gerite erga extraneos, opportunitatem redimentes, 6. Sermo vester semper cum gratia sit sale conditus, vt sciatis quomodo oporteat vos vnicuiq; respondere, 1.Thess.c.4.22. abomni specie mali abstinete, Coloss.c.3.17. & quidquid egeritis sermone aut facto, in nomine Domini Iesu facite, Ephes.c.4.29. Nullus sermo putris ex ore vestro egreditur, sed si quis est commodus ad aedificationis vsum, vt gratiam auditoribus adferat, Ephes.c.5.15. Videte igitur quomodo accurate incedatis, non vt insipientes, sed vt sapientes Rom.c.14.19. Nempe igitur quae ad pacem faciunt sectemur & quae ad mutuam aedificationem, 1.Pet.c.2.12. & conuersationem vestram habeatis honestam inter gentes, Eccles.c.3.9. Opere & sermone honora patrem Iacob.c.2.12. ita loquimini, ita facite, &c. Roman.c.15.2. Itaq; vnusquisq; nostrum proximo placeat in bonum, id est, ad eius aedificationem, 1.Tim.c.4.12. Esto exemplar fidelium in sermone & conuersatione, &c.1.Pet.c.3.1. Similiter vxores sese subiiciant viris suis, vt etiam si qui non obediunt sermoni, per vxorum conuersationem absq; sermone lucrifiant, 2. vbi spectarint cum reuerentia coniunctiam castam conuersationem vestram, & seqq. Prou. c. 14. 33. In animo prudentis requiescit sapientia, quod autem est in stolidis, se cognoscendum prabet. Nam hisce duobus instrumentis sermone nimirum, & actione, res & operas nostras & praxin reliquarum artium cum proximo communicamus & societatem humanā colimus, vel in eam peccamus & affectiones animi in aliis excitamus, arg. Matth. c. 12. 34. & seqq. Psalm. 10. 7. & seqq. & 140. 3. 5. 10. & 118. Iacob. c. 3. Eccles. c. 17. 7. 1. Cor. c. 11. adeo vt I. C. ex hisce, sermone nimirum & actionibus sen gestibus hominum, præsumptiones & indicia tam licitorum quam illicitorum recte sumant. Vide Menoch. De præsumption.
units.tr: Manners and propriety of this kind are expressed either by the speech of the one conversing, or by his decorous action. Cicero, De oratore, Book 1: There are some, he says, who hesitate in their speech, or are discordant in voice, or are so rustic and boorish in face and bodily movement that, even if they excel in talent and art, they cannot come into the number of learned men. There are others who are so naturally fitted for the same things and so adorned that they seem not to be born but to be given by some god. Colossians 4:5: Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time. Verse 6: Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man. 1 Thessalonians 5:22: Abstain from all appearance of evil. Colossians 3:17: And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus. Ephesians 4:29: Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers. Ephesians 5:15: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools but as wise. Romans 14:19: Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another. 1 Peter 2:12: Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles. Ecclesiasticus 3:9: Honour thy father in word and deed. James 2:12: So speak ye, and so do, etc. Romans 15:2: Let every one of us please his neighbour for good, to his edification. 1 Timothy 4:12: Be thou an example of the believers in word, in conversation, etc. 1 Peter 3:1, 2: Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives, while they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear. Proverbs 14:33: Wisdom resteth in the heart of him that hath understanding; but that which is in the midst of fools is made known. For by these two instruments, namely speech and action, we communicate our works and the practice of the other arts with our neighbour, and cultivate human society, or sin against it and stir up the feelings of the mind in others. Cf. Matthew 12:34 and following; Psalm 10:7 and following; Psalm 140:3, 5, 10; Psalm 118; James 3; Ecclesiasticus 17:7; 1 Corinthians 11. So much so that the jurist may rightly draw from these, namely the speech and actions or gestures of men, presumptions and indications both of what is lawful and of what is unlawful. See Menochius, De praesumptionibus.

units.la: Mores vero eiusmodi & conuersatio iudicio & prudentia in ciuili hominum societate & commercio est regenda, arg. Prou. c. 23. 12. vbi Iun. & c. 14, 35. Psalm. 14. 1. 3. vbi Iunius in Notis. inprimis vero modestia, & verecundia & grauitate, quibus externi affectus reguntur, reprimuntur & cohibentur.
units.tr: Such manners and conversation, however, must be governed by judgement and prudence in civil human society and dealings, cf. Proverbs 23:12, where Junius; and 14:35; Psalm 14:1, 3, where Junius in his Notes. Above all they must be governed by modesty, shamefastness and gravity, by which external emotions are ruled, restrained and checked.

units.la: Sermo hominis est quo decore animi cogitata & proposita in conuersatione ciuili prose- rentes aliis communicamus.
units.tr: Speech is that by which we communicate to others, in civil conversation, the thoughts of the mind that we have conceived and purposed, expressed with propriety.

units.la: Decorum sermonis hic nobis conciliatur ex eo, quod virtutibus congruenter, habita ratione loci, temporis, personæ, reive loquimur, vnde præsumptio & coniectura animi bene & recte affecti ab audientibus colligitur. Indecorû contra. Ergo verba sunt indicia animi & cogitationis honesta vel inhonesta. Matth. c. 12. 34. Progeniesvipe-rarum quomodo possitis bona loqui, cum sitis mali? nam ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. 35. Bonus homo ex bono thesauro cordis profert bona, & malus homo ex malo thesauro profert mala, 35. Sed dico vobis, quodcunq; verbum otiosum locuti fuerint homines, de eo reddituros rationem in die iudicii 36. Ex sermonibus tuis condemnaberis, Luc. c. 6. 45. Et Graecis dicitur καρπὸς τῆς διανοίας ὁ λόγος, fructus mentis sermo. Clemens Alexand. lib. 2. Paedag. c. 5. & lib. 3. c. 11. ubi sermone & gestu affectiones animi in aliis nos excitare recte dicit. Ideo Seneca De morib. ait, quoties scripturus aliquid vel dicturus es, scito morum tuorum te hominibus chirographum dare. De lingua & sermonis commodis, usu & abusu praeter ea vid. Iacob. c. 3. Proverb. c. 4. 23. imprimis c. 18. 20. 21. Fructu oris cuiusq; satiatur venter eius, proventu labiorum suorum quisq; satiatur, Mors & vita sunt in potestate linguae, prout amat quisq; uti ea, comedet fructum eius, & c. 16. 2. 23. c. 14. 23. c. 15. per tot c. 21. 23. Qui observat os suum conservat ab angustiis animam suam, Eccles. c. 28. 16. & seqq. c. 4. 29. Ex sermone cognoscitur sapientia & erudito ex verbis linguae, & c. 5. 15. c. 22. 31. Gloria & ignominia est in loquutione, & lingua hominis ruina ipsi est, & c. 10. 12. 28. Sapiens sibi ipsum reddit amabilem sermonibus, stultorum vero gratia effunduntur. Sapiens prouectus est sibi ipsum sermonib. & vir prudens magnatum, placiturus, & c. 21. 8. notus e longinquo est qui valet lingua.
units.tr: Here the propriety of speech is recommended to us by this: that we speak in a way that agrees with virtues, taking account of place, time, person and matter. From this the hearers gather a presumption and conjecture of a mind well and rightly disposed. The opposite is indecorous. Therefore words are signs of an honest or dishonest mind and thought. Matthew 12:34: O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh. 35. A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things, and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things. 35. But I say unto you, that every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgement. 36. By thy words thou shalt be condemned, Luke 6:45. And the Greeks say that speech is the fruit of the mind [καρπὸς τῆς διανοίας ὁ λόγος]. Clement of Alexandria, Book 2 of the Paedagogus, chapter 5, and Book 3, chapter 11, where he rightly says that by speech and gesture we stir up the feelings of the mind in others. Therefore Seneca, De moribus, says: whenever you are about to write or say something, know that you are giving men a written record of your manners. On the uses and abuses of the tongue and speech, besides these, see James 3; Proverbs 4:23, especially 18:20, 21: A man's belly is satisfied with the fruit of his mouth; with the increase of his lips shall he be filled. Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof, etc.; 16:2, 23; 14:23; 15 throughout; 21:23: Whoso keepeth his mouth keepeth his soul from troubles. Ecclesiasticus 28:16 and following; 4:29; Ecclesiasticus 5:15; 22:31: In the speech there is glory and dishonour, and the tongue of man is his downfall. 10:12, 28: A wise man makes himself lovable by his words, but the favour of fools is poured out. A wise man is commended by his words, and a prudent man will please great men. 21:8: He who has a skilful tongue is known from afar.

units.la: Cogitata animi sunt hic nobis quaecunq; aliis artibus singulis, vel omnibus praecipiuntur, vel prohibentur, quae per sermonem aliis communicamus, aliter tamen quam in Grammatica, vel Rhetorica. In Grammatica cogitata animi proferimus sermone puro & congruo per Etymologia & Syntaxin. In Rhetorica sermone ornato & eleganti per tropos ps & figuras. In Ethica vero decoro & ciuili sermone atq; concinno. In vsu & praxi coniungi & concurrere hi tres sermonis artes possunt, vel seperari. Fieri enim potest vt quis pure quidem loquatur, non tamen elegan-ter. Similiter vt eleganter quis loquatur, qui tamen non decore. & contra, vt quis decore loquatur, non tamen pure vel eleganter & ornate. Distinguamus igitur ita, vt Grammatica sermonis puritate, Rhetorica ornatu, & Ethica decorum, vrbanitatem & ciuilitatem sermonis tribuamus.
units.tr: Here we are concerned with the thoughts of the mind, whatever is taught or forbidden by the individual arts, or by all of them, and which we communicate to others through speech, though in a different way from grammar or rhetoric. In grammar we express the thoughts of the mind in pure and correct speech, through etymology and syntax. In rhetoric, in ornate and elegant speech, through tropes and figures. In ethics, however, in becoming and civil speech, and in harmonious speech. In use and practice these three arts of speech can be joined and combined, or separated. For it can happen that someone speaks purely but not elegantly; similarly, that someone speaks elegantly but not becomingly; and conversely, that someone speaks becomingly but not purely or elegantly and ornately. Let us therefore distinguish so that grammar assigns purity of speech, rhetoric ornament, and ethics propriety, courtesy and civility of speech.

units.la: Actio hic nobis est gestus & habitus hominis cuiusdam conuersantis. Hoc est modus, quo illa quae in aliis artib. traduntur, motu membrorum, corporis & habitu decoro & ciuili exequimur, seu, quo reliquarum artium praxin decore & venuste exercemus. Prou. c. 20. 11. Actionibus suis praebeat se cognoscendum etiam puer, an purum vel rectum sit opus suum, 1. Cor. c. 11. 4. Omnis vir orans aut prophetans operto capite dedecorat caput suum, 5. Omnis vero mulier orans aut prophetans, non operto capite dedecorat caput suum, nam vnum ac idem est ac si rasa esset, 6. Nam si non operitur mulier, etiam tondeatur. Quod si turpe mulieri tonderi aut radi vetetur, 14. An ne natura quidem ipsa hoc vos docet, quod viro quidem comatum esse dedecori sit, 15. contra mulieri comatam esse decori sit? nam coma ei pro velamento data est, Philip. c. 2. 8. Et habitu compertus vt homo, & c. 1. Pet. c 2. 12. & conuersationem vestram habeatis honestam inter gentes, &c. 1. Tim. c. 4. 12. Esto exemplar fidelium in sermone, in conuersatione, &c. Hebr. c. 13. 18. Vt qui in omnib. cupiamus honeste conuersari, Tit. c. 2. 3. Anus itidem vt sint habitu qui sanctimoniam deceat, 1. Cor. c. 13. 6. Charitas non agit indecore, 1. Pet. cap. 1. 15. sed sicut is qui vos vocauit sanctus est, ipsi quoque sancti in omni conuersatione reddamini, & verf.17. & c.3.1. 2.16. Nam gestus & habitus corporis etiam sermo dicitur, adeo vt quidam solo gestu spectantibus sine voce omnia significare possint, vt tanquam communis hominum sermo esse videatur, in tanta per tot gentes linguarum diuersitate. Imo etiam bestiarum actiones & gestus sunt, quibus tanquam signa affectus suos enunciant. vt ait Talæus libr.2.Rhetor.c.7. Nam ex gestu cognoscitur vir, ex obuia persona specie cognoscitur qui valet mente, ornatus viri & vsus dentium greffusq; hominis enunciant constitutionem eius, vt loquitur Ecclef.c.19.26.27. & c.25.21.c.13.30.31.c.9.18. & seqq. c.42.12.13.c.13. Prou.c.26.12. c.17.24. c.22.9.c.16. 28.29.c.10.10.c.6.13. qua de re latius suo loco,
units.tr: Here by action we mean the bearing and demeanour of a person who is conversing. That is, it is the manner in which we carry out, by the movement of our limbs, body and bearing, becoming and courteous, those things which are taught in the other arts, or in other words, the manner in which we practise the rest of the arts becomingly and gracefully. Prov. 20:11: even a child makes himself known by his actions, whether his work is pure and upright. 1 Cor. 11:4: Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonours his head. 5: But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonours her head; for it is one and the same as if she were shaved. 6: For if the woman is not covered, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be covered. 14: Does not nature itself teach you that for a man to wear long hair is a dishonour, 15: but for a woman to have long hair is a glory? For her hair is given to her as a covering. Phil. 2:8: And being found in fashion as a man. 1 Pet. 2:12: Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles, etc. 1 Tim. 4:12: Be an example of the faithful in speech, in conversation, etc. Heb. 13:18: That in all things we desire to live honestly. Titus 2:3: Likewise the aged women, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness. 1 Cor. 13:5: Charity does not act unbecomingly. 1 Pet. 1:15: but as he who called you is holy, so you also be holy in all your conversation; and v. 17; and 3:1-2, 16. For the gesture and bearing of the body is also called speech, so much so that some can signify everything by gesture alone, without voice, to those who look on, so that it seems to be a common speech of humankind, amid such diversity of languages among so many peoples. Indeed, even the actions and gestures of beasts are signs by which they declare their feelings, as Talaeus says in book 2 of the Rhetoric, chapter 7. For a man is known by his gesture, and the one who is of sound mind is recognised by his appearance when met face to face; the dress of a man, the use of his teeth and the gait of a man declare his constitution, as Ecclesiasticus 19:26-27 says; and 25:21; 13:30-31; 9:18 and following; 42:12-13; 13:... Prov. 26:12; 17:24; 22:9; 16:28-29; 10:10; 6:13. On this matter more fully in its proper place.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De materia sermonis.
units.tr: On the matter of discourse.

units.la: HAEc de generalibus ciuilis conuersationis, seu Ethicae adfectionibus sequitur de speciebus eiusdem.
units.tr: These are the general features of civil conversation, or Ethics. There follows a discussion of its species.

units.la: Species igitur Ethicae duę sunt. Est enim quędam communis, quędam propria.
units.tr: There are therefore two species of Ethics. One is common, the other proper.

units.la: Communis est, quæ mores & modum eum cuiusuis conditionis & status hominibus conuersandi docet.
units.tr: The common Ethics is that which teaches morals and the manner of conversing with people of any condition and status.

units.la: Plerasq; virtutes, vt iustitiam, pietatem, probitatem, castitatem, patientiam, amicitiam, societatē, verecundiam, veracitatem, humilitatem, charitatem, prudentiam, scientiam, benevolentiam, sapientiam, candorem, temperantiam, sobrietatem, constantiam, liberalitatem, fidelitatem, obedientiam, lenitatem, nemesin, misericordiam, & si quæ sunt plures, quas alii ad Ethiad Ethicam referunt, ego, iubente lege Logica, ad suas quasq; facultates & artes remitto, partim nimirum ad Theologiam, partim ad Iurisprudentiam & partim ad Physicam, & Politicam, partim quoq; ad Logicam, in quibus virtutes suas habent sedes & ex quibus earū plena & vera cognitio haurienda, in quibus illa homogenea & essentialis. Nec etiamsi quis harum virtutum cognitionem habet & praxin, ideo statim bonis illis moribus, quos dixi, praditus duci potest, qui tamen est huius artis finis summus, ad quem praecepta eius de collimare necesse est. Modus & via hic prescribenda, qua virtutes in aliis artibus prescriptas, exercere, in actum & publicum producere & aliis communicare possis: nimirum quomodo & quibus verbis, sermone, enunciatione, gestu, habitu actioneve corporis, praxin virtutum ex aliis artibus perceptarum, percipias, habeas, qui solus finis Ethica proprius & genuinus, ad quem omnia illius praecepta referri debent. Quam ob causam male, meo iudicio, vulgo dicunt Theologiam & Iurisprudentiam Ethica rivulos esse; cum contra, virtutes quae vulgo Ethica propriae adscribuntur, ex his & reliquis artium regulis & praeceptis fuerint desumpta, earumq; consectaria ac μεταφορα saepe dicantur, quae plenius, uberius & rectius in suis locis, & propria arte docentur & traduntur, quam seorsim & separatim in Ethica, iustitiae lege repugnante. Siquidem eiusdem est artis docere praecepta & proxime inde nascentia consectaria. Soli igitur huic Ethicae relinquitur propria morum honestorum & decentium scientia & usus, quibus virtutes in aliis artibus tradutas exprimamus. Nam ex aliis artibus ut bene & recte agamus discimus; ex Ethica vero ut id ipsum quod recte fit, etiam decore, venuste, eleganter, cum gratia & concinne secundum naturā rei, persona vel causa agamus, percipimus, quib. scilicet verbis alii exhilarentur, quibus offendantur, quib. opinionem & indicium virtutis vel vitii nobis apud alios procreemus & quo habitu & actione corporis congrua quaelibet peragenda & tractanda. Quam ob causam recte Lambertus Danæus, & Zacharias Vrsinus virtutes, quas vulgo ad Ethicam referunt, ad praecepta Decalogi, adcommodauerunt. Et ego, nisi res manifesta esset, pluribus demonstrarem, & fontes ex quibus hiriuuli Ethici ex Theologia, Iurisprudentia, Logica, Politica vel Physica, sunt derivati ostenderem & aperirem. Paucis vero sedes virtutum, quas Ethici μεγαλοπρεπεῖς ad Ethicam referunt, quasi digito demonstrabo. Iustitiam Ethici omnes adscribunt Ethicae. At male: quis enim, quaeso, exacte scire poterit quid sit iustitia, nisi prius quid sit ius cognouerit eiusq; species? Ex iure enim, iustitia. Species iustitiae distributiuam & commutatiuam docere qui poterit, qui comercia, maleficia, munera & officia, praemia & poenas nondum tradidit? Versatur siquidem commutatiua iustitia in commerciorum permutatione, in conuenientib. & contractibus. Distributiua vero in praemiorum & poenarum distributione. De conuentionib. vero, rerum contractarum fide & constantia, earumq; speciebus, item de maleficiis eorumq; poenis & speciebus, de muneribus, honoribus & officiis nulla ars alia, quā Iurisprudentia tractare debet vel potest, quae si huic arti ademeris, nihil habebit amplius in quo consistere possit. Nimis itaq; aperte & violenter Ethici de Iustitia praecepta tradeties, Iurisprudentiae opes & patrimonium inuadunt & diripiunt, & nimis ieiune & imperfecte sine praceptis Iurisprudentiae iustitiae doctrinam docere conantur. Ab hac iustitia non separanda sunt alia anancillantes virtutes, lenitas & Nemesis, in quib. culpa, dolus, temeritas, imprudentia, casus & reliqua circumstantia, uti tempus, locus, persona & eventus de quibus abunde Iurisprudentia docet, & in qua haec praecipuè sibi locum vendicant. Pietatem & probitatem, mirum est Theologiae admi & Ethicae annumerari: Viram quidem enim sola Theologia informat, sicuti & Dei cognitione, timorem, precationem & gratiarum actionem quae fidei effecta. Prudentia virtus, quae est recte agendorum cognitio, ex ςυνεχείας vel cognitione artium reliquarum existit, atque sine usu rerum quoque experientia existere non potest. Consectarium igitur potius cuiusque artis dixerim, quod male ad separatam quandam & peculiarem artem constituendam refertur. Physici etiam proprium est de rationali potentia in anthropologia agere.
units.tr: Most virtues, such as justice, piety, uprightness, chastity, patience, friendship, fellowship, modesty, truthfulness, humility, charity, prudence, knowledge, benevolence, wisdom, candour, temperance, sobriety, constancy, liberality, fidelity, obedience, gentleness, nemesis, mercy, and any others that some refer to Ethics, I, following the law of Logic, return to their own faculties and arts: partly to Theology, partly to Jurisprudence, partly to Physics and Politics, and partly also to Logic. In these they have their own seats, and from these their full and true knowledge is to be drawn, and in these they are homogeneous and essential. Nor, even if someone has the knowledge and practice of these virtues, can he for that reason at once be led to be endowed with those good morals which I have mentioned, though these are the highest end of this art, to which its precepts must necessarily aim. The method and way to be prescribed here is by which you may exercise the virtues prescribed in other arts, bring them into act and public view, and communicate them to others: namely, how and with what words, speech, utterance, gesture, bearing or action of the body you may perceive, possess and display the practice of the virtues learned from other arts. This alone is the proper and genuine end of Ethics, to which all its precepts ought to be referred. For this reason, in my judgement, people wrongly say commonly that Theology and Jurisprudence are streams of Ethics. On the contrary, the virtues commonly ascribed to Ethics proper have been derived from these and the remaining rules and precepts of the arts, and they are often called their consequences and metaphors [μεταφορα]. These are taught and handed down more fully, richly and correctly in their own places and by their own art than separately and apart in Ethics, which is contrary to the law of justice. For it belongs to the same art to teach the precepts and the consequences arising immediately from them. Therefore to this Ethics alone is left the proper knowledge and practice of honourable and seemly morals, by which we express in action the virtues handed down in other arts. For from other arts we learn to act well and rightly; but from Ethics we learn to do what is rightly done also gracefully, elegantly, charmingly and harmoniously, according to the nature of the matter, the person or the cause. That is, we learn with what words we may cheer others, with what we may offend them, by what means we may produce in others an opinion and sign of virtue or vice, and with what bearing and action of the body any fitting thing is to be carried out and handled. For this reason Lambert Danaeus and Zacharias Ursinus rightly adapted the virtues commonly referred to Ethics to the precepts of the Decalogue. And I would demonstrate this at greater length, were the matter not obvious, and would show and reveal the sources from which these Ethical rivulets have been derived from Theology, Jurisprudence, Logic, Politics or Physics. Briefly, however, I will point out, as it were with a finger, the seats of those virtues which the high-minded [μεγαλοπρεπεῖς] Ethicists refer to Ethics. All Ethicists ascribe justice to Ethics. But wrongly: for who, I ask, will be able to know exactly what justice is, unless he has first learned what right is and its kinds? For justice comes from right. Who will be able to teach the kinds of justice, distributive and commutative, if he has not yet taught commerce, wrongs, gifts and duties, rewards and punishments? For commutative justice is concerned with the exchange of goods, in agreements and contracts; distributive justice with the distribution of rewards and punishments. But concerning agreements, the faith and constancy of contracted things and their kinds, likewise concerning wrongs and their punishments and kinds, and concerning gifts, honours and offices, no art other than Jurisprudence ought or is able to treat. If you take this art away, Ethics will have nothing further on which it can stand. Too openly and violently, therefore, do the Ethicists, in delivering precepts about justice, invade and plunder the resources and patrimony of Jurisprudence, and too meagrely and imperfectly do they try to teach the doctrine of justice without the precepts of Jurisprudence. Not to be separated from this justice are the other virtues that serve it, gentleness and nemesis, in which fault, guile, rashness, imprudence, chance and the other circumstances, such as time, place, person and outcome, are at issue. Jurisprudence teaches abundantly about these, and in these it especially claims a place for itself. That piety and uprightness should be numbered among the virtues of Theology and Ethics is strange. For indeed Theology alone forms the man, as also the knowledge of God, fear, prayer and thanksgiving, which are effects of faith. Prudence, the virtue which is the knowledge of what is to be done rightly, arises from the connection [ςυνεχείας] or knowledge of the other arts, and cannot exist without the use of things and experience. I would therefore call it rather a consequence of each art, and it is wrong to refer it to some separate and peculiar art to be set up. It is also the proper task of Physics to treat of rational power in anthropology.

units.la: Sapientiam, qua quid in negotiis honestum sit, inquirimus & exacte perspicimus nonne duce Logica, comite cognitione cuiusque artis, ad quam negotium, in quo sapientia requiruntur pertinet, adquirimus? Nonne tanquam ἀντίλογια & fructus communis ex omnium artium Theoria existit? Quare igitur peculiarem hic artem excogitas, quam alienis plumis exornas, & quam sine adminiculo logicae & artis cuiusque discere vel docere non potes? Taciturnitatem & silentium Ethica relinquo & suis in locis propono, sicuti & virtutem vocalem. Candor, bona fides, veracitas partim Theologicae in rebus divinis, partim iuridica in politicis sunt virtutes. Imo leges artium informa darum κ' αυτὸ & κ' αὐτὸ πρῶτον. partim has virtutes respiciunt, & singula artium praecepta necessario vera, genuina, essentialia, homogenea & reciproca esse praecipiunt, & I.C. de falsi & mendacii speciebus prolixe differunt, & de testimonio, de candore, bonaq; fide & dolo malo in vltimis voluntatibus, contractibus, modis adquiren-di dominii & maleficiis; ex quibus necesse est sumant Ethici, si perfecte de hac virtute in Ethica docere volunt. Humanitatem, quatenus Ethica propria, suo loco trado; Temperantiam eiusq; species, frugalitatem, mansuetudinem, humilitatem, sobrietatem, pudicitiam, castitatem & verecundiam ad suas quasq; artes referGo, quae cupiditates & voluptates hominis honestas explicant. Nam in quacunq; arte peccatur in excessu, vel defectu, ibi contra iustitiam temperantiamq; peccatur, contra, cum medium tenetur, temperantia & iustitia colitur. Ad Physicam igitur refero temperantiam, quae praecipit de victu, cibo & potu, diaeta, laboribus, exercitiisq; corporis, secundum crasin & constitutionem cuiusq; naturae & complexionis, ut bona valetudo & natura vires conserventur, non opprimantur vel laedantur, quo quis ad vocationis officia obeunda ineptus fiat. Physica igitur cines erunt continentia, sobrietas, castitas, frugalitas & pudicitia. Ad iurisprudentiam vero refero illam temperantiam, quae praecipit de mediocritate & iustitia in vocationis officiis & in amictu, ubi & de excessu in luxu & prodigalitate plura I. C. imo & politici in sua arte tradunt. Verecundiam & modestiam in Ethica retineo, atq; de iis suo in loco lib. 2. c. 1. & seqq. ago latius. Humilitatem quo nisi ad Theologiam referrem? ad praeceptum nimirum primum, ubi de illa Zachar. Vrsinus & Danaeus pluribus agunt cum caeteris Theologis. Ad Politicam pertinet temperantia & parsimonia in administratione rei familiaris. Politica enim praescribit cuiq; ordini & statui modum in victu, & amictu, quem qui excedit luxuriosus, prodigus; qui in defectu peccat, sordidus dicitur. Sumptuum & impensarum necessariarum, vti-
units.tr: Wisdom, by which we inquire into and exactly perceive what is honourable in affairs: do we not acquire it under the guidance of Logic, with the companion of knowledge of whatever art the affair in which wisdom is required belongs to? Does it not exist as the counterpart [ἀντίλογια] and common fruit of the theory of all the arts? Why then do you devise here a peculiar art, which you adorn with borrowed feathers, and which cannot be learned or taught without the aid of logic and of each art? I leave silence and taciturnity to Ethics and set them out in their places, as also the vocal virtue. Candour, good faith and truthfulness are partly theological virtues in divine matters, partly juridical virtues in political ones. Indeed the laws of the arts, in themselves and first in themselves [κ' αυτὸ & κ' αὐτὸ πρῶτον], partly regard these virtues, and each precept of the arts requires that they be true, genuine, essential, homogeneous and reciprocal. The jurists discuss at length the kinds of falsehood and lying, and about testimony, candour, good faith and malicious deceit in last wills, contracts, modes of acquiring dominion and wrongs. From these the Ethicists must take what they need, if they wish to teach this virtue perfectly in Ethics. Humanity, insofar as it is proper to Ethics, I set out in its place. Temperance and its kinds (thrift, gentleness, humility, sobriety, modesty, chastity and shamefastness) I refer to their own arts, which explain the honest desires and pleasures of man. For in whatever art one sins by excess or by defect, there one sins against justice and temperance; conversely, when the mean is kept, temperance and justice are cultivated. I therefore refer to Physics that temperance which prescribes food, drink, diet, labours and exercises of the body, according to the temperament and constitution of each nature, so that good health and natural strength are preserved, not oppressed or harmed, and a person does not become unfit for performing the duties of his calling. Thus continence, sobriety, chastity, thrift and modesty belong to Physics. To Jurisprudence I refer that temperance which prescribes moderation and justice in the duties of one's calling and in dress, where the jurists, and even the politicians in their art, teach much about excess in luxury and prodigality. I retain shamefastness and modesty in Ethics, and about them I treat at greater length in its place, in book 2, chapter 1 and following. Humility, to what else should I refer it, if not to Theology, namely to the first precept, where Zacharias Ursinus and Danaeus, with the other theologians, treat it at length? To Politics belong temperance and thrift in the management of household affairs. For Politics prescribes for each order and status a measure in food and dress; whoever exceeds it is called luxurious or prodigal, and whoever sins by defect is called sordid. Of necessary expenses and outlays, of use-

units.la: { } Note: the marginal notes on the right edge are not legible enough to transcribe. [illegible, ~12 letters]vel voluptuariarum modum alium diuiti, a- [illegible, ~6 letters]pauperi, alium priuata, alium publica personæ, a- [illegible, ~5 letters]rursus masculo, fœmina, iuuenì, nobili egregio, generoso, humili, inferiori, subdito, opifici, literato, idio- ta, &c. præscribit pro ratione personæ, ordinis, officii, status, conditionis, temporis, & loci, de qua re prolixè Politica & non nihil Iurisprudentia de sumptibus & impensis, præcipit. Quid etiam de diligentia Ethicus præscriberet, quam sibi Iurisprudentia vindicat & do- cet in muneribus, officiis & honoribus suscipiendis & gerendis, in administratione negotiorum alienorum, & propriorum, atq; ob id negligentiam, cessationem & culpam & otium in delictis ponit & punit. Imo vl- terius hæc iurisprudentia progreditur, dum quantita- tem & qualitatem & gradus diligentiæ in quouis ne- gotio & administratione hominum præscribit & deter- minat, de qua re altum apud Ethicos silentium. Pati- entia, constantia, fortitudo & magnanimitas sunt co- munes affectiones, pertinentes ad munerum iniun- ctorum executionem. Ideoq; Iurisprudentia & Politi- ca, quibus officia personis secundum iustitiam distri- butiuam adsignantur, propria. Beneficentia, gratifica- tio, liberalitas & munificentia pertinent ad proximi dilectionem, ideoq; Theologia propria quadam etiam iurisprudentia, de quibus sub tit. De donat. & tit. De quasi contractib. tit. De commodato, De deposito & mandato, & tit. De pollicitat. qui contractus gratuiti, beneficentiæ, gratificationis, liberalitatisq; rationem, viam, modum subiectum & caussas tradunt, quæ ab Ethicis in explicatione harum virtutum omittuntur. Hospitalitas, quid aliud quam species gratuita locatio- nis & beneficentiæ particula, pertinens ad tit. Naut. caup. stab. tit. De locat. & conduct. tit. De exercit. act.
units.tr: [Note: the marginal notes on the right edge are not legible enough to transcribe. illegible, ~12 letters] prescribes a different measure for the rich and the poor, for a private person and a public one, [illegible, ~5 letters] for a man and a woman, a young man, a nobleman, an eminent or generous person, a humble person, an inferior, a subject, a craftsman, a literate person, an unlettered person, and so on, according to the person's rank, office, status, condition, time and place. Politics treats this at length, and Jurisprudence says something about expenses and outlays. What would Ethics prescribe about diligence, which Jurisprudence claims for itself and teaches in assuming and discharging duties, offices and honours, and in managing the affairs of others and one's own? For this reason it counts negligence, neglect, fault and idleness as offences and punishes them. Jurisprudence goes further still, prescribing and determining the amount, quality and degrees of diligence in any business and administration of men, a matter on which Ethicists keep a deep silence. Patience, constancy, fortitude and magnanimity are common affections, pertaining to the carrying out of imposed duties. Therefore Jurisprudence and Politics, which assign offices to persons according to distributive justice, claim them as their own. Beneficence, kindness, liberality and munificence pertain to love of neighbour, and so Theology has a kind of jurisprudence of its own on these matters, under the titles On Gifts, On Quasi-Contracts, On Loan for Use, On Deposit and Mandate, and On Promises. These gratuitous contracts set out the reason, way, measure, subject and causes of beneficence, kindness and liberality, which Ethicists omit when explaining these virtues. Hospitality is nothing other than a species of gratuitous letting and a part of beneficence, pertaining to the titles on shipmasters, innkeepers and stables, on letting and hiring, and on the actions arising from such exercise.

units.la: Ethicus igitur de hac traduturus, doceat primum de locatione & conductione, & de iure hospitii ex iurisprudentia, ut exacte intelligatur id quod praecipit. Fidelitas pertinet ad fidem constantiamque conventionum, quam si Ethicus docere vult, necesse etiam habet praemittere quid sit conventio eiusque species, item quando inutilis, invalida turpisve sit conventio, ut fidem servare non sit necesse; item a quo & quibus modis & quando conventio impleri debeat & de rebus, quae deducuntur in conventionem. Hoc si fecit, plane contra fidem egerit & finem suae artis excedet & malefidei possessor rei alienae existet, quam sine titulo honesto & legitimo usurpabit, sed nunquam usucapiet. De misericordia Ethico item intentabit Physica, quae de illa in anthropologia & anima potentia agit, sicut & de affectibus aliis, συμπαθείας, laetitia, spe, amore, tristitia, metu, pudore, odio, ira & omnibus interioribus sensibus. Vide Physicam Freigii libr. 36. Idem de πρῶτοι & amore liberorum, parentum & cognatorum iudicium. Si Ethicus etiam perpenderet causam efficientem amicitiae, quomodo illa mutuo consensu duorum vel plurium contrahatur, illam iurisprudentiae sine dubio relinquerent, quae de illa praecipit sub tit. De adoptionibus & innominatis contractibus, sine quorum cognitione exacte intelligi non potest doctrina de amicitia & fraternitate, seu ἀδελφοποιΐα. De amicitia sociali res est manifestior, eam plene & perfecte in iurisprudentia tradit, ibique fixam sedem & domicilium habere sub tit. de societate & tit. De matrimonio, ubi quid sit, inter quos contrahi possit & in quibus consistat socialis amicitia, plenissime exponitur. De sociali vita & hominum consortio inuita huius commodis & incommodis, sola politica vberrime agit, & proponit media vtilia & necessa- cessacessaria ad continuanda, conseruandam & colendam societatem humanam, cuius haec admissis, nihil habitura ecти illa omnino in quo consistere possit. Mirum etiam est quo iure obedientia ex iurisprudentia & politica agro in Ethicam ab aliis translata fuerit. Obseruantia & reuerentiam veros & naturales Ethicae cines agnosco & recipio, de quibus forte latius quam ullus Ethicorum lib.1. tractatu. De pietate & obseruantia diuina, cane vt in Ethica agas, non pralucente fide & cognitione de Deo, eiusq; operibus. Sacrilegium est ex hoc sacrario aliquid rapere, usurpare & sibi adscribere. Profana- tio est sacra illa mundanis hisce miscere. Inscitia & confusio connexa & coherentia diuellere & separatim tradere. Gratitudinem ad iustitiae species suum cuique tribuentes & permutationis genera, l. 25. sed etsi, §. 11. consuluit. de petit. hared. refero, & ob id iurisprudentia attribuo, in qua domi est & habitat: in Ethica vero agens ab aduibus & larib. domesticis peregrinatur.
units.tr: Ethics, then, when it is going to treat of this, should first teach about letting and hiring, and about the right of hospitality from Jurisprudence, so that what it prescribes is understood exactly. Fidelity pertains to the faithfulness and constancy of agreements. If Ethics wishes to teach this, it must first set out what an agreement is and its kinds, and likewise when an agreement is ineffective, invalid or dishonourable, so that there is no need to keep faith with it; also by whom, in what ways and when an agreement ought to be fulfilled, and concerning the things that are brought into an agreement. If it does this, it will plainly have acted against fidelity, will have gone beyond the end of its own art, and will become a possessor of another's property in bad faith, which it will usurp without an honest and lawful title, but will never acquire by prescription. Concerning mercy, Ethics will likewise make use of Physics, which treats of it in the anthropology and in the faculties of the soul, and likewise of the other affections, sympathy, joy, hope, love, sadness, fear, shame, hatred, anger and all the inner senses. See Freigius's Physics, book 36. The same holds for the first movements and the love of children, parents and kindred. If Ethics also considered the efficient cause of friendship, how it is contracted by the mutual consent of two or more, they would undoubtedly leave this to Jurisprudence, which prescribes on it under the titles On Adoptions and On Innominate Contracts, without whose knowledge the doctrine of friendship and brotherhood, or adelphopoiia, cannot be exactly understood. Social friendship is a clearer matter; Jurisprudence treats it fully and perfectly, and has its fixed seat and dwelling there, under the titles On Partnership and On Marriage, where what it is, between whom it may be contracted, and in what social friendship consists, is set out most fully. Concerning social life and the fellowship of men, with its benefits and drawbacks, Politics alone treats at length, and proposes the useful and necessary means for continuing, preserving and cultivating human society; without these, Ethics would have nothing at all in which it could consist. It is also remarkable by what right obedience was transferred from Jurisprudence and Politics, as from a foreign field, into Ethics by others. I acknowledge and accept observance and reverence as true and natural citizens of Ethics, concerning which I perhaps treat more fully than any Ethicist, in book 1, in the treatise On Piety and Divine Observance. Do not practise Ethics like a dog, when faith and knowledge of God and his works do not shine forth. It is sacrilege to snatch anything from this sanctuary, to usurp it and claim it for oneself. It is profanation to mix those sacred things with these worldly ones. It is ignorance and confusion to tear apart what is connected and coherent and to teach it separately. I refer gratitude, which assigns to each his due, to the species of justice and the kinds of exchange, as the law of Digest 25 "But although" section 11, under "On Petition of Inheritance" has advised, and so I assign it to Jurisprudence, in which it is at home and dwells; but in Ethics it wanders like a stranger away from its household gods and hearth.

units.la: De ingratitudine plurima I.C. passim tradunt in tit. De ingrat. liber. & tit. De renocand. donat. & passim alibi. Gratiatem & verecundiam virtutes Ethicas libenter agnosco, earumque mores in verbis & gestis exprimo, quod ab aliis omissum. Innocentiam vero ex Ethica ad iurisprudentiam relego & de ea latius ago suo loco, sub cap. de Fama & dignitate, quamuis etiam non male hac quasi communis quidam Theologia, Politica & Iurisprudentia fructus & effectus dicatur. His ita accurate examinatis & omnibus virtutibus ad κεφαλεων ac tribunal legum artium & methodi renocatis, quid tandem Ethica aliud, quam ars multarum artium spoliis consarcinata & ditata? cui si aliena bona auferantur, quid aliud erit quaridicula illa aut alienis pennis exornata, deplumata, & nudata? Quid aliud pleraque Ethicæ virtutes quam rivuli ex aliis artibus deducti & derivati? quid aliud quam consectaria ex aliarum artium regulis & præceptis formata, vel per consequentiam deducta axiomata? Quid aliud quam flores in amplissimus aliarum artium campis decerpti & collecti? Excipio hic paucas quasdam virtutes, quas ut Ethica proprium patrimonium & possessionem adsigno & refero, & suis in locis trado. Respiciunt enim illa ad summum Ethicæ scopum & finem, nimirum conversationem infermoxe & gestu seu habitu consistentem. Ideoque in aliis artibus heterogenea & peregrina. Reliquæ virtutes, quacunque ex his ad pie vivendum ab hoc fine dependent, ad Theologiam referuntur: quæ ad commode degendum & humanam societatem colendam, ad Politicam: quæ ad ius in humana societate colendum, ad Iurisprudentiam: quæ ad naturales rei proprietates & affectiones cognoscendas spectant, ad Physicam: quæ ad rationem bene differendi, ad Logicam. Quodcunque enim præceptum ad summum artis alicuius bonum & finem directè tendit, & reciproce cum forma & fine artis congruit, hoc eidem etiam homogeneum & essentiale constituendum est, ut Logici docent. Sed pergamus ad divisionem Ethicæ communis.
units.tr: Jurisprudence sets out a great deal about ingratitude throughout, under the title On Ingratitude of Freedmen, and under the title On Revoking Gifts, and in many other places. I gladly acknowledge gratitude and modesty as Ethical virtues, and I express their characters in words and deeds, which others have omitted. But I relegate innocence from Ethics to Jurisprudence, and I treat it more fully in its place, under the chapter On Reputation and Dignity, although it may not badly be called a kind of common fruit and effect of Theology, Politics and Jurisprudence alike. Having examined these matters so carefully, and having called all the virtues back to the head and tribunal of the laws, the arts and the method, what else is Ethics but an art patched together and enriched with the spoils of many arts? If the goods of others were taken away from it, what would remain but that ridiculous figure, adorned with borrowed feathers, stripped of them and left bare? What else are most of the virtues of Ethics than streams drawn and derived from other arts? What else are they than corollaries formed from the rules and precepts of other arts, or axioms deduced by consequence? What else than flowers plucked and gathered from the wide fields of other arts? Here I except a few virtues, which I assign and refer to Ethics as its proper patrimony and possession, and which I treat in their places. For these look to the highest aim and end of Ethics, namely conversation, which consists in speech and in bearing or conduct. Therefore in other arts they are foreign and alien. The remaining virtues, whichever of them depend on this end for living piously, are referred to Theology; those for living decently and cultivating human society, to Politics; those for cultivating right in human society, to Jurisprudence; those which concern knowing the natural properties and affections of things, to Physics; and those for the right manner of arguing, to Logic. For whatever precept is directly aimed at the highest good and end of any art, and agrees reciprocally with the form and end of the art, must also be counted as homogeneous and essential to it, as the logicians teach. But let us proceed to the division of common Ethics.

units.la: Usus linguæ & sermonis decorus in hac communi Ethica, consistit in duob. membris: nimirum in conceptione verborum & enunciatione conceptorum.
units.tr: The proper use of language and speech in this common Ethics consists of two parts: namely, the conception of words and the expression of what has been conceived.

units.la: Conceptio verborum est, qua animi nostri cogitata aliis, quibus cum conversamur, significanda, & verba præmeditamur. Nam qui aut tempus quid postulet non videt, aut plura loquitur, aut se ostentat, aut eorum quibus cum est, vel dignitatis, vel comcommodi rationem non habet, aut denique in aliquo genere aut inconcinnus, aut multus est, ut ineptus dicitur, Cicer. 2. De orat.
units.tr: The conception of words is the process by which we rehearse the words with which we are to signify the thoughts of our mind to those with whom we converse. For whoever does not see what the time requires, or speaks too much, or shows off, or takes no account of the dignity or convenience of those he is with, or who is in any kind of matter either clumsy or verbose, is called inept, Cicero, De oratore, book 2.

units.la: Ergò verborum conceptio reliquarum artium adminiculo perpendit qualitatem rerum, personarum & verborum, de quibus scilicet rebus, ad quas personas, & quibus verbis sermone instituere & habere conueniat, quae est διάθεσις quaedam, & διάμετρα sermonis nostri, arg. Hebr. c. f. 14. Huius formulam exprimit Plutarchus: Quis (inquit) hic sermo est? quidnam boni adquiram si dixero? quidve molesti si tacuero? Non enim sermone tanquam onus quoddam promentem deponere oportet, quoniam & dictus similiter permanet, sed aut nostri causa effamur, si qua re indigemus; aut prosumus audientibus, aut gratiam aliquam inter nos conciliamus, quemadmodum sale, ut sermonib. condientes conversationem actionemque, in qua sumus. Sin vero neque dicenti est utile id quod dicere volumus, neque necessarium audientibus, nullaque voluptas adiuncta est & gratia: cur dicitur? Non minus enim sermones quam opera frustranei sunt & inanes. Plutarch. De garrul. in sin. Isocrat. ad Demon. Quidquid dicturus es, prius apud animum tuum expende: multorum enim cogitationem lingua praecurrit. Cicer. Orat. ad Brut. Debemus considerare in omni re quid aptum sit & consentaneum tempori & personae, tum quid in dictis factisque dedeceat, & ibid. Non omnis fortuna, non omnis honos, non omnis authoritas, non omnis aetas, nec vero locus, aut tempus, aut auditor omnis eodem aut verborum genere tractandus est aut sententiarum semperque in omni parte orationis, ut vita quid deceat est considerandum: quod & in re de qua agitur, expositum, &
units.tr: Therefore the conception of words, aided by the other arts, weighs the quality of things, persons and words: that is, what things, to which persons, and in what words one ought to speak and converse. This is a certain disposition [διάθεσις] and measure [διάμετρα] of our speech; see Hebr. c. f. 14. Plutarch gives its form: "What sort of talk is this?" he says. "What good will I gain if I speak? What harm if I keep silent?" For one should not put speech down like a burden that one unloads, since what is said remains as it was. Rather we speak either for our own sake, when we need something; or to benefit those who hear us; or to win some favour between us, just as with salt, seasoning our conversation and the action we are engaged in. But if what we wish to say is neither useful to the speaker nor necessary to the hearers, and no pleasure or favour is attached to it, why is it said? For speeches are no less idle and empty than deeds. Plutarch, On Talkativeness, at the end. Isocrates to Demonicus: Whatever you are about to say, first weigh it in your own mind; for the tongue runs ahead of the thought of many. Cicero, Orator to Brutus: We must consider in every matter what is fitting and consistent with the time and the person, and also what is unbecoming in words and deeds; and in the same place: Not every fortune, not every honour, not every authority, not every age, nor indeed every place, time or hearer, is to be addressed in the same kind of words or sentences; and in every part of a speech we must always consider what suits life; which is set out both in the matter under discussion, and

units.la: B in personis eorum qui dicunt & eorum qui audiunt. Ecclesiastic. c. 28.29.30. Ergo sermonis tui trutinam confice & oris tuo fac tantum & vectem, & attende ne quando labaris illis ut non concidas coram insidiatore. Proverb. c. 15.28. Os improborum eructat temere & inconsiderate mala, &c. verf. 10.14. Sapiens diligenter ponderat verba sua. Ecclesiastic c. 21.28. c. 11. 7. Psalm. 37.30. Proverb. c. 33.4. Eccles. c. 13.14. c. 14. 21. Beatus vir qui cum sapientia res honestas meditatur & qui intelligentia sua res sanctas disserit, & verfic. seqq. 1. Theffal. c. 5.21. Senec. alibi, Quicquid dicturus es, antequam aliis dixeris, tibi dicito. Nam ad poenitendum properat, qui cito dicit, vel iudicat. Dictum enim indictum fieri nequit: non dictum facile dici. Et cor fons linguae dicitur. Matth. c. 15.19. Ex corde prodeunt cogitationes malae, furta, maledicta &c. Psalm. 51.17. Domine aperi labia mea & os meum enunciabit laudem tuam. Prov. c. 16.1. Intellectus est dux linguae & comes. Lingua vero mentis nuncius & imago.
units.tr: in the persons of those who speak and of those who hear. Ecclesiasticus 28, 29, 30: So weigh your words, and make for your mouth a balance and a bridle, and take heed lest at any time you slip on them and fall before the ambusher. Proverbs 15, 28: The mouth of the wicked pours out evil rashly and inconsiderately, etc. v. 10, 14: The wise man weighs his words carefully. Ecclesiasticus 21, 28; 11, 7. Psalm 37, 30. Proverbs 33, 4. Ecclesiastes 13, 14; 14, 21: Blessed is the man who meditates on honourable things with wisdom, and who discourses on holy things by his understanding, and the following verses. 1 Thessalonians 5, 21. Seneca elsewhere: Whatever you are about to say, say it to yourself before you say it to others. For he who speaks quickly is hastening to repent, or judges quickly. What has been said cannot be made unsaid; what has not been said can easily be said. And the heart is called the fountain of the tongue. Matthew 15, 19: Out of the heart come evil thoughts, thefts, slanders, etc. Psalm 51, 17: Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. Proverbs 16, 1: Understanding is the leader and companion of the tongue. The tongue is the messenger and image of the mind.

units.la: Αὐτὸς ἐξ ἀπάντων igitur haec est rerum, personarum, & verborum, de quibus ordine videbimus.
units.tr: Himself out of all [Αὐτὸς ἐξ ἀπάντων]: so this is the matter of things, persons and words, which we shall see in order.

units.la: In rebus, de quibus sermonem instituere volumus, videndum, quas decorum & honestum sit proferre & enunciare, & quas tacere.
units.tr: In the matter of what we wish to discuss, we must consider what it is fitting and honourable to bring forward and state, and what to keep silent.

units.la: Decorum & honestum est loqui de rebus cognitis, convenientibus, utilibus, necessariis & veris. Vt testantur exempla Christi & aliorum piorum hominum, qui de variis rebus sanctis, piis, utilibus, necessariis cum aliis collocuti leguntur in sacris literis. De quare vide differentem Macrobium lib. 7. Saturn. c. 1 Plutarch. lib. 1. Sympos. & Ioh. Guil. Stuckium lib. 3. c. 18. & seqq. Convivial. antiqu. ubi plures, prout est sit vir doctus & plurima lectionis, in hanc sententiam adducit. Isocrates ad Demonic. Duo tibi tempora ad dicendum deputa, vel cum sunt aliqua, de quibus exploratum habeas, vel de quibus dicere est necesse. In solis enim istis potior est silentio sermo: in reliquis melius fuerit tacere, quam loqui.
units.tr: It is fitting and honourable to speak of things that are known, suitable, useful, necessary and true. As the examples of Christ and of other pious men testify, who are read in Sacred Scripture to have conversed with others about various holy, pious, useful and necessary things. On this see Macrobius, who differs, Saturnalia 7.1; Plutarch, Symposiacs 1.1; and John William Stuck, Antiquities of Banquets, 3.18 ff., where many more are cited. As a learned and well-read man, he brings them to this view. Isocrates to Demonicus: Set aside two times for speaking: either when there are some matters of which you have sure knowledge, or when it is necessary to speak about something. For only in these cases is speech preferable to silence; in other cases it is better to be silent than to speak.

units.la: Ergo sermo sit de iis rebus quas loquens optime intelligit, aut de iisad quę dicenda necessario constringitur, & vrgetur, aut quæ loco, tempori & personæ conuenire intelligit, vsu frequenti, conuersatione & prudentia edoctus, ilIæ sint Theologicæ, siue Iuridicæ, siue Philosophicæ, Logicæ, Physicæ, Politicæ, Ethicæ, aut Oeconomicæ, aut alterius cuiusdam artis, Agriculturæ, Architecturæ & similium. In his enim melius & satius loqui quam tacere. Ephes.c. 4.29. Sed si quis sermo est commodus ad ædificationis usum vt gratiam auditoribus adferat, & 1.Cor.c.14. 19. In ecclesia malim quinque verba ex intelligentia mea loqui vt & alios instituam, &c. & vers. 1.2. & seqq. Ecclesiastic. c.20.4.s.20.c.3.23.c.4.27. Prouerb. c. 10.20.21.
units.tr: Therefore let speech be about those things which the speaker understands very well, or about those things to which he is necessarily constrained and urged to speak, or which he understands to suit the place, time and person, having been taught by frequent practice, conversation and prudence. These are theological, juridical or philosophical, logical, physical, political, ethical, economic, or of some other art, such as agriculture, architecture and the like. For in these matters it is better and more advantageous to speak than to be silent. Ephesians 4, 29: But if any speech is suitable for the use of edification, so that it brings grace to the hearers; and 1 Corinthians 14, 19: In the Church I would rather speak five words with my understanding, so that I may also instruct others, etc.; and verses 1, 2 ff. Ecclesiasticus 20, 4; 20; 3, 23; 4, 27. Proverbs 10, 20, 21.

units.la: De eiusmodi rebus sermo institutus, de loquente bonam opinionem procreat. Nam lingua sapientum bonam profert scientiam. Os autem stolidorum, eructat stultitiam. Prou.c.s.2. & labia sapientum spargūt scientiam, & animus stultorum quod abest à recto, vers. 7. Ephes.d.c.s.19. Et vt lumen oculorum lætificat animum, ita auditio bona pinguefacit ossa. Prou.c.15.30.31. & labia insta diligit rex. Prou.c.16.13. Et qui intelligentes sunt, ii sermonibus suis testatur sapientiam. Eccles.cap.18.30. & qui respondet recta verba, eius labia osculabitur. Prov. c. 24. 26. & c. 12. Iacob. c. 3. 10. Et vir qui regiones multas peragrauit, nouit multa; & qui multa est expertus, enarrat sermones intelligentia, qui non est tentatus, nouit pauca. Ecclesiastic. c. 34. 9. 10. 11. c. 39. 5. & vir callidus eruditor multorum, Eccles. c. 37. 12. Plura de subiectis sermonis vid. Proverb. c. 6. c. 18. 20. 21. c. 21. 23. c. 16. 2. 21. 26. Ecclesiast. c. 4. 29. c. 27. 4. 5. 6. c. 5. 15. c. 22. 31. c. 18. 30.
units.tr: Speech conducted about such matters creates a good opinion of the speaker. For the tongue of the wise brings forth good knowledge; but the mouth of fools pours out folly. Proverbs 15, 2: the lips of the wise scatter knowledge, but the heart of fools is far from what is right, v. 7. Ephesians 4, 29. And as the light of the eyes gladdens the heart, so good hearing makes the bones fat. Proverbs 15, 30, 31: The king loves upright lips. Proverbs 16, 13: Those who are intelligent show their wisdom in their speech. Ecclesiasticus 18, 30; and whoever answers with right words, his lips will be kissed. Proverbs 24, 26; 12. James 3, 10. A man who has travelled through many regions knows much; and he who has had much experience tells of things with understanding; he who has not been tried knows little. Ecclesiasticus 34, 9, 10, 11; 39, 5. And a crafty man is a teacher of many, Ecclesiasticus 37, 12. More on the subjects of speech: Proverbs 6; 18, 20, 21; 21, 23; 16, 2, 21, 26. Ecclesiasticus 4, 29; 27, 4, 5, 6; 5, 15; 22, 31; 18, 30.

units.la: Materia igitur sermonis est de Deo vel de proximo, vel de nobismetipsis.
units.tr: The matter of speech, therefore, concerns God, or our neighbour, or ourselves.

units.la: De Deo si est, videndum, ut nomen illius sanctè visurpetur. Exod. c. 20. 7.
units.tr: If it concerns God, we must take care that his name is used reverently. Exodus 20, 7.

units.la: De proximo si dicendum, considerandum est, an causa sit bona, vel mala. In bona promptè veritati testimonium est perhibendum. Iohan. 12. In mala nihil est dicendum, nisi propria, conscientia & vocatio vrgeat, aut postulet.
units.tr: If we must speak of our neighbour, we must consider whether the cause is good or bad. In a good cause, testimony must be given readily to the truth. John 12. In a bad cause nothing should be said, unless one's own conscience and calling urge or require it.

units.la: Vocatio postulat vt i. dicat quis requisitus & iussus à magistratu: 1. in admonitione quâ Christiana caritas exigit. Matth. c. 18. ad aedificationem proximi. 3. ad futura mala & pericula praecaueda. Genef. c. 37. 2. ibi referebat q. Ioseph famam eorum malam ad patrem ipsorum. 2. Reg. c. 6. 9. Mittebat vir Dei ad regem Israelis dicendo caue tibi ne transeas per locum istum: nam ibi Syri insidiantur. 1. Cor. c. 1. 11. dictum est mihi de vobis quod lites sint inter vos. Act. c. 23. 20. 21. 22. vbi de insidiis Iudaeorum Paulo struetis admonetur Tribunus.
units.tr: A calling requires that someone speak when he is asked and ordered to do so by the magistrate; (1) in admonition, which Christian love demands, Matthew 18; (2) for the edification of a neighbour; (3) to guard against future evils and dangers. Genesis 37, 2: there Joseph reported their evil reputation to their father. 2 Kings 6, 9: The man of God sent to the king of Israel, saying, Take care that you do not pass by that place, for the Syrians are lying in ambush there. 1 Corinthians 1, 11: It has been reported to me about you that there are quarrels among you. Acts 23, 20, 21, 22: where the tribune is warned about the ambushes of the Jews plotted against Paul.

units.la: De arcaniis & dubiis non in malam partem vel finiistre est iudicandum. 1. Corint. c. 13. 5. & c. 4. 5.
units.tr: Things that are secret and doubtful should not be judged in a bad or sinister sense. 1 Corinthians 13, 5; and 4, 5.

units.la: De nobismetipsis nihil dicendum quod ad laudem, vel vituperium pertinet. Proverb. c. 27. 2. vti infra dicetur latius.
units.tr: Concerning ourselves, we should say nothing that pertains to praise or blame. Proverbs 27, 2, as will be said more fully below.

units.la: Est vero sermo gratiosus & acceptus, quando habet comites sapientiam, veritatem, lenitatem, fidem & curam famæ proximi. Coloss.c.4.6. contra sermo dicitur futilis. Ephef.c.4.29.1.reg.c.21.10.Proverb.c.10.32.
units.tr: Speech is pleasing and acceptable when it has as its companions wisdom, truth, gentleness, faithfulness and care for the reputation of a neighbour. Colossians 4, 6. On the other hand, speech is called frivolous. Ephesians 4, 29; 1 Kings 21, 10; Proverbs 10, 32.

units.la: Sapiens sermo dicitur, in quo habetur ratio circumstantiarum, loci, temporis, personæ & causæ. Proverb.c.29.11. totum spiritum suum profert stolidus, at Sapiens pone reprimit eum. &c.25.11. velut mala aurea cum figuris argenteis est verbum dictum commode. Sapientiæ vero indicium est timor Domini. Psalm.14.1. Prov.c.1.7. qui cogitat semper Deum esse præsentem. Act.c.16.33. & diuinam præsentiam reueretur. Genes.c.39.9. eique se submittit. 1.Sam.c.16.10.
units.tr: Wise speech is that in which due account is taken of the circumstances: place, time, person and cause. Prov. 29:11: "A fool utters all his spirit, but a wise man keeps it back"; Prov. 25:11: "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver."
