The mark of wisdom, however, is the fear of the Lord (Ps. 14:1; Prov. 1:7), which means always thinking of God as present (Acts 16:33) and revering his presence (Gen. 39:9) and submitting oneself to him (1 Sam. 16:10).

units.la: Verus sermo, rem vti est, profert. Psalm.15.2. Prov.c.12.22. in iudicio. Prov.c.17.7. in Professione Christi. Matth.c.10.32. Unde mendacium officio suum est prohibitum. Iacob.c.3.12. Prov.c.12.22. Rom.c.3.8. De rebus diuinis etiam cum reuerentia loquitur. Deut.c.28.58.
units.tr: True speech sets forth things as they are (Ps. 15:2; Prov. 12:22), in judgement (Prov. 17:7), and in the confession of Christ (Matt. 10:32). Hence lying is forbidden by its very office (James 3:12; Prov. 12:22; Rom. 3:8). It also speaks of divine things with reverence (Deut. 28:58).

units.la: Lenis sermo est humanus, benignus ad auditoris captum & palatum pium accommodatus. Coloss.c.4.6. Sermo vester semper cum gratia sit sale conditus, ut sciatis, quomodo oporteat vos, unicuique respondere. Hæc humanitas apparet potissimum in affabilitate & salutatione, quibus dilectio & charitas conseruatur inter homines.
units.tr: Gentle speech is humane and kind, suited to the understanding and the pious taste of the hearer (Col. 4:6: "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person"). This humanity appears chiefly in courtesy and greeting, by which love and charity are preserved among people.

units.la: Salutantur autem homines nominibus vel cognominibus suis, aut etiam officiis suis honorificis. Ita Moses & Samuel propriis suis nominibus à Deo vocantur. Ita Christus à suis discipulis Rabbi vocatur. de quare cap.4.latius. Lenis sermo etiam in aliis prout rei necessitas & utilitas exigit adhibendus. Iudic. c. 8. 3. vbi Gideon leni sermone iram mitigauit suorum cognatorum. 1. Sam. c. 25. 10. 24. vbi Abigael animum iratum Dauidis leni oratione sedauit. Proverb. capit. 15. 1.
units.tr: People are greeted by their names or surnames, or even by their honourable offices. Thus Moses and Samuel are called by God by their own names; thus Christ is called Rabbi by his disciples (see more fully below, chapter 4). Gentle speech is also to be used toward others as the need and advantage of the matter require. (Judg. 8:3, where Gideon with gentle words calmed the anger of his kinsmen; 1 Sam. 25:10, 24, where Abigail soothed David's angry mind with a gentle address; Prov. 15:1.)

units.la: Propositum dictum conditionem habere debet, si Deus volet. Iacob. cap. 4. 15. 1. Chron. capit. 13. 1. 2. Corinth. cap. 1. 17. 23.
units.tr: A proposed statement ought to carry the condition, "if the Lord wills" (James 4:15; 1 Chron. 13:1–2; 1 Cor. 1:17, 23).

units.la: Ea que tacenda sunt, duorum sunt genera. Vel enim omnino sunt tacenda, vel aliquatenus, & quandoque sermone silentium temperandum.
units.tr: Things that ought not to be said are of two kinds. Some must be wholly passed over in silence; others must be passed over in part, and sometimes speech must be tempered by silence.

units.la: Omnino tacendum & sermo cohibendus, quando honesta & conueniens dicendi materia, vel scientia deest.
units.tr: Silence must be kept entirely, and speech restrained, when there is no honest and suitable subject of speech, or no knowledge of one.

units.la: Materia honesta deest in rebus auditu odiosis, quae decoro & honestati aduersantur.
units.tr: An honest subject is lacking in matters that are odious to hearing and opposed to propriety and honesty.

units.la: Decoro aduersantur res inconuenientes, taediosae, alienae & falsae. Vnde homo dicitur insulsus, bardus, rudis, fatuus.
units.tr: Matters opposed to propriety are those that are unfitting, tedious, foreign and false. Hence a man is called insipid, a blockhead, rude or foolish.

units.la: De rebus inconuenientibus sermo instituitur, quando eadem sunt alienae, impertinentes, non conuenientes negotio quod agitur, vel personis loquentis, & illius ad quem sermo dirigitur, cui praesenti ruborem incutiant, vel in cuius ignominiam & notam vergunt, vel quae indicio esse possunt, eos, quorum communione vtimur, non valde a nobis amari, aut certe non magni feri.
units.tr: Speech about unfitting things arises when those things are foreign, irrelevant, not suited to the business in hand, or to the person speaking or the one to whom the speech is addressed, and so either shame the person present, or redound to the disgrace and reproach of someone, or give indication that those with whom we associate are not much loved by us, or at least not greatly esteemed.

units.la: De rebus taediosis & foetidis sermo habetur, quando ex verbis & sermone nostro per imaginationem sensus aliquis externus audientis, visus, au-
units.tr: Speech is tedious and foul when, through our words and discourse, some external sense of the hearer, of sight,

units.la: auditus, gustus, olfactus, tactusve offendi potest.
units.tr: hearing, taste, smell or touch, can be offended.

units.la: Honestati aduersantur res facta, audita & dicta turpes. Unde homo talia proloquens, κὶ cognoscitur & Epicureus. Eiusmodi sunt res turpes, spurcæ, obscœnæ, impiæ & illicitæ. Clemens Alex. lib. 2. Pædag. c. 6. De hisce rebus omnino tacendis, vide Psalm. 141. 3. Compone Iehova, observa os meum custodiens, moderare quidquid efferunt labia mea, (hoc est, ut Iunius explicat, ut Deus sermones ipsius componat & informet prudentia, qua sibi ab omni maleficio caveat) & sermones meos rege, ne quid temere profundam, aut aduersarii mei subdole aliquid hauriant ex imprudentis animo & ore. & 1. Timoth. c. 5. 13. de reb. profanis, anilibus fabulis, futilibus, vanis, nugacibus, stultis, friuolis, inutilibus, scurrilibus, garrientes, quæ non oportet, de quibus etiam 1. Timoth. c. 1. 4. c. 4. 7. 2. Timot. c. 2. 23. Tit. c. 3. 9. Ephes. c. 5. 4. & Iacob. c. 1. 26.
units.tr: Matters opposed to honesty are deeds, things heard and words that are shameful. Hence a man who utters such things is recognised as an Epicurean. Such things are filthy, foul, obscene, impious and unlawful. (Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2.6.) On these matters that must be wholly passed over in silence, see Ps. 141:3: "Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips" (that is, as Junius explains, that God may order and shape my words by a prudence by which I guard myself from all evil), "and keep my speech from rashly pouring out anything, or my adversaries from craftily drawing something from the heart and mouth of an imprudent man." Also 1 Tim. 5:13 (of worldly, old-wives' tales, frivolous, vain, trifling, foolish, empty, useless, buffoonish matters, speaking things that are not fitting; see also 1 Tim. 1:4; 4:7; 2 Tim. 2:23; Titus 3:9; Eph. 5:4; James 1:26).

units.la: Si quis videtur religiosus inter vos, non frenans linguam suam, sed suum ipsius cor seducens, huius vana est religio, & c. 3. 2. Si quis in sermone non impingit, hic perfectus est vir, ut qui possit frenno moderari totum etiam corpus. & verf. 8. Linguam enim nullus hominum domare potest. Malum quod coercere non potes, plena est veneno. Coloss. c. 3. 8.
units.tr: "If anyone among you thinks himself religious, and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his own heart, this man's religion is vain" (James 1:26). "If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body also" (James 3:2). And verse 8: "No one can tame the tongue; it is a restless evil, full of deadly poison." (Col. 3:8.)

units.la: At nunc deponite vos hæc omnia, iram, malitiam, excandescentiam, maledicentiam, verborum obscenitatem ab ore vestro. Matth. c. 12. Dico vobis, quodcunque verbum otiosum (id est malum, leve, vanum & futile) loquuti fuerint homines, de eo rationem redditurosin die iudicii. Ex sermonibus enim tuis iustificaberis, & ex sermonibus tuis condemnaberis. Clem. Alexand. lib. 2. c. 6. Turpiloquio, & nos omnino abstinere oportet, & iis qui illo utuntur os obstruere, & aspectu
units.tr: But now put off all these things: anger, malice, wrath, slander, obscene talk from your mouth (Col. 3:8). "I tell you, for every careless word (that is, evil, light, vain and trifling) that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgement. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned" (Matt. 12:36–37). Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2.6: We too must altogether abstain from foul speech, and stop the mouths of those who use it, both with a sterner look and a turning away of the face, and with what is called rebuke, and often with a harsher address.

units.la: [Remainder of page is partly illegible due to damage and show-through.] seueriore & vultus auersione, & ea qua vocatur sub-Jannatione & sæpe etiam asperiore oratione. vbi etiam αἰσχρολογίας definitur ᾧ περὶ τῶν τῆς κακίας ἐργῶν λογισμῶν. 'Αδολεσχίαν φλυαρίαν, nugas ineptas. Ephef.c.5.3. Scorta-tio vero & omnis impuritas aut auaritia ne nomina-tor quidem inter vos sicut decet sanctos, 4. Et obscœni-tas & stultiloquium & scurrilitas qua non conuenìut,sed potius gratiarum actio, 12. Nam qua occulte fiunt,ab istis turpe est vel dicere, & c.4.29. Nullus sermoputris egrediatur ex ore vestro. Ecclesiastic.c.37.21.Lingua dominatum assidue obtinet, & 1.Pet.c.3.10.Itaq; qui vult vitam diligere, & videre dies bonos, co-erceat linguam suam à malo & labia sua ne loquan-tur malum, vel dolum. & Prou.c.25.28. Vt ciuitasdisrupta absq; muro, ita est cuicunq; non est imperiumin suum spiritum, & c.16.26. qui res molestas temereaut improbe eloquitur, molestiam sibi adsert & refle-ctitur in ipsum eius os, & c.13.3. Remoue à te peruersi-tatem oris tui & labiorum. vbi Iun.& c.4.24. & c.8.13.in dicto libro Prou. quibus ex Psalmis adde Psalm.50.16. Quid tu enarres decreta mea & assumas fœdusin ore tuo, 19. Ostuum adhibes ad malum & linguatua concinnas dolum, 20. Sedens fratri tuo obloqueris,in filium matris tuæ edis infamiam: & Psalm.34.13.Quis est vir ille qui amat dies, delectatur vita & fruibono? Custodi linguam tuam à malo, & labia tua neloquantur fraudem. & Psalm.52.4. & 140.4.12. &141.3. & Prou.c.13.3. Qui custodit os suum ne extrametas officii sui excurrat aut diuagetur sermo, seipsumconseruat. & Prouerb.c.4.24.c.10.18.19.c.11.9.c.12.13.14.19.c.15.2.c.16.27.28.c.17.20.27.c.18.21.c.21.23.c.23.c.23.c.25.28.28. Matth.c.12.36.Luc.c.6.45.1.Corinth.c.15.33. Eccles.c.41.19. Senec. De morib.
units.tr: [The remainder of the page is partly illegible due to damage and show-through.] …with a sterner look and a turning away of the face, and with what is called rebuke, and often with a harsher address. Here also obscene speech (aischrologia) is defined as speech concerned with the works and thoughts of wickedness [αἰσχρολογία]. Idle chatter and silliness, foolish trifles (adolescha, phlyaria) (Eph. 5:3–4: "But fornication and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor filthiness, nor foolish talk, nor crude joking, which are not fitting, but rather thanksgiving." Verse 12: "For it is shameful even to speak of the things done by them in secret"; Eph. 4:29: "Let no corrupt word come out of your mouth"); Sirach 37:21: "The tongue holds sway continually"; 1 Pet. 3:10: "Therefore whoever wishes to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit"; Prov. 25:28: "Like a city broken through without a wall is a man who has no rule over his spirit"; Prov. 16:26–27: "He who speaks troublesome things rashly or wickedly brings trouble on himself, and the words of his mouth recoil upon him"; Prov. 13:3: "Put away from you a perverse mouth and crooked lips." To these from the Psalms add Ps. 50:16–20: "What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips? … You sit and speak against your brother; you slander your mother's son"; Ps. 34:13: "Who is the man who desires life and loves many days that he may see good? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit"; also Ps. 52:4; 140:4, 12; 141:3; Prov. 13:3: "He who keeps his mouth keeps his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin" (where the one who guards his mouth keeps speech from running beyond the limits of his duty and wandering); Prov. 4:24; 10:18–19; 11:9; 12:13–14, 19; 15:2; 16:27–28; 17:20, 27; 18:21; 21:23; 23:…; 25:28; Matt. 12:36; Luke 6:45; 1 Cor. 15:33; Ecclus. 41:19. Seneca, De moribus.

units.la: Turpia ne dixeris, Paulatim enim pudor p verba discutitur. 1. Cor.c.15. Corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava. Seneca lib.3. De ira: Sumuntur à conuersantibus mores.
units.tr: "Do not say shameful things, for modesty is gradually shaken loose by words" (cf. 1 Cor. 15:33). "Bad company corrupts good morals" (1 Cor. 15:33). Seneca, De ira 3: Manners are taken on from those we associate with.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: In quibus rebus sermo silentio temperandus.
units.tr: On what matters speech must be restrained by silence.

units.la: ATque haec fuerunt res de quibus omnino in conuersatione non loquendum. Sequitur de quibus quandoque tacendum & sermo silentio,&silentium sermone temperandum, quod est indicium hominis animi sui compotis.
units.tr: These are the subjects about which one should not speak at all in conversation. Next come the subjects on which we must sometimes be silent, and speech must be tempered by silence, which is a sign of a man who is master of his own mind.

units.la: Temperandus itaq; sermo silentio 1. in assensu & dissensu. 2. in commendatione. 3. in mentione aliorum facienda. 4. in iocis. 5. in irrisione & censura. 6. in increpatione & reprehensione. 7. in contentione.
units.tr: Speech, then, must be tempered by silence: (1) in assent and dissent; (2) in commendation; (3) in mentioning others; (4) in jests; (5) in mockery and censure; (6) in rebuke and reproof; (7) in contention.

units.la: Assensus, vel dissensus, qui sermone fit, silentio ita temperari debet, ut in eis non fit levitas, vel vitiosus pudor; neq; etiam malitiosa affectatio & obstinatia.
units.tr: Assent or dissent expressed in speech must be so tempered by silence that no levity or faulty shame arises in them, nor any malicious affectation or obstinacy.

units.la: Levitas est flexibilitas & mollities, qua in sermone promiscuè sine delectu quæuis præpropere & inconsiderate approbantur, vel obvitiosam & immodicam verecundiam non denegatur. Nam qui cuiuis voci acclamat, homo levis dicitur, adulator, aut imperitus & ineptus.
units.tr: Levity is a pliancy and softness by which, in speech, one approves indiscriminately and without judgement whatever is put forward, too hastily and thoughtlessly, or does not refuse what is offered out of a faulty and excessive bashfulness. For he who cheers every voice is called a light man, a flatterer, or unskilled and foolish.

units.la: Immodica & vitiosa verecundia est, qua ex vana suspicione & metu cuiusdam probri, vel ob imaginationem existimationis offensæ & præsumptionem mali poslulantibus & petentibus postulata non recusamus, vel pollicemur quae præstare non possumus.
units.tr: Excessive and faulty bashfulness is that by which, from a vain suspicion and fear of some disgrace, or from imagining offence to one's reputation and presuming some harm, we do not refuse what those who make demands and ask for things request, or we promise what we cannot perform.

units.la: De hoc vitioso pudore & verecundia, quae Graecis δυσωπία, ἀπὸ δὺς & ὤψ, eleganter Plutarch. De vitiosa verecundia, Imminet illa, ait, mollibus & effeminatis, nec valet ad ullam petitionem renuere aut contradicere, quod iudices auertit à iustitia, multaq; cogit tu dicere tum facere inconsulte, dum nullam interpellationem potest repellere, aut remouere perinde ut ager supinus & mollis turpissimis tum factis tum cupiditatib. perius est, omnia præbet inuadentib. immunita, patentia, procliuia. Talesverecundi perdunt ingenia sceleratissima, persuadendo vero & exorando corrumpunt etiam proba. Talis pudor immodicus mutuum dat, quib. diffidit: spondet, pro quib. non vult, & multa damna patitur. Ex hoc periit Dion, non quod ignoraret sibi à caldipo struí insidias, sed quia puduit obseruare amicum & hospitem. Ex hoc ebrietas quod propinati ob pudorem satis facere volumus. Atq; sic etiam multis instanter improbeq; flagitantibus damus non quod velimus dare, sed quod negare non valeamus. Malu pudor, malu rerum dispensator. Sic sæpe adsumitur padagogus ob petitionem vel intercessionem amicorum, qui non aptus neq; idoneus. Accidit itaq; pudori & verecundia immodica, ut in damna qui sumum ignominia & lenem reprehensionem vitat, incidat & se coniiciat in ignem & pudorem confessum, qui pœnitentiam perpetuum comitem habet.
units.tr: Concerning this faulty shame and bashfulness, which the Greeks call dysopia [δυσωπία, from δύς and ὤψ], Plutarch speaks elegantly in his work On Faulty Bashfulness: "It besets," he says, "the soft and effeminate, who cannot bring themselves to refuse or contradict any request. It turns judges away from justice and compels many people to say and do things rashly, since they cannot repel or turn aside any appeal. Like a limp and slack field, open, yielding and inclined to every sort of filthy act, whether deed or desire, it offers itself unguarded to all who attack. Such bashful persons ruin the most wicked schemes; by persuading and entreating they corrupt even honest men. Such immoderate shame lends money to those it distrusts, gives surety for those for whom it does not wish to, and suffers many losses. Dion perished because of this, not because he did not know that a plot was being built against him by Calippus, but because he was ashamed to watch over a friend and a guest. From this comes drunkenness, because out of shame we wish to satisfy those who pour us drinks. And so too we give to many who demand insistently and shamelessly, not what we wish to give, but what we cannot refuse. Bad shame is a bad steward of things. Thus often someone is taken on as a tutor, on the petition or intercession of friends, though he is neither suitable nor fit. It happens, then, that immoderate shame and bashfulness, which avoids the disgrace of a slight rebuke, falls into harm, casts itself into the fire, and confesses a shame that has repentance as its constant companion."

units.la: Remedium huic verecundiae vitiosæ ponit Plutarch. primò silentium, quod responsi loco: Deinde excusationem coram illis, qui nostro pudori vim faciunt, proponendam ait. Et tertiò, firmum propositum; de non cedendo do territantibus, vel assentantibus nobis.
units.tr: Plutarch prescribes a remedy for this faulty bashfulness: first, silence, which serves as the answer; then, he says, an excuse should be offered before those who put pressure on our shame; and thirdly, a firm resolve not to yield to those who threaten us or flatter us.

units.la: Vitiosæ verecundiæ contraria est impudentia; cuius indicia sunt, quando quis non confunditur ob ea, quæ existimationis offensionem & ignominiam procreant. Vt, petere mutuum abeo qui à te pecuniam mutuam petiturus videbatur: vel nonam summam petere, ne prior à te repetatur. Item, accurate quid laudare, vt id ipsum tibi donetur ab alio qua occulta & impudens petitio. Item, repulsam passum nihilominus instare & molestum esse. Alium in os laudare, vel virtutes eius extollere & vitia praeterire. Supra modum in alterum calamitate dolere. Non sustinere posse labores quos seniores, delicati, vel nobiliores sustinuerunt. Ab alio beneficium accipere & eidem saepe molestum esse. De seipso magna praedicare & polliceri. Alienam gloriam sibi adscribere. Vide Aristotelem lib. 2, Rhetoric.
units.tr: The opposite of faulty bashfulness is impudence, whose signs are when someone is not embarrassed by things that bring offence to reputation and disgrace. For example: to ask a loan of one who seemed about to ask you for money; or to ask for a sum you do not need, so that the one you lent it to is not repaid first. Likewise, to praise carefully something so that it may be given to you by another, a hidden and shameless request. Likewise, to keep pressing after a rebuff and to be a nuisance. To praise another to his face, to extol his virtues and pass over his faults. To grieve for another's calamity beyond measure. To be unable to endure labours which elders, delicate persons or nobles have endured. To receive a benefit from another and often be a burden to him. To boast and promise great things about oneself. To claim another's glory for oneself. See Aristotle, Rhetoric book 2.

units.la: Silentium, quod tendit ad Dei gloriam & proximi vtilitatem commendatur.
units.tr: Silence that tends to the glory of God and the usefulness of our neighbour is commended.

units.la: Aliquando in totum veritas silentio tegitur: aliquando pro parte. In totum, quando verbum etiam minimum obesse potest: vt si pater aegrotus de filii aegrotantis morte quaerat, qui iam est mortuus, reticenda est veritas, ne parenti mortem, vel aegritudinem augeat accelerate. Ita quoque Christiani in persecutionibus tyrannis non indicandi.
units.tr: Sometimes the truth is hidden by silence entirely, and sometimes in part. Entirely, when even the smallest word could do harm: for example, if a sick father asks about the death of his sick son, who has already died, the truth must be withheld, lest he hasten the death or the sickness of the parent. Likewise Christians are not to be revealed to tyrants in persecutions.

units.la: Pro parte non dicitur veritas, quando quaedam reticentur, vel omittuntur; quod concessum in rebus & causis licitis ad Dei gloriam pertinentibus. Ita Samuel in vnctione Dauidis egit vt habetur 1.Sam.c.16.12.3.Ita Ieremias.Ierem.c.38.24.25.26. & Paulus actor. c.23.6.
units.tr: The truth is told only in part when certain things are passed over or omitted; this is permitted in lawful matters and affairs that pertain to the glory of God. So Samuel acted in the anointing of David, as is recorded in 1 Sam. 16.12.3. So Jeremiah, Jer. 38.24.25.26, and Paul, Acts 23.6.

units.la: Ministris Christianæ Ecclesiæ secreta & arcana tegere conuenit. Nec stratagemata hostibus indicanda.
units.tr: It is fitting for the ministers of the Christian Church to keep secrets and mysteries hidden, and not to disclose stratagems to enemies.

units.la: Defectus & infirmitas proximi tegenda nisi forte vocatio & caritas aliud postularent. Prou. c.19.11.
units.tr: The defects and weaknesses of a neighbour are to be covered, unless perhaps calling and charity require otherwise. Prov. 19.11.

units.la: Malitiosa obstinacia & affectatio est: contra rigor & immobilitas, qua nos austeros & refractarios erga alios præbemus in sermonis allen-su, vbi imprimis odiosa est vana contradictio & pertinacia.
units.tr: Malicious obstinacy and affectation are the opposite; and so is harshness and immovability, by which we show ourselves austere and unyielding toward others in our assent in speech, where especially empty contradiction and pertinacity are hateful.

units.la: Veritati ne contradicas vllo modo, sed verecundia cohibetor, ne mentiaris inopia eruditionis tuæ. Eccles. c.4.30.neq; intelligentia propria contra alios innititor, neq; sapiens esto iudicio tuo. Prou.c.3.5.7.c.26.12. Ecclef.c.7.23.
units.tr: Do not contradict the truth in any way, but restrain yourself with modesty, lest you lie from a lack of your own learning. Eccles. 4.30. Nor lean upon your own understanding against others, nor be wise in your own judgement. Prov. 3.5.7; 26.12; Eccles. 7.23.

units.la: Nihil inexpertum affirmes, vel neges; quia no omne verisimile, statim verum est: sicut & sapius, quod incredibile, non continuo falsum est. Crebro siquidem faciem mendacii veritas retinet: Crebro mendacium specie veritatis occultatur.
units.tr: Affirm or deny nothing without experience; for not everything likely is at once true, just as, more often, what is incredible is not straightway false. Truth frequently wears the face of a lie; a lie is frequently concealed under the appearance of truth.

units.la: Non singulis aliorum verbis & dictis te opponas. vel de iis disputes, aut alterceris cum audacia & confidentia, Eccles.c.4.34. Prouerb.c.28.14.
units.tr: Do not set yourself against the individual words and sayings of others, or dispute about them, or quarrel with boldness and confidence. Eccles. 4.34; Prov. 28.14.

units.la: Non contradicas aliis causa victoriæ, vel vincendi studio, sed quemuis in sua, nō impia opinione, relinquas. Amamus enim eos qui nobis iratis aut feria agentibus non aduersantur.
units.tr: Do not contradict others for the sake of victory or from a desire to win, but leave each man in his own opinion, provided it is not impious. For we love those who do not oppose us when we are angry or acting wildly.

units.la: Qui animo obstinato & feroci aliorum opinionibus cōtradicunt & obstiftunt, & quibus vis emiéminere volunt consilio & scientia, sibi aliorum maleuolentiam & tædium conciliant, & per arrogantiam, subtilitatem & vigorem intellectus sui ostentant. Est enim stultitiae gradus velle videri sapientem. Nam qui sapientem agit in verbis, odiosus est, & omni sapientia destituitur. Ecclesiast. c. 37.23. & seqq. c. 7.23. Prov. c. 26. 12. c. 3. s. 7. Vidisti virum sapientem in oculis suis? expectatio est de stulto maior quam de illo. Agricolae spicas inclinatas versus terram libentius vident, quam eas quae sursum attolluntur; quae inanes & cassae: Ita qui maxime vani sunt, & gravitatis expertes, audaciam habent speciem, & incessum vultumque plenum superbia, ac contemtus: ubi vero impleri incipiunt fructumque e doctrina colligere, tum ferocia ista & vanitas deponitur. Ita fit ut ad scholam accedentes, primum sibi sapientes esse videantur, deinde fiant philosophi, postea oratores, tandem temporis progressu rudes & plebei, ut ait Plutarchus.
units.tr: Those who with an obstinate and fierce spirit contradict and oppose the opinions of others, and wish to stand out above them by counsel and learning, win for themselves the ill will and weariness of others, and display through arrogance, subtlety and the vigour of their understanding. For it is a degree of folly to wish to seem wise. For he who plays the wise man in words is hateful and is destitute of all wisdom. Ecclesiasticus 37.23 and following; 7.23; Prov. 26.12; 3.5.7. Have you seen a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him. Farmers prefer to see the ears of grain bent towards the ground rather than those raised upwards, which are empty and hollow. So those who are most vain and lacking in seriousness have a bold face, a gait and countenance full of pride and contempt; but when they begin to be filled and to gather fruit from learning, then that ferocity and vanity is laid aside. So it happens that those who come to school at first seem to themselves wise, then become philosophers, afterwards orators, and at last, as time goes on, rough and common, as Plutarch says.

units.la: Stultorum genera tria vulgo constituunt: Vnum est eorum, qui sine discretione & arrogantia iudicant, vid. Prouerb. c. 12. c. 13. qui insulsi sine sale, simplices, incauti, improuidi, & inepti vocantur. Quidam cum stulti quidem sint, tamen se sapientes arbitrantur, quorum numerus, teste Salomone, est magnus. Quidam cum sint stulti, alios tamen stultos putant, seque solos sapientes, minimam scintillam mentis habentes, nec se neque alios cognoscentes, interim tamen superbe, omnia iudicantes & prae se contemnentes: qui fatui dicuntur, quod omnino desipiant. Dementes & furiosi dicuntur qui nihil mentis habent. De quibus videre licet Menoch. lib. 6. Praef. 45. & lib. 2. caf. 519. arb. iud. quæst. Pet. Gregor. lib. 15. Synt. c. 5. & Proverb. c. 26. c. 27. & passim alibi. Proverb. c. 28. 11. Sapiens videtur in oculis suis stultus, & vir dives: sed tenuis prudens perscrutatur eum, &c. 12. 14. Gal. c. 6. 3. nam si quis sibi aliquid videtur quòd nihil sit, hunc suus ipsius animus seducit. Intelligentia tua ne innitctor, neque sapiens esto iudicio tuo. Proverb. c. 3. 5. 7. c. 26. 12. Ecclesiast. c. 7. 23. Esai. c. 5. 21. Væ sapientib. iudicio suo, 1. Corinth. c. 10. 12.
units.tr: Men commonly distinguish three kinds of fools. One kind is of those who judge without discernment and with arrogance, see Prov. 12, 13; these are called unsalted, simple, incautious, improvident and foolish. Some, though they are fools, nevertheless think themselves wise, and their number, as Solomon testifies, is great. Others, though they are fools, think other men fools, and consider themselves alone wise, having the least spark of mind, knowing neither themselves nor others, yet meanwhile judging everything proudly and despising everyone before them; these are called fools, because they are utterly senseless. Those who have no mind at all are called demented and mad. On these one may see Menochius, book 6, Preface, 45, and book 2, case 519, On Arbitrary Judgement; Pietro Gregorio, book 15, Syntagma, chapter 5; and Proverbs 26, 27, and passim elsewhere. Prov. 28.11: A man who is wise is in his own eyes foolish, but the poor man of understanding searches him out, etc. 12.14. Gal. 6.3: for if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, his own mind deceives him. Lean not on your own understanding, nor be wise in your own judgement. Prov. 3.5.7; 26.12; Eccles. 7.23; Isa. 5.21: Woe to those who are wise in their own judgement; 1 Cor. 10.12.

units.la: Vir cerebrosus & ἀνήδυς perunicax pro desiderio quarit & omnibus quæ sunt se immiscet, hoc est in sensu animi sui conquiescit, seque ab omni consortio subducit & nihil non præse fastidit & cuncta ex arbitrio facit. Proverb. c. 18. 1. 2. 3. Ecclesiast. c. 6. 2. & sibi ipsi confidit & contentiones miscet, Proverb. c. 28. 25. 26. vid. Exemplum 1. Samuel. c. 25. 3. 17. Vocatur eiusmodi (ἀληθῆς, ἀνήδυς, δυσχερής, δυσπαθιστής, ἐσ ipsum amat eiusmodi sine corrivali.
units.tr: A man who is quarrelsome and unpleasant [ἀνήδυς], and very contentious, seeks out what he desires and thrusts himself into everything. That is, he rests in the opinion of his own mind, withdraws himself from all company, despises everything before him, and does everything at his own discretion. Proverbs 18:1-3; Ecclesiastes 6:2. He trusts in himself and stirs up quarrels, Proverbs 28:25-26; see the example in 1 Samuel 25:3, 17. Such a man is called true [ἀληθῆς], unpleasant [ἀνήδυς], difficult [δυσχερής], hard to deal with [δυσπαθιστής], and one who loves himself without a rival.

units.la: Huc quoq; refero, studium alteri aduersandi eiusq; conatus impediendi, non vt commodum aliquod ipse ex ea re nancisca​ris, verum vt alterius commoda interuertas & corrumpas, quod vitium vocant ἐμφυτικόν, quod ὀλιγωρία indicium est. Proverb. c. 13. 10. Mera superbia vir edit iurgiu, at penes consultos est sapientia. industrie cauens ab accendendis, inflammandis & fouendis iurgiis.
units.tr: To this I also refer the eagerness to oppose another and to hinder his undertakings, not so that you yourself gain some advantage from the matter, but so that you overturn and ruin another's advantages. The Greeks call this fault [ἐμφυτικόν], and it is a sign of [ὀλιγωρία], contempt. Proverbs 13:10: "By pride comes only strife, but wisdom is with those who take counsel." He takes care to avoid kindling, inflaming and feeding quarrels.

units.la: Ethicus igitur ex modestia alium se præstantiorem existimabit. Philip. c. 2. 3. Roman. c. 12. 10. & ad omnia verba non adhibebit animum suum: sed dissimulabit lege charitatis & prudentia, Ecclesiast. c. 7. 21. arg. Galat. c. 6. 1. 1. Sam. c. 3. 38. c. 16. 10. & Proverb. 6. 17. 9. 10.
units.tr: The ethical person, therefore, out of modesty, will judge others to be better than himself, Philippians 2:3; Romans 12:10. He will not give his mind to every word, but will overlook it, in accordance with the law of love and prudence, Ecclesiastes 7:21; compare Galatians 6:1; 1 Samuel 3:38, 16:10; Proverbs 6:17, 9:10.

units.la: Importuni & fastidiosi sagaces vocantur, qui sub-
units.tr: Those who are troublesome and fastidious are called shrewd, those who sharpen their wit by a certain subtlety against others,

units.la: Importuni. subtilitate quadam ingenium suum cóntra alios acuunt, dictis eorum laqueos intendentes & insidias.
units.tr: troublesome: setting snares and traps for others by their words.

units.la: Sequitur de commendatione, iactantia & adulatione. Commendatio est sui ipsius, vel aliorum laudatio.
units.tr: Next comes the matter of commendation, boasting and flattery. Commendation is either praise of oneself or praise of others.

units.la: Causa suæ laudis est φιλαυτία: deinde, laus proximi, quæ ex æmulatione quadam incendit eos qui intemperáter erga gloriā sunt affecti: Quemadmodum esurientium aliis comedētib. magis irritatur & concitatur appetitus. Tertio, aliquando etiam feliciter ex animi sententia gestorum narrationes abripiūt aliquos in iactantiā. Quarto, quidam de se aliorum laudes & beneficia recitantes, seipsos de philautia suspectos reddunt. Quinto, quidē in reprehensionib. captant gloriam, quod ipsimet semper virtute præditi fuerint. Plane per alterius ignominiam, gloriam sibi venari & captare, & dum propriā laudem immiscet, alterius vituperio & depressione euehi velle, malitiosum & detestabile est. Plutarchus De sua ipsius laude.
units.tr: The cause of praising oneself is self-love [φιλαυτία]. Then there is praise of a neighbour, which kindles in those who are immoderately affected by glory a certain rivalry, just as the appetite of the hungry is more aroused and stirred when others eat. Third, sometimes even the narrating of deeds that turned out well, to one's liking, carries some people off into boasting. Fourth, some who recount the praises and benefits they have received from others make themselves suspect of self-love. Fifth, some seek glory in rebukes, by saying that they themselves have always been endowed with virtue. Plainly to hunt and seize glory for oneself at another's shame, and while mixing in one's own praise to wish to be raised up by the belittling and humbling of another, is malicious and detestable. Plutarch, On Self-Praise.

units.la: Laudem propriam semper sequitur alienum vituperiū, & gloriæ illius finis est ignominia. Nā qui seipsum laudat, primo suspectū se reddit de gloriæ cupiditate & arrogantia, vitiis pessimis. Deinde, quod sui ipsius sit amator & admirator sine corriuali. Tertio, se laudat vt ab aliis laudetur, & alios obscuret & deprimat. Quarto, desiderium suū ostendit; Nam quemadmodum is qui dolet, ibi etiam manū habere solet, vbi dolet: sic etiam talis in eo quo delectatur voce suā habet, & linguā circumagit. Nauita enim de ventis, de tauris narrat arator. Et qui sui ipsius amator est & ambitiosus, is plurimam diei partem eò impendit, ut ipse videatur optimus. In historiis, legendi studiosus; in sermonis artificio grammaticus; in peregrinis narrationibus, qui multas terras peragrarit & peruagatus sit. Ergo in hisce sermone cohibendus. Garrulitas enim inescata ab hisce progreditur & molesta redditur. Plutarch. De garrulitate.
units.tr: Self-praise always brings with it the blame of another, and the end of that glory is disgrace. For he who praises himself, first, makes himself suspected of a desire for glory and of arrogance, the worst vices. Second, that he is a lover and admirer of himself without a rival. Third, he praises himself so that he may be praised by others, and overshadows and depresses others. Fourth, he shows his own desire. For just as the one who is in pain usually also has his hand where he is in pain, so such a man has his voice and turns his tongue toward that in which he takes delight. For the sailor tells of winds, the ploughman of bulls. And one who loves and is ambitious for himself spends most of the day on this, so that he himself may seem the best. In histories, he is studious of reading; in the art of speech, a grammarian; in accounts of foreign places, he who has travelled through many lands and wandered over them. Therefore, in these matters he must restrain his speech, for chatter, once it has been drawn out by these things, becomes tedious. Plutarch, On Talkativeness.

units.la: Quinto, qui seipsum laudat, impudens praesumitur; quod scilicet non erubescit sibi tribuere, quae eum ab alio accipere oportebat. Sexto, de se indicium etiam praebet contemptus cuiusdam aliorum, qui tacentes praesentes molestè ferunt iactantiam & tacite obscuri redduntur & deprimuntur, & quasi testes virtutum praedicatarum laudantis tacite rogantur, qui id minimè volent testificari.
units.tr: Fifth, he who praises himself is presumed to be shameless, since he does not blush to claim for himself what he ought to have received from another. Sixth, contempt for others also reveals something about him: those present, who keep silent, bear his boasting with displeasure, are silently obscured and depressed, and are as it were silently asked, as witnesses of the virtues he proclaims, to bear witness to what they are least willing to attest.

units.la: Studium de se dicendi, cum alii laudantur, ob invidiam, aemulationemq;, in medium non est proferendum, ac neq; alii nos laudantes, tum sustinendi, sed concedendum tempus & locus iis, qui honore digno afficiuntur. Quod si illo honore illi indigni, haud tamen decet ut nostris laudibus, illorum laudi detrahamus, Plutarchus de se ipsum laude.
units.tr: The eagerness to speak of oneself when others are praised, out of envy and rivalry, is not to be brought forward in public, nor should we, when others praise us, endure it; rather, time and place should be yielded to those who are honoured with due esteem. But if they are unworthy of that honour, it is still not fitting that we should detract from their praise by our own. Plutarch, On Praising Oneself.

units.la: Gloriam vir civilis, non ut mercedem, aut solatium appetit, amatq; actionibus adstantem, sed quod fides & bonitatis opinio de se, apud alios, plurium ac praestantiorum actionum occasiones praebeat, ut ait Plutarch. d. loco. sed haec, si praedicatio non ab ipso, sed alio proficiscatur. Laudet te potius os extranei, non autem os tuum; alieni, non autem labia tua. Prou. c.27. 2. & opus ipsum potius potius te commedet, & c. 18.2. vbi Lauater. Ecclesiast. c.9.21.2. Corinth. c.10.18. non enim qui seipsum commendat, is probatus est, sed is quem Dominus commendat. Vide Plutarch. De garrulitate.
units.tr: The civil man seeks glory not as a reward or consolation, and loves to stand by his actions, but because the trust and the opinion of goodness that others have of him give occasions for more and greater actions, as Plutarch says in the same place. But this holds if the proclamation comes not from himself but from another. Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth; another, and not your own lips. Proverbs 27:2; and let the work itself commend you rather than your words, and compare Proverbs 18:2, where Lavater comments; Ecclesiasticus 9:21; 2 Corinthians 10:18. For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom the Lord commends. See Plutarch, On Talkativeness.

units.la: De bonis & honoribus nostris, virtutibus vxoris, liberorum, famulorum, item, de propriis diuitiis, rebusve gestis, officio, natalibus, neque gloriose loqui, neq; contemptim dicere conquenit. Prouerb c.13.7. Est enim illud aliis defectus suos exprobrare: hoc vero virtutes aliorum habere ludibrio. Et eum qui peccat in animam suam, quis iustum pronuntiabit? & eum qui vitam suam afficit ignominia, quis ornabit gloria? Ecclesiast.c.10.32. Et qui sibi ipsi malus, cui erit bonus? Ecclesiast.c.14.4 f. Siquidem non minus malum est tibi adscribere malu quod non admiseris, quam arrogare tibi bonum aliquod, quod non feceris, quo alludit Cato in Distichis: Nec te collaudes, nec te culpaueris ipse. Hoc faciunt stulti, quos gloria vexat inanis, adde Eccles. c.34.1.2.& seq. c.4.6. Iacob. c.4.16. Non obstat illud Pauli de se, quod peccatorum omnium sit primus, ad Timoth. & quod est Prou. c.30.2.3. & illud Christi de se, Vermis sum, non homo.
units.tr: Concerning our goods and honours, the virtues of our wife, children and servants, likewise concerning our own riches, deeds, office or birth, it is fitting neither to speak boastfully nor to speak with contempt. Proverbs 13:7. For it is one thing to reproach others for their defects, another to mock the virtues of others. And who will pronounce just one who sins against his own soul? And who will adorn with glory one who brings disgrace on his own life? Ecclesiasticus 10:32. And one who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good? Ecclesiasticus 14:5 f. For it is no less an evil to attribute to yourself a fault you have not committed than to claim for yourself some good you have not done. Cato alludes to this in his Distichs: Do not praise yourself, nor blame yourself. Fools do this, those whom empty glory troubles; add Ecclesiasticus 34:1-2 and following; Ecclesiasticus 4:6; James 4:16. Paul's saying about himself, that he is the first of all sinners, in 1 Timothy, does not stand in the way, nor does Proverbs 30:2-3, nor Christ's saying about himself, I am a worm and not a man.

units.la: Quando de erratis aliorum vel communiu est dicendum, sibi praecipua adscribet, vti fecit Paulus. 1. Timoth. c.1.13. qui prius eram blasphemus & persecutor, & c.15. vt peccatores seruaret, inter quos ego primus sum. & c.16.
units.tr: When we must speak of the errors of others, or of what is common to all, we shall ascribe the chief place to ourselves, as Paul did. 1 Timothy 1:13: who was before a blasphemer and persecutor; and chapter 15, that he might save sinners, of whom I am the first; and chapter 16.

units.la: Conditionem itaq; suam extenuare minime decet: Ecclesiast. c.10.32. & seqq. Prouerb. c.13.7. Habet siquidem speciem gloriationis. Vnde etiam haud decet valde recusare debita obsequia & honores conuenientes, quod est honore se
units.tr: Therefore it is by no means fitting to belittle one's own standing, Ecclesiasticus 10:32 and following; Proverbs 13:7. For this has the appearance of boasting. Hence it is also not fitting to refuse strongly the due services and fitting honours, which is to prefer oneself to others in honour and to despise those same people.

units.la: C
units.tr: C

units.la: aliis præferre & eosdem vilipendere. quæ est φιλοπτωχία, aut modestiæ & humilitatis simulatio quædam, quætamen duplex superbia recte vocatur. Recusare vero, quod officiose beneuolentiæ causa ab alio præstatur, est rustici, barbari, austeri & inhumani. Vide de Nabale, 1. Sam. c. 25. nisi impii & illicitis quid exhiberetur, quod contestatione recusandum, exempla Petri & Pauli, Actor. c. 14. 11. 2. & seqq. cap. 12. 21. & seqq. c. 10. 25. 26.
units.tr: This is the love of poverty [φιλοπτωχία], or a certain pretence of modesty and humility, which is nevertheless rightly called double pride. To refuse, however, what is offered by another out of courtesy and goodwill is the mark of the rustic, the barbarian, the harsh and the inhuman. See of Nabal, 1 Samuel 25; unless something impious and unlawful is offered, which must be refused with protest; examples of Peter and Paul, Acts 14:11; 2 and following; chapter 12:21 and following; chapter 10:25-26.

units.la: Non extollas neq; deiicias quenquam. Lauda parce & parcius vitupera. Nam nimia laudatio adulationem, & nimia vituperatio, malignitate sapit. Et nimia parsimonia & tenacitas in laudandis aliis indicat hominem adhuc laudis inopem & famelicum. Plutarch. de auditione. Qui hyperbolice laudat, traducit laudatos, quasi sc. hi superbia impulsi, nimias laudes affectarent.
units.tr: Do not exalt or cast down anyone. Praise sparingly and rebuke more sparingly. For excessive praise savours of flattery, and excessive rebuke savours of malice. And excessive parsimony and stinginess in praising others shows a man still lacking and hungry for praise. Plutarch, On Hearing. He who praises with hyperbole slanders those he praises, as if they, impelled by pride, were striving after excessive praises.

units.la: Nemo quoq; in faciem laudandus; sed dicendum potius constare tibi de præsentis laude & virtutibus, sed excusabis te nolle præsente laudare. Qui laudat ea, de quorum possessione & præsentia dubitat laudatus, gratiam & amorem sibi conciliat: qui vero certus est de re laudata, iudicat se non egere præconio.
units.tr: Nor is anyone to be praised to his face; rather, one should say that the praise and virtues of the present person are plain to you, but you will excuse yourself from praising him in his presence. He who praises those things about which the praised man is in doubt as to their possession and presence wins favour and love for himself; but he who is certain of the thing praised judges that he has no need of a herald.

units.la: Neq; laudes quæquam de pulchritudine ipsius, neq; abominaris quemquam ex aspectu ipsius, Eccles. c. 11. 2.
units.tr: Do not praise anyone for his beauty, nor despise anyone for his appearance, Eccles. 11. 2.

units.la: 1. Seipsum laudare ciuile aliquando & conueniens est, quando nimirum id facis ad defensionem honoris & famæ tuæ, aduersus calumniam, vel accusationem, vel iniurias, vti Paulus fecit 2. Corinth. c. 3. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. & c. 4. c. 12. & Samuel 1. Sam. c. 12. adde Ioh. c. 8. 14. vid. Chassan. part. 1. confid. 60. catal. gloriæ mundi.
units.tr: 1. It is sometimes proper and fitting to praise yourself, namely when you do so to defend your honour and reputation against slander, accusation or injury, as Paul did 2 Cor. 3. 1, 2, 3 and following, and ch. 4, ch. 12; and Samuel, 1 Sam. 12; add John 8. 14; see Chassan. part 1, consid. 60, catal. gloriae mundi.

units.la: 1. Deinde infortunatis & calamitosis superbia & iactantia conuenire potest, quando se hac contra fortunam erigere, animumq; suffulcire volunt, & omnibus modis commiserationem & lamentationem à rebus insperatis prouenientem ac deiectionem vitare & propellere, vt ait Plutar. de sua ipsius laude. & fecit Iob. Iob. c. 29.
units.tr: 1. Again, pride and boasting may suit the unfortunate and the afflicted, when they wish to raise themselves against fortune and sustain their spirit, and to avoid and drive off, by every means, the pity and lamentation that arise from unexpected misfortunes and the dejection that goes with them, as Plutarch says in On Praising Oneself; and as Job did, Job 29.

units.la: 2. Tertio etiam ille qui reprehenditur ob ea quæ recte fecit, is si facta sua laude euehat, venia dignus est. hic enim non exprobrare, sed defendere se dicitur.
units.tr: 2. Thirdly, the man who is reproved for things he has done rightly deserves pardon if he extols his own deeds, for he is not then said to reproach others but to defend himself.

units.la: 3. Horum quoq; habetur laudare alium, qui iisdem quibus laudator, est præditus virtutibus; hoc est, ille qui seipsum ob similitudinem virtutis in alio laudat, vel aliud agens, aut per aliud obliquè, non affectatè, laudes suas introducit: vt fecit Paulus 1. Corinth. c. 12. 2. nouit hominem in corpore, &c. & Iohannes Iob c. 19. 26. 27.
units.tr: 3. It is also allowed to praise another who has the same virtues as the one praising him. That is, a man who, because of a similarity of virtue, praises himself in another, or, while doing something else, or indirectly and without affectation, introduces his own praises by means of another. So Paul did, 1 Cor. 12. 2, "I knew a man in Christ," etc., and John, Job 19. 26, 27.

units.la: 4. Qui seipsos laudare coguntur, minus sunt molesti, quando Deo & aliis causis laudem suam communicant.
units.tr: 4. Those who are compelled to praise themselves are less objectionable when they share their praise with God and with other causes.

units.la: Sic pii homines suas virtutes etiam magnificè prædicasse legūtur, 1. Sam. c. 12. 7. vbi Pet. Martyr. Sed de iis non gloriantur, quas sciunt dona Dei esse, quas sciunt sibi datas ad proximi salutem. Ita & Apostolus commemorat & commendat sua dona. 1. Corinth. c. 9. 1. 2. & seqq. & 2. Corint. c. 9. 12. & seqq. capitib.
units.tr: So we read that pious men have also boasted of their virtues with some magnificence, 1 Sam. 12. 7, where Peter Martyr. But they do not boast of those gifts which they know to be gifts of God, which they know were given to them for the salvation of their neighbour. So the Apostle also recounts and commends his own gifts, 1 Cor. 9. 1, 2 and following, and 2 Cor. 9. 12 and following, in the chapters.

units.la: Sunt etiam, qui seipsos laudare quandoque coguntur, sed tum conuenit extenuare facta sua vt fecit Paulus. 1. Corinth. c. 15. minimus sum inter Apostolos, qui non sum dignus, &c.
units.tr: There are also those who are sometimes compelled to praise themselves, but then it is fitting to diminish their own deeds, as Paul did, 1 Cor. 15, "I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy," etc.

units.la: 6. Similiter qui correctione quadam mitigat laudem apud feroces & inuidos, vel iniiciunt leuia peccata, fraftrationes & excessus, vel defiderant aliquid, vel afferunt aliud potius laudandum, vel ob alia, vel deteriora abscondi, vel alios quibus maior laus debetur non laudari. qualis non infert, sed transfert laudem. vt aut Plutar.
units.tr: 6. Similarly, a person who softens his praise by some qualification before fierce and envious hearers, either admits small faults, errors and excesses, or expresses a desire for something, or names something else that is rather to be praised, or conceals other, greater or worse things, or does not praise others to whom greater praise is due. Such a person does not bring in praise but shifts it. As in Plutarch.

units.la: 7. Ob exhortationem quoq; & imitationem contentionemq; auditorum semet ipsum quis laudare ciuiliter potest. Vti fecit Paulus. 1. Corinth. c. 11. & c. 12. Nam exhortatio factum simul & sermonem habens, exemplum & imitationem propriam & familiarem, viuax mouet & incitat cum impetu, & proposito spem de rebus possibilibus commouet. Chaffan. late part. 1. confider. 60. Cat. glor. mund.
units.tr: 7. A man may also praise himself in a civil manner for the sake of exhorting and imitating his hearers and stirring them to emulation. Paul did so, 1 Cor. 11 and 12. For exhortation, which combines deed and speech and offers its own familiar example for imitation, moves and incites with force and kindles hope for things that are possible to do. Chassan., late, part 1, consid. 60, Catal. glor. mund.

units.la: 8. Interdum quoq; perterrefactionis correptionisq; gratia ad humiliandum subiiciendumque contumacem & improbum, conuenit gloriari aliquid de fe ac magnifice praedicare. Talis enim laus est non populi gratiam emerétis, aut sophistam agentis, neq; plausum, aut popyfmu petentis, sed eius qui virtutem fcientiamq; pro pignore fiduciae offerat amicis. Magnum eftenim momentum in temporibus periculosis ad salutem gloria fidesq; viri, imperatoriam experientiam ac potentiam habentis. Hic itaque lei-pfum laudas, prodest audienti, eiusq; iudicium corrigit. Plutarch. de fuaipfius laude.
units.tr: 8. Sometimes too, for the sake of terrifying and rebuking, in order to humble and subdue the stubborn and wicked, it is fitting to boast of oneself a little and to speak of oneself with some magnificence. For such praise is not that of a man seeking the favour of the people, or acting the sophist, or seeking applause or popular acclaim, but of one who offers his virtue and knowledge as a pledge of trust to his friends. For in dangerous times the reputation and faithfulness of a man who has military experience and authority carry great weight for safety. Thus when you praise yourself in this way, you benefit the hearer and correct his judgement. Plutarch, On Praising Oneself.

units.la: Sanctos quoq; quandoq; laudaffe sua facta constat. 1. Sam. c. 12. f. vbi Martyr. 2. Corinth. c. 9. & feqq. Efaiae c. 18. 3. & feqq. 1. Reg. c. 18. 13. 14. sed non oltentant, imo potius haec ad Deum autorem refe-
units.tr: It is also agreed that the saints sometimes praised their own deeds. 1 Sam. 12, where Martyr; 2 Cor. 9 and following; Isaiah 18. 3 and following; 1 Kings 18. 13, 14. But they do not make a display of them. Rather they refer these things to God as their author,

units.la: referunt & sua vita gloriam Dei illustrant;& pō- dus doctrinæ suæ addunt & gratias Deo agunt, non sicut Pharisæus apud Matth.
units.tr: and they make their life illustrate the glory of God, add weight to their teaching, and give thanks to God, and not as the Pharisee in Matthew did.

units.la: Sequitur de adulatione: Blanda benignaque oratio ciuilis est; sed assentatoria, indecora & turpis, qua nimirum quis in consuetudine, conuictu, sermonis negotiorumq; communicatione, omnia gratificatur omnibus, eandem affectionem animi fingit & imitatur, omnia collaudat quæ aliis placere putat, neque cuiquam, vbi vel maxime opus est, aduersatur, sed ita sibi persuadet, molestiæ nemini quidquam esse creandum, 1.Thessalon.cap 2.vers.3.4.5.6.
units.tr: There follows a discussion of flattery. Pleasant and kindly speech is proper to civil life; but fawning, unbecoming and base speech, by which a man, in habit, companionship and in the mutual exchange of talk and business, courts everyone in everything, feigns and imitates the same feeling of mind, praises all that he thinks will please others, and opposes no one, even when opposition is most needed, but persuades himself that nothing that might cause anyone trouble should be done. 1 Thess. 2. 3, 4, 5, 6.

units.la: Est igitur adulatio blandus quidem sermo, sed talis, quo homini placere volumus, quo studemus lucrum aliquod, vel beneuolentiam captare ab alio, eo quod alii attribuimus quod non habet, vel bonum quod habet nimium extollimus, vel vitium laudamus, vel æquum rectumque dissimulamus, vel maiora quam decet tribuimus. Tectissimus vero est adulator, qui cum maxime adulatur, tamen eam præ se fert specie libertatis vt possit videri non adulari, sed potius refragari. Ita Dauid Regi Achi hoc astutissimo genere adulationis adulatur. 1. Samuel. cap.28. vbi Martyr. & 1.Samuel.cap.29.8. Ideo adulatio animi depraedatio, amicitia ficta, corruptio, infatuatio, venenum placidum & iucundum, atq; incantatio vocatur, & adulator coruus, parasitus, hirudo, musca, tinea, & amicus ollaris.
units.tr: Flattery, then, is indeed a smooth speech, but of such a kind that by it we wish to please a man, by which we strive to win some gain or goodwill from another: when we ascribe to someone what he does not have, or extol a good quality he does have beyond measure, or praise a vice, or conceal what is fair and right, or bestow more than is fitting. The most crafty flatterer is he who, while flattering most of all, yet presents himself with such an appearance of frankness that he may seem not to flatter but rather to contradict. Thus David flatters King Achish with this most cunning kind of flattery. 1 Sam. 28, where Martyr; and 1 Sam. 29. 8. Therefore flattery is called the plunder of the mind, false friendship, corruption, infatuation, a gentle and pleasant poison, and an enchantment; and the flatterer is called a raven, a parasite, a leech, a fly, a moth, and a friend of the pot.

units.la: Adulator ergo hominem malum peiorem reddit, bonum vero corrumpit, vitia nutrit & auget, virtutes sistit & languefacit.De quo sermonis vitio vide Plutareh. De discrim. adulatoris & amici, & Senecam lib. 4. epist. 31. & libr. 8. epist. 60. Roman. c. 16. 18. Nam qui eiusmodi sunt, Domino nostro Iesu non serviunt, sed suo ventri: & per blanditloquentiam & assentationem corda hominum minime malorum seducunt. 1. Thessal. cap. 2. 4. 5. 6. Coloss. cap. 3. 21. 23. 24. Actor. c. 12. 22. Ierem. cap. 6 13. 14. 2. Sam. c. 15. 6. 3. 4. 5. c. 13. 3. 4. 5. c. 16. 1. 2. 3. 4. Genes. cap. 31. 20. 26. 27. 1. Corinth. cap 7. 33. 34. & passim alibi: Labia autem blanda exscindet Iehoua. Psalm. 12. 4. & Psalm. 5. 10. & mali lingua sua dolose blandiuntur. & Psalm. 140. 4. 10. Psalm. 10. 7. Psal. 55. 22. Cuius blanda sunt butyrina verba, dum bellum insidet animo eius, cuius molliora quidem verba oleo, sed strictli gladii sunt. Et ei qui benedicit amico suo voce magna & tempestive surgendo, maledictio imputabitur ei, hoc est, assentator, qui officia sua singulis momentis fingit & praedicat, maledictus est, ut Iunius explicat. Prou. cap. 27. 14. Ecclesiastic. cap. 6. 8. 9. & seqq. c. 12. 14. & seqq. c. 28. 14. Nam vir qui blanditur animo suo, rete & insidias pandit circa pedes eius. Prouerb. c. 29. 5. c. 6. 24. c. 7. 6. 21. & ore blando perficit impulsionem. Prouerb. c. 26. 28. Ecclesiast. c. 5. 16. c. 21. 29. cap. 6. 9. 10. 11. Adulatores Plutarchus ait esse similes pediculis, qui a morientibus discedunt, eorumque corpora relinquunt, simulatque sanguis extinctus est, quo nutriri solebant. Sic & adulatores nobilibus & potentibus imminent hisque aluntur; sed iisdem rebus commutatis, statim auolant. Iatius de aulicis adulatoribus in politicis dixi.
units.tr: The flatterer therefore makes a bad man worse, corrupts a good man, nurtures and increases vices, and checks and weakens virtues. On this vice of speech see Plutarch, On the Difference between a Flatterer and a Friend, and Seneca, letter 31 of book 4 and letter 60 of book 8. Rom. 16. 18. For those of this sort do not serve our Lord Jesus but their own belly, and by smooth talk and flattery they lead astray the hearts of men who are by no means evil. 1 Thess. 2. 4, 5, 6. Col. 3. 21, 23, 24. Acts 12. 22. Jer. 6. 13, 14. 2 Sam. 15. 6; 3, 4, 5; ch. 13. 3, 4, 5; ch. 16. 1, 2, 3, 4. Gen. 31. 20, 26, 27. 1 Cor. 7. 33, 34, and elsewhere throughout. "But the LORD will cut off flattering lips," Ps. 12. 4; and Ps. 5. 10, "and with their tongues they deal deceitfully"; and Ps. 140. 4, 10; Ps. 10. 7; Ps. 55. 22. "Whose words are softer than butter, while war is in his heart; whose words are softer than oil, yet they are drawn swords." And to him who blesses his friend with a loud voice, rising early, it will be counted as a curse, that is, the flatterer, who feigns and proclaims his services at every moment, is cursed, as Junius explains. Prov. 27. 14. Ecclus. 6. 8, 9 and following; ch. 12. 14 and following; ch. 28. 14. "For a man who flatters his neighbour spreads a net and snares at his feet," Prov. 29. 5; ch. 6. 24; ch. 7. 6, 21; "and with smooth lips he brings about a fall," Prov. 26. 28; Ecclus. 5. 16; ch. 21. 29; ch. 6. 9, 10, 11. Plutarch says that flatterers are like lice, which leave dying men and abandon their bodies as soon as the blood by which they were nourished is gone. So too flatterers hang about nobles and the powerful and are fed by them; but when those circumstances change, they immediately fly away. I have spoken more fully about courtly flatterers in my Politics.

units.la: Adulatoribus similes sunt delatores malitiosi, Vide 1. Samuel. cap. 22. 9. 10. cap. 23. 19. & foemina malicmalitiosa, qua blanditiis suis maritos suos seducunt & decipiunt. de quibus vide Prouerb. c. 31. 3. Ecclesiast. c. 4. 1. 2. 3. c. 19. 2. & seqq. c. 25. per tot. quales fuere uxores Salomonis & Achabi, & aliorum.
units.tr: Slanderers are like flatterers: malicious informers. See 1 Samuel 22:9-10; 23:19. Likewise a malicious woman, who by her flatteries seduces and deceives her husband. On these see Proverbs 31:3; Ecclesiastes 4:1-3; 19:2 ff.; 25 throughout, such as were the wives of Solomon and Ahab, and of others.

units.la: Adulationi contrarius est candor, quo illud quod sentimus ingenue & sine dissimulatione dicimus.
units.tr: The opposite of flattery is candour, by which we say frankly and without pretence what we think.

units.la: Sequitur de maledicentia: De aliis quidem loqui ciuile saepe est, sed male de aliis loqui, vel arcana eorundem reuelare, hominis inciuilis. Fieri enim id solet ideo, vt proximum, adducat in inimicitiam & odium, aut contra eum vindictam excitet, vel commodum inde consequatur maledicus.
units.tr: Next comes slander. To speak well of others is often civil, but to speak ill of others, or to reveal their secrets, is the mark of an uncivil man. This is usually done so that the neighbour is drawn into enmity and hatred, or so that vengeance is stirred up against him, or so that the slanderer gains some advantage from it.

units.la: Maledici autem inciuiles varii sunt. Quidam sunt personati, quidam Rhetores, quidam hypocritae, quidā scorpiones mordaces, vel ignoti. vt Guazzius loquitur.
units.tr: Uncivil slanderers are of various kinds. Some are masked, some are rhetoricians, some are hypocrites, some are biting scorpions, or anonymous. As Guazzo says.

units.la: Personati seu larvati maledici sunt, qui larua modestiae se obducunt & interim tamen ab omnibus cognosci cupiunt. Tales sunt qui dicunt se nolle nomen exprimere eius, cuius famam laedunt, interim tamen satis describunt & declarant, vt ab audientibus cognoscantur. Atq; tales mel in ore, nouaculam sub cingulo gerere dicuntur.
units.tr: Masked or veiled slanderers are those who cover themselves with the mask of modesty and yet at the same time want to be recognised by all. Such are those who say they do not wish to name the person whose reputation they harm, yet describe and point him out so clearly that the hearers recognise him. Such people are said to carry honey in the mouth and a razor under the belt.

units.la: Rhetores maledici sunt, qui sub specie & colore occupationis simulant se nolle maledicere, & tamen eo ipso male, imo peius loquuntur & per ironiam pungunt. Item, qui sub specie laudis exagitant, vt qui timidissimum Achilli vel Herculi comparant, aut iniustum Aristidi, vid. Macrob. lib. 7. Saturnal. c. 3.
units.tr: Rhetorical slanderers are those who, under the appearance and colour of a duty, pretend that they do not want to slander, and yet by that very act speak ill, or rather worse, and sting through irony. Likewise those who attack under the guise of praise, as when they compare a most cowardly man to Achilles or Hercules, or an unjust man to Aristides. See Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 7, chapter 3.

units.la: Hypocritae maledici sunt, qui sub specie doloris & compassionis lacrymabili, lenta atq; lassa voce & verbis quasi coactis extortisve, aliorum infortunia vel excessus commemorant, quo eorundem exístimationem minuant & laedant, & petunt ne cuipiam reueletur. Vide Lauater. Proverb. c. 18. 8. Tales quoq; sunt qui clam proximi vitia aliis manifestant. Ro. c. 1. 30. similes Chamo. Genes. c. 9. 22.
units.tr: Hypocritical slanderers are those who, under the show of grief and compassion, with tearful eyes, a slow and weary voice, and words as if forced or wrung out, recall the misfortunes or faults of others, in order to diminish and damage their reputation, and yet ask that nothing be revealed to anyone. See Lavater on Proverbs 18:8. Such also are those who secretly disclose a neighbour's faults to others. Romans 1:30. Like Ham, Genesis 9:22.

units.la: Tales quoq; sunt qui bene & recte dicta factave, aliorum glossa & interpretatione maligna & sinistra in alium peruersum sensum detorquet, vel falsos testes iubornant contra innocentem hominem, quib iuris praetextum habeant. Matt. c. 26. 60. Ierem. c. 37. 13.
units.tr: Such also are those who twist things done or said well and rightly, by malicious and sinister gloss and interpretation, into a perverse sense against another, or who suborn false witnesses against an innocent man, so that they have a pretext of law. Matthew 26:60; Jeremiah 37:13.

units.la: Maledici scorpiones sunt, qui primo commedant & postea appendunt maculam, & quasi cauda feriunt & laedunt, ut, Non credo honoratiorem Pamphilo, nisi scortator esset.
units.tr: Scorpion slanderers are those who first bite and afterwards hang on a stain, and strike and wound as with a tail, as in: I do not believe anyone more honourable than Pamphilus, unless he were a whoremonger.

units.la: Maledici mordaces sunt iocommatum & facetiarum eiaculatores, ex quorum ore breues quaedam & aculeatae proiiciuntur orationes, quae aliorum corda plusquam sagittae feriunt, ut meminimus, quando brachio te emungebas. Etalia plura exempla recenset Macrobius lib. 7. Saturn. c. 3. & foetum contumeliae vocat. Sunt tamen quaedam scommata minus aspera quasi edentatae belluae morsus, quae plus urbanitatis, minus amaritudinis habent, quorum exempla vide apud Macrob. d. c. 3. Praesertim quando dicuntur in eos, qui a dictis sunt alienissimi, vti si nimis & notorie casto dicas ipsi meretrices gratas, &c. Sunt etiam quae coram quibusdam personis nobis obiici & dici nolimus, & coram aliis libenter audire possumus. Conditio dicentis etiam
units.tr: Biting slanderers are the shooters of jests and witticisms, from whose mouths short, barbed speeches are hurled, which strike men's hearts more than arrows, as when you blew your nose with your arm. Macrobius, Saturnalia book 7, chapter 3, lists many other examples and calls it the offspring of insult. Yet some jests are less harsh, like the bite of a toothless beast, having more wit and less bitterness; examples of these are in Macrobius, ibid. chapter 3. Especially when they are aimed at those who are most remote from the charge, as if you were to say to a man notoriously chaste that prostitutes love him. There are also things that we would not want said to us in the presence of certain persons, yet can gladly hear in the presence of others. The standing of the speaker also commends the jibe,

units.la: scomcomma commendiar, si in eadem sit causa, vt ii alium de paupertate pauper irrideat.
units.tr: if he is in the same situation, as when a poor man mocks another for poverty.

units.la: Ignoti maledici sunt qui pasquillos, picturas, aut scripturas famosas spargunt, iisque aliorum famam & existimationem transfigunt.
units.tr: Anonymous slanderers are those who spread lampoons, pictures, or defamatory writings, and by these pierce the good name and reputation of others.

units.la: De hisce maledicis singulis passim Scriptura loquitur. Coloss. cap. 3. 8. At nunc deponite vos haec omnia, iram, maledicentiam. 9. Ne mentiamini alii aduersus alium. 1. Timoth. cap. 3. 2. Necui maledicant, vt sint a pugnis alieni, aequi, omnes exhibentes lenitatem, erga quosuis homines, & verf. seqq. Psalm. 140. 12. Vir maledicus ne stabilitatur in terra, & verf. 4. 6. 10. Psalm. 50. 20. Roman. c. 1. 30. 2. Corinth. c. 12. 20. Exod. c. 23. 1. ne efferto rumorem mendacii: 1. Sam. c. 24. 10.
units.tr: Scripture speaks everywhere of each of these slanderers. Colossians 3:8-9: "But now put off all these: anger, slander... Do not lie to one another." 1 Timothy 3:2-3: "Let no one slander, but be free from quarrels, fair, showing all gentleness to all men," and the following verses. Psalm 140:12: "A slanderer shall not be established in the earth," and verses 4, 6, 10. Psalm 50:20. Romans 1:30. 2 Corinthians 12:20. Exodus 23:1: "Do not spread a rumour of falsehood." 1 Samuel 24:10.

units.la: Dixitq; Dauid Sauli, quare auscultas verbis cuiusquam dicentis, Ecce, Dauid quaerit malum tuum. Ierem. c. 40. 14. 16. & Iacob. c. 3. 9. 10. c. 4. 11. & Luc. c. 7. 33.
units.tr: David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to the words of anyone who says, 'Behold, David seeks your harm?'" Jeremiah 40:14, 16; James 3:9-10; 4:11; Luke 7:33.

units.la: Venit Ioannes Baptista neq; edens, neque bibens vinum, & dicitis Daemonium habet, 34. Venit filius hominis edens & bibens, & dicitis: Ecce homo edax, vini potor & amicus publicanorum & peccatorum.
units.tr: John the Baptist came neither eating nor drinking wine, and you say, "He has a demon." The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, "Behold, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners."

units.la: Matth. c. 26. 61. Dixerunt, ipse dixit: possum destruere templum Dei & triduo ipsum aedificare, & verf. 59.
units.tr: Matthew 26:61: "They said, 'This man said, I am able to destroy the temple of God and to build it in three days,'" and verse 59.

units.la: Quaerebant falsum testimonium contra Iesum vt eum morte afficerent. Marc. c. 14. 55. 56. Ioh. c. 2. 19. & sic finistre salutationem Dauidis accipiebant. 2. Sam. c. 10. 3. 4. Reg. c. 11. 8. & seqq. vbi & de Iezebel uxore Achabi notabilis subernatio testium & quaesitus color iuris narratur.
units.tr: They sought false testimony against Jesus so that they might put him to death. Mark 14:55-56; John 2:19. And so they received David's greeting ill-naturedly. 2 Samuel 10:3-4; 1 Kings 11:8 ff., where also a notable subornation of witnesses and a pretended colour of law is recorded concerning Jezebel, the wife of Ahab.

units.la: Prouerb. c. 16. 27 Vir nequam & maledicus effodit malum, eiusq; labiis insidet, velut ignis adurens.
units.tr: Proverbs 16:27: "A worthless and slanderous man digs up evil, and on his lips dwells, like a burning fire."

units.la: Eccles. c. 19. 8. ne enarra apud amicum aut inimicum rationes aliena vita, 9. Nam qui audierit te & observauerit te, is suo tempore odio habiturus est te,
units.tr: Ecclesiasticus 19:8-9: "Do not relate to friend or foe the affairs of another's life; for whoever has heard you and observed you will at his time hate you."

units.la: 10. Audiuisti sermonem? moriatur apud te, & bono animo esto, non enim rumpet te, 11. A sermone stultus cruciatur doloribus, vt a fœtu parturiens. Prou. c. 26.23. Vt argenti scoria obducta testa; ita sunt labia prosequentia & animus malus, 24. & labiis suis alium se simulat ofor, quam in medio sui disponit dolum. 25. & quando gratiosam prabebit vocem suam, ne fidito ei. Nam septem abominationes insunt animo eius. Roman. c. 3. 13. Sepulchrum apertum guttur eorum, linguis suis ad dolum abusi sunt, venenum aspidum sub labiis ipsorum. 14. quorum os diris & amarulentia plenum est. Psalm. 5.10. & Psalm. 140. 4. Exacuunt linguam suam similem serpentis: venenum pryados subest labiis eorum maxime. Psalm. 52.4. Ærumnas excogitatas depromis, linguatua similis est nouacula acuta, o artifex doli. 5. Diligis malum potius, quam bonum, mendacium, quam loqui iustitiam, diligis vehementissime, 6. Dilexisti omnia verba perniciosa, linguam dolosam, & Prouerb. c. 26. 28. Vir lingua fallace odit quos attriturus est, & ore blando perficit impulsionem, & cap 11.9. Ore hypocrita corrumpit proximum suum, at scientia insti liberatur. Leuitici cap.19.16. Non ambulandum cū detractatione tanquam si nundineris verba & honorem proximi, & Prouerb. c.11.12.13. Ecclesiastic.cap. 41.28. & cap.22.22. Qui pungit oculos, elicit lachrymas, & qui pungit eor, prouocat scutum, 28. Et qui mittit lapidem in volucres, abigit illas, & qui probris afficit amicum, dissoluit amicitiam, & vers.23. & cofringit ossa. Ecclesiastic.c.28.20. & perdit, vers. 21. & seqq. & cap. 23.18. Homo consuescens sermonibus probrosis, omnibus diebus suis nequaquam erudietur. Prouerb.cap. 14.21. qui contemnit proximum suum, suum, futurus est peccator. Ecclesiast. cap. 41. 14. Pu-deat te si quis te contumeliis probrosis infamibus, ex-aget, cum eo colludere & conventione pacisci ad ma-lum, 28. Pudeat apud amicum sermonum probri, & postquam dederis, ne exprobrato.
units.tr: 10. "Have you heard a word? Let it die within you, and be of good courage; it will not burst you." 11. "A fool is racked with pains from a word, as a woman in labour from a child." Proverbs 26:23: "Like a potsherd covered with silver dross, so are smooth lips with a wicked heart." 24. "With his lips the enemy pretends, but within he lays up deceit." 25. "When he makes his voice gracious, do not trust him, for seven abominations are in his heart." Romans 3:13: "Their throat is an open sepulchre; they have used their tongues to deceive; the venom of asps is under their lips." 14. "Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness." Psalm 5:10; Psalm 140:4: "They sharpen their tongues like a serpent; the poison of asps is under their lips." Psalm 52:4: "You devise ruin; your tongue is like a sharp razor, O worker of deceit." 5. "You love evil rather than good, lies rather than to speak righteousness, you love most vehemently." 6. "You have loved all destructive words, a deceitful tongue." And Proverbs 26:28: "A man with a lying tongue hates those whom he will crush, and with a smooth mouth he brings about ruin." And Proverbs 11:9: "With his mouth the hypocrite destroys his neighbour, but by knowledge the righteous are delivered." Leviticus 19:16: "You shall not go about as a slanderer among your people, as if you were trading in words and in your neighbour's honour." Proverbs 11:12-13. Ecclesiasticus 41:28. Ecclesiasticus 22:22: "He who pricks the eye brings forth tears, and he who pricks the heart provokes the shield." 28. "And he who throws a stone at birds drives them away, and he who heaps reproaches on a friend dissolves the friendship," and verse 23, "and breaks the bones." Ecclesiasticus 28:20, "and destroys," verse 21 ff., and 23:18: "A man accustomed to reproachful words will never be instructed all his days." Proverbs 14:21: "He who despises his neighbour will be a sinner." Ecclesiasticus 41:14: "Be ashamed if someone with insulting and shameful reproaches drives you, to collude with him and make a bargain for evil." 28. "Be ashamed before a friend of reproachful words, and after you have given, do not upbraid."

units.la: Eius modi maledici, suspecti & odiosi ideo sunt, quod existimentur id quod de aliis apud nos loquuntur, id ipsum de nobis etiam dicere apud alios. Ideo Seneca recte dicit: Multi cum alii male dicunt, sibi ipsis conuicium faciunt & iram aliorum excitant.
units.tr: Slanderers of this kind are suspected and hated for this reason: people think that whatever they say about others among us they also say about us among others. So Seneca rightly says: Many people, when they speak ill of others, heap insults on themselves and stir up the anger of others.

units.la: Contra amantur qui nec propria, neq; proximorum suorum mala & defectus scire videntur, sed tantum bona. Bonus enim homo mala tegit & dissimulat, contra bona ostentat & celebrat. Huc etiam pertinent imprecantes aliis diram, eosq; execrantes, quae imprecationes & execrationes prohibitae. Vide Martyr. ad Rom. c. 11. 9. & c. 12. 14. & Iudic. c. 1. 17.
units.tr: On the other hand, those are loved who seem to know neither their own faults nor those of their neighbours, but only their good points. A good man covers and overlooks faults, but displays and celebrates good qualities. This also applies to those who call down a curse on others and execrate them, which imprecations and execrations are forbidden. See Martyr on Rom. 11.9, Rom. 12.14, and Judg. 1.17.

units.la: Secreta, praesertim amici, non sunt revelanda. Prauerb. c. 20. 19. Reuelanti arcana qui ambulat cum detractatione & ei qui seducitur labiis suis, ne admisceto te. & c. 25. 9. Causam tuam age cum proximo tuo; sed arcanum alterius ne retegito, 10. ne probro afficiat te qui audit, & infamia tua fit irrevocabilis. & c. 11. 13. Ambulans cum detractione revelat arcanum; at fidus animo tegit rem. Ecclesiastic. c. 22. 25. c. 27. 16. Qui revelat arcana, amittit fidem, ac nequaquam amicum inventurus est ex animo suo. & verf. 18. 23. Matth. cap. 18. 15. Si vero peccaverit in te frater tuus, veni & argue eum inter te & ipsum solum, & c. De exemplo Iosephi vid. Matth. c. 1. 19. Eccles. c. 19. 13. & seqq.
units.tr: Secrets, especially a friend's, must not be revealed. Prov. 20.19: He who goes about as a slanderer reveals secrets, so do not associate with one who opens his lips wide. Prov. 25.9–10: Plead your cause with your neighbour, but do not disclose another's secret, lest he who hears it put you to shame, and your infamy never be undone. Prov. 11.13: The slanderer goes about revealing secrets, but the faithful in spirit keeps a matter hidden. Ecclus. 22.25; Ecclus. 27.16: He who reveals secrets loses trust, and will never find a friend to his heart; ver. 18, 23. Matt. 18.15: If your brother sins against you, go and show him his fault between you and him alone. For Joseph's example, see Matt. 1.19 and Ecclus. 19.13ff.

units.la: De maleficio perpetrando secreta reuelare & indicare decorum, & ciuile & æquum, si fiat ab eo, qui eorum habet certam scientiam, vt futurum delict im præcaueatur & impediatur, qui alias peccatis alienis communicare diceretur. An vero, quatenus & quis & qua commissa malefi-cia indicare & reuelare teneatur, iuridica quæstio est, quam late examinauit lib. 1. Dicaolog. cap. De seduc-tione. ex Anton Gabriel concluf. 37. lib. 7. Farinac. quæst. 51. de indi. & tortura. Menoch. caf. 355. arb. iu-dic. quæst. & caf. 414. & 537. ex Theolog. probati. vid. Iacob. c. 5. 9. 20: Genef. c. 37. 2. 1. Cor. c. 11. Matt. c. 18. 16.
units.tr: To reveal and point out secrets in order to prevent a crime being committed is seemly, civil and fair, if it is done by someone who has certain knowledge of the matter, so that a future offence may be forestalled and prevented; otherwise he would be said to share in other people's sins. But how far, and who, and for which crimes committed, one is bound to indicate and reveal them, is a legal question, which the author examined at length in book 1 of the Dicaeologicon, in the chapter On Seduction, from Antonius Gabriel, conclusion 37; book 7 of Farinacius, question 51, on indication and torture; Menochius, case 355 and question on arbitrary judgments, and cases 414 and 537, approved from the theologians. See Jas. 5.9, 20; Gen. 37.2; 1 Cor. 11; Matt. 18.16.

units.la: Sequitur de Iocis. Iocari quandoq; decorum & ciuile est: sed in rebus grauibus iocari non licet, neq; in flagitiosis, obscœnis, & impiis, neq; cum intractabilibus & austeris hominibus. vid. Gell. lib. 4. c. 10. Macrob. lib. 2. Saturnal. Ephes. cap. 4. 19.
units.tr: Next comes jesting. Jesting is sometimes seemly and civil, but one may not jest about serious matters, nor about shameful, obscene and impious things, nor with intractable and austere people. See Gellius, Attic Nights 4.10; Macrobius, Saturnalia 2; Eph. 4.19.

units.la: Ioci autem subtiles & faceti esse debent, non longe repetiti, sed faciles & iucundi, alias tædiosi & molesti. Commode igitur exerceri non possunt, nisi ab homine cauto acuta & prompta sagacitate ex improuiso se exerente: & in peculiari quadam promtitudine, venustate & celeribus animi motibus consistunt. Ideo non conueniunt ioci hominibus plebeis, stupidis & tardis, sed eis, qui possint, non qui velint iocari iocis venustis, urbanis, lepidis, facetis, elegantibus, subtilibus & salibus breuibus, qui exhilarant & suauiter recreant. Vtendum enim ioco tanquā somno & quietibus cæteris tum, cum grauibus seriisq; rebus satisfecerimus, vide Plutarch. lib. Sympos. Concessus iocus itaq;,si est sobrius & sine scandalo;vel, si est cum acrimo-
units.tr: Jests should be subtle and witty, not long drawn out, but easy and pleasant; otherwise they are tedious and annoying. They cannot be fittingly exercised except by a cautious man, whose sharp and ready shrewdness shows itself unexpectedly; they consist in a particular quickness, charm and swift movements of the mind. So jests do not suit common, dull and slow people, but those who are able, not those who merely want, to jest with pleasant, urbane, witty, elegant and subtle jests and brief witticisms, which cheer and gently refresh. For jesting should be used like sleep and other rests, once we have attended to serious and weighty matters. See Plutarch, Symposiacs. Permitted jesting, then, is that which is sober and without scandal, or which is with some sharpness.

units.la: Iocis scurrilib.insulsum se fingere aut stultū, valde indecorum est.Ephef.cap.4.29. nullus sermo putris ex ore vestro egreditor, Prouerb.c.14.28. Plu-tarch.de liber.educ. Quia se comparant,vt homini-bus,nullam honestatis rationem habentibus,voluptates concilient & placeant, ii mali & inciviles sunt.
