Fugienda itaq; hæc scurrilitas in iocis & dicis,quaiñhonestis verbis,risum volumus exci-tare.quæ sunt ineptiæ sannionum. Clem. Alex. lib.2.Padag.c.5.Macrob.lib.7.Saturn.c.3.& lib. 2.c. 2. &seqq. Siquidem scurræ,vndequaq; aucupātur ridicula & potius hoc student, vt risum moueant,quam vt acute quid dicant, imprimis qui in hoc loco tempori vel dignitati cuiusque non parcunt, sibiq; hanc licentiam sumunt, neq; in eo se peccare ai bitrantur, vt quemlibet & quacunq; in re ludificent. Imo nonnunquam & se-metipsos aliis ridiculos probris & irrisione dis-gnos præbent. vt ait Clemens Alex.lib.2.Padag.c. 5.& c.7.vbi ... id est, vrbane nobis lepideq; loquendum, non risu mouendus: vt hunc allegat & explicat doctissimus vir D.Stuck.libr. 3.c.19.comminal.antiquit.
units.tr: To pretend to be a buffoon or a fool in jests is very unseemly. Eph. 4.29: Let no corrupt talk come out of your mouth; Prov. 14.28; Plutarch, On the Education of Children. Those who make themselves like men who have no regard for honour, in order to win pleasures and please, are wicked and uncivil. So this buffoonery in jokes and quips, which wants to raise laughter by dishonest words, must be avoided; these are the silly antics of mockers. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2.5; Macrobius, Saturnalia 7.3, and 2.2ff. For buffoons everywhere hunt after ridiculous things and aim rather to cause laughter than to say something cleverly; especially those who in this spare neither the place nor anyone's dignity, and claim this licence for themselves, nor think they sin in mocking anyone in any matter whatever. Indeed, they sometimes make themselves ridiculous and worthy of scorn to others by their insults and mockery. As Clement of Alexandria says, Paedagogus 2.5 and 7, we must speak urbanely and wittily, not be moved to laughter; as the most learned Stuckius explains and cites it, Antiquitates convivales 3.19.

units.la: Risum quoq; comprimere, quandoq; præse fert decorum & honestatem, Clementis Alex. d.c. §
units.tr: Restraining laughter, too, sometimes shows seemliness and honesty. Clement of Alexandria, loc. cit.

units.la: Neq; enim, inquit, apud quoslibet ridendum est, neq; omni in loco: sed neq; omnibus, neque propter omnia. Maxime enim adolescentulis & mulieribus risus est proclivis ad calumniam, & praesentibus odiosus. Unde Seneca: Miscebis interdum feriis locos, sed temperatos sine detrimento dignitatis & verecundiae. vid. Macrob. lib.2.c.1. & seqq. & libr.7.c.3. Saturn. Probatur risus, quando coniunctus est 1. cum timore Dei Eccles.c.2.2. Luc.c.6.25. 11. cum sympathia. Amos c.6.6. 111. cum moderatione. 2.Timoth.c.3.4. & sine peccatis est. Hebr.c.11.25. De risu Christi non legitur de lachrymis Luc.c.19.41. Ioh.c.11.35. Heb. cap.5.7. Per risum multum debes cognoscere stultum: locis vel dicteriis uti convenit & alium amabili modo ludere, si error illius non sit coniunctus ignominia, neque damnum ei sit coniunctum, ut iocationes ab iniuriis discernantur. Vide Psal. 35.14. & seqq. Unde Seneca: Sales tui sint sine dente, loci sine vilitate, risus sine cachinno, vox sine clamore, incessus, sine tumultu.
units.tr: For, he says, one should not laugh in front of just anyone, nor in every place, nor at everyone, nor at everything. Laughter is especially prone to slander in young men and women, and is offensive to those present. Hence Seneca: You will sometimes mix festive occasions into your days, but keep them moderate, without loss of dignity and modesty. See Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.1ff and 7.3. Laughter is approved when it is joined (1) with the fear of God, Eccles. 2.2; Luke 6.25; (2) with sympathy, Amos 6.6; (3) with moderation, 2 Tim. 3.4, and is free from sin, Heb. 11.25. Of Christ's laughter nothing is read, but of his tears, Luke 19.41; John 11.35; Heb. 5.7. Through much laughter you must recognise a fool. It is fitting to use pleasantries and witticisms, and to play with another in an agreeable way, provided his error is not joined with disgrace or with loss to him, so that jokes are distinguished from injuries. See Ps. 35.14ff. Hence Seneca: Let your witticisms be without a tooth, your places without vileness, your laughter without guffaws, your voice without shouting, your gait without tumult.

units.la: Loci igitur mordentes, aculeati & dentati sermones omnino sunt fugiendi. Sub his enim iocis iniuriae latent, Prou.c.17.5. & 4. Psal.35.16. & seqq. Eccles.cap.21. 22. 28. Psalm.22 7.8. vide latius Ioh. Guil. Stuck. libr.3.c.17. conv.antiq. Macrob.d.c. 3. Plutar.lib.1. Problem.1.quid sint [Greek], & tales φιλεχωμένοις dicuntur, caulandi cupidi: Macrob.lib 7. Saturn.c 3.
units.tr: Therefore biting jests, pointed and toothed speeches, must altogether be avoided, for injuries lie hidden beneath such jokes. Prov. 17.5; Prov. 4; Ps. 35.16ff.; Ecclus. 21.22, 28; Ps. 22.7–8. See more fully Joh. Guil. Stuckius, Antiquitates convivales 3.17; Macrobius, loc. cit. 3; Plutarch, Problems 1, on what such people are; those who delight in mockery are called [φιλεχωμένοις], lovers of mockery. Macrobius, Saturnalia 7.3.

units.la: loci & risus Sardonici fugiendi, qualis fuisse dicitur Caligulae risus, plane crudelis & immanis, de quo vide apud Sueton.in Caligula.
units.tr: Sardonic jests and laughter must be avoided, such as Caligula's laughter is said to have been, plainly cruel and monstrous. See Suetonius, Caligula.

units.la: Qui honestis nominibus in conuiciando v-tuntur, vel res bonas periocum nominibus pro-brofis afficiunt, laudant magis quàm vituperat’ Elegans quoq; dicterium fit, quando vituperatione gratiarum actio adiicitur, ita vt non offendant, neq; laedant eos qui laudantur. Vt quan-do qui ex paupere factus diues à rege, dicit per insidias sibi otium & somnum esse ereptum. Plutarch. Symposiacon lib. 2. quaest. 1. vide Macrob. lib. 2. Saturn. cap. 2. & seqq. & lib. 7. c. 5.
units.tr: Those who use honourable names when reviling, or who attach disreputable names to good things, praise rather than blame. An elegant jest also arises when thanksgiving is added to blame, so that it neither offends nor harms those who are praised: as when a man who has risen from poverty to wealth through a king's favour says that his leisure and sleep were snatched from him by treachery. Plutarch, Symposiacs 2, question 1; see Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.2ff. and 7.5.

units.la: Qui in eludendis & perferendis falsis & iocis dextri sunt, eleganterque possunt falsè dicta excipere, & lepide eadem retorquere, gratiosi sunt. vide exempla in Colloquiis Erasmi, & apud Macrob. d. lib. 2. c. 2. & seqq.
units.tr: Those who are skilful at parrying and bearing false and jesting words, and who can elegantly take up what is falsely said and neatly turn it back, are gracious. See examples in the Colloquies of Erasmus, and in Macrobius, loc. cit. 2.2ff.

units.la: Loci captati ex syllabarum permutatione, mordentes sepe sunt, vt pro Decretum, Dreccetum, pro Virgilius, Vormilius, pro medicus, mendicus, mendicus, pro Polycarpus, Polycopros: Sic & quidam ex syllabarum quarundam ellipsi iocimordentes, vt pro Cafimirus irus, pro Marcus, arcus, pro vinosus, osus, pro sacerdotium, otium, pro Augustus, vstus, pro Musculus, culus.
units.tr: Jests based on altering syllables are often biting: for example, Decretum turned into a mangled form, Virgilius into Vormilius, medicus into mendicus, Polycarpus into Polycopros. So too some jests bite by eliding certain syllables: Casimirus into "irus", Marcus into "arcus", vinosus into "osus", sacerdotium into "otium", Augustus into "ustus", Musculus into "culus".

units.la: Nemo etiam vt aliis placeat, seipsum vilem, abiectum ve facere debet, aut insulsum & scurrilem se fingere, neq; personam ad peccandum sui-cipere. Eccles. cap. 42. 1. vel damno animae suae. Eccles. cap. 4. 26. Nam stultus seipsum conturbat labiis suis. Proverb. cap. 10. 8. 10. Fili mansuetudine compara gloriam animae tuae: & da honorem ei, prout digna est. nam eum qui peccat in animam suam, quis ipsum pronuntiabit? Et eum qui vitam suam afficit ignominia, quis ornet gloria? Eccles. cap. 10. 31. 32. Fatuum igitur ne agito labiis tuis. Prouerb.c.24.28. Clem.Alex.lib.1.c.5.de Pædag.
units.tr: Nor should anyone, in order to please others, make himself cheap or abject, or feign himself foolish and buffoonish, or assume a role that leads to sin, Eccles. cap. 42. 1. or to the loss of his soul. Eccles. cap. 4. 26. For a fool troubles himself with his own lips. Proverbs cap. 10. 8. 10. My son, win glory for your soul by gentleness, and give it honour as it deserves; for who will declare him who sins against his own soul? And who will adorn him who brings shame upon his own life with glory? Eccles. cap. 10. 31. 32. Therefore do not wag your lips at a fool. Proverbs cap. 24. 28. Clement of Alexandria, book 1, chapter 5, On the Instruction of Children.

units.la: Sequitur de irrisione.Ludibrio habeti & ri-deri nemo facilè debet,Eccles.c.7.10. Fiunt enim iniurię ex ira &alia cupiditate.Ecclesia.c.8.5.Psal. 22.7.8.Matth.c.27.29:Psalm.40.16.& Psalm.41. 6.&70.4.5. Nam quoslibet verbis exagitare & deridere irrisorum est & iurgia excitat. Prouerb c.26. 10.vide Genes.c.21.9. Clem.Alex.d.lib.1.c.7. De irrisione, ironia & subsannatione Eliae in Baalitas extat 1.Reg.c.18.17.quae non ex odio vel ultione proficisce-batur, sicut & Esa. c.44.festiua idoli irrisio,& c.46.
units.tr: Next comes mockery. No one should readily be treated with contempt or be laughed at. Eccles. cap. 7. 10. For injuries arise from anger and other passions. Ecclus. cap. 8. 5. Ps. 22. 7. 8. Matt. cap. 27. 29. Ps. 40. 16, and Ps. 41. 6 and 70. 4. 5. For to harass or deride anyone with words is the mark of a mocker, and it stirs up quarrels. Proverbs cap. 26. 10. See Genesis cap. 21. 9. Clement of Alexandria, book 1, chapter 7. The mocking, ironic and scornful taunting of Elijah against the prophets of Baal is found in 1 Kings cap. 18. 17, which did not proceed from hatred or a desire for revenge; so too the festive mockery of idols in Isaiah cap. 44 and cap. 46.

units.la: Qui ludibrio alium habet, is ex despicientia, contemptu,defectu vel ignominia illius sibi volu-ptatem quaerit & crabrones irritat, & futurus est peccator. Prou.c.14.21.& adiram provocat eum quę deridet, subsannat & illudit. maxime vero quando non ultionis, neq; alicuius utilitatis gratia ludit, aut eas res contemnit, in quibus alius magnam operam & studium posuit, & in quib. excellere se putat. Spernente vero proximum suum demente, vir prudentissimus, sordum agit.Prou. c.11.12.13. Ideo Seneca alibi, Nullius imprudentiam despicias,Iohann.c.9.34. Dixerunt ei, tu in peccatis natus es totus, & tu doces nos? & eiecerunt eum foras.
units.tr: Whoever mocks another seeks pleasure from his contempt, scorn, weakness or disgrace, stirs up hornets, and will become a sinner. Prov. cap. 14. 21. And he provokes to anger the one whom he derides, scorns and mocks, most of all when he does not jest for the sake of revenge or any advantage, or when he despises those things in which another has put great effort and zeal, and in which he thinks himself superior. But when a foolish man despises his neighbour, a very prudent man keeps silent. Prov. cap. 11. 12. 13. Therefore Seneca elsewhere says: Do not despise anyone's lack of wisdom. John cap. 9. 34. They answered him, "You were born wholly in sins, and do you teach us?" And they cast him out.

units.la: Qui ludit alium,ex errore admisso, eiusdem non tam voluptatem, quam recreationem percipit,licet is qui luditur,saepe pro probro habeat & indignetur,qui alias eauillatores faceti & iucundi dicuntur.Eccles.c.19.
units.tr: One who mocks another for a mistake he has made does not so much take pleasure in it as in amusement, although the one who is mocked often regards it as an insult and is indignant; yet those who are witty jesters are called pleasant and agreeable. Eccles. cap. 19.

units.la: Communicatio eorum quae obiiciuntur dicteria,ficit tolerabiliora, ut cum in paupertate pauper, in ignobilitatem ignobilis; in amatore amaamatoraliquid iacit. Scommata etiam facile negligit is, qui compertum habet notorium esse sibi iniuriam fieri. vid. Macrob. lib. 7. c. 3. Saturnal.
units.tr: Sharing the things that are thrown at us as insults makes them more bearable: as a poor man with the poor, an ignoble man with the ignoble, a lover with a lover, one throws something back. A person who knows that an injury done to him is publicly known also easily disregards gibes. See Macrobius, book 7, chapter 3, Saturnalia.

units.la: Homines derisores inflammant vrbem, at sapientes auertunt iram. Prouerb. c. 29. 8. Et quousque derisores derisionem sibi desiderabunt? Prou. c. 1. 22. Deus enim derisores deridet. Prouerb. c. 3. 34. & punit. Ecc. c. 7. 10. & si sapias, sapies tibi: sin derisor eris, solus reportabis. Prou. c. 9. 12. Eccles. c. 6. 2. Testis nequam deridet ius, sed parata sunt in istos derisores iudicia & contusiones tergo stolidorum, Prou. c. 19. 28. 29.
units.tr: Scoffers inflame a city, but the wise turn away wrath. Prov. cap. 29. 8. And how long will scoffers desire their mockery? Prov. cap. 1. 22. For God mocks the scoffers. Prov. cap. 3. 34. and punishes them. Eccles. cap. 7. 10. And if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself; but if you are a scoffer, you alone will bear it. Prov. cap. 9. 12. Eccles. cap. 6. 2. A worthless witness mocks justice, but judgments and blows are prepared for these scoffers, and for the backs of fools. Prov. cap. 19. 28. 29.

units.la: Neque vitia verbis, vel gestu aut imitatione aliì exprobare, vel cum risu & exultatione de iis nobis gratulari, & libenter alios rubore suffundere debemus. Eccles. c. 8. 6. 7. 8. vid. 1. Cor. cap. 13. 4. 4. 5. 6. 7. Vel quicquam loquendum quod alteri pudorem, vel pudoris aut existimationis laesa imaginationem excitare possit. quod facilius fieri potest apud eos, quos alius admiratur & observat; aut apud quos in admiratione esse cupit, aut apud eos, cum quibus de honore contendit.
units.tr: We ought not to reproach others for their vices, by word, gesture or imitation, nor to rejoice over them with laughter and exultation, and we ought not gladly to bring others to blush. Eccles. cap. 8. 6. 7. 8. See 1 Cor. cap. 13. 4. 5. 6. 7. Nor should we say anything that could arouse shame in another, or a sense of having been hurt in his modesty or reputation. This can more easily happen before those whom the other admires and respects, or before those in whose esteem he wishes to stand, or before those with whom he contends for honour.

units.la: Sermo profectus ex fatuitate excusandus, aut cooperiendus, vel dissimulandus, quatenus bona fide & conscientia fieri potest. Prouerb. cap. 19. 8. 1. Samuel. c. 3. 38. c. 16. 10. Nam qui tegit defectionem, quaerit dilectionem, Prouerb. c. 17. 9. 10. c. 10. 12. vid. 1. Corinth. cap. 13. 4. 5. 6. Charitas non cogitat malum, 7. Omnia credit, omnia sperat. Aut ex συμπα- θείᾳ corrigendus proximus, Leuit. c. 19. 7.
units.tr: Speech that proceeds from foolishness should be excused, or covered over, or overlooked, so far as this can be done in good faith and with a clear conscience. Prov. cap. 19. 8. 1 Sam. cap. 3. 38. cap. 16. 10. For he who covers a fault seeks love. Prov. cap. 17. 9. 10. cap. 10. 12. See 1 Cor. cap. 13. 4. 5. 6. Love thinks no evil; 7. it believes all things, hopes all things. Or else the neighbour should be corrected out of sympathy [συμπαθείᾳ]. Lev. cap. 19. 17.

units.la: Sequitur de exprobratione, quae civilis quadoq; ex monentis officio ob ingratitudinem,
units.tr: Next comes reproach, which is sometimes civil, arising from the duty of admonition, on account of ingratitude

units.la: D vel maleficium. Quod si vero quis in narratione erratum, vel falsum aspersit, vel beneficium aliquod præstitit, non verbis hoc illi exprobrandum, quod acrimoniam & acerbitatem naturæ rusticæ & asperæ indicat, quæ illos exprobrantes in mutua sermonum & officiorum communicatione ita odiosos reddit, ut quilibet eos aucrsetur. Eccles.c.8.6.7. cum contra, dilectionem quærere dicatur, qui tegit defectionem; qui vero rem renouat, disiungit ducem. Prou.c.17.9.vid.1.Cor.c.13.4.& seqq.2. Pet.c.1.6.7. & re-le Cato:
units.tr: or wrongdoing. But if anyone has made a mistake in his account, or spoken something false, or has done some kindness, this should not be thrown in his face with words, since that shows a harshness and bitterness of rustic and rough nature, which makes those who reproach others so hateful in the mutual exchange of talk and service that everyone shuns them. Eccles. cap. 8. 6. 7. Whereas it is said that one who covers a fault seeks love, but one who repeats the matter separates close friends. Prov. cap. 17. 9. See 1 Cor. cap. 13. 4. and following; 2 Pet. cap. 1. 6. 7. And see Cato:

units.la: Alterius dictum aut factum ne carpseris unquam:
units.tr: Never find fault with another's word or deed.

units.la: Exemplo similis ne te derideat alter.
units.tr: Lest, made like the example, another mock you.

units.la: Beneficia præstita nemini exprobranda. Ecclesiastic.c.18.19.c.20.14. Postquam dederis, ne exprobrato c.41.28. neque prædicanda apud alios, sed potius celanda. Idenim cum fit, intelligitur eius solummodo gratia factum esse, nullamque ob aliam causam. Nam præclaras sæpe gratias corrumpit, quæ ex ingenii vanitate nascitur, beneficiorum commemoratio. Cicero de amicit. Officia meminisse debet is in quo collata sunt, non commemorare qui contulit. Senec.lib.2. De benefic.c.11. Qui dedit beneficium, taceat; narret qui accepit, & li.1.c.2. Beneficia in vulgus non effunden-da. Nam qui beneficia se dedisse dicit, petit, vt Mimus aut: Exprobrationis maligna exemplavid.1.Sam. c.1.6.14. Matth.c.27.42.Iob.c.9.34. 1.Sam.c.25. 10 11.12. Isocrates ad Demonic. Cave cuiquam calamitatem exprobres. Considerans (vt Paulus ait) teipsum ne & tu tenteris.
units.tr: Benefits once conferred must never be thrown in someone's face. Ecclus. cap. 18. 19. cap. 20. 14. After you have given, do not reproach. Ecclus. cap. 41. 28. Nor should they be proclaimed to others, but rather concealed. For when this happens, it is understood that the thing was done only for his sake and for no other reason. For the recounting of benefits often corrupts even splendid thanks, and it arises from vanity of mind. Cicero, On Friendship. The one to whom favours were given ought to remember them; the one who conferred them ought not to mention them. Seneca, book 2, On Benefits, chapter 11. Let him who gave a benefit be silent; let him who received it speak. And book 1, chapter 2: Benefits must not be poured out for the crowd. For he who says he has conferred benefits seeks payment, like an actor. Malicious reproach: see 1 Sam. cap. 1. 6. 14. Matt. cap. 27. 42. Job cap. 9. 34. 1 Sam. cap. 25. 10. 11. 12. Isocrates, To Demonicus: Beware of reproaching anyone with his misfortune. Considering yourself (as Paul says), lest you too be tempted.

units.la: Neq; exprobrandæ veteres iniuriæ, neq; crimina commissa recolenda sunt, sed placabilem & mansuetum esse convenit. Qualis enim quis erga alium esse apparet, talis quoq; in nos futurus esse existimatur.
units.tr: Neither old injuries should be thrown in people's faces, nor committed offences recalled; rather, it is fitting to be forgiving and gentle. For as someone appears towards another, so he is thought likely to be towards us as well.

units.la: Inprimis vero indecorum, exprobrare alteri, qui & tibi par reponere potest. Vt, si gibboso cuidam oculorum imbecillitatem exprobranti respondeatur, humanum virium & infortunium mihi exprobras, cum ipse Nemesin in dorso gestes. vide Plutarch. De capiend. ex inimic. utilit. ubi exemplis hoc ipsum illustrat. In primis illo, quod Dominus Crasso obiecit, dicens, Nonne tu ob mortem murenæ, quam in vivario tuo alebatur, plorasti? Cui Crassus: nonne tu absque ullis lacrimis tres tuas uxores extulisti? Hinc illud, Qui dicit quod vult, etiam audiet, quod non vult. Qui quæ vult, dicit, quæ non vult, audiet ipse.
units.tr: Above all, it is unseemly to reproach someone who can answer you back in kind. For example, if someone reproaches a hunchback for his weak eyes, he may be answered: "You reproach me with human weakness and misfortune, when you yourself carry Nemesis on your back." See Plutarch, On Profiting from One's Enemies, where he illustrates this very point with examples. Especially that one, which the lord Crassus received: "Did you not weep over the death of the lamprey that was kept in your fishpond?" To which Crassus replied: "Did you not bury your three wives without any tears?" Hence the saying: "He who says what he wishes will also hear what he does not wish. He who says what he wishes, will himself hear what he does not wish."

units.la: Sequitur de censura. Iudicare quidem de aliorum factis decorum & civile, si id iuste fiat, ex necessitate publici officii, at privati illi censores importuni ius rigidæ censuræ in alios sibi vsurpantes gravius iudicium accipiunt. Iacob. d. c. 3. 1. c. 4. 11. Matth. c. 7. 1. 2. & seqq. 1. Cor. cap. 4. 3. Eccles. c. 11. 7. Job. c. 1. 9. 11. 1. Sam. c. 22. 9. Matth. cap. 11. 19. Tales, inquam, sunt qui de aliis exacte iudicandi quanti precii & æstimationis sint sibi censoriam sumunt potestatem. vid. exemplum. Actor. c. 28. 4. 1. Sam. c. 17. 28. Actor. c. 2. 13. 14. 15. 1. Sam. c. 1. 13. vid. Petr. Martyr. 1. Cor. c. 4. 5.
units.tr: Next comes censure. To judge the deeds of others is indeed fitting and proper for a citizen, if it is done justly, from the necessity of public office; but those private censors who presume to claim for themselves the right of harsh censure over others will receive a heavier judgment. James, cap. 3. 1. cap. 4. 11. Matt. cap. 7. 1. 2. and following. 1 Cor. cap. 4. 3. Eccles. cap. 11. 7. Job cap. 1. 9. 11. 1 Sam. cap. 22. 9. Matt. cap. 11. 19. Such people, I say, are those who take upon themselves the censor's power to judge exactly of others, how much value and worth they have. See the example, Acts cap. 28. 4. 1 Sam. cap. 17. 28. Acts cap. 2. 13. 14. 15. 1 Sam. cap. 1. 13. See Peter Martyr on 1 Cor. cap. 4. 5.

units.la: Censura
units.tr: Censure

units.la: Addo, quod qui promptus & cupidus est aliorum defectus vel errata corrigere, aut reprehendere (quod ludi magistris & parentibus relinquendum, & magistratui, Matth.c.12.27. 41.42.) arrogantiam sapientiæ & dominationis suæ demonstrat, præsertim illi qui lolium ex alienis agris euellere volunt, & proprios sentibus & & vrticis totos occupari sinunt. cMatth.d.c.7. Rom.c.2.1.2.3.4.1. Cor.c. 4.3.4.5.6. Iacob. c.3.1.2.
units.tr: I add that whoever is quick and eager to correct or rebuke the faults or errors of others (a task to be left to schoolmasters and parents, and to the magistrate, Matt. cap. 12. 27. 41. 42.) shows the arrogance of his own wisdom and dominance, especially those who want to pull out the darnel from other people's fields while allowing their own fields to be wholly overrun with brambles and nettles. See Matt. cap. 7. Rom. cap. 2. 1. 2. 3. 4. 1 Cor. cap. 4. 3. 4. 5. 6. James cap. 3. 1. 2.

units.la: Vnde fit vt qui adsunt, de talibus censoribus peius existiment. Ergo dum alienam existimationem minuere volunt, in damnum & periculum propria incidunt. Contra in vita communi & quotidiana consuetudine suaues & iucundi sunt faciles, neq; proclives ad redarguendum peccata & errores, non contentiosi aut litigiosi. Omnes enim eiusmodi sunt pugnaces. Ideoq; videntur velle contraria: quod cum amicitia vnice pugnat. Ad omnia igitur verba ne adhibeto animum tuum, sed dissimula lege charitatis & prudentiæ. Ecclesiast.7.21. arg. Galat.c.6.1.1. Sam. c.10.27. c.11.13. Iacob. c.3.1. & Coloss.c.3.13. Tolerantes alii alios & condonantes vobis mutuo. Ephes.c.4.32. Estote alii in alios benigni, misericordes, condonantes vobis mutuo offensas, & 1.Cor.c.13.4. & seqq. & 1.Petr.c.4.8. Ecclesiast.c.19.13. Argue amicum ne quando fecerit: Et, si fecerit, ne quando pergat, 14. Argue proximum, ne quando dixerit, & si dixerit, vt non repetat, 15. Argue amicum, nam sæpe existit vana calumnia, & ne cuius sermoni credito animus tuus. Nam qui facile credit, facile decipitur & leuis esse iudicatur.Conuenit itaq; semper in mitiorem partem in dubio iudicare, secundum legem caritatis.
units.tr: Hence it happens that those who are present think worse of such censors. So while they want to diminish another's reputation, they bring harm and danger on themselves. On the other hand, in common life and daily company, people should be pleasant and agreeable, easygoing, not quick to rebuke sins and errors, not quarrelsome or litigious. For all such people are combative, and so they seem to want the opposite, which fights wholly against friendship. Therefore do not give your mind to every word, but overlook things, in accordance with the law of charity and prudence. Eccles. 7:21; Gal. 6:1; 1 Sam. 10:27; 11:13; Jas. 3:1; Col. 3:13: "Bearing with one another and forgiving one another." Eph. 4:32: "Be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another your offences," and 1 Cor. 13:4ff.; 1 Pet. 4:8; Eccles. 19:13: "Rebuke a friend before you act against him, and if he has acted, do not let him go on; 14: rebuke a neighbour before he has spoken, and if he has spoken, so that he does not repeat it; 15: rebuke a friend, for often a vain calumny arises; and do not let your mind believe every word. For he who believes easily is easily deceived and is judged to be foolish." It is therefore fitting always to judge in doubtful matters in the milder sense, according to the law of charity.

units.la: Sunt autem 4. potissimum, de quibus omnino non iudicare concessum est. Primum, de arcanis diuinæ prouidentiæ & prædestinationis & Dei consiliis, Rom.c.9. Secundum est, sacra Scriptura, ptura,quam nō debemus ideo legere, vt ibi aliquid condemnemus, aut ad nostrum sensum & affectum torqueamus. Tertium est, de hominibus extra ecclesiam constitutis, quos nō statuemus deploratæ salutis esse. Neq; deniq; de irregularibus Dei factis iudicandum, sed tacendū, Iob.cap.39.37. Leuit.c.10.ǂ.actl.c.11.18. Psal.41.1.
units.tr: There are, however, four matters above all about which it is not permitted to judge at all. The first concerns the hidden things of divine providence and predestination and the counsels of God: Rom. 9. The second is Holy Scripture, which we ought not to read in order to condemn something in it, or to twist it to our own sense and feeling. The third concerns people who are outside the Church; we should not declare that their salvation is hopeless. Nor, finally, should we pass judgment on the irregular works of God, but keep silent. Job 39:37; Lev. 10; Acts 11:18; Ps. 41:1.

units.la: Sunt etiam quædam quæ tam bono, quam malo animo fieri possunt, hæc non oportet in malam partem accipere in dubio. Sunt alia quæ bono animo fieri non possunt; vt adulteria, homicidia: in his de autore non male iudicandum, qui mutari non possit, & bonus fieri.
units.tr: There are also some things which can be done with a good intention as well as a bad one; in doubtful cases one ought not to take these in the worse sense. There are other things which cannot be done with a good intention, such as adultery and murder; in these cases one should not judge badly of the author, who can be changed and made good.

units.la: Qui controuersias sua sententia finire & vnicuique legem præscribere vult, odiosus est. Eccles.c.20.6. & cerebrosus seu ἀνθρωπος, qui nihil nona præse fastidit, vt supra ex Prou.c.18.1.2.3. cap.28.2 s. 26. Eccl.c.6.2.
units.tr: He who wants to end disputes by his own opinion and prescribe the law to everyone is hateful; and so is the hot-headed person [ἄνθρωπος] who despises every counsel, as above from Prov. 18:1–3; 28:2, 26; Eccles. 6:2; Eccles. 20:6.

units.la: Qui in aliorum præsentia expostulationibus alios obiurgant, vel castigant, insolescentes & tyranni videntur: sic etiam qui proprios ministros conuitiis & reprehensionibus aliis præsentibus exagitant, argumentum superbiæ & dominationis de se præbent. Seneca De moribus: Qui in seruos irascitur & crudelis est, satis ostendit potestatem aduersus alienos sibi deesse.
units.tr: Those who rebuke others with reproaches in the presence of other people, or chastise them, seem arrogant and tyrannical; so too those who harass their own ministers with insults and reproaches in the presence of others give evidence of pride and domineering in themselves. Seneca, On Morals: He who is angry with his slaves and is cruel shows well enough that he lacks power over those who belong to others.

units.la: Sequitur de contentione: quæ pro veritate licita & ciuilis est, sed tamen non temere, imprudenter & quocunq; in loco & tempore fieri debet. Nam qui hasce circumstantias non obseruat merito contentiosus & rixosus, in disputationes & altercationes temerarias pronus, qui quocunque inloco, quoscunq; inter homines, de rebus etiam difficilimis, aut non necessariis, argutissime disputare contendit, quinq; omne suum studium ponit in carpendis & reprehendendis aliis, & nulla de causa quemlibet adoriuntur. De contentiosis talibus, vide 1. Timoth. cap.6.4. Insaniens circa quaestiones ac verborum pugnas; ex quibus nascitur invidia, lis, maledicentia, suspiciones malae, verse.20. Auersare illos profanos de rebus inanibus clamores & oppositiones falso nominata scientia, & c.5.13. Nam sermones stolidi, eunt contentiones & os eius contentiones aducat & contritionem sibi ipsi, Proverb. c.28.6.7. Philip. cap. 2.3. Nihil gerentes per contentionem, aut per inanem gloriam, sed ex modestia alius alium se praestantiorem existimans. ad Tit. c.3.9. Stultas quaestiones, genealogias, contentiones & pugnas legales cohibe. Sunt enim inutiles & vana. 1. Timoth. c.1.7. & seqq. c.4.4. 2. Timoth. c.2.11. & Proverb. cap.13.10. Mera superbia animo ferociente & inconsulto vir edit iurgium, at consultus cauet sibi ab accendendis, inflammandis & fouendis iurgiis. Eccles. c.28.20. & seqq. & Psalm.12.4. Exscindet Iehoua linguam grandiloquentem.5. Eos qui dicunt lingua nostra magnificabimus, labia nostra penes nos sunt, quis esset dominus nobis? Ut deficientibus lignis extinguitur ignis, ita cum non est susurro, silet contentio. Proverb. c.26.20. & diligit defectionem qui diligit iurgia. Proverb. c.17.14. 19. nam susurro contentiones excitat & odiosus est, Eccles. c.20.20. c.21.31. cap.28.10.13.15.16. Proverb. c.18.8. c.26.20. & seqq. quibus adde Galat. c.5.19.20. Ephes. c.4.31.
units.tr: Next comes the matter of contention, which is lawful and civil in defence of the truth, but nevertheless must not be undertaken rashly, imprudently, or in any place and at any time. For whoever does not observe these circumstances is rightly called contentious and quarrelsome, prone to rash disputes and wrangling, one who in any place and among any people strives to dispute most subtly even about very difficult or unnecessary matters, and who puts all his effort into carping at and censuring others, and attacks anyone for no reason. On such contentious persons see 1 Tim. 6:4: "Raving about questions and disputes over words, from which come envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions," v. 20: "Avoid those profane babblings and oppositions of falsely named knowledge," and 5:13: "For foolish talk brings quarrels, and his mouth brings contentions and destruction to himself," Prov. 28:6–7; Phil. 2:3: "Doing nothing through contention or vainglory, but in humility each regarding the other as better than himself"; Titus 3:9: "Avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions and legal quarrels, for they are unprofitable and vain"; 1 Tim. 1:7ff.; 4:4; 2 Tim. 2:11; Prov. 13:10: "Pure pride in a fierce and unadvised mind produces a quarrel, but the wise man takes care not to kindle, inflame or foster quarrels"; Eccles. 28:20ff.; Ps. 12:4: "May the LORD cut off the tongue that speaks great things, those who say, 'With our tongue we shall prevail, our lips are our own; who is lord over us?'" As wood fails and the fire goes out, so where there is no whisperer, strife is silent; Prov. 26:20; "He who loves transgression loves strife," Prov. 17:14, 19; for a whisperer stirs up contentions and is hateful, Eccles. 20:20; 21:31; 28:10, 13, 15, 16; Prov. 18:8; 26:20ff. To these add Gal. 5:19–20; Eph. 4:31.

units.la: Susurro est qui apud eos quorum perniciem machinatur sese suis verbis abiicit, & contendit dit ut abiectissimus videatur ad regendas fraudes suas & fidem conciliandam,Prouerb. c. 18. 8. 9. vbi Iunius. Psalm. 10. 10. & 35. 16. & seqq. Eccles. c. 5. 16. c. 27. 25. c. 28. 14. & seqq. Nam proprium est viri peruersitatibus dediti, ut immittat contentiones, & susurro & emissarius explorator dissidia excitat. Prouerb. c. 16. 28. Verba enim susurronis similia sunt verbis eorum, qui sape contusi sunt, tamen ea descendunt in penetralia ventris. Prou. c. 26. 22. Prehendit autem aures canis quitransiens furentem agit in lite non sua. Prouerb. c. 26. 17. Ideoque litibus & rixis imprimis supersedendum. Prouerb. c. 20. 3. c. 26. 20. 21. 22. potissimum vero cum potentiore rixoso ve aduersario. Eccles. cap. 8. 1. 2. 5. cap. 13. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. c. 9. 22. ut peccatorum occasio praecidatur. Prou. c. 25. 8. 9. & seqq. Ecclesiast. cap. 28. 10. 11.
units.tr: A whisperer is one who casts himself down before those whose destruction he plots, with his words, and strives to appear most humble, in order to conceal his deceits and win trust; Prov. 18:8–9, where see Junius; Ps. 10:10; 35:16ff.; Eccles. 5:16; 27:25; 28:14ff. For it is characteristic of a man given to perversities that he stirs up contentions, and the whisperer and the spy sow discord. Prov. 16:28. For the words of a whisperer are like the words of those who have been struck, yet they go down into the inner parts of the belly; Prov. 26:22. But he who passes by and takes hold of a dog's ears stirs up a fury in a quarrel not his own. Prov. 26:17. Therefore one must above all refrain from quarrels and brawls, especially with a more powerful or quarrelsome opponent, Prov. 20:3; 26:20–22; Eccles. 8:1–2, 5; 13:1–3ff.; 9:22, so that the occasion of sin may be cut off; Prov. 25:8–9ff.; Eccles. 28:10–11.

units.la: De re vero quae non attinet te, ne litiges vel contendas. Ecclesiastic. cap. 11. verf. 9. cap. 27. verf. 28.
units.tr: Do not quarrel or contend about a matter which does not concern you. Eccles. 11:9; 27:28.

units.la: Quibus de rebus libere te proloqui pudet, visq; cum amicis aliquibus de eis communicare, verbis veluti de alieno negotio vtere: Sicenim & illorum sententiam nosces, teq; ipsum haudquaquam manifestum reddes.
units.tr: In matters about which you are ashamed to speak freely, and if you want to share them with some friends, use words as if the matter belonged to someone else. For in this way you will also learn their opinion, and you will by no means reveal yourself.

units.la: CAP. IV. Cum quibus personis & quibus verbis sermo habendus.
units.tr: CAP. IV. With what persons, and in what words, conversation is to be held.

units.la: HActenus de rebus, de quibus decore sermo instituitur, vel silentio temperatur. Sequitur ad quas personas & quibus verbis sermo habendus.
units.tr: So far concerning the subjects on which discourse may fittingly be undertaken, or is better restrained by silence. Next comes the question with what persons, and in what words, conversation is to be held.

units.la: Cum illis autem loquendum, quibus ex officio teneris, vel quibus cum conuersari necessitas, vel vtilitas tua, vel alterius te vrget.
units.tr: One must speak with those to whom you are bound by duty, or with whom association is required, or whom your own advantage or that of another urges you to deal with.

units.la: Alloquium autem hoc quod cum aliis instituitur, est vel Affabilitas, vel commercium & collatio humana, benigna & suauis.
units.tr: This address with others takes the form either of affability, or of human intercourse and conversation, kindly and pleasant.

units.la: Affabilitate & comitate erga quosuis suaues & humani esse debemus, aliis in congressu, vel digressione verbis benignis & humanis bene precantes & bene dicentes, felicia & fausta precantes in accessu & discessu. Sienim Dei iussu pro nobis inuicem precari debemus, & cum gaudentibus gaudere & cum flentibus flere, Rom. cap. 12. 15. certe etiam nos mutuo salutare conuenit, sicuti Christus, Apostoli & sanƈti viri fecerunt. Siquidem fausta & felix precatio non postremum charitatis erga proximū officium. Ideo August. serm. 42. De sanƈtis ait, si quis obuium hominem sibi non salutarit, aut salutanti non reddiderit salutem, à viatore non habebitur homo, sed truncus, lapis aut Mercurius, qui stans in via monstrat iter & nihil loquitur. & Christus Matth. c. 5. 44. Si tantum salutaueritis eos qui salutant vos, quam mercedem habebitis? nonne publicani hoc faciunt? Isocrates ad Demonic. Comitatis est, ait, benigne obuios appellare: affabilitatis familiariter cum ipsis verba communicare. Benignum te cunctis praebeas, optimis autem vtaris. Sic & illis inimicus non eris & istis amicus sies. & Cicer. De legibus Difficile dictu est, aut, tantopere concilliet animos hominum comitas affabilitasq; sermonis, quia curatur inuidia & suspicio, atque ira animis hominum eximitur.
units.tr: With affability and courtesy we ought to be pleasant and humane toward everyone, greeting others when we meet and when we part with kind and gracious words, wishing them well and blessing them, and invoking good and prosperous things at arrival and departure. For by God's command we ought to pray for one another, and to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15). Surely it is also fitting that we greet one another, as Christ, the apostles and holy men did. For a joyful and fortunate greeting is no small part of the duty of love toward a neighbour. So Augustine says in Sermon 42 On the Saints: if someone does not greet a man he meets, or does not return the greeting of one who greets him, he will not be regarded by the traveller as a man, but as a stump, a stone or a Mercury, which stands on the road and points the way but says nothing. And Christ, Matt. 5:44: If you greet only those who greet you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? Isocrates, To Demonicus: It is a mark of courtesy, he says, to address those we meet kindly; of affability, to share words with them in a familiar way. Show yourself kind to all, but make use of the best. Thus you will not be an enemy to those, nor a friend to these. And Cicero, On the Laws: It is hard to say how greatly courtesy and affability of speech win men's minds, since envy and suspicion are cured and anger is taken out of men's hearts.

units.la: Hæc humana, benigna & suauis affabilitas præcipitur erga omnes, adeò vt etiam inimicos nostros salutare iubeamur, Matt.c.5. nisi ob festinationem vel alia grauiora impedimenta nō possimus. Luc.c.10.2.Reg.c.4.29.vbi Pet. Mart. neq; aue dicendum excommunicatis, vt Iob.ait. De hac εὐλογίᾳ & affabilitate passim quoq; alibi præcipitur, vti 2.Tim.c.3.2. omnem exhibentes lenitatem erga quosuis homines, 1.Cor.c.13.4.5.6. Caritas patiens est, comis est, i.e. facilis ad congressum & collocutionem. Rom.c.16.3.21.22.&seqq.1.Cor.c.1. Genef.cap. 29.6.c.37.14.c.41.16.
units.tr: This human, kindly and pleasant affability is enjoined toward all, so much so that we are commanded to greet even our enemies (Matt. 5), unless haste or other more serious hindrances prevent us (Luke 10; 2 Kings 4:29, where Peter Martyr). Nor should we say 'hail' to the excommunicate, as Job says. This blessing [εὐλογίᾳ] and affability is enjoined everywhere else too: 2 Tim. 3:2, showing all gentleness toward all men; 1 Cor. 13:4-6, love is patient, it is courteous, that is, easy to approach and to converse with; Rom. 16:3, 21-22 and following; 1 Cor. 1; Gen. 29:6; 37:14; 41:16.

units.la: Absit ergo hic contemtus, despicientia, incommodatio, contumelia, ὑπερηφανίας, studium alteri aduersandi, eiusq; conatus sine vlla commodi spe impediēdi. Sunt enim hæc πρὸς ἀλυγωρίας indicia. Adde ad Rom.c.12.10. Fraterna charitate alii ad alios amandos propensi, honore alii aliis præeuntes, Colos.c.3.12. Induimini igitur, vt electi Dei sancti & dilecti, visceribus miserationum, comitate, modestia, mansuetudine, lenitate animi. 13. tolerantes alii alios, &c. Senec.alibi: Cunctis esto benignus, nemini blandus paucis familiaris, omnibus æquus. 1.Pet.c.3. 8. deniq; omnes estote concordes mutuo molestiarum sensu affecti, fraterna præditi charitate, ad misericordiam proni, comes, &c.1.Pet.c.5.14. Salutate alii alios charitatis osculo. Rom. c.16.16. Salutate alii alios osculo sanĉto. Eccles.c.4.7. amicum te exhibe congregationi. Exemplum huius humanitatis extat in Iofepho fratres suos perterritos humanissimis verbis alloquente. Genef.c.45. & Labano Abrahami seruum hospitio excipienti. Genef.c.24. & in Abigale. 1.Sam. c.25. adde præcepta moralia Prou.c.15. de responsione molli, &c.25.
units.tr: Let there therefore be far from this any contempt, disdain, rudeness, insult, pride [ὑπερηφανίας], or eagerness to oppose another and hinder his efforts with no hope of any advantage. For these are signs of carelessness [πρὸς ἀλυγωρίας]. Add Rom. 12:10: in brotherly love inclined to love one another, going before one another in honour. Col. 3:12-13: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, long-suffering, bearing with one another, and so on. Seneca elsewhere: be kind to all, flatter no one, be familiar with a few, fair to all. 1 Pet. 3:8: finally, be all of one mind, sympathizing with one another's troubles, endowed with brotherly love, prone to mercy, courteous, and so on. 1 Pet. 5:14: greet one another with the kiss of charity. Rom. 16:16: greet one another with a holy kiss. Ecclus. 4:7: show yourself friendly to the congregation. An example of this humanity is in Joseph, addressing his terrified brothers in the most humane words (Gen. 45), and in Laban receiving Abraham's servant with hospitality (Gen. 24), and in Abigail (1 Sam. 25). Add the moral precepts of Prov. 15 on the soft answer, and Prov. 25.

units.la: Fieri autem debet hæc affabilitas eo modo quo vsitatum est in loco, in quo commoramur, idque in salutando, compellando, excipiendo, valedicendo, vel dimittendo, cuius rei exempla vide Exod. cap. 18. 7. Ruth cap. 2. 4. 1. Sam. c. 25. 4. & seqq. sic & Angelus Mariam salutans dicit, Dominus tecum & Gideonem, & Christus discipulos, Pax vobis, & Iudas Christum, Ave Rabbi, sic itaque ergo alios nos decet esse iucundos & quasi domesticos & familiares ut cum iis colloqui, ipsis respondere vel eos interrogare, si res postulat, non detrectemus: atque haec omnia blande & suaviter, Eccles. cap. 4. 7. 8. Hoc est, (ut scriptura loquitur) ad cor. arg. Genes. cap. 34. 3. c. 50. 21. Iudic. c. 19. 3. Ruth. c. 2. 13. 2. Sam. c. 19. 7. Esa. c. 40. 2. Osea c. 1. 14. c. 2. 14. ut inde appareat & elucceat charitas, humanitas & benevolentia salutantium, quibus contraria morositas, fastus, inhumanitas & contemptus.
units.tr: This affability ought to be practised in the manner customary in the place where we live, in greeting, addressing, receiving, bidding farewell and dismissing. For examples of this see Exod. 18:7; Ruth 2:4; 1 Sam. 25:4ff. So too the angel greeting Mary says, 'The Lord is with you'; and Gideon; and Christ to his disciples, 'Peace be with you'; and Judas to Christ, 'Hail, Rabbi.' Thus we ought to be pleasant to others, and as it were domestic and familiar, so that we do not refuse to converse with them, to answer them or to question them if the matter requires it; and all of this blandly and sweetly (Ecclus. 4:7-8). That is, as Scripture speaks, 'to the heart' (Gen. 34:3; 50:21; Judg. 19:3; Ruth 2:13; 2 Sam. 19:7; Isa. 40:2; Hos. 1:14; 2:14), so that from this the love, humanity and goodwill of those who greet may appear and shine forth, to which are opposed moroseness, haughtiness, inhumanity and contempt.

units.la: Veteres salutationis ergo suos nomenclatores habuisse leguntur. Alex. ab Alex. genial. dier. lib. 2. cap. 19. de meritoria salutatione Roman. vid. Senecam, De vita breuit. & de salutatione per formulam aue, Senec. libr. 6. De benefic. & de iis qui salutandi causa domos introeunt, lib. 12. epist. 8 y. & in sapient. non cadminiur. Fiebat quoque apud hosce Romanos salutatio more prisco, dexteram dexterae iungendo, nonnunquam osculo, plerunque adsurgendo, caputque denudando, ut refert Alex. ab Alexand. lib. 5. gen. dier. cap. 24. vbi addit, non foris tantum, sed & intra domesticos lares libertos seruosque salutatores coperimus, quibus in die frequentes adorant, ut mane salue re & vesperi valere domino aut patrono dicerent. Salutatio fieri solet nominibus & titulis honorificis, vel certis verborum formulis & phrasibus. Stuck. lib. 2. cap. 31. antiquit. conuiuial. Exempla salutationis eiusque formuformulas apud Iudaeos visitatas vid. 1. Sam. cap. 10. 4. Ruth. c. 2. 4. 10. Exod. c. 18. 7. Iudi. c. 6. 12. Luc. c. 1. 28. 1. Sam. c. 25. 23. 24. 2. Sam. c. 9. 6. c. 14. 22. 33. 2. Reg. c. 4. 23. 29. vbi Pet. Martyr. Matt. c. 28. 9. 10. 11. Act. c. 21. 7. 18. 19. c. 25. 13. 2. Corint. c. 13. 12. Philip. c. 4. 12.
units.tr: The ancients are read to have had their own nomenclators for greetings. Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, book 2, ch. 19, on the meritorious greeting of the Romans; see Seneca, On the Shortness of Life, and on greeting by the formula 'ave', Seneca, book 6, On Benefits; and on those who enter houses for the sake of greeting, book 12, letter 8 (unclear). The Romans also greeted in the old manner, joining right hand to right, sometimes with a kiss, mostly by rising and baring the head, as Alexander ab Alexandro reports, book 5, Genial Days, ch. 24, where he adds: we found that not only outside but also within the household hearths freedmen and slaves greeted, who came in the day in numbers to pay their respects, saying in the morning 'be well' and in the evening 'farewell' to master or patron. Greeting is usually made with honorific names and titles, or with fixed formulas and phrases. Stuckius, book 2, ch. 31, Antiquities of Feasting. For examples of greeting and of the formulas used among the Jews, see 1 Sam. 10:4; Ruth 2:4, 10; Exod. 18:7; Judg. 6:12; Luke 1:28; 1 Sam. 25:23-24; 2 Sam. 9:6; 14:22, 33; 2 Kings 4:23, 29, where Peter Martyr; Matt. 28:9-11; Acts 21:7, 18-19; 25:13; 2 Cor. 13:12; Phil. 4:12.

units.la: Patres veteres ex hac vita discessuri salutem suis dixerunt, vti Moses Israelitis, Iacobus liberis suis, & Isaac. Imo & salutationes gratulatorias de parta victoria, de reditu, de abitu, de officio suscepto & similibus, dicebat, vt Martyr. d. loco refert. Rom. c. 16. per tot. Salutatio & bene precatio quaedam solemnis apud Iudaeos in coetib. sacris & concionib. visitata erat, & praescripta extat Num. cap. 6. Benedicat tibi Dominus, custodiat te, illuminet faciem suam super te & misereatur tui. Leuet Dominus faciem suam super te & ponat te in pace. De modo & formulis salutandi Apostolis visitatis in epistolis, vid. in princip. & fine epistolarum Apostolicarum, & Christus formulam salutandi suis discipulis praescribit. Matt. c. 10. 11. & c. 5. De formula salutandi apud Graecos visitata refert Stuck. d. loco, c. 31 scil. χαίρειν, εὐπεφίλειν, εὖ ἄγειν, ὑγιαίνειν. Apud Latinos erant Aue, qua formula mane vtebatur, & salue, qua vesperi, & vale in digressionib. Vnoquoque vale & salue vtebantur discedentes ab iis quos nunquam visuri essent. Plaut. in Curcul.
units.tr: The ancient fathers, about to depart from this life, bade farewell to their own, as Moses to the Israelites, Jacob to his children, and Isaac. They also spoke greetings of congratulation for a victory won, a return, a departure, an office undertaken and similar things, as Martyr reports in the place cited. Romans 16 throughout. A greeting and a certain solemn blessing was customary among the Jews in sacred assemblies and sermons, and it is prescribed in Num. 6: "The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you; the Lord lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace." On the manner and formulas of greeting used by the apostles in their epistles, see the beginnings and endings of the apostolic letters. Christ also prescribes a formula of greeting to his disciples, Matt. 10:11 and 5. On the formula of greeting used among the Greeks, Stuckius reports in the same place, ch. 31, namely farewell [χαίρειν], fare well [εὐπεφίλειν], go well [εὖ ἄγειν], be in health [ὑγιαίνειν]. Among the Latins there was 'ave', a formula used in the morning, and 'salve', used in the evening, and 'vale' at departures. Everyone used 'vale' and 'salve' when parting from those whom they would never see again. Plautus, in Curculio.

units.la: --- vale atque salue
units.tr: --- vale atque salue

units.la: Nam & opera & pecunia benigne praebuisti. Et in Cistellaria: Quando ita tibi lubet, vale atq; salue. & in Mercat. & in Capteiuis. & Virgilius alibi, lib. 11. & lib. 6. Hodie apud nos varia formula salutandi usurpantur, quae secundum hominum congressum, vel digressum, vel secundum tempora, secundum varias actiones, illarumque euentum, vel secundum, vel ad. uersum alias, deniq; circumstantias distingui possunt.
units.tr: For you have generously provided both help and money. And in the Cistellaria: "Since it pleases you so, farewell and be well." Likewise in the Mercator, in the Captivi, and Virgil elsewhere, book 11, and book 6. Today among us various forms of greeting are in use, which can be distinguished according to the coming together or parting of people, according to the times, according to the various actions and their outcomes, and according to other aspects and finally the circumstances.

units.la: Gott grüsse dich/ Willkomme/ Gott behüte dich/ ein guten morgen/ guten tag/ guten abend/ gute nacht/ Gott helffe dir/ Gott sey mit dir/ Gott gebe dir ein gut glückhafftig jahr/ Gott beleite dich/ Gott gebe daß wir wider mit freuden zusammen kommen/ Biß Gott willkom/ Gott segne dir das bad/ den trunck/ Gott helffe euch/ Gott gebe dir vil glücks/ Gott gesegne das essen/ Gott tröste dich vnd stercke dich/ &c. similes.
units.tr: God greet you; Welcome; God keep you; good morning; good day; good evening; good night; God help you; God be with you; God give you a good and fortunate new year; God accompany you; God grant that we meet again with joy; Till God welcomes you; God bless your bath; the drink; God help you all; God give you much luck; God bless the meal; God comfort and strengthen you; etc. and similar.

units.la: Commercium & collatio sermonis cum iis esse debet, quorum conuersatio te meliorem, non deteriorem reddere potest. De qua re Senec. lib. 14. epist. 93. Nulla res, inquit, magis animos honestate induit, dubiosq; & in prauum inclinantes reuocat ad rectum, quam bonorum virorum conuersatio. Paulatim enim descendit in pectora & vim praeceptorum obtinet frequenter audiri, aspici frequenter. Occursus ipse sapientium iuuat. Est & aliquid quod ex magno viro vel tacente proficias. Nec tibi facile dixerim quemadmodum prosit, sicut illud intelligam, profuisse. Minuta quaedam vt ait Phædon animalia, cum mordent non sentiuntur, adeo tenuis illis & valens in periculum vis est, tumor indicat morsum, & in ipso tumore nullum vulnus apparet. Idem tibi in conuersatione virorum sapientum euenit, non deprehendes quemadmodum, aut quando tibi prosit: profuisse deprehendes, & lib. 19. epist. 110. Nam vt aromata longe lateq; odorem emittunt, sic teras: sic boni virtute praediti, sic illis vtaris in conuersatione: contra malignus comes, quamuis candido & simplici rubigine suam affricat. Senec. lib. 1. epist. 7. & mores a conuersantibus sumuntur. Idem lib. 3. De ira, c. 7. & colloquia prava prava corrumpunt bonos mores.1.(or.c.1.Prou.c.13.
units.tr: Intercourse and conversation should be had with those whose company can make you better, not worse. On this matter Seneca, letter 93 of book 14, says: "Nothing so imbues minds with honour, or recalls the doubtful and those inclining toward wrong to what is right, as the company of good men. For it gradually sinks into the breast and gains the force of precepts by being often heard and often seen. Even the mere approach of wise men helps. There is also something you may gain from a great man even when he is silent. I could hardly tell you how it benefits you, but you will understand that it has benefited you. Small creatures, as Phaedo says, when they bite are not felt, so subtle and yet so potent is their power to harm; the swelling shows the bite, and no wound appears in the swelling itself. The same happens to you in the company of wise men: you will not perceive how or when it benefits you; you will perceive that it has benefited you." And letter 110 of book 19: "For as spices send out their fragrance far and wide, so will you rub off on others; so good men endowed with virtue, so you will be used by them in conversation. On the other hand, a malicious companion will rub his own rust onto even a candid and simple man." Seneca, letter 7 of book 1: "Manners are taken from those we associate with." The same, On Anger, book 3, ch. 7: "Evil talk corrupts good morals." 1 Corinthians 15; Proverbs 13.

units.la: 20. Qui ambulat cum sapientibus sapientior fiet, qui vero se consociat stolidis, efficietur peior, Eccles. c. 11.
units.tr: 20. He who walks with the wise will become wiser; he who joins himself to fools will become worse. Ecclesiastes 11.

units.la: Ne quemuis hominem inducas in domum tuam nam multae sunt insidiae Diaboli, & verf. seqq. & cap. 9. per tot. Ecclesiast. c. 9. 19. Pro viribus tuis coniecturam fac de altero & cum sapientibus ini consilia: cum intelligentibus esto confabulatio tua, & tota narratio tua de lege altissimi, 20. Viri iusti sunto conuictores tui & in reuerentia Domini esto gloriatio tua, late Clemens Alexand. lib. 3. Padag. c. 4.
units.tr: Do not bring just any man into your house, for many are the snares of the Devil, and the following verses; and Ecclesiasticus 9 throughout; Ecclesiasticus 9:19. Make a judgment of another according to your strength, and take counsel with the wise; let your conversation be with the intelligent, and let all your talk be of the law of the Most High. 20. Let righteous men be your table companions, and let your boast be in the fear of the Lord. Widely cited by Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 3, ch. 4.

units.la: Videndum tamen ut haec conversatio sit temperata, non nimia neq; rara. Ibi enim rerum & conuersationis est satietas, hic vero ignoti nulla cupido neq; delectatio. Temperata conuersatio amorem conciliat. Siquidem amamus eos qui se aliquo modo studiose & cum quadam animi propensione erga nos gerunt & nostra consuetudine delectantur, & nostri aemuli & imitatores esse volunt.
units.tr: Yet care must be taken that this conversation be moderate, neither excessive nor rare. For where there is too much, there is a surfeit of things and of conversation; where it is rare, there is no desire for the unknown and no delight in it. Moderate conversation wins love, since we love those who show themselves toward us in some way with zeal and with a certain goodwill of mind, who delight in our company, and who want to be our emulators and imitators.

units.la: Ethicus ergo cum bonis & virtute praeditis colloqui & sermonem habere debet, cum malis vero & nequam hominibus, quantum ratione officii & conscientiae licet, sermones conferre & colloqui non debet. Est enim delicti species conversari cum malis, vel eorum consortio uti. Psalm. 26. 4. 5. & Psalm. 1. & 50. 18. Prou. c. 16. 15. 16. 17. Nam talis quis iudicatur qualis est ille cum quo conversatur. Similis enim simili gaudet. Eccles. c. 13. 1. 18. 19. 20. 21. cap. 9. 19 20. Et qui tangit picem, inquinabitur ab ea. Eccles. c. 13. 1. 2. 1. Cor. c. 5. Ex quo argumento Iudaei de Christo iudicabant, Matth. c. 9. 9. 10. 11. 12.
units.tr: The ethical person, therefore, ought to converse and hold discourse with good people endowed with virtue, but he ought not to confer and converse with wicked and worthless people beyond what the demands of duty and conscience allow. For it is a kind of offence to associate with the wicked or to make use of their company. Psalm 26. 4, 5; Psalm 1; 50. 18. Prov. 16. 15, 16, 17. For a person is judged by the one with whom he keeps company, since like delights in like. Eccles. 13. 1, 18, 19, 20, 21; 9. 19, 20. And whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it. Eccles. 13. 1, 2. 1 Cor. 5. From this argument the Jews judged concerning Christ, Matt. 9. 9, 10, 11, 12.

units.la: Quibus vero conditionibus & cautionibus
units.tr: But under what conditions and cautions

units.la: liceat cum infidelibus conuersari, vel eorum consortio & familiaritate vti, docet Pet. Martyr. Iudic. c. 1. verf. 6. vbi distinguit inter homines priuatos, eruditos, constantes, indoctos, infirmos, & Magistratus.
units.tr: Pet. Martyr. Iudic. c. 1. verf. 6. teaches when it is lawful to converse with unbelievers, or to make use of their company and familiarity, distinguishing between private persons, the learned, the steadfast, the unlearned, the weak, and the magistrates.

units.la: Priuatus doctus & constans cum infidelibus licitè conuersatur. Primò, quando id facit quo alienos à pietate doceat & ad religionem synceram inducat, quod quo commodius faciat, conuenit esse blandum, comem, benignum erga eos, quos Christo lucrifacere vult.
units.tr: A private person who is learned and steadfast may lawfully associate with unbelievers. First, when he does so in order to teach them, estranged from piety, and to lead them to pure religion; and to do this more conveniently, he should be affable, courteous, and kind toward those whom he wishes to win for Christ.

units.la: Deinde videndum est, inquit, vt sancte, iuste & honeste viuat, ne quod vna manu extruit, id altera destruat.
units.tr: Next, he must see, he says, that he lives holily, justly, and honourably, lest what he builds with one hand he tears down with the other.

units.la: Tertio, ne praetextu comitatis cuiusdam & amicitiae sese impiis ritibus & actionibus immiscceat. Non enim sunt mala facienda, vt bona eueniant.
units.tr: Third, lest under the pretext of a certain courtesy and friendship he mix himself into impious rites and actions. For evil things must not be done so that good may come of them.

units.la: Quarto, ne sua causa, vel ne sua quaerat commoda, dum cum eis versatur, atque sua compedia sectetur.
units.tr: Fourth, lest he seek his own advantage or his own conveniences while he lives among them, and pursue his own gain.

units.la: Quod si desperatio subsit in hisce, tum non cum infidelibus amplius agendum, nisi quantum necessitas vel nostra, vel eorum postulat, id est, quando forte ipsi infideles laborarent grauissime, necesse aliunde quam opera nostra posset subuenire, aut si nos ipsi, quae ad victum necessaria sunt alibi, quam apud eos nancisci non valeremus. Conuersari quoque cum illis licebit, quantum naturales & ciuiles necessitudines exigunt, vt si nostri principes fuerint, patres, coniuges, heri, domini, & similia horum.
units.tr: But if despair lies beneath these matters, then one must no longer deal with unbelievers, except as far as the need of either ourselves or them requires; that is, when perhaps the unbelievers themselves are in the gravest distress and help must come from elsewhere than from our efforts, or when we ourselves could not obtain the things necessary for life anywhere but among them. It will also be lawful to associate with them as far as natural and civil ties demand, as when they are our princes, fathers, spouses, masters, and the like.

units.la: Nam qui suorum praesertim domesti-corum curam non habet, fidem, Apostolo testante, abnegauit & infideli deterior. Et ser-uientiam duris & impiis dominis obedire iubentur a Petro. Et vxor fidelis, infidelem maritum non deserere, sed cohabitare illi iubetur, 1.Cor.c.7.arg.precum qua funduntur etiam pro impio rege.Jerem.c.29.Baruch.c.1.
units.tr: For he who has no care for his own, especially those of his household, has denied the faith, as the Apostle testifies, and is worse than an unbeliever. Servants are also commanded by Peter to obey harsh and impious masters. And a believing wife is commanded not to desert an unbelieving husband but to live with him, 1 Corinthians 7; the argument of the prayers that are poured out even for an impious king, Jeremiah 29; Baruch 1.

units.la: Priores distinctiones idem Martyr testimoniis & exemplis probat. Ita enim Christus cum publicanis, peccatoribus & Pharisaeis & Scribis versabatur, vt eos de salute instituert & a peccatis ad pietatem conuerteret. Ita prophetae cum populo idololatra vna versabantur, & Apostoli inter Ethnicos & Paulus cum Athenien-sibus, Abraham ex iussu Dei inter Ethnicos. Loth inter Sodomitas, Nahaman inter idolatras.
units.tr: The same Martyr proves the former distinctions by testimonies and examples. For thus Christ associated with tax collectors, sinners, Pharisees, and scribes, in order to instruct them concerning salvation and to turn them from sins to piety. Thus the prophets lived together with an idolatrous people, and the Apostles among the Gentiles, and Paul with the Athenians; Abraham, by God's command, among the Gentiles; Lot among the Sodomites; Naaman among the idolaters.

units.la: Homines infirmi & indocti non debent nacum infidelibus agere, nisi quantum patitur necessitas corporis, & necessitudo ciuilis. Illud vero, 1.Corinth.cap.10.27. Quod si quis infidelium vos vocat & vultis ire, quidquid apponitur vobis, edite, &c. intelligendum caeteris paribus.
units.tr: Weak and unlearned men ought not to have dealings with unbelievers except as far as bodily need and civil obligation require. But the passage in 1 Corinthians 10:27, "If any of the unbelievers invites you and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you," etc., must be understood with the other things being equal.

units.la: In aliis omnino infidelium commercium & familiaritas est fugienda. vid.Matt.c.5.c.18. Ita enim accipitur ibidem de abiiciedis iis quae nobis offendiculo aut impedimento sunt. Ita quoque Paul. 1.Cor.c.5. Ne paululum fermenti totam massam polluat, & ibid.c.15. ne mores bonos colloquia prava corrumpant, ne qui tangit pice ab ea inquinetur, & supra vires onus suscipipiamus.Eccles.c.13. adde 2.Cor.c.6.Matth. cap.5. 18.1.Cor.c.15.33.34. cap.5. 9.10.11. Psalm.43.63.84. Rom.c.12.Hoc etiam exemplis Israelitarum, qui 70. annos in Babylone captiui fuerunt & infecti probatur, vt licet videre ex Esra, Nehemia, Zacharia. Idem etiam ex commercio Aegyptiorum & aliorum vitia contraxerunt, vt constat ex gestis Exod.c.32. & Num.c.22. Matth.c.26.58.59.70. & seqq. c.6.5. Quid quod impari iugo copulari cum infidelibus prohibeatur? 2.Cor.c.6.14.15.16. Quae enim communio lucis cum tenebris? & qui consensus Christo cum Belial? Ideo Deus prohibuit ne ab exteris regionibus & infidelibus Iudaei auxilium peterent, vel foedus facerent. Ideo Iudaei cum Samaritanis commercium habere nolebant, Joh.cap.4. & Moses aulam Pharaonis fugit, Heb.c.11. Et David conqueritur in Psalmis quod cogatur degere cum impiis.
units.tr: In other matters the fellowship and familiarity of unbelievers is wholly to be avoided. See Matthew 5 and 18; for there it is understood of casting away those things that are a stumbling block or hindrance to us. So also Paul, 1 Corinthians 5: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump"; and in the same place, chapter 15: "Evil communications corrupt good manners," "he who touches pitch will be defiled by it," and that we should not take up a burden beyond our strength. Ecclesiasticus 13; add 2 Corinthians 6; Matthew 5:18; 1 Corinthians 15:33-34; chapter 5:9-11; Psalms 43, 63, 84; Romans 12. This is also proved by the examples of the Israelites, who were captives in Babylon for seventy years and were infected, as may be seen from Ezra, Nehemiah, and Zechariah. Likewise they contracted vices from dealings with the Egyptians and others, as is clear from the deeds recorded in Exodus 32 and Numbers 22; Matthew 26:58-59, 70, and following; chapter 6:5. What of the fact that being yoked unequally with unbelievers is forbidden? 2 Corinthians 6:14-16. For what fellowship has light with darkness? And what agreement has Christ with Belial? Therefore God forbade the Jews to seek help from foreign lands and unbelievers, or to make a covenant with them. Therefore the Jews did not want to have dealings with the Samaritans, John 4; and Moses fled the court of Pharaoh, Hebrews 11. And David complains in the Psalms that he is forced to dwell among the impious.

units.la: Indistinctè omnes docti, indocti, fortes, imbecilles cum infidelibus conuersari non debet, quando coguntur impiis eorum ritibus & actionibus interesse. 1.Cor.c.10.20.21.22. Plane in rebus adiaphoris licet se fratris infirmitati accommodare, 1.Cor.c.8. vt Paulus dicit, se omnia facit omnibus vt complures lucrifaceret Christo, vid. Pet. Martyr. Judic.d.c.1.36. Virsinum lib.2. Dispositum III, & seq.
units.tr: Everyone, whether learned or unlearned, strong or weak, ought not to mix with unbelievers when they are compelled to take part in their rites and actions. 1 Cor. 10:20-22. Plainly, in matters indifferent it is permitted to accommodate oneself to a brother's weakness, 1 Cor. 8, as Paul says, that he became all things to all men that he might win many to Christ. See Peter Martyr, Judges 1:36; Virsinus, book 2, Dispositum III, and following.

units.la: Cum insipiente ne habeas sermonem multum, neque ambules cum eo qui caret intelligentia. Prou.c.23.9. Eccles.c.22,13. caue potius ab illo vt molestiam non habeas & quisquiliis eius inquineris. 14. & seqq. sed cum intelligentibus sit confabulatio tua. Eccles.c.9.19.
units.tr: Do not hold much talk with a fool, nor walk with one who lacks understanding. Prov. 23:9; Eccles. 22:13. Rather, beware of him, lest you have trouble and be defiled by his trifles, 14 and following; but let your conversation be with the wise. Eccles. 9:19.

units.la: Neque cuiuis homini exponas animum tuum.
units.tr: Do not open your mind to every man.

units.la: Eccles. cap.8.21. & consiliarii tui pauci sint, vnus e millenis. c.6.6. non tamen stultus & irascundus. Eccles.c.8.20.21. Qui vero non in consilium adhibendi,vid. Prou.c.37.11.& seqq. & cap. 21.17.& seqq.c.23.19.12.c.20.19. vbi lun. Eccl.c.9. 19.20.c.8.9.10.11. & quod facturus es ne praedixeris frustratus enim spe, irrideberis. infortunium tuum celato, ne gaudio afficias inimicos.
units.tr: Eccles. 8:21. Let your counsellors be few, one in a thousand, Eccles. 6:6, and not a fool or a hothead, Eccles. 8:20-21. But do not take into counsel those who... See Prov. 37:11 and following, and ch. 21:17 and following, ch. 23:19, 12, ch. 20:19, where Lun. reads; Eccles. 9:19-20, 8:9-11. And do not tell beforehand what you are about to do, for if you are disappointed in your hope you will be mocked. Hide your misfortune, lest you give joy to your enemies.

units.la: Arcana vero nemini dicas,Plutarch.de garrulit.Nam,inquit, si sermonem nesciri oportebat, male dictus estad alium, sin vero secretum ex te emissum,continesin alio,in alienam fidem profugisti,tua prodita. Et,si tui similis is fuerit, iuste perisi:si vero melior te quum sit,id praeter spem seruet,alium inuenisti super te fideliorem. Prolem vero ac multiplicationem accipit intempestantiae sermo. Vt enim vnitas suum terminum excedit, quando accedit alius numerus, ita & sermo in primo remanens, vere arcanus est, si vero in alterum egreditur,instar famae est,& volat irreuocabile verbum. Clausula garrulitatis communis est,Nemini dixeris. Quod si vero tibi imperare non potuisti in silentio, quomodo ab alio id ipsum sperare potes? Amore tamen videntur prosequendi qui nihil secum fingunt,nihil obtegunt;quales sunt qui etiam res suas adversas & miserias nobis aperiunt. Arist. libr. 2. Rhetor.
units.tr: Do not tell secrets to anyone. Plutarch, On Garrulity. For, he says, if it was necessary that the matter be unknown, it was badly spoken to another; but if you have let a secret out of yourself and it is held in another, you have fled into another's trust and your own is betrayed. And if he is like you, you have justly perished; but if he is better than you and keeps it beyond expectation, you have found another more faithful than yourself. Talk of indiscretion, however, takes on offspring and multiplication: just as unity exceeds its limit when another number is added, so speech that remains in the first person is truly secret, but if it passes into another it is like rumour, and a word once uttered cannot be recalled. The formula of the chatterbox is common: "Tell no one." But if you could not command yourself to silence, how can you hope that another will do so? Yet they seem worthy of love who feign nothing with themselves and conceal nothing, such as those who also open to us their adverse affairs and miseries. Aristotle, Rhetoric, book 2.

units.la: Facile vero ad iram commoueri exist imari di ii, qui dolore aut aegritudine aliqua laborant. Cum enim omnes dolore affecti aliquid cupiscant,facile quoque commoueri possunt in
units.tr: Those who are suffering from grief or some sickness are easily judged to be moved to anger. For since all who are afflicted with grief desire something, they can also easily be moved

units.la: E eos qui ipsorum desideriis videntur obstare. Idcoque ad iram proni, aegroti, pauperes, amantes, sitientes, aliquid concupiscentes, voti non compotes, aut frustrati exspectato rei eventu. Pro varietate autem insiti irae etiam ira ut plurimum variatur.vid. Aristot. 2. Rhetor.
units.tr: against those who seem to stand in the way of their desires. Hence the sick, the poor, lovers, the thirsty, those who long for something, those who have not obtained their wish, or who are disappointed in the expected outcome of a matter, are prone to anger. But anger itself, according to the variety of the innate disposition, mostly varies. See Aristotle, Rhetoric, book 2.

units.la: Non est quoque facile admittendus in colloquium ἐκγυνάσκον, qui ea quae videt audite, eliminat & multis enunciat: qui diligenter intentus est, curiosus & solicitus, ut maculam aliquam aliis aspergat.
units.tr: Nor is one who is a babbler [ἐκγυνάσκον] easily to be admitted into conversation: he who repeats what he hears, spreads it abroad, and tells it to many; he who is diligently attentive, inquisitive and anxious to spatter some stain upon others.

units.la: Neque etiam is qui in aliorum erratis exagitandis & enunciandis totus occupatur, ut est subsannator, scriptor cum aediarum & qui μισοφυλάκιος colligit alienorum vitiorum, vid. Horat. lib. 1. Serm. satyr. 4.
units.tr: Nor is one to be admitted who is wholly occupied in pursuing and publishing the errors of others, such as a mocker, a writer of lampoons, and one who collects the faults of others [μισοφυλάκιος]. See Horace, Satires, book 1, satire 4.

units.la: Omnes hi metuunt, versus odere poetas.
units.tr: All these fear verses; they hate poets.

units.la: Fanum habet in cornu; longe fuge, dummodo risum.
units.tr: He has a cudgel in his horn; flee far off, provided he shakes out a laugh.

units.la: Excutiat sibi, non hic cuiquam parcet amico.
units.tr: He spares no friend of his own, nor here spares anyone.

units.la: Et quodcunq; semel chartis illeverit, omnes
units.tr: And whatever he has once daubed on paper, all

units.la: Gestiet a furno redeuntes scire lacus,
units.tr: will be eager to know, from the baker's oven to the returning vats,

units.la: Et pueros & anus, &c.
units.tr: and boys and old women, and so on.

units.la: Non pugnandum etiam cum homine verbosis & loquacibus. Eccles. c. 8. 20. 22. neque potentiore. d. cap. 8. 1. 2. 3. 15. 17. neque audace, impudenti & iracundo, d. c. 8. 18. 19. & carente intelligentia. Eccles. c. 27. 12. neque plurimum iurante. d. c. 27. 13. 14. neque stulto. Eccles. d. cap. 8. 20. 22. Proverb. c. 23. 9. qui omnia tua nihili facturus est, Eccles. cap. 2. 13. 14. c. 27. 12. Prov. d. c. 23. neque cum dissimulatoribus, simulatoribus, callidis & vafris, neq; etiam cum obseruatore tuo & corycaeo. Eccles. c. 37. 7. ri.
units.tr: One must also not quarrel with a man who is verbose and talkative, Eccles. 8:20, 22; nor with one who is more powerful, ibid. 8:1-3, 15, 17; nor with one who is bold, shameless and angry, ibid. 8:18-19; nor with one who lacks understanding, Eccles. 27:12; nor with one who swears much, ibid. 27:13-14; nor with a fool, Eccles. ibid. 8:20, 22; Prov. 23:9, who will count all your things as nothing, Eccles. 2:13-14, 27:12; Prov. ibid. ch. 23. Nor with dissemblers, pretenders, the crafty and the sly, nor even with your spy and flatterer, Eccles. 37:7, ri.

units.la: 11. neque cum susurrone & bilingue. Eccles. c. 28. verf. 15.16. neque enim inimicis tuis. Eccles. cap. 6. verf. 13. Neque cum homine duro, malis actionibus dedito & nequam. 1. Samuel c 25.3 sed vir illius erat durus & malis actionibus deditus. & verf. 17. ipse autem nequior est quam ut alloquar eum & verf. 9.10.11.12. Neque vis adferenda defluxioni fluminis. Eccl. c. 4. 32. Velin turbam se immutendum. Eccles. c. 7. 7.
units.tr: 11. Nor with a whisperer and a double-tongued man, Eccles. 28:15-16. Nor indeed with your enemies, Eccles. 6:13. Nor with a hard man, given to evil deeds and worthless, 1 Sam. 25:3, "but he was hard and given to evil deeds," and v. 17, "he himself is too worthless for me to speak to him," and vv. 9-12. Nor must force be applied against the flood of a river, Eccles. 4:32. Nor must one let oneself be changed into a crowd, Eccles. 7:7.

units.la: Illis qui male de nobis loquuntur non est male respondendum. Rom. c. 12. 14. benedicite iis qui vos insectantur, benedicite, inquam, & ne impre-camini. 1. Pet. c. 3. 8. 9. ubi exemplum Christi nobis proponitur hac in re. vid. Psalm. 109. Decorum itaque hic est silere, vel iusta defensione uti. Ita ratum put-pulus Dei ad maledictionem & blasphemiam regis Assyriae. 2. Reg. c. 18. 36. Excusatione & defensione vsus est Samuel. 1. Sam. c. 12. Hanna. 1. Sa. c. 1. 15. Daniel. Daniel c. 6. 22. Paulus. act. c. 23. 1. adde Gen. c. 40. 15. de qua re infra latius.
units.tr: Evil must not be answered with evil to those who speak ill of us. Rom. 12:14, "Bless those who persecute you, bless, I say, and do not curse." 1 Pet. 3:8-9, where the example of Christ is set before us in this matter. See Ps. 109. Therefore it is fitting here to be silent or to use a just defence. Thus the people of God answered the blasphemy and reproach of the king of Assyria, 2 Kings 18:36. Excuse and defence were used by Samuel, 1 Sam. 12; Hannah, 1 Sam. 1:15; Daniel, Dan. 6:22; Paul, Acts 23:1. Add Gen. 40:15, concerning which matter more below at greater length.

units.la: Contentioio & rixoso ita respondendum, ut prudentia locum det temeritati, & obsecundet stulto contentioso, ut contentionis finis fiat. Ec-clef. cap. 18. verf. 10. 11. & seqq. 1. Sam. c. 25. verf. 9. 10. 11. 12. 17. Seneca: Requirenti facile responde: & contemnenti facile cede. & magnanimi est iniurias & offensiones despicere.
units.tr: To a contentious and quarrelsome man one must so answer that prudence gives place to rashness and yields to the contentious fool, so that there may be an end to contention. Ecclus 18:10-11 and following; 1 Sam. 25:9-12, 17. Seneca: "Answer easily the one who asks; yield easily to the one who despises." It belongs to a magnanimous man to disregard injuries and offences.

units.la: Adulatoribus respondendum cum protestatione ut taceant: te, cum laude opus sit, remetipsum laudaturum, cum hac vel simili forma: Non scio quid cum tuis laudibus agam. Si enim reiicio te, adulatorem arguo; sin recipio, me inanis gloriæ cupidum ostendo.
units.tr: To flatterers one must answer, with a protest, that they should be silent: "If you should need praise, you will praise yourself," in this or a similar form: "I do not know what to do with your praises. For if I reject you, I accuse you of flattery; but if I accept them, I show myself to be a lover of empty glory."

units.la: Affici verò & commoueri laude improborum, est instar suum se gerere; qui, dum fricantur & titillantur, se ipsos præbent vti volenti.
units.tr: To be moved and stirred by the praise of wicked men is to act like those who, while they are rubbed and tickled, offer themselves to whoever wishes to use them.

units.la: Quod si sunt qui alios irridĕt, tacendum nobis est & superflua verba tanquam plena pocula à nobis transmittĕda. Lubricus enim & periculosus est eiusmodi ludus. Clemens Alexand. lib.2.Pædagog.c.7.
units.tr: But if there are those who mock others, we must be silent and send back superfluous words from ourselves as if they were full cups. For such play is slippery and dangerous. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, book 2, ch. 7.

units.la: Inanem auditionem non suscipies. Neque vnà cum iniusto sedebis, vel communicabis, vt sis falsus testis, neque in calumniis neque in maledictis, sed neq; in improbitate. Clemens Alexand. dicto lib.2.c.7.
units.tr: You will not receive an idle hearing. Nor will you sit or associate with the unjust, so that you become a false witness, neither in calumnies nor in insults, nor indeed in wickedness. Clement of Alexandria, cited, book 2, ch. 7.

units.la: Consilia sua non requisita præter officium & vocationem suam obtrudere, est hominis stulti, vani & superbi.
units.tr: To thrust one's counsel upon others, unasked and beyond one's office and calling, is the mark of a foolish, vain and proud man.

units.la: Ne contendito cum vllo homine immerito. Prouerb.cap.3.30. & sermo intelligentiæ ingratus est stulto. Prou.cap.17.7. Malignos ne æmulator, neque desiderato cum eis esse. Prouerb.cap.24.1.2. Neque cum irrisoribus conferendum. Prou.d.cap.24.verf.9. & Psalm.101. Sed euciendi illi, & contentio cessabit. Prouerb.c.22.10. neque cum ludibrio & vilipendio quod sanctum porcis proiiciendum, Matt. c.7.6.
units.tr: Do not contend with any man without cause. Prov. 3:30. "A word of understanding is unwelcome to a fool," Prov. 17:7. Do not emulate the malicious, nor desire to be with them, Prov. 24:1-2. Nor is one to confer with scorners, Prov. ibid. 24:9, and Ps. 101. But drive them out, and the contention will cease, Prov. 22:10. Nor is that which is holy to be cast to dogs amid mockery and contempt, Matt. 7:6.

units.la: Homo peccator declinat redargutionem, & pro voluntate sua invenit iudicia sibi convenientia, & quærit homines qui adblandiuntur sua nequitia, Eccles.c.32.20.
units.tr: The sinner avoids correction, and according to his own will finds judgements suited to himself, and seeks men who flatter his wickedness, Ecclus 32:20.

units.la: Apud senes & honoratiores ne multa dicas. Eccles.c.32.12.c.7.13. Sed eos attende, v.6.34.35. cap.8.9.10.11.12. & ab illis disce, quomodo magnatibus
units.tr: Among elders and men of honour do not say much. Ecclus 32:12; 7:13. But attend to them, vv. 6:34-35, ch. 8:9-12, and learn from them how you ought to serve great men

units.la: gnatibus ministrare debeas, & tempore necessitatis respondere,Eccles.c.8 9.10.11.12.
units.tr: and answer in time of need. Eccles. 8:9-12.

units.la: Cum hæreticis aliisq; atheis hominibus & profanis sermo habendus illi, cui hoc ratione officii incumbit, vel cuiuis alii, qui de suado-ctrina & constantia certus est, neab illis sedu-catur,& horum salutem quærit,& impiis ritibus eorum & actionibus abstinet. Exemplo Christi, Luc. c.15.12.& seqq. Vide Pet. Martyr. de com.pio-rum cum impiis. Iudic.c.1.36. Alias minime, arg.1. Cor.c.10. Matth.c.5.18. ob periculum, Eccl.cap.13. Exemplo Israelitarum. Exod. c.32. Num. c.22. & Petri in aula versantis, & dixi supra de hac re. Neque cum hostibus religionis. Matth.c.7.6. c.27.14. co-metudo & sermo habendus.
