units.tr: Discourse with heretics and other godless and profane men is to be held by one to whom this belongs by reason of his office, or by anyone else who is certain of his doctrine and steadfastness, who is not seduced by them, who seeks their salvation, and who abstains from their impious rites and actions. Following the example of Christ, Luke 15:12 and following. See Peter Martyr, On the Communion of the Pious with the Impious, Judges 1:36. Otherwise by no means: argument from 1 Cor. 10; Matt. 5:18; because of danger, Eccles. ch. 13; following the example of the Israelites, Exod. 32; Num. 22; and of Peter, who was in the high priest's court, as I said above on this matter. Nor is the sermon to be held with enemies of religion, Matt. 7:6; 27:14, a fear and a discourse to be held.

units.la: Odiosa & fastidiosa est consuetudo vel conversatio cum hominibus teneris, qui instar vitrifragilis obseruari&mollibrachio tractarivo- lentin sermone, qui quando non satis ciuiliter forte fuerunt, vel non titulis suis appellati, conqueruntur, exempli causa, tu tuissas me in singularì numero, mecum loqueris; vocasti me amicum, non Dominum: Ego vero (vt scias,) sum Dominus Iacobus. Item, non eo quo decet loco in mensa accubui. Tales molles aliospro suis mancipiis habere videntur; & seipsos amantes sine corriuali, aliis se longe præferunt.
units.tr: Keeping company with tender, delicate people is tiresome and irksome. They must be handled like fragile glass and treated with great care, and they take offence at words. If they have not been greeted quite politely, or have not been addressed by their titles, they complain, for example: "You address me in the singular and speak to me as an equal. You called me friend, not Lord. But I am Lord James, so you should know." Likewise, if they have not reclined at table in the place that suits them. Such effeminate people seem to treat others as their slaves, and, loving only themselves with no rival, they put themselves far above everyone else.

units.la: Non ad quosuis sermones cuiusuis respondendum, neque animus ad omnia verba adhibendus, Eccles.c.7.21. Fatuus credit omnibus rebus. Proverb.c.14.c.15. & quife prosternit ad sermones quosuis, contritionem parat. Prouer. c.13.3. Ideo recte Seneca: Morbum esse scias, non hilaritatem, semper arridere arridentibus & ad omnium æstimationem ipsum quoq; os diducere. Nam stulto non se subsistendum, Eccles. c. 4. 32. neq; stulto est respondendum secundum stultitiam suam, Eccles. c. 26. 4. 5. Sed abeundum à conspectu viri stolidi, quem nosti non praeditum verbis intelligentia, Prou. c. 24. 7. 1. Sam. c. 10. 27. at homines nequam dicebat, quid seruaret nos iste? & contemnentes eum, ut ne afferrent ei munus: tamen plane conticuit, & 1. Sam. c. 25. 9. & quiete se continuerunt, 2. 17. Ipse nequior est quam ut alloquar eum. Eccle. c. 19. 15. Ne cuiuis sermoni credito animum tuum. Leuitas enim in credendo leuem notat mentem. Senec. ad Lucilium, epist. 3. Utrum quid, inquit, vitium est, & omnibus credere, & nulli. Itaque quod dicitur, non esse facile credendum, intelligendum, nisi is sit probus & fide dignus, vid. Tiraquel. De poen. temperand. cauff. 51. num. 27. & seqq. gloss. & Bartol. in l. Titio fundus, de condit. & demonstr. Cito & temere credere assertioni cuiusuis non debemus, l. 1. §. dolum, de eo per quem factum l. 3. §. sed si. de in rem verf. l. 2. quod falsum tut. l. nimia credulitate, C. de act. & oblig. l. sicut, C. de fid. instrum. l. non omnes, §. a barbaris, de re militari. & Cato: Noli tu quadam referenti credere semper: Exigua est tribuenda fides quia multa loquuntur.
units.tr: One should not answer every speech of every person, nor give heed to every word. "The fool believes everything" (Eccles. 7:21; Prov. 14:15). "He who rushes headlong into every kind of talk prepares his own ruin" (Prov. 13:3). So Seneca rightly says: "Know that it is a sickness, not good cheer, always to smile at those who smile and to stretch one's own mouth to match everyone's judgement." One must not stay to argue with a fool, whom you know to lack the wit of words (Eccles. 4:32; Prov. 24:7). Nor should one answer a fool according to his folly (Eccles. 26:4-5). Rather, one must withdraw from the sight of a stupid man, whom you know to be without understanding in words (1 Sam. 10:27; Prov. 24:7). Thus the wicked men said, "What shall this man save us?" and despised him, so that they brought him no gift; yet he held his peace (1 Sam. 10:27). And the men (1 Sam. 25:9) and those who were quiet kept themselves still (2 Sam. 17:?). "He is too wicked for me to speak to him" (Eccles. 19:15). Do not give your mind to every speech that is told you, for lightness in believing marks a light mind. Seneca, in his letter to Lucilius, epistle 3: "What is the fault? To believe everyone, or to believe no one." Hence it is to be understood that one should not readily believe, unless the man is upright and worthy of trust; see Tiraquellus, De poenis temperandis, cause 51, nn. 27 ff., gloss, and Bartolus on l. Titio fundus, de condit. et demonstr. We ought not to believe quickly and rashly any assertion whatever (D. 47.8 l. 1 §. dolum; l. 3 §. sed si; l. 2 quod falsum tut.; C. 2.? l. nimia credulitate; C. l. sicut, de fid. instrum.; l. non omnes §. a barbaris, de re militari). And Cato: "Do not always believe what a man tells you; little trust is to be given, for many people talk too much."

units.la: De illis rebus quae efferendae non sunt, noli communicare cum vllis, nisi quorum forte no minus quam tua interest silentium. Isocrat. ad Demonicum imprimis vero curiosis nihil communicandum. Nam quae hi libenter audiunt, ea etiam libenter effutiunt; & quae ab aliis studiose colligunt, apud alios cum voluptate efferunt. Solent etiam etiā curiosi eiusmodi colligere & congerere alienæ vitæ lapsus, errata, solœcismos & odiosissimū malorum grammatophylaciò circumferre, & ἱστορίας laborare, quâ malorum arinnam, nouitates & mutationes exoptant, quas poltea venales gerunt & sæpe non petentibus obtrudunt. Unde recte Plutarchus De curiositate ait esse eam paralysin & tabem atq; renudationem rerum, non efferendarum, libidinem audiendi secreta retrusaq;, eaq; mala quibus gaudet & latatur, ex quo homo curiosus seipsum reddit odiosum, molestum, in cuius præsentia nihil dicitur vel fit, & cuius commercium vitatur. Nam sicut ventus, qui nobis pallia reuellit est molestus, ita & curiosus qui parietes detegit, fores referat, & non aliter ac ventus penetrat, irrepitque ad arcana & omnia omnium negotia scrutatur. Unde Plutarchus recte dicit, curiosum hostibus suis utilorem quam sibi. Siquidem illorum mala coargui & profert, commonstrans illis quid cauendum, corrigendumve. Pleraq; vero quæ domi geruntur, non animadvertit.
units.tr: Do not share with anyone those matters which ought not to be made known, except with those whose silence is of no less concern to you than to yourself. Isocrates, to Demonicus. Above all, nothing should be shared with the curious. For what they gladly hear, they also gladly blab; and what they eagerly gather from others, they pass on with pleasure to still others. Curious people are also accustomed to gather and heap up the slips, errors and solecisms of others' lives, and to carry about the most hateful register of evils, and to labour at gossip [ἱστορίας], longing for the misfortunes and novelties and upheavals of others, which they afterwards hawk for sale and often thrust upon people who have not asked for them. Hence Plutarch rightly says in his essay On Curiosity that it is a paralysis and a rot, and an uncovering of things that should not be divulged, a lust to hear secrets hidden away, and that they delight and rejoice in evils. By this a curious man makes himself hateful and troublesome, so that when he is present nothing is said or done, and his company is avoided. For just as a wind which tears away our cloaks is troublesome, so the curious man, who uncovers walls, unlocks doors, and, like the wind, creeps into hidden places and searches all the affairs of everyone. Hence Plutarch rightly says that the curious man is more useful to his enemies than to himself, for he exposes and brings to light their evils, showing them what must be guarded against or corrected, while he does not notice the many things that happen at home.

units.la: Qui erudit hominem deridentem, hoc est, hominem desperatæ salutis, qui oblatrat & obgrunnit verbo salutari, ac nefariè ludificatur, recipit sibi ignominiam; & qui corripit improbum, recipit sibi conuicium. Prou. c. 9. 7. 8. Ne igitur corrigas derisorem, ut non odio prosequatur te; corripe sapientem, & amabit te. Da sapienti, ut sapiat adhuc, hoc est, qui animo ita comparatus est ut recipiat sapientiam, & non derideat. Prou. c. 10. 8. Nam virga & correptio dat sapientiam. Prou. c. 29. 15. Stultum si contunderes in mortario cum mola pistillo, non recederet ab eo stultitia. Prou. c. 27. 22. Quocunq; ergo modo sapiens conetur stultum corrigere, nihil tamen efficit, sed ille inquieto animo permanet. Prov. cap. 29. 9. vbi Iun. Nam conglutinat testam, qui docet stultum & excitat dormientes e profundo somno: & narrat dormitanti, qui narrat stulto, Eccles. c. 22. 8. Sed tamen vt Seneca lib. 1. De ira, c. 14. ait, non est prudentis, errantes odisse, alioquin ipse sibi odio erit.
units.tr: He who instructs a scoffer, that is, a man past hope of salvation, who snarls and growls at a healthful word and mocks it wickedly, gets insult for himself; and he who rebukes a wicked man gets abuse for himself (Prov. 9:7-8). So do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you. Give to the wise, and he will become still wiser; that is, to one who is so disposed in mind that he receives wisdom and does not scoff (Prov. 9:8). For the rod and correction give wisdom (Prov. 29:15). If you were to crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle, his folly would not depart from him (Prov. 27:22). Whatever way a wise man tries to correct a fool, he achieves nothing, but the fool remains restless in mind (Prov. 29:9, where Junius). For he who teaches a fool glues a broken pot together, and he who tells a tale to a fool wakes sleepers from a deep sleep, and he who tells a tale to a man who is dozing (Eccles. 22:8). But as Seneca says in book 1 of On Anger, ch. 14, it is not the mark of a wise man to hate those who err, otherwise he would become a hatred to himself.

units.la: Qui recipit documentum & correptionem sapiens est. Prov. c. 10. 8. c. 12. 32. c. 12. 14. c. 13. 1. 18. 19. 20. c. 15. s. 10. 12. 31. 32. c. 19. 20. 25. 27. c. 21. 11. & qui auscultat corripienti, scientia praeditus est, Eccles. c. 10. 28. c. 20. 7. c. 21. 7. qui vero sapius correptus, obdurat cervicem suam, repente confringetur, vt non sit curatio. Prov. c. 29. 1. & peccator declinat redargutionem, & quaerit homines qui adblandiuntur sua nequitia. Eccles. c. 32. 20.
units.tr: "He who receives instruction and correction is wise" (Prov. 10:8; 12:32; 12:14; 13:1, 18-20; 15:5, 10, 12, 31-32; 19:20, 25, 27; 21:11). And he who listens to one who rebukes has understanding (Eccles. 10:28; 20:7; 21:7). But he who, often rebuked, hardens his neck will suddenly be broken, so that there is no cure (Prov. 29:1). The sinner shuns reproof and seeks men who flatter his wickedness (Eccles. 32:20).

units.la: Nunc de verbis sermonis, quae elegantia, modesta & iucunda esse debent, quibus nihil infit saporis amari, nec quae veneno quodam doloris & contumeliae sint imbuta, atque in recessu aculeos habeant. Hisce enim vtentis consortium quilibet fugit, ne a sentibus, aut tribulis pungatur, aut laedatur. Exempli gratia, quando verba alius minus acutus aut promptus, non intelligit, dicendum potius, Ego pro dignitate non possum exprimere, quam, tu me non intelligis. Item, satius ita loqui, cogitemus aliquantulum, an res se sic habeat; quam ita, Tu erras: aut, res se ita non habet: aut, tu hac non intelligis. Quod si amicus tuus solus erraverit, & errorem utriq; vestrum facere communem decorum est, hoc modo: Nos vehementer erramus, nos non sumus recordati. Ita enim satius est loqui, quam ita, si modo modo vera sunt quae dicis. Sic ubi quis non fecit, quae debebat, loquendum potius his verbis, Forte oblitus necircumuentus, meum negotium non expediuisti; aut, tu forte illud facere non potuisti. Vel, forte tibi intermentem non venit: ita, inquam, potius loquendum, quam aculeatis hisce verbis utendum; Tu non solus fidem, tu non liberasti fidem, tu fefellisti, tu mentitus es, tu non es candidus. Est enim honesta & amabilis constudo alium excusare etiam in eo, in quo intelligis iure eum culpari posse. Neq; etiam tam facile fides & existimatio aliorum in dubium vocanda.
units.tr: Now concerning the words of speech: they ought to be elegant, moderate and pleasant, with nothing bitter in their flavour, nothing steeped in a kind of poison of pain and insult, and nothing with stings hidden within. For everyone avoids the company of one who uses such words, lest he be pricked or hurt by thorns or thistles. For example, when another, who is less quick or sharp, does not understand, it is better to say, "I cannot express it as I ought," than "you do not understand me." Likewise, it is better to speak thus: "Let us think a little whether the matter is so," than thus: "You are wrong," or "the matter is not so," or "you do not understand this." But if your friend alone has erred, and it is fitting to make the error common to both of you, speak like this: "We have gone badly wrong; we did not remember." For it is better to speak thus than, "If only what you say is true." So when someone has not done what he ought, it is better to speak in these words: "Perhaps you forgot or were prevented, and so did not carry out my business," or "perhaps you could not do that." Or: "Perhaps it did not occur to you in the moment." I say it is better to speak thus than to use these stinging words: "You alone did not keep faith; you did not free faith; you deceived; you lied; you are not sincere." For it is an honourable and lovable custom to excuse another even in that where you understand he may rightly be blamed. Nor should the trust and reputation of others be called into doubt so easily.

units.la: Honestas vocabulorum consistit in eorum sono & significatione, quorum utrumq; nihil turpe aut odiosum exprimat, nihil indecorum, vel impurum. Sic meretricem, tu honestius mulierem impudicam dixeris, & pro anofeu podice, natibus ve, rectius posteriora, vel sedes, dixeris; & pro latrina aut cloaca, locum secretum; pro stercore humano excrementum; pro coitre, concumbere, vel cognoscere: ita enim Scriptura loquitur, Genef. c. 4. 1. 17. 25. ca. 6. 4. vel introire ad mulierem, Psal. 51. 1. &, pro cacare, aluum exonerare, purgare, pedes tegere, Iudic. c. 3. 34. 1. Sam. c. 24. 4. vel sedere. Deut. cap. 23. 12. 13. 14. Pro mingere, vel lotium reddere, necessitati & naturae parere, & sic in similibus.
units.tr: The honesty of words consists in their sound and meaning, and neither of these should express anything shameful or hateful, nothing indecent or impure. Thus you would more decently say "an unchaste woman" rather than "a whore"; and for the anus (podex), you should more properly say the "hinder parts" or "seat"; and for a latrine or sewer, a "private place"; for human dung, "excrement"; for coitus, "to lie with" or "to know"; for so Scripture speaks (Gen. 4:1, 17, 25; 6:4), or "to go in to a woman" (Ps. 51:1). And for defecating, "to relieve the bowels," "to purge," "to cover the feet" (Judg. 3:24; 1 Sam. 24:4), or "to sit" (Deut. 23:12-14). For urinating, "to pass water" or "to render urine," "to obey necessity and nature," and so in similar cases.

units.la: Non vtendum etiam verbis sordidis & humilioribus, quam quae rei dignitati respondent. veluti si quis amicum ac familiarem, congerronem; literarum auidum, helluonem dixerit. vid. Erasm. De cop. verb. lib. 1. cap. 11. neque inusitatis, insolentibus, priscis, obsoletis, duris, peregrinis, obscaenis, Cynicis, neque nouatis. de quibus Erasmus late d. lib. 1. c. 11. De cop. rer. & verb. quae omnia ex vsu & consuetudine hominum sunt metien-da. Phavorinus philosophus apud Gell. lib. 1. c. 10. cuidam adolescenti veterum verborum cupidissimo & plerasq; voces nimis priscas & ignotas in quotidianis sermonibus expromenti, sesquium dedit responsum: Vive morib. praeteritis, loquere verbis praesentibus, &c. vide Macrob. lib. 1. Saturn. c. 3.
units.tr: We should also not use dirty and humbler words that do not match the dignity of the subject, as when someone calls a friend and familiar a "fellow-reveller" (congerro), or a lover of letters a "glutton". See Erasmus, De copia verborum, book 1, chapter 11. Nor should we use unusual, strange, archaic, obsolete, harsh, foreign, obscene, Cynic, or newly coined words. Erasmus discusses these at length in the same book, chapter 11, De copia rerum et verborum. All of these must be judged by the usage and custom of people. Phavorinus the philosopher, in Gellius, book 1, chapter 10, replied to a young man who was very keen on old words and kept producing archaic and unknown terms in everyday conversation: "Live by the customs of the past, speak in the words of the present," etc. See Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 3.

units.la: Non vtendum tropis, tacitum tædium, nauseam, vel molestiam, vel odium norantibus; vel sensum turpem, præposterum insinuantibus; vel rei spurcæ aut obscænæ imaginationem inducentibus, vti melius, ex animo molestiam eiicere, quam euomere.
units.tr: We should not use figures of speech that show silent weariness, disgust, annoyance or hatred to those who know us, or that insinuate a base or perverse sense, or that bring to mind an image of a filthy or obscene thing. It is better to cast the annoyance out of the mind than to vomit it up.

units.la: In familiari sermone omnis affectatio oratoria, vel poetica tædiosa.
units.tr: In familiar conversation, all oratorical or poetical affectation is tiresome.

units.la: Verba loquentis sint clara, aperta, significantia, rebus adcommodata, non inuoluta, intricata, aut nimis ambitiosè huc traiecta, turbata, vel insinuata, sed bene, aptè collocata, prout vsus quotidiani sermonis exigit, vide Senec. lib. 21. Epist. 116. & lib. 20. epist. 115.
units.tr: A speaker's words should be clear, open and meaningful, fitted to the things they describe, not involved, tangled, or awkwardly and ambitiously transposed, disordered or insinuated, but well and aptly arranged, as the usage of everyday speech requires. See Seneca, Letters 116 and 115.

units.la: Genus dicendi tragicum & theatrale fugiendum; quia nimio turgens fastu, ad res ciuiles & cóuersationem inter homines est ineptum. Nimis quoq; gracile & exile fugiendum, quia nihil habet ad percellendum roboris, cum oratio nō morbo tantum carere, sed & vires habere debeat. Plutarch. de educ. liberor.
units.tr: The tragic and theatrical style is to be avoided, since it swells with excessive pomp and is unfit for civil affairs and conversation among people. The overly slender and meagre style is also to be avoided, since it has no strength to strike, whereas speech should not only be free from defect but also have vigour. Plutarch, On the Education of Children.

units.la: Non vtendum etiam abiecto, vili, plebeiove sermone, quo cerdones, baiuli & lotrices, vel infima plebs vti solet. vide Senec. d. loc. sed medio genere, quod artificiolum dicit Plutarchus de liber. educ.
units.tr: We should also not use a low, cheap or plebeian speech, such as cobblers, porters, washerwomen, or the lowest common people are accustomed to use. See Seneca, the passage cited above. Instead we should use the middle style, which Plutarch, in On the Education of Children, calls the "somewhat artful" style.

units.la: CAP. V. De pronunciatione, eiusque primo requisito.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On delivery, and its first requirement.

units.la: HVcusque de verborum conceptione. Sequitur nunc de conceptorum enunciatione: quod secundum membrum vsus sermonis diximus.
units.tr: So far on the formation of words. Now follows the utterance of what has been conceived, which we named as the second part of the use of speech.

units.la: Pronunciatio igitur alterum membrum sermonis est, quo verba concepta, tempestiue, & vocis sono congruo proferimus.
units.tr: Delivery, then, is the second part of speech, by which we utter conceived words at the right time and with a fitting sound of voice.

units.la: Pronunciationis itaque requisita duo sunt: quorum prius est, vt illa sit tempestiua. Alterum, vt sit congruo & decenti sono prolata & expressa.
units.tr: There are therefore two requirements of delivery. The first is that it be timely. The second is that it be uttered and expressed with a suitable and becoming sound.

units.la: Tempus sermonem instituendi tum opportunum est, quando eius rei, de qua dicendum est, formam animo concepisti, & auscultanti & dicenti tibi est commodum. Sic enim oratio tua erit partus legitimus, non abortus: vt opus non habeas alios interrogare in medio orationis cursu, vel teipsum corrigere, vel impingere & balbutire cum aliorum molestia. Eccl. c. 18. 20. & 11. 8. Prou. c. 18. 13. c. 33. 4.
units.tr: The time for beginning a discourse is opportune when you have formed in your mind the shape of the matter you are to speak about, and when both the listener and yourself are free for it. For your speech will then be a lawful birth, not a miscarriage, so that you have no need to ask others questions in the middle of your discourse, to correct yourself, or to stumble and stammer, to the annoyance of others. Eccl. c. 18. 20. & 11. 8. Prou. c. 18. 13. c. 33. 4.

units.la: Tempestiua igitur enunciatio est, quae primo auscultanti adfert commodum, non taedium, molestiam, pudorem, vel iracundiam procreat. Deinde, quae dicenti seu proferenti gratiam, nō suspicionem vel praeiudicium generat.
units.tr: Therefore an utterance is timely if it first brings convenience to the listener, not tedium, annoyance, embarrassment or anger. Then, it is timely if it wins favour for the speaker or utterer, and does not give rise to suspicion or prejudice.

units.la: De utroque genere tempestiue pronunciationis sunt accipienda dicta. 1. Chron. c. 2. 32. Et e filiis Issachar qui noscentes scite tempora, vt nosce-rent Israelita quid sibi faciendum esset. Esther c. 1. 13. Quapropter dicente sibi faciendum esset. Rege sapientibus noscentibus tempora, &c. Prouerb. c.25.11. Velut mala aurea cum figuris argenteis, est verbum dictum commode & tempestiue, habita temporis, loci & auscultantium ratione. & c. 15.23. nam res suo tempore dicta, o quam bona! Esaiae cap. 50.4. Dedit mihi Dominus linguam eruditissimam, ut sciam tempestiue eloqui defessō verbum, &c. Eccles. c.20.21. Ab ore stulti prolata parabola reprobatur, nequaquam enim eam dicit tempore suo. Iacob.c.1.19. Omnis homo sit velox ad audiendum, tardus ad loquendum, Eccles. c.5.13. cum tolerantia responsionem rectam eloquere, 14. Si tibi est intelligentia, responde to proximo; sin minus, manus tua super os tuum esto, & c.41.20. Verecundia quilibet moueatur, non enim bonum est, omnem pudorem conseruare, neq; omnia omnibus probantur, & verf.19. Praestat homo abscondens stultitiam suam hominis abscondenti sapientiam suam.
units.tr: What has been said must be understood of both kinds of timely utterance. 1 Chron. c. 2. 32. And of the sons of Issachar, who knew well the times, so that the Israelites might know what ought to be done. Esther c. 1. 13. Therefore, when the king's wise men, who knew the times, etc., said what ought to be done for him. Proverbs c. 25. 11: As golden apples in settings of silver, so is a word spoken fitly and in good time, with regard to the occasion, the place and the hearers. And c. 15. 23: a word spoken in its season, oh how good! Isaiah c. 50. 4: The Lord has given me the tongue of the learned, that I may know how to speak a word in season to him who is weary, etc. Ecclesiasticus c. 20. 21: A parable uttered from the mouth of a fool is rejected, for he does not speak it in its season. James c. 1. 19: Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak. Ecclesiasticus c. 5. 13: speak a right answer with patience. 14: If you have understanding, answer your neighbour; if not, put your hand over your mouth. And c. 41. 20: Let a man be moved by shame, for it is not good to keep every kind of shame, nor is everything approved for everyone. And verse 19: Better is the man who hides his folly than the man who hides his wisdom.

units.la: Silentium moderatum & tempestiuum, signum est pudoris, verecundiae & modestiae. Sermo tempestiuus, index animi prudentis. Vide Plutarch. in libello, περὶ τῆς ἀδολεσχίας. Contra nullum potus vel cibus non debito modo apparatus, tam insuauis est, quam sermo ἀκαιρῶν καὶ ἀσόντων, ut ait idem Plutarch. Problem. 1. Sympos.
units.tr: A silence that is measured and timely is a sign of modesty, shame and courtesy. Timely speech is the mark of a prudent mind. See Plutarch in his little book, On Talkativeness [περὶ τῆς ἀδολεσχίας]. On the other hand, no drink or food, if it is not prepared in the proper way, is as unpleasant as speech [out of season and out of measure, ἀκαιρῶν καὶ ἀσόντων], as the same Plutarch says in Problems 1, Symposiacs.

units.la: Considerare etiam oportet, ne imprudens, iis qui risus aut contumeliae causa ad sermones prouocant, respondeas serio. Ideoque non cito ad sermones prosiliendum, sed interro-gantis mores & necessitatem contemplari con-uenit. Et, si apparet, quod interrogans reuera velit dicere, adsuefaciamus nos responsum re-primere, interuallum aliquod facientes inter quæstionem & responsionem, quo interro-gans, siquid velit, adiicere possit; quique inter-rogatur, consideret quid respondeat & non præcurrat, neque obruat responsionem. Non raro etiam solet accidere vt præ festinatione interrogantibus alia pro aliis demus responsa. Quin etiam impetus & fames sermonis acris retundenda est, ne videatur veluti fluentum iam olim linguæ obsistens libenter ab interro-gatione educi.
units.tr: One must also consider, lest you carelessly answer in earnest those who provoke speech for the sake of laughter or insult. Therefore one should not leap quickly into speech, but ought to weigh the character and the need of the questioner. And if it appears that the questioner really wants to say something, let us accustom ourselves to hold back the answer, leaving some interval between question and answer, so that the questioner may add anything he wishes; and let the one questioned consider what he is going to answer, and not run ahead nor overwhelm the answer. It also often happens, through haste, that we give one answer in place of another to those who ask. Indeed, the eager and sharp appetite for speech must be checked, lest it seem, like a stream long held back, to be drawn out gladly by the question.

units.la: Sunt autem tria genera respondendi ad in-terrogationes. Vnum, necessarium; vti si inter-rogetur quis, an sit intus Socrates: ibi inuitus cogitur respondere, non est intus. Alterum, est humanum, vti si respondeat, non est intus, sed apud trapezitas agens ibidem, &c. Tertium, est superfluum, vti, non est intus, sed apud trapezitas, hospites ex Ionia exspectans, pro quibus illi scripsit Alcibiades, &c. ex quo gar-rulus molestus fit. vide Plutarchum, De garrulitate.
units.tr: There are, moreover, three kinds of answering to questions. One is necessary: as when someone asks whether Socrates is inside, and one is forced, against one's will, to answer, "He is not inside." Another is human: as when one answers, "He is not inside, but is at the bankers' with some business," and so on. The third is superfluous: as, "He is not inside, but is at the bankers', waiting for guests from Ionia, for whom Alcibiades wrote to him," and so on, from which a person becomes a tiresome chatterbox. See Plutarch, On Talkativeness.

units.la: Sermonem tuum in alterius loquentis ora-tionem & pronuntiationem ne immittas. Eccles.cap. 11.8. Molesta enim est consuetudo, alterius verba quæ in ore habet, obstrependo interrumpere. Eccles.c.18.16. quod quidem tanto-pere ei qui id patitur, placet, quanto pere placeret, si aliquis te pleno cursu ad metam contendentem dentem subito retraheret. Neque enim conue-nit vt alio quopiam loquente, ruvel nouialiquid monstrando, vel praesentium attentionem aliorsum se vocando, efficias vt ab auditoribus negleͣctus deseratur. neque enim decet, vt tu eum, qui non a te, sed a loquente est inuitatus, demittas. Addo, quod qui auscultando sunt impatientes, iudicando fiant temerarii.
units.tr: Do not thrust your speech into the speech and delivery of another speaker. Ecclesiasticus 11. 8. For it is an annoying habit to interrupt another's words that are in his mouth by clamouring over him. Ecclesiasticus 18. 16. This is as pleasing to the one who suffers it as it would be if someone, while you were racing at full stride towards the goal, suddenly pulled you back by the tooth. For it is not fitting, while someone else is speaking, to bring about, by showing some novelty or by calling the attention of those present elsewhere, that he is neglected and deserted by his listeners. Nor is it proper for you to dismiss the one who has been invited not by you but by the speaker. I add that those who are impatient in listening become rash in judging.

units.la: Nequaquam igitur aliorum sermo interceptus, interrumpendus ex insatiabili dicendi ingluie, sicuti videmus in rusticorum fimetis, pullos gallinaceos, aliis ex roftellis grana praeripere; nisi forte priuatus quis sit affectus, inhibitionem requirens, aut morbus admonitionis egens.
units.tr: Therefore, a speech that has been begun by others must not be interrupted out of an insatiable gluttony for talking, as we see in the dunghills of country folk, where the cockerels snatch grains from one another's beaks, unless perhaps someone is affected by some private matter that calls for a hearing, or by an illness that needs a warning.

units.la: Neque etiam quando quis in loquendo est tardior, is anteuertendus, aut verba eidem suppediranda: tanquam tu opulentus, ille vero egenus videatur.
units.tr: Nor, when someone is slower in speaking, should he be hurried along, or words be supplied to him, as if you appeared rich and he needy.

units.la: In diebus & tempore publicae laetitiae, non recitentur historiae melancholicae, aut tragoe-diae: nihil de morte, morbis; de furum, praedonum, piratarum & venef icarum extremis & capitalibus supplicis, & quibusuis aliis auditoribus horrorem incutientibus & hilarita-ti repugnantibus. Nam vt musicorum sonorum in luctu narratio intempestiua est, Ecclesiastic. cap. 22. verf. 6. Sic concentus musicorum tempore laetitiae instar carbunculi est, Ecclesiastic. cap. 32. 6, 7. Et vt qui imponit sibi vestem tempore frigoris, aut acetum nitro, ita est qui canit cantica apud animum male affectum: Prouerb. 25. 20. adde Iacob. 4. 5. 13. Est enim tempus ridendi, tempus plangendi & tempus saltandi, Ecclesiast.c.3.4. Flendum enim cum flentibus & gaudendum cum gaudentibus, Roman. c.12.15. Quando itaque accurata scientia agitur, mu-sicos etiam modulos impedi, ubi est concentus, ne ef-fundas eloquium, neq; intempestiue agas sapientem, Ecclesiast.c.32.s.6. & feria aliis agentibus non tuio-ceris aut nugas agas, & contra. Nemo libenter tristi conuersatur, nedum tristitia, vt Senec.lib.16.epist.100. & contra, omni tempore laetis & iocantibus.
units.tr: On days and at times of public rejoicing, no melancholy stories or tragedies are to be recited: nothing about death or diseases, nothing about the extreme and capital punishments of thieves, robbers, pirates and poisoners, and nothing else that strikes horror into the hearers and is opposed to cheerfulness. For just as the narration of musical sounds in mourning is out of season, Ecclesiasticus c. 22, verse 6. So the harmony of musicians in a time of joy is like a carbuncle, Ecclesiasticus c. 32. 6, 7. And as one who puts on a garment in cold weather, or vinegar on nitre, so is one who sings songs to a heart that is ill-disposed: Proverbs 25. 20. Add James 4. 5. 13. For there is a time to laugh, a time to mourn, and a time to dance, Ecclesiastes c. 3. 4. For we must weep with those who weep, and rejoice with those who rejoice, Romans c. 12. 15. Therefore, when serious learning is under way, hold back even the musical tunes where there is harmony, lest you pour out words, or play the wise man out of season, Ecclesiasticus c. 32. 6, and on a holiday do not keep silent when others are at work, nor play the fool; and the reverse. No one willingly keeps company with the sad, still less with sadness, as Seneca says in Letter 100 of Book 16; and conversely, one should always be with the cheerful and the jesting.

units.la: De rebus personis audientibus contrariis etiam loquimur, quando in praesentia suspectarum personarum de pudicitia Lucretiae, vel Iosephi castitate, sermo instituitur: aut in praesentia deformium, corpore vitiosorum vel mutilatorum, de Therfite disputatur; aut in conuentu militum, de vitiis Thrasonis disseritur; velin consessu anicularum, disseritur de modestia adhibenda in choreis, vel de iucundo matrimonio & pie educandis liberis.
units.tr: We also speak in ways that clash with the hearers. When a discussion is started in the presence of people under suspicion, about the chastity of Lucretia or the purity of Joseph, or in the presence of deformed people, those with bodily defects or mutilations, we discuss Thersites. In a gathering of soldiers we discourse on the vices of Thraso, and in a gathering of old women we discuss the modesty to be kept at dances, or a happy marriage and the pious upbringing of children.

units.la: Risus quoque intempestiuus grauis auditu est, & vt Menander dixit, γέλως ἀκαίρῳ ἐν βεγμῆ δεινὸν πάγχυ.
units.tr: Untimely laughter is also unpleasant to hear, and as Menander said, "laughter at an unseasonable time in a serious matter is utterly dreadful" [γέλως ἀκαίρῳ ἐν βεγμῆ δεινὸν πάγχυ].

units.la: Risus vero neq; multus sit, neque ob multa, neque solutus & effusus. Ecclesiast. c. 21. & c.7. Ergo neque semper est ridendum, neque omnibus, neq; apud quoslibet, neque propter omnia, neq; omni in loco, sed diligens & accurata est & personarum, & rerum & loci, & temporis habenda ratio. Vide Clem. Alex. lib.2. Paedag.c.5. Nam omnibus dictis & factis arridere, stultorum est; nullis arridere stupidorum. Isocrates ad Demon. Neq; inter ridicula seriis, neq; inter seria ridiculis gaudeas. Intempestivum enim ubi, est molestum.
units.tr: Laughter should be neither frequent, nor over many things, nor loose and unrestrained (Ecclesiasticus 21 and 7). So one should not always laugh, nor at everyone, nor in front of anyone, nor at everything, nor in every place. Instead, careful and exact attention must be paid to the persons, the matter, the place and the time. See Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2.5. For to smile at everything said and done is the mark of fools, and to smile at nothing is the mark of dullards. Isocrates to Demonicus: do not take delight in jokes during serious matters, nor in serious matters during jokes. For what is untimely is annoying wherever it occurs.

units.la: Garrulus, si quis sermo incidit, nude discere aliquid & audire queat, quae nescie bat, cum relicit & repellit, mercedem sibi paruam silendo dare non valens: circumiens autem in gyro in veteres ac detritos centones sermonem impellit de iis rebus, quibus delectatur, vel in quibus valet scientia & alios excellere se putat. Plutarch. De garrulitat. in sin. Macrob. lib. 7. c. 2. Saturnal.
units.tr: A chatterbox, if any conversation arises, cannot simply learn or hear something he did not know. He breaks in and rejects it, unable to give himself the small reward of silence. Instead he goes round and round, driving the talk back onto old, worn-out patches, onto the things he enjoys or in which he thinks he has skill and surpasses others. Plutarch, On Talkativeness, near the end; Macrobius, Saturnalia 7.2.

units.la: Alienaa professione alicuius, ab eodem ne quaeras. Praebes enim suspicionem malignitatis & odii. Neque multa, neque frequenter quaerenda: quod signum ostentationis & superbiae.
units.tr: Do not ask a man about another's profession when that man is the one concerned. For this gives grounds for suspicion of malice and hatred. Nor should one ask many things or ask often, since that is a sign of showing off and pride.

units.la: Audiente quoque stolido ne loquaris, Eccles. 23. 9. Prov. c. 23. 9. Nam sermo intelligentiae stulto ingratus est, Prov. c. 17. 7. Apud senes etiam ne multa dicas, Eccl. c. 32. 12. c. 7. 13.
units.tr: Do not speak even in the hearing of a fool (Ecclesiasticus 23:9; Proverbs 23:9). For speech is unwelcome to a foolish man who lacks understanding (Proverbs 17:7). Nor should you say much before old men (Ecclesiasticus 32:12; 7:13).

units.la: Qui balbus est, blaesus aut raucus, prae aliis omnibus garrulus & vocalis esse non debet, sed potius linguae suae defectum silentio & auscultatione tegere.
units.tr: Whoever stammers, lisps or is hoarse should not be more talkative or vocal than everyone else. Rather, he should cover the defect of his tongue by silence and by listening.

units.la: In reprehensionibus, ut decorae & civiles sint, considerandae sunt res & personae. Res, ut talis sit, quae reprehensionem mereatur; quod ex aliis artibus iudicandum. Persona vero reprehendentis & reprehendendi. In persona reprehendente requiritur, 1. innocentia & integritas. 2. forma & modus iustus reprehendendi: & 3. tempus. Ideo recte dicitur, Prius cognoscendum, & tum increpandum. Eccles. c. 11. 7. & c. 19. 28.
units.tr: In rebukes, to make them proper and courteous, the matter and the persons must be considered. The matter must be such as deserves rebuke, which is to be judged by the standards of other disciplines. The persons must be considered, both the one rebuking and the one rebuked. In the one rebuking, three things are required: (1) innocence and integrity; (2) a just form and manner of rebuking; and (3) timing. Hence it is rightly said: first know, and then rebuke (Ecclesiasticus 11:7; 19:28).

units.la: Integritas & innocentia reprehendentis in eo consistit, ut ipse se excutiat, ne huius vitii, cu-
units.tr: The integrity and innocence of the one rebuking consist in this: he should examine himself, so that he cannot be charged with the very fault of which he wishes to accuse another.

units.la: F ius alium arguere vult, argui possit. Psalm.141. 5. corrigat me iustus & erit mihi unguentum praestantissimum, &c. vbi lautius. Et Plut. de lib. educ. aut; Quorum vita turpis est, u obiurgandi libertatem sibi adimant: & reprehendentes alios, seipsos accusant. Quod si vero ipse reprehensor est culpae reus, vel moribus non integris, conuenit ut se quoque culpae admisceat, quomodo benevolus videtur, & fides illi habetur in iis, quibus seipsum corrigit, & se ingenue fatetur obnoxium, & magis penetrant in affectus, & magis credunt homines iis, qui communibus tanguntur affectibus. Corripiens vero qui seipsum tactat quasi liber & immunis a vitiis omnibus sit, grauis & molestus cotemptor habetur. Plutarch. de discr. adulat. & amici. Matth. c.7.3 4.5. & c.5.7. Hypocrita, eice primum trabem illam ex oculo tuo, & tum dispicies ut eicias festucam ex oculo fratris tui, Luc. c.6.41.42. Ioh. c.8.7. 1. Timoth. c.3.2. Tit. c.1.6. & Seneca De moribus, nihil turpius quam sibi obiicendum, alteri obicere, juxta illud Catonis, Turpe est doctori cum culpa redarguit ipsum.
units.tr: Psalm 141:5: "Let the righteous correct me, and it shall be an excellent ointment to me," and so on, where it is more fully treated. Plutarch, On the Education of Children: those whose lives are shameful take away from themselves the freedom to rebuke, and when they rebuke others they accuse themselves. But if the rebuker himself is guilty of a fault, or is not of upright morals, it is fitting that he also include himself in the fault. In this way he appears kindly, and he is trusted by those whom he corrects by including himself, and who sees himself as liable to fault. Such a man penetrates the feelings more deeply, and people believe those who are touched by the same feelings as themselves. But one who rebukes while treating himself as if he were free and immune from all faults is regarded as a harsh and annoying censor. Plutarch, On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend. Matthew 7:3–5; 5:7. "Hypocrite, first cast out the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to cast out the speck from your brother's eye" (Luke 6:41–42). John 8:7; 1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6. Seneca, On Morals: nothing is more shameful than to object to another what is objected to oneself, in line with Cato's saying: "It is a shame for a teacher to rebuke another for a fault he has himself."

units.la: Deinde corrigens semper ignoscere prius debet alii erranti: sibi vero nunquam. Qualis enim est iudex, talis est quoq; minister & subditus, Eccl. c.10.2.
units.tr: Further, the one rebuking must always be ready to pardon the erring other, but never himself. For as the judge is, so too are the minister and the subject (Ecclesiasticus 10:2).

units.la: Deniq; admonentis & reprehendentis munus est, offensam ex admonitione natam inde recipere.
units.tr: Finally, it is the duty of the one who admonishes and rebukes to bear calmly the offence that arises from the admonition.

units.la: Forma & modus reprehendendi ciuilis est, quo increpatio secundum personarum, quibus fit, qualitates, temperatur, vt fiat benevole, humaniter, fraterne, paterne, reuerenter, Christiane, ex amore fideque sincera, cum spiritu manmansuetudinis & lenitatis, & συμπαθείας, non cupidè, affectatè & ἐπιχαριτικῶς, sed cum dolore. Isocrat. ad Demon. Neq; fueris cupidus culpandi, quia grave est; vel castigandi, quia est acerbum: neq; sis contentiosus & contumax in admonendo.
units.tr: The form and manner of rebuking is civil when the reproof is tempered according to the qualities of the persons to whom it is given, so that it is done kindly, humanely, brotherly, fatherly, respectfully and Christianly, out of love and sincere faith, with a spirit of gentleness and mildness and sympathy, not eagerly, affectedly or flatteringly, but with sorrow. Isocrates to Demonicus: do not be eager to find fault, because it is burdensome, or to punish, because it is harsh; nor be contentious and stubborn in admonishing.

units.la: Neq; libertas admonendi vulgo iactanda & circumferenda, sed ad iuuandum & sanandum proximum eâ duntaxat vtamur.
units.tr: The freedom to admonish is not to be boasted of or spread about among the common people. Rather, we should use it only to help and heal our neighbour.

units.la: Neque coram pluribus quis reprehendendus. Nam peccati detectionem, quae sit reprehendendo, secretam esse conuenit, clandestinam, priuatam & verecundam; quae ex alienis erratis gloriam non captet, Plut. De discr. adulat. & amici.
units.tr: No one should be rebuked in the presence of many. For the disclosure of a sin, which is what rebuke is, ought to be private, secret, personal and modest, and should not seek glory from another's errors. Plutarch, On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend.

units.la: In genere vitia sunt perstringenda in persona tertii, vt fecit Nathan in Dauidis reprehensione. 2. Sam. c. 12. & in genere omnes senes, vt patres, & iuuenes, vt fratres monendi. 1. Tim. c. 5. 1. 2.
units.tr: In general, faults should be censured in the person of a third party, as Nathan did in rebuking David (2 Samuel 12). And in general, elders should be admonished as fathers, and young men as brothers (1 Timothy 5:1–2).

units.la: Neque etiam conuenit non inficiantes acerbius coarguere, neque obsistere sese purgantibus, sed potius excusandi occasiones quasuis admittere & à peioribus caussis abstinere ad hoc, vt leuius peccasse videatur admonendus: vt, Ignorasti, potius dicendū quam iniuriam fecisti, &c. Plutarch. d. loco. Neq; purgandi sui potestas adimenda, sed in argumentis honesti praetextus excogitandis adiuuand² est: & causa deteriore omissa, tolerabiliores suggerendae. Senec. lib. 7. De benef. Admonitio interueniat, quae non poscat nec in ius vocet, & lib. 2. De benef. Admonitio taedium facit, exprobratio odium, 2. Timoth. cap. 2. 24. Seruum autem Domini non oportet pugnare, sed placidum esse erga omnes, aptum ad docen-dum, tolerantem malos, 2 s. cum lenitate erudientem eos qui contrario animo sunt affecti. &c.
units.tr: It is also not fitting to censure harshly those who do not deny their fault, nor to oppose those who defend themselves. Rather, one should grant any opportunities for excuse and refrain from more serious charges, so that the one admonished may seem to have sinned more lightly. For example, it is better to say "You did not know" than "You did wrong," and so on. Plutarch, in the same place. Nor should the power of defending oneself be taken away, but one should help the other to devise honourable pretexts, and set aside the worse cause and suggest more tolerable ones. Seneca, On Benefits 7: let an admonition come in that does not demand or summon to court. And On Benefits 2: admonition causes weariness, reproach causes hatred. 2 Timothy 2:24–25: "The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, apt to teach, patient with the evil, correcting with gentleness those who are opposed, and so on.

units.la: Inprimis etiam hic cauendum is qui obiurgant, ne post obiurgationem monitum destitu-ant; neue committant, vt ita contristent & irritent familiares, vt ea res finiat consuetudinem & familiaritatem, vt ait Plutarch. d. loco. Sed potius aliis colloquiis & sermonibus lenibus demulceant ac recreent. Quare obseruandum ne verbis amicum castigantes, colloquium veibis molestiam afferentibus & irritantibus abrumpentes, discedamus, Galat. c. 6. 1. Instaurate huiusmodi hominem cum spiritu mansuetudinis, considerans temetipsum, ne & tu quandoque tenteris, 2. Tim. c. 4. 2. Exhortare cum omni lenitate & doctrina, 1. Thess. c. 5. 14. Patientes estote erga omnes, 1. Timoth. c. 5. 1. 2. Seniorem ne increpato, sed hortare ut patrem, & seqq. verf. De qua forma admonendi & reprehendi exempla & praecepta vide latius Iacob. cap. 3. 1. Ne estote multi Doctores, fratres mei, scientes forte graviius iudicium auferamus, 1. Iohann. c. 2. 1. 7. 12. 13. 14. Levit. c. 19. 17. 18. Proverb. c. 1. 20. c. 9. 7. cap. 10. 17. c. 12. 1. c. 13. 1. c. 15. 31. Matth. c. 18. 15. & seqq. 1. Sam. c. 25. 37. Gen. c. 19. 7. cap. 37. 2. Exod. cap. 2. 12. c. 18. 14. 1. Sam. c. 24. 15. 16. 2. Sam. c. 2. 21. 22. Nehem. c. 5. 7. Daniel cap. 5. 22. & passim alibi. Ita verecundi serui dominum Nahaman reprehenderunt 2. Reg. c. 5. 15. 23. Ideo Seneca recte: Alienorum vitiorum neque curiosus scrutator, neque acerbus reprehensor, sed sint exprobratione reprehensi: ita vt admonitionem hilaritate praeuenias & errori facile veniam des. Nam, vt pressura lactis educit butyrum, & pressura nasi educit sansanguinem, ita pressura irarum educit litem, ut Sapientiae Prouerb. c. 30. 33. & velut monile aureum & ornamentum ex insigni auro est reprehensor sapiens, Eccl. c. 1. 24.
units.tr: Here especially, those who rebuke must take care not to abandon the one they admonish after the rebuke, nor to allow the rebuke to so sadden and provoke their friends that it ends the friendship and familiarity, as Plutarch says in the same place. Rather they should soothe and refresh them with other conversations and gentle talk. Hence we must take care not to end the conversation abruptly, while rebuking a friend with words that cause pain and provoke. "Brethren, if a man is overtaken in a fault, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you too be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). "Reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all patience and teaching" (2 Timothy 4:2). "Exhort with all gentleness and teaching" (1 Thessalonians 5:14). "Be patient toward all" (1 Timothy 5:1–2). "Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father," and what follows in that verse (1 Timothy 5). For examples and precepts on this manner of admonishing and rebuking, see more fully James 3:1; 1 John 2:1; 7, 12–14; Leviticus 19:17–18; Proverbs 1:20; 9:7; 10:17; 12:1; 13:1; 15:31; Matthew 18:15ff.; 1 Samuel 25:37; Genesis 19:7; 37:2; Exodus 2:12; 18:14; 1 Samuel 24:15–16; 2 Samuel 2:21–22; Nehemiah 5:7; Daniel 5:22; and elsewhere. So the modest servants of Naaman rebuked their master (2 Kings 5:15, 23). Hence Seneca rightly says: be neither a curious searcher into the vices of others nor a bitter reprover, but let the reproached be rebuked by reproach; so anticipate admonition with cheerfulness and readily grant pardon for error. For as pressing milk brings out butter, and pressing the nose brings out blood, so pressing anger brings out strife, as in Proverbs 30:33. And a wise rebuker is like a golden necklace and an ornament of fine gold (Ecclesiasticus 1:24).

units.la: Quapropter in reprehensionibus honestum est reprehensionis amaritudinem, laudis alicuius dulcedine & lenitate miscere; aut ostendere, nos alios culpare ob eosdem defectus vel excessus, quibus is, quem corrigere cupimus, laborat; aut vero nos ipsos etiam arguamus, inuentes eidem errori nos quandoque obnoxios. 1. Corinth. c. 4. 6. hæc autem fratres mei propter vos proposui sub exemplo meo & Apollo ut in nobis discatis non sapere supra id quod scriptum est. Plutarch. de lib. educat. Clem. Alexandrin. libr. 2. Pædagog. c. 7.
units.tr: Therefore, in rebukes it is proper to mingle the bitterness of the reproof with the sweetness and gentleness of some praise; or to show that we blame others for the same faults or excesses that afflict the one we wish to correct; or indeed that we also accuse ourselves, finding that we too are sometimes liable to the same error. 1 Corinthians 4:6: "These things, brethren, I have set forth in a figure in my own person and Apollos', for your sakes, that in us you might learn not to think beyond what is written." Plutarch, On the Education of Children; Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, book 2, ch. 7.

units.la: Per id quod non adest, id quod adest reprehendere conuenit, aut sub aliena persona castigare, ut Plutar. d. loco ait. Vnde Seneca de moribus Obiurgationi semper aliquid blande admisce. Facilius enim penetrant verba quae molli vadunt via, quam asperà. In summa itaq; alius ita corrigendus, ut sit grata correctio; eaq; emendatum nobis obligatum reddat, neq; videatur corrigens cupidus vanae cuiusdam praestantiae aut dignitatis, arrogantiae, aut diffamationis cuiusque in correctum. Elegans huius reprehensionis exemplum extat 1. Sam. cap. 25. 25. & seqq. Vbi Abigail prudenter Danidis temeritatem & vindictæ cupiditatem corrigit. Et aliud iudic. c. 8. 1. 2. 3. vbi Gideon arrogantiam & ambitionem Ephraimitarum tacite reprehendit, aliud 2. Samuel. c. 14. & Galat. c. 3. Actor. c. 19. Plutarch. De liberor. educat. Conuenit, inquit seueritatem & acerbitatem reprehensionis lenitate temperare, ut medici amara medicamenta dulcibus succis permisceat, quo accessum inveniant: & De discrim. adulat. & amici, ait; Laus leniter admiscenda reprehensioni, quae asperitas illius corrigatur, & aemulatio significatur erga seipsum, ut secum ipse certet, dum honestè factorum commemoratione turpium pudefcit, & ob id fe meliorem exemplum praestare studet. Sanè qui laude potius, quàm reprehensione ad mores emendandos utitur libere, maximè monet & offendit minime, & sanat maximè. Plut. De discrim. adulat. & amici.
units.tr: It is fitting to rebuke what is present in the absence of the person, or to chastise under another's name, as Plutarch says in the same place. Hence Seneca, On Morals: always add something gentle to a rebuke, for words that go by a soft path penetrate more easily than harsh ones. In sum, another should be corrected in such a way that the correction is welcome, and leaves the one corrected obliged to us; and the corrector should not seem to be eager for some vain pre-eminence or dignity, for arrogance, or for any defaming of the one corrected. An elegant example of this kind of rebuke is in 1 Samuel 25:25 and following, where Abigail prudently corrects David's rashness and desire for revenge. Another is Judges 8:1-3, where Gideon quietly rebukes the arrogance and ambition of the Ephraimites; another is 2 Samuel 14, and Galatians 3, and Acts 19. Plutarch, On the Education of Children: it is fitting, he says, to temper the severity and harshness of rebuke with gentleness, as a physician mixes bitter medicines with sweet juices so that they may be received. And in On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend he says: praise is to be mixed gently into rebuke, so that its harshness is corrected, and a rivalry is shown towards oneself, so that one contends with oneself, while by recalling honourable deeds one shames base ones, and so strives to set a better example. Indeed, he who uses praise rather than rebuke to amend manners, freely, most of all admonishes, offends least, and heals best. Plutarch, On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend.

units.la: Quod si tamen manuetudo reprehendetis ferociorem redderet reprehensum, ut Benadadus respondeo placido Achabi efferebatur. 1. Reg. c. 20. tunc secundum eorum superbiam & stultitiam ipsi respondendum, ut Iephte fecit. Judic. c. 11. & praecipitur Eccl. c. 17.
units.tr: But if gentleness would make the rebuked person more fierce, as Ben-hadad was puffed up by Ahab's mild answer (1 Kings 20), then one must answer him according to his pride and folly, as Jephthah did (Judges 11); and Ecclesiasticus 17 so commands.

units.la: Tempus reprehendendi idoneum censerent illud, quo corrigendus est admissurus facilius correctionem vel admonitionem. Nam in reversa, ut ait Seneca, crudelis est obiurgatio, & in ebrietate hominis corrigendi, ira & furore, vel pertinacia. Est enim tempus curandi, tempus loquendi, silendi, tempus amandi & odio habendi, tempus belli & tempus pacis, ut ait Eccles. c. 3. 5. 7. 8. Et honestè serviit qui tempori serviit. Eccles. c. 19. 28. Est redargutio quae intempestiva est; & qui tacet eam, is quoque prudens est.
units.tr: Those who thought about it considered the proper time for rebuking to be when the one to be corrected is more likely to accept correction or admonition. For, as Seneca says, a rebuke is cruel when a man is in a fit of anger, and when a man who is to be corrected is drunk, it arouses rage, fury, or obstinacy. There is a time for healing and a time for speaking, a time for silence, a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace, as Ecclesiastes 3:5, 7, 8 says. And he who serves the occasion serves honourably (Ecclesiasticus 19:28). A rebuke given at the wrong time is useless, and he who keeps silent about it is also wise.

units.la: In rebus adversis crudelis est obiurgatio, ideo, quia adflicto adderet afflictionem, & charitatis expers esset, quae iubet esse flendum cum flentibus. Rom. c. 12. 15. eosque erigendos esse. Hinc Plutarch. De discrim. adulat. & amici, rectè ait, res afflictorum non recipere obiurgandi libertatem, aut sententisententia dictionem, sed humanitatem & subsidium desiderare.
units.tr: In adversity, rebuke is cruel, because it adds affliction to one who is afflicted, and lacks charity, which bids us weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), and raise up those who are cast down. Hence Plutarch, On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend, rightly says that the affairs of the afflicted do not admit the liberty of rebuke or the pronouncing of a sentence, but desire humanity and help.

units.la: Quod si tamen petulantia sua sibi malum quis attraxit, praesertim cum de illo cauendo aliquoties fuit admonitus, grauiter, non tamen acerbè talis admoneri debet, ut cogitet se sibi tale malum attraxisse, & proinde agnoscat iustam Dei gubernationem, quae tamen iis qui diligunt eum, omnia ad bonum conferat.
units.tr: But if someone has brought evil upon himself by his own wantonness, especially when he has been warned several times to guard against it, he should be admonished in a serious but not harsh manner, so that he may reflect that he has brought such evil upon himself, and so acknowledge God's just government, which nonetheless works all things for good for those who love him.

units.la: In ebrio reprehensio & obiurgatio intempestiva est ideo, quia non aedificat, sed crabrones irritat. vide Plutarchum De garrulitate & De discrimine adulator. & amici, vbi dicit hinc oriri tam laetitiae privationem & hilaritatis ac obleetationis ademptionem. Ideoque reprehendenti ebrium, Non pudet te ebrietatis foetidae? recte ab ebrio responsum dicitur; Non pudet te ebrium hominem reprehendere? Et Eccles. c. 31. 35. praecipit: In conuiuio vinosso neredarguas propinquum, neque facias eum nihil in latitia sua. 36 Sermonem probrosum ne dixeris, neque arguas eum obseruantem tibi. Prou. c 20.1. Deriso est vinum tumultuosus potus inebrians. Cuius exemplum extat 1. Sam. c. 25. 36. Ecce conuiuium erat Nabal domi, in quo animus eius laetus erat, adeo ut pervalde ebrius esset. Quamobrem illa non indicavit ei quicquam parui aut magni usque in lucem matutinam. & v. 37. Sed fuit mane, cum abiisset crapula a Nabale & indicaret ei uxor eius res istas, ut obstupuerit animus eius.
units.tr: Rebuke and reproof of a drunk man is out of place, because it does not build up but stirs up hornets. See Plutarch, On Garrulity and On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend, where he says that from this arises the loss of joy and the taking away of cheerfulness and pleasure. Therefore, to a drunk man who is being rebuked, the reply is rightly given: "Are you not ashamed of your foul drunkenness?" and the drunk may answer: "Are you not ashamed to reprove a drunken man?" And Ecclesiasticus 31:35-36 commands: "Do not rebuke your neighbour at a drinking party, nor make him anything in his merriment. Do not speak a reproachful word, nor reproach him who is watching you." Proverbs 20:1: "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging." An example is in 1 Samuel 25:36: "Now Nabal had a feast in his house, like the feast of a king, and his heart was merry, for he was very drunk; therefore she told him nothing, small or great, until the morning light." And verse 37: "But in the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him."

units.la: Eodem modo obiurgatio intempestiva in furore vel ira concitato & occupato homine, quae apud eum locum non habet. Isocrates ad Demon. Eris autem comis, si neque iurgator sis, neque implacid^o, neque cum omnibus contendas, neq; ira eorum cum-quibus agis, celeriter occurras, neque si iniuste quidem fuerint irati, sed efferuescentibus concedas, deinde ipsos vbi relanguerit, reprehendas. Eccles. c. 8. 4. Ne contendas cum homine verbosó, neque exaggeres ad ignem illius ligna. 13. Ne in endas carbones peccatoris, ne comburaris igne flammante illius. 19. Cum iracundo ne ineas certamen, ac ne facias cum eo iter solutarium. Ita enim videtur sanguis in oculis ipsius, quasi nihil esset, & vbi non est auxilium, ibi deficiet te.
units.tr: In the same way, rebuke is out of place when a man is stirred up with anger or fury and is preoccupied, since such a man has no room for it. Isocrates, To Demonicus: You will be agreeable if you are neither quarrelsome nor implacable, if you do not contend with everyone, and if you do not rush to meet the anger of those you deal with; nor, if they are angry without cause, should you yield to them while they boil over, but rebuke them once they have cooled down. Ecclesiasticus 8: "Do not contend with a talkative man, nor heap wood on his fire" (v. 4). "Do not blow on the coals of a sinner, lest you be burned by his flaming fire" (v. 13). "Do not enter into a contest with a wrathful man, nor go with him on a journey of leisure; for his blood is in his eyes as if it were nothing, and where there is no help, there he will fail you" (v. 19).

units.la: In reprehendendo considerandum an sit admissurus correctionem, & an aedificari possit. Derisorem igitur reprehendere intempestiuè, hoc est, hominem desperatæ salutis, qui oblatrat & obgrunnit verbo salutari. Talis enim admonitor & reprehensor recipit sibi ignominiam & conuicium. Prouerb. c. 9. 7. 8. & c. 30. 33. Matth. c. 7. 6. Corripe potius sapientem & amabit te. Prou. c. 10. 8. Nam stultum quocunq; modo sapiens conetur corrigere, nihil tamen efficiet, sed ille inquieto animo permanet. Prou. c. 29. 9. vbi lux.
units.tr: In rebuking one must consider whether the person is likely to accept correction, and whether he can be built up. To rebuke a scorner at the wrong time, that is, a man whose salvation is hopeless, who barks and grumbles at a wholesome word, is therefore improper. For such an admonisher and reprover brings disgrace and insult upon himself. Proverbs 9:7-8; 30:33; Matthew 7:6; Proverbs 9:8: "Reprove a wise man and he will love you." Proverbs 10:8: "For however a wise man tries to correct a fool, he will achieve nothing, but the fool remains restless in spirit." Proverbs 29:9: see the light.

units.la: Cauendum quoque diligenter ne in admonendo sis contentiosus, vel contumax; deinde, ne assidua sit seueritas, quæ amittit authoritatem & beneuolentiam, sed sit temperata cum clementia & lenitate. Ideo alternis vicibus increpationes & collaudationes vsurpandæ & adhibendæ, vt cum exultant animi reprehensionibus, ad pudorem redigantur: & cum deiecti sunt, rursus laudibus erigantur. Plutarch. de liber. educat.
units.tr: Also take care that you are not quarrelsome or obstinate in admonishing; and further, that your severity is not constant, for constant severity loses authority and goodwill, but let it be tempered with mercy and gentleness. Therefore reproofs and commendations should be used and applied in turn, so that when minds grow proud under reproof they are brought back to shame, and when they are cast down they are raised up again by praise. Plutarch, On the Education of Children.

units.la: Nonnunquam etiam tempus hortatur vt voluvoluptate, ira vel ferocitate præcipitem coer-ceas, aut auaritiam cohibeas, aut vt aduersus stultum aliquem animi motum reluctēris.
units.tr: Sometimes also the occasion urges you to restrain someone rushing headlong in pleasure, anger, or ferocity, or to curb avarice, or to resist some foolish motion of the mind.

units.la: Nonnunquam etiam amici ipsi opportunitates admonendi & reprehendendi ministrat, quas arripere oportet & vti. Sic enim percontatio, narratio, vel aliud factum reprehendendi præbet causam & monendi ansam. Sic etiam ab aliis affecti probris, sua vitia illis exprobrant.
units.tr: Sometimes friends themselves provide opportunities for admonishing and rebuking, which one ought to seize and use. Thus a question, a narrative, or some other event offers the cause for rebuke and the occasion for admonition. Thus also, when they have been wounded by the reproaches of others, they reproach them in turn for their own faults.

units.la: Quandoq; etiam verba de aliis faciendo corrumpitur amicus, dum in illis culpatur, quod scit culpans committi ab amico. Plutarch. De discrim. adulat. & amici. Qui vero in quibusuis vulgaribus & leuibus non necessariis ad quæli-bet acerbus & molestus est monitor, is more pædagogorum imperiosè incessit, & in rebus arduis hebes & inefficax erit monitor, Plutarch. d. loco.
units.tr: Sometimes too a friend is corrected by speaking of others, while he is blamed in them for what he knows the friend himself commits. Plutarch, On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend. But one who is a harsh and troublesome monitor about any trivial and unnecessary matters, and who acts domineeringly after the manner of schoolmasters, will be a dull and ineffective monitor in weighty affairs. Plutarch, ibid.

units.la: Eos etiam reprehendere & corrigere cum quibus conuersari & commercium habere, & sermonem non decet, intempestiuum est. De quibus dixi supra cap. 4. Quod si tamen officii necessitas onus reprehendendi tibi imponit, tum nihil referr an tempestiue, vel minus illud facias. 2. Tim. c. 4. 2. 1. Thess. c. 5. 14. c. 4. 18. Matth. cap. 14. 4. c. 16. 23. Luc. c. 5. 22. Act. c. 3. 12. c. 7. 51. cap. 8. 20. c. 13. 10. Gal. c. 3. 1. c. 5.
units.tr: It is also inappropriate to rebuke and correct those with whom you live and have dealings, and whom it is not fitting to talk with. I have spoken of these above in chapter 4. If, however, the necessity of duty lays on you the burden of rebuking, then it makes no difference whether you do so at a suitable time or not. 2 Tim. 4:2; 1 Thess. 5:14; 4:18; Matt. 14:4; 16:23; Luke 5:22; Acts 3:12; 7:51; 8:20; 13:10; Gal. 3:1; 5:

units.la: De admonendo Seneca alicubi ita: Admonebe-ris libenter & reprehendēris patienter. Si immerito quis reprehendit, scito quod voluit prodesse, si merito, quia profuit, adde Plut. De auditione. Qui recte monet, talentum sibi concessum cum vsuris locare dicitur & augere. Matth. c. 25. 15. & seqq. c. 13. 12. Luc. cap. 8. 18. & dona concessa exuscitare, 2 Tim. c. 1. 6. 1 Timoth. c. 4. 14. 15. atq; tum non est bonum sapien-tiam abscondere. Eccles. iast. c. 41. 18. 19. c. 5. 14. 1 Pet. c. 4. 10. & seqq.
units.tr: Seneca says somewhere about admonition: You will be glad to be admonished and patient in being rebuked. If someone rebukes you undeservedly, know that he meant to help you; if deservedly, then because he has helped you. Add Plutarch, On Listening. He who admonishes rightly is said to lend out the talent entrusted to him at interest and to increase it. Matt. 25:15ff.; 13:12; Luke 8:18; and to stir up the gifts bestowed (2 Tim. 1:6; 1 Tim. 4:14–15), since it is not good to hide wisdom (Eccles. 41:18–19; 5:14; 1 Pet. 4:10ff.).

units.la: Reprehenso conuenit se gratum & docilem exhibere. Psalm. 141. 4. 5. Prou. c. 17. 10. c. 27. 5. Vnde ille qui admonetur, non vicissim admonentem moneat & libertatem opponat libertati: quae resincendit animos & contentionem parit, & suspicionem hominis non volentis ferre & acceptare admonitionem, sed regerentis,Plut. De discrim. adul. & amici.
units.tr: It becomes the one who is rebuked to show himself grateful and teachable (Ps. 141:4–5; Prov. 17:10; 27:5). Hence the one who is admonished should not in turn admonish the admonisher and set his own freedom against the other's freedom. That kind of response stirs up minds and produces strife, and it breeds suspicion of a man who is unwilling to bear and accept admonition, and instead answers it back. Plutarch, On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend.

units.la: Secundi vel alterius generis sunt, quae dicenti gratiam adferunt & beneuolentiam conciliant; ea, inquam, tempestiue in medium adferuntur. Contra vero intempestiue, quae praeiudicium & suspicionem generant, reticenda non efferenda.
units.tr: Some things, of a second or other kind, bring grace to the speaker and win goodwill for him. Such things, I say, are brought forward at a suitable time. On the contrary, things said at an unsuitable time, which produce prejudice and suspicion, should be held back, not brought out.

units.la: Hinc stultum & ignominiosum existimatur, si quis respondeat priusquam audiuerit, Eccl. c. 11. 8. Prou. c. 18. 13. Nam vtcunq; interrogatio manifesta est, sermonem tamen prapara & post eruditionem responde. Prouerb. c. 33. 4. Eccl. c. 33. 4. Ideo inciuile dicitur iudicare de re non tota perspecta & audita, vel discretione non habita. Hebr. cap. 5. 14. 1. Thess. cap. 5. 21. Imprimis non festinandum quando spondes pro alio, Prouerb. cap. 6. 1. 2. & seqq. Sermones suos vir sciens & frigidus spiritu cohibet, Prouerb. c. 10. 19. c. 12. 22. c. 13. 16. c. 17. 27. Ecclesiast. cap. 17. 20. & suo tempore & loco profert. Prouerb. c. 29. 11. Totum spiritum suum profert stultus, at sapiens pone reprimit eum, & c. 12. 22. c. 13. 16. c. 14. 8. Nam vt aut mala aurea cum figuris argenteis est verbum dictum Tum commode & tempestiue, habita loci, temporis & personarum ratione. Prouerb. c. 25. 11. c. 15. 23. Itaque conuenit quandoq; ad tempus occultare sermones suos, ne illi sint intempestiui, Eccles. cap. 20. 20. c. 1. 23. 24. Salutis autem tempore sermonem suum non probibet sapiens. Eccles. c. 4. 27. & semper paratus est, ad respondendum cuilibet petenti rationem spei suae, 1. Pet. c. 3. 15.
units.tr: Hence it is considered foolish and discourteous if someone answers before he has heard (Eccles. 11:8; Prov. 18:13). For although the question is plain, nevertheless prepare your speech and answer after reflection (Prov. 33:4; Eccles. 33:4). So it is called uncivil to pass judgment on a matter that has not been fully examined and heard, or without discernment (Heb. 5:14; 1 Thess. 5:21). Above all, do not hurry when you stand surety for another (Prov. 6:1–2ff.). A wise and calm man restrains his words, with the spirit held in check (Prov. 10:19; 12:22; 13:16; 17:27; Eccles. 17:20), and utters them in their proper time and place (Prov. 29:11). A fool pours out his whole spirit, but a wise man holds it back (Prov. 29:11; 12:22; 13:16; 14:8). For a word spoken fittingly and at the right time is like golden apples in silver settings (Prov. 25:11), when regard is had to place, time and persons (Prov. 15:23). Therefore it is sometimes fitting to keep one's words hidden for a time, so that they may not be unseasonable (Eccles. 20:20; 1:23–24). But the wise man does not hold back his speech at a time of salvation (Eccles. 4:27), and he is always ready to answer anyone who asks him for a reason for his hope (1 Pet. 3:15).

units.la: Iucunda dicitur interrogatio de illis rebus, in quibus promptum & facile est respônsum. Nam de ignotis interrogati, cum non habeant quod respondeant, aegre ferunt, vel perturbantur & haerent. Quod si responsio non modo facilis, sed etiam subtilis est, id respondenti voluptatem adfert, qui gaudet se interrogari de iis rebus, quas se habere cognitas nesciri non vult. vid. Macrob. lib. 7. c. 2. Saturnal.
units.tr: A question is called pleasant when it concerns things about which the answer is ready and easy. For those questioned about things they do not know, since they have nothing to answer, are vexed or become confused and stuck. But if the answer is not only easy but also clever, this brings pleasure to the one answering, who is glad to be asked about things that he does not want to be thought ignorant of. See Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 7, ch. 2.

units.la: Cauendae vero sunt interrogationes de calamitatibus praesentibus rebusq; ingratis, vel in quibus verecundiae damnum est si dicantur, vel metus infamiae. Contra gaudemus interrogari de laetis amicorum successibus, de filiorum profectibus, de rebus bene a nobis gestis, de periculis, & aerumnis superatis, de repentina felicitate, de illis quae quis sponte non audet dicere, vel tacere, metu iactantiae, vel malitiae, & similibus, quod ex studiis & affectione illorum qui interrogantur aestimandum est. Senes videmus delectari si dicendi copia illis datur. vid. Macro. d. lib. 7. c. 2.
units.tr: Questions about present calamities and unwelcome matters must be avoided, or about things in which it would be a loss of modesty to speak, or in which there is fear of infamy. On the other hand, we are glad to be asked about the happy successes of friends, the progress of our children, things we have done well, dangers and hardships overcome, sudden good fortune, and those things which a person does not dare to say or to keep silent about of his own accord, from fear of boasting or of malice, and the like. This must be judged from the zeal and goodwill of those who are asked. We see old men delight when they are given opportunity to speak. See Macrobius, cited above, book 7, ch. 2.

units.la: Qui voluptatem malunt quam molestiam afferre, huiusmodi quaestiones proponant, quarum responsa non vituperatio, sed laus; non odium aut inuidia, sed benevolentia & gratia auditorum comitatur. Sunt quædam malorum genera, quæ non vult qui pertulit, vel transacta meminisse, nec minus interrogatus offenditur, quam cum in ipsis malis fuit. Caue interroges ne videaris obiicere, vt dicitMacrob. d.c.2.lib.7. Saturn.
units.tr: Those who prefer to bring pleasure rather than annoyance should put questions of this kind, whose answers bring not blame but praise, not hatred or envy, but goodwill and favour from the hearers. There are certain kinds of evils which one who has endured them does not wish to remember, or to recall things past, and he is no less offended when questioned than he was while in the evils themselves. Take care not to ask questions in a way that seems to reproach, as Macrobius says, book 7, ch. 2, of the Saturnalia.

units.la: Sunt etiam qui cupiunt interrogari, quibus loquacitas familiaris. Sunt qui parci sunt verborum & morosi, quibus molesta interrogatio.
units.tr: There are also those who want to be questioned, and for whom talkativeness is familiar. There are those who are sparing of words and peevish, for whom questioning is troublesome.

units.la: Magna quoque & ciuilis res est vocis & silentii temperamentum. Nimia enim loquacitas odiosa & inciuilis,& nimia raciturnitas. Ergo duo extrema hic vitanda, loquacitas & silentium.Loquacitas & garrulitas effusa & effrænis est in excessu. Taciturnitas, siue silentium, pertinax & perpetuum in defectu.vid. Gell.lib.13.c.11. Noct.Cicer.2.De orat.Tempus, ratio & ipsius dicacitatis moderatio & temperantia, & raritas dictorum distinguit oratorem à scurra.& Gellius lib.1.cap.15.ex Hesiodo refert linguam non vulgandam,sed recondendam esse,perinde vt thesaurum; eiusque in promendo gratiam plurimam, si moderata & parca & modulata sit. Garrulitas siue loquacitas Græcis eleganter dicitur ἀδολεσχία, φλυαρία, ἀπ-γγελία, λογοδιαρροία, ἀπρα-τογία, μικρολογία, λαλία, πηχο-λογία, λογοφιλία, γλωσσαλγία. vide Cle.Ale.lib.2.c.7.& Guil.Stuckiuli 3.c.17. Communiter antiquit.qui & aliorum testimonia citat. Gellius vocat linguam prodigam,effrenem, quæ semper fluit & æstuat collusione verborum teterrima, & blaterones linguaces, garrulos, loquaces.
units.tr: The tempering of voice and silence is also a great and civil matter. For excessive talkativeness is odious and uncivil, and excessive reticence likewise. So the two extremes are to be avoided here: loquacity and silence. Loquacity and garrulousness are unrestrained and unbridled in excess; taciturnity, or silence, is obstinate and perpetual in deficiency. See Gellius, book 13, ch. 11, Attic Nights; Cicero, On the Orator, book 2. Timing, reason, and the moderation and temperance of wit itself, and the rarity of sayings, distinguish the orator from the buffoon. Gellius, book 1, ch. 15, relates from Hesiod that the tongue should not be spread about but kept hidden, just as a treasure is; and that its use is most pleasing when it is moderate, sparing and well-measured. Garrulity or loquacity is elegantly called by the Greeks [adoleschia] (idle prattle), [phlyaria] (silly nonsense), [apangelia] (boasting), [logodiarrhoia] (verbal diarrhoea), [apraktologia] (busy idleness), [mikrologia] (pettiness), [lalia] (chatter), [pēchologia] (windy talk), [logophilia] (love of words), [glossalgia] (tongue-itch). See Clement of Alexandria, book 2, ch. 7, and Guillaume Stuck, book 3, ch. 17. The ancients commonly cite also the testimonies of others. Gellius calls the tongue prodigal and unbridled, which always flows and seethes with a most foul jumble of words, and calls chatterers blaterones, talkative, garrulous, loquacious.

units.la: Loquacitas & garrulitas arguit futilitatem, leuitaleuitatem, temeritatem, inconstantiam, super- biam, scurrilitatem & vanitatem hominis, vid. Plutarch. De garrulitat. Contra, temperati silentii encomia sunt grauitas, sanctitas, secretum, my- sticum, ob quod admirationi sunt aliis, & diligunter, sapientiores̄ videntur. Plutar. de garrul. Iudaei sapientiae sepem vocarunt silentium.
units.tr: Loquacity and garrulousness show frivolity, lightness, rashness, inconstancy, pride, buffoonery and the vanity of a man. See Plutarch, On Garrulity. On the other hand, the praises of temperate silence are gravity, holiness, secrecy, and mystery, on account of which people are admired by others and are thought to be wiser. Plutarch, On Garrulity. The Jews called silence a hedge around wisdom.

units.la: Ergo omnis homo velox ad audiendum & tardus ad loquendum esse debet. Iacob. c. 1. 19. Ideo enim natura nobis duas aures & vnam linguam eamq; muro dentium circumuallatam dedit, quod nimirum plura & sapius audienda quam loquenda sint. Vnde Ecclesiasticus eleganter dicit, Sepem spinosam praetexis tuis praediis; quare non potius ori tuo obdis ostium & repagulum? Hinc ora, [illegible, ~6 letters] Plutarch. De garrul. Silentii enim tutum praemium. Vnde recte Horatius lib. 1. Epist. —ne fidos inter amicos Sit, qui dicta foras eliminet. ibid. Sed tacitus pasci si posset coruus, haberet Plus dapis, & rixae multo minus invidiaeque.
units.tr: Therefore every man should be quick to hear and slow to speak (James 1:19). For nature gave us two ears and one tongue, and that tongue walled round with a fence of teeth, because surely more things are to be heard and more often than are to be spoken. Hence Ecclesiasticus says elegantly: You hedge your fields with thorns; why do you not rather put a door and bar on your mouth? Hence… [illegible] Plutarch, On Garrulity. For silence brings a safe reward. Hence Horace rightly says, book 1 of the Epistles: lest there be among trusted friends one who blurts out what was said. Ibid. But if a crow could be fed while silent, it would have more food, and much less strife and envy.

units.la: Deinde loquaces existimantur esse leues & futiles, vt ait Gellius lib. 1. c. 15. quiq; nullo rerum pondere innixi, verbis humidis & lapsantibus defluunt, quorum oratio in ore, non in pectore nascitur. Allegat Ciceronem libro 1. De Orat. dicentem, Quid tam est furiosum quam verborum vel optimorum & ornatissimorum sonitus manis, nulla subiecta sententia nec scientia? Nunquam, inquit, tacet quem morbus loquendi tenet, tanquam veternosum bibendi & dormiendi. & alibi: Malim equidem inudistam prudentiam, quam stultam loquacitatem.
units.tr: Next, talkative people are considered light and frivolous, as Gellius says, book 1, ch. 15, and they, leaning on no weight of matter, flow away in watery and slipping words, whose speech is born on the lips and not in the heart. He quotes Cicero, book 1 of On the Orator, saying: What is so mad as the mere sound of words, even the finest and most ornate, with no thought or knowledge underlying them? Never, he says, does the one who is afflicted with the disease of talking keep silent, like one suffering from the drowsiness of drinking and sleeping. And elsewhere: I would indeed rather have an unlearned prudence than a foolish loquacity.

units.la: His addo quod immodicè sermo fastidiũ pa-riat. Eccles.c.7.13.c.19.cap.20.3.5.6. Ecclesiast.cap. 2.3. πολύλογος stultus dicitur. Ecclesiast. c.5.2.3. 6.10.11. & seipsum odiosum reddit loquacitate,sua Ec-clesiast.cap.20.3.5.6. & vox stolidi ex multitudine verborum cognoscitur, Ecclesiast.d.c.5.2.3. Atqʒ in multitudine verborum non cessabit defeƈtio, & intel-ligens cohibet labia sua. Proverb.c.17.28. Etiam stul-tus cum tacet, sapiens reputatur; & qui obdurat la-bia sua intelligens & c.25. Sicut vrbs patens & abs-que murorum ambitu, ita vir qui non potest in lo-quendo cohibere spiritum suum. & Iob. c.13. & Prou. c.10.19. Et parcus verborum sapiens iudicatur. Eccles. cap.5.3.4.6. Est enim tacens, qui sapiens deprehen-ditur, & est aliquis odiosus pro nimia loquacitate sua. Eccles.c.10.3. Est tacens, eo quod non habet respon-sionem, & est tacens qui opportunitatem nouit. d cap. 20.4. Vir sapiens taciturus est ad opportunitate vsq; procax vero & insipiens opportunitatem transilit.5.
