Et qui abundat sermone abominationi est, 6. & vers.20. Hominis ingrati & inepti sermones alieni sunt, vbi Iunius. Plutarch. De garrul. Garruli volentes amari sunt odio, & gratificari volentes sunt molesti & putā-tes se admirari,deridentur & lucrantes nihil capiunt, ita vt nec vera dicentibus credatur, Eccles.cap.7. Ne sis loquax apud seniores, & cum oras tempera tibi à multiloquio. Proverb. c.17.27. Cohibet eloquia sua qui scit sapientiam, & pretiosus spiritus est vir intel-ligens.Eccles.c.6.11. Sane verba multa multiplicant vanitatem, quid amplius hominis? Alii garrulitatem proditionem, nullo pretio conductam, vocarunt. vid. Plutarch. De garrul. vbi historicis exemplis idillu-strat.Ephef.c,5.vocatur dicacitas futilis & scurrilis, & c.4. Quam
units.tr: To this I add that excessive talk breeds weariness. Eccles. 7.13; 19.; 20.3, 5, 6; Ecclesiast. 2.3. The one who talks much is called foolish [πολύλογος]. Ecclesiast. 5.2, 3, 6, 10, 11. Loquacity makes a man hateful to himself. Ecclesiast. 20.3, 5, 6. The voice of a fool is known from the multitude of his words. Ecclesiast. 5.2, 3. In the multitude of words there will not be lack of sin, but the prudent man restrains his lips. Prov. 17.28. Even a fool, when he holds his peace, is counted wise; and he who shuts his lips is intelligent. And ch. 25: like an open city without walls, so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking. Job 13. Prov. 10.19: he who is sparing of words is judged wise. Eccles. 5.3, 4, 6: for he who is silent is found wise. Some man is hateful because of his excessive talk. Eccles. 10.3: one is silent because he has no answer. And one is silent who knows the right moment. Ch. 20.4: a wise man keeps silent until the right time, but a forward man, and a fool, lets the opportunity pass. 5: he who abounds in speech is an abomination. 6, and verse 20: the speeches of an ungrateful and foolish man are not his own. Junius there. Plutarch, On Garrulity: talkative people, wanting to be loved, are hated; wanting to please, they are a nuisance; thinking they are admired, they are laughed at; and gaining nothing, they receive nothing, so that even when they speak the truth they are not believed. Eccles. 7: Do not be talkative before the elders, and keep your ears from much talk. Prov. 17.27: he who knows wisdom restrains his words, and a man of understanding is a precious spirit. Eccles. 6.11: Indeed, many words multiply vanity; what is more for man? Others have called garrulity a betrayal, hired by no price. See Plutarch, On Garrulity, where he illustrates this with examples from history. Eph. 5: frivolous and buffoonish wit is called dicacitas, and ch. 4: Which

units.la: Quam praterea indecora, inhonesta & odiosa sit hac effrenata & immoderata dicendi libido, late Plutarch.d.loco differt. Quod si enim garrulus (aut) exiguum audiuerit, id arreptum instar affluentis maris illico multiplicatum reddit. Et ut portuum Olympia unam vocem, multis reflexionibus resonabat, unde ἐπιλάθων; sic garrulitas vel minima voce sit tangitur, statim sonos reddit varios, ita ut auditu foramina garrulis, non in animum, sed in linguam desinere videantur. Deinde cum aliis vitiis deditu, ut auaritia, ambitioni, intemperantia plerunque iis quae appetunt potiantur, garruli contra voto suo magna cum animi sui molestia fruntrantur. Cupiunt enim habere multos auditores, at omnes illos fugiunt & adversantur. Itaque, quemadmodum orto silentio in collocutione aliqua, Mercurium aiunt subintrasse: ita cum in confessum aut conuiuium notorum garrulus aliquis sese infert, omnes obticescunt, ne illi loquendi ansam prabeant, etsi ille vel ultro hiscit, illico vniuersi digrediuntur, astum & nauseam, veluti Borea circa maritimum promontorium fremente praeuidentes. Ita Plutarch.
units.tr: How otherwise unbecoming, dishonourable and odious this unbridled and immoderate lust for speaking is, Plutarch explains at length in the same place. For if a talkative man hears even a small thing, he at once seizes it and, as if a sea were flowing in, multiplies it and gives it back. Just as at Olympia a single voice was echoed back in many reflections, whence it is called echo <bl>[ἐπηχεῖν]</bl>, so a talkative man, touched by even the smallest voice, immediately returns various sounds, so that his ears seem to have holes that lead not to the mind but to the tongue. Moreover, since talkative people are also given to other vices, such as greed, ambition and intemperance, they usually obtain what they desire, but the talkative, on the contrary, are disappointed in their wish, to their great distress of mind. For they want to have many listeners, yet all of them flee from and oppose them. Therefore, just as when silence falls in some conversation they say Mercury has slipped in, so when some talkative man intrudes into a gathering or a banquet of acquaintances, everyone falls silent so as not to give him an opening to speak; and even if he gapes on of his own accord, all at once they leave, foreseeing his tedium and disgust, as when Boreas roars around a sea promontory. Thus Plutarch.

units.la: Hisce addo quod qui minimum sciunt, fere plurimum loqui soleant, sicuti dolia inania & vacua si pulsentur, maximum sonum edunt; contra plena, exiguum; & agricolae spicas ubentius vident quae inclinata versus terram vergunt, quae ob lauitatem attolluntur sursum, eas inanes putant & vassas. Difficile quoque vnum & eundem simul & multa loqui & non multum errare, atque ita ex loquacitate quasi ἀπειρία nascitur. Est etiam tyrannidis cuiusdam species, semper loqui velle & nemini auscultare, & signum arrogantiae & praestantioris fortunae. Nam qui verbosus est, cuput excellentior videri iis qui auscultat, sicuti praeceptor suis discipulis praestantior & dignior habetur. Et si tibi non imperasti, quomodo ab alio sperare poteris silentium? Nescit loqui qui tacere nescit. Et sat scit qui tacere scit, velrari sermonis est & loquentium patiens. Primum igitur discendum silere & deinde loqui. Plutarch. De garrulit.
units.tr: To these I add that those who know least are usually the ones who talk most, as empty and hollow casks, when struck, give the loudest sound, but full ones give little; and farmers see more readily the ears of grain that lean toward the ground, while those that are lifted up because of their lightness they think empty and worthless. It is also difficult for one and the same person to speak much and at the same time not to err much, and thus loquacity arises from something like inexperience [ἀπειρία]. There is also a kind of tyranny: always to want to speak and to listen to no one; and it is a sign of arrogance and of a more exalted fortune. For the man who is wordy seems to himself to be superior to those who listen, just as a teacher is regarded as superior and more worthy than his pupils. And if you have not commanded yourself, how can you hope for silence from another? He does not know how to speak who does not know how to be silent. And he knows enough who knows how to be silent; it is the mark of a rare speech, and of one who bears with speakers. Therefore one must first learn to be silent and then to speak. Plutarch, On Garrulity.

units.la: Ut ergo redundantes sint sermones tui, ne curiose laborato. Eccles. c. 3. 23. Sed finis dicendi & loquendi tempestive faciendus, ne sermo in tui solius possessionem venisse videatur, & alios excludas, ut Cicero alibi loquitur; & monet animadvertendum quatenus sermo delectationem habeat, ut & incipiendi ratio fuerit ita & desinendi modus. vid. Plutarch. Sympos. problem. 1. Senec. lib. 3. Contro. aiebat Scaurus, dicit, rem veram minus magnam virtutem esse scire dicere, quam scire desinere.
units.tr: So that your speeches may be abundant, do not labour over them with excessive care. Eccles. 3.23. But the end of speaking and talking must be made at the right time, lest your speech seem to have come into your own possession alone and you shut others out, as Cicero says elsewhere; and he advises us to note how far speech gives pleasure, so that the manner of ending is as much to be observed as that of beginning. See Plutarch, Symposiac Problems 1. Seneca, Controversiae book 3: Scaurus used to say that it is a smaller virtue to know how to speak than to know how to stop.

units.la: Suramiatim vero contrahere sermonem & paucis multa dicere convenit, Eccles. c. 32. 10. 11. quae est βραχυλογία. vid. Plut. De garrul. ubi Laconicam brevitatem vocat & summe laudat; sed tamen sermo tuus non sit brevior quam res ipsa requirit, ne sit necesse amplius interrogare, Plutar. De garrul.
units.tr: But to compress one's speech, and to say much in few words, is fitting. Eccles. 32.10, 11. This is brevity [βραχυλογία]. See Plutarch, On Garrulity, where he calls it Laconic brevity and praises it highly. Yet your speech should not be shorter than the matter itself requires, lest it be necessary to ask more questions. Plutarch, On Garrulity.

units.la: Ταυτολογία & repetitio sermonis prolati molesta & odiosa est, Ecclesiast. cap. 7. 13. cap. 19. 7. cap. 41. 29. vid. Joh. Guil. Stuckium de convivi. antiq. lib. 3. cap. 17.
units.tr: Tautology [ταυτολογία] and the repetition of a speech once delivered are tiresome and odious. Ecclesiast. 7.13; 19.7; 41.29. See Johann Wilhelm Stuck, On Ancient Banquets, book 3, ch. 17.

units.la: Tacitumitas nimia seu perpetuum & pertinax silentium & ἀφωνία improbatur, & parit suspicionem odii, inimicitiae, fallidii, superbiae, arrogantiae, cupiditatis, insciciae vel stultitiae. Nam omnis e linguis & mutus ob unam ex his causis talis esse videtur. Et tibi tacere, ubi alii per vices loquuntur, quid aliud videtur esse, quam ad conconuiuium pro parte sua symbolum conferre? Et ibi tacere, vbi loquendum est, quid est nisi odium proximi & inuidia? Nam Amyclas silentium perdidisse dicitur. Itaque mutos iistos in laetis & amicis congressibus nemo libenter videt. vid. Gell. lib. 13. c. 11. Nec loquaces neque mutos legere oportet. Eloquentia in foro & apud subsellia: Silentium vero non in conuiuio, sed cubiculo esse debet. Suo ergo loco & tempore loquendum & tacendum est alternatim. Eccles. c. 4. 27. c. 41. 20. Cogitabundi enim eo in loco esse vbi quis est, quasi abreptum & extra se constitutum est hominis melancholici habitus.
units.tr: Excessive taciturnity, or perpetual and stubborn silence, and speechlessness [ἀφωνία], is disapproved of; it breeds suspicion of hatred, enmity, deceit, pride, arrogance, covetousness, ignorance or stupidity. For a man who is mute from any one of these causes seems to be of that kind. And to be silent when others speak in turn, what else does it seem but to refuse to contribute one's share to the common feast? And to be silent where one must speak, what is it but hatred and envy of one's neighbour? For the Amyclaeans are said to have lost their silence. So nobody gladly sees such mute people at cheerful and friendly gatherings. See Aulus Gellius, book 13, ch. 11. One should read neither the talkative nor the mute. Eloquence belongs in the forum and before the benches; but silence ought to be kept not at the banquet but in the bedchamber. Therefore one must speak and be silent in turn, each in its place and time. Eccles. 4.27; 41.20. For to be lost in thought in the place where one is, as if one were carried away and set outside oneself, is the habit of a melancholy man.

units.la: Arcanorum silentium commendatur. siquidem secreta & arcana nemini committenda. vid. Plut. De garr. Et Ouidium, qui ait:
units.tr: The keeping of secrets is commended, since secrets and confidences must be entrusted to no one. See Plutarch, On Garrulity, and Ovid, who says:

units.la: Eximia est virtus praestare silentia rebus;
units.tr: Rare is the virtue of keeping silence about things;

units.la: At contra grauis est culpa, tacenda loqui. & Prou. c. 20. Ne verseris cum illo qui arcana detegit. & c. 11. Qui ambulat fraudulenter, revelat arcana: qui autem fidelis est, celat amici commissum. adde Eccles. c. 27. Iudic. c. 14. vbi Simsoni revelatio arcanorum nocuit.
units.tr: but on the other hand it is a grave fault to speak what ought to be kept silent. Prov. 20: Do not associate with the one who uncovers secrets. Ch. 11: He who walks deceitfully reveals secrets, but he who is faithful conceals what has been committed to a friend. Add Eccles. 27 and Judg. 14, where the revelation of a secret harmed Samson.

units.la: CAP. VI. De altero pronunciationis requisito.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. On the second requirement of pronunciation.

units.la: TAntum de primo pronunciationis requisito. Sequitur de altero; congruo nimium & decenti sono pronunciationis, quo vocis sono rebus adcommodato, secundum earundem naturam verba concepta proferimus. Graecis recta pronunciatio est Ὀρθοέπεια.
units.tr: That is enough on the first requirement of pronunciation. Next comes the second: a sound of pronunciation that is fitting and decent, by which we utter the words we have formed, adapting the tone of the voice to the things so that it matches their nature. For the Greeks, correct pronunciation is orthoepeia [Ὀρθοέπεια].

units.la: G Nam lingua vocem moderatur & ad animi mo-tum adcommodat. Ideo affectibus & natura negotii de quo quis loquitur, se adcommodare debet in pro-nunciatione: qua de causa lingua data, Eccles. cap. 17. 7. 1. Cor. c. 14. 7. 8. 9. & seqq. Nisi distinctionem tonis dederint, quomodo cognoscetur quod tibia canitur, aut cithara? & ideo lingua clavo navis comparatur, qua si suavis est, tibia & psalterium superat, Eccl. c. 40. 21.
units.tr: The tongue governs the voice and fits it to the motion of the mind. So in pronunciation a speaker ought to adapt himself to the emotions and the nature of the matter he is speaking about. For this reason the tongue was given, Ecclesiasticus 17:7; 1 Corinthians 14:7-9 and following. Unless the notes give a distinction of tones, how will it be known what is played on the pipe or the harp? Therefore the tongue is compared to the rudder of a ship, which, if it is pleasant, surpasses the flute and the psaltery, Ecclesiasticus 40:21.

units.la: Pronunciatio eiusmodi male & contra leges Logicas, Rhetorica adscribitur, qua praeter tropos & figuras non habet essentialia alia membra, vel species. Nam tropi & figura omnem sermonem & orationem semper reciproce exornant, ita ut infinitis ipsis verbis, atque sermonis pronunciati vel scripti natura & adfectioni adhaereant, tanquam essentialia & cognata membra, adeo ut absque sermone illo usum nullum habeant, & ab eadem Rhetorica separata, per se consistere non possint, neque ad aliam artem referri. Finem etiam huius artis Rhetoricae, qui est bene dicere, affectutus ille dicitur, qui sermonem & orationem suam tropis & figuris exornavit, etiamsi orationem suam non pronuntiaverit, vel non decore, seu voce, sono & gestu non congruentibus enunciaverit. Hic enim elegantem quidem & ornatam orationem pronuntiavit, quod negari non potest, sed voce, sono vel gestu ineptis, indecoris, inconcinnis & inciuilibus. Unde constat orationem ornatam aliam esse, & alium sonum seu vocem vel gestum decoru & inciuilem. Quando haec concurrunt, & aliarum artium scientia atque usus a Rhetore coniungitur, praeclarum & eximium opus quoddam existere certum est; sed huc non solus Rhetorica beneficio. Troporum igitur & figurarum doctridoctrinam, ut essentialem & sibi cognatam recte & iure Rhetorica sibi vindicat: Pronuntiationem vero minime. Nam haec non ex natura vel medullis sermonis & verborum, sed aliunde sumitur ad exornandam orationem vel sermonem, neque semper, perpetuo, & omnem sermonem ornatum comitatur; cum & sermo scriptus, vel verba scripta, sine pronuntiatione consistere per se possint: imo etiam sonus quidam sine sermone, quamvis sermo sono & voce enuncietur. De habitu & gestu corporis, qui pronuntiationis species a Talaeo dicitur, manifestius est hunc etiam tacentium esse; & dicetur latius infra cap. 7. seq.
units.tr: Pronunciation of this kind is wrongly and contrary to the rules of logic assigned to rhetoric, which, apart from tropes and figures, has no other essential parts or kinds. For tropes and figures always adorn every speech and oration reciprocally, so that they cling to the words themselves, and to the nature and character of the spoken or written discourse, as essential and kindred parts. So much so that without that discourse they have no use, and cannot exist on their own, separated from rhetoric itself, nor be assigned to another art. Moreover, the end of this art of rhetoric, which is to speak well, is said to be attained by the one who has adorned his speech and oration with tropes and figures, even if he has not delivered his oration, or has delivered it without fitting voice, sound and gesture. For he has indeed delivered an elegant and ornate oration, which cannot be denied, but with a voice, sound or gesture that is unsuitable, indecorous, incongruous and ungraceful. Hence it is clear that an ornate oration is one thing, and a decorous or ungraceful sound, voice or gesture is another. When these come together, and the knowledge and practice of the other arts are joined by the orator, there is certainly some outstanding and remarkable work; but this is not due to rhetoric alone. Rhetoric therefore rightly and justly claims for itself the doctrine of tropes and figures as essential and kindred to it. But pronunciation it does not claim at all. For this is not drawn from the nature or the very marrow of the speech and words, but is taken from elsewhere to adorn the oration or discourse, and it does not always and constantly accompany every adorned discourse; since written discourse, or written words, can exist on their own without pronunciation; indeed, even a certain sound can exist without speech, although speech is uttered with sound and voice. As for the bearing and gesture of the body, which Talaeus calls a species of pronunciation, it is more evident that this also belongs to those who are silent; and it will be discussed more fully below, in chapter 7 and following.

units.la: At pronunciatio seu sonus & vox orationem exornat? Itaque est. Sed non quidquid sermonem orationemve exornat, statim Rhetoricum dici debet. Sic enim dispositio, prudentia & scientia artium reliquarum atque reliquae virtutes hominis, magnum sermoni & orationi ornamentum, decus, pondus & authoritatem conciliant, quae tamen ideo non germana, genuina & essentialia Rhetorica sunt dicenda; nisi praxin reliquarum artium Rhetoricum definire velis. Cicero & Quintilianus, & alii plerique ad perfectum oratorem constituendum & efformandum haec requirunt, quos Pet. Ramus lib. 2. & 3. Scholarum Rhetoricarum refutavit. Quod si interne, simili modo quo tropi & figurae, orationem pronuntiatio exornaret & afficeret, eodem quoque cum hisce iure gauderet. Et quo iure Rhetorica pronuntiationem sibi vindicaret, quae etiam Grammatica communis; quae quando agit de accentu acuto, grani & circumflexo, nec no de vocalibus & consonantibus, literarum & syllabarum pronuntiationem informat, quae scilicet deductio contractove ore efferri debeant. Quo iure etiam arti Musica doctrinam pronunciationis & formationem soni vocisve adimet & sibi adscribet? Dices forte Rhetoricam sibi ornatam pronunciationem sermonis arrogare, non simplicem, rudem vel musicorum sonorum doctrinam; haec enim suis cuiusque artis praeceptis informari & doceri. Nego Rhetoricam tradere praecepta de ornata pronuntiatione; sed de pronuntiatione dicere, non ut illam exornet, sed ut illa oratio exornetur, ut huius beneficio oblectet, moveat, persuadeat, atque illam tu ex Ethica sumit sicuti dispositionem & methodum prudentia ex Logica, puritatem sermonis ex Grammatica, & res quas tractat ex aliis artibus, quibus coniunctis persuadeat & vincat. Pariergo ratione de methodo prudentiae ex Logica, de puritate sermonis ex Grammatica, & ex Physica de affectibus praecepta tradere posset, quibus mirifice exornatur oratio & persuasio attentioque apud auditores & gratia excitatur. Sed hoc est limites transfilire, & aliena aliis eripere contra legem secundam artium informandarum. In usu & praxi omnes artes coniunguntur & inuicem communicant, atque virum bonum, perfectum non solum Rhetorem, sed & Physicum, Logicum, I.Cum & Theologum & Philosophum efficiunt. Non igitur, (ut repetam quod supra dixi,) quidquid orationem exornat, vel pronunciationem, statim Rhetoricum dici debet; sicuti non quidquid vile, vel necessarium est ad Logicam percipiendam, intelligendam, vel exercendam, hoc statim Logicum haberi debet, & in Logica tradi, uti nec in aliis artibus: sed potius illud quod essentiale, genuinum & homogeneum, & ad finem summum cuiusque artis tendit, illi inhaeret perpetuoque comitatur, neque per se extra illam consistit; hoc, inquam, illius patrimonium & possessio possessio dicitur, quæ illi sine iniuria adimi & alii ad-scribi non potest. Hoc solum etiam reciprocum & catholicum præceptum artis constituit. Sed nunc ad pronunciationis præcepta reuertamur.
units.tr: But does pronunciation, that is, sound and voice, adorn the oration? Yes, it does. But not everything that adorns a speech or oration must at once be called rhetorical. For disposition, prudence, the knowledge of the other arts, and the other virtues of a man likewise bring great ornament, dignity, weight and authority to speech and oration; yet these should not for that reason be called the genuine, proper and essential parts of rhetoric, unless you wish to define rhetoric as the practice of the other arts. Cicero, Quintilian and many others require these things to constitute and form the perfect orator, and Peter Ramus refuted them in books 2 and 3 of the Scholae rhetoricae. But if pronunciation adorned and moved the oration internally, in the same way as tropes and figures, it would also enjoy the same right with them. And by what right would rhetoric claim pronunciation for itself, when grammar also claims it? Grammar, when it treats of the acute, grave and circumflex accents, and likewise of vowels and consonants, shapes the pronunciation of letters and syllables, namely how they ought to be brought out with an open or closed mouth. By what right also would rhetoric take from the art of music the doctrine of pronunciation and the formation of sound and voice, and ascribe it to itself? Perhaps you will say that rhetoric claims for itself an ornate pronunciation of speech, not the simple, rough, or musical doctrine of sounds; for these are formed and taught by the precepts of their own arts. I deny that rhetoric hands down precepts about ornate pronunciation; rather it speaks about pronunciation not in order to adorn it, but so that the oration may be adorned by it, so that by its help it may delight, move, persuade. And it takes that from ethics, just as prudence takes its disposition and method from logic, the purity of speech from grammar, and the matters it treats from other arts, by which, when united, it persuades and conquers. In the same way, for the sake of a side-benefit, logic could hand down precepts on the method of prudence, grammar on the purity of speech, and physics on the emotions, by which the oration is wonderfully adorned, and persuasion, attention and grace are aroused in the hearers. But this is to leap over the limits and to snatch what belongs to others away from them, contrary to the second law of forming the arts. In use and practice all the arts are joined and communicate with one another, and they make a good man, a perfect person, who is not only a rhetorician but also a natural philosopher, logician, lawyer, theologian and philosopher. Therefore, to repeat what I said above, whatever adorns an oration or pronunciation must not at once be called rhetorical; just as whatever is trivial or necessary for grasping, understanding or practising logic is not at once to be regarded as logical and taught in logic, nor in other arts either. Rather, that which is essential, genuine and homogeneous, and which aims at the highest end of each art, adheres to it and constantly accompanies it, and does not exist on its own outside it; this, I say, is called its patrimony and possession, which cannot be taken from it without injury and ascribed to another. This alone also constitutes the reciprocal and universal precept of the art. But now let us return to the precepts of pronunciation.

units.la: Pronunciationis præcepta quædam sunt generalia, quædam speciala, Generale præceptum vnum est de mediocritate, ne vox sit grauissima, neve acutissima, hoc est, in defectu, vel excessu peccet. ut Talus notauit.
units.tr: Some precepts of pronunciation are general, others special. There is one general precept, concerning moderation: the voice should be neither very deep nor very high, that is, it should not err by deficiency or excess, as Talaeus noted.

units.la: Specialia præcepta pronunciationis sunt de voce formanda in singulis verbis, vel tota sententia. Vocis & pronunciationis sonus in tota sententia, rursum alius in figuris, alius vero in affectibus.
units.tr: The special precepts of pronunciation concern forming the voice in individual words or in the whole sentence. The sound of voice and pronunciation is one way across the whole sentence, another in figures, and another in the emotions.

units.la: Deinde vocis & pronunciationis sonus, alius in miseratione, alius in iracundia, alius in metu & verecundia, alius in voluptate & lætitia, alius in dolore, alius in aliis mentis affectibus pronunciandis.
units.tr: Next, the sound of voice and pronunciation is one in expressing pity, another in anger, another in fear and shame, another in pleasure and joy, another in grief, and another for the other emotions of the mind.

units.la: In miseratione vox sit flebilis, flexibilis, plena & interrupta. In iracundia vox contraria, acuta, incitata & crebro incidens. In metu & verecundia sonus vocis contractus, hæsitans & lentus. In dolore vox grauis, imò pressa & sono obducta & lachrymabilis. Eccl. c. 38. 16. 17. In risu & lætitia, vox pura & exultans.
units.tr: In pity the voice should be tearful, flexible, full and broken. In anger the voice is the opposite: sharp, urged on and frequently interrupted. In fear and shame the sound of the voice is contracted, hesitant and slow. In grief the voice is heavy, indeed pressed down, overcast with sound and tearful, Ecclesiasticus 38:16, 17. In laughter and joy the voice is clear and exultant.

units.la: Vox afflicta & tenera, dolorem, commiserationem & miseriam arguit. Daniel. c. 6. 21. & adpropinquando ad fouceam, Danielem voce tristi inclamauit, Ecclesiast. c. 4. 7. 8.
units.tr: A afflicted and tender voice indicates sorrow, compassion and misery. Daniel 6:21; and when he drew near to the den, he cried out to Daniel with a sad voice; Ecclesiastes 4:7, 8.

units.la: In supplicante quoq; & petente sit vox tenuis, demissa, flebilis, humilis, lenis, & mollis, Eccl. cap 29. 5. Propecunius propinqui submittit vocem. Proverbior. cap.18. 23. Supplicationes eloquitur pauper: dives autem loquitur superbe. Esai. cap. 26.16. Iehoua, in ipsa angustia visitarunt te, fuderunt submissam orationem, castigatione tua premente ipsos. Iudic. c.8 1.2.3.1. Sam. cap. 25. Eccles. cap.35.16.17. & seqq.19. Oratio humilis vim transit nubes. Quaim re peccauit Ioab. 2. Samuel. c.19 6. & seqq 2. & seqq. cap.20.18.19. & seqq. Intra quoque lenienda submissa voce & humili utendum & molli. Prouer. cap.25 15. Lingua mollis frangit ossum durum & rigidum. Iudic.c.8.1. Sed dixerunt viri Ephraimita, quae est haec res quam fecisti nobis, non vocando nos, quum proficisceretis ad pugnam contra Madianitas? contenderuntq; cum eo valde, 2. Qui dixit eis, quid feci nunc, cuiusmodi vos? nonne meliores sunt racemationes Ephraimitarum vindemia Abiezeritarum? 3. In manum vestram tradidit Deus Principes Madianitarum, Horebum & Zeebum, quid ergo potui facere cuiusmodi vos? Tunc destitit iratus illorum animus ab eo, cum loquutus esset verbum hoc. Aliud exemplum extat 2. Sam.c.25. ubi iratum animum Dauidis, spirantis caedem & vindictam, prudens feminea Abigail leni & submissa oratione sua mitigavit, & aliud, 2. Sam. c.14.3. & seqq. de Tecoitide, qua Dauidis animum ad clementiam & filii Absalomi revocationem commouit.
units.tr: In one who supplicates and petitions, the voice should be thin, lowered, tearful, humble, gentle and soft. Ecclesiasticus 29:5: the one who is near to the wealthy lowers his voice. Proverbs 18:23: The poor man speaks supplications, but the rich man answers roughly. Isaiah 26:16: LORD, in their distress they sought you, they poured out a lowered prayer, when your chastisement pressed upon them. Judges 8:1-3; 1 Samuel 25; Ecclesiasticus 35:16, 17 and following, 19: The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds. Why did Joab sin? 2 Samuel 19:6 and following; 2 Samuel 20:18, 19 and following. Within, too, one must soften with a lowered and humble voice, and use a gentle one. Proverbs 25:15: A soft tongue breaks a hard and rigid bone. Judges 8:1: But the men of Ephraim said to him: What is this thing you have done to us, not calling us when you went to fight against the Midianites? And they contended with him sharply. 2. He said to them: What have I done now, such as you? Are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? 3. God has given into your hand the princes of the Midianites, Oreb and Zeeb; what then could I have done, such as you? Then their anger subsided from him when he had spoken this word. Another example is found in 2 Samuel 25, where the prudent woman Abigail, with her gentle and lowered speech, softened the angry mind of David, who was breathing slaughter and vengeance. And another, 2 Samuel 14:3 and following, concerns the woman of Tekoa, who moved David's mind to clemency and to the recall of Absalom his son.

units.la: Leni quoq; & benignā voce utendum in correctione & admonitione, Galat.cap 6.1.2. Timoth.c.4.2.1. Thessal.c.5.14. & erga superiores, Ecclesiast.cap.9.19. Verba sapientium submissorum audienda esse potius, quam clamorem dominantis cum stolidis suis.
units.tr: Gentle and kindly speech should also be used in correction and admonition (Gal. 6.1–2; 2 Tim. 4.2; 1 Thess. 5.14), and towards superiors: "The words of the wise who are humble are better heard than the shouting of a ruler among fools" (Eccles. 9.19).

units.la: Vox alta, vel clamor, hostilem tumultum desiderium indicat, Esa.c.42.2.11. Attollam vocem desertum & civitates eius, villa quas inhabitat Kedar, &c. & seqq. verf. Jerem. c.25.30. Tuaque prophetato ad illos omnia verba ista, & dicas illis: Iehova ex alto rugiet, & ex habitatione sanctitatis sue edet vocem suam, omnino rugiet in habitaculo suo: celeusma, quale est vnas calcantium, efferet contra omnes habitatores istius terra.
units.tr: A raised voice, or a shout, indicates a hostile uproar and a desire for it: Isa. 42.2.11: "Let the desert and its cities raise their voice, the villages where Kedar dwells," etc., and following verses; Jer. 25.30. "Prophesy to them all these words, and say to them: Jehovah will roar from on high and give forth his voice from his holy habitation; he will roar mightily over his dwelling; a shout, like that of those who tread the grapes, will rise against all the inhabitants of this land."

units.la: Aliquando etiam indignationem demonstrat, Mich.c.6. dolorem & cruciatum magnum, Esa. c.26.17. Ut pragnans propinqua partui dolet, exclamat in doloribus suis, ita fuimus a conspectu tuo Iehova. & verf.18. Iob c.2.12. Sed vbi sublatis oculis suis e longinquo, non agnouissent eum, postea vociferantes fleuerunt, & verf. seqq. Aliquando quoque vim & iniuriam, Esa.c.5.29. Rugitus eius vt immanis leonis, rugiensq; vt iuuenes leones, fremet, &c. & verf.30. Iob c.19.7. En exclamans violentiam, non tamen exaudior, vociferanti non adest iudicium, & v. 16. Esa c 22.4.5.6.
units.tr: Sometimes it also shows indignation, Mic. 6. and great grief and anguish, Isa. 26.17: "As a woman with child, near her delivery, writhes and cries out in her pains, so have we been before you, Jehovah," and verse 18; Job 2.12: "But when they lifted up their eyes from afar and did not recognise him, they wept aloud," and the following verses. Sometimes also violence and injury: Isa. 5.29: "Its roaring is like that of a fierce lion, and it roars like young lions; it will growl," etc., and verse 30; Job 19.7: "Behold, I cry out of violence, but I am not heard; I shout, but there is no justice," and verse 16; Isa. 22.4, 5, 6.

units.la: Vocis elevatio est signum imperii, superbiae & arrogantiae, 2.Reg.c.18.28. Itaq; subsistens Rabschake exclamauit magna voce Iudaice, & locutus est dicens: Audite verbum Regis maximi, Regis Assyriae. Ecclesiastic.cap.9.19. Verba sapientum submissorum audienda potius esse quam clamorem dominantis cum stultitia suis. Vocis elevatio cum risu, est stultitiae nota. Ecclesiastic. c.21.23. Vocem suam stultus in risu extollit: vir autem sapiens vix placide est arrisurus. Clemens Alexandrinus libr. 2. Paedagog. cap.7. Vterque qui disserit, vocem suam mutatur iusta proportione atque moderatione. Elatus clamor pronunciationis est res sanis. sima. Cum proximis autem ira loqui ut non audiatis, eius est qui nullo sensu est praeditus: estq; ἀγνωσίας, pusilli & abiecti animi, sicut illud, αὐθάδεια, audaciae & arrogantiae. Vide latius Iohan. Guilelm. Stuckium polyhistor. praestantiss. lib. 3. cap. 19. conviv. antiqui. & Plutarch. De liber. educat.
units.tr: Raising the voice is a sign of command, pride and arrogance: 2 Kings 18.28: "So Rabshakeh stood and cried out loudly in the Jewish language, and spoke, saying: Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria." Eccles. 9.19: "The words of the wise who are humble are better heard than the shouting of a ruler among fools." A raised voice together with laughter is a mark of folly: Eccles. 21.23: "The fool raises his voice in laughter, but the wise man will hardly smile quietly." Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2.7: "Each one who speaks changes his voice in fitting proportion and measure. A loud, strained tone of delivery is a sign of an unsound mind. But to speak in anger with those nearby, so that they do not hear, belongs to one who has no sense at all; it is a sign of ignobility [ἀγνωσίας], of a small and abject spirit, just as that self-will [αὐθάδεια] is a sign of boldness and arrogance." See more at length Johann Wilhelm Stuck, the most distinguished polymath, Antiquitates convivales 3.19, and Plutarch, On the Education of Children.

units.la: Vox fracta & enervata, feminae propria est; Stuckius d. loco, ex Clem. Alex. d. c. 7. Cantilena unius tenoris ubiq; in pronunciatione, facietatem adfert & offendit. Varietas contra delectat.
units.tr: A broken and feeble voice belongs to a woman. Stuck, in the passage cited, from Clement of Alexandria, chapter 7: "A monotonous chant throughout the delivery brings weariness and offends. Variety, on the other hand, delights."

units.la: Vociferatio etiam demonstrat affectum hominis audiri cupientis, Iob c. 30. 5. e corpore expellebantur, vociferabantur homines contra nos, ut contra furem, & v. 28. Ezech. c. 25. 15. & seqq.
units.tr: Shouting also shows the emotion of a man who wishes to be heard: Job 30.5: "They were driven out from among men; they shouted after them as after a thief," and verse 28; Ezek. 25.15 and following.

units.la: Cantus est argumentum laeti affectus vel gratulationis, gaudii & laetitiae. Psal. 70. 5. 6. Gaudeant & laetentur in te ac dicant iugiter, Magnificetur Deus amantes salutis tuae, & Psalm. 136. & 134. & seqq. & 67. 5. & Psalm. 126. & Psalm. 88. 2. Exo. 32. & c. 15. Esa. c. 38. 20. c. 65. 13. 14. c. 51. 12. c. 59. 1. Sam. c. 28. Ose. c. 2. 15. Quandoque tamen est nota opprobrii & exprobrationis & conuicii. Psal. 69. 13. Confabulantur de me sedentes in porta; & canunt odas lyricas, bibentes potum inebriantem, Iob. c. 30. 9. nunc, inquam, modulatio istorum sum; & sumus sermonis argumentum. Intra dentes cantillare, est argumentum, hominis praesentes alios fastidientis.
units.tr: Singing is a sign of a joyful feeling, of congratulation, joy and gladness: Ps. 70.5, 6: "Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you, and let those who love your salvation say continually, 'God be magnified';" and Ps. 136, 134 and following, 67.5, Ps. 126, Ps. 88.2; Exod. 32, and 15; Isa. 38.20; 65.13, 14; 51.12; 59.1; 1 Sam. 28; Hos. 2.15. Sometimes, however, it is a mark of scorn, reproach and reviling: Ps. 69.13: "They who sit in the gate talk about me, and those who drink strong drink make songs about me"; Job 30.9: "And now I have become their song; I am their byword." To hum between the teeth is a sign of a man who despises those present.

units.la: In officio deferendo, non vtendum verbis vel pronunciatione morosa, aspera vel dura, sed amica & suaui. Gen. c. 14. 18. 19. 20. 31. 32. & seqq. Vbi exemplum sermonis benigni & suauis extat Rebecca, becca, officia sua deferentis Abrahami seruo, & La-banis excipientis eundem, & Genes.cap.18.3.4. Exemplum Abrahami tribus Angelis prompte officia sua deferentis, & Judic.cap.19.18.19.20.21. Lenita à sene perhumaniter & benigne excipitur, Ruth.cap.2. 8.9.11. & seqq.cap.3.1.2.3. & Eccl.c.4.8. Inclina au-rem tuam ad pauperem libenter, & responde ei man-suete verbis pacis.
units.tr: In performing a duty one should not use words or delivery that are fussy, harsh or hard, but friendly and sweet. Gen. 14.18, 19, 20; 31.32 and following. Here an example of kindly and sweet speech is Rebekah, performing her duty to Abraham's servant and receiving the same from Laban; Gen. 18.3, 4: the example of Abraham promptly performing his duty to three angels; Judg. 19.18–21: a Levite is received most courteously and kindly by an old man; Ruth 2.8, 9, 11 and following, 3.1, 2, 3; Ecclus. 4.8: "Incline your ear to the poor gladly, and answer him gently with words of peace."

units.la: Lingua suauis, humana, & benigna, superat tibias & psalteria. Eccl.c.40.21. Et suum venenum habet blanda oratio, ut Seneca dicit. Et hac pronun-ciatione & voce vtens, ad cor audientis loqui dicitur, hoc est, qui blande & suauiter eloquitur, gratus est. Vide exempla. Genes.c.34.3.c.50.21. Iudic.cap.19.3. Ruth.c.2.19. 2.Sam.c.19.7.8. Esa.c.40. 2. Osea c.1. 14.c.2.13.14. Eccles.c.41.25. Qua amica pronuncia-tione maxime vtendum erga afflictos. 2. Reg.c.25.28. Eccles.c.4.3.4.5. & seqq. Et sapientibus adscribitur, Eccl.c.9.19. Qua in re peccauit. Nabal, 1. Sam.c.25. v.10.11. Vbi dure & aspere & inhumaniter affliclo Dauidi respondet per nuntios eiusdem.
units.tr: A sweet, humane and kindly tongue surpasses flutes and harps: Ecclus. 40.21. "Flattering speech also has its poison," as Seneca says. Using this kind of delivery and voice, one is said to speak to the heart of the hearer; that is, whoever speaks pleasantly and sweetly is welcome. See examples: Gen. 34.3; 50.21; Judg. 19.3; Ruth 2.13; 2 Sam. 19.7, 8; Isa. 40.2; Hos. 1.14; 2.13, 14; Ecclus. 41.25. This kindly delivery is to be used above all towards the afflicted: 2 Kings 25.28; Ecclus. 4.3, 4, 5 and following. And it is ascribed to the wise: Eccles. 9.19. In this matter Nabal sinned, 1 Sam. 25.10, 11, where he harshly, roughly and inhumanely answers David, who was in distress, through David's messengers.

units.la: In minis & correctione adhibetur vox aspera, dura & incitata. Cicero lib.1. Offic. Obiurgationes etiam nonnunquam incidunt necessaria, in quibus vtendum est forti & vocis contentione maiore, & verborum granitate acriore. Prov.c.18.23. Supplica-tiones eloquitur pauper, dines autem loquitur aspere. 2.Sam.c.19.2.3.4. & seqq. vbi ita proterue, dure, minaciter & aspere lugentem Dauidem Magi-stratum suum alloquitur Ioab. & v.42.43.44. Mat. c.23.13. & seqq. Va vobis Scriba & Pharisaei, &c. Esa.c.30.1. Va filiis cotumacibus, dicitur Iehona, &c. & c.31.c.33. Volubiliter & præcipitanter non loquendū. vid.Clem.Alexand.lib.2.Paed.c.7. ῥᾳχαλὰς καὶ ἀπεκρινον ἀνωμολόγησεν.
units.tr: In threats and correction a harsh, hard and vehement voice is used. Cicero, De officiis 1: "Rebukes also sometimes become necessary, in which one must use a strong tone, greater vehemence of voice and a sharper weight of words." Prov. 18.23: "The poor man speaks with entreaties, but the rich man answers roughly." 2 Sam. 19.2, 3, 4 and following, where Joab, the commander of David, addresses David, who is mourning, so insolently, harshly, threateningly and roughly. Matt. 23.13 and following: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees," etc. Isa. 30.1: "Woe to the rebellious children, says Jehovah," etc.; and ch. 31, 33. One should not speak in a rolling or headlong manner. See Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2.7. [ῥᾳχαλὰς καὶ ἀπεκρινον ἀνωμολόγησεν.]

units.la: Qui præceps est sermone, odiosus est. Eccles.c.9.22. in quo lingua mentem præcurrere dicitur, cum præsumptione quadam stultitiæ. Quando itaq; vides virum præcipitem verbis suis, de eo est melior exspectatio stultitiæ. Proverb. c.29.20. Addo, quod peccare solet, qui præceps lingua est & inconsideratus in pronunciatione. Prover.b.c.19.2. & sibi nocere dicitur. Prov.c.21.5. Vocem & pronuntiationem præcipitem, nec non hæsitantiam, titubantiam & barbarologiam emendat mollis, sedata, explanata & lenta pronuntiatio.
units.tr: He who is headlong in speech is disagreeable. Eccles. 9.22: where the tongue is said to run ahead of the mind, with a certain presumption of folly. When, therefore, you see a man rash in his words, there is a worse expectation of folly from him. Prov. 29.20. I add that he who is headlong in tongue and thoughtless in delivery is accustomed to sin, and is said to harm himself, Prov. 19.2; Prov. 21.5. A soft, calm, clear and slow delivery corrects a hasty and headlong voice and delivery, as well as hesitation, stammering and barbarous speech.

units.la: Non conuenit quoque sententiam & opinionem suam timide dicere, ut cum molestia audiaris, maxime coram hominibus eruditis & intelligentib. arg.Eccl.c.4.23.24.25.28. sed tamen non intrepide, confidenter, & audacter. Eccles. c.19.21.
units.tr: It is also not fitting to state one's opinion timidly, so that one is heard with discomfort, especially before learned and intelligent people; argument from Eccles. 4.23, 24, 25, 28. But neither should it be stated fearlessly, confidently and boldly: Eccles. 19.21.

units.la: Confessio proprii delicti spontanea, non extorta, est indicium hominis ingenui, pœnitentis & dolentis, & fatentis se iuste puniri, & aliorum commiserationem excitat. Contra vero negare & inficiari ea quæ sunt nota, est hominis impudentis & iram sibi conciliantis; quæ verecundia & subiectione mitigatur.
units.tr: A voluntary confession of one's own fault, not extorted, is a sign of an honest man, who repents and grieves, and who admits that he is justly punished, and it stirs the pity of others. On the contrary, to deny and disown what is well known is the mark of a shameless man who wins anger for himself; this is softened by modesty and submission.

units.la: Rogare & deprecari, est hominis humilis, leniorem alium sibi reddentis.
units.tr: To ask and to entreat is the mark of a humble man, who makes the other more gentle towards him.

units.la: Sunt etiam quidam soni & voces pronunciatæ, quæ affectus internos hominum tacite exprimunt; uti est eiulatio, gemitus, fremitus, anhelitus, risus, sibilatio. Eiu-
units.tr: There are also certain sounds and voices uttered which silently express the inner feelings of men, such as ululation, groaning, growling, panting, laughter, hissing. Ulu-

units.la: Eiulatio est hominum plangentium & calamitosorum, Esa. c. 65. 14. Ecce serui mei canent prae hilaritate animi. Vos autem clamabitis prae dolore animi, & prae contritione spiritus eiulabitis, c. 16. 3. Super tecta eius & in plateis eius quisque eiulabit descen-surus cum fletu suo, & verf. seq. c. c. 23. 1. 2. Ierem. cap. 25. 30. 31. 34. 36. Iac. c. 5. 1. Mich. c. 1. 8. & seqq. c. 2. 1. Cor. c. 7. 30. Ezech. c. 30. 2. in Tremel. & Iun. verf. 7. Eiulate dicentes, Ah de die ista. & seqq. v. & Ezech. c. 26. 15. & seqq.
units.tr: Ululation belongs to men who mourn and are in calamity: Isa. 65.14: "Behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for sorrow of heart, and shall wail for breaking of spirit"; 16.3: "Upon her housetops and in her streets everyone shall wail, going down in weeping," and the following verse; 23.1, 2; Jer. 25.30, 31, 34, 36; Jas. 5.1; Mic. 1.8 and following, 2.1; 1 Cor. 7.30; Ezek. 30.2, in Tremellius and Junius, verse 7: "Wail, saying, Ah, what a day!" and following; Ezek. 26.15 and following.

units.la: Fletus & planctus idem fere indicat & signum moestitiae & desiderii. Psal. 137. Esa. c. 22. 4. 5. c. 65. 19. Gen. c. 50. 4. Deut. c 34. 8 Ierem. c. 48. 3. Iacob. c. 5. 1. sicuti & lachryma & lamentatio. vd. Lament. Ier. c. 1. & seqq. 2. Sam. c. 19. 1. 2. 3. Eccl. c. 3. c. 4. Eccl. c. 3. 4.
units.tr: Weeping and wailing mean roughly the same thing, and they are a sign of sorrow and longing. Psal. 137. Esa. c. 22. 4. 5. c. 65. 19. Gen. c. 50. 4. Deut. c 34. 8 Ierem. c. 48. 3. Iacob. c. 5. 1. So too with tears and lamentation. See Lament. Ier. c. 1. & seqq. 2. Sam. c. 19. 1. 2. 3. Eccl. c. 3. c. 4. Eccl. c. 3. 4.

units.la: Quandoque tamen lachrymę signum impotentis laetitiae. Ierem. c. 50. 4. Diebus illis & tempore illo dictum Iehoua, veniant filii Israelis ipsi cum filiis Iehuda una indesinenter flendo eant & Iehovam Deum suum quaerant. Gen. c. 45. 14. 15. Tum ruens in collum Beniaminis fratris sui flebat. Beniamin quoq; flebat, ad collum eius. 15. Osculatusq; fratres suos, flebat super eos. Et postea demum loquuti sunt fratres eius cum eo, & c. 5. 6. 29. Quumq; Ioseph se adspicien-dum obtulisset ei, irruit Iacob in collum eius, fleuitq; ad collum eius diu.
units.tr: Yet tears are sometimes a sign of uncontrolled joy. Ierem. c. 50. 4. In those days and at that time, says the LORD, the children of Israel shall come, they and the children of Judah together, going and weeping, and they shall seek the LORD their God. Gen. c. 45. 14. 15. Then he fell on the neck of his brother Benjamin and wept; Benjamin also wept on his neck. 15. And he kissed all his brothers and wept over them. And after that his brothers talked with him. And c. 5. 6. 29. And when Joseph presented himself to Jacob, Jacob fell on his neck and wept on his neck for a long time.

units.la: Gemitus est signum & index oppressionis. Iacob. c. 5. 9. Ne ingemiscite alius aduersus alium fratres, ut ne condemnemini, ecce iudex ante tanuam adstat. Ezech. c. 24. 23. Et tiaris vestris inditis ad capita vestra, calceisq; vestris ad pedes vestros, non plangetis neq; flebitis, sed tabescitis in iniquitatibus vevestris & gemetis alter cum altero, & Ezech. cap. 26. 15. & seqq. c. 30. 24. Esa. c. 22. 4. 5. & seqq. c. 38. 14. Ut grus, aut hirundo, ita pipiebam, Psalm. 102. 6. Pra voce gemitus mei adhaesit os meum carni meae. Prov. c. 29. 2. Nehem. c. 2. 7.
units.tr: Groaning is a sign and indication of oppression. Iacob. c. 5. 9. Do not groan against one another, brothers, that you may not be condemned; behold, the judge stands before the door. Ezech. c. 24. 23. And you shall keep your turbans on your heads and your shoes on your feet; you shall not mourn or weep, but you shall waste away in your iniquities and groan one to another. And Ezech. cap. 26. 15. & seqq. c. 30. 24. Esa. c. 22. 4. 5. & seqq. c. 38. 14. Like a crane or a swallow, so I chattered. Psalm 102. 6. Because of the voice of my groaning my bones cleave to my flesh. Prov. c. 29. 2. Nehem. c. 2. 7.

units.la: Quandoq; ingemiscere significat συμπάθειαν & commiserationem. Marc. c. 8. 12. Ille vero cum alte ingemuisset spiritu suo, dixit. & quandoque poenitentiam. Prov. c. 5. 11. Gemasq; tandemq; consumta carne tua & corpore tuo, 12. ac dicas, quomodo odi eruditionem & correctionem spreuit animus meus? & quandoque coactionem, Ezech. cap. 26. 15.
units.tr: Sometimes to groan signifies sympathy and compassion. Marc. c. 8. 12. But he, sighing deeply in his spirit, said. And sometimes it signifies repentance. Prov. c. 5. 11. And you groan at the last, when your flesh and body are consumed, 12. and say, how did I hate instruction, and how did my heart despise correction? And sometimes it signifies compulsion. Ezech. cap. 26. 15.

units.la: Fremitus & rugitus vocis significat vehementem & alacrem animum, valde commotum, incitatum & fortem in bello, Esa. c. 42. 13. Ierem. c. 25. 30.
units.tr: Snorting and roaring of the voice signify a vehement, eager spirit, greatly stirred, roused and brave in war. Esa. c. 42. 13. Ierem. c. 25. 30.

units.la: Anhelare est hominis anxii & soliciti, Jeremia cap. 4. 31. Vocem filiae Sionis subinde anhelantis, &c.
units.tr: Panting belongs to a man who is anxious and troubled. Jeremiah cap. 4. 31. The voice of the daughter of Zion panting now and then, etc.

units.la: Risus in voce arguit gaudium, felicitatem & voluptatem. Genes. c. 17. 17. c. 21. 6. Prov. cap. 14. 13. Job c. 8. 21. Luc. c. 6. 21, 25. Jacob. c. 4. 4. Prov. c. 29. 9. Psalm. 126. 2. 5. 6. & quandoque admirationem. Rom. c. 4. 17. Genes. c. 17. 14. 15. 16. Quandoque irrisionis, insultationis & contemptus indicium praebet. Psalm. 52. 8. Quod videntes justi reverebuntur, & de isto ridebunt, dicentes, &c. Ecce virum illum, &c. Psalm. 2. 4. Sedens in caelis ridet, Dominus subsannat eos. Habacuc c. 1. 10. Job c. 19. & c. 30. 1. Nunc autem ridet me minores me tempore qui spreuissem parentes eorum apponere canibus gregis mei.
units.tr: Laughter in the voice indicates joy, happiness and pleasure. Genes. c. 17. 17. c. 21. 6. Prov. cap. 14. 13. Job c. 8. 21. Luc. c. 6. 21, 25. Jacob. c. 4. 4. Prov. c. 29. 9. Psalm. 126. 2. 5. 6. And sometimes it signifies astonishment. Rom. c. 4. 17. Genes. c. 17. 14. 15. 16. Sometimes it shows mockery, insult and contempt. Psalm 52. 8. The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him, saying, etc. Behold the man, etc. Psalm 2. 4. He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord scoffs at them. Habakkuk c. 1. 10. Job c. 19. and c. 30. 1. But now those younger than I mock me, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock.

units.la: Rifus fi iufto debitoque modo proferatur, {a}hoc eft, decorum & honeftatem: fin minus, {b}id eft, intemperantiam præ fe fert. Plato De legibus. In ipfo rifu dicit maximum inefle fignum tum grauitatis, tum leuitatis.Nam quia eft vehementiffimus motus & impetus natus, videmus quofdam in eo genere diffolute effufeq; ridere, vt modeftia in his deffderetur.
units.tr: If laughter is uttered in a just and fitting measure, that is, {a} with decorum and honesty, it is well; if not, {b} it shows intemperance. Plato, De legibus. He says that in laughter itself there is a very great sign both of seriousness and of lightness. For since it is a most violent and impetuous motion by nature, we see some people laughing loosely and wildly in this way, so that modesty is lacking in them.

units.la: Rifus igitur non nimis intentus, effufus, aut immoderatus effe debet, in quo eft vultus decora & concinna remiffio, ita vt in vultu modeftia appareat & refideat. Alius eft rifus immoderata & inconcinna vultus diffolutio. qui eft, rifus folutus; qui in mulieribus dicitur γυναικῶδης: in viris, ἀνδρῶδης cachinnatio. Priorem rifum moderatum, Græcis vocant μειδίαμα, ὑπέρτονον καὶ σύμφωνον. Alter ipfis dicitur rifus ἀκμαλής, & ἀσθενής ἰκνός, Clem. Alexand. d. c. 5. lib. 2. Pædagog. Non oportet enim rifum effe triftem, fed grauem & cogitantem. Si de rebus turpibus excitatus eft, erubefcere potius videri debet, ne per confensum affentiri vel lætari videatur, fi de rebus moleftis, triftitiæ potius quam lætitiæ fpeciem præ nobis in rifu præferre debemus. Illud λογισμὸς πλανήσιον: Hoc crudelitatis fufpicionem adfert. Clem. Alex. d. c. 5. Eccle. c. 7. Melior eft indignatio rifu; quia triftis vultus pariet lætum cor. Et paulo poft: Qualis eft fonus fpinarum fub olla, talis eft rifus ftulti, quod etiam eft vanum, & v. 21.
units.tr: Laughter therefore ought not to be too tense, unrestrained or immoderate; it should be a decorous and harmonious relaxing of the face, so that modesty appears and dwells in the countenance. There is another kind of laughter, an immoderate and unbecoming breaking up of the face, which is loose laughter; in women it is called womanish [γυναικῶδης], in men manly [ἀνδρῶδης] guffawing. The moderate laughter the Greeks call a smile [μειδίαμα], high-pitched and harmonious [ὑπέρτονον καὶ σύμφωνον]. The other kind they call unrestrained [ἀκμαλής] and weak and sickly [ἀσθενής ἰκνός]. Clem. Alexand. d. c. 5. lib. 2. Pædagog. For laughter ought not to be gloomy, but grave and thoughtful. If it is provoked by shameful things, we ought rather to appear to blush, lest by consenting we seem to assent or to rejoice. If it is provoked by troubling things, we ought to show in our laughter the look of sadness rather than of joy. The former is a reasoned deception [λογισμὸς πλανήσιον]; the latter brings suspicion of cruelty. Clem. Alex. d. c. 5. Eccle. c. 7. Anger is better than laughter, for a sad face makes the heart glad. And a little later: Like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool, which is also vain; and v. 21.

units.la: Solum, aut ob nullam euidentem cauffam ridere, vel ftultitiæ tribuitur, vel infaniæ. Si quid tamen eiufmodi fuerit obortum, ciuilitatis erit aliis aperire risus causam: aut, si non putes eam proferendam, aliud afferre debes, ne quis se derideri suspicetur. vt Erasmus monet.
units.tr: To laugh alone, or for no evident cause, is attributed either to foolishness or to madness. If, however, something of that kind has arisen, it is a matter of courtesy to tell others the cause of the laughter; or, if you think it should not be told, you ought to offer some other reason, so that no one suspects he is being laughed at. As Erasmus advises.

units.la: In calamitoso risus etiam iniuria est, vide Eccles. c. 2. 3.
units.tr: Laughter in calamity is also an injury. See Eccles. c. 2. 3.

units.la: In risu vocem extollere, stulti hominis est indicium, Ecclesiast. c. 21. 23. Vocem suam in risu stultus extollit: vir autem solers vix placide arrisurus est: Itaque a cachinnis istis fatuis, agrestibus & insulsis est abstinendum. Nam risus immodicus reprehensibilis, si pueriliter effusus, vel muliebriter fractus. Ideo Seneca dicit, hominem risum facere odibilem, quando est superbus, clarus, malignus, furtivus, aut alienis malis enocatus.
units.tr: To raise the voice in laughter is a sign of a foolish man. Ecclesiast. c. 21. 23. A fool lifts up his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely smile quietly. Therefore one must abstain from those foolish, rustic and vulgar guffaws. For immoderate laughter is blameworthy, whether it is poured out like a boy's or broken up like a woman's. So Seneca says that a man makes his laughter hateful when he is proud, boastful, spiteful, sly, or draws it out of other people's misfortunes.

units.la: Ridere ad iocos & dicteria a te ipso prolata, est hominis se ipsum laudatis; siquidem auscultantis est, non dicentis ridere.
units.tr: To laugh at jokes and witticisms uttered by yourself is the mark of a man who praises himself; for it is the part of a listener, not of a speaker, to laugh.

units.la: Cachinni & clamores & frequens exscreatio, indicant habitum animi soluti, & securi & stulti. Et ideo stultorum voces sunt, Risu diffluo, dissilio, emorior, &c.
units.tr: Loud laughter, shouting and frequent spitting show a loose, careless and foolish state of mind. That is why these are the voices of fools: I melt, I burst, I die with laughter, etc.

units.la: Sibilatio est irridentis & insultantis hominis, Esa. cap. 5. 26. c. 7. 18. Ierem. cap. 25. 9. Ezech. cap. 27. 36.
units.tr: Hissing belongs to a man who mocks and insults. Esa. cap. 5. 26. c. 7. 18. Ierem. cap. 25. 9. Ezech. cap. 27. 36.

units.la: Quae autem dicenda sunt, ea prudenter & distincte proferenda tono & sono distincto, 1. Cor. c. 14. 7. 8. 9. neq; res diversae & valde dissimiles inter se coniungendae. Vitium igitur est eodem tono pariq; mora, omnes syllabas pronuntiare, paribusq; interuallis, quasi syllabae singulae singulas voces absoluerent; quod est latrare, non loqui.
units.tr: What must be said should be delivered prudently and distinctly, with a clear tone and sound, 1. Cor. c. 14. 7. 8. 9. and unlike and very dissimilar things should not be joined together. It is therefore a fault to pronounce all the syllables with the same tone and equal delay, with equal intervals, as if each syllable released a separate sound; this is to bark, not to speak.

units.la: In sermonis pronuntiatione neque ita lentus tus eris, vt aliquis in mensa, qui omnium rerum est fatur; neque ita auidus, vt quispiam famelicus: sed ita loqueris & pronunciabis, vt homo moderatus facere consueuit, literas aut syllabas cum conuenienti quadam dulcedine, sed ita tamen, vt non more pædagogi alicuius, qui in ratione legendi & literas coniungendi pueros informat, enunties. Neque verba instar manducantium, dentibus conficies, vel ea inter se conglutinata & compacta quasi deglutiies: neque literæ vel syllabæ exprimendæ vltra modum, qui est mocacifmus; neque supprimendæ, quæ est ἰχνόμτ. Erasm. De pronunt.
units.tr: In delivering speech you should be neither so slow as someone at table who is full of everything, nor so greedy as a starving person; but you should speak and pronounce as a moderate man customarily does, with a certain pleasant sweetness in the letters and syllables, yet not in the manner of some schoolmaster who trains boys in the method of reading and joining letters. Nor should you chew the words as those who eat, nor swallow them as if glued and crammed together; nor should you pronounce the letters or syllables beyond measure, which is mocacismus, nor suppress them, which is ichnomos. Erasm. De pronunt.

units.la: Vitia pronunciationis enumerat Erasmus in libello De pronunciatione ex Aristotele, ex quibus sunt sequentia.
units.tr: Erasmus, in his little book On Pronunciation, drawing on Aristotle, lists the faults of pronunciation, of which the following are some.

units.la: Labdacismus, qui est impotentia sonandi literam R. vt pellucidum, pro perlucidum; pellegere, pro perlegere; Valesius, pro Velerius, Fuscus, pro Furius.
units.tr: Labdacism, which is the inability to pronounce the letter R: for example pellucidum for perlucidum; pellegere for perlegere; Valesius for Velerius, and Fuscus for Furius.

units.la: Iotacismus, quo literæ cognatæ mutantur, vt, pro iecit, gecit, pro eiicio, egicio, pro e, i, & pro a, o.
units.tr: Iotacismus, in which kindred letters are interchanged, as gecit for iecit, egicio for eiicio, i for e, and o for a.

units.la: Ψελλισμός, qui est impotentia exprimendi literam S, vnde blæsi.
units.tr: Psellismus [ψελλισμός], which is the inability to pronounce the letter S, whence "blæsi" (lisping).

units.la: Τραυλισμὸς vel βαρβαρισμὸς, qui est iteratio syllabæ, vt pro cane, cacaue, pro Tullius, Tutullius, pro Roma, Romana. Huic vitio cognata est βατταλογία, Titubantia, & hæsitantia, μογιλαλία.
units.tr: Traulismus or barbarismus [τραυλισμὸς, βαρβαρισμὸς], which is the repetition of a syllable, as cacaue for cane, Tutullius for Tullius, and Romana for Roma. Akin to this fault are battalogia [βατταλογία], stammering and hesitation, and mogilalia [μογιλαλία].

units.la: Κοιλοσωμία est, qua vox velut e cauo specu atque oris recessu resonat.
units.tr: Koilosomia [κοιλοσωμία] is when the voice sounds as if from a hollow cave and the recess of the mouth.

units.la: Ἰχνόμτ, est exilitas & angustia qua vox labiis femiclufis promitur. cui contrarium est, cum nimium diductis faucibus & ore plus satis patulo sermo promitur sono pinguiore & crassiore. Græcis dicitur <bl>*</bl>.
units.tr: Ischnophonia [ἰσχνόφωνον] is a thinness and narrowness of voice, uttered with the lips half closed. Its opposite is when, with the jaws opened too wide and the mouth more open than enough, speech is delivered with a fuller and coarser sound. In Greek this is called [παχύφωνον].

units.la: Sunt etiam coruicines, quibus sonus per nasum erumpit potius quam per os.
units.tr: There are also nasal speakers, whose sound comes out through the nose rather than through the mouth.

units.la: Gargarismus est, quo sermonis tenor quasi intercidit ructu quodam, singultu, crepitu, stridore, sibilo, gemitu, screatu, tussi vel risu interloquendum.
units.tr: Gargarismus is when the flow of speech is broken, as it were, by a belch, a hiccup, a crackle, a hissing, a whistle, a groan, a spitting, a cough or a laugh.

units.la: Porro pronunciatio secundum partium morem formanda est, etiamsi hospes aliquis idioma seu Dialectum illam non intelligat, argum. 1. Cor. c. 14. per tot.
units.tr: Moreover, pronunciation must be shaped according to the custom of one's own part of the country, even if some stranger does not understand that idiom or dialect; argument from 1 Cor. 14, throughout.

units.la: Valde igitur inciuile & indecorum est, affectare in pronunciatione peregrinam Dialectum, vt puta, quando Germanus Belgicè & Belga Germanicè, & Bauarus Weftphalicè, & hic Misnicè sermonis sui pronunciationem & locutionem formare vellet, 1. Corinth. c. 14. 9. Ita & vos nisi per linguam edideritis bene significantem sermonem, quomodo cognoscetur quod dicitur? Eritis enim in aerem loquentes, & v. 11. & seqq. Loquendum ergo cum multis & sentiendum cum paucis. Omnis enim affectatio enunciationem reddit obscuram & ingratam, imo de contemptu vitatae linguae suspectam.
units.tr: It is therefore very ill-mannered and unbecoming to affect a foreign dialect in pronunciation, as when a German wished to shape his pronunciation and speech in Dutch, or a Dutch speaker in German, or a Bavarian in Westphalian, or a man from Meissen in his own speech. 1 Cor. 14:9: So also you, unless you utter by the tongue speech that is easy to understand, how will it be known what is said? For you will be speaking into the air, and verses 11 and following. So one must speak with many but think with few. For all affectation makes utterance obscure and unpleasant, and even brings suspicion of contempt for one's own native tongue.

units.la: Plebeius quoque non more nobilium & patriciorum, atq; aliorum eruditorum hominum pronunciationem suam formare debet, neque hi ad consuetudinem & morem rusticorum & artificum suam dialectum, vel elocutionem instituere. In pronunciatione seipsum auscultare, φιλαυ- τίας suspicionem præbet. Et inter oscitandum sermo non continuandus.
units.tr: Nor should a commoner shape his pronunciation in the manner of nobles, patricians and other educated men; nor should these men adapt their dialect or speech to the habits and custom of rustics and craftsmen. To listen to oneself while pronouncing gives an impression of self-love (philautia). And speech should not be continued through yawning.

units.la: CAP. VII. De habitu & gestu naturali hominis loquentis & audientis.
units.tr: CAP. VII. On the natural bearing and gesture of a man who speaks and listens.

units.la: HActenus de vsu sermonis in communi Ethica. Sequitur nunc de actionibus hominis.
units.tr: Hitherto we have discussed the use of speech in general ethics. Now follows the subject of human actions.

units.la: Actio igitur, siue habitus & gestus hominis communi Ethicæ & ciuili conuersationi inser- uientes, sunt motus situsque corporis, ex quibus hominis mores, affectiones internæ, bonæ malæve, vel status, aut conditio vitæ, cognoscitur quoad virtutes & vitia.
units.tr: Actions, that is, the bearing and gestures of a man, which serve general ethics and civil conversation, are the movements and postures of the body by which a person's morals, inner dispositions, good or bad, or condition and manner of life, is recognised with respect to virtues and vices.

units.la: Eiusmodi habitus & gestus hominis male & contra legem iustitiæ Rhetoricæ essentialis dicitur, & pensius pronunciationis species, aut pars constituitur. Nam quidquid est Rhetoricum, hoc semper necessario & omnem orationem exornare debet & inesse sermonis natura, ita ut separatim sine oratione per se consistere non possit. At gestus & habitus hominis, non semper & necessario ornant orationem, atq; per se etiam & separatim consistunt & considerari possunt, licet sermo, vel oratio nulla habeatur; cum etiam tacentibus gestus & habitus adscribatur, ut cap. 8. latius dico: & gestus quidam sint orationem non exornantes, & quidam etiam eandem deformantes. Unde etiam apparet, habitum & gestum ad summum illum finem & scopum Rhetorica non semper collimare, qui est, ut ornatè dicere doceat. Quod vero præceptum Rhetoricum non bene dicere semper & perpetuo, necessario & uniuersaliter docet, id huic non essentiale, vel homogeneum sed heterogeneum & alienum a Rhetorica: neque κατὰ παντὸς, neque καθ' αὑτὸ, neque καθόλε αὐτῶν. Habitus ergo Rhetorica non est. Sed actiones & gestus forte Iurisprudentia, Theologia practicis artibus adscribes, in quibus bene & recte operandi, agendi & tractandi praecepta traduntur, & in quibus omnino actione opus, si exercitium & usum earum spectauteris: sine qua actione, usus & praxis earundem consistere nequit. Ita est. Distinguendum vero existimo inter actiones, usum & exercitium reliquarum artium, & Ethica. Non est enim huius & caeterarum actio eadem, sed dissimilis & longè alia. Nam actiones hominum, ut recta bonaeque sint, reliquis artib. docetur, quae eas informant bonas, rectas & iustas. Ut vero decora, venusta, concinna, ciuiles & urbanae sint, sola Ethica; sic Logica informat rationem, ut ea bene utamur, tam in inueniendis argumentis, quam inuentis disponendis & iudicandis. Haec extra suam praxin in nuda speculatione consistit: in praxi vero & actionibus sola non est, sed reliquarum artium materiam tractat. Sic Iurisprudentia docet quae actiones iustae & aequae sint, quaeq; iniquae, iniustae, & quae hominum societati colenda conseruandaq; apte, convenientes & necessarie, quaque contra inutiles & perniciose; idque tractat in distributione praemiorum & poenarum, quibus utraque actiones remuneratur. Theologia vero tradit, quae hominum actiones sint sanctae, pie salutares & necessarie ad vitam aeternam consequendam: quid fides, poenitentia; bonum, sanctum, pium opus, quid regeneratio, quae sigilla gratiae diuinae. Physica doctrinam operationum & actionum rerum naturalium continet. Quomodo vero & qua ratione actiones homihominum iusta, pia vel naturales in superioribus artibus informata, decore, venuste & ciuiliter & decenter fiant, sola Ethica praescribit. Fieri enim potest, ut aliquid iuste, recte, pie, sancte, naturaliter fiat, quod tamen minus decore & rite fiat, habita ratione rei, personae, loci, temporis & aliarum circumstantiarum. Si quid iniuste fit, poena in iure praescripta est. Unde tota materia maleficiorum exorta, & Iurisprudentia propria & Magistratui concessa, ut puniat. Si quid contra fidei analogiam creditur, vel aliter non Christiane, hoc Theologi verbis & reprehensionibus & admonitionib. indicant; sed no quomodo bona actiones remunerandae neque quomodo impia puniendae; vel quomodo ad societatem humanam externamque disciplinam colendam & conservandam, actiones hominum sint instituenda praescribu, vel tradit. Hoc enim I. C. torum traditiones, & precepta Iurisprudentiae abunde docent, qua cum Magistratus proponit, etiam ob conscientiam huic obtemperandum Theologi docent cum Apostolo.
units.tr: Such bearing and gesture of a man is said, wrongly and against the law of essential rhetorical justice, to constitute a more weighty species or part of pronunciation. For whatever belongs to rhetoric must always and necessarily adorn every speech and be inherent in the nature of discourse, so that it cannot exist apart from speech on its own. But the gestures and bearing of a man do not always and necessarily adorn a speech; they exist and can be considered on their own and separately, even when there is no speech or oration at all, since gestures and bearing are also attributed to those who are silent, as I explain more fully in chapter 8. Some gestures do not adorn a speech, and some even disfigure it. Hence it is also clear that bearing and gesture do not always aim at that highest end and goal of rhetoric, which is to teach how to speak ornately. But a rhetorical precept which teaches that one should not speak well always, perpetually, necessarily and universally is not essential to rhetoric or of its kind, but foreign and alien to it: neither universally [κατὰ παντὸς], nor per se [καθ' αὑτὸ], nor in general [καθόλου αὐτῶν]. Therefore bearing is not part of rhetoric. But actions and gestures perhaps you may assign to the practical arts of jurisprudence and theology, in which precepts are handed down about doing, acting and dealing well and rightly, and in which action is wholly needed if you consider their exercise and use; without such action the use and practice of these arts cannot exist. That is so. Yet I think one must distinguish between the actions, use and exercise of the other arts and of ethics. For the action of this art is not the same as that of the others, but different and quite other. For men's actions, that they be right and good, are taught by the other arts, which shape them as good, right and just. But that they be becoming, graceful, elegant, civil and courteous is the business of ethics alone. Thus logic shapes the reasoning so that we use it well, both in finding arguments and in arranging and judging what has been found. Logic, outside its practice, consists in pure speculation; in practice and in actions it is not alone, but treats the matter of the other arts. So jurisprudence teaches which actions are just and fair, which unjust and wrong, and which are fitting, necessary and apt for cultivating and preserving human society, and which are, on the contrary, useless and harmful; and it treats of the distribution of rewards and punishments by which each kind of action is repaid. Theology teaches which human actions are holy, pious, salutary and necessary for attaining eternal life: what faith is, what repentance is, what a good, holy and pious work is, what regeneration is, and what the seals of divine grace are. Physics contains the doctrine of the operations and actions of natural things. But how and in what manner human actions which are just, pious or natural, as formed by the higher arts, are to be done becomingly, gracefully, civilly and decently, ethics alone prescribes. For it can happen that something is done justly, rightly, piously, holily and naturally, and yet is done less becomingly and properly, given the nature of the thing, the person, the place, the time and the other circumstances. If something is done unjustly, a penalty is prescribed in law. Hence the whole matter of crimes arises, and it belongs to jurisprudence proper and is committed to the magistrate, so that he may punish. If something is believed contrary to the analogy of faith, or is otherwise done un-Christianly, theologians point this out by words, rebukes and admonitions; but they do not prescribe or hand down how good actions are to be rewarded, nor how impious ones are to be punished, nor how human actions are to be instituted for cultivating and preserving human society and external discipline. For the traditions and precepts of the jurists teach this abundantly, and when the magistrate proposes them, theologians teach, with the Apostle, that they must be obeyed also for conscience' sake.

units.la: Sic, si res naturalis non habeat suas naturales vires & operationes, quas ordinatione divina accepit; si degeneret, labefactata, corrupta, vel alterata sit, hoc physicus perpendit & examinat, & Medicus postea ad naturale habitum reducere conatur. Quod si quid inciviliter, agreste, inconcinne fit, hoc Ethicus ex sua arte iudicat & reprehendit, sed (uti & Theologus) no punit aut quomodo puniri debeat, praescribit. Neque etiam si Iurisprudentia decorum civilitatem, morum remuneratione dignam iudicet; id tamen quod inciviliter, vel indecore factum est, si modo iustum, rectum, vel aequum sit, non punit. Hac vero illa tantum persequitur & tradit quae ad hominum societatem tuendam conseruandamq; faciunt; non vero quae ad illam decorandam, quae solius sunt Ethica. Neq; enim societatem humanam eiusve continuationem & commune bonum turbas, si quid non decore, vel venuste aut ciuiliter feceris, quod per se alias iustum & pium. Quae igitur in iurisprudentia, vel cateris artib. traduntur praecepta, necessaria & utilia sunt humano generi; quae in Ethica vero, illa tantum honestatem, voluptatem, decorum & urbanitatem respiciunt; quae ratione etiam utilia dici possunt; quos limites hac non egrediuntur. Atque ita intra proprios & essentiales cuiusq; artis fines, haec sunt regenda & coercenda, ne alienam possessionem sibi usurpent. Sed iam pergamus dicere de habitu & gestu.
units.tr: So, if a natural thing does not have its natural powers and operations, which it received by divine ordinance; if it degenerates, is weakened, corrupted or altered, the physicist weighs and examines this, and the physician afterwards tries to restore it to its natural state. But if something is done uncivilly, rustically or ungracefully, the ethicist judges and rebukes this from his own art, but (as does the theologian) he does not punish it or prescribe how it ought to be punished. Nor, if jurisprudence judges something decorous and civil and worthy of reward in manners, does it punish what was done uncivilly or unbecomingly, if only it was just, right or fair. These matters pursue and hand down only what serves to protect and preserve human society, not what serves to adorn it, which belongs to ethics alone. For you do not disturb human society, its continuation or the common good, if you have done something not becomingly or elegantly or civilly, which is otherwise just and pious. Therefore the precepts handed down in jurisprudence or the other arts are necessary and useful to the human race; those in ethics concern only honesty, pleasure, decorum and courtesy, which may also be called useful in a certain sense; these precepts do not go beyond those limits. And thus, within the proper and essential ends of each art, these matters are to be governed and restrained, lest they usurp another's possession. But now let us proceed to speak of bearing and gesture.

units.la: Ex habitu igitur & gestu hominis, variae dee-iusdem affectibus, tam bonis quam malis, tam virtutibus quam vitiis, variae, inquam, sumuntur coniecturae. Nam ut sapiens Eccl. c. 19. 26. ait, Ex aspectu cognoscitur vir, & ex obuia persona specie, cognoscitur quae valet mente. & v. 27. Ornatus viri & risus dentium, gressusq; hominis, enunciant constitutionem eius. & v. 19. & Idem Eccl. c. 13 30. Cor hominis mutat vultum ipsius, sive ad bona spectet, sive ad mala. nam animus virescens in delectatione bonum vultum efficit, & v. seq. & latius de hisce videm c. 25. 21. c. 31. 12. & seqq. & Eccl. habet in cap. 19. 18. Prou. c. 23. 29. 20. & seqq. & c. 25. 23. Et mala mulier ex habitu & actione sua describitur, Eccles. c. 26. c. 36. 25. 26. 27. 28. & tot. c. 25. & habitus pigri. Prou. c. 19. 24. c. 26. 13. 14. 15. 16. Constantis & placidi viri, Prouerb. c. 17. 24. c. 22. 9. c. 11. 2. Impii, Prou. c. 16. 28. 29. cap. 17. 25. c. 10. 10. c. 6. 13. c. 26. 12. c. 7. 10. 11. c. 6. 13. vbi homo nequam dicitur nictare oculis suis, facere verbapedibus suis & docere digitis suis. & Apostolus Tit.c.2.3.dicit,anus sint habitu quisanctimoniam decet. Et Clemens Alex.lib.2.Pædag.c.6.dicit; Quisquis insolenter,inhonestè & inconcinne gerit,facit ille, ut meditentur inhonestè facere. Et Cic.3. De orat. Omnis motus animi suum quendam a natura habet vultum,& sonum & gestum.
units.tr: From the bearing and gesture of a man, therefore, various conjectures are drawn about his dispositions, both good and bad, both virtues and vices. For, as the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus 19:26, "A man is known by his look, and a person who has sense is known by his outward appearance," and v. 27, "The adornment of a man and the laughter of his teeth, and his gait, declare what he is." And v. 19, and the same Ecclesiasticus 13:30, "A man's heart changes his countenance, whether it looks to good or to evil; for a mind that flourishes in delight makes the face good," and the following verses; and more fully on these matters see Ecclesiasticus 25:21, 31:12 ff. And Ecclesiasticus 19:18; Proverbs 23:29, 20 ff., and 25:23. An evil woman is described by her bearing and conduct, Ecclesiasticus 26, 36:25–28, and throughout chapter 25; and the bearing of the sluggard, Proverbs 19:24, 26:13–16. Of the steadfast and gentle man, Proverbs 17:24, 22:9, 11:2. Of the ungodly, Proverbs 16:28–29, 17:25, 10:10, 6:13, 26:12, 7:10–11, where the worthless man is said to wink with his eyes, to speak with his feet and to teach with his fingers. And the Apostle in Titus 2:3 says that the older women should be in bearing such as becomes holiness. And Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, chapter 6, says: whoever behaves insolently, dishonourably and ungracefully makes others inclined to act dishonourably. And Cicero, De oratore book 3: every motion of the mind has by nature its own look, sound and gesture.

units.la: Refert Apuleius 1. Apologia, Socratem discipulis suis suasisse, ut crebro se in speculo contemplarentur, ne dignitatem corporis malis moribus dedecorarent: & Demosthenem semper ante speculum quasi ante magistrum caussas meditatum, & pronunciandi concinnitatem à speculo didicisse. vide Senec.1. natural. & De quatuor virtutibus in Continentia ait: Si continens es,animi tui motus corporisque observa, ne indecori sint. De quibus omnibus generaliter hic monuisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Apuleius, in his first Apology, reports that Socrates urged his disciples to look often at themselves in a mirror, so that they would not disgrace the dignity of the body with bad morals; and that Demosthenes always rehearsed his cases before a mirror, as if before a teacher, and learned the polish of his delivery from it. See Seneca, Natural Questions 1; and in his book On the Four Virtues, on Continence, he says: "If you are continent, watch the movements of your mind and body, so that they are not unseemly." It is enough to have given this general warning about all of these.

units.la: Est autem in gestibus ea dignitas seruanda, quæ tacendo loquitur,&quasi mandando in sui admirationem & reuerentiam alios constringit.
units.tr: In gestures, however, that dignity must be preserved which speaks by being silent and, as it were, commands others to admire and revere us.

units.la: Deinde, perpetuò hic regula illa obseruanda, ut talem quis se habitu & gestu exhibeat, qualis cupit videri; & talis reuera intus sit, quales apparere exterius cupit.
units.tr: Next, this rule must always be observed: a person should present himself in bearing and gesture as he wishes to be seen, and should be inwardly what he wishes to appear outwardly.

units.la: Tertiò, gestus & habitus nostri ita comparati esse debent, ut aliquam reuerentiæ præclaræq; de iis, apud quos sumus, existimationis significationem testentur,non desideriis, vel sentibus aliorum contrarii. Contra igitur habitus, qui indicant, non amari, vel æstimari alios, quibus cum conuersamur, fugiendi: Inprimis ex quibus indicia ἀλογείας elucent, contemtus, despicientia, incommodatio, contumelia, & studium aduersandi.
units.tr: Thirdly, our gestures and bearing should be arranged so that they bear witness to some reverence and considerable esteem for those among whom we are, and do not run contrary to the wishes or feelings of others.
