On the contrary, we should avoid those bearings which show that the people with whom we associate are not loved or valued: above all, those in which signs of thoughtlessness [ἀλογεία] shine forth, such as contempt, disdain, disregard, insult, and a zeal for opposing.

units.la: Quarto cauendum hic, ne quis quo ad habitum in defectu peccet & fiat instar statuarum immobilium; vel in excessu, simiarum instabilitatem frequentia gestuum, & libertate nimia repraesentet.
units.tr: Fourthly, care must be taken here lest anyone err in bearing by deficiency and become like an immobile statue, or by excess, and by frequent gestures and excessive freedom represent the restlessness of monkeys.

units.la: Quinto cauendum omnino, ne actiones & habitus eiusmodi, notae esse possint & indicia exi-stimationis laesae & ignominiae imaginationem & significationem habeant, vt pudorem agentibus incutere possint. Vti, Non facere aliquem participem istarum rerum, quarum participes fecit omnes pares, vel plurimos. Non sustinere vel le vel posse labores, quos delicati, seniores, vel nobiliores sustinent. Neque scire quae omnes sui ordinis sunt; vel pati quod probrum & ignominiam afferre possit: qualia sunt foeda illa corporis obsequia & ministeria in rebus inhonestis & turpibus.
units.tr: Fifthly, one must be wholly careful that actions and bearings of this kind do not become marks of lost esteem, carrying the image and meaning of disgrace, so that they could cause shame in those who perform them. That is: not to make someone a sharer in those things of which all equals or most are sharers; not to be willing or able to endure the labours which the delicate, the elders, or the nobles endure; nor to know what all of one's own rank know; or to suffer what can bring reproach and disgrace, such as those foul services and ministries of the body in shameful and base matters.

units.la: Habitus autem siue gestus sunt duplices. Quidam enim sunt insiti; quidam adsumpti habitus, 1. Corinth. c. 11. 13. Apud vos iudicate, num decorum est mulierem non opertam Deum orare. 14. An ne natura quidem ipsa hoc vos docet, quod vir quidem comatum esse dedecori sit? 15. Contra mulieri comatam esse decori sit. nam coma pro velamento data est ei, & c. 14. 40. Omnia decenter & ordine fiant.
units.tr: Bearings or gestures are of two kinds. For some are innate, while others are assumed habits. 1 Corinthians 11:13: "Judge among yourselves: is it fitting that a woman pray to God unveiled? 14: Does not nature itself teach you that for a man to wear long hair is a disgrace? 15: But for a woman to wear long hair is a glory, for her hair is given to her as a covering." And 14:40: "Let all things be done decently and in order."

units.la: Insiti siue naturales habitus sunt, qui naturae vi cogente, ex hominum affectionibus naturalibus proficiscuntur. Vnde fit, vt omnibus nationibus eiusmodi sint communes, atq; perpetuam & certam apud omnes significationem habeant. Nam iisdem omnium animi motibus concitantur, & eos iisdem notis etiam in aliis agnoscunt & in se ipsi iudicant, ut supra c. 1. in fine generaliter monui. Cicero lib. 1. Offic. Nos autem natu-ram sequamur, & ab omni quod abhorret ab ipsa oculorum auriumque approbatione fugiamus: status, incessus, sessio, accubatio, vultus, oculi, manuum motus teneant illud decorum.
units.tr: Innate or natural bearings are those which arise from natural human feelings, under the compelling force of nature. Hence it comes that they are of this kind common to all nations, and have a perpetual and certain meaning among all. For all are stirred by the same movements of the mind, and recognise them by the same signs in others and judge them in themselves, as I said in general at the end of chapter 1 above. Cicero, On Duties, book 1: "Let us follow nature, and flee from everything that is repugnant to the very approval of our eyes and ears: posture, gait, sitting, reclining, expression, eyes, and movements of the hands should keep that decorum."

units.la: In sit eiusmodi habitus & gestus, sunt dupli-ces. Alii enim hominis loquentis vel audientis, alii silentis ut plurimum.
units.tr: Of such bearings and gestures there are two kinds: some belong to a man who is speaking or listening, others to one who is silent for the most part.

units.la: Gestus loquentis sunt, qui eiusdem verbis eorum q; sensui sunt adcommodati.
units.tr: The gestures of the speaker are those which are fitted to his words and to the meaning of his words.

units.la: Huius praecepta respiciunt totum hominis loquentis corpus, vel partes eiusdem.
units.tr: The precepts for these concern the whole body of the speaking man, or its parts.

units.la: Totum corpus hominis; ut nimirum huius virilis sit gestus in masculo, & muliebris in femina; & status corporis secundum naturam erectus & excelsus.
units.tr: As for the whole body: the gesture of a man should be manly, and of a woman womanly; and the posture of the body, according to nature, should be upright and lofty.

units.la: Ergo contrà, omnis gesticulatio, mutatio & vacillatio, indecora & inciuilis.
units.tr: Therefore, on the contrary, all gesticulating, shifting and swaying is unseemly and uncivil.

units.la: Praecepta partes corporis respicientia, sunt de capite, fronte, oculis, brachiis, manibus, digitis.
units.tr: The precepts concerning the parts of the body are about the head, forehead, eyes, arms, hands and fingers.

units.la: De capite praeceptum est, ut sit demissum, quo modestia & metus quidam significatur; eoque verlum quo sermo dirigitur, exceptis iis quae aut damnanda sunt, aut remouenda: tum enim illius auersione auersari aliquid cognoscimur.
units.tr: Concerning the head the precept is that it be held lowered, by which a certain modesty and fear is signified; and that it be turned toward the one to whom the speech is directed, except in things which must be condemned or set aside; for then, by turning the head away, we show that we shun something.

units.la: Frons, oculi & vultus, imaginem affectionis internae seu animi bene vel male affecti praebent. haec itaque membra secundum affectum quem in aliis loquens excitare vel insinuare & generare vult, conformare & fingere debet. Vultus enim ac frons, animi est ianua, quę significat voluntatem abditam & retrufam. & Cicero 3. De Oratore: Oculi sunt, quorum intentione, tum coniectu, tum hilaritate motus animorum apte significemus.
units.tr: The forehead, eyes and face present an image of the inner affection, or of a mind well or ill disposed. These members, therefore, ought to be shaped and fashioned according to the feeling which the speaker wishes to arouse, insinuate or produce in others. For the face and forehead are the gate of the mind, signifying the hidden and withdrawn will. And Cicero, On the Orator, book 3: "There are the eyes, by whose gaze, by whose glance and by whose cheerfulness we aptly signify the movements of the mind."

units.la: Inter loquendum oculi intenti spectabunt placide in eum, cui loqueris.
units.tr: While speaking, the eyes should look calmly and intently at the one to whom you speak.

units.la: Manus inprimis loquentem adiuuat, quando fecundum affectus naturales rei seu negotii, de quo sermo habetur, regitur & gubernatur à loquente. Ex hisce constat quæ vitia loquēti seu sermonem habenti homini sint fugienda; nimirum, vt non caput titubet, oculisve limis, seu intuitu obliquo, adspiciat eum, cum quo loquitur; vel altero oculo in frontem sublato, altero ad mentum depresso supercilio, Proverb. 6.4.25.
units.tr: The hands above all help the speaker, when they are guided and steered by him according to the natural feelings about the matter or business under discussion. From these points it is clear which faults the man who speaks or holds a discourse must avoid: namely, that the head should not wobble, nor that he should look at the one he is speaking with out of the corner of his eyes or with an oblique glance; nor with one eye raised toward the forehead and the other eyebrow lowered toward the chin (Proverbs 6:4, 25).

units.la: Vultum in varios habitus, vt instar Protei, transformare, corrugare nasum, contrahere frontem, attollere supercilia, distorquere labra, diducere os, aut premere, capite concusso iactare comam, scabere caput, aureis scalpere, suffricare occiput, rotato capite negare, reducto accerfcere, & breuiter gestibus & nutibus loqui, indecorum.
units.tr: To transform the face into various expressions, like Proteus; to wrinkle the nose, contract the brow, raise the eyebrows, twist the lips, stretch or press the mouth; to toss the hair with the head shaken, scratch the head, scrape with the fingers, rub the back of the head; to refuse with the head turned, to call back with the head drawn back; and in short to speak by gestures and nods: all this is unseemly.

units.la: Deinde non os distorqueat, non sputo suo faciem eius, cum quo loquitur, adspergat, neque ronchos ducat neque cantillet, neque pituitam naribus propendentem cum sono quodam ingratiffimo subinde retrahat, neque manus inter loquendum agitet, instar muscas à fe depeldepellentis; neque ita prope adstet alii, vt suo illum halitu contingere possit; cum inuenias etiam qui alterius animam, etiam non graueolentem, ferre nequeunt.
units.tr: Further, one should not distort the mouth, nor spatter the face of the one he speaks with by spitting, nor snort or sing through the nose, nor repeatedly draw back the phlegm hanging from the nostrils with some most unpleasant sound, nor wave his hands while speaking, like one shooing away flies; nor stand so close to another that he can touch him with his breath; for you will find some who cannot bear even another's breath, though it is not foul-smelling.

units.la: Neque labra inter loquendum subinde lambenda vel mordenda; vel inter oscitandum, sermo ore hiante continuandus.
units.tr: Nor should the lips be licked or bitten again and again during speech; nor should one go on talking with the mouth gaping open in a yawn.

units.la: Ventrem & pectus proiicere, valde quoque inciuile & indecorum est; sicuti & pedibus in dextrum, vel lævum latus vacillare, alternis pedibus insistendo, vel discurrere, ridiculum est.
units.tr: To thrust out the belly and chest is also very uncivil and unseemly; and likewise to sway to the right or left side, shifting the weight from one foot to the other, or to run about, is ridiculous.

units.la: Odiosum & molestum valde est, quando loquens subinde eidem cum quo loquitur, fodit latus & cubito suo ad interrogationes suas, vel intentionem & auscultationem stimulat.
units.tr: It is very irritating and troublesome when the speaker repeatedly jabs the one he is speaking with in the side with his elbow, to prompt his answers or to stir up his attention and listening.

units.la: Vehemens contentio pro inani verborum victoria, valde indecora est & procliuis ad tumultum & perturbationem. Clemens Alex. lib. 2. Paedag. c. 7.
units.tr: Vehement contention for an empty victory in words is very unseemly, and prone to tumult and disturbance. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, chapter 7.

units.la: Poppysmata, sibili, digitis expressi soni, quibus accersuntur famuli, cum sint rationis expertes significationes, ratione praeditis hominibus vitandi sunt. Clemens Alexandrin. d. libr. 2. cap. 7.
units.tr: Smacking of the lips, whistling, and the sounds made by snapping the fingers, by which servants are summoned: since these are signs devoid of reason, they are to be avoided by men endowed with reason. Clement of Alexandria, the same book 2, chapter 7.

units.la: Indecorus risus habetur qui oris rictum latè diducit, corrugatis buccis, ac nudatis dentibus; qui caninus est & Sardonius dicitur.
units.tr: An unseemly laugh is one which stretches the mouth wide open, wrinkles the cheeks and bares the teeth; it is called dog-like and Sardonic.

units.la: Ad tertium etiam verbum exspuere indecorum; sicuti & identidem inter loquendum tussire, vel ad tertium quoq; verbum eructare vel screare, nasum emungere, demulcere faciem, humeros diducere, iactare brachia, ab imo pulmone pituitam trochleis adducere, gesticulari digitis, pedibus vacillare, toto corpore loqui, inciuile.
units.tr: Spitting at the third word is also unseemly; likewise, coughing repeatedly during speech, or belching or hawking at the third word, blowing the nose, stroking the face, spreading the shoulders, tossing the arms, hauling phlegm up from the bottom of the lungs as if with pulleys, gesticulating with the fingers, swaying on the feet, speaking with the whole body: all this is uncivil.

units.la: In auditione quieta vultus constitutio, hominem constantem & prudentem arguit, qui continenter, patienter & verecunde audit loquentem, is quod vtile est in sermone percipit & falsum facilius deprehendit, & veritatis studiosus habetur, non contentionis cupidus.
units.tr: In quiet listening, the composure of the face shows a steady and prudent man, who listens continently, patiently and modestly to the speaker; he grasps what is useful in the discourse and more easily detects what is false, and is regarded as a lover of truth rather than a lover of contention.

units.la: Grauitas supercilii in audiendo, vultus parū iucundus, oculi vagi, corporis circumactio indecora, femorum inter se permutatio, sed & nutus & susurrus, ad alterum fubrifio, & somnolentae oscitationes ac demissio vultus, & quidquid tale est, in vitio ponitur & accurate cauendum. Plutar. De auditione.
units.tr: A frown while listening, a rather unpleasant face, wandering eyes, an indecorous turning of the body, crossing of the thighs, as well as nods and whispering to another, drowsy yawns and a drooping face, and whatever is like these, is counted among faults and must be carefully avoided. Plutarch, On Listening.

units.la: Inuidia & liuor peffimus adsessor & consiliarius auditori, & dicta molesta & iniucunda efficit, & iudicium eorum inuertit, abripit & attentionem adimit, & memoriam & recordatione dictorum abolet.
units.tr: Envy and spite, the worst of advisers and counsellors to a listener, make what is said seem unpleasant and disagreeable, twist his judgement, distract his attention, and wipe out both the memory and the recollection of what was said.

units.la: In vsu sermonis prius est accipere recte quam emittere, sic vt conceptio & retentio foetus, partum antecedat. Accipimus vero & haurimus sermones auribus. Nam auris est ianua, quâ aditus ad animum virtutibus & vitiis datur. Ideoq; vacua illa a prauis sermonibus seruanda, & a nugis, sed necessariis & vtilibus & honestis aperienda.
units.tr: In the use of speech, it is first necessary to receive correctly before one sends out, just as conception and retention of the offspring come before birth. We receive and drink in speech through the ears. For the ear is the gate through which access to the mind is given to virtues and vices alike. Therefore those empty spaces must be kept free of bad speech and trivial talk, and opened instead to what is necessary, useful and honourable.

units.la: Vbi corrigendae vitae gratia sermone acriter arguente quis vtitur, tanquam medicamento mordente, ibi non audire submisse, neque pudore animum accensum vertigine corripi & pudore suffundi; sed immotum audire, deducti sq; Iuctifque in risum labiis dissimulare dolorem, est signum mali hominis a verecundia omni alieni.
units.tr: When someone uses a sharp, reproving speech for the sake of correcting one's life, like a biting medicine, it is a sign of a bad man, alien to all modesty, not to listen humbly, but to hear it unmoved, and, with lips drawn into a grin, to hide the pain; or to be seized with dizziness and suffused with shame as the mind burns with anger.

units.la: Contrà correptus & reprehensus, ob verecundiam nimiam dolorisque morsum fugiens, neque se curari sustinens, nimis ille delicatus, mollis & desperabundus dicitur. Cum etiam immeritæ correctiones homini forti perferendæ & sustinendæ. Et falsè in se iactum aliquod dictum, citra tamen iniuriam, cum facetia, ferre sine dolore & hilarè, non sit indignum ingenuo & disciplinam experto homini, sed omnino liberale.
units.tr: On the contrary, a man who is rebuked and reproved, who flees from excessive shame and the sting of pain and cannot bear to be cured, is called overly delicate, soft and despairing. Even undeserved corrections must be borne and endured by a brave man. And to bear without pain and cheerfully some saying falsely thrown at oneself, provided it is without injury and in a witty spirit, is not unworthy of a well-born man who has experienced discipline, but is altogether gentlemanly.

units.la: Præterea inter loquentem & audientem, quædam debet esse proportio, quemadmodum in pilæ ludo, qui excipit, iacenti se motibus corporis concinnè adcommodare solet. Dicenti igitur se adcommodare & attentionem loquenti adhibere conuenit, ne quid utiliter dictorum effugiat.
units.tr: Moreover, between speaker and listener there ought to be a certain proportion, as in the game of ball, where the one who catches usually adjusts his bodily movements neatly to the one who throws. It is fitting, then, for the listener to accommodate himself to the speaker and to give attention to him, so that nothing of what is said may usefully escape him.

units.la: Ideoque molestus & importunus est audi-tor, qui nulla orationis parte mouetur & delinitur, repletus fastu quodam, invidia, & insita sui solius approbatione, veluti qui aliquid iis quæ dicuntur melius dicere se posse præ se ferat: cum neque supercilium pro decoro moueat, neq; vllam emittat vocem, quæ eam animo æquo audire testetur, sed silentio & fictitia grauitate, atque habitu opinionem venetur constantis & profundi hominis, qui contemptu suam grauitatem metiatur. Plutarch. De audiione.
units.tr: Therefore the listener is troublesome and tiresome who is not moved or softened by any part of the speech, filled with a certain haughtiness, envy and an innate self-approval, as if he wished to show that he could say better than what is being said; since he neither moves his eyebrow to show decorum, nor utters any sound that would testify that he hears it with an even mind, but by silence and feigned gravity and bearing seeks the reputation of a steady and profound man, who measures his own dignity by contempt. Plutarch, On Listening.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De habitu & gestu naturali singulorum hominis membrorum.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. On the natural bearing and gesture of each of the human limbs.

units.la: ATque hi sunt habitus naturales hominis loquentis. Sequitur de illis, qui vt plurimum sunt silentis; qui licet quandoq; loquentem comitentur, diuersam tamen à sermone dicentis rationem habent.
units.tr: These are the natural bearings of a person who is speaking. Next come those of a person who is mostly silent; although these sometimes accompany a speaker, they have a different character from the speech of the one who is talking.

units.la: Atque eiusmodi rursum sunt in hominis membris singulis, vel in toto corpore eiusdem.
units.tr: Such bearings occur again in each of the human limbs, or in the whole body of the same person.

units.la: Natiui habitus qui sunt in singulis hominis membris, spectantur in eiusdem capite, fronte, ceruice, capillis, auribus, oculis, ore, labiis, osculo, lingua, barba, dentibus, facie tota, vultu, collo, humeris, brachiis, manibus, digitis, dextera, tergo, lumbis, cruribus, genibus, pedibus, & colore hominis: de quorum singulorum habitu, item, malo bono ordine dicemus hoc capite.
units.tr: The natural bearings found in the individual limbs of a person are seen in the head, forehead, neck, hair, ears, eyes, mouth, lips, kiss, tongue, beard, teeth, the whole face, countenance, throat, shoulders, arms, hands, fingers, right hand, back, loins, shins, knees, feet, and the complexion of the person. We shall speak of the bearing of each of these, likewise, in this chapter, in due order.

units.la: Velatio capitis est habitus & gestus hominis melancholici, moestitia, dolore, vel pudore affecti, aliorum occursum, colloquium & consolationem declinantis, 2.Sam.c.15.30. Dauid autem ascendit per cliuum montis oliuarum, indesinenter flens, opertus capite suo & pergens discalceatus; similiter totius populi, qui erant cum eo, operuerant quisque caput suum & ascendebant indesinenter flendo. c.19.5. Rex vero obvoluerat faciem suam, & clamabat Rex voce magna, Fili mi Absalom, Absalom, fili mi. Ezech.c.24.17. Clamare desiste, mortuorum luctum ne facito, tiaram tuam alliga tibi, & calceos tuos apponito pedibus tuis: neque obuelato mystacem, & cibum bum vllorum ne comedito. Esler c.6.12. Ierem.c.14.
units.tr: Covering the head is the bearing and gesture of a melancholy person, one affected by sadness, grief or shame, who avoids the approach, conversation and consolation of others. 2 Sam. 15:30. And David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping continually, with his head covered and going barefoot; and all the people who were with him had each covered his head and went up, weeping continually. 19:5. But the king had covered his face and cried with a loud voice, My son Absalom, Absalom, my son, my son. Ezek. 24:17. Cease to cry out, do not make mourning for the dead; bind your turban on you and put your shoes on your feet; do not cover your mustache, and do not eat the bread of mourners. Esther 6:12. Jer. 14.

units.la: 3. Etiam magnifici eorum reuertentur suis vasis vacuis: erubescent & pudore suffusi, operient caput suum.
units.tr: 3. Even their great men shall return with their vessels empty; they shall be ashamed and confounded, and shall cover their heads.

units.la: 4. Propter terram attritam, eo quod non fuerit pluuia in terra, erubescentes agricola operient caput suum. Leuit.c.10.21. Joh. Guil. Stuckius lib.2. c.28. Connubial antiquitat. Quandoque etiam habitus eorum qui gratia exciderunt. Esther d.c.6.12. Posteaquam Mordecai ad portam Regis: Haman vero proripuit se domum suam, lugens & opertus capite. vbi Jun. Esther c.7.8. Simulatq; verbum hoc prodiit ex ore Regis facie Hamanis operuerunt satellites. Job c.9.24.
units.tr: 4. Because the ground is parched, since there has been no rain on the earth, the farmers, ashamed, shall cover their heads. Lev. 10:21. Joh. Guil. Stuckius, book 2, chapter 28, Connubial Antiquities. Sometimes also it is the bearing of those who have fallen from favour. Esther 6:12. After Mordecai had gone to the king's gate, Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered. Where Junius (on Esther). Esther 7:8. As soon as the word came out of the king's mouth, the attendants covered Haman's face. Job 9:24.

units.la: In vxore autem velatio capitis, est habitus notans subiectionem, 1.Cor.c.11.3.4.5.6.13. Apud vos indicate, num decorum est mulierem non opertam Deum orare? 14. At ne natura quidem ipsa hoc vos docet, quod viro quidem comatum esse dedecori sit, 15. Contra mulieri comatam esse decori sit. Nam coma pro velamento data est ei. Genef. cap.20.16. & cap. 24.65. Alexand. ab Alexand. libr.2. Genial.dier. cap.29.
units.tr: In a wife, however, covering the head is a bearing that marks subjection. 1 Cor. 11:3, 4, 5, 6, 13. Judge among yourselves: is it fitting that a woman pray to God uncovered? 14. Does not nature itself teach you that for a man to wear long hair is a dishonour, 15. but for a woman to wear long hair is a glory? For her hair is given to her as a covering. Gen. 20:16 and 24:65. Alexander ab Alexandro, book 2, Genial Days, chapter 29.

units.la: Capitis demissio est habitus luctus, doloris & humiliationis, Esa.c.58.5. An huiusmodi esset ieiunium quod eligo, dies quo homo affligit animam suam? an incurvare, ut iuncum, caput suum? an ut quis cilicium ac cinerem sibi sternat? Genef.c.4.6. Tum dixit Iehova Cain, quare accensa est ira tua? & quare cecidit vultus tuus? Eccl.c.4.7.c.7.4.5.6.c.8.1. c.16. 13.c.20.39.c.13.10. &seqq.
units.tr: Lowering the head is the bearing of mourning, sorrow and humiliation. Isa. 58:5. Is this the fast that I choose, a day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head like a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Gen. 4:6. Then the LORD said to Cain, Why is your anger kindled? and why has your countenance fallen? Eccl. 4:7; 7:4, 5, 6; 8:1; 16:13; 20:39; 13:10, and following.

units.la: Caput erectum & altum gerere, est habitus victorum; Esa.c.35.10. & c.51.11. Luc.c.21.28. Cum autem haec fieri incipient, suspicite & attollite capita vestra, quoniam appropinquat redemtio vestri, Psal.83.3.
units.tr: To carry the head erect and high is the bearing of victors. Isa. 35:10 and 51:11. Luke 21:28. When these things begin to take place, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near. Ps. 83:3.

units.la: Caput depilatum & humerus leuis, magni & assidui laboris argumentum & nota est. Ezech. c.5 o.2. Omne caput decaluatu est. & c.7.18. In omni facie erit pudor, & in omnibus capitibus ipsorum calvitium, Esa. c.3.19.20.
units.tr: A shaven head and a light shoulder are a sign and mark of great and constant labour. Ezek. 5:2. Every head shall be made bald. 7:18. Shame shall be on every face, and baldness on all their heads. Isa. 3:19, 20.

units.la: Mouere caput solent, qui alienam calamitatem admirantur, vel irridෙnt & ludibrio habent alios, Jerem.cap.18.16. Vt exponam terram desolationi sibilo perpetuo: quisquis transiturus est per eam, obstupescat & agitet caput suum, Ecclesiastic. cap.2.16. Psalm.44.15. Posuisti nos parabola argumentum in gentibus, agitationis capitis in nationibus, & Psalm.109.25. Insuper ego probro sum illis: Videntes me, mouent caput suum. 2. Reg.cap.19.21. vbi notat Iunius. Psalm.22.8. Omnes videntes me subsannant me, diducunt labium, mouent caput. Job c.16.10. Matth. cap.27.39. & seqq. Marc.cap.15.29.30.
units.tr: Those who marvel at another's calamity, or mock and make a sport of others, are wont to shake the head. Jer. 18:16. To make their land a desolation, a perpetual hissing; everyone who passes by it shall be astonished and shake his head. Ecclus. 2:16. Ps. 44:15. You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples. And Ps. 109:25. I also am a reproach to them; when they see me, they shake their heads. 2 Kings 19:21, where Junius notes this. Ps. 22:8. All who see me mock me; they part their lips, they shake the head. Job 16:10. Matt. 27:39 and following. Mark 15:29, 30.

units.la: Capillorum capitis euulsio & laceratio, est habitus arguens indignationem, luctum & dolorem. Hesra c.9.3. Itaque audiens rem hanc, lacerauit vestem meam & pallium meum, & vellens de capillis capitis mei & barbae mea, sedebam desolatus, & seqq. Ier.c.16.6. & c.47.5. Mich.c.1.16. Leuit. c.19.27.c.21. Deut.c.14.1.2. Ier.c.7.29. Gen.c.41.14. c.50.4. Esa.c.4. 2. Job c.4.
units.tr: Plucking out and tearing the hair of the head is a bearing that shows indignation, grief and sorrow. Ezra 9:3. So when I heard this matter, I tore my garment and my mantle, and plucking hair from my head and my beard, I sat down desolate, and following. Jer. 16:6; 47:5. Mic. 1:16. Lev. 19:27; 21. Deut. 14:1, 2. Jer. 7:29. Gen. 41:14; 50:4. Isa. 4:2. Job 4.

units.la: Annuere capite, vel manu, est habitus hominis affirmantis & approbantis, Luc. c.1.62. Innuebant autem patri eius, quid vellet eum vocari, c.7. Et innuerunt sociis qui erant in altero nauigio, vt venirent & sibi opitularentur. Contra, capite renuere & id circumflectere, habitus est improbantis & negantis.
units.tr: Nodding with the head or the hand is the bearing of a person affirming and approving. Luke 1:62. And they made signs to his father, asking what he wished him to be called. Luke 5:7. And they beckoned to their partners in the other boat, that they should come and help them. On the other hand, to refuse by turning the head aside is the bearing of one who disapproves and denies.

units.la: Habere
units.tr: Having

units.la: Habere caput asperum, introrsum, vel incultum est habitus negligentis, & pertæsi hominis. vid. Senec. lib. 1. epist. 5.
units.tr: Having the head rough, unkempt or uncombed is the bearing of a careless man, one weary of life. See Seneca, letters, book 1, letter 5.

units.la: Caput vnctum habentis gestus, ostendit & arguit lætitiæ affectum. Esa. c. 61. 3. Matth. c. 6. 17. Luc. c. 7. 46.
units.tr: A head anointed with oil shows and betokens a feeling of joy. Isa. 61. 3. Matt. 6. 17. Luke 7. 46.

units.la: Frons dura significat obstinationem & impudentiam, Esa. c. 48. 4. Exprascientia mea erat, ut durum esse, & nervum ferreum esse cervicem tuam, frontem tuam chalybeam. Ezech. c. 3. 17.
units.tr: A hard brow signifies obstinacy and shamelessness. Isa. 48. 4. "Because I knew that you are stubborn, and your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead bronze." Ezek. 3. 17.

units.la: Frons rugosa cum attractis superciliis est habitus attente meditantis, cogitabundi & philosophici. Sen. lib. 20. epist. 114. & lib. 14. epist. 90.
units.tr: A wrinkled brow with the eyebrows drawn together is the bearing of one who thinks intently, pondering and philosophising. Seneca, letters 114 and 90.

units.la: Auris inclinatio notat habitum libenter rem cognoscere cupientis, vel hominis attenti. Psal. 102. 3. Non abscondas faciem tuam à me, quo die est angustia mihi; Inclina ad me aurem tuam, quo die inclamo, & Psal. 10. 17. Confirma animum horum, adverte aurem tuam, & Psalm. 31. 3. Inclina ad me aurem tuam, cito eripe me, & Psal. 130. 2. Sint aures tuæ intentæ ad vocem deprecationum mearum, Prov. c. 4. Quandoq; etiam est habitus obedientis. Ier. c. 7. 24. Matth. c. 13.
units.tr: Bending the ear signifies the bearing of one eager to learn something gladly, or of an attentive man. Ps. 102. 3. "Do not hide your face from me in the day of my trouble; incline your ear to me in the day when I call." Ps. 10. 17. "Lord, you have heard the desire of the meek; you will prepare their heart, you will incline your ear." Ps. 31. 3. "Incline your ear to me, deliver me speedily." Ps. 130. 2. "Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications." Prov. 4. Sometimes it is also the bearing of one who obeys. Jer. 7. 24. Matt. 13.

units.la: Contrà autem obturare & occludere, est habitus attentionem & auscultationem negantis, & non persuaderi sibi cupientis, Psalm. 58. 5. Venenum est illis simile veneno serpentis, sicut aspidis surdæ obturantis aurem suam. Esa. c. 33. 15. Qui occludit aurem suam, ne audiat cædes, &c. Prouerb. c. 21. 13.
units.tr: On the other hand, stopping up and closing the ears is the bearing of one who refuses to attend and listen, and who wishes not to be persuaded. Ps. 58. 5. "Their poison is like the poison of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear." Isa. 33. 15. "He who stops his ear from hearing blood, etc." Prov. 21. 13.

units.la: Auris tinniens, est habitus maxime pauescentis, cui sensus audiendi hebetatur. 2. Reg. c. 2. 12. Mich. c. 7. 16. 1. Sam. 3. 11.
units.tr: A ringing ear is the bearing of one who is greatly terrified, whose sense of hearing is dulled. 2 Kings 2. 12. Mic. 7. 16. 1 Sam. 3. 11.

units.la: Oculi sunt lucerna corporis, qua interna apparent, Matth. c. 6. Hos placidos esse, verecundos & compositos decet; qui animum sedatum & compositum indicant.
units.tr: The eyes are the lamp of the body, by which the inner things appear. Matt. 6. It is fitting that they be calm, modest and composed, for they indicate a settled and composed mind.

units.la: Oculi sublimes & elati, sunt habitus & indices superbiæ. Prou. c. 21. 4. Elatio vero oculorum & aptitudo animi, oratio deniq; improborum, peccatum est, c. 26. 12. Esa. cap. 2. 11. & Iob c. 22. 29. Luc. c. 18. 13. 2. Reg. c. 19. 22. Quod attollis in sublime oculos tuos contra sanctum Israelis. Psalm. 10. 4. Improbos in elatione vultus sui non inquirere nullum esse Deum, sunt omnes cogitationes eorum. Eccles. c. 23. 4. 5. 7. Luc. c. 18. 13.
units.tr: Eyes raised high and haughty are the bearing and marks of pride. Prov. 21. 4. "A haughty look and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, is sin," Prov. 26. 12. Isa. 2. 11. Job 22. 29. Luke 18. 13. 2 Kings 19. 22. "Whom have you mocked and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel." Ps. 10. 4. "The wicked, in the pride of his countenance, does not seek God; God is not in all his thoughts." Ecclus. 23. 4, 5, 7. Luke 18. 13.

units.la: Oculi nutantes innuentes, loquaces, notant mores malicicos, cogitationesque peruersas & malas. Eccles. c. 27. 24. Qui nictat oculo, fabricatur mala. Prou. c. 6. 13. Homo nequam nictat oculis suis, verba facit pedibus suis, docet digitis suis. Prou. c. 10. 10. c. 16. 30. c. 4. 25. c. 26. 12. Eccl. c. 27. 24. Et oculis conniuentibus, circumactis & lasciuis intueri, nihil aliud est quam oculis maechari, ut dicit Clemens Alex. lib. 3. c. 11. Paedag. Quia per eos cupiditas ineat prima pugnæ præludia.
units.tr: Winking, nodding and talking eyes betoken wicked manners and perverse and evil thoughts. Ecclus. 27. 24. "He who winks with the eye devises mischief." Prov. 6. 13. "A worthless man winks with his eyes, speaks with his feet, and teaches with his fingers." Prov. 10. 10; 16. 30; 4. 25; 26. 12. Ecclus. 27. 24. And to look with half-closed eyes, or with roving and wanton glances, is nothing other than to commit adultery with the eyes, as Clement of Alexandria says, Paedagogus, book 3, chapter 11. because through the eyes desire enters, the first skirmishes of the battle.

units.la: Oculi torui sunt truculentorum; vagi & volubiles leuium vel insanorum; limi, suspiciosorum & insidiantium; immodice diducti, stolidorum; stupentes & defixi, attonitorum; acres, iracundorum.
units.tr: Fierce eyes belong to the savage; roving and restless eyes to the frivolous or mad; shifty eyes to the suspicious and those who lie in wait; eyes immoderately wide open to the dull-witted; staring and fixed eyes to the astonished; sharp eyes to the angry.

units.la: Indecorum etiam & contemptus indicium est, clauso oculorum uno, alium intueri, quod nihil aliud est quam seipsum quasi eluscare: qui est gestus iaculantium, & fabrorum ad Lesbiam suam regulam opus suum examinantium.
units.tr: It is also an indecent sign of contempt, with one eye closed, to look at someone with the other, which is nothing other than to squint at oneself, as it were. This is the gesture of archers and of craftsmen who test their work against their Lesbian rule.

units.la: Attollere oculos, est attente, cupide & promte obseruare. Ezech. c. 33. 25. Psalm. 33. 16. Oculi vero clausi, cogitantem & meditantem produnt. Prou. c. 16. 30. Oculos aperire, est vigilantium & attendentium. Prouerb. c. 20. 13. Iob c. 27. 19. Oculus deficiens, vel languens, significat animum fatiscentem & defessum. Psal. 119. 82. 123. & Psal. 88. 10. & Psal. 38. 11. Marc. c. 8. 3. Ierem. c. 14. Psal. 69. 4. Deficiunt oculi mei sperantes in Deum. Esa. c. 38. 14. Exhauriuntur oculi mei, &c.
units.tr: To raise the eyes is to observe attentively, eagerly and readily. Ezek. 33. 25. Ps. 33. 16. Closed eyes, on the other hand, reveal one who is thinking and meditating. Prov. 16. 30. To open the eyes is the bearing of those who are watchful and attentive. Prov. 20. 13. Job 27. 19. A failing or languishing eye signifies a spirit faint and weary. Ps. 119. 82; 123; Ps. 88. 10; Ps. 38. 11; Mark 8. 3; Jer. 14; Ps. 69. 4 "My eyes fail while I hope in God." Isa. 38. 14 "My eyes are worn out," etc.

units.la: Oculi praeterea sunt indices nequitiæ & impudentiæ, Ecclesiast. cap. 26. 12. Scortatio mulieris in elatis oculis atque in palpebris eius cognoscitur, & v. 14. 11. Prou. c. 26. Oculi vagi stolidorum hominum. Prou. c. 17. 24. Adest faciei prudentis sapientia: oculi autem stolidi, vagantur ad extremitatem terræ.
units.tr: Moreover, the eyes are signs of wickedness and shamelessness. Ecclus. 26. 12. "The harlotry of a woman is known by her haughty eyes and her eyelids." Ecclus. 14. 11. Prov. 26. Roving eyes belong to foolish men. Prov. 17. 24. "Wisdom is before the face of the prudent, but the eyes of fools wander to the ends of the earth."

units.la: Sunt etiam indices auaritiæ & inuidiæ. Matt. c. 20. 15. An non licet mihi, quod volo facere in meis rebus? an oculus tuus malus est, quia ego sum bonus? Deut. c. 15. 9. Ne oculus tuus sit malignus. & cap. 28. 54. Vir mollis, & malignus erit oculus in fratrem suum. &c. & v. 56. Eccles. c. 14. 8. 9. c. 31. 14. Marc. c. 7. 22.
units.tr: The eyes are also signs of covetousness and envy. Matt. 20. 15. "Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? Or is your eye evil because I am good?" Deut. 15. 9. "Let not your eye be evil." And 28. 54. "The man who is soft and whose eye is evil toward his brother will be..." etc. And v. 56. Ecclus. 14. 8, 9; 31. 14. Mark 7. 22.

units.la: Sunt etiam oculi indices curæ & custodiæ, Psal. 33. 18. Ecce, oculus Ieho͞uæ, attendit ad timentes se, ad exspectantes benignitatem ipsius.
units.tr: The eyes are also signs of care and watchfulness. Ps. 33. 18. "Behold, the eye of the LORD is upon those who fear him, upon those who hope in his steadfast love."

units.la: Oculi demissi & humiles, sunt modestiæ habitus. Iob cap. 22. 29. Tum demissum oculis seruabit Deus, Luc. c. 18. 13. Nolebat vel oculos in cælum attollere. Prou. c. 16. 19. Melius est submissum esse spiritu cum mansuetis, &c. Osea c. 7. 10.
units.tr: Eyes cast down and humble are signs of modesty. Job 22. 29. "When men are cast down, you will say, 'Lift up'; then God will save the humble of eye." Luke 18. 13. He would not lift his eyes to heaven. Prov. 16. 19. "It is better to be of a humble spirit with the lowly, etc." Hos. 7. 10.

units.la: Oculi in aliquem conuersi, indicant attentionis petitionem. Luc. c. 6. 20. Sublatis oculis suis in discipulos, dixit. quandoq; obseruationem.Psal. 10.8.9.Psalm.34.16. Oculi Iehoua ad iustos, Ezech. c.33.25.Genes.c.4.4.c.19.17.& Deut.c.26.15.Exod. c.4.31.c 12.25.
units.tr: Eyes turned upon someone indicate a request for attention. Luke 6. 20. "And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples and said." Sometimes they indicate observation. Ps. 10. 8, 9; Ps. 34. 16. "The eyes of the LORD are upon the righteous." Ezek. 33. 25. Gen. 4. 4; 19. 17; Deut. 26. 15. Exod. 4. 31; 12. 25.

units.la: Oculi auersi vel transuersi negantem, fastidi-entem, dissimulantem, vel negligentem fignifi-cant.Psal.119.37. Auerte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem. Iob c.36.7. Non subtrahit a iusto oculos. Eccles.c.4.1. Prou.c.21.v.28.
units.tr: Eyes turned away or sideways signify one who refuses, disdains, dissembles or neglects. Ps. 119. 37. "Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity." Job 36. 7. "He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous." Eccles. 4. 1. Prov. 21. 28.

units.la: Oculos obstipare, velare, vel auertere, est habitus non cupientis videre. Isa.c.33.15.Et obstipat oculos suos, ne videant malum. Iob d.c.36.7. Contra oculos aperire, habitus est vigilantis. Prou.c.20.13.Iobc.27.19.
units.tr: To cast down, veil or turn away the eyes is the bearing of one who does not wish to see. Isa. 33. 15. "And shuts his eyes so as not to see evil." Job 36. 7. On the contrary, to open the eyes is the bearing of one who is watchful. Prov. 20. 13. Job 27. 19.

units.la: Testis oculatus maiorem fidem meretur, quam auritus, Prou.c.21.28.vbi Iun.
units.tr: An eyewitness deserves greater trust than one who only hears. Prov. 21. 28, where Junius.

units.la: Lachrymae oculorum, animum & affectum lugentem & maerentem arguunt.1.Cor.c.7.30.vbi Beza.2.Reg.c.20.5.vidi lacrymas tuas, &c. Marc. c.9.24. Gen.c.21.16.c.27.38. Hebr.c.12.17. Indic. c.11.37.Ruth.c.1.9.1.Sam.c.1.7.8.c 11.4.c.15.35.cap. 20.41.2.Sam.c.1.17.24.1.Esd.cap.10.1.Esth.c.8.3. Iob cap.30.25.31.Matth.cap.26.75.Esa. cap.38.3.4.5. & Psalm.137.Marc.c.5.38.Luc.c.19.41. & locis pluribus aliis.
units.tr: Tears of the eyes show a mind and feeling that mourns and grieves. 1 Cor. 7. 30, where Beza. 2 Kings 20. 5. "I have seen your tears," etc. Mark 9. 24. Gen. 21. 16; 27. 38. Heb. 12. 17. Judg. 11. 37. Ruth 1. 9. 1 Sam. 1. 7, 8; 11. 4; 15. 35; 20. 41. 2 Sam. 1. 17, 24. Ezra 10. 1. Esther 8. 3. Job 30. 25, 31. Matt. 26. 75. Isa. 38. 3, 4, 5. Ps. 137. Mark 5. 38. Luke 19. 41, and in many other places.

units.la: Quandoq; lachrymae etiam impotentis alicuius laetitiae argumentum, Genes.c.43.30.c.33.4. c.45.14.15.Ier.c.30.4.
units.tr: Sometimes tears are also a sign of a joy that is too great to contain. Gen. 43. 30; 33. 4; 45. 14, 15. Jer. 30. 4.

units.la: Supercilia exporrecta, indecora; adducta, toruitatis; sublata in altum, arrogantiae; in oculos depressa, male cogitantis indicium praebent.
units.tr: Eyebrows stretched out are unbecoming; drawn together they show a fierce look; raised high they show arrogance; pressed down over the eyes they reveal a man thinking evil.

units.la: Frons sit hilaris & explanata: quae animi aperti perti signum est & liberalis; in rugas contracta, est senum & iracundorum; torua, taurorum.
units.tr: The forehead should be cheerful and smooth, which is the sign of an open and generous mind; drawn into wrinkles it belongs to the old and the angry; fierce, to bulls.

units.la: Nares vento, vel fumo incensæ, iram gravissimam & vltionis præsentis auidam significant. 1.Reg.c.22.9. Psal.18.9. Ascendit fumus per nares eius, &c. Iob c.39.23.
units.tr: Nostrils inflamed by wind or smoke signify very grievous anger and a desire for present vengeance. 1 Kings 22. 9. Ps. 18. 9. "Smoke went up from his nostrils," etc. Job 39. 23.

units.la: Nares habere muco, fœtore & purulentia oppletas, est hominis fœtidi, & sordidi; præsertim quando veste, brachio, cubito, vel manu emunxerit, vel in solum eiecerit.
units.tr: To have the nostrils filled with mucus, stench and pus is the mark of a foul and filthy man, especially when he has blown his nose on his garment, arm, elbow or hand, or has flung it upon the ground.

units.la: Ronchos naribus ducere, est furiosorum, nisi orthopnœa quis laboret: naribus vocem emittere, est cornicinum & elephantorum. Nasum crispare, est irrisorum & sannionum.
units.tr: To snort through the nose belongs to madmen, unless one suffers from orthopnoea; to make a noise through the nose is the habit of horn-blowers and elephants. To wrinkle the nose belongs to mockers and buffoons.

units.la: De sternutationis habitu & significatione quid senserint veteres, refert Alex. ab Alexan. libr.2. Gen.dier.cap.26. & Plin.lib.28. cap.3. quae præsentibus molesta esse solet. vide Clement. Alexand.lib.2. Padag.c.7. Ideoque sternutantibus corpus auertendum, ne cui in os quid ingerat vel indecorum quid exhibeat: non vero sonitus quem natura fert, reprimendus.
units.tr: What the ancients thought about the bearing and meaning of sneezing, which is usually troublesome to those present, is reported by Alexander ab Alexandro, Dies Geniales, book 2, chapter 26, and by Pliny, book 28, chapter 3. See Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, book 2, chapter 7. Therefore, those who sneeze should turn their body away, lest they spray anything into someone's face or display anything unbecoming; but the sound that nature produces is not to be suppressed.

units.la: Os apertum tribuitur iis, qui initium dicendi faciunt. Matth.c.5.2. Psalm.78.1. Act.cap.8. 35.Dilatatio oris, quandoque est gestus irridentis, insultantis, illudentis & contemnentis. Esa. cap.57.4. vbi Iun. Psalm.35.21. & 22. Videntes me subsannant me, & diducunt labium, & verf.14. Dilatant contra me os suum, & Psalm.22.14. Iob c.16.10. Diiciendum contra me os suum, &c. Os vero percutere, est detestantis hominis, Actor. c.23. & Matth.c.27.
units.tr: An open mouth is attributed to those who begin to speak. Matt. 5:2; Ps. 78:1; Acts 8:35. Opening the mouth wide is sometimes the gesture of one who mocks, insults, jeers and scorns. Isa. 57:4, where Junius; Ps. 35:21-22: "They gaped at me and said, 'Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it'"; v. 14: "They opened their mouths wide against me"; Ps. 22:13: "They open their mouths against me like a ravening and roaring lion"; Job 16:10: "They have gaped upon me with their mouths." To strike the mouth is the gesture of a man who detests, Acts 23:2; Matt. 27.

units.la: Inflare buccas, fastus indicium est; demittere easdem, est animum despondentis. vt Erafm. in Ciuilit. morum ait.
units.tr: Puffing out the cheeks is a sign of pride; letting them fall is the mark of a despondent spirit. As Erasmus says in his book on good manners.

units.la: Os pressum, est metuentis alterius halitum haurire; hians vero est morionum. Labiis subin-de porrectis, veluti poppysmum facere, indeco-rum, & felium est & canum.
units.tr: A pressed mouth means one who breathes in the breath of someone he fears; a gaping mouth belongs to fools. To thrust out the lips now and then, as if making a kissing sound, is unseemly and belongs to cats and dogs.

units.la: Oscitatio vola vel strophiolo vel corporis auersione tegenda & occultanda. Declare & so-nore oscitante infamia notato refert Gellius libr.4. cap.20.
units.tr: A yawn should be covered and hidden with the hand, a handkerchief or a turning away of the body. Gellius, book 4, chapter 20, relates that a loud, gaping yawn is marked with disgrace.

units.la: Oris sputo, alium conspuere, est habitus ho-minis contemnentis, abominantis & auersan-tis. Marc.c.10.34. Et ipse illudent eum, & flagellabunt eum & inspuent in eum, &c. Matth.c.27.30. Et cum inspuissent in eum, & seqq. Esa.c.50.6. Faciem meam non abscondo a contumeliis & sputo. Iob c.30.10. Abo-minantur me, longe recedunt a me, & a facie mea non cohibent sputum. Num.c.12.14. Si pater inspuisset in faciem eius, &c.
units.tr: To spit from the mouth at someone is the gesture of a man who scorns, loathes and turns away. Mark 10:34: "They will mock him, and scourge him, and spit upon him"; Matt. 27:30: "And they spat upon him"; Isa. 50:6: "I hid not my face from shame and spitting"; Job 30:10: "They abhor me, they flee far from me, and spare not to spit in my face"; Num. 12:14: "If her father had but spit in her face."

units.la: Sputum eiectum ne cui nauseam moueat, pede proterendum, vel terrae puluere tegen-dum. Resorbere saliuam, sordidum est & ca-num & suum, qui ad vomitum & volutabrum redeunt.
units.tr: Spittle that has been cast out should, so that it does not cause anyone nausea, be trodden under foot or covered with dust. To swallow back one's saliva is filthy, and belongs to dogs and pigs, who return to their vomit and their wallowing.

units.la: Frequenter spuere, violentius exscreare & emungere, arguit nauseam & intemperantiam, & parit molestiam & tædium. Vel signum in-temperantiae est ex immoderata exhibitione humidorum, vt Clem. & Alex. Pædag.lib.2.c.2.
units.tr: To spit often, to hawk and blow the nose violently, shows nausea and intemperance, and causes annoyance and disgust. Or it is a sign of intemperance, arising from an immoderate intake of moist food. As Clement of Alexandria says, Paedagogus, book 2, chapter 2.

units.la: Ori manus imposita, indicat habitum eorū qui veritate conuicti, aut potestate & authori-tate superati, obmutescunt pudefactiq; tacent. Mich.c.7.16. Imponent manum ori & videntes eru-bescent. befcent.Pfal.39.10. Obmutesco, non aperio os meum. Esai.cap.52.15. Propter eum reges obdent os suu, &c.
units.tr: A hand laid on the mouth indicates the attitude of those who, convicted by the truth or overcome by power and authority, fall silent, put to shame and mute. Micah 7:16: "They shall lay their hand upon their mouth, and their ears shall be deaf"; Ps. 39:9: "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth"; Isa. 52:15: "Kings shall shut their mouths at him."

units.la: Osculum sanctum & pudicum, charitatis symbolum est & amicitiæ mutuæ signum: & in salutationibus vt plurimum vsurpatur,1.Theff.c. 5.26.1.Pet.c.5.14.1.Cor.c.16.20.c.13.2. Cor.c.13.12. Rom.c.16.16. Act.c.20.37. Gen.c.29.13. cap.33.4. c.45.14.c.48.10.c.49.34.Exod.c.4.27. Luc.cap.15. 20.c.7.45. De hoc habitu vide qua infra cap.14. dico & c.11.
units.tr: A holy and chaste kiss is a symbol of love and a sign of mutual friendship, and is commonly used in greetings. 1 Thess. 5:26; 1 Pet. 5:14; 1 Cor. 16:20; 1 Cor. 13:12; Rom. 16:16; Acts 20:37; Gen. 29:13; Gen. 33:4; Gen. 45:14; Gen. 48:10; Gen. 49:34; Exod. 4:27; Luke 15:20; Luke 7:45. On this gesture see what follows in chapter 14, and chapter 11.

units.la: Labia mouere fine eloquio, est habitus ardenter & vehementer precantis & meditantis. 1.Sam.1.13. Nam Channa loquebatur cum animo suo: tantum labia eius mouebantur, vox autem eius non audiebatur, & verf.15.ib.d. Mulier agra animo sum, effundo desiderium animi mei coram Iehoua. & verf.16. Nam pra magnitudine meditationis mea & indignationis mea locuta sum hactenus.
units.tr: Moving the lips without speaking is the attitude of one who prays and meditates fervently and earnestly. 1 Sam. 1:13: "For Hannah spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard"; v. 15: "I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit; I have poured out my soul before the LORD"; v. 16: "For out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken hitherto."

units.la: Labrum inferius premere dentibus superioribus, vel superius inferioribus, est habitus minantis.
units.tr: To press the lower lip with the upper teeth, or the upper lip with the lower teeth, is the attitude of one who threatens.

units.la: Lingua palato inhærens, silentium indicat. Iob c.29.10.Ezech.c.3.11.12.Psalm.22.16. Mandere linguam, est dolentis & exacerbati hominis. Apocalyps.c.16.10. Et mandebant linguas suas pra dolore. Linguam exerere, est habitus insultantis & irridentis hominis. Esa.c.57.8. Contra quem oblectatis vos? contra quem dilatatis os, protrahitis linguam, &c. Psal.22.13. &35.31.
units.tr: A tongue cleaving to the palate indicates silence. Job 29:10; Ezek. 3:11-12; Ps. 22:15. To bite the tongue belongs to a man in pain and fury. Rev. 16:10: "And they gnawed their tongues for pain." To thrust out the tongue is the attitude of one who insults and mocks. Isa. 57:4 (LXX-style rendering of v. 8): "Against whom do you make merry? Against whom do you open your mouth and stick out the tongue?"; Ps. 22:13; Ps. 35:21.

units.la: Silere & tacere tum, quando homines loqui solent, est habitus vehementissime commoti & perculsi, cui præ dolore & consternatione verba sunt intercepta. Iob c.2.13. Itasedebant cum eo humi septem diebus & noctibus, neque erat qui alloquere‑tur eum vllo verbo; quia videbant magnum esse illum dolorem valde. Psalm. 32. 3. Hesra c. 9. 3. & quandoque patientiam significat. Ierem. cap. 8. 14. & Psalm. 39. 3. Obmutui taciturus, sedebam etiam, &c. Psalm. 38. 14. Quos ego tanquam surdus non audio, & tanquam mutus, non aperiens os meum, 15. Sum tanquam is, in cuius ore non sunt argumenta. Esa. c. 30. 15. Leuit. c. 10. 3. Tum dixit Moses Aaroni, Il‑lud est quod locutus erat Iehoua dicendo, In propin‑quis meis sanctificabor, &c. sed conticuit Aaron. 1. Sam. c. 10. 27. 2. Reg. c. 18. 36. Iesa. c. 36. 21. cap. 42. 14. Matth. c. 26. 63. c. 27. 14. Quandoq; habitus conuiͤcti conscientia. Neh. c. 5. 8. Qui silenerunt, neque invenerunt quod responderent. Iob c. 36. 37. 38. Aliquando signum & habitus melancholici & Ecstasi correpti. Sed & saepe silentium alias animi affectiones indicat; de quib. dixi supra c. 4. ex Prou. c. 10. 19. Eccl. c. 20. 3. 4. 5. 6. 20. c. 5. 4. 5. Eccl. c. 5. 2. 3. 10. 11. Prou. c. 17. 27. 28.
units.tr: To be silent and keep quiet at the very time when people are wont to speak is the attitude of a man greatly moved and struck down, whose words are cut off by grief and dismay. Job 2:13: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great." Ps. 32:3; Ezra 9:3. Sometimes it signifies patience. Jer. 8:14; Ps. 39:2-3: "I was dumb with silence, I held my peace, even from good; and my sorrow was stirred"; Ps. 38:13-14: "But I, as a deaf man, heard not; and as a dumb man, who openeth not his mouth." Ps. 38:15: "I am as a man that heareth not, and in whose mouth are no reproofs." Isa. 30:15; Lev. 10:3: "Then Moses said unto Aaron, This is it that the LORD spake, saying, I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me... and Aaron held his peace." 1 Sam. 10:27; 2 Kings 18:36; Isa. 36:21; Isa. 42:14; Matt. 26:63; Matt. 27:14. Sometimes it is the sign of a conscience that feels itself convicted. Neh. 5:8: "They held their peace and found nothing to answer"; Job 36:37-38. At other times it is the sign and attitude of melancholy or of one seized by ecstasy. But silence often indicates other emotions of the mind too, of which I spoke above in chapter 4, from Prov. 10:19; Eccl. 20:3-6, 20; Eccl. 5:4-5; Eccl. 5:2-3, 10-11; Prov. 17:27-28.

units.la: Frendere dentibus, eosq; instar canis exacerbati labiis diductis ostendere, est irascentium, dolentium, & quandoq; irridentium & insultantium. Psal. 35. 16. Inter hypocritas facetos, sannio-nes faceti frendentes contra me dentibus suis. Psal. 101. 10. Improbus videns indignatur, dentibus suis frendes contabescit. Act. c. 7. 54. Audientes haec, findebantur cordibus suis & stridebant dentibus suis.
units.tr: To grind the teeth, and to show them like an enraged dog with the lips drawn back, belongs to those who are angry, in pain, and sometimes mocking and insulting. Ps. 35:16: "With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth"; Ps. 112:10: "The wicked shall see it and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth and melt away"; Acts 7:54: "When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth."

units.la: Barbae & capillorum canities, auctoritatis & reuerentiae habitus dicitur. Prouerb. cap. 16. 31. Leuit. c. 19. 17. De barba velata vide Ezech. cap. 24. 17. Leuit. c. 19. 45. Conuellere alicui barbam, est habitus ignominiam & iniuriam inferentis.
units.tr: Grey hair on the beard and head is said to be the mark of authority and reverence. Prov. 16:31; Lev. 19:32. On the veiled beard see Ezek. 24:17; Lev. 19:45. To pull out someone's beard is the gesture of one who inflicts disgrace and injury.

units.la: Corpus meum expono percussoribus & malas meas depilantibus. Barba horrens, est habitus mæsti & sordidati hominis, 2.Sam.c.19.f. c.10.4. f.6.Ierem.c.41.f. Barbam subinde intorquere, est habitus affectati muliebris ornatus. vid. Senec. lib.21.epist.116. De barba habitu Clem. Alex.lib.3. c.11. Pædagog.ita scribit: Quod si quis non nihil barba tondeat; ea tamen non omnino est tondenda & denudanda, quod turpe est spectaculum. Barba enim tonsa ad cutem usque non videtur multum abesse à vulsione & leuore.vid.Psal.132.
units.tr: "I gave my body to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair." A bristling beard is the attitude of a sorrowful and squalid man. 2 Sam. 19; 2 Sam. 10:4-6; Jer. 41. To twist the beard now and then is the attitude of an affected, womanish adornment. See Seneca, book 21, letter 116. On the beard's attitude Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, book 3, chapter 11, writes thus: "But if someone trims his beard a little, it should nevertheless not be shaved off completely and stripped bare, for that is an ugly sight. For a beard shaved right down to the skin does not seem much different from plucking and baldness." See Ps. 132.

units.la: Pili capitis qui descendentes, visum impediunt, & qui in superiori labri parte intercomedendum polluuntur, tondendi sunt tonsorum forficibus. Barbæ pili qui nihil molestiæ adferunt, non sunt vexandi, ut qui vultui gravitatem adferant, & quendam paternum terrorem incutiant. Clem. Alex.d.loc.
units.tr: Hairs of the head that hang down and obstruct the view, and those that defile the upper part of the lip, should be trimmed with barbers' shears. Hairs of the beard that cause no inconvenience should not be harassed, since they lend gravity to the face and strike a kind of paternal awe. Clement of Alexandria, in the same place.

units.la: Facies hominis, gestus & habitus tam bonos quam malos multiplices, admittit & induit ex interiore hominis affectione. Eccl.c.13.30.31. Cor hominis mutat vultum ipsius sive ad bona spectet, sive ad mala & seqq. & ex aspectu cognoscitur vir. Eccl.c.19.26.27. & vultus formatio & fictio ex corde hominis est, Eccl.d c.13.& c.37.20. & animus latus beneficit vultum, Prov.c.15.13.
units.tr: The face of a man admits and takes on many gestures and attitudes, both good and bad, from the inner disposition of the man. Eccl. 13:30-31: "A man's heart changes his countenance, whether for good or for evil," and following; a man is known by his look, Eccl. 19:26-27; the shaping and feigning of the countenance comes from the heart of man, Eccl. 13 and Eccl. 37:20; and a cheerful spirit makes the face glad, Prov. 15:13.

units.la: Faciem in rem aliquam ponere, est gestus intentionem, studium & operam præstantis, Ezech.c.6.2 c.28.21. c.29.2. cap.14.8. cap.25.2. Disponere faciem suam contra aliquid, est offendere quò, & ad quem dirigatur sermo. Ezech.d. cap.6.2.cap.28.21. c.29.2. Ierem. c.3.7. Faciem abscondere & auertere, est hominis auersantis, negligentis & alienati animi. Psalm.11.25. Non abscondit faciem suam ab eo. & Psalm.44.25. Quare faciem tuam absconderas? &c. 2.Reg.c.3.14. Nisi personam Josaphati regis Judæ susciperem, non intuerer te neque aspicerem te. Contrà, faciem illustrare & conuertere ad aliquem. Psal.119. 135. Num. c.6. 26.
units.tr: To set one's face upon something is the gesture of one who gives attention, zeal and effort. Ezek. 6:2; Ezek. 28:21; Ezek. 29:2; Ezek. 14:8; Ezek. 25:2. To set one's face against something is to show whither and against whom the speech is directed. Ezek. 6:2; Ezek. 28:21; Ezek. 29:2; Jer. 3:7. To hide and turn away the face is the mark of one who turns away, neglects and is estranged in mind. Ps. 11:25 (with the notion of not hiding his face from him); Ps. 44:24: "Wherefore hidest thou thy face?"; 2 Kings 3:14: "Were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, I would not look toward thee, nor see thee." On the contrary, to make the face shine and to turn it towards someone: Ps. 119:135; Num. 6:25-26.

units.la: Vultus placidus & iucundus, est habitus hominis compositi & morati, ciuilis & sua sorte contenti. Prou.c.17.24. c.22.9. Eccles.cap.26.4. & vultus lætus hilaritatis index. Prouerb.c.15.13.15.16. c.17.22. Eccles.d.c.26.4. cum stolidorum oculi dicantur vagi. Prou.c.17.25.
units.tr: A calm and pleasant countenance is the attitude of a man who is composed, well-mannered, civil and content with his lot. Prov. 17:24; Prov. 22:9; Eccl. 26:4; and a cheerful countenance is a sign of gladness, Prov. 15:13, 15-16; Prov. 17:22; Eccl. 26:4, whereas the eyes of fools are said to wander, Prov. 17:25.

units.la: Faciem demittere, est habitus eorum, quos conscientia accusat & caussa sua premit. Genes. c.4.6. Quare cecidit vultus tuus? Quandoque etiam adorantis & trementis, 2.Chron.c.7.3. Inflexerunt se facie in terram versus pauimentum, &c. Matth.c.26.39. Procidit in faciem suam & precans. Et gratiam humiliter habentis. Ruth.c.2.10.
units.tr: To lower the face is the habit of those whom conscience accuses and whose cause weighs down. Gen. 4.6: Why has your face fallen? Sometimes it is also the habit of one who worships and trembles, 2 Chron. 7.3: They bowed down with their faces to the ground, upon the pavement, etc.; Matt. 26.39: He fell on his face and prayed. And of one who humbly receives a favour. Ruth 2.10.

units.la: Operire faciem, est habitus videre non cupientis, Ezech.c.12.6. Operito faciem tuam, ne videas hanc terram. Velata facies, hominis est turbati & damnati. Ester.c.7.8. Operuerunt faciem Haman. Iob c.9.24. Faciem iudicum eius obtegit, &c. Quandoq; etiam pudoris & verecundiæ signum. Daniel.c.13.33. vt dixi sup. in capitis velatione. Et quandoque luctus. Mich.c.3.9. Ezech. c.24.17. Leuit. c.19.45.
units.tr: To cover the face is the habit of one who does not wish to see. Ezek. 12.6: Cover your face, that you may not see this land. A veiled face belongs to a troubled and condemned man. Esth. 7.8: They covered Haman's face. Job 9.24: He covers the faces of its judges, etc. Sometimes it is also a sign of shame and modesty, Dan. 13.33, as I said above in the discussion of veiling the head; and sometimes of mourning. Mic. 3.9; Ezek. 24.17; Lev. 19.45.

units.la: Facies sordida, est habitus lugentis & mærentis, atq; miseriam arguit. Matth.c.6.16. Deformât faciem suam, vt videantur hominibus ieiunare. Iob c.16.16. Facies mea lutulenta affecta est pra fletu. Contra, tra, facies lota & pura, animum sedatum & com-positum indicat. Matth. c. 6. 17. Tu vero cum ieiu-nas, faciem tuam laua, ut ne appareas hominibus ie-iunare. & Gen. c. 43. 31. Postea lota facie suâ egressus continebat se, &c.
units.tr: A dirty face is the habit of one who mourns and grieves, and it shows misery. Matt. 6.16: They disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting. Job 16.16: My face is swollen with weeping. On the other hand, a washed and clean face shows a calm and composed mind. Matt. 6.17: But when you fast, wash your face, so that you do not appear to men to be fasting; and Gen. 43.31: Afterwards he washed his face, came out, and restrained himself, etc.

units.la: Faciem alterius conspurcare & conspuere, probat contemptum & detestationem eiusdem. Malach. c. 2. 3. Sparsurus sum fimum in facies vestras. Matth. c. 26. 67. Tunc insputerunt in faciem eius & colaphos infixerunt; alii vero bacillis eum ceciderunt. Esa. c. 50. 6. 7. Iob c. 30. 10. Abominantur me; a facie mea non cohibent sputum. Marc. c. 10. 3. 4. Num. c. 12. 14. Si pater insputisset in faciem eius, an non rubore suffusa esset?
units.tr: To defile another's face or spit in it shows contempt and detestation of that person. Mal. 2.3: I will spread dung on your faces. Matt. 26.67: Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists; others beat him with rods. Isa. 50.6-7; Job 30.10: They abhor me; they do not hold back from spitting in my face. Mark 10.33-34; Num. 12.14: If her father had spat in her face, would she not have been ashamed?

units.la: Facies rubore suffusa, verecundiae index est. arg. d. Num. c. 12. 14. Esa. c. 13. 8. Ezech. c. 7. 18. In omni facie erit pudor. Ierem. c. 8. 12. Neque illi prorsus erubescunt, neque ignominia sciunt affici, &c. Num. cap. 12.
units.tr: A face suffused with blushing is a sign of shame. Cf. Num. 12.14; Isa. 13.8; Ezek. 7.18: Shame will be on every face. Jer. 8.12: They are not at all ashamed, nor do they know how to be disgraced, etc. Num. ch. 12.

units.la: Facies, seu vultus pallidus, maestitiam, dolorem, timorem & luctum in illo, qui talis natura non est, indicat. Ierem. cap. 30. 6. Conuersos esse vultus in speciem morbi regii, id est, ut Iunius in Notis explicat, expallescere. Ficuti & ater vultus. Ioel. cap. 2. 6. Nahumi cap. 2. 10. Facies eorum contrahet nigrorem; & vultus rectus, luctus indicium. Mich. cap. 3. 9.
units.tr: A pale face, or a pallid countenance, indicates sadness, pain, fear and grief in one who is not by nature like that. Jer. 30.6: Faces turned into the likeness of jaundice, that is, as Junius explains in his notes, to grow pale. So also a dark face. Joel 2.6; Nah. 2.10: Their faces gather blackness; Mic. 3.9: and a downcast face is a sign of mourning. Mic. 3.9.

units.la: Vultus afflictus, aegritudinem corporis, vel animi indicat, Nehem. c. 2. 2. 3. Quare vultus tuus afflictus est, cum non sis aegrotus? Non est hoc nisi affli-ctio animi, &c. 2. Macchab. c. 3. 16. Nam aspectus & mutatus color declarabat angustiam, qua vrgebat animum ipsius. & verf. 17. Nam turbatione animi vultus quoq; turbatur. Daniel.c.3.19. Tum Nebu- cadnezar adeo repletus fuit excandescentia, vt imago vultus eius immutaretur. & vers.24. & Eccles.c.25. 21. Mulier improba mutat faciem & vultum indignabundum lingua simulantis parit. Prouerb.c.25. 23. Et vultus placidus & constans sapientia indicium. Prouerbior. cap.17.14. cap.22.9. & hilaritatis. Eccles.4.c.26.4. & laetus vultus, animi laeti index, Prou. c.15.13 & animus laetus hominem bene afficit. Prou. c.17.v.22.
units.tr: A troubled face indicates sickness of body or mind. Neh. 2.2-3: Why is your face troubled, since you are not sick? This is nothing but affliction of the mind, etc. 2 Macc. 3.16: For the look and the changed colour revealed the anguish that gripped his soul; and v. 17: For in disturbance of the mind the face is also disturbed. Dan. 3.19: Then Nebuchadnezzar was so filled with rage that the image of his face was changed; and v. 24; Ecclus 25.21: A wicked woman changes her face and gives birth to an indignant look, the sign of a deceitful tongue. A calm and steady face is a sign of wisdom. Prov. 25.23; Prov. 17.14; Prov. 22.9; and of cheerfulness. Eccl. 4 (Ecclus) 26.4; and a joyful face is a sign of a joyful mind. Prov. 15.13; and a joyful mind makes a man well disposed. Prov. 17.22.

units.la: Collum erectum, nonnunquam libertatem significat. Job c.15.26. & extentum seu exsertum, arrogantiam, Esa. c.3.17. collum curuum & depressum, seruitutem & obedientiam, Ier.c.27.8. Genti quae non indet collum suum regi Babylonia, & c.28.10.11.14. Esa.c.52.2.c.10.27. Mich.c.2 3. Incuruare collum, valde inciuile est.
units.tr: An erect neck sometimes signifies liberty. Job 15.26. A neck stretched out or thrust forth signifies arrogance. Isa. 3.16-17. A bent and lowered neck signifies servitude and obedience. Jer. 27.8: The nation that does not put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon; and ch. 28.10-11, 14; Isa. 52.2; Isa. 10.27; Mic. 2.3. To bow the neck is very uncivil.

units.la: Amplexus colli & procubitus significat desiderium personae charissimae, Gen.c.33.4. Accurrens Esau obuiam ei, amplexatus est eum, & ruens in collum eius, deosculatus est eum, Genes.c.45.14. Tum ruens in collum Beniaminis fratris sui, flebat: Beniamin quoq; flebat ad collum eius. Actor. c.20.37. Et ruentes in collum Pauli deosculabantur eum, & Marc. c.10.16. & amplexans eos, & imponens manus super eos, benedicebat eis.
units.tr: Embracing the neck and falling upon it signifies longing for a most dear person. Gen. 33.4: Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, and falling on his neck kissed him. Gen. 45.14: Then he fell on the neck of his brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck. Acts 20.37: They all wept aloud and, falling on Paul's neck, kissed him; and Mark 10.16: And taking them in his arms, and laying his hands on them, he blessed them.

units.la: Humerus nudatus, index oneris & seruitutis & laboris magni. Ezech. cap 30.2. Omne caput decalvatum est, & omnis humerus nudatus. Humeris enim onus suscipimus, 2.Chron.cap 2.18. Luc.cap.5.5. Humerus recedens, est hominis detrectantis seruire. Nehem.c.9.29. Nahum.cap.11. Ezech.c.19.7.
units.tr: A bared shoulder is a sign of burden, servitude and great labour. Ezek. 29.18: Every head is made bald and every shoulder is rubbed raw. For we take up a burden on our shoulders, 2 Chron. 2.18; Luke 5.5. A receding shoulder is the habit of one who refuses to serve. Neh. 9.29; Nah. 1.13 (ch. 11); Ezek. 19.7.

units.la: Brachium extensum, vel eleuatum, significat potentiam & facultatem, ad rem gerendam conficiendamque. Exo. c.6.6. redimamq; vos brachio extento & iudiciis magnis, & v.7. Sic experieminime esse Iehouam, &c. Deut. c.4.34. Bello & manu forti, & brachio extento. & vers.seq.35. Tibi sunt exhibita videnda, vt cognoscas Iehouam esse Deum ipsum.
units.tr: An outstretched or raised arm signifies power and ability to carry out and accomplish a thing. Exod. 6.6: I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments; and v. 7: Thus you shall know that I am the LORD, etc. Deut. 4.34: By war and a strong hand and an outstretched arm. And the following verse, 35: To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God himself.

units.la: In cubitum recumbere, est immorantium & familiariter & secure agentium, Eccles.c.9 9.
units.tr: To recline on the elbow is the habit of those who dwell and act familiarly and securely. Eccl. 9.9.

units.la: Manus, multiplicis habitus artifex est: & varias cordis affectiones internas exprimit. Nam manus sublata, erecta & extenta, vim, robur potentiamque indicat. Exod.c.15.12. Extendisti dexteram tuam: deglutiuit eos terra. Esai. cap.5.25. Et extendens manum suam contra eum, percussit eum. Et his omnibus non est auersa ira eius, sed adhuc manus eius extenta.
units.tr: The hand is the skilled artificer of many kinds of habit, and it expresses the various inner affections of the heart. For a hand raised, upright and stretched out signifies force, strength and power. Exod. 15.12: You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them. Isa. 5.25: He stretched out his hand against them and struck them. And for all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.

units.la: Manus pendulæ, pigri habitus.
units.tr: Hanging hands are the habit of the lazy.

units.la: Brachia & manus modo in hanc, modo in illam partem iactare, aut proiicere instar serentis, est habitus hominis stolidi & inertis.
units.tr: To toss the arms and hands now this way, now that, or to cast them out like a sower, is the habit of a foolish and idle man.

units.la: Manu dextera elata, iuramentum præstare solemus. Genes.c.14.21. dixit Abraham, Iuraui elata manu mea ad Iehouam, Ezech c.36.7. Idcirco sic aut Domin Iehoua, Ego sublata manu mea iuro. Daniel. cap.12.7. Qui efferens dexteram suam & sinistram suam versus cælos, iurauit per viuentem in æternum. Apocalyps. cap.10.5. Angelus sustulit manum suam ad cælum. 6. & iurauit per eum qui viuit in secula seculorum. In iuramentis quæ à domesticis exigebantur, aliud Iudæis vsitatum fuisse, apparet ex Gen.c.24.2.9.c.47.29.
units.tr: We customarily raise the right hand when we swear an oath. Gen. 14.21: Abraham said, I have sworn with my hand raised to the LORD. Ezek. 36.7: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: I lift up my hand and swear. Dan. 12.7: He who lifted his right hand and his left hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever. Rev. 10.5: The angel lifted his hand to heaven, 6: and swore by him who lives for ever and ever. That among the Jews something else was customary in oaths demanded of members of the household appears from Gen. 24.2, 9; 47.29.

units.la: Manus extensio est habitus locuturi, silentium & attentionem indicentis. Actor. cap.19. 33. Manu silentio postulato, volebat reddere rationem populo, & c.21.40. Paulus stans in gradibus, silentium manu postulauit a plebe: & silentio facto, locutus est, & c.26.1. Tunc Paulus extenta manu, hac defensione vsus est, & cap.13.16. Cum surrexisset igitur Paulus, manu silentio postulato dixit. Prou.c.1.24. Quando-quidem multo & renuntis, extendo manum meam & ad illos agitate manum, vt ingrediantur portas ingenuorum.
units.tr: Stretching out the hand is the habit of one about to speak, showing silence and attention. Acts 19.33: Alexander, having motioned with his hand for silence, wished to give an account to the people; Acts 21.40: Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people for silence, and when there was silence he spoke; Acts 26.1: Then Paul, stretching out his hand, used this defence; Acts 13.16: So Paul stood up, and with his hand motioned for silence, and said. Prov. 1.24: Because I called and you refused, I stretched out my hand and no one paid attention.

units.la: Manus porrecta & extensa, est habitus indicantis & demonstrantis aliquid. Matth. c.12.49. Et protensa manu sua in discipulos, dixit, Ecce mater mea & fratres mei. Et quandoque opem & auxilium ferentis. Matth.c.14.31. Statim vero Iesus extenta manu apprehendit eum. Actor c.9.34. Matth. c.20.34. Esa. c.51.18. Et nemo apprehendebat manum eius ex omnibus filiis quos educauerat.
units.tr: A hand held out and stretched forth is the habit of one indicating and pointing something out. Matt. 12.49: And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, Behold my mother and my brothers. And sometimes of one who brings help and aid. Matt. 14.31: Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and took hold of him. Acts 9.34; Matt. 20.34; Isa. 51.18: Not one of all the sons she bore took her by the hand.

units.la: Manus ori admota, est habitus tacentis & modeste agentis; & quandoq; admirantis secumque reputantis. Prou.c.30.32. Si stultus fuisti efferendo te, sine cogitasti, manum ori tuo imponito. Iob c.21.5. Respicite ad me, & stupore corripiamini; & apponite manum ad os. & c.29. Principes continebant sermones & manum imponebant ori suo, & vers.seq.& c.9.
units.tr: A hand placed to the mouth is the habit of one who is silent and acts modestly; and sometimes of one who is amazed and reflects within himself. Prov. 30.32: If you have been foolish in exalting yourself, or if you have thought evil, put your hand on your mouth. Job 21.5: Look at me and be struck with horror, and lay your hand on your mouth. And ch. 29: The princes held back their words and laid their hands on their mouths; and the following verse; and ch. 9.

units.la: Manum dare, vel porrigere, est habitus fidedantis & promittentis, Ezech.cap.17.18. Quia ecce tunxit manum suam, &c. Ierem.c.50.51. iunxit sua manum, Iob c.17.2. Quis est? manui mea plaudatur, 2.Reg.c.10.15. Si est, inquit, animus tuus rectus, cedo manum tuam: & vbi dedisset manum suam, iussit eum conscendere ad se in currum. & Galat. c.2 9. Iacobus cobus & Cephas & Iohannes, &c. dexteras dederunt mihi. 1. Macchab. c. 6. 58. 2. Macchab. c. 13. 50. 1. Chronic. c. 29. 24. Omnesq; principes & robusti & omnes filii regis Danidis dederunt manus, se fore subditos regi Salomoni. quod alibi exprimitur per manus complosionem & iunctionem. Proverb. c. 6. 1. 2. Complosisti extraneo manum tuam: illaque easti te sermonibus tuis. 3. Fac istud iam, fili mi, & eripe te: quadoquidem convenisti in manum proximi tui. & c. 11. 15. Qui odit complodentes, securus est. Contra, qui spondet pro extraneo, confringitur. & c. 17. 18. Homo demens complodit manum, spondens sponsionem ante amicum suum.
units.tr: To give or offer the hand is the habit of one who pledges faith and promises. Ezek. 17.18: For behold, he gave his hand, etc. Jer. 50.15: He has given his hand; Job 17.2: Who is there who will strike my hand in pledge? 2 Kings 10.15: If, he said, your heart is right, give me your hand. And when he had given his hand, he had him come up to him into the chariot. Gal. 2.9: James and Cephas and John, etc., gave me their right hands. 1 Macc. 6.58; 2 Macc. 13.50; 1 Chron. 29.24: And all the princes and the mighty men and all the sons of King David submitted to King Solomon and gave their hands. This is expressed elsewhere by clapping and joining of hands. Prov. 6.1-3: You have struck your hand with a stranger, and you are caught by the words of your mouth. Do this now, my son, and deliver yourself, since you have come into the hand of your neighbour. Prov. 11.15: He who hates those who clap is secure; but he who stands surety for a stranger is broken. Prov. 17.18: A foolish man claps his hand, pledging surety before his friend.

units.la: Alias complodere manus, est etiam laetantium habitus, 2. Reg. c. 11. 12. Et complodentes voluis dicebant, Viuat Rex. Esa. c. 55. 12. Omnes agri arbores complodent manum. Nahum. c 3. in sin. Quicunq; audient rumorem tuum, complodent manum super te. & Psalm. 47. 2. Omnes populi plaudite manibus, clangite Deo voce canora. Quandoq; etiam lugentium.
units.tr: Otherwise, clapping the hands is also a sign of rejoicing: 2 Kings 11:12, "And they clapped their hands and said, Long live the king." Isa. 55:12, "All the trees of the field shall clap their hands." Nahum 3, at the end, "All who hear the report of you shall clap their hands over you." Ps. 47:1, "Clap your hands, all peoples; shout to God with loud songs of joy." Sometimes it is also a sign of mourning.

units.la: Manu dentes scalpere, vel corpus fricare, vel vlcera vel pustulas refricare atq; cruentare, habitus est hominis impudentis & sordidi. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Padag. c. 7. in sin.
units.tr: To pick the teeth with the hand, or to rub the body, or to scratch and make bloody sores or pustules, is the habit of a shameless and filthy man. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2, ch. 7, at the end.

units.la: Manum attollere, est habitus negotium suscipientis. Genes. c. 41. 44. Attamen sine te non attollet quisquam manum suam, aut pedem suum, in universa Ægypti terra. Psalm. 119. 48. Attollam manus meas ad praecepta tua quae diligo.
units.tr: To lift up the hand is the habit of one who undertakes a task. Gen. 41:44, "Yet without you no one shall lift up his hand or foot in all the land of Egypt." Ps. 119:48, "I will lift up my hands to your commandments, which I love."

units.la: Expansa manus, est habitus petentis & rogatis. Esa. c. 65. 2. Expanderam manus meas toto die ad populum rebellem, c. 1. 15. Psal. 141. 2. Elatio manuum mearum, ut munus vespertinum coram te. Ier. c. 4. 31. Vox e filia Tzion is subinde anhelantis, pandentis manus suas, dicendo, Vae mihi, &c. Exod. c. 9. 29. Cum egressus fuero, extendam manus meas ad Dominum.
units.tr: An outstretched hand is the habit of one who asks or begs. Isa. 65:2, "I have stretched out my hands all day to a rebellious people." Isa. 1:15. Ps. 141:2, "Let the lifting up of my hands be as the evening sacrifice before you." Jer. 4:31, "The voice of the daughter of Zion, gasping, spreading out her hands, saying, Woe is me, etc." Exod. 9:29, "When I have gone out, I will spread out my hands to the Lord."

units.la: Manus exequi ere, est habitus demonstrantis non habere vel no cupientis habere. Isa. c. 33. 15. Qui sipernit lucrum ex fraudibus, qui excutit manus suas, ne teneat munus, &c.
units.tr: To shake out the hands is the habit of one who shows that he does not have, or does not desire to have, something. Isa. 33:15, "He who despises gain from fraud, who shakes his hands so as not to hold a bribe, etc."

units.la: Manus remissa, est indicium timoris, consternationis & animi deiecti. Esa. c. 13. 7. Idcirco omnes manus remissae erunt, & omne cor humanum colliquescet & conturbabitur, &c. Ezech. c. 7. 17. Omnes manus debilitabuntur, & omnia genua in aquas fiunt abitura. Ierem. c. 50. Audientes Regis Babylonis rumorem de eo, illico remittent se manus, angustia apprehendet eum, dolor tanquam parturientis. Manuum remissio, complicatio & complosio & complexus, brachiorum in sinu vel manica occultatio, est habitus pigrorum & desidum. Eccl. c. 3. 14. 15. c. 2. 14. Prov. c. 19. 24. Abdutam habet piger manum suam in manica sua, etiam ad os non reducit illam. & c. 26. 15. 16. & c. 21. 25. c. 22. 13. Hebr. c. 12. 12. Quapropter manus remissas & genua soluta surrigite. Psal. 74. 11.
units.tr: Hands hanging limp are a sign of fear, dismay and a dejected spirit. Isa. 13:7, "Therefore all hands shall be feeble, and every human heart shall melt and be dismayed, etc." Ezek. 7:17, "All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall run with water." Jer. 50:43, "When the king of Babylon hears the report of them, his hands shall fall helpless; anguish shall seize him, pain like that of a woman in labour." Letting the hands fall limp, folding them together, clasping them, or hiding the arms in the bosom or in the sleeve, is the habit of the lazy and idle. Eccl. 3:14, 15; Eccl. 2:14; Prov. 19:24, "The sluggard buries his hand in his bosom; he will not even bring it back to his mouth." Prov. 26:15, 16; Prov. 21:25; Prov. 22:13; Heb. 12:12, "Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees." Ps. 74:11.

units.la: Pectinatim manus inter se complicare, ominosum creditur & tristitiae indicium. Manus membro corporis laboranti impolita, dolorem arguit. Ierem. cap. 30. 26. Capiti impolita, lugentium foeminarum habitus, Iere. c. 2. 37. & 2. Sam. c. 13. 19. Utrumque brachium in tergum detorquere, pigritiae speciem habet: sicut & alteram manum in illa vel tergum iniectam habere & adstare, vel sedere.
