units.tr: To fold the hands together, finger locked in finger, is thought to be an ill omen and a sign of sadness. A hand laid on a suffering limb of the body shows pain. Jer. 30:26. To lay the hand on the head is the habit of women mourning. Jer. 2:37; 2 Sam. 13:19. To twist both arms behind the back has the appearance of laziness, as does having one hand thrown behind the other or on the back, whether standing or sitting.

units.la: Digitus ori impositus,est habitus silentis, Judic. c.18.19. Qui dixerunt et sile, impone manum tuam ori tuo & veni nobiscum. Job.c.29.37.
units.tr: A finger laid on the mouth is the habit of one keeping silence. Judg. 18:19, "They said to him, Be silent, put your hand on your mouth and come with us." Job 29:9-10.

units.la: Quandoq; digitus docentem & demonstra-tem aliquid tacite significat. Prou.c.6.13. docet digitis suis.
units.tr: Sometimes a finger silently signifies one who is teaching and showing something. Prov. 6:13, "He teaches with his fingers."

units.la: Digitis concrepare cum talitris, est habitus & signum hominis insultantis & contemnen-tis,seu vilipendentis.
units.tr: To snap the fingers with a snapping sound is the habit and sign of one who insults, despises or scorns.

units.la: Proprios digitos conspuere, est habitus hominis sordidi.
units.tr: To spit upon one's own fingers is the habit of a filthy man.

units.la: Tympanorum pulsum digitis imitari & alterna pedum iactatione vti; est hominis alios praefentes non curantis vel fastidientis.
units.tr: To imitate the beating of drums with the fingers and to use an alternating stamping of the feet is the mark of one who ignores or disdains the others present.

units.la: Tergum vertere in bello, est fugientium habitus. Gen.c.14.10. post tergum reiicere, est negligere,non curae habere,vel obliuioni tradere. Esa.c.38.17. Quia abiecisti post tergum tuum omnia peccata tua. Ierem. c.2.27. Quia obuerterunt mihi ceruicem,non autem faciem. Iudic.cap.10.10. Ierem. cap.32.33. Quia obuerterunt mihi ceruicem, non autem faciem: & docenti eos minime auscultant.
units.tr: To turn the back in battle is the habit of those who flee. Gen. 14:10. To cast behind the back is to neglect, to have no care for, or to consign to oblivion. Isa. 38:17, "For you have cast all my sins behind your back." Jer. 2:27, "For they have turned their back to me, and not their face." Judg. 10:10. Jer. 32:33, "For they have turned their back to me, and not their face," and "they do not listen at all when I teach them."

units.la: Dorsum & ceruicem alicui praebere, est habitus patienter plagas sustinentis. Psalm.18.41. Et inimicorum meorum exponis mihi ceruicem, ut ofores meos exscindam.
units.tr: To offer one's back and neck to someone is the habit of one who patiently endures blows. Ps. 18:41, "You have made my enemies turn their backs to me, and I destroy those who hate me."

units.la: Quandoque fugientis & cedentis. Deut.cap.33.11.Psalm.18.41. Psalm.21.17. Verticem inclinare,est annuere & approbare cum reuerentia Nehem. c.8.7. Respondit totus populus Amen, amen. Cum elatione manuum suarum verticem inclinarunt.
units.tr: Sometimes it is the sign of one who flees or yields. Deut. 33:11; Ps. 18:41; Ps. 21:17. To bow the head is to nod in assent and approval with reverence. Neh. 8:6-7, "All the people answered, Amen, amen, and they bowed their heads and worshipped with their hands lifted up."

units.la: Lumbos accingere& lumbi accincti,indicant habitum hominis parati & promti, 2.Reg.cap.4. 29. Edixit Elisa Gehazi, Accinge lumbos tuos; & sumpto scipione in manum tuam, abi.2.Reg.9.1.Elisa vocato uno e filiis prophetarum, edixit ei: Accinge lumbos tuos, & accipiens lenticulam olei hanc in manu tua, abi Ramothas Gilhadis, 1. Reg.c.20. c.99.2. Reg.c.4. Luc.c.12. Iob c.38.3. Accinge nunc vt vir lumbos tuos, & quod interrogabo te, notum facmihi. Jerem.c.1.17. Tuitaq; accinge lumbos tuos, & surgens eloquaris apud eos, quidquid ego praecepero tibi, Luc. cap.12.35. Sint lumbi vestri praecincti, &c. Exod.c.12. 11.12. Ita eam comedite: lumbis vestris succinctis, calceamentis vestris ad pedes vestros, & baculo vestro in manu vestra, sic comedetis eam cum festinatione. Psal.45.4.5. Esa.c.11.5. Luc.c.11.31.
units.tr: Girded loins, and loins girded up, indicate the habit of a man who is ready and prompt. 2 Kings 4:29, "Elisha said to Gehazi, Gird up your loins, take my staff in your hand, and go." 2 Kings 9:1, "Elisha called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, Gird up your loins, take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead." 1 Kings 20; 2 Kings 4; Luke 12. Job 38:3, "Now gird up your loins like a man, and I will question you, and you shall declare to me." Jer. 1:17, "But you, gird up your loins, and arise and speak to them all that I command you." Luke 12:35, "Let your loins be girded, etc." Exod. 12:11-12, "Thus shall you eat it: with your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste." Ps. 45:4-5; Isa. 11:5; Luke 11:31.

units.la: Contrà vero lumbi dissoluti & confracti habitum dolentium & infirmorum indicant. Esa. c.21.3. Jerem.c.30.6. Iob c.16.5. vide Iob. Guil. Stuck lib.2.c.19. Conuiualium antiquit.
units.tr: On the contrary, loosened and broken loins indicate the habit of those in pain and weakness. Isa. 21:3; Jer. 30:6; Job 16:5; see Job. Wilhelm Stucki, Antiquitates convivales, book 2, ch. 19.

units.la: Inflectere ceruicem & adducere scapulas, pigritiam arguit. Ceruicem in laeuum, vel dextrum vergere, est habitus hypocriticus; nisi colloquium, aut alia necessitas id postulet.
units.tr: To bend the neck and draw the shoulders forward betrays laziness. To incline the neck to left or right is the habit of a hypocrite, unless conversation or some other necessity requires it.

units.la: Humeros aequo libramine temperare, habitus bene compositi: at in morem antennarum alterum tollere, alterum deprimere, pigri.
units.tr: To hold the shoulders level in even balance is the habit of a well-composed man; but to raise one and lower the other, like the yards of a ship, belongs to the lazy.

units.la: Femur siue coxam ferire, est habitus eorum, qui se deceptos, aut alios errantes agnoscunt, Jer.c.31. 9.Ezech.c.21.19.
units.tr: To strike the thigh or hip is the habit of those who recognise that they have been deceived or that others are in error. Jer. 31:19; Ezek. 21:12.

units.la: Oscitare, praesertim clare & sonore, est habitus satietatis, fastidii, socordiae, otii, somnolentiae, animi vagi, fluxae & apertae securitatis & molestiae, Gell.lib.4.c.20. Ronchos ducere,&pituitam propendentem cum sono retrahere subinde, est hominis sordidi & fœtidi.
units.tr: To yawn, especially loudly and resonantly, is the habit of satiety, disgust, sloth, idleness, drowsiness, a wandering mind, and a careless and open security and annoyance. Gellius, book 4, ch. 20. To make snoring noises, and to draw back with a sound the phlegm that keeps dripping, is the mark of a filthy and foul man.

units.la: Singultus, est indicium diaphragmatis nimio cibo distenti, & propterea antegressæ signum. Clemens Alexand. Padag.lib. 2.c.2.c.7.
units.tr: Hiccupping is a sign of a diaphragm distended by too much food, and so a sign of what has gone before. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2, ch. 2 and ch. 7.

units.la: Cum screatu & tussi saliuam & mucum expectorare, aut postquam nasum emunxeris in ftrophiolum diductum, mucum inspicere, quasi fieri potuerit, vt margarita aut pyropus tibi e cerebro exciderit, est hominis sordidi, naufeabun-di, tædiofi & immunditiæ amantis.
units.tr: To spit out phlegm and mucus with hawking and coughing, or after blowing one's nose to inspect the mucus in the handkerchief spread out, as if a pearl or a garnet might have fallen out of your brain, is the mark of a filthy man, a nauseating, tedious man, one who loves uncleanness.

units.la: Ructus incidés, cum exspirato aere est transmittendus ore decoré composito, nec instar personarum tragicarum diduéto & hiante. Cle. Alex.lib.2.Padag.c.7. Sternutationis autem qui conturbat strepitus, respiratione leniter repref-faacretenta, auferendus est, dicto c.7. Hacenim ratione quam honestissime fieri poterit, conglobatæ spiritus minæ intus sunt extinguendæ, prouidendo vt ita transeat, vt etiam cæteros latere conetur, fi vi expressus aer aliquod secum excrementum eduxerit. Impudentiæ autem & insolentiæ signum est, ipsis velle sonis aliquid addere, non autem detrahere, d.c.7.
units.tr: A belch should be let out through the mouth, with the air expelled, arranged in a decorous manner, not gaping wide like tragic actors. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2, ch. 7. A sneeze that breaks out with a disturbing noise should be suppressed gently by holding the breath, so that it is removed; the same chapter 7. For by this method, as decently as possible, the gathered threats of the breath are to be extinguished within, taking care that it passes in such a way as to try to escape notice even by the others, if the expelled air has drawn out some excrement with it. It is a sign of shamelessness and insolence to wish to add something to the sounds themselves rather than to take something away; ibid., ch. 7.

units.la: Tussi & sternutamento sonitum excitare, & pituitæ suæ aspergine faciem vel vestes aliorum collinere, est habitus aliorum præsentiam non curantis. vide Clement. Alexand.lib.2. cap.7. Padag.
units.tr: To make a noise by coughing and sneezing, and to smear the face or clothes of others with the spray of one's phlegm, is the habit of one who does not care about the presence of others. See Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2, ch. 7.

units.la: Crepitum & efflatum ventris emittere, est hominis gulosi & intemperantis indicium, &
units.tr: To emit a fart and a puff of wind from the belly is a sign of a gluttonous and intemperate man, and

units.la: K præsentes alios vilipendentis. vide Sueton. in Claudio. Quod si tamen hoc fiat ex libertate quadam familiaritatis, vel apud viliorem & abiectum, non ita vitio vertitur: unde Martialis in Crispum;
units.tr: of one who despises the others present. See Suetonius, in the life of Claudius. However, if this is done from a certain freedom of familiarity, or among inferiors and the lowly, it is not held so much against a man; whence Martial, on Crispus:

units.la: Nil aliud video quo te credamus amicum;
units.tr: I see nothing else by which we may believe you a friend,

units.la: Quàm quòd me coràm pedere, Crispe, soles.
units.tr: Except that you, Crispus, are in the habit of farting in front of me.

units.la: Alias eos testamur nos amare, apud quos ea facere erubescimus, quæ reuera turpitudinem in se habent. Apud amicos enim omnes viri boni haberi volunt, ideoq; sua vitia cupiunt celare.
units.tr: Otherwise we show that we love those before whom we are ashamed to do things that are in truth disgraceful. For all good men wish to be thought well of by their friends, and therefore they desire to hide their faults.

units.la: Anhelare, est habitus anxiè & solicitè sperantis & laborantis. Psal. 119. & 131. Os meum diffendo & anhelo; quia præceptorum tuorum cupidus sum. Ierem. c. 4. 31. Vocem filiæ Tzionis subinde anhelantis, pandentis manus suas, dicendo, Væ mihi. Prouerb. c. 29. 2. Quum dominatur improbus, suspirat populus.
units.tr: To pant is the posture of one who hopes anxiously and eagerly and is weary with longing. Ps. 119 and 131: I open my mouth and pant, because I long for your commandments. Jer. 4.31: I hear a cry as of a woman in labour, the voice of the daughter of Zion gasping, spreading out her hands and saying, Woe is me. Prov. 29.2: When the wicked rule, the people sigh.

units.la: Ingemiscere, est commoti & commiserantis cum συμπαθείᾳ. Marc. c. 8. 12. Ipse vero quum alte ingemuisset spiritu suo, dixit, &c. & spiritu fremere, est commoueri. Ierem. c. 4. 19. Fremit cor meum: non possum silere.
units.tr: To groan is the sign of one who is moved and sympathises [συμπαθείᾳ]. Mark 8.12: But he, sighing deeply in his spirit, said, etc. To snort in the spirit is to be stirred. Jer. 4.19: My bowels, my bowels! I am pained at the very walls of my heart; my heart makes a noise within me; I cannot hold my peace.

units.la: Spiritus languens, angustus & tenuis, est index pauoris & metus. Iohan. c. 2. 11. Quod audientibus nobis liquefactum est cor nostrum, neq; constat animo quisquam amplius metu vestri: & Psal. 119. 32. Quum dilataueris animum meum.
units.tr: A languid, narrow and thin spirit is a sign of dread and fear. John 2.11: Our hearts melted when we heard it, and there remained no courage in any man any more because of you. And Ps. 119.32: When you enlarge my heart.

units.la: Crura fæminarum vestibus didu-ctis altiusque præcinctis nuda, migrandi longiusque peregrinandi cogitationem & habitum indicant. Isa. c. 47. 2. c. 20. 2. 3.
units.tr: Women's legs, bared by garments drawn aside and girded up higher, show a thought and posture of departing and of travelling far. Isa. 47.2; 20.2, 3.

units.la: Genuum curuatio, est habitus supplicantium um & orantium, 1.Reg.c.8.54.Cum absoluisset Salomo orare, surgens ab anteriore parte altaris Iehoua, ab inflexione sua in genua, manibusq; suis passis versus caelum.& Hefra,c.9.5. Surrexi ab afflictione mei, idq; laceratam habens vestem & pallium meum, & flectens in genua mea, expandi manus meas ad Iehouam.2.Reg.c.19.18. Relinquam mihi septem millia, quorum genua non sunt curuata ante Baal.Luc.c.3.22. Quod cum vidisset Petrus, procidit ad genua Iesu, dicens,&c.
units.tr: Bending the knees is the posture of suppliants and those who pray. 1 Kings 8.54: When Solomon had finished praying, he rose from before the altar of the LORD, from kneeling on his knees, with his hands spread towards heaven. Ezra 9.5: I rose up from my affliction, with my garment and cloak torn, and falling on my knees I spread out my hands to the LORD. 2 Kings 19.18: I will leave me seven thousand, all whose knees have not bowed to Baal. Luke 3.22: When Peter saw this, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, etc.

units.la: Genuum dissolutio, aut tremor, debilitatis & infirmitatis indicium est. Psalm.109.24. Genua mea labant praeieiunio, & caro mea emaciatur. Ezech.c.7.17. Omnes manus debilitabuntur & omnia genua in aquas abitura sunt. Esai.c.35.3. Confirmate manus remissas, & genua labantia fortificate. Nahum.c.2.Iob c.4. Daniel.c.5.6. Quum singula lumborum eius dissoluta essent, genuaq; eius colliderent alterum alteri. Iob cap.4.4. Et labantem confirmabant sermones tui, & fortificabas genua sine cur-nantia.
units.tr: Loosening or trembling of the knees is a sign of weakness and infirmity. Ps. 109.24: My knees totter from fasting, and my flesh wastes away. Ezek. 7.17: All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall run like water. Isa. 35.3: Strengthen the weak hands and confirm the feeble knees. Nahum 2. Job 4. Dan. 5.6: Then the king's loins were loosed and his knees struck one against the other. Job 4.4: Your words have upheld the one who was falling, and you have strengthened the feeble knees.

units.la: Pede plaudere & percutere terram, est habitus insultantis alienis calamitatibus. Ezech.cap.25.6. Nam sic ait Dominus Iehoua, eo quod complodis manum & plaudis pede, & laetaris ex animo de tota populatione tua contra terram Israelis, &c. Prou.c.6.13. Homo nequam verba facit pedibus suis. Pes constans, rectus & certus, recti studii & firmi propositi affectionem indicat. Contra motus, inconstans & titubans, sententiae mutationem, aut dubitationem metumve arguunt.Psal.56.14. & Psal. 73.2. Equidem pene declinauerant pedes mei, & Psal. 38.17. Ut non latentur de me nutante meo pede, & Psal.94.18. Cum dico dimoueturpes meus,&c.Ieremiæc.14.10.
units.tr: To stamp the foot and strike the ground is the posture of one who exults in the calamities of others. Ezek. 25.6: For thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have clapped your hands and stamped your feet, and rejoiced in heart with all your scorn against the land of Israel, etc. Prov. 6.13: A worthless man speaks with his feet. A foot that stands firm, upright and sure shows a disposition of right purpose and settled resolve. On the other hand, a foot that moves, is unsteady and stumbles, betrays a change of opinion, or doubt or fear. Ps. 56.14; Ps. 73.2: But as for me, my feet had almost gone; Ps. 38.17: Lest they rejoice over me when my foot slips; Ps. 94.18: When I said, My foot slips, your mercy, O LORD, held me up; Jer. 14.10.

units.la: Pedum festinatio temeritatem indicat & inconsultam actionem eorum, qui affectus suos impotenter sequuntur.Rom.c.3.15. Pedes eorum veloces ad effundendum sanguinem, Prou.c.6.18. Pedes festinanter currentes ad malum, & c. 28.1. Fugit improbus nemine persequente, & c.19.2.ac præceps pedibus suis peccat,& c.7.11.c.25.8.
units.tr: Hasty feet indicate the rashness and ill-considered action of those who follow their passions without restraint. Rom. 3.15: Their feet are swift to shed blood. Prov. 6.18: Feet that run swiftly to evil; 28.1: The wicked flee when no one pursues; 19.2: Whoever is hasty with his feet sins; 7.11; 25.8.

units.la: Turpe est adstantem diuaricare crura;turpius vero crebrò motitare,aut contorquere.
units.tr: It is shameful for someone standing to spread his legs apart; but it is more shameful still to shift or twist them often.

units.la: Ad pedes prouolui, est habitus adorantis & supplicantis,Ester.c.8.3. Deinde rursum Ester elocuta est coram Rege,procidens ante pedes eius,& flens deprecabatur.Matth.c.27.29. Et genu ante eum summisso illudebant ei. Marc.cap.5.22.Iairus videns eum,procidit ad pedes eius,&c.& c.10.17.& Matth. cap.28.9. Illa autem accesserunt & tenuerunt pedes eius,& adorauerunt eum.
units.tr: To fall prostrate at the feet is the posture of one who adores and supplicates. Esther 8.3: Then Esther spoke again before the king, falling at his feet and weeping, and begged him. Matt. 27.29: And kneeling before him, they mocked him. Mark 5.22: Behold, one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, came, and when he saw him he fell at his feet, etc. Mark 10.17; Matt. 28.9: And they came and took hold of his feet and worshipped him.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De habitu & gestu totius corporis.
units.tr: On the bearing and gesture of the whole body.

units.la: TAntum de habitu naturali singulorum membrorum corporis hominis. Sequitur nunc de omnium membrorum & totius corporis hominis habitu & gestu.
units.tr: So much for the natural bearing of the individual limbs of the human body. Now follows the bearing and gesture of all the limbs together and of the whole body.

units.la: Totius corporis habitus respectu eius qui est partium,rectè compositus vocari potest, quod omnium membrorum gestus & habitus simplices hic quasi coniunguntur, ex qua coniunctione totius corporis gestus existit.
units.tr: The bearing of the whole body, with respect to the parts that make it up, may rightly be called composite, because the simple gestures and bearings of all the limbs are here joined together, and from this joining the gesture of the whole body arises.

units.la: Eiusmodi habitus cõsideratur primò in ipsis memmembris per se, eorumque motu & actione: Deinde in horum vestitu & amictu.
units.tr: A bearing of this kind is considered first in the limbs themselves, in their own movement and action, and secondly in their clothing and dress.

units.la: Habitus in motu corporis totius seu plurium membrorum, consistit in incessu, statione, surrectione, sessione, cursu, lapsu, obstupefactione, pudore, tremore, abscondione, pinguedine, inedia, sudore, procubitu, somno, &c.
units.tr: The bearing in the movement of the whole body, or of several limbs, consists in walking, standing, rising, sitting, running, falling, being stupefied, shame, trembling, hiding, fatness, hunger, sweating, lying down, sleeping, and so on.

units.la: Incessus non furiosus, sed honestus & lentus, non tardus nimis, decorus & civilis est, non fractus neq; praeceps, neq; vacillans, sed planus & aequabilis, nec exultatione nec lentitudine, neq; festinatione culpabilis.
units.tr: A gait that is not wild but dignified and unhurried is decorous and civil. It is neither too slow, nor broken, nor headlong, nor unsteady, but level and even, and it is blameworthy neither for exultation, nor for sluggishness, nor for haste.

units.la: Incedere cum exserto collo, erectis cervicibus, frontis protensione, minutim & numerose passus conferre, & gressus suos modificare, more astrarconum & tolutariorum, est habitus hominis lasciuientis, luxuriantis & superbientis, ut graviter describit Propheta Esai. c. 3.17. Praeterea ait Iehova, eo quod altae sunt filiae Tzionis & ambulant extento gutture & nutantes oculis, indesinenter minutis passibus incedunt, pedibusq; suis compeditas agunt. 18. Idcirco scabie afficiet Dominus verticem filiarum Tzionis & Iehova pudendum earum nudabit. vbi eleganter Iunius. Deut. c. 28. 56. Mollis in te & delicata, quae non tentarat plantam pedis sui figere super terram pra deliciis, & pra mollitie, oculus malignus erit, & v. 54. Clemens Alex. lib. 2. Paedagog. c. 11. & lib. 3. c. 11.
units.tr: To walk with the neck stretched out, the head held high, the forehead thrust forward, taking small and quick steps and affecting one's stride in the manner of the mincing and strutting sort, is the bearing of a wanton, luxurious and proud person, as the Prophet Isaiah describes it gravely, Isa. 3.17. Moreover the LORD says: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with outstretched neck and wanton eyes, going continually with mincing steps, and making a tinkling with their feet. 18. Therefore the Lord will smite the crown of the daughters of Zion with a scab, and the LORD will uncover their secret parts. Where Junius puts it elegantly. Deut. 28.56. The tender and delicate woman among you, who would not venture to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness, her eye shall be evil. And v. 54. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, ch. 11, and book 3, ch. 11.

units.la: Meretricum & lasciuarum faeminarum est, fractis motibus & effaeminatis, atq; ingressibus mollibus & oculis scintillantibus, reflexo collo in obliquum incedere. Clem. Alex. lib. 3. c. 11. Paedag. In via fluctuare, resupinare corpus, vel supina ceruice obuios respicere an se aspiciant; hominis est superbi & arrogantis, vt Clem. Alex. d. loco ait.
units.tr: To walk with broken, effeminate movements, with soft steps, sparkling eyes, and the neck bent to one side, belongs to harlots and wanton women. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 3, ch. 11. To sway in the street, to throw the body back, or to look at those one meets over the shoulder with the neck thrown back, to see whether they are looking at oneself, is the mark of a proud and arrogant man, as Clement of Alexandria says in the place cited.

units.la: Vir honestus in via non curret, aut nimium properabit, qui est habitus cursoris, & incon-stantis hominis. Incessus lentus, mollis & restu-dineus & tener, est faeminae alicuius primariae, aut sponsae. Cic. lib. 1. Officior. Hinc Seneca libr. 7. natural. tenero & molli incessu gradum suspendere, aut repere, non ambulare est mulierum. Clem. Alex. lib. 3. c. 11. Paedag.
units.tr: An honourable man will not run in the street or hurry too much; that is the bearing of a runner and of an inconstant man. A slow, soft, languid and delicate gait belongs to some woman of rank, or to a bride. Cicero, De Officiis book 1. Hence Seneca, Natural Questions book 7: to lift the step with a tender and soft gait, or to creep, rather than walk, is the mark of women. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 3, ch. 11.

units.la: In incedendo ita altè pedes tollere, vt eos ex medimno educere videaris, est habitus & incessus equi pauidi. Pedem terrae ita fortiter rantoque cum sonitu impingere, vt plaustrorum strepitus vix maior esse possit, est habitus minacis, ferocis & superbi hominis.
units.tr: To lift the feet so high when walking that you seem to draw them out of mire is the bearing and gait of a frightened horse. To strike the ground so hard and with such a noise that the racket of carts can scarcely be louder is the bearing of a threatening, fierce and proud man.

units.la: Pedes in obliquum impellere & quodam modo calcitrare, vel tibias collidere, est habitus hominis temulenti & ebrii.
units.tr: To thrust the feet sideways and kick out in a certain way, or to knock the shins together, is the bearing of a drunk and intoxicated man.

units.la: In incessu ad vnumquemq; passum caligas attrahere & se inclinare, est habitus ad alui purgationem properantis hominis; sicuti & motu clunium indecoro incessum fractum & quasi anatinum prae se ferre; aut solutis genibus incedere, grelsum frangere, vel ludentibus pedibus incedere, est habitus hominis petulantis & luxuriantis.
units.tr: To drag the stockings up at every step and bend forward, as those hurrying to empty their bowels do; likewise to move the buttocks indecorously, showing a broken gait like a duck's; or to walk with loose knees, breaking the stride, or to walk with playful feet, is the bearing of a wanton and luxurious man.

units.la: Modò huc, modò illuc se mouere, contorquere, & modò in hoc, modo in illud latus se conuertere, est habitus febricitantis hominis & fastidientis.
units.tr: To move now here, now there, to twist about, and now to turn to this side, now to that, is the bearing of a feverish and fastidious man.

units.la: Femur vnum alteri supponere, vel manu fustensustentare mentum, pedem pedi imponere, est habitus pigri, seipsum non ferentis.
units.tr: To lay one thigh over the other, or to prop the chin on the hand, or to set one foot on the other, is the bearing of a lazy man who cannot hold himself up.

units.la: Sæpe vero moueri, habitum & figuram mutare, est signum leuitatis. Clemens Alexand. lib. 2. cap. 7. Pædag.
units.tr: To shift often, changing posture and figure, is a sign of levity. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, ch. 7.

units.la: Ex consessu honestorum hominum inter se confabulantium surgere, & per cubiculum, vel conclaue inambulare, est habitus fastidientis & vilipendentis præsentes. sicuti etiam forpicula, aut culcello vngues resecare, dentes scalpere fricare corpus, vlcera cruentare, vel modo hanc, modo illam epistolam ex pera extrahere & legere, vt Galatæus ait, & Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Pædag. c. 7. in sin.
units.tr: To rise from a gathering of honourable men talking together and to stroll about the room or chamber is the bearing of one who despises and looks down on those present; likewise to pare the nails with scissors or a knife, to scratch the teeth, rub the body, make ulcers bleed, or draw out now this letter, now that one, from one's wallet and read it, as Galataeus says, and Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, ch. 7, at the end.

units.la: Status rectus & decorus fit, non cum decussatim compositis tibiis. Stare in concionibus & orationibus audiendis, est habitus attente & obsequiose auscultantis 2. Chron. cap. 6. 2. Postea rex conuersa facie sua benedixit cum tota congregatione Israelis, tota congregatione Israelis stante, & vers. 4 ac dixit, Benedictus Iehoua, &c. Luc. cap. 4. 6. Et surrexit vt legeret. Num. c. 23. 22. Tum protulit sententiam suam, dicens: Surge Balac & audi, aures attende ad me fili Tzipporis. vbi Iunius in hanc sententiam præterea allegat Genef. c. 49. 33. c. 47. Iudic. c. 3. 20. 2. Reg. c. 23. 2. 2. Chronic. c. 34. 31. Nehem. c. 8. 6. Act. c. 1. 15. 16. Et per eos dies cum assurrexisset Petrus in medio discipulorum dixit. &c. 13. 16. Cum surrexisset Paulus, dixit: Nam stando verbo & maiestati verbi Dei, honor exhibetur, vt expressis locis apparet: quibus adde Ierem. c. 23. 22. Zachar. c. 3. 7. Est. c. 8. 4. Alibi adstare, est comprobantis habitus. Act. c. 22. 20.
units.tr: A standing posture should be upright and decorous, not with the shins crossed. To stand while sermons and speeches are heard is the bearing of one who listens attentively and respectfully. 2 Chron. 6.2. Then the king turned his face and blessed the whole congregation of Israel, while the whole congregation of Israel stood; and v. 4, and said: Blessed be the LORD, etc. Luke 4.16. And he stood up to read. Num. 23.22. Then he uttered his oracle, saying: Rise up, Balak, and hear; give ear unto me, son of Zippor. Where Junius, for this view, further cites Gen. 49.33; 47.31; Judg. 3.20; 2 Kings 23.2; 2 Chron. 34.31; Neh. 8.6; Acts 1.15-16: And in those days Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples and said, etc.; 13.16: Then Paul stood up and said: for standing before the word and majesty of God, honour is shown to it, as the passages cited make plain; to which add Jer. 23.22; Zech. 3.7; Esth. 8.4. To stand near elsewhere is the bearing of one who approves. Acts 22.20.

units.la: Surgere est habitus curantis rem aliquam agendam operiq; instantis. Ierem. c.1.17. Tu ergo accinge lumbos tuos vt surgens eloquaris apud eos, quidquid ego praecepero tibi. Matth.c. 26.62. Surgens princeps sacerdotum, aut ei. Habacuc. c.2.1. In custodia mea stanti & considenti mihi in munitione ac speculanti ad videndum quid responsurus essem, 1.Reg.c. 11.40. Act.c.13.16. Luc.c.4.6.
units.tr: To rise is the bearing of one who takes care to carry out some matter and is pressing on with it. Jer. 1.17: So gird up your loins, and rise, and speak to them whatever I command you. Matt. 26.62: The high priest rising up... Hab. 2.1: I will stand upon my watch and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say to me, and what I shall answer. 1 Kings 11.40; Acts 13.16; Luke 4.6.

units.la: Sessio plana & aequabilis sit.
units.tr: Sitting should be level and even.

units.la: In sedendo etiam pedes & manus otiosa esse debent, nisi necessario quid hisce agendum. & in sedendo corpus, aequo libramine erectum habere, non in sella vacillare, nō iam huic, nunc alteri nati vicissim insidere decet, neq; ex adverso sedentem molestare, vel hinc inde vacillare.
units.tr: While sitting, the feet and hands too should be idle, unless something must be done with them; and while sitting one should keep the body upright and balanced, not wobble in the chair, nor be fitting to sit now on this one's, now on another's, knee in turn, nor annoy the person sitting opposite, or sway this way and that.

units.la: Sedere in agris, hortis, vineis, est habitus indicans quietem, tranquillitatem & pacem. 1. Macch. c.14 12.1. Reg.4.2. Et sedit vnusquisq; sub vinea sua, & sub ficulnea sua, & non erat qui eos deterreret. Mich.c.4.4. Sed confideant quisque sub vite sua, & sub ficu sua nemine deterrente. Psal.50.20. Sedens fratri tuo obloqueris, &c. Psal.119.23.1. Sam.c. 4.13. Esaiae c.33.16.
units.tr: To sit in fields, gardens or vineyards is the bearing that indicates rest, tranquillity and peace. 1 Macc. 14.12; 1 Kings 4.25: And every man sat under his vine and under his fig tree, and there was none to make them afraid. Mic. 4.4: But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and none shall make them afraid. Ps. 50.20: You sit and speak against your brother, etc. Ps. 119.23; 1 Sam. 4.13; Isa. 33.16.

units.la: Sedere quoq; quandoq; habitus est docentis, eorum in primis, qui in cathedra sedet. Matt. cap.23.2. In cathedra Mosis sedent Scribae & Pharisaei. & c.26.55. Quotidie apud vos sedebam, docens in templo, Luc.c.2.46. Invenerunt eum in templo sedentem in medio Doctorum.
units.tr: Sitting is also sometimes the bearing of a teacher, especially of one who sits in a chair. Matt. 23.2: The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat. And Matt. 26.55: Every day I sat with you teaching in the temple. Luke 2.46: They found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers.

units.la: Aliquando etiam habitus quietè auscultantis. Marc. c.3.32. Sedebat autem circa eum turba, Luc.c.10.39. Et huic erat soror, qua vocabatur Maria, via qua etiam assidens ad pedes Iesu, audiebat eius sermonem. Quandoq; etiam dolentis habitus. Job 2.13. Itaque sedebant cum eo humi diebus &c. Esa.c.3.26. Ier.c.13.18. Ezech.c.26.16, c.47.2.
units.tr: Sometimes it is also the bearing of one who listens quietly. Mark 3.32: And the crowd sat around him. Luke 10.39: And she had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus' feet and heard his word. Sometimes too it is the bearing of one who grieves. Job 2.13: So they sat down with him on the ground for seven days, etc. Isa. 3.26; Jer. 13.18; Ezek. 26.16; 47.2.

units.la: Didu&tis genibus sedere, aut diuaricatis distortiue tibiis stare, Thrasonum est, vt dicit Erasmus. Tibia altera altero genu suspensa sedere, vel dextero pede in lævum femur iniecto, inciuile est.
units.tr: To sit with knees spread apart, or to stand with legs wide apart or twisted, is the way of braggarts, as Erasmus says. To sit with one shin hung over the other knee, or with the right foot laid on the left thigh, is unbecoming.

units.la: Cursus hominis arguit desiderium & magnam curam rei gerendæ, Genef.c.18. Quos vides Abraham accurrit obuiam eis ex ostio tentorii sui, & Genef.c.24.28. Itaq; currens puella, nunciauit in domo matris suæ, vt se habebant ista. Sic Genef.c.29.13. Laban obuiam occurrit Iacobo ad illum hospitio excipiendum.1.Reg.c.19.20. Tum relictis bobus accurrens post Eliam, dixit. Psal.119.32. Viam præceptorum tuorum percurram, postquam dilataueris animum meum. Ier.c.8.6. Prouer.c.1.16. Pedibus suis, ad malum concurrunt & festinant ad effundendum sanguinem. Rom.c.3.15.
units.tr: Running signifies a man's desire and great concern to get something done. Gen. 18. Abraham sees them and runs to meet them from the door of his tent. Gen. 24, 28: So the girl ran and told in her mother's house how matters stood. Likewise Gen. 29.13: Laban ran to meet Jacob to welcome him into his house. 1 Kings 19.20: Then, leaving the oxen, he ran after Elijah and said. Ps. 119.32: I will run the way of your commandments, when you have enlarged my heart. Jer. 8.6. Prov. 1.16: Their feet run to evil, and they hurry to shed blood. Rom. 3.15.

units.la: Quandoq; etiam animum consternatum & timidum atq; sibi male conscium arguit. Prou. c.28.1. Fugit improbus quisq; nemine persequente. Leuit.c.17.38. Vt persequente eos strepitu folii agitati, fugiant fuga, &seq. Deut. c.28.7.25. & 2.Sam.cap. 10.13.18.
units.tr: Sometimes it also signifies a dismayed and fearful mind, conscious of wrongdoing. Prov. 28.1: The wicked flee when no one pursues. Lev. 26.36: So that the sound of a driven leaf shall chase them and they shall flee as from the sword, etc. Deut. 28.7, 25; 2 Sam. 10.13, 18.

units.la: Lapsus&casus dicitur esse periclitantis. Deut. c.32.35. Mea est ultio & retributio, tempore suo vacillabit pes eorum. Ierem.c.23.12. Idcirco erit via sua ipsis, quasi lubricissima cum caligine, in qua impellantur vt cadant. 1.Sam. c.4.18. Vt caderet Heli e sedili retrorsum, ante latus porta. Vid. plura in hanc rem
units.tr: Stumbling and falling is said to belong to one in danger. Deut. 32.35: Vengeance and recompense are mine; in due time their foot shall slip. Jer. 23.12: Therefore their way shall be to them as slippery paths in the dark, in which they are driven so that they fall. 1 Sam. 4.18: So that Eli fell backward from his seat beside the gate. See more on this matter.

units.la: Num.c.14.3. Genesc.14.10. 1.Reg.c.1.19. Psalm.27. 2. & 91.7. & 121.3.8. Actorum cap.27.34. & Ierem.cap.8.4.12. & Psalm.17.5. Contine gressus meos in orbitis tuis, ne dimoueantur pedes mei. & Psalm. 18.37.
units.tr: Num. 14.3; Gen. 14.10; 1 Kings 1.19; Ps. 27.2; 91.7; 121.3, 8; Acts 27.34; Jer. 8.4, 12; Ps. 17.5: Hold up my steps in your paths, that my feet may not slip; and Ps. 18.37.

units.la: Aliquando habitus est hominis lugentis. Iosc.7.6. Procidit in faciem suam in terram ante arcam Iehoua, &c. Matth. cap.26.39. Et progressus paululum procidit in faciem suam, &c. 1.Sam.c.15. 23.24.
units.tr: Sometimes it is the posture of one who mourns. Josh. 7.6: He fell on his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD, etc. Matt. 26.39: And going a little further he fell on his face, etc. 1 Sam. 15, 23, 24.

units.la: Conculcare est habitus contemnentis & dominantis. Matt.c.7.6. Ne forte conculcent eas, &c. Esai.c 28.3. Pedibus conculcabitur corona superbiae Ephraimi. Iosc.c.10.24. Imponito pedes vestros cervicibus ipsorum regum, &c.
units.tr: To trample underfoot is the posture of one who despises and dominates. Matt. 7.6: Lest perhaps they trample them underfoot, etc. Isa. 28.3: The crown of pride of Ephraim shall be trodden under foot. Josh. 10.24: Put your feet upon the necks of these kings, etc.

units.la: Obstupescere est habitus rem nouam & improuisam mirantis. 1.Sam. c.14.16. Quapropter fuit trepidatio in castris illius in agro, & in toto illo populo, stationarii & populatores milites trepidauerunt quoq; & seqq. & praeced. 1.Sam.c.21.1.2. Aduentante autem Dauide Nobum ad Achimelecum sacerdotem, trepidus accurrens Achimelec obuia Dauidi, &c. dicebat ei, Quare tu solus es? Et nemo tecum? Esa.c. 10.29. Transierunt transitum Gebaliin diuersorium, verterunt, trepidauit Rama, Gibba Saulis fugit, praeced. & seqq. Eze. c.28.19. Quicunq; norant te in populis, obstupuerunt de te, terrori summo es, quod nulla sis vsq; in seculum.
units.tr: To be astonished is the posture of one who marvels at a new and unforeseen thing. 1 Sam. 14.16: Then there was trembling in the camp, in the field and among all the people; the guards and the raiding soldiers also trembled, etc., and what goes before and after. 1 Sam. 21.1, 2: When David came to Nob to Ahimelech the priest, Ahimelech trembled and came running to meet David, etc., and said to him, Why are you alone, and no one with you? Isa. 10.29: They have crossed the pass, they have lodged at Geba; Ramah trembles, Gibeah of Saul flees, and what goes before and after. Ezek. 28.19: All who knew you among the peoples are astonished at you; you have become a terror, and you shall be no more for ever.

units.la: Pudefieri & confundi, est habitus eius, qui voti & consilii sui concepti non fit compos. Psalm. 25.2. Deus mi, in te confido, ne erubescam, ne exsultent inimici mei de me. 3. Etiam illi exspectantes te, ne erubescant. Erubescant qui perfide agunt agunt immerito. 1. Pet. cap. 3. 16. & Psalm. 35. 4. Pu- defiant & rubore perfundantur, quarentes animam meam; agantur retrorsum & erubescant machinantes malum meum. Psalm. 31. 18. ne erubescam. Esa. c. 44. 4. 6. Ierem. c. 31. 19. 2. Sam. c. 19. 4. 5. cap. 10. 5. Ezech. cap. 7. 18. Psalm. 71. 13. Pudefiant, deficiant aduersantes animae meae: operiantur opprobrio & ignominia, quarentes malum meum. & Psalm. 97. Pudore suffundantur omnes colentes sculptile, qui se iactant de idolis. & Psalm. 35. 26 Pudefiant & erubescant simul gaudentes de malo meo, induantur pudore & ignominia. Ioel. c. 1. 11. Erubescunt agricolae, eiulant vinitores propter triticum & hordeum, quia periit messis agri. Ierem. cap. 20. 11. Iehova adest mihi, idcirco qui persequuntur me, impingent, neque praevalebunt; erubescent valde cum non secundabuntur, ignominia perpetua non poterit tradi oblivioni. & vers. vlt. Esa. c. 50. 7. 2. Sam. c. 19. 4. Populus rubore suffusus ac si fugisset in praelio. & vers. 6. Pudefecisti hodie vultum omnium servorum tuorum. 1. Cor. c. 15. 34. Ad pudorem vobis incutiendum loquor. 2. Thessal. c. 3. 14. Quod si quis non auscultat nostro per epistolam sermoni, hunc notate & ne commercium habete cum eo, ut eum pudeat, Genes. c. 3. 10.
units.tr: To be put to shame and confounded is the posture of one who is not master of the wish and plan he has formed. Ps. 25.2: O my God, in you I trust; let me not be put to shame, let not my enemies exult over me. 3: Let none who wait for you be put to shame. Let those be ashamed who deal treacherously without cause. 1 Pet. 3.16. Ps. 35.4: Let them be turned back and brought to shame who seek my life; let them be turned back and be ashamed who plot my harm. Ps. 31.18: Let me not be ashamed. Isa. 44.4, 6; Jer. 31.19; 2 Sam. 19.4, 5; 10.5; Ezek. 7.18; Ps. 71.13: Let them be put to shame and consumed who oppose my soul; let them be covered with reproach and dishonour who seek my harm. Ps. 97: Let all who serve graven images be put to shame, who boast of idols. Ps. 35.26: Let them be put to shame and confusion together who rejoice at my harm; let them be clothed with shame and dishonour. Joel 1.11: The farmers are ashamed, the vinedressers wail over the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. Jer. 20.11: The LORD is with me, therefore my persecutors shall stumble and not prevail; they shall be greatly ashamed when they do not succeed; their everlasting disgrace shall not be forgotten; and the last verse. Isa. 50.7; 2 Sam. 19.4: The people stole into the city, ashamed, as if they had fled in battle; and verse 6: You have today put to shame the faces of all your servants. 1 Cor. 15.34: I say this to shame you. 2 Thess. 3.14: If anyone does not obey our word in this letter, mark that man and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed. Gen. 3.10.

units.la: Ossium tremor & trepidatio, est habitus hominis pauescentis, dolentis & meruentis. Psalm. 119. 120. Horret pavore tui caro mea, adeo a iudiciis tuis timeo, Deut. c. 2. 25. Die hoc incipiam imponere pavorem & timorem tui populis sub universo caelo, qui audierint famam tuam, ut trepidabunt & languescent a facie tua. Psalm. 55. 5. 6. Ierem. c. 46. 24. Fiet ut conuertat se ad fugiendum & horrorem febrilem prehendet, &c. 2. Macchab. c. 3. 17. Iere. cap. 23.9. Frangitur cor meum in me, eliduntur omnia os- fa mea. Ezech.c.5.15. Sam.c.13.7. Totus populus tre- pidi accurrerunt post eum. Psal.48.7. Ezech.cap.26. 16. Trepidationes induent, in terra sedebunt, & trepi- dantes singulis momentis stupebunt de te, & c.7.16. 1. Sam.c.28.20.21.22.
units.tr: Trembling of the bones and quaking is the posture of a man who is terrified, grieved and fearful. Ps. 119.120: My flesh trembles for fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgments. Deut. 2.25: This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you upon the peoples under the whole heaven, who shall hear the report of you, so that they shall tremble and be in anguish before you. Ps. 55.5, 6; Jer. 46.24: It shall come to pass that she turns to flee, and seizes a feverish horror, etc. 2 Macc. 3.17; Jer. 23.9: My heart is broken within me, all my bones are shaken. Ezek. 5.15; 1 Sam. 13.7: All the people followed him trembling. Ps. 48.7; Ezek. 26.16: They shall clothe themselves with trembling, they shall sit on the ground, and tremble every moment and be astonished at you, etc. 7.16; 1 Sam. 28.20, 21, 22.

units.la: Denudatio partium corporis quas denuda- re non decet, habitus & signum est hominis ob- scæni, immodesti & turpis, & libidinosi. arg. Ge- nef.c.9. Clem. Alex.lib.2. Paedag.2.6.
units.tr: Uncovering the parts of the body which ought not to be uncovered is the posture and sign of a man who is obscene, indecent, shameful and lustful. Cf. Gen. 9. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, bk. 2, ch. 6.

units.la: Abscondere se, est habitus fallentis & decipientis, vel male sibi conscii. Genef.c.3.9. Timui, eo quod nudus essem & abscondi me. 1. Sam.c.10.22. Prou.c.1.11. Si dixerint, veni nobiscum, insidiemur sanguini, abscondamus nos contra innocentem impu- ne. Psalm.35.7. Absconderunt mihi in fovea rete, & v.8.2. Sam.c.19.4. Iof.c.10.16.17. Psalm.110.1.
units.tr: To hide oneself is the posture of one who deceives and beguiles, or who is conscious of wrongdoing. Gen. 3.9: I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself. 1 Sam. 10.22. Prov. 1.11: If they say, Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood, let us lurk secretly for the innocent without cause. Ps. 35.7: They have hidden for me their net in a pit, and v. 8. 2 Sam. 19.4. Josh. 10.16, 17. Ps. 110.1.

units.la: Abscondere etiam aliquando est seponentis & custodientis, Pf.31.20.21. Psal.27.5. Nam ab- scondit me in tugurio suo tempore adversitatis, ab- dit me in abdito tentorii sui. Ofea c.13.12. Iob cap.31. 33.34.
units.tr: Hiding also sometimes signifies setting aside and keeping safe. Ps. 31.20, 21; Ps. 27.5: For he shall hide me in his shelter in the time of trouble; he shall hide me in the secret place of his tent. Hos. 13.12. Job 31.33, 34.

units.la: Pinguedine & obesitate corporis instar Mo- nachorum saginatorum uti, est habitus & signū pacis, tranquillitatis & abundantiae eorum fere, qui secundum carnem viuunt, Rom.c.7.f. Iob c. 15.27. Qui operuit vultum suum adipe suo & effecit flrigas ad ilia; hoc est (ut Iunius explicat,) obesuit corpus, ut pingue in cute plicaturas effecerit. Psalm. 17.10. Adipem suum obesant: ore suo loquuntur super- be. hoc est, (ut ibidem Iunius dicit) praepingues sunt & desiderius suis omnibus circumfluunt, & Psal.73 7. Exiit cat prae pinguedine uterq; oculus eorum, superat cogi. cogitationes animi, Ier.c.31.14.25. Lament. Ierem. c. 4.5. c.3.
units.tr: Having fat and a bloated body, like well-fed monks, is the posture and sign of peace, tranquillity and abundance, of those who for the most part live according to the flesh. Rom. 7; Job 15.27: Because he has covered his face with his fat and made folds on his loins; that is, as Junius explains, he has grown fat, so that his body has made folds of fat in his skin. Ps. 17.10: They have closed up their fat; with their mouth they speak proudly; that is, as Junius says in the same place, they are very fat and flow around with all their desires. Ps. 73.7: Their eyes bulge out from fatness; they exceed the imaginations of the heart. Jer. 31.14, 25; Lam. 4.5; Jer. 3.

units.la: Contrà caro attenuata & pellis consumpta, est habitus afflictorum. Job c.30.28. Ater ambulo, non à sole: surgens in congregatione vociferor. 30. Cutis mea denigrata est super me, & ossa mea exaruerunt prae siccitate. Psalm. 73.26. Deficiente carne mea, & verf.12.4.5.6. & Psal. 22.15.18. Psal. 31.11. Lament. Ier. cap. 4.8.9. Concreta est cutis eorum cum osse ipso-rum, aret, est similis ligno, & c.3. Ezec. c.4.17. Psf. 42. 11. Esa. c.52.2.3.
units.tr: On the contrary, a wasted body and a skin consumed is the posture of the afflicted. Job 30.28: I go about blackened, not by the sun; I stand up in the assembly and cry out. 30: My skin has turned black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat. Ps. 73.26: My flesh and my heart fail, and verses 12, 4, 5, 6. Ps. 22.15, 18; Ps. 31.11; Lam. 4.8, 9: Their skin cleaves to their bones; it is dried up, it is like wood; and ch. 3. Ezek. 4.17; Ps. 42.11; Isa. 52.2, 3.

units.la: Abstinere ab alimentis, est habitus lugentis & tristitia affecti. 1.Sam. c.7. Vt fleret, ac non comederet, 8. Quam nis diceret ei Elcana vir eius, Channa quare fles? & quare non comedis? & quare male habet animus tuus? 1.Reg. c.21.2. Sam. c.12.17. 20.21. Petiit ut apponerent cibum & comedit, 1.Sam. c.28. 20.21.22.23. Quad re videndum in ieiunio, Iudic. c. 20.26. Ioel c.2.12. Ion. c.3.5.7.1. Sam. c.7.6.2. Sam. c.1.11.12.2. Chron. c.23. Nehem. c 9.1. Esth. c.4.3. Ier. c.36.9. Act. c.13.2.3. & passim alibi.
units.tr: Abstaining from food is the posture of one who mourns and is affected by sadness. 1 Sam. 1.7: So that she wept and did not eat. 8: Then Elkanah her husband said to her, Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart grieved? 1 Kings 21.2; 2 Sam. 12.17; 20, 21: He asked that food be set before him, and he ate. 1 Sam. 28.20, 21, 22, 23. Concerning this see fasting: Judg. 20.26; Joel 2.12; Jonah 3.5, 7; 1 Sam. 7.6; 2 Sam. 1.11, 12; 2 Chron. 23; Neh. 9.1; Esth. 4.3; Jer. 36.9; Acts 13.2, 3, and passim elsewhere.

units.la: Sudare est habitus defessi & laboriosi homi-nis. Ezech. cap.2.11. c.24.12. Genes. cap 3.19. Luc. c.22.44.
units.tr: To sit on the ground is the posture of a weary and laborious man. Ezek. 2.11; 24.12; Gen. 3.19; Luke 22.44.

units.la: Iacere in terra, est imbecillium, defessorum & deiectorum, moerentium ve habitus. Esa. c.51. 20. Filii tui dilecti animo, iacent in capite omnium platearum, ut bubalus irretitus pleni excandescen-tia & increpatione Dei sui, & vers. vlt. Qui dicebant animatua, Abiicete, ut transeamus, quibus expone-bas tanquam humus corpus tuum & tanquam pla-team transeuntibus. Esa. c.50.11. In dolore iacebitis, 1. Sam. c.28.10.21.22.2. Sam. cap.12.16,17.18.20.21. Iacere in confusione, Ierem. c.3.20. Iacemus in pudo-re nostro, & operit nos ignominia nostra; quia Deo nostro peccauimus, &c. 1.Chron.c.21.16. Hesra cap. 10.12.
units.tr: To lie on the ground is the posture of the weak, the weary and the cast down, or of the mourning. Isa. 51.20: "Your sons, your beloved, lie at the head of all the streets, like a bull caught in a net, full of the wrath and rebuke of their God;" and last verse: "who said to your soul, Bow down, that we may pass over; you laid your body as the ground and as a street for passers-by." Isa. 50.11: "You shall lie down in sorrow." 1 Sam. 28.10, 21, 22; 2 Sam. 12.16, 17, 18, 20, 21. To lie in confusion: Jer. 3.20 ("We lie in our shame, and our disgrace covers us, because we have sinned against our God," etc.); 1 Chron. 21.16; Ezra 10.12.

units.la: Dormire, est habitus securè & pacificè viuen-tis.Leuitic.c.26.s.6. Ita ut cubetis & non sit qui exterreat.Psalm.3.6.Ego cubui & dormiui: Exper-gefeci me,quia Iehoua sustentat me.Psalm.4.9. In pace simul cubabo & dormiam: cum tu Iehoua fa-cias,vt securè habitem, 1.Thessal.cap.5.6. Nempe igitur, ne dormiamus vt reliqui, sed vigilemus & so-brii simus, & vers.7.8.9.10. Ezech.cap.4.4.s.6. Psalm.121.4. Psalm.44.24. Marc.cap.13.36. Ne quum repente venerit, inueniat vos dormientes, Prou.c.6.
units.tr: To sleep is the posture of one who lives securely and peacefully. Lev. 26.6: "so that you shall lie down and no one shall make you afraid." Ps. 3.6: "I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the LORD sustains me." Ps. 4.9: "In peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you, LORD, make me dwell in safety." 1 Thess. 5.6: "Therefore let us not sleep as others do, but let us watch and be sober;" and verses 7, 8, 9, 10. Ezek. 4.4, 6; Ps. 121.4; Ps. 44.24; Mark 13.36: "lest, coming suddenly, he find you sleeping." Prov. 6.

units.la: Contravigilare, est hominis soliciti anxiique. 1.Thess.d.c.s.6.2. Cor.c.6. & c.11.33. Cauete,vigilate & orate,& v.34 35.36.37.Luc.12.37.38. Psalm.63. & 126. & Psal.120.3.4.Prou.c.8 Iob c.21. & Psalm. 127.2.
units.tr: To keep watch against is the posture of a man who is anxious and troubled. 1 Thess. 5.6; 2 Cor. 6; 11.33; "Take heed, watch and pray," and verses 34, 35, 36, 37; Luke 12.37, 38. Ps. 63; 126; Ps. 120.3, 4; Prov. 8; Job 21; Ps. 127.2.

units.la: Obdormire in loco & tempore quibus cum aliis conuersamur, est habitus non magni faciē-tis colloquia & praesentiam aliorum.
units.tr: To fall asleep in a place and at a time when we are in company with others is the habit of one who does not value conversation and the presence of others.

units.la: Salutatio, est habitus & signum pacis & mu-tuae charitatis,Exod.cap.18.7. 1.Sam.c.13.10. c.10. 4.Rom.c.16.16.1. Corinth.c.16.20. Matth.cap.10.12. Iudic.cap.6.12.1. Sam.cap.25 s.c.30.21.2. Sam.c.8. 16.c.15.s. Marc.c.9.15. Luc.c.1.28.40. Act.cap.18. 21.dixi sup.
units.tr: Greeting is the habit and sign of peace and mutual love. Exod. 18.7; 1 Sam. 13.10; 10.4; Rom. 16.16; 1 Cor. 16.20; Matt. 10.12; Judg. 6.12; 1 Sam. 25; 30.21; 2 Sam. 8; 16; 15; Mark 9.15; Luke 1.28, 40; Acts 18; 21; said above.

units.la: CAP. X. De vestitu & cultu.
units.tr: CHAP. X. On clothing and adornment.

units.la: HActenus de motu plurium membrorum corporis simul. Sequitur de horum vestitu & amictu.
units.tr: Hitherto I have treated of the movement of several parts of the body together. What follows concerns their clothing and covering.

units.la: Vestitus decorus dicitur, qui personae vtentis eo, vocationem, vitae genus, aetatem, pietatem, temperantiam, sanctimoniam & grauitatem decet. Tit. c. 2. 3. Anus itidem vt sint habitu qui sanctimoniam deceat. 1. Tim. c. 2. 9. Itidem & mulieres amictu honesto cum verecundia & modestia ornare se, non cincinnis vel auro, vel margaritis vel pretiosa veste. 1. Pet. c. 3. 3. 4. Eccl. c. 9. 8. Esa. c. 3. 16. & seqq. & ad 1. Tim. c. 2.
units.tr: Clothing is called seemly when it suits the person who wears it: their calling, way of life, age, piety, self-control, holiness and dignity. Titus 2:3. Likewise the older women should be dressed in a way that befits holiness. 1 Tim. 2:9. Likewise women should adorn themselves with modest apparel, with shamefastness and sobriety, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly garments. 1 Pet. 3:3-4. Eccles. 9:8. Isa. 3:16ff., and on 1 Tim. 2.

units.la: Decorus autem & honestus vestitus est, qui comparatus est 1. ad necessitatem & vtilitatem corporis eius, qui eo vtitur. 2. qui est conformis & aptus corpori. vide Clement. Alexandri. libr. 3. Padag. c. 11. Varro. de Latina lingua, Pet. Greg. lib. 4. de Repub. c. 11.
units.tr: Seemly and respectable clothing is that which is fitted (1) to the need and usefulness of the body of the one who wears it, and (2) which is suited and adapted to the body. See Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 3.11; Varro, On the Latin Language; Petrus Gregorius, Republic 4.11.

units.la: Necessitas & vtilitas vestitus in eo est, vt corpus contra iniurias caloris, vel frigoris muniatur. Deinde, vt tegatur nudi corporis deformitas, quae secuta est post peccatum. Genes. c. 3. 7. 21. & vt excessus, vel defectus quo corpus seu membrum aliquod corporis, a natura vel casu deformatum est, quantum fieri potest, occultetur veste. unde vestimentum, quasi nuditatis velamen dicitur, 1. Corinth. cap. 12. 23. Et quae putamus membra corporis maxime esse inhonesta, iis honore ampliore circumponimus; Et quae sunt in nobis indecora, copiosiore habet. 24. Nam quae sunt in nobis decora,iis decore non est opus: sed Deus contempera-uit corpus,ei cui deerat copiosiore tributo honore, 25. utne sit dissidium, &c. Ad vestiendum igitur impelluntfrigus, turpitudo corporis, deformitas membrorum,defectus, &c. Deniq; vt ex eo appareat distinctiosexus, aetatis & vocationis, seu status in quo quilibet est collocatus. Deut. c. 22. s. Ne esto instrumentum virile super faeminam, neque induitovir vestem faeminae: nam abominationi est Iehouae Deo tuo quisquis facit ista. Esa. c. 3. 17. & seqq. Tit. c. 2. 3. Clem. Alexand. lib. 3. c. 2. c. 3. Padagog. Ec-clef. cap. 19. 27. Vestitus viri & gressus pedis, & risus dentium, enuntiant constitutionem eius. Pet. Greg. de Repub. lib. 4. c. 11. Aretius problem. 120.
units.tr: The need and usefulness of clothing lie in this: that the body be protected against the harms of heat or cold. Next, that the ugliness of the naked body, which followed upon sin, be covered. Gen. 3:7, 21. And that any excess or lack by which a body or some part of it has been deformed, whether by nature or by accident, be hidden by clothing as far as possible. Hence clothing is called, as it were, a veil of nakedness. 1 Cor. 12:23. "And those parts of the body which we think to be least honourable, we clothe with more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness. For our comely parts have no need; but God hath tempered the body together, giving more abundant honour to that part which lacked, that there should be no schism in the body." Therefore cold, the shame of the body, the deformity of the limbs, defects and so on, drive us to clothe ourselves. Finally, so that the distinction of sex, age and calling, or of the station in which each is placed, may appear from it. Deut. 22:5. The woman shall not wear that which pertaineth to a man, neither shall a man put on a woman's garment: for all that do so are an abomination unto the LORD thy God. Isa. 3:17ff.; Titus 2:3; Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 3.2-3; Ecclesiasticus 19:27. "The apparel of a man, the walk of his foot, and the laughing of his teeth, declare what he is." Petrus Gregorius, Republic 4.11; Aretius, Problem 120.

units.la: Conformis vestitus est, qui pro ratione vocationis, opificii & vitae est comparatus, & ad-commodatus conditioni vtentis, & aptus corpori, & tempori & loco, in quo viuit qui eo vtitur.
units.tr: Conformable clothing is that which is prepared in accordance with the reason of one's calling, trade and way of life, and which is adapted to the condition of the wearer, fitted to the body, and suited to the time and place in which the wearer lives.

units.la: Mulieribus vestes delicatiores concessae, sed quae tamen honestatem in matronis & pudicitiam non offenduntiuxta mores regionu. 1. Pet. c. 3. 3. 4. 1. Timot. c. 2. 9. arg. l. 7. §. si quis, de iureiur.
units.tr: Women are allowed more delicate garments, provided they do not offend the modesty and chastity of matrons, according to the customs of the region. 1 Pet. 3:3-4; 1 Tim. 2:9; the argument of Digest 12.2.7 "si quis", on oaths.

units.la: Viros seu masculos vestitus non nimium ornatus, neque adfectatus, vel preciosus decet, Gregor. d. loco. vid. tit. C. Theodof. De habitu, quo vti oporteat intra urbem, lib. 4. tit. 10.
units.tr: Men and males should not wear clothing that is excessively ornate, affected or costly. Gregorius, loc. cit.; see Codex Theodosianus, On the dress one ought to wear within the city, book 4, title 10.

units.la: Ex hisce colligitur, quis vestitus indecorus, inciuilis & incompetens sit dicendus, qui nimirum necessitati, vel vtilitati non respondet; vel corpori non est adcommodatus & aptus; vel inconueniens circumstantiis.
units.tr: From these points it may be gathered what dress is to be called unseemly, unbecoming and unsuitable: namely that which does not answer to need or usefulness; or which is not adapted and fitted to the body; or which is out of keeping with the circumstances.

units.la: Vtilitati & necessitati in excessu repugnat vestivestitus superuacaneus, alienus; in defectu vero, nuditas.
units.tr: Excess is contrary to usefulness and need: superfluous and foreign clothing. In defect, however, there is nakedness.

units.la: Superuacaneus vestitus cernitur in sumptuoso, luxurioso, superfluo nimis & exquisito vestitu, & in prodigioso inaurium pretio. vid. tit. C. de vestibus holoseric. & aurat. Senec. De remed. fortun. & lib. 7. De benef. & De beat. vita. Iuuenal. Satyr. 6. Plin. 12. in Proœm. Isidor. Etymol. lib. 19. c. 21. Lev. c. 4. 30. Esa. c. 3. 18. & seqq.
units.tr: Superfluous clothing is seen in sumptuous, luxurious, excessively superfluous and affected dress, and in the extravagant price of earrings. See Codex, On silk and gold-embroidered garments; Seneca, On Remedies for Fortune, and On Benefits book 7, and On the Happy Life; Juvenal, Satire 6; Pliny, Preface to book 12; Isidore, Etymologies 19.21; Lev. 4:30; Isa. 3:18ff.

units.la: Huc refero etiam eos qui habent cerussatam, vel oblitam faciem rubore, croco, cerussa, stibio, pigmento, fuligine, spuma. de quo fuco, vnde agunt personas laruatas, cerussatas, purpurissatas, stibiatas & fucatas impudenter mentientes, vide Ierem. c. 43. 30. 31. Esai. c. 57. Ezech. c. 23. 13. 14. & seqq. 2. Reg. c. 9. 30, 31. Prou. c. 7. 10. 11. Tiraquell. De legib. connub. lege 3. num. 1. & seqq. & dixi latius lib. 1. Dicæolog. cap. De falso. Atq; talis habitus dicitur meretricius & impudicus. vid. Clem. Alex. lib. 3. c. 2. Padag. & c. 3.
units.tr: To this I also refer those who have a face smeared or painted with red, saffron, white lead, antimony, pigment, soot or foam, by which deceitful fraud they impudently play masked, painted, rouged, antimony-tinted and made-up roles, lying shamelessly. See Jer. 4:30-31; Isa. 57; Ezek. 23:13-14ff.; 2 Kings 9:30-31; Prov. 7:10-11; Tiraquellus, On Marriage Laws, law 3, nos. 1ff.; and I have discussed this more fully in the Dicaeologia, chapter On Falsehood. Such dress is called harlot-like and immodest. See Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 3.2-3.

units.la: Eiusmodi quoq; sunt, qui pilos tingunt, canos vngunt, coloribusque oblinunt, ad specu-lum componunt, genas radunt, vellunt, aures perforatas habent, in quibus pendiles gerunt margaritas, vel aurum, argentum, lapidesve pretiosos. Clem. Alex. libr. 3. c. 11. Padag. Refert Gellius lib. 3. c. 5. Archesilaum philosophum cum vocem delicati diuitiis infractam, capillumq; arte compositū & oculos ludibundos, atq; illecebra voluptatisq; plenos videret, dixisse; Nihil interest, quibus membris cinædi sitis, posterioribus an prioribus. De Demosthene & Hortensio delicatulis, idem Gellius lib. 1. c. 5. tradit.
units.tr: Of the same kind are those who dye their hair, anoint their grey hairs, smear them with colours, arrange themselves before a mirror, shave or pluck their cheeks, have their ears pierced so that they wear pendant pearls, gold, silver or precious stones. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 3.11. Gellius, book 3, chapter 5, reports that the philosopher Arcesilaus, seeing a pampered man whose voice was broken by wealth, his hair artfully arranged, his eyes wanton and full of allurement and pleasure, said: "It makes no difference with which of your parts you are a catamite, the rear or the front." Gellius, book 1, chapter 5, relates the same of Demosthenes and Hortensius, the dainty fops.

units.la: L
units.tr: L

units.la: Alienus autem vestitus dicitur, qui sexum vtentis non decet; vt puta, si vir muliebri,& mulier virili vestitu, vel amiƈtu incederet. qualis est abominationi Iehouæ, Deut. c. 22 f. quò pertinet etiam vestitus larvatorum hominum. Item delicatorum illorum, qui instar mulieris se comunt, atq; exornant; ita vt aliud sit ornatus, aliud persona; quales sunt illi, qui capillitium, barbam & cæsariem ita in anulos crispatam ferro candenti habent, vel cirris & miris artibus intortas comas; & faciem, collum, manus ita præter modum cerussatas & fricatas, vt talis ornatus, quamcunq; mulierculam dedeceret; imo meretricem quoq;, quæ pretio pudorem suum prostituit.
units.tr: Clothing is called foreign when it does not suit the sex of the wearer: for instance, if a man went about in women's dress, or a woman in men's dress or garb. Such is an abomination to the LORD, Deut. 22 ff. To this also belongs the dress of masked men. Likewise that of those effeminate men who adorn and deck themselves like women, so that the ornament is one thing and the person another: such as those who curl their hair, beard and locks into ringlets with a hot iron, or have their tresses twisted with curls and wondrous arts; and who smear and rub their face, neck and hands beyond measure with white lead, so that such adornment would disgrace any little woman, indeed even a harlot who sells her modesty for money.

units.la: Eiusmodi cincinnatuli & calamistrati Androgyni, ingenia sua monstrosa & effæminata hoc habitu, & vestitu & amiƈtu suo omnibus ostendunt. Martial. Satyr. 1. & 12. Epigram. Paul. lib. 3. Sent. tit. 6. §. 8. Senec. lib. 6. epist. 47. & libr. 22. epist. 125. & lib. 7. Natur. & De vita breuitate, vbi dicit, de corporis sui decore magis hosce quam desa-lute sollicitos esse, qui comptiores, quam honestiores esse malunt: hos tu otiosos vocas inter peĉtinem specu-lamque occupatos? vid. Tertullian. De cultu fœmin. an vnguentis & coronis vtendum sit; vid. Clement. Alexand. libr. 2. Paed. c. 8. & lib. 3. c. 2. c. 3. vbi etiam de effaminato cultu masculorum & lasciuo vestitu mulierum disserit late. & c. 11. de suco; vid. Martyr. 2. Reg. cap. 9. & Pet. Gregor. lib. 4. cap. 11. de Repub. Huc etiam refero vestitum exoticum, peregrinum & alienum à vestitu recepto, & vsitato. vid. Pet. Greg. lib. 4. c. 11. De Republica.
units.tr: Such curled and frizzed androgynes show their monstrous and effeminate natures to all by this dress, clothing and garb. Martial, Epigrams 1 and 12; Paulus, Sentences 3.6.8; Seneca, Letters 47 and 125 (book 22), and On Nature book 7 and On the Shortness of Life, where he says that such men are more anxious about the beauty of their bodies than about their health, and prefer to be more elegant than more honourable: do you call these men idle, who are busy with comb and mirror? See Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women, whether ointments and garlands are to be used; Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2.8 and 3.2-3, where he also discusses at length the effeminate dress of men and the wanton clothing of women; and 3.11, on the dye; Martial, 2 Kings 9; and Petrus Gregorius, Republic 4.11. To this I also refer foreign clothing, strange and alien to the accepted and customary dress. See Petrus Gregorius, Republic 4.11.

units.la: Nuditas post lapsum hominis est habitus inopis & egeni hominis. & quandoque hominis lymphatici, phrenetici, furiosi, impudentis, ebriosi & malitiosi: & quandoque obscoeni, & libidinosi hominis, ostendentis ea, quae natura occulta esse voluit.
units.tr: Nakedness after the fall of man is the mark of a poor and needy man, and sometimes of a deranged, frenzied, raving, shameless, drunken or malicious man; and sometimes of an obscene and lustful man, displaying those things which nature wished to be hidden.

units.la: Paedagog.
units.tr: Paedagogus

units.la: Corpori non adcommodatus vestitus, dicitur inhabilis, ineptus, qui modo maior, modo minor corporis membris. Maior, uti quando quis more agasonum & aurigarum dissolutis vestibus utitur, ut thorax cum caligis confligere velle videatur. Eiusmodi sunt praegrandes illi pilei & corrugatae fasciae, circa collum serpentes, necnon thoraces illi tumidi, ac si hydropicum aliquem tegerent, vel pullos instar praegnantis scrophae: tales, inquam, prodigiose prominentes illi ventres, goffipio aut pilis infarti, quibus multi faciunt se <bl>ਅ</bl>
units.tr: Clothing that does not fit the body is called unsuitable and unbecoming. It is either larger or smaller than the limbs of the body. It is larger when someone, in the manner of carters and charioteers, wears loose clothes so that his doublet seems to be fighting his breeches. Such are those enormous caps and crumpled bands wound about the neck, and those swollen doublets, as if they covered some dropsical man, or a sow heavy with piglets. I mean those prodigiously protruding bellies, stuffed with padding or hair, by which many make themselves

units.la: Tales etiam sunt prolixae illae faeminarum caudae. Tales etiam vestes aptae quidem corpori, sed quae tamen in alterum latus defluant, aut in tergum ad renes usque inaequaliter & incompositè; vel reiectis circa humeros tunicis, ac manticis in terram propendentibus atq; demissis incessus.
units.tr: Such too are the long trailing tails of women. Also such are clothes that fit the body but hang down to one side, or down the back to the buttocks, unevenly and untidily; or tunics thrown back over the shoulders, with wallets and sleeves hanging down to the ground and dragging the gait.

units.la: Mulieribus crines sufficit mollite & tenui aliqua fibula comam alligare frugaliter, simplici cultura pudicas comas in veram & germanam pulchritudinem alentibus. Alienorum capillorum appositiones sunt omnino reiiciendæ. vide Clem. Alex. lib. 3. c. 11. Padag.
units.tr: Women should be content to bind their hair simply with some soft, thin clasp, and to nourish their modest locks with plain dressing, so that they achieve true and genuine beauty. Additions of other people's hair are to be rejected altogether. See Clem. Alex., Paedagogus, bk. 3, ch. 11.

units.la: Pilos tingere, vel canos colorare neq; honestum, neq; decorum, sed potius, quod Dei decus, in apertum proferendum, vt id honorent adolescentes. d. c. 11.
units.tr: To dye the hair or colour grey hair is neither honourable nor becoming. Rather, the glory of God should be displayed openly, so that young people may honour it. Ibid., ch. 11.

units.la: Huc refero etiam laserationes, dissectiones, alligationes & varietates vestium versicolorum, qui est habitus morionum & simiarum. Vestes etiam aspergine lotii, atramenti, luti, pituitæ, pingere vel incrustare, est sordidorum.
units.tr: To this I refer also the slashing, cutting, tying up and variegating of clothes in many colours, which is the custom of buffoons and monkeys. To spatter clothes with urine, ink, mud or phlegm, or to paint or crust them, belongs to the dirty.

units.la: Huius generis est quoque nimium studium & cultus corporis & vestitus, quæ hominem delicatum, mollem & sui ipsius amantem arguit, de quibus Cato:
units.tr: Of this kind too is excessive zeal for the care of body and clothing, which shows a man to be effeminate, soft and a lover of himself. Of such men Cato says:

units.la: Inuidiam nimio cultu vitare memento:
units.tr: Remember to avoid envy by excessive display:

units.la: Quæ si non lædit, tamen hanc sufferre molestum est.
units.tr: Which, even if it does not harm, is still troublesome to endure.

units.la: Minore vestitu vtuntur, qui pileis illis parvis gaudent, pallio breui, caligis angustis, quibus ad viuum membra corporis, quæ vestiuntur hisce, exprimuntur: ita vt nonnunquam illa quæ natura tegi voluit, occultari vix possint, aut aduersus iniurias externas corpus protegere nequeant. C. m. Alex. d. c. 2. & c. 3. qui vestitus conuenit cinædis, similiis & cercopithecis.
units.tr: They wear too little clothing who delight in those tiny caps, short cloaks and tight breeches, through which the limbs covered by them are expressed to the life, so that sometimes those parts which nature wished to be covered can scarcely be hidden, or they cannot protect the body against external injuries. See Clem. Alex., ibid., ch. 2 and ch. 3. Such dress suits catamites, mimics and monkeys.

units.la: Vestitus circumstantiis inconueniens est, qui non respondet vitæ generi & professioni vtentis, quive non est adcommodatus tempori, loco, vel co, vel consuetudini; quibus ostenditur con-temptus eorum, qui aliter vestiti incedunt.
units.tr: Clothing is unbecoming to circumstances when it does not correspond to the way of life and profession of the wearer, or is not adapted to the time, place, or custom; by such dress contempt is shown for those who go dressed otherwise.

units.la: Non respondet vitæ generi, officio & vocationi, quando scholasticus more militis, & hic instar scurræ vel histrionis fcenici harenarii amictus incedit: Ecclesiasticus, ciuis, aliusque honoratus, vestitu rustico, sordido; honesta fæmina, vel matrona, habitu & amictu meretricio vtitur. l. 1 §. item, §. 1 §. fi quis de iniur. vbi Gothofr. Genef. c. 38. & c. 24. vid. Macrob. lib. 1. Saturn. cap. 6. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 5. c. 18. Genial. dier. & Pet. Greg. lib. 9. Syntagm. c. 19. & tit. De vit. & honest. cleric. Gellius lib. 9. c. 2.
units.tr: It does not correspond to way of life, office and calling when a student walks about dressed like a soldier, or a man walks in the manner of a buffoon or a stage actor or gladiator in the arena. An ecclesiastic, a citizen, or any other man of honour who dresses in rustic, dirty clothes does so inappropriately; an honest woman or matron who uses the dress and adornment of a harlot does so inappropriately. See Digest 1 §1 and §1 ‘Si quis’, De iniuriis, where Gothofredus; Gen. ch. 38 and ch. 24; Macrobius, Saturnalia 1, ch. 6; Alexander ab Alexandro, Genialium dierum 5, ch. 18; Peter Gregory, Syntagma 9, ch. 19, and the title De vita et honestate clericorum; Gellius 9, ch. 2.

units.la: Huc pertinent illi, qui vestitu altioris ordinis & status vtuntur, digitos anulis, pileos ac vestes bullis & gemmis exornant, vel collum torquibus aureis onerant, ac fi genere, familia, dignitatis, honore & gloria potiores effent; quo habitu produnt vanitatem, inanis gloriæ cupiditatem & falsum suum. vid. Sueton. in Iul. Cæsare, Dion. libr. 49. histor. & constitut. Imperii, & Cod. Theodos. tit. 10. De habitu quo uti oporteat, &c. lib. 4. Inferiorem & humiliorem vestibus illis induere est illudentis. Marc. c. 15. 18. 19. 20. Matth. c. 27. 28. & seqq.
units.tr: To this belong those who dress in the attire of a higher rank and status, who adorn their fingers with rings and their caps and clothes with bosses and gems, or load their necks with golden collars, as if they were superior in birth, family, dignity, honour and glory. By such dress they betray their vanity, their desire for empty glory and their falsehood. See Suetonius, Julius Caesar; Dio, Histories 49, and the constitutions of the Empire; and Codex Theodosianus, title 10, On the dress that ought to be worn, bk. 4. To put on clothes lower and humbler than one's own is the mark of a mocker. Mark ch. 15:18–20; Matt. ch. 27:28ff.

units.la: Tempori accommodatus vestitus non est, quando tempore pacis, lætitiæve quis vtitur vestitu vsitato tempore belli, vel luctus, aut contra. Similiter, quando quis capitis integumento nocturno, interdiu vtitur, eoq; in conspectum aliorum prodit; vel dentiscalpium fiue auriscalpium omni tempore & loco è collo vel alio loco suspensum, vel pendile gestat. Loco, consuetudini receptæ, & personis præsentibus vestitus inconueniens est, qui harum dignitati non respondet. Matth. c. 22. 11. Intrauit autem Rex, vt videret discumbentes & vidit ibi hominem non vestitum veste nuptiali. 12. Et ait illi, Quomodo huc intrasti, non habens vestem nuptialem? Iudit. c. 12. 15. Genes. 41. 14. Ioseph. cum abraderet caput, venit ad Pharaonem, & c. 50. 4. vbi lun. Daniel c. 1. 4. & seqq. Luc. c. 7. 25. Ecce, qui vestiuntur magnifico vtuntur sunt in palatiis regum, Ester c. 4. 2. & seq.
units.tr: Clothing is not suited to the time when someone wears in time of peace or joy the dress customary in time of war or mourning, or the reverse. Likewise, when someone wears a nightcap by day and goes out in public in it; or carries a toothpick or ear-pick hung from his neck or some other place at all times and in all places, or wears it as a pendant. Clothing is unsuited to place, custom and the persons present when it does not match their dignity. Matt. 22:11–12: "But when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man who did not have on a wedding garment. And he said to him, 'Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?'" Judges 12:15; Gen. 41:14, when Joseph shaved his head and came to Pharaoh; Gen. 50:4; Daniel 1:4ff.; Luke 7:25: "Behold, those who wear splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' palaces." Esther 4:2ff.

units.la: Vestis variæ sunt formæ & species. Alia enim est manicata, alia sine manicis.
units.tr: Clothes come in various forms and kinds. Some have sleeves, others are sleeveless.

units.la: Manicatas longas & integras manicas voco, quæ ad manus & ipsos manuum digitos vsque extenduntur: Breues manicas habent, quæ ad cubitum vsque porriguntur.
units.tr: I call sleeves long and full when they extend down to the hands and the very fingers; they are short when they reach only to the elbow.

units.la: Exomides vestes sunt, quæ carent manicis, Ärmellos ohne Ermel. Aliæ vestes porrò ornantur plicis: aliæ simplices sunt sine plicis.
units.tr: Garments without sleeves are called sleeveless, Ärmellos ohne Ermel. Some clothes are further decorated with pleats; others are plain, without pleats.

units.la: Alia vestis patagium habet, alia fimbrias: alia his caret. Patagium affui solet ad summam tunicam ex alia pretiosa materia. Fimbriata vestis dicitur, quæ circa imas extremitates ornatum habet.
units.tr: One garment has a patagium, another a fringe, another neither. A patagium is usually attached to the outer tunic and made of another costly material. A garment is called fringed when it has ornament around its lower edges.

units.la: A coloribus quoque plurimæ vestis species sumuntur, vt purpura simplex, bis tincta, dibapha, ostrina, tyrianthina, violacea, leucophæa, chlorea, hyacinthina, crocea, sulca, nigra vestis.
units.tr: Very many kinds of clothing are also named from their colours: plain purple, twice-dyed, dibaphic, ostrine, Tyrian, violet, white-grey, green, hyacinth, saffron, sulphur-coloured, and black clothing.

units.la: Alia vestis est vnius coloris, alia diuersorum variorum. vid. Aret. problem. 120.
units.tr: Some clothing is of one colour, other of several different colours. See Aretaeus, Problems 120.

units.la: Vestis vsus secundum partes humani corporis tis consideratur, vt capitis diadema, tiara, mitra, galerus, petasus, pileus, birretum, capitium, vitta, reticulum, peplum, &c.
units.tr: Clothing is also considered according to the parts of the human body: for the head, the diadem, tiara, mitre, galerus, petasus, pileus, biretta, hood, fillet, hairnet, peplum, etc.

units.la: Pedis vestimentum est calceus ex corio, ligno, vel alia materia, calopodia, calones, sandalium, perones, ocreæ, &c.
units.tr: Clothing for the foot is a shoe of leather, wood or other material: calopodia, calones, sandal, peronés, greaves, etc.

units.la: Manus vestimentum est chirotheca, anulus, gemma.
units.tr: Clothing for the hand is the glove, ring and gem.

units.la: Trunci corporis vestimentum est thorax, pallium, chlæna.
units.tr: Clothing for the trunk of the body is the breastplate, cloak and chlaina.

units.la: Vestitus candidus, est habitus puritatis & innocentiæ, Apocalyps. c. 3. 4. Qui non inquinarunt vestimenta sua, ideoq; incedent mecum albati: digni enim sunt. 5. Qui vicerit, amicietur vestimentis albis, &c. 19. 8. Et datum est ei ut amiciatur bysso pura & splendida. Byssus enim iustificationes sunt sanctorum, Iohann. cap. 20. 12. Matth. cap. 17. 2. Ador. cap. 1. 10. Ecce viri duo adstiterunt illis albo vestitu. Sic enim Angeli boni visi leguntur albo vestitu. Matth. cap. 28. Marc. c. 16. Ioh. cap. 20. & Christus, Marc. c. 9. & Matth. c. 17. Luc. cap. 23. vid. Ecclesiast. c. 9. 10. Baptizandorum vestitus olim quoque candidus erat in primitiva Ecclesia. Stuckius libr. 2. cap. 26. convivial. antiquit. & Clemens Alexand. Pædag. lib. 2. c. 10. & lib. 3. c. 11. Aret. problem. 120.
units.tr: White clothing is a sign of purity and innocence. Rev. 3:4: "They have not soiled their garments, and so they shall walk with me in white, for they are worthy." 3:5: "He who conquers shall be clothed in white garments," etc. 19:8: "It was given to her to clothe herself in fine linen, bright and pure"; for fine linen is the righteousnesses of the saints. John 20:12; Matt. 17:2; Acts 1:10: "Behold, two men stood by them in white clothing." Thus good angels are read of as clothed in white. Matt. 28; Mark 16; John 20; and Christ, Mark 9 and Matt. 17; Luke 23. See Eccl. 9:8–10. In the early Church the clothing of those to be baptized was also white. Stuckius, Antiquitates convivales 2, ch. 26; Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 2, ch. 10 and 3, ch. 11; Aretaeus, Problems 120.

units.la: Ergo lætitiæ, puritatis, integritatis, fincerita-tis, felicitatis, libertatis, victoriæ habitum indi-cat color vestium albus. vid. Lipf. Electi. c. 13. lib. 1. Stuck. d. lib. 2. c. 26. Clement. Alex. d. loco. Pau. libr. 1. Sentent. tit. de sepulch. Alex. ab Alex. libr. 5. Genial. dier. c. 18. Ideo in honorum & munerum petitione co-petitores albo vestitu utebantur, & candidati diceban-tur. Stuck & Plut. d. locis.
units.tr: Therefore white colour of clothing indicates a habit of joy, purity, integrity, sincerity, happiness, liberty and victory. See Lipsius, Electa 1, ch. 13; Stuckius, loc. cit., 2, ch. 26; Clement of Alexandria, loc. cit.; Paulus, Sententiae 1, title De sepulchris; Alexander ab Alexandro, Genialium dierum 5, ch. 18. For this reason, in seeking offices and honours, rival candidates used to wear white clothing, and were called candidates. Stuckius and Plutarch, loc. cit.

units.la: Contrà autem vestitus ater & vestes pullatę, habitus & signum sunt tristitiæ & luctus. Psalm. 35.14. Tanquam ad proximum, tanquam ad fratrem mihi indesinenter itarem, tanquam lugens matrem atratus curuarem me. Psal. 42. Quare atratus incedo propter oppressionem inimici? Jerem. c.8.21. Propter contritionem filiæ populi mei, conteror, atratus incedo, stupor corripit me. Vestium lugubrium color apud Romanos erat ater, vel caeruleus. vid. Alexand. ab Alex. lib.3. Gen. diur. cap.7. Paul. lib.1. Sent. tit. De sepulch. Stuck. libr. 1. cap. 26. connubial. antiquit.
