units.tr: Conversely, black clothing and dark garments are the dress and sign of sadness and mourning. Psalm 35.14: I went about as though it were my friend or my brother; I bowed down in mourning, as one who grieves for a mother. Ps. 42: Why do I go about in black because of the oppression of the enemy? Jer. 8.21: For the breaking of the daughter of my people I am broken; I go about in black, and astonishment has seized me. The colour of mourning garments among the Romans was black or dark blue. See Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial. dier. bk 3 ch. 7; Paulus, Sent. bk 1, title De sepulchro; Stuck, bk 1 ch. 26, De connubiali antiquitate.

units.la: Vestitus varii coloris, index est animi inconstantis: contrà, purus, simplex, moderati & temperantis. Clem. Alex. lib.3. c.11. Pædag.
units.tr: Clothing of varied colours is a sign of an inconstant mind; on the contrary, plain, simple and moderate clothing belongs to a temperate and self-controlled person. Clem. Alex. Paedag. bk 3 ch. 11.

units.la: Vestes ægrotantium, peculiares quoq; esse solent. vid. Senec. li.4. Natur. c.13. Sueton. in Claud. c.2. Quintil. 11. c. vlt.
units.tr: The garments of the sick are also customarily distinctive. See Seneca, Nat. bk 4 ch. 13; Suetonius, Claudius ch. 2; Quintilian, bk 11, last ch.

units.la: Vestitus decorus, mundus, purus, ætati & vocationi respondens, index est animi honesti & moderati. Clem. Alex. lib.3. c.11. Pædag.
units.tr: Decent, clean, pure clothing suited to one's age and calling is a sign of an honourable and moderate mind. Clem. Alex. Paedag. bk 3 ch. 11.

units.la: Vestitus sordidus, est habitus miserorum aut occupatorum hominum, 2. Sam. c.19.25. Mephiboseth quoq; nepos Saulis, descenderat obuiam regi, non curauerat autem pedes suos, neq; curauerat mystacem suum, & vestes suas non lauerat, ex quo die abierat Rex. Et quandoque pauperis. Jacob. c.2.2. Ingrediatur autem & pauper cum sordida veste. Hebr. c.11.37. Oberrarunt cum ouillis & caprinis pellibus, destituti, pressi & male vexati, Zach. c.3.3.
units.tr: Shabby clothing is the habit of wretched or busy people. 2 Sam. 19.25: Mephibosheth also, the grandson of Saul, had gone down to meet the king; he had not cared for his feet, nor trimmed his moustache, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed. And sometimes it is the habit of the poor. James 2.2: And a poor man in shabby clothing comes in. Heb. 11.37: They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed and badly treated. Zech. 3.3.

units.la: Vestitus luxuriantium & lasciuientium, & superbientium faeminarum, graphicè describitur ab Esa. c.3.18.19. & seqq. vbi Iun. Vestitus sacerdotalis, Zachar. c.3. Nimius etiam cultus corporis nitidus, ve- nustus,& nimis accuratus summis viris probro datur, vt scribit Gell.lib.1.cap.5.de Demosthene & Hortensio.
units.tr: The dress of luxurious, wanton and haughty women is vividly described in Isa. 3.18-19 and following, where Junius... Priestly dress is described in Zech. 3. Excessive bodily adornment, too polished, elegant and over-careful, is also a reproach to great men, as Gellius writes, bk 1 ch. 5, concerning Demosthenes and Hortensius.

units.la: Vestitus regius & amplissimæ dignitatis, de- scribitur Est.c.15.16. Tu scis necessitatem mihi im- positam, me detestari signum illud meum superbia, quod in capite meo gero, quibus me speciandam præ- beo, me detestari istud vt pannunculum ex mensibus. Est.c.8.15. Ita Mardochai egrediebatur è conspectu Regis,cum indumento regio, hyacinthino & albo, coronaq; aurea magna & stola byssina, aut purpurea. Daniel.c.5.29. Matth.c.11.8. Ecce, qui gerunt molles vestes, in domibus regum sunt. Luc.c.7.25. Eccl.cap. 40.4. Æque ferenti hyacinthinum & coronam, at- que amicienti linum crudum. Daniel 5.7. Quisquis legerit scripturam hanc & interpretationem eius in- dicauerit mihi, purpura induetur, cumq; torque au- reo ad collum ipsius, ac tertius in hoc regno dominabi- tur,& vers.16.29. Genef.c.41.41. Vide, constitui te super vniuersam terram Ægypti, 42. Detrahensq; Pharao anulum suum è manu sua, indidit in manum Josephi, iussitq; illum induere vestes xylinas, & appo- suit torquem aureum collo eius, Ester cap.6.8.9.10.11. Corona index gloriæ & dignitatis. Iob cap.19.9. c.31.36. Psalm.21.4. vid. Esa.c.28.1. vid.tit. C.de ve- stib.holoseric.& aurat. Clem. Alex.lib.2.c.8.Pædag. & c.10.c.12.& de Repub.lib.4.c.11. P.Gregor.& lib. 9.Syntagm.c.19. & infra in Ethica propria.
units.tr: Royal dress of the highest dignity is described in Esth. 15.16: You know the necessity laid upon me; I loathe that sign of my pride which I wear on my head, and I display myself to be looked at; I loathe it as a rag of a menstruous woman. Esth. 8.15: So Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal robes of violet and white, with a great golden crown and a fine linen and purple cloak. Dan. 5.29. Matt. 11.8: Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings. Luke 7.25. Ecclus 40.4: Equally to the one who wears violet and a crown, and to the one who clothes himself in raw linen. Dan. 5.7: Whoever reads this writing and shows me its interpretation shall be clothed in purple, with a golden chain about his neck, and he shall rule as third in the kingdom; and v. 16, 29. Gen. 41.41: See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt. 42: And Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand, and clothed him in fine linen garments and put a golden chain about his neck. Esth. 6.8-11; the crown is a sign of glory and dignity. Job 19.9; 31.36. Ps. 21.4; see Isa. 28.1; see title C. De vestibus holosericis et auratis. Clem. Alex. Paedag. bk 2 ch. 8, and ch. 10, ch. 12; and De Republica bk 4 ch. 11. P. Gregor. bk 9 Syntagm. ch. 19; and below in Ethica propria.

units.la: Arma gestare & circumferre secum, est ha- bitus hominis sibi metuentis, & se contra vim & iniuriam illatam, aut læsurum defendere cu- pientis. Nehem.c.4.13. Constitui etiam populum per familiam cum gladus suis, sputulis suis & arcubus suis, & verf. 14. & seqq. Est. c. 8. 11. 12. Matth. cap. 26. 47. Iudas unus ex duodecim venit, & cum eo turba multa cum gladiis & fustibus, a primariis sacerdotibus & senioribus populi. & verf. 55. Vt aduersus latronem exiuistis cum gladiis & fustibus, ut comprehenderetis me. & 1. Sam. cap. 25. 13. dixit David hominibus suis, Accingite quisque gladium suum, quibus accingentibus singulis gladium suum, accinxit quoque Dauid & Matth. c. 26. 51. Et ecce vnus ex eis quaerant cum Iesu, extensa manu distrinxit gladium suum, & percussò seruo Pontificis maximi, abstulit auriculam eius, 1. Chron. c. 12. 34. & seqq. 1. Sam. c. 17. 5. 6. & seqq. 43 49. c. 21 9. Praeterea dixit Dauid Achimeleco, an non est hic penes te hasta aut gladius? nam nec gladium meum, nec arma mea acceperim manum meam, &c. & verf. 10. c. 14. 7. & seqq. 21. c. 13. 19. 20. 21. 22. Genes. c. 14. 14. Deut. c. 19. 11. Psalm. 7. 13. 14. Ezech. c. 32 11. 12. 13. Exod. cap. 15.
units.tr: To carry arms and bear them about with oneself is the habit of a man who fears for himself and wishes to defend himself against violence and injury inflicted or about to be inflicted. Neh. 4.13: I set the people by families with their swords, spears and bows. v. 14 and following. Esth. 8.11, 12. Matt. 26.47: Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs from the chief priests and elders of the people. v. 55: Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs, to seize me? 1 Sam. 25.13: David said to his men, Gird on each his sword. And when each had girded on his sword, David also girded on his. Matt. 26.51: And behold, one of those with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. 1 Chron. 12.34 and following. 1 Sam. 17.5, 6 and following, 43, 49; 21.9. Moreover David said to Ahimelech: Is there not here with you a spear or a sword? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons, etc.; v. 10. 1 Sam. 14.7 and following; 21; 13.19-22. Gen. 14.14. Deut. 19.11. Ps. 7.13, 14. Ezek. 32.11-13. Exod. 15.

units.la: Principatus insignia sunt corona, diadema, fascia, pileus, sceptrum, vid. Greg. lib. 6. cap. 20. de Rep.
units.tr: The insignia of rule are the crown, diadem, fillet, cap and sceptre. See Gregory, bk 6 ch. 20, De Republica.

units.la: Vestitus Aaronicus describitur Exod. cap. 28. cap. 29. Levit. cap. 8. Num. cap. 15. 1. Sam. c. 2. De monastico sacerdotum, Episcoporum, Cardinalium & Pontificis vestitu vide alios. hypocritarum vestitus extat Matth. c. 23. Luc. c. 20.
units.tr: The dress of Aaron is described in Exod. 28; Exod. 29; Lev. 8; Num. 15; 1 Sam. 2. On the monastic dress of priests, bishops, cardinals and the Pope, see others. The dress of hypocrites is found in Matt. 23; Luke 20.

units.la: CAP. XI. De habitu & gestu adsumpto.
units.tr: CAP. XI. Of adopted dress and gesture.

units.la: ATque talis fuit habitus naturalis, insitus & innatus, communiq; hominum omnium iudicio approbatus: sequitur de adsumpto.
units.tr: Such, then, was natural dress, implanted and innate, and approved by the common judgment of all men. What follows concerns adopted dress.

units.la: Est autem adsumptus habitus, qui ex placito & iudicio plurium hominum efformatur & assumitur: Unde est quod hic non omnibus communis sit, neq; idem & similis semper, neq; eandem certamque apud omnes significationem habeat.
units.tr: Adopted dress, however, is that which is formed and taken up by the approval and judgment of many people. Hence it is that it is not common to all, is not always the same or similar, and does not carry the same fixed meaning among everyone.

units.la: Eiusmodi habitus & gestus adsumptus rursus est consuetudinarius, vel arbitrarius.
units.tr: Such adopted dress and gesture is in turn either customary or arbitrary.

units.la: Consuetudinarius dicitur, qui ex frequenti alicuius loci, vel hominum quorundam vsurpatione frequentatur.
units.tr: It is called customary when it is practised through the frequent usage of some place or of certain people.

units.la: Hic igitur habitus consuetudinarius non a nostra voluntate aut libero arbitrio originem suam trahit, sed a lege, hoc est, communi consuetudine nobis imponitur. In illis autem rebus, quae nullo cum scelere, sed potius cum specie quadam virtunitatis sunt coniunctae, oportet & decet communi consuetudini obedire, eique neque disputationem neque litem movere, ut Galateus ait. Itaque consuetudini Ethicus se prudenter accommodare debet tanquam Polypus, ne alias ipse suo singulari & discrepanti habitu & gestu alios contemnere, vel vilipendere videatur, vel improbare eosdem, eorumque mores publicos, quo nomine inuisos sibi populares reddit, eorumque oculos in se converrit, quorum commune & publicum iu-
units.tr: Customary dress of this kind does not derive its origin from our will or free choice, but is imposed on us by law, that is, by common custom. In matters that are joined with no wrongdoing, but rather with some appearance of decency, it is right and fitting to obey common custom, and neither to dispute with it nor to stir up strife against it, as Galateus says. Therefore the ethical person ought prudently to accommodate himself to custom, like a polyp, lest he appear to despise or hold in contempt others by his own singular and discordant dress and gesture, or to disapprove of those same people and their public manners, by which name he makes the people hostile to himself and draws their eyes upon himself, while he scorns their common and public judgment in dress or manners by not conforming to them. Rightly therefore Seneca says: the wise man will not disturb the public customs that have been received, nor the judgments [of others], nor will he turn the people against himself by the novelty of his life. And Cato:

units.la: dicium in vestitu vel moribus contemnit, dum se iisdem non conformat. Ideo recte Seneca: Nō conturbabit sapiens mores publicos receptos; nec iudicia, vel populum in se vitæ nouitate conuertet. & Cato,
units.tr: Never despise the judgment of the people, not even of one man: lest you please no one, while you wish to despise many.

units.la: Iudicium populi nunquam contempseris unum: Ne nulli placeas, dum vis contemnere multos.
units.tr: Never disregard the judgment of a single person, lest you please no one while you wish to scorn many.

units.la: In Italia blandi & nimii gestus grati sunt; si-cut & in Gallia. In Germania moderatio & gra-uitas in gestibus accepta.
units.tr: In Italy, flattering and excessive gestures are welcome, as they are also in France. In Germany, moderation and gravity in gestures are accepted.

units.la: Eiusmodi actiones & gestus seu ceremoniæ plurimæ hodie sunt, aliæ tamen atq; aliæ in di-uersis nationibus & regionibus: in quorum ge-stuum vsu, ratio habenda regionis, vt dixi, eius, in qua viuis; item, temporis, ætatis & conditio-nis cum illius, apud quem viuis, & veteris hisce ceremoniis, tum etiam nostræ conditionis. Re-feram autem hic habitus & gestus consuetudi-narios & vsitatos potissimum apud Iudæos, qui quatenus & quantum in qualibet alia regione & populo sunt recepti, experientiâ & ciuiles po-litici testari possunt.
units.tr: Such actions and gestures, or ceremonies, are very many today, but they differ among different nations and regions. In using these gestures, one must consider, as I said, the region in which you live, and likewise the time, age and condition of both yourself and the one among whom you live, together with the ceremonies of the past and of our own condition. I shall describe here the habits and gestures that were customary and in common use, especially among the Jews, which, insofar as and to the extent that they have been taken up in any other region and people, can be attested by experience and by civil and political writers.

units.la: Salutatio ceremonialis gestu motuq; corpo-ris totius, vel certarum partium, fiebat apud Iu-dæos, Romanos & Græcos. Eratq; duplex: Pri-or, quæ fiebat sine contactu illius qui salutaba-tur. Illa erat capitis certus quidam motus & ha-bitus, quod in salutationibus moueri & inclina-ri solebat, & aliquando velari atq; regi, aliquan-do aperiri & denudari.
units.tr: Ceremonial greeting by the movement of the whole body, or of certain parts, was practised among the Jews, the Romans and the Greeks. It was twofold. The first kind was made without touching the person greeted. This was a certain movement and posture of the head, which was customarily moved and bowed in greetings, and sometimes covered and arranged, and at other times uncovered and bared.

units.la: Detecto capite Romani, homines & Deos salutabant. Ioh. Guil. Stuckius lib. 2. c. 32. comment. antiquit. vbi hoc ipsum multis exemplis probat. Egnat. lib. 9.
units.tr: Romans, with head uncovered, greeted both men and gods. Johann Wilhelm Stuckius, book 2, chapter 32, Commentaries on Antiquity, where he proves this very point with many examples. Egnatius, book 9.

units.la: Salutatio gestus facta.
units.tr: A greeting made by a gesture.

units.la: lib.9.c.11.Bonfin.lib.10. Decad.3. Olaus lib.11. c.11.1. Cor. c.11. vbi inter masculos & faeminas recte Apostolus distinguit.
units.tr: Book 9, chapter 11. Bonfinius, book 10, Decade 3. Olaus, book 11, chapter 11. 1 Cor. chapter 11, where the Apostle rightly distinguishes between men and women.

units.la: Manibus quoque salutatio fiebat, quando scilicet dextera ad osculum referebatur & corpus circumagebatur, Plin.lib.28. c.2.vid. Caelium Rhodigin.lib.7. c.15. De manuum extensione & expansione in supplicationibus, vid.1.Reg.cap.8. Hodie manus osculantur & deinde porrigunt in salutando. Huc pertinet quoq; geniculatio, γονυκλισία, quae hodie visitata, ut dixi supra in Incurvatione. Huc etiam totius corporis prostratio. Genes.cap.48.11.Esa.c.44.15.41.43. Matth.cap.4. c.18. Apocalyps.c.7. Act.c.10.arg. Rom.c.14. Act. c.7. & 20.
units.tr: Greeting was also made with the hands, namely when the right hand was carried to the mouth in a kiss and the body was turned around. Pliny, book 28, chapter 2; see Caelius Rhodiginus, book 7, chapter 15. On the stretching out and spreading of the hands in supplications, see 1 Kings, chapter 8. Today people kiss the hands and then extend them in greeting. To this belongs also genuflection [γονυκλισία], which is in use today, as I said above under bowing. To this also belongs the prostration of the whole body. Gen. 48:11; Isa. 44:15; 41; 43; Matt. 4; 18; Rev. 7; Acts 10 (argument); Rom. 14; Acts 7 and 20.

units.la: Salutatio, quae fit cum apprehensione sive contactu eorum qui salutantur, varia & olim, & hodie est. Osculum vero olim & hodie valde visitatum. Moris olim fuit mentum attingere eius, qui salutabatur, ut probat Io.Guil.Stuckius ex Homero, quo refert etiam exceptionem illam filii perditi. Luc.c.15.20. & seqq.
units.tr: Greeting that is made with the taking hold of, or touching, those greeted is varied, both in former times and today. The kiss, however, was and is very much in use. It was formerly the custom to touch the chin of the person being greeted, as Johann Wilhelm Stuckius proves from Homer, where he also reports that exception of the prodigal son. Luke 15:20 and following.

units.la: Veteres manus quoque dexterae apprehensione, atque osculatione, seinuicem salutabant & pacta inibant, ut ex Homero probat Stuckius sic Iacobus Rahelem osculo salutabat, & Laban Iacobum. Sic Paulus osculo charitatis alios salutare iubet, 1.Cor.c.ult. sic Christus salutantes se osculo excepit. vid.Polyd.Virgil.lib.4. De inuent.c.13. & Plutar. in Quaestion.Roman.quaest.6. De dexterae apprehensione praeterea vid.Sabellic.lib.5. Ennead. Plautum in Panulo, & in Asinariam, ubi Leonida ad Philenium hisce ceremoniis utitur, & in Amphit. & Virgil.lib.7. Pars mihi pacis erit, dextram tetigisse Tyran-ni. Valer. Maxim. lib.5. c.5. Bonfin.libr.7. decad.1.
units.tr: The ancients also greeted one another by taking hold of the right hand and kissing it, and made agreements in this way. As Stuckius proves from Homer. So Jacob kissed Rachel and Laban kissed Jacob. So Paul bids others to greet one another with a holy kiss, 1 Cor. last chapter; so Christ received those greeting him with a kiss. See Polydore Vergil, book 4, On Inventions, chapter 13, and Plutarch, Roman Questions, question 6. On the taking of the right hand, moreover, see Sabellicus, Enneads, book 5; Plautus in the Pseudolus and in the Asinaria, where Leonida uses these ceremonies toward Philaenium; in the Amphitryon; and Virgil, book 7: "It will be a part of peace for me to have touched the hand of the tyrant." Valerius Maximus, book 5, chapter 5; Bonfinius, book 7, Decade 1.

units.la: Hodie quoque dexterarum coniunctione salutare solemus. Pithæus lib.1. Aduersar. cap.7. vbi Iob c.30.13. Eccl.c.29. explicatur, & Pierus in suis Hieroglyphicis lib.3f.
units.tr: Today too we are accustomed to greet by joining right hands. Pithaeus, book 1, Adversaria, chapter 7, where Job 30:13 and Ecclesiasticus 29 are explained, and Pierius in his Hieroglyphics, book 3.

units.la: Ad genua vel pedes procidere, siue procumbere, ea attingere, exosculari denique in salutationibus & supplicationib.veteres consueuerūt, vti ex Homero, Virgil.lib.3.& 10. Ouid.lib.9. Metamorph.& 13. Plauto in Rudente, Liuio lib.45. Suetonius in Tybe.& Claudio,2. Reg.c.4. Genes.c.48.12. Stuck. d.loco. probat.
units.tr: The kissing of feet was also practised in the greetings and supplications of the ancients. Luke 7, and a mutual kiss: Exod. 18; Gen. 33; 39; Tobit 7; Gen. 45; Luke 15:1; 1 Kings 19, 20; Gen. 48:10; Ruth 1; Gen. 31; 2 Sam. 19; Tobit 10. From these passages it is clear that among the Jews greetings by kiss were customary in the meeting and parting of friends.

units.la: Pedum exosculatio vsitata quoque fuit in salutationibus & supplicationibus veterum. Luc. c.7.& osculum mutuum. Exod. c.18. Genes.c.33. c.39. Tob.c.7. Genes.c.45. Luc.c.15.1. Reg cap.19.20. Genes.c.48.10. Ruth.c.1. Genes.c.31. 2 Sam. cap.19. Tob.c.10. ex quibus constat, ludæis vsitatas fuisse salutationes per osculum in congressu & digressu amicorum.
units.tr: Sometimes a kiss was also a symbol of reconciliation, as in 2 Sam. 14; Luke 15, or of approved virtue in another, 3 Ezra 4; Prov. 24; Matt. 26; 2 Sam. 20; 15. See Caelius Rhodiginus, book 15, chapter 9, and book 4, chapter 3. Plutarch, Problems, problem 6. Pierius, Hieroglyphics.

units.la: Erat etiam quandoque osculum reconciliationis symbolum, vti 2.Sam.c.14. Luc.c.15. vel virtutis approbatæ in alio, 3. Efd.c.4. Prou.c.24. Matt.c.26.2.Sam.c.20.c.15. vide Cæl. Rhodigin.libr. 15.c.9.& lib.4.c.3. Plutar.in Probl.problem.6. Pier. in Hieroglyph.
units.tr: Sometimes a kiss was also a symbol of reconciliation, as in 2 Sam. 14; Luke 15, or of approved virtue in another, 3 Esdras 4; Prov. 24; Matt. 26; 2 Sam. 20; 15. See Caelius Rhodiginus, book 15, chapter 9, and book 4, chapter 3; Plutarch, Problems, problem 6; Pierius, Hieroglyphics.

units.la: Ab osculo differt basium, quod est pudicorum affectuum; & suauium, quod libidinum, vel amoris; cum osculum officiorum sit habitus & gestus.
units.tr: A basium differs from a kiss in that the basium belongs to chaste affections, while a suavium belongs to lust or love; whereas the kiss is a habit and gesture of duty.

units.la: Pompon. Latus in compend. Rom. hist. dicit Imperatores suas manus osculandas suis nobilibus libus præbuisse, quos postea suis manibus subleuabant ad oris osculum. Vulgus genua osculabatur. Diocletianus sanxit, ut omnes sine generis discrimine, prostrati, pedes ipsius exoscularentur. Sueton. in Caio Caligula, qui manum, vel pedem ad osculandum præbebat etiam senatoribus. Seneca idem testatur de Iulio Cæsare. vid. Polyd. Virgil. lib. 4. cap. 13. & Alex. ab Alexand. lib. 2. c. 19. Blond. decad. 2. lib. 2. & lib. 1. decad. 1. Crantz. in Metropol. lib. 2. c. 1. & Platin. in vitis Pontif.
units.tr: Pomponius Laetus, in his Compendium of Roman History, says that emperors offered their hands to be kissed by their nobles, whom they afterwards raised with their own hands to the lips for a kiss. The common people kissed the knees. Diocletian decreed that all, without distinction of rank, should prostrate themselves and kiss his feet. Suetonius in the life of Caius Caligula, who offered his hand or foot to be kissed even to senators. Seneca attests the same of Julius Caesar. See Polydore Vergil, book 4, chapter 13; Alexander ab Alexandro, book 2, chapter 19; Blondus, Decade 2, book 2, and Decade 1, book 1; Crantz, Metropolis, book 2, chapter 1; and Platina, Lives of the Popes.

units.la: Ratio quare veteres in salutationibus & supplicationibus caput, dexteram, genua eorum quos salutabant, attingebant, & osculabantur, erat quod hisce partibus corporis inest præstantior facultas, quam in cæteris, & quia auguria, finis supplicandi, hisce inerat. Vide Plin. lib. 11. cap. 45. Isidor. lib. 11. origin. Stuck. d. loc.
units.tr: An embrace of the whole body in greetings was customary among many. Gen. 48:10. In our regions we see it customary, to show and display mutual goodwill and respect, to uncover the head, bow the body, fall upon the breast, and extend the right hand, by which we testify that we are ready to give ourselves up to our friends.

units.la: Complexus totius corporis in salutationibus apud multos visitatus fuit. Genes. cap. 48. 10. In nostris regionibus ad mutuam benevolentiam obseruantiamque præstandam & demonstrandâ videmus visitatum esse caput aperire, corpus inclinare, procidere in pectus, dexteram porrigere, quibus testamur nos paratos esse nos ipsos amicis tradere.
units.tr: An embrace of the whole body in greetings was customary among many. Gen. 48:10. In our regions we see it customary, to show and render mutual goodwill and respect, to uncover the head, bow the body, fall on the breast, and extend the right hand, by which we testify that we are ready to give ourselves to our friends.

units.la: Capitis nudatio ad honorem præstandum & testandum facere videtur, & simul eodem gestu aures quoq; deregimus, quo ipso indicamus, nos ad audiendum, iussu capessendum & obediendum cum quodam prolubio promptos esse. vid. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 2. c. 19. Gen. dier. Stuck. lib. 2. c. 32. & c. 31. commuial. antiquit.
units.tr: Uncovering the head seems to be done to render and bear witness to honour, and at the same time by the same gesture we also turn the ears, by which very act we show that we are ready, with a certain willingness, to listen, to take up commands and to obey. See Alexander ab Alexandro, book 2, chapter 19; Gen. dier.; Stuckius, book 2, chapter 32, and chapter 31, Commentaries on Antiquity.

units.la: Apud Iudæos habitus lugentium, erat caput caluum,rasum, & barba præcisa, & saccus in lu-bis. Ierem.c.48.37. Nam omni capiti caluitium erit & omnis barba exsecta,in omnibus manibus casura & super lumbos cilicium. Eiusdem argumenti erat habitus caput terra inspergentis, operientis, vestes lacerantis,&similes.de quibus Iob c.2.12. Postea vociferantes fleuerunt & lacerantes quisque pallium suum,insperserunt puluerem capitibus suis, vociferantes in cælum vsque. 1.Sam.c.4.12. Tum currens quidam Biniaminita ex ipsa acie venit Schiluntem eodem die,vestibus suis laceris, & terra capiti suo inspersa. 2.Sam,c.1.2. Quidam venit castris Saulis vestibus suis laceris & terra impositá capiti suo, c.15.32. Ecce Chusai Arcaus obuiam veniret ei lacerata tunica sua & terra impositá capiti suo. Nehem.c.9.1. Congregatis Israelitis in ieiunio & cilicijs, & terra ipsis impositá. Ester cap.4.2. Lacerans Mordecai vestimenta sua, induit cilicium cum cinere, & seqq. Ierem.cap.2. Atrati erunt humi iacentes, 3.Erubescent & pudore suffusi operient caput suum, & verf. 4.2. Sam,c.15.30. Dauid opertus capite suo & pergens discalceatus,& seqq. 1.Chron.c.21.16. Ideoq; procidit Dauid & seniores tecti cilicijs in faciem. Ezech.c.42. 17. Clamare desiste,mortuorum multum ne facito,tiaram tuam alligatibi & calceos tuos apponito pedibus tuis,neq; obuelato myflacem,&c.& verf.2.2.Levit.c.13.45.c.19.27.28.c.21.5.Mich.c.3.7. Esai. cap.16.2. Moab ejulabit:in omnibus capitibus eius caluitium, & omnis barba excisa. 3.In compitis eius accingentur cilicio,&c. Iof.c.7.6. Iehosua autem lacerans vestimenta sua,procidit super faciem suam in terram ante arcam Iehova vsq; ad vesperam,ipse & seniores Israelis: lu imposuerunt q3 pulverem quisq3 capiti suo, 1. Chron. c.21.16. Apocalyps. c.18.19. Act. c.22.23. Ier. c.41.5. Ut venirent homines Schecemo, Schilunti, & Schoñ rone, octoginta viri rasi barba & laceri vestibus, ac incidentes sese, &c. & c.48.37. Nam omni capiti calui-tium erit & omnis barba exsecta, in omnibus manib. cæsura, & super lumbos cilicium, 2. Macchab. c.3.19. Etsuccincta sub mammas mulieres ciliciis vias implebant, &c. Luc. c.23.48. Et omnis turba quæsimul ad hoc spectaculum accesserat, spectans quæ factae-rant, verberans pectora sua, reuertebatur. & c.18.13. Publicanus autem procul stans, nolebat veloculos in-calum attollere, sed percutiebat pectus suum dicens, Deus placator mihi peccatori, & Actor. cap.14.14. Quod cum audissent Apostoli Barnabas & Paulus disruptis palliis suis, insiluerunt in turbam, & c.22.23. Clamantibus autem iis & proiicientibus pallia, & pulverem iactantibus in aera. Ioel c.2.12. Quapropter etiam nunc dictum Jehova, convertimini ad me ex toto animo vestro & ieiunio & fletu & planctu, 13. Lacerate igitur corda vestra, ac non vestes vestras. Ierem. c.30.6. Interrogate iam & videte, an pariat mas. Cur video vnumquemq3 virum stare manibus suis appositis ad lumbos suos, velut puerperam & conuersos esse omnes vultus in speciem morbi regi? 2. Sam. c.19.25. Mephiboseт quoq3 nepos Saulis descenderat obuiam regi, non curauerat autem pedes suos, neq3 curauerat mystacem suum, & vestes suas non lauerat, ex quo die abierat rex. Iesa. c.20.2. Abi & solue illud cilicium à lumbis tuis & calceamentum tuum extra-he de pede tuo. Qui fecit ita, incedens nudus & discal-ceatus, & vers. seq. 1. Chron. c.21.16. Ideoq3 procidit Dauid & seniores tecti ciliciis in faciem suam, &c.
units.tr: Among the Jews the habit of mourners was a bald head, a shaved beard and sackcloth on the loins. Jer. 48:37: For every head shall be bald and every beard cut off; upon all hands shall be cuts, and sackcloth upon the loins. Of the same kind was the habit of one who sprinkles or covers his head with earth, tears his garments, and the like, of which Job 2:12: Then they lifted up their voices and wept, and each tore his mantle and sprinkled dust on their heads, crying out toward heaven. 1 Sam. 4:12: Then a certain Benjamite ran out of the battle line that same day to Shiloh, with his clothes torn and earth on his head. 2 Sam. 1:2: A certain man came from Saul's camp with his clothes torn and earth on his head; 15:32: Behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his tunic torn and earth on his head. Neh. 9:1: The Israelites were assembled in fasting, in sackcloth, and with earth upon them. Esther 4:2: Mordecai tore his garments, put on sackcloth with ashes, and so on. Jer. 2: They shall be clothed with mourning, lying on the ground; 3: they shall be ashamed and confounded and cover their heads; and verse 4. 2 Sam. 15:30: David went up with his head covered and his feet bare, and so on. 1 Chron. 21:16: Therefore David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces. Ezek. 24:17: Cease to cry out, make no great mourning for the dead; bind your turban on you and put your shoes on your feet, do not cover your mouth, etc.; and verse 22. Lev. 13:45; 19:27–28; 21:5. Mic. 3:7. Isa. 15:2: Moab shall wail: on all its heads there shall be baldness, and every beard cut off. 3: In its streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth, etc. Josh. 7:6: Joshua tore his garments and fell on his face to the earth before the ark of the LORD until evening, he and the elders of Israel, and they put dust on their heads. 1 Chron. 21:16; Rev. 18:19; Acts 22:23; Jer. 41:5: That men came from Shechem, from Shiloh and from Samaria, eighty men with shaven beards and torn garments, having cut themselves, etc.; and 48:37: For every head shall be bald and every beard cut off, upon all hands shall be cuts, and sackcloth upon the loins. 2 Macc. 3:19: The women, girded with sackcloth beneath their breasts, filled the streets, etc. Luke 23:48: And all the crowd that had come together to this spectacle, seeing what had happened, returned beating their breasts. And 18:13: But the tax collector, standing afar off, would not lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. Acts 14:14: When the apostles Barnabas and Paulus heard this, they tore their garments and leapt into the crowd. And 22:23: As they cried out and cast off their garments and threw dust into the air. Joel 2:12: Therefore now also, says the LORD, turn to me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning. 13: Rend your hearts and not your garments. Jer. 30:6: Ask now and see whether a man bears a child. Why do I see every man with his hands on his loins, like a woman in labour, and all faces turned pale? 2 Sam. 19:25: Mephibosheth also, grandson of Saul, went down to meet the king; he had neither cared for his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his garments, from the day the king departed. Isa. 20:2: Go and loose the sackcloth from your loins and take off your shoe from your foot. He did so, walking naked and barefoot; and the following verse. 1 Chron. 21:16: Therefore David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces, etc.

units.la: Esa.c.51.2 Excute te ipsam è pulvere, surge, sede,c.3.
units.tr: Isa. c.51.2 Shake yourself from the dust, arise, sit down, c.3.27.25.

units.la: 27.25. Loco operis impexi calvitium, & loco segmen-tatæ cycladis, cinctus cilicio, vsfio loco pulchritudinis,
units.tr: Instead of well-set hair, baldness; instead of a finely pleated robe, a girdle of sackcloth; branding instead of beauty.

units.la: 1.Samuel.c.18.20.21. & seqq. 2.Sam. c.12 16.17.18. 19.20.21.Ezech.c.26.16. Ionæ c.3.6.7. Debabitu fe-mina lugentis vid.Jer.c.2.37.1.Reg.c.18 42. & va-rius variarum gentium gestibus lugendi, vid.apud Alex.ab Alex.lib.3. Genial.dier.c.7. De vestium lace-ratione vide Genes.c.37.29.34.c.44.13. Num.c.14. 6.Iudic.c.11.35.1.Sam. c.4.11.12.2.Sam.c.13.19.31. c.15.32.1.Reg.c.21.27.c.5.7.c.6.30.c.11.14.c.18.37. c.22.11.1.Esd.c.9.3.Iob c.1.20.c.2.12.Matth.c.26.65. Marc.c.14.63.
units.tr: 1 Sam. c.18.20.21 and following; 2 Sam. c.12.16.17.18.19.20.21; Ezek. c.26.16; Jonah c.3.6.7. On the habit of a mourning woman, see Jer. c.2.37; 1 Kings c.18.42. On the varied gestures of mourning among different peoples, see Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial. dier. lib.3 c.7. On the tearing of garments see Gen. c.37.29.34; c.44.13; Num. c.14.6; Judg. c.11.35; 1 Sam. c.4.11.12; 2 Sam. c.13.19.31; c.15.32; 1 Kings c.21.27; c.5.7; c.6.30; c.11.14; c.18.37; c.22.11; 1 Esd. c.9.3; Job c.1.20; c.2.12; Matt. c.26.65; Mark c.14.63.

units.la: Erat quoq; peculiaris vestitus pœnitentium, deprecantium & lugetium apud Iudæos.1.Sam. c.14.3. Dixitq; ei, age quaso, lugentem, & induete iam vestibus lugubribus, neq; vngitor oleo, sed esto sicut mulier iam dies multos lugens de mortuo, & c.12. 20.Ezech.c.7.17.18.Et accingent cilicia, Jon.d.c.3.6. 7.Esa.c.3.25.Esth.c.4.2. Psal.30.12. Nehem.c.9.1.1. Chron.c.21.16.Matt.11.21. Si Tyri & Sidoni edita fuissent virtutes, &c.2.Sam.c.3.31. Postea edixit David Ioabo & toti populo, Lacerate vestimenta vestra & accingite vos cilicius, & plangite ante Abnerum, 2.Chron.c.13.13.1.Reg.c.21.27.28.
units.tr: There was also a peculiar dress of penitents, suppliants and mourners among the Jews. 1 Sam. c.14.3. "And he said to her, Come, I pray you, feign mourning, and put on mourning garments now, and do not anoint yourself with oil, but be like a woman who has been mourning for the dead for many days" (2 Sam. c.14.2). Also c.12.20; Ezek. c.7.17.18; "And they shall gird themselves with sackcloth" (Jonah c.3.6.7; Isa. c.3.25; Esth. c.4.2; Ps. 30.12; Neh. c.9.1; 1 Chron. c.21.16). Matt. c.11.21: "If the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon..." 2 Sam. c.3.31: "Afterwards David commanded Joab and all the people: Rend your garments, gird yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner" (2 Chron. c.13.13; 1 Kings c.21.27.28).

units.la: Peculiaris quoq; vestitus sacerdotum erat, de quo Exod.c.28.29.c.39.c.40.Zachar.c.3.3.4. & seqq.Levit.c.8. Num.c.15.38. Pharisæorum item & Scribarum,de quo Marc.c.12.38.Luc.c.20.45. & Prophetarū,1.Reg.c.19.19.Matt.c.3.4.5.Marc. c.1.6.Et Regum,1.Macc.c.10.21.Esth.c.8.3.1.Reg. c.10.Dan.c.5.Zach.c.6. Esa.c.28.1.2.3.4.5. & Diuitum,Luc.c.16.19.Iac.c.2.Primogenitorū, Gen. c.27.
units.tr: A peculiar dress was also that of the priests, concerning which see Exod. c.28.29; c.39; c.40; Zech. c.3.3.4 and following; Lev. c.8; Num. c.15.38. Likewise that of the Pharisees and scribes, see Mark c.12.38; Luke c.20.45; and of the prophets, 1 Kings c.19.19; Matt. c.3.4.5; Mark c.1.6. And of kings, 1 Macc. c.10.21; Esth. c.8.3; 1 Kings c.10; Dan. c.5; Zech. c.6; Isa. c.28.1.2.3.4.5. And of the rich, Luke c.16.19; James c.2. Of the firstborn, Gen. c.27.

units.la: Lasciuientium, Esa.c.3.17. & seqq. vbi Iun.viduarum, Gen. c.38.14. nuptialium, Matt.c.22. De Romanorum toga praetexta, candida, pura, sordida, picta, palmata, purpurea; item trabea, stola, pallio, tunica, penula, & aliis vestium generibus, vid. Joh. Rosin. lib.5. c.31. & seqq. antiquit. Rom. Lazarum Bayfium de re vestiaria. Sigon. lib.3. de Iudic. Isidor lib.19. Etymol. c.22. & seqq. Pet. Greg. lib.9 Syntag. c.19. & lib.4. c.11. De Repub. Deregum vestitu Est. c.5. c.8. Greg. de Rep. c.vlt. lib.6. Bulla Caroli 4. Imp.
units.tr: Of wanton women, Isa. c.3.17 and following, where Junius; of widows, Gen. c.38.14; of brides, Matt. c.22. On the Roman toga praetexta, candida, pura, sordida, picta, palmata and purpurea; likewise the trabea, stola, pallium, tunica, paenula and other kinds of clothing, see Joh. Rosinus lib.5 c.31 and following, Antiquitates Romanae; Lazarus Bayfius, De re vestiaria; Sigonius lib.3 De iudiciis; Isidore lib.19 Etymologiae c.22 and following; Petrus Gregorius lib.9 Syntagma c.19, and lib.4 c.11, De republica. On the clothing of kings, Esth. c.5, c.8; Greg., De republica c.vlt. lib.6; Bull of Emperor Charles IV.

units.la: Pileus, libertatis habitus erat. Vid. Lipf. lib.3. Antiq. lection. Alexan. ab Alex. Genial. dier. lib.5. cap.21. De cingulorum atque zonarum vario multiplicique vsu, vid. Stuckium libr.2. cap.29. antiquit. convivial. De veteri Germanorum habitu & gestu & vestitu vid. Tacit. De morib. German. & Senec. De consol. ad Albin. & lib.5. Epist. 56. & lib.2. De ira.
units.tr: The pileus was a habit of liberty. See Lipsius lib.3 Antiquae lectiones; Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial. dier. lib.5 cap.21. On the varied and manifold use of belts and girdles, see Stuckius lib.2 cap.29, Antiquitates convivales. On the old habit, gesture and dress of the Germans, see Tacitus, De moribus Germanorum; Seneca, Consolatio ad Albinam, and lib.5 Epist. 56, and lib.2 De ira.

units.la: Operto capite esse, vel loqui, apud Iudaeos erat signum & habitus subiectionis. 1. Corinth. c.11.4. Apud Germanos capitis nudatio habitus honorantis alium, vid. Alex. ab Alex. Genial. dier. lib.2. c.19. & Joh. Wilhel. Stuckius lib.2. cap.32. convivial. antiquit. vid. infra, vbi de Honore & reverentia tractato.
units.tr: To have the head covered, or to speak with it covered, was among the Jews a sign and habit of subjection. 1 Cor. c.11.4. Among the Germans, baring the head was a habit of honouring another; see Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial. dier. lib.2 c.19, and Joh. Wilhelm Stuckius lib.2 cap.32, Antiquitates convivales. See below, where honour and reverence are treated.

units.la: Manus super caput habens faemina, prodit animi dolorem & turbationem, Jerem. c.2.37. 1. Reg. c.18.42.
units.tr: A woman with her hands on her head shows grief and disturbance of mind. Jer. c.2.37; 1 Kings c.18.42.

units.la: Nazaraeatus voto obstricti apud Iudaeos comam in capite alebant. Num. c.6. s. Iudic. c.13.7. 14. c.16.17. & Act. c.24. s. c.18. 8. c.21.24.
units.tr: Those bound by a Nazirite vow among the Jews let the hair grow on their heads. Num. c.6; Judg. c.13.7.14; c.16.17; Acts c.24; c.18.8; c.21.24.

units.la: Osculum Iudaeis erat charitatis & mutuae salutationis signum, 1. Thess. c. 5. 26. Luc. 7. 45. 2. Sam. c. 20. 8. 1. Cor. c. 16. Actor. c. 16. 16. 1. Pet. c. 5. 14. & passim alibi.
units.tr: A kiss was among the Jews a sign of love and mutual greeting. 1 Thess. c.5.26; Luke 7.45; 2 Sam. c.20.8; 1 Cor. c.16; Acts c.16.16; 1 Pet. c.5.14, and passim elsewhere.

units.la: Pectoris percussio erat illis gestus miseriam suam profitentis & dolentis, Luc. cap. 23. 48. cap. 18. 13.
units.tr: Striking the breast was for them a gesture of one professing and lamenting his misery. Luke c.23.48; c.18.13.

units.la: Iurantes suis dominis domestici, manum sub femore ponebant. Genes. c. 24. 2. 9. c. 47. 29.
units.tr: Servants swearing to their masters put their hand under the thigh. Gen. c.24.2.9; c.47.29.

units.la: Manus elevatae, erant habitus orantis. Psal. 28. 2. Psal. 77. 2. 3. & 88. 10. Nehem. c. 8. 6. sicuti quoq; manus orantis expansae. Exod. c. 17. 11. 1. Reg. c. 8. 21. 2. Chron. c. 6. 13. 1. Esd. c. 8. 9.
units.tr: Raised hands were the habit of one praying. Ps. 28.2; Ps. 77.2.3; and 88.10; Neh. c.8.6; likewise outstretched hands were the habit of one praying. Exod. c.17.11; 1 Kings c.8.21; 2 Chron. c.6.13; 1 Esd. c.8.9.

units.la: Manus posita super lumbos, arguebat dolorem impotentem. Ierem. cap. 2. 37. 1. Reg. cap. 18. 42.
units.tr: A hand placed on the loins signified helpless grief. Jer. c.2.37; 1 Kings c.18.42.

units.la: Impositio manus, habitus erat significans potestatis & authoritatis communicationem, & officii & muneris concessionem & traditionem, Matth. 8. 3. 1. Timoth. c. 5. 22. c. 4. 14. 2. Timoth. c. 1. 6. Actor. c. 6. 6. Levit. c. 1. 4. Actor. c. 8. 16. Deut. cap. 34. 6 9. & quandoque signum benedictionis erat. Genes. c. 48. 14. Matth. 19. 15. Marc. c. 10. 16. c. 6. 5. 6. c. 8. 23. Luc. c. 4. 40. Act. c. 8. 17. c. 13. 3. c. 19. 5. c. 28. 8. c 9. 12. 17.
units.tr: The laying on of hands was a habit signifying the communication of power and authority, and the granting and handing over of an office and duty, Matt. c.8.3; 1 Tim. c.5.22; c.4.14; 2 Tim. c.1.6; Acts c.6.6; Lev. c.1.4; Acts c.8.16; Deut. c.34.6.9; and sometimes it was a sign of blessing. Gen. c.48.14; Matt. c.19.15; Mark c.10.16; c.6.5.6; c.8.23; Luke c.4.40; Acts c.8.17; c.13.3; c.19.5; c.28.8; c.9.12.17.

units.la: Manus implere, Iudaeis erat initiari & inaugurari in munere impositio. 1. Chron. c. 29. 5. Esa. cap. 23. 2.
units.tr: Filling the hands: among the Jews, to be initiated and inaugurated into an office by the laying on of hands. 1 Chron. c.29.5; Isa. c.23.2.

units.la: Lauare manus, innocentiam indicabat. Psal. 73. 13. Matth. cap. 27. 24. Psalm. 26. Amos cap. 9. 31.
units.tr: Washing the hands indicated innocence. Ps. 73.13; Matt. c.27.24; Ps. 26; Amos c.9.31.

units.la: Alia lotio manuum superstitiosa Iudaeorum, describitur Matth. c. 15. 2. ubi Martin. Bucer. in Enarrat. Luc. cap. 11. 38. Deut. cap. 21. 6. 7. vide Stuck. Stuck lib. 2. c. 33. Conuiuial. antiquit. Macrob. libr. 3. Saturn. c. 1.
units.tr: Another superstitious washing of hands among the Jews is described in Matt. c.15.2, where Martin Bucer, in his Enarrationes on Luke c.11.38; Deut. c.21.6.7; see Stuckius lib.2 c.33, Convivia, Antiquitates; Macrobius lib.3 Saturnalia c.1.

units.la: De pedum lotione Iudaeorum, vid. Genes. c. 18. 4. c. 19. 2. Ioh. c. 13. 4. 14. 1. Timoth. c. 5. 10. 2. Sam. c. 19. 25. Pedes illoti habitus squalore & maerore hominum affectorum erant. 2. Sam. c. 19. 25.
units.tr: On the washing of feet among the Jews, see Gen. c.18.4; c.19.2; John c.13.4; 14.1; 1 Tim. c.5.10; 2 Sam. c.19.25. Unwashed feet were marks of the squalor and grief of those afflicted. 2 Sam. c.19.25.

units.la: Pede percutere, est irridere. Ezech. cap. 25. 6. Prou. c. 6. 12.
units.tr: To strike with the foot is to mock. Ezek. c.25.6; Prov. c.6.12.

units.la: Puluerem pedibus excutere, erat habitus communionem & conuersationem cum alio detrectantis. Luc. c. 10. 11. Act. c. 13. 51.
units.tr: Shaking dust from the feet was a habit of one who refused fellowship and association with another. Luke c.10.11; Acts c.13.51.

units.la: Discalceatum incedere, erat lugentium. Esa. c. 20. 2. 3. 2. Samc. c. 19. 25. Ierem. c. 13. 23.
units.tr: Walking barefoot was the habit of mourners. Isa. c.20.2.3; 2 Sam. c.19.25; Jer. c.13.23.

units.la: Procubitus erat illis habitus deprecantis. 1. Esd. c. 10. 1. 1. Mach. c. 4. 39. 2. Mach. c. 3. 15. Act. c. 19. Matth. c. 26. 39. Erat quoq; olim situs & habitus conuiuarum, quo tempore lectis ad mensam stratis recubebant. 1. Sam. c. 28. 22. 23. 24. 25. Luc. c. 22. 27. Nam uter maior est, qui discumbit, an qui ministrat? c. 14. 6. 7. 8. c. 9. 14. 15. Matth. c. 14. 6. & seqq. cap. 26. c. 8. Luc. c. 7. 37. 38. vid. Rosin. in antiquit. Roman. & Stuck. libr. 2. conuiuial. antiquit. cap. 34.
units.tr: Prostration was for them a habit of one who entreats. 1 Esd. c.10.1; 1 Macc. c.4.39; 2 Macc. c.3.15; Acts c.19; Matt. c.26.39. There was also formerly the posture and habit of diners, who reclined on couches laid out at the table. 1 Sam. c.28.22.23.24.25; Luke c.22.27: "For which is greater, he who reclines or he who serves?"; c.14.6.7.8; c.9.14.15; Matt. c.14.6 and following; c.26; c.8; Luke c.7.37.38; see Rosinus in Antiquitates Romanae, and Stuckius lib.2 Convivia, Antiquitates, cap.34.

units.la: Genibus flexis veteres ut plurimum orabat. 2. c. Chron. c. 6. 13. c. 7. 3. Dan. c. 6. 9.
units.tr: The ancients for the most part prayed with bent knees. 2 Chron. c.6.13; c.7.3; Dan. c.6.9.

units.la: Stare in templis, habitus erat orantis 2. Chronic. cap. 7. 9. cap. 6. 2. Esa. cap. 49. 7. Luc. cap. 18. 13. Matth. cap. 26. 62. Esther cap. 8. 4. Habacuc. cap. 2. 1. Act. c. 1. 2.
units.tr: Standing in the temples was the habit of one praying. 2 Chron. c.7.9; c.6.2; Isa. c.49.7; Luke c.18.13; Matt. c.26.62; Esth. c.8.4; Hab. c.2.1; Acts c.1.2.

units.la: Ambulare, Hebraeis erat habitus hominis suum munus expedientis, Zach. c. 3. 7. 2. Sam. cap. 4. 35. Marc. c. 10. 2. Matth. c. 23. 8. Psalm. 70. 21. Nah. c. 3. 7. Iob c. 2. 11.
units.tr: Walking was for the Hebrews the habit of a man carrying out his office. Zech. c.3.7; 2 Sam. c.4.35; Mark c.10.2; Matt. c.23.8; Ps. 70.21; Nah. c.3.7; Job c.2.11.

units.la: Vnctio Iudæis erat habitus, officii grauis im-positi: nimirum regii, sacerdotalis, vel prophe-tici, Levit.c.43. Num.c.3.3.1. Sam.c.19. 1.cap.16.13. Exod.c.29.7.1. Reg.c.19.16. Exod.c.30.23. & seqq. Luc.c.7.38.39.44.45.46. Esa.c.61.1. Psalm.89.21. Corpora etiam mortuorum vngebantur, Genes. c.50.2. & ægrotorum. Marc.c.6.13. Iacob.c.5.14. & regum deliciis vnctio adscribitur. 2. Reg.c.20.1. Chron.c.9.2.1. Chron.c.16. Esr.c.14. Esa.c.57. Dan. c.10.2. Sam.12.20.21.
units.tr: Anointing among the Jews was the habit of one who had taken up a weighty office: namely the royal, priestly or prophetic. Lev. c.4.3; Num. c.3.3; 1 Sam. c.19.1; c.16.13; Exod. c.29.7; 1 Kings c.19.16; Exod. c.30.23 and following; Luke c.7.38.39.44.45.46; Isa. c.61.1; Ps. 89.21. The bodies of the dead were also anointed, Gen. c.50.2, and of the sick, Mark c.6.13; James c.5.14. And anointing is ascribed to royal luxury. 2 Kings c.20.1; 2 Chron. c.9.2; 1 Chron. c.16; Ezra c.14; Isa. c.57; Dan. c.10.2; 2 Sam. c.12.20.21.

units.la: Huc refero omnes actiones, functiones & leges ceremoniales Iudaicas, quarum exercitium & visus ex Dei ordinatione suas significationes & typos habebat; vti erat velamen Moßis. Exod. c.34.34. 2.Cor. c.3.13.14. & alia Genes.c.24.65.1. Cor.c.11.7. Genes.c.20.16. Ruth.c 3.9. Esa. c.4. Circumcisio, comestio agni paschalis, festum pentecostes, seu tabernaculorum, festum Iubilæi, & id genus plures, de quibus in Exod. Levit. & Num. & Deut.
units.tr: I refer here to all the Jewish ceremonial actions, functions and laws, whose performance and appearance, by God's ordinance, carried their meanings and types, such as the veil of Moses. Exod. c.34.34. 2.Cor. c.3.13.14. and others: Genes.c.24.65.1. Cor.c.11.7. Genes.c.20.16. Ruth c 3.9. Esa. c.4. Circumcision, the eating of the paschal lamb, the feast of Pentecost or of Tabernacles, the feast of Jubilee, and many others of this kind, which are described in Exod., Levit., Num. and Deut.

units.la: Qui præterea sint alii habitus & gestus cuiusq; nationis, regionis & populi, discendum est ex historiis & experientia.
units.tr: What other customs of dress and gesture belong to each nation, region and people must be learned from histories and experience.

units.la: Sequitur de habitu arbitrario, qui ex voluntate & pro arbitrio vtentis eodem instituitur. Hic, si est rationabilis, vel hominum opinione probabilis, qui ex ratione quadam probabili est institutus, gratiam habet; secus vero sapit stultitiam & temeritatem.
units.tr: Next comes arbitrary dress, which is adopted by the will and at the discretion of the one who uses it. If it is reasonable, or approved by the opinion of men, having been instituted on some probable ground, it finds favour; otherwise it smacks of folly and rashness.

units.la: Huc refero habitus portentosos, qui rarâ & illustri actione sua singularem aliquam & memorabilem significationem etiam præter naturam suam denotant & exprimunt Dei iussu.
units.tr: I refer here to portentous dress and gestures, which by some rare and striking action, at God's command, denote and express a singular and memorable meaning even beyond their natural function.

units.la: Huius generis sunt actiones quædam prophetarum & legatorum Dei: de quibus videre licet Exod.c.9.8.9.10.& seqq. De sparsa fauilla fornacis versus cælum, unde vlcera eruperunt, &c. Iosuæ c.8.18. c.6.6.7. & seqq. Deque Elisæo, 2.Reg.c.3.15.c.4.34. & seqq. & cap.13 15.16.17.18. & de quo legitur 1.Reg.c.18.42. Iohan. cap.9.6.7. 1.Sam.c.19.23.24. & passim alibi. Exod.c.3. Act.c. 7.Iosc.7.
units.tr: Of this kind are certain actions of the prophets and envoys of God: see Exod.c.9.8.9.10.& seqq. the ashes of the furnace scattered toward heaven, whence ulcers broke out, etc. Iosuæ c.8.18. c.6.6.7. & seqq. and concerning Elisha, 2.Reg.c.3.15.c.4.34. & seqq. & cap.13 15.16.17.18. and what is read in 1.Reg.c.18.42. Iohan. cap.9.6.7. 1.Sam.c.19.23.24. & passim alibi. Exod.c.3. Act.c. 7.Iosc.7.

units.la: IOHANNIS ALTHVSII I. C. clarissimi, CIVILIS CONVERSATIONIS, seu Ethicæ Liber II. qui est De Ethica propria. Caput I.
units.tr: JOHANNES ALTHUSIUS, J.U.D., most distinguished, CIVIL CONVERSATION, or Ethics, Book II, which concerns Particular Ethics. Chapter I.

units.la: De dignioribus, honoratioribus & vilibus, popularibus, vulgaribus personis, earumq; affectione mutua in conuersatione ciuili.
units.tr: Of more worthy, more honourable, lowly, common and ordinary persons, and of their mutual regard in civil conversation.

units.la: Tv_ve hactenus de illa, quæ ad Ethicam & conuersationem communē, hoc est, ad mores cuiusq; conditionis & status homines pertinent, perstrinximus. Sequitur de Ethica propria.
units.tr: So far we have outlined that part of ethics and general conversation which concerns the manners of people of every rank and condition. What follows concerns particular ethics.

units.la: Propria Ethica est, quæ mores & modum conuersandi cum certis hominum generibus, certis quibusdam personis praescribit.
units.tr: Particular ethics is that which prescribes manners and the manner of conversing with certain kinds of men and with certain particular persons.

units.la: Species huius Ethicae sunt duae. Vna est conuersatio statui cuiusque proprio conueniens. Altera est conuersatio actui conuiuiali conueniens.
units.tr: There are two species of this ethics. One is conversation suited to each person's own station. The other is conversation suited to the act of feasting together.

units.la: Priorilla, statum & conditionem cuiusque respiciens, est rursum duplex; Imparium nimirum, vel parium.
units.tr: The former, which regards each person's status and condition, is again twofold: it concerns either unequals or equals.

units.la: Imparium personarum Ethica est, quae rationem conuersandi cum honoratioribus, dignioribus; aut cum se inferioribus, vulgaribusve personis docet.
units.tr: The ethics of unequal persons teaches the manner of conversing with those who are more honourable and more worthy, or with those who are inferior, or with common people.

units.la: Huius requisita sunt duo. Primum est, de dignioribus vilibusque personis, atque earum affectione mutua inter se inuicem in ciuili conuersatione. Alterum est de officio alterius erga alterum in sermone & habitu.
units.tr: It has two requirements. The first concerns the more worthy and the lowly persons, and their mutual regard for one another in civil conversation. The second concerns the duty of each toward the other in speech and bearing.

units.la: Digniorem voco, qui illum cum quo conuersatur, antecedit, ipsique in existimatione & pretio praefertur.vide Chassan. in catal. gloriae mun-di part.1. Esse vero inter homines alium alio excellentiorem & praestantiorem, satis puto constare ex Philip. c.2.3.29. Act. c.5.34. c.17.4.12. cap. 12.23. c.14.11. c.13.30. c.17.4.12.1. Thessal. c.5.12.13.2. Corinth. c.10. per tot. 1. Chronic. c.27. per tot. 2. Sam. c.23. per tot. Matth. c.18.1. c.8.8.9. c.6.2. Marc. c.9. 34. Luc. c.9.46. c.14.9.10. c.7.1.2.4. 5. c.22.27.28. Ephes. c.5.21. Act. c.5.34. Luc. c.7.28. Galat. c.2.6. Roman. c.12.10. Iohan. c.5.44. Psal. 49.3.21.13. Esa. c.2.9.11.12.17. c.3.4.5.6. Eccles. c.40.3.4. c.3.1.2.3. 4. & seqq. c.10.26.27. Exod. c.11.5.2. Reg. c.24.14. 16,17. c.25.15. Nehem. 8.1.2. Chron. c.24.17,23. c.12. 5. cap. 5. cap.26.11.12. c.28.14. cap.29.20.30. c.30.2.5. late differt ex prophanis autoribus Tiraquel.in tractat.de nobilit. c.21. & de iur. primogenior. in prafation. & Chassan.in lib.de gloria mundi & Flaminius in lib.de honore. Hinc dignitas,honor, auctoritas, gloria, eminentia,excellentia. Rom.c.13.1.2.3.2.Chronic.c.1.12, 13.Matth.c.15.4.1.Pet.c.2.17. & Num.c.16. 1.Iudic.c.9.1.1.Sam.c.10.27.2.Thess.c.1.4.Proverb.cap.26.1.2.Corinth.c.15.5.Sapient.c 8.11.1.Reg.cap.2.9. 10.11.1.Chron.c.18.8.9.1.Reg.c.8.16.17. & seq. Philip.c.2.9. & in magna domo non tantum aurea & argentea vasa,sed etiam fictilia & lignea. 2.Tim.c.2.& ordines,1.Reg.c.10.5.
units.tr: I call a person more worthy when he surpasses the one with whom he converses and is preferred to him in esteem and value. See Chassanaeus, Catalogue of the Glory of the World, part 1. That among men one is more excellent and outstanding than another, I think is sufficiently clear from Phil. 2:3, 29; Acts 5:34; 17:4, 12; 12:23; 14:11; 13:30; 17:4, 12; 1 Thess. 5:12-13; 2 Cor. 10 throughout; 1 Chron. 27 throughout; 2 Sam. 23 throughout; Matt. 18:1; 8:8-9; 6:2; Mark 9:34; Luke 9:46; 14:9-10; 7:1-2, 4-5; 22:27-28; Eph. 5:21; Acts 5:34; Luke 7:28; Gal. 2:6; Rom. 12:10; John 5:44; Ps. 49:3, 21, 13; Isa. 2:9, 11-12, 17; 3:4-6; Eccles. 40:3-4; 3:1-4 and following; 10:26-27; Exod. 11:5; 2 Kings 24:14, 16-17; 25:15; Neh. 8:1-2; 2 Chron. 24:17, 23; 12:5; 26:11-12; 28:14; 29:20, 30; 30:2, 5. Indeed it differs in profane authors: Tiraquellus, in his treatise on nobility, ch. 21, and on the right of primogeniture, in the preface; Chassanaeus, in his book on the glory of the world; and Flaminius, in his book on honour. Hence dignity, honour, authority, glory, eminence and excellence. Rom. 13:1-3; 2 Chron. 1:12-13; Matt. 15:4; 1 Pet. 2:17; Num. 16; Judg. 9:1; 1 Sam. 10:27; 2 Thess. 1:4; Prov. 26:1; 2 Cor. 15:5; Wisd. 8:11; 1 Kings 2:9-11; 1 Chron. 18:8-9; 1 Kings 8:16-17 and following; Phil. 2:9; and in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of earthenware and wood. 2 Tim. 2; and orders, 1 Kings 10:5.

units.la: Dignitas igitur haec, est praeclara hominum multorum de alio opinio,sermone vel gestu testata,Iohan.c.5.44.Matth.c.6.2.Act.c.12.23. c.14. 11.Galat.c.6.3.2.Corinth.c.10.seu praesumptio virtutis & praestantiae ac excellentiae egregiae. Menoch.lib.6.praesumpt.59.Tiraquel. De nobilit. c.37. c.20. & Sene. lib.17.Epist.103. Ad gloriam & famam non est satis unius opinio: sed gloria multorum,claritas bonorum iudiciis constat.
units.tr: Dignity, then, is a high opinion of one person held by many others, shown in speech or bearing: John 5:44; Matt. 6:2; Acts 12:23; 14:11; Gal. 6:3; 2 Cor. 10; or the presumption of virtue, worth and outstanding excellence. Menochius, Presumptions, book 6, no. 59; Tiraquellus, On Nobility, ch. 37 and 20; and Seneca, Letters, book 17, letter 103. One person's opinion is not enough for glory and fame; glory rests on the judgement of many, and the renown of good men rests on their verdicts.

units.la: Causae efficientes huius opinionis & dignitatis sunt maiora a Deo accepta dona, virtutes, potentia,magistratus & imperium, diuitiae, senectus,officium, aut munus, quod quis gerit nobile, excellensve, aut merita in Rempub. Prov.c.26.1.2.3.arg. Deut.c.1.13.14. & seqq. Exod. c.18. Eccles.c.10.14. Eccles.c.40. per tot. & cap.seqq. c.3.2.& seqq.1.Timoth.c.3.13.c.5.17. 1.Sam.c.18.29. Flaminius de honore c.7.c.8.c.10.c.12. Nam quod nos allicit ad amandum & colendum, id honore dignum iudicamus late Chassan.in catalog glor. mundi part. 1. confid. 5. Iustum etiam est vt iis qui nos iuuant & Dei donis instructi sunt, aliquid rependamus. Honore autem melius nihil habemus. Deinde, honorem exhibemus, vt ipsi & illorum similes pergant sediutius atque constantius exercere in alias adiuuandis & conseruandis. Ad haec, vt addita huiusmodi reuerentia authoritatem illis conciliemus, quo aptius & commodius queant suo fungi munere & in Repub. administranda & munere suo sint feliciores & ita pergant. Chass part. 1. confid. 46. & seqq. Martyr Iud. cap. 9. 5. Cassidior. copiose libr. 1. Variar. epist. 3. & 13. asserit honores veluti praemia quaedam & aculeos esse, qui animos ad virtutem impellant, alioqin in laboribus desides & torpentes. Cicer. de clar. orator. Honor est praemium virtutis, studio iudicioque ciuium ad aliquem delatum. Idem alibi: Si quis ad gloriam adsequendam laborat, talem se efficiat qualis vult haberi. Quod si ostentatione inani & ficto sermone vel vultu stabilem se gloriam adsequi opinatur, vehementer errat. Vera enim gloria radices agit, ficta omnia celeriter, tanquam flosculi, decidunt: neque simulatum quidquam potest esse diuturnum.
units.tr: The efficient causes of this opinion and dignity are the greater gifts received from God: virtues, power, magistracy and rule, riches, old age, an office or duty which a person discharges nobly or excellently, or merits toward the commonwealth. Prov. 26:1-3 (argument); Deut. 1:13-14 and following; Exod. 18; Eccles. 10:14; Eccles. 40 throughout and the following chapters; 3:2 and following; 1 Tim. 3:13; 5:17; 1 Sam. 18:29. Flaminius, On Honour, ch. 7, 8, 10, 12. For what attracts us to love and cherish a person, that we judge worthy of honour; see Chassanaeus, Catalogue of the Glory of the World, part 1, consideration 5. It is also just that we repay something to those who help us and who are furnished with God's gifts. Now we have nothing better to give than honour. Further, we show honour so that they themselves, and others like them, may go on exercising more diligently and constantly their work of helping and preserving others. Moreover, by adding such reverence we win them authority, so that they may perform their office more fitly and conveniently in administering the commonwealth, and be more fortunate in their office and go on so. Chassanaeus, part 1, consideration 46 and following; Martyr, Judges, ch. 9; Cassiodorus, at length, Variae, book 1, letters 3 and 13, maintains that honours are as it were rewards and goads which drive minds to virtue, otherwise they would be idle and sluggish in their labours. Cicero, On Famous Orators: Honour is the reward of virtue, conferred on someone by the zeal and judgement of citizens. Cicero, elsewhere: If anyone labours to attain glory, let him make himself such as he wishes to be thought. But if he supposes that he can gain lasting glory by empty display and feigned speech or look, he is gravely mistaken. For true glory takes root; all that is feigned quickly falls away, like little flowers; nothing simulated can last.

units.la: Accidit etiam quandoque, vt sola hominum opinione quis habeatur dignior & honoratior, qui tamen hisce omnibus vacat. Nam, vt Seneca lib. 2. in sapient. non cad. iniur. ait, Honores & iniuriae vulgi in promiscuo habendae. Unde Fernand. Vasquius lib. 1. in praefat. num. 86. & seqq. ait illum demum maiorem, digniorem & excellentiorem esse, quem generaliter talem esse omnes homines iudicant. per l. Athletas. de his qui not. infam. Boer. decif. 286. num. 9. Ratio vero ob quam hisce virtutibus praeditis honor habeatur, est, quod imago Dei, quae in hisce elucet, agnoscenda est. Nam in Magistratu quaedam potentiae & gloriae diuinae imago cernitur. Psalm. 82. In diuite imago diuinae opulentiae; in docto, diuinae sapientiae; in patre, diuinae paternitatis & potestatis patriae. Matth. c. 23. 9. In marito, authoritatis diuinae, 1. Corinth. cap. 11. In sene, quaedam aeternitatis diuinae imago: In iudice, iustitiae & seueritatis diuinae, 2. Chron. c. 19. in aliis virtus excellens. vide Flaminium de honore c. 8. & c. 10.
units.tr: It also sometimes happens that someone is held more worthy and more honourable by the opinion of men alone, although he lacks all these things. For, as Seneca says, book 2, On the Wise Man, not to be cast down by injuries, honours and the injuries of the crowd are to be counted as of little account. Hence Fernandus Vasquius, book 1, preface, nos. 86 and following, says that he is finally considered greater, more worthy and more excellent whom all men generally judge to be such. By the law Athletae, On those who are noted for infamy; Boerius, decision 286, no. 9. The reason why those endowed with these virtues are held in honour is that the image of God, which shines forth in them, must be acknowledged. For in the magistrate a certain image of the power and glory of God is seen. Ps. 82. In the rich, an image of divine opulence; in the learned, of divine wisdom; in the father, of divine fatherhood and paternal power. Matt. 23:9. In the husband, of divine authority. 1 Cor. 11. In the old man, a certain image of divine eternity. In the judge, of divine justice and severity. 2 Chron. 19. In others, excellent virtue. See Flaminius, On Honour, ch. 8 and 10.

units.la: Quamuis autem fieri non potest, vt aliquis Dei imagine careat, vt huius respectu recte etiam suus cuique honos debeatur, vt dicitur 1. Pet. cap. 2. 17. Rom. c. 12. 10. Philip. cap. 2. 3. 29. Ephes. cap. 5. 21. nihilominus tamen cum in aliis atque aliis magis atque magis diuina haec imago sit illustris, & pluribus virtutibus donisque diuinis exornata & aucta, fit vt alius alio excellentior, honoratior, eminentior, maiorisque existimationis & pretii recte dicatur: imo inter dignitates ipsas recte quoddam discrimen constitutum sit.
units.tr: Although it cannot happen that anyone is without the image of God, so that in respect of this each person is rightly owed his own honour, as it is said in 1 Pet. 2:17; Rom. 12:10; Phil. 2:3, 29; Eph. 5:21; nevertheless, since this divine image shines forth more and more in some than in others, and is adorned and enlarged with more virtues and divine gifts, it comes about that one is rightly called more excellent, more honourable, more eminent, and of greater esteem and value than another. Indeed, a certain distinction has been rightly established even among the dignities themselves.

units.la: Dignitas & excellentia est duplex. Naturalis, vel ciuilis.
units.tr: Dignity and excellence are twofold: natural or civil.

units.la: Naturalis est, qua propter naturae dotes eximias, alius alio est & habetur excellentior pro virtutis, qua praeditus est, qualitate, vel quantitate. arg. 1. Corinth. c. 12, 4. 5. 6. & seqq. cap. 13. c. 14. Rom.c.2.7.Ephes.c.4. Philip. c.2.29. Eccles.cap.18, 26.27.33.34.c.11.1. sic masculus dignior fœmina. Eccles.c.42.15.1.Timoth.c.2.12. Levit. c.27.2.3.4. Ierem.c.50.c.51.Esa.1.c.27. & Deuter. c.28.56.Siracid. c.14.ibi honora personam senis. Gell.lib.2.c.15. late Chass.de gloria mundi consid.17.part.11. & consid.4.dixi late lib.1. Dicaeologica mea, c.4. de homin. ἀγωνίως. Sic senex dignior iuuene. 1.Timoth.c.5.1. 2.3.4.17. & Tit.c.2.1.2.Levit.c.19.32.1.Pet.cap.5.5. Similiter iuniores subiecti esse senioribus, &c. Proverb.c.20.29.& c.16.31.in Dicaeolog.d.lib.1.c.25. dixi latius. Sic publica persona priuatâ praestantior est. Luc.c.21.25.26.27. Matth.c.20.25. & seqq. Marc.c.10.42.& seqq. Eccles.c.10. verf.13.26.27. 1.Timoth.c.2.12. Sic virtus & gloria militaris, seu bellica, praestantior virtute togatâ, tempore belli, non pacis. 1.Timoth.c.5.17. Philip.c.2.29.1.Chro. c.11.11.& seqq.c.12.7.8.2.Sam.c.23.18.& seqq. Eccle. c.44.6.c.10.26.27.c.7.29.30.31. Eccles.c.9.17.18.19. Sapient.c.7.Pet. Gregor.de Rep.lib.4.c.10.num.8.14. vid.l.unic.C.de profess.qui in urbe Constantinop. seu in negotiis bellicis, non Reip. ut dicit Chass.per l. nemo.C.de sum.trinit.& fid.cath.l.1. C.de Codic.Iustin.comp.l.1.C.de iur. vet. enunc.l. his honoribus, de vacat.vniuer. in actibus pacis literati praeferuntur. d. lege nemo clericus. Chass.part.9. consid.1. catal.glor.mundi. Diues honoratior paupere. Eccle. c.10.33.34.c.13.24.& seqq.Ecclesiast.c.9.17.& seqq. Iacob.c.2.2.3.4.& seqq. Levit.c.19.5. Mich.cap.6. 12.Luc.c.6.24. late Tiraquel. De nobilit.c.3.cap.25. Chassan.consid.27.par.11.per.l.honor.de hon.& mun. l.3.de testibus vasq lib.1.in praefat.num.77.& seqq.illust.controu. Boet. decis.286. Nam opes pariunt potentes. potentiam & dignitatem.ut dicit Farn. Vasq. & Chass.d.locis. Sic dominus seruo, pater filiofam. maritus vxore honoratior est. Malach.c.1.6.Eccles.c.3.9. c.16 30. & verf.26. & 28. Luc.cap.12.37. & seqq.c.17.7.8.9.10.1. Pet.c.3.1. 2. Deut.c.27.maledictus qui non honorat patrem suum. Syrac. honora patrem ex animo. Deut.c.5. & Exod.cap.20. honora patrem & matrem. Sic honoratior persona ecclesiastica persona politica. Eccles. cap.3. & persona politica in magistratu constituta. 1. Pet.c.2. Regem honorate, &c. senex literatus. Levit.c.19. Coram cano capite, &c. quidam ob bonitate suam honoratiores Philip.c.2. tales honorate.
units.tr: Natural dignity is that by which one person is, and is held, more excellent than another, on account of outstanding gifts of nature, in respect of the quality or quantity of the virtue with which he is endowed. Argument from 1 Cor. 12:4-6 and following; ch. 13; 14; Rom. 2:7; Eph. 4; Phil. 2:29; Eccles. 18, 26-27, 33-34; 11:1. Thus the male is more worthy than the female. Eccles. 42:15; 1 Tim. 2:12; Lev. 27:2-4; Jer. 50; 51; Isa. 27; and Deut. 28:56; Sirach 14, where it says "honour the person of the old man." Gellius, book 2, ch. 15; at length Chassanaeus, On the Glory of the World, consideration 17, part 11, and consideration 4; I have spoken at length in book 1 of my Dicaeologica, ch. 4, on human contests. Thus an old man is more worthy than a young one. 1 Tim. 5:1-4, 17; Titus 2:1-2; Lev. 19:32; 1 Pet. 5:5. Likewise the younger are to be subject to the elders, etc. Prov. 20:29; 16:31; I have spoken more fully in Dicaeologica, book 1, ch. 25. Thus a public person is superior to a private one. Luke 21:25-27; Matt. 20:25 and following; Mark 10:42 and following; Eccles. 10, verses 13, 26-27; 1 Tim. 2:12. Thus military virtue and glory, or the glory of war, is superior to the virtue of the gown, in time of war rather than of peace. 1 Tim. 5:17; Phil. 2:29; 1 Chron. 11:11 and following; 12:7-8; 2 Sam. 23:18 and following; Eccles. 44:6; 10:26-27; 7:29-31; Eccles. 9:17-19; Wisd. 7; Gregory Peter, On the Commonwealth, book 4, ch. 10, nos. 8 and 14; see the single law, Code, On the professors who are in the city of Constantinople, or in military affairs, not in civil ones. As Chassanaeus says, by the law Nemo, Code, On the Supreme Trinity and Catholic Faith, law 1; Code, On the Codex of Justinian, compilation, law 1, Code On Ancient Right, enunciation; the law his honoribus, On Exemption from All Burdens. In the affairs of peace, the learned are preferred. By the said law Nemo clericus; Chassanaeus, part 9, consideration 1, Catalogue of the Glory of the World. The rich man is more honourable than the poor. Eccles. 10:33-34; 13:24 and following; Eccles. 9:17 and following; James 2:2-4 and following; Lev. 19:15; Mic. 6:12; Luke 6:24; at length Tiraquellus, On Nobility, ch. 3, ch. 25; Chassanaeus, consideration 27, part 11; by the law Honor, On Honours and Offices; law 3, On Witnesses; Vasquius, book 1, preface, no. 77 and following; the illustrious controversy; Boerius, decision 286. For riches produce powerful men, power and dignity, as Farinacius Vasquius and Chassanaeus say in the places cited. Thus a lord is more honourable than a slave, a father than a son in his power, a husband than a wife. Mal. 1:6; Eccles. 3:9; 16:30 and verse 26 and 28; Luke 12:37 and following; 17:7-10; 1 Pet. 3:1-2; Deut. 27: "cursed is he who does not honour his father"; Sirach: "honour your father from the heart"; Deut. 5 and Exod. 20: "honour your father and mother." Thus a person holding ecclesiastical office is more honourable than a person of political standing. Eccles. 3, and a person placed in magistracy is more honourable than a private citizen. 1 Pet. 2: "Honour the king," etc. A learned old man. Lev. 19: "Before the grey head," etc. Some are more honourable on account of their goodness. Phil. 2: "Honour such men."

units.la: Sic quoq; honestus, in honesto & infami praefertur. arg.l.1, de testib. Chass.part.11. conf.28. diligens & utilis, otioso pigro & inutili praefertur. confider.29. Vxorati praeferuntur non vxoratis, nam per matrimonium consequitur quis dignitatem. Novell.de nupt. §.deinceps.Chassan.part.11.confid.10. Gellius lib.2.c.15. & filios vel liberos habens praefertur non habenti coelibi l.spurii.in sin.de Decurion.l.in albo. C.d.tit.lib.10. Chass.confid.12.d.loc. Legitimi bastardis illegitimis etiam nobilibus praeferuntur. Sap.c.3. Chass.d.loc.confid.15. part.11. Parens quoq; liberis suis dignior. arg.1. Timoth.c.5. Coloss.c.3.l.parentib.l.generaliter.de in-ius vocand. Et inter liberos primogenitus caeteris praestantior & dignior habetur. Genes.c.4.9. & cap.49.2.3. c.48.19.20. c.25.23. & seqq. Tiraquell. paff. in tract. de primigen. Sic literatus imperito honoratior & praestantior, Ecclesiastic. c.26.35. c.10.5.33.c.38.1.2.3.4.37.38.39. 1.Thessal.c.5.12.13. Mich.c.3.1.2, Eccles.cap.44.1.2. & seqq. Sapiens Ier.c.31.37.38. Inde nimirum ab Abrahamo vsq; serie & genealogia perpetua, non interrupta. Iohan.c.8.33.37.Ezech.c.16.3.4.5.6.
units.tr: Likewise, the honest man is preferred to the one who is dishonest and infamous. arg.l.1, de testib. Chass.part.11. conf.28. The diligent and useful man is preferred to the idle, lazy and useless. confider.29. Married men are preferred to unmarried men, for a man gains dignity through marriage. Novell.de nupt. §.deinceps. Chassan.part.11.confid.10. Gellius lib.2.c.15. A man who has sons or children is preferred to a celibate who has none. l.spurii.in sin.de Decurion.l.in albo. C.d.tit.lib.10. Chass.confid.12.d.loc. Legitimate children are preferred to illegitimate bastards, even noble ones. Sap.c.3. Chass.d.loc.confid.15. part.11. A parent is also more worthy than his own children. arg.1. Timoth.c.5. Coloss.c.3.l.parentib.l.generaliter.de in-ius vocand. And among children the firstborn is regarded as more outstanding and worthy than the others. Genes.c.4.9. & cap.49.2.3. c.48.19.20. c.25.23. & seqq. Tiraquell. paff. in tract. de primigen. Likewise the learned man is more honourable and outstanding than the unskilled. Ecclesiastic. c.26.35. c.10.5.33.c.38.1.2.3.4.37.38.39. 1.Thessal.c.5.12.13. Mich.c.3.1.2, Eccles.cap.44.1.2. & seqq. The wise man Ier.c.31.37.38. Indeed, from Abraham onwards there is a continuous and uninterrupted series and genealogy. Iohan.c.8.33.37.Ezech.c.16.3.4.5.6.

units.la: Apud Romanos qui imagines suorum maiorum habuerunt, ii nobiles; qui suas tantum, illi novi vocabantur. Vnde constat, ius nobilitatis esse iisdem ius imaginis habendae & collocandae. Nam, vt imago a magistratu, quem gerere necesse est illi, qui imaginem ponere volebat; sic nobilitas ab imagine proficiscitur, quae in celebriore domus parte, atrio, armario, vel lararío ligneo ponebatur. vid. Sigon. lib. 2. cap. 20. De antiq. iur. ciu. Rom. & lib. De nomin. Roman & Senec. lib. 5. epist. 44. & lib. 3. De benefic. c. 28. & lib. 9. epist. 63. Hodie, apud nos, quis nobilis, & quae nobilitas vocari debeat, arbitrio iudicis relinquitur. Menochius li. 2. caf. 67. & seq. arb. iud. quaest. qui id pro ratione circumstantiarum, loci, consuetudinis, regionis, temporis, personaeque aestimare debet. Sicuti quoque quae sit grauis, discreta & honesta persona, eiusdem arbitrio relinquitur. Menoc. d. lib. 2. caf. 69. & quae diues, caf. 65. & quae egregia persona. Idem caf. 70. arb. iud. quaest. Contra vero quae persona popularis, humilis, plebeia, vilis, abiecta, ignobilis, nullius pretii, aut existimationis, arbitrio recte iudicantis relinquitur, qui plerunque id ex genere, professione, conditione, statu, officio, vita ve sordida, opificio mechanico, vili, humili, vel ex consuetudine, & more cuiusque regionis, vel vulgi opinione, aut hominum prudentum arbitrio, vel vita antea acta, iudicat. Menoch. lib. 2. caf. 71. arb. iud. quaest. Similiter quae sit persona miserabilis. bilis.Idem caf.66.& caf.532.num.2.3.4. pauper& inopscaf.65. Vilis& plebeia persona apud Iudæos vocabatur homo paruus,Matth.c.10.42.c.18.f.10.1.Corinth.c.3.1.1.Sam.c.15.17.c.9.21.& eanis.2.Sam.c.9.2.c.3.8.1.Sam.c.24.15.2.Reg.c.8.13.c.25.15.Matth.c.15.26.c.7.6.Iohan.cap.7.47.48.Nehem.cap.8.1.& pulex.Sam.cap.16.20. Metaphoricè.
units.tr: Among the Romans, those who had images of their ancestors were nobles; those who had only images of themselves were called "new men." Hence it is clear that the right of nobility is the right to have and to set up such images. For just as an image derives from the magistracy which the man wishing to set up the image must have held, so nobility arises from the image, which was placed in the more prominent part of the house: the atrium, a cabinet, or a wooden lararium. See Sigon. lib. 2. cap. 20. De antiq. iur. ciu. Rom. and De nomin. Roman; and Seneca lib. 5. epist. 44, lib. 3. De benefic. c. 28, and lib. 9. epist. 63. Today among us, who is noble and what nobility ought to be called is left to the judgment of the judge, who must assess this according to the circumstances of place, custom, region and time, and the person. Menochius li. 2. caf. 67. & seq. arb. iud. quaest. In the same way, who is a grave, discreet and honest person is left to his judgment, Menoc. d. lib. 2. caf. 69. and who is rich, caf. 65. and who is an eminent person. Idem caf. 70. arb. iud. quaest. On the contrary, who is a person of the common people, humble, plebeian, vile, abject, ignoble, of no worth or reputation is left to the judgment of the one judging rightly, who for the most part judges this from birth, profession, condition, status, office, or a squalid life, a mechanical, base or humble trade, or from the custom and manner of each region, or the opinion of the common people, or the judgment of prudent men, or from the life lived previously. Menoch. lib. 2. caf. 71. arb. iud. quaest. Likewise, who is a wretched person: Idem caf.66. and caf.532.num.2.3.4. a poor and needy man: caf.65. Among the Jews a vile and plebeian person was called a "little man," Matth.c.10.42.c.18.f.10.1.Corinth.c.3.1.1.Sam.c.15.17.c.9.21. and a "dog," 2.Sam.c.9.2.c.3.8.1.Sam.c.24.15.2.Reg.c.8.13.c.25.15.Matth.c.15.26.c.7.6.Iohan.cap.7.47.48.Nehem.cap.8.1. and a "flea." Sam.cap.16.20. Metaphorically.

units.la: Dignitas autem & excellentia atque auctoritas crescit & decrescit ex superioris, vel consuetudinis cuiusque loci, vel hominum opinione,& arbitrio vt exemplis patet. Esther c.3.2.c.5.11.c.1.6.6.7.8.9.10.Daniel.c.5.7.29. c.2.48.Genes.c.41.37.39.41. & seqq.1. Macchab.c.10.20.64.65.66.2.2.c.14.38.39.40.43.44.c.15.32.8.9.c.11.27.28. vel ex vitæ statu & honestate.§ 7.pœna.Iust.de inur.Tiraquel.De nobilit.c.37.num.68.& seqq.Menoch.lib.2. casu 67.arb.iud.quæst. Nam quo quis melioribus & præstantioribus negotiis & laboribus occupatur, vel vacat, aut quo propius ad superioris dignitatem accedit, aut præstantioribus est proximior, eo dignior & venerabilior haberi debet.Esther c.1.14.15 c.6.7.Nehem.c.4.14.19.c.5.7.1.Reg.c.10.5. 2.Timoth.c.2.20. Roman. c.12.10. Philip. c.2.3. Matth.c.20.21.& seqq.1. Corinth.c.10.Exod.c.11.8.c.8.3.31.c.7.13.23.Genes.cap.41.39.40.41.42.Est.c.10.3. Tiraquel. De nobil.c.5. c.6.7.& seqq Pet. Gregor.de Repub.lib.4. c.3.4.10. Fernand.Vasq.lib.1. in præfat. num.26.& 126.& seqq. Chassan.part.11. confid.38. catal. glor. mundi.
units.tr: Dignity, excellence and authority, however, rise and fall according to the judgment of superiors, or the custom of each place, or the opinion and judgment of men, as examples show. Esther c.3.2.c.5.11.c.1.6.6.7.8.9.10.Daniel.c.5.7.29. c.2.48.Genes.c.41.37.39.41. & seqq.1. Macchab.c.10.20.64.65.66.2.2.c.14.38.39.40.43.44.c.15.32.8.9.c.11.27.28. Or they rise and fall according to one's state of life and honesty. § 7 pœna. Iust. de inur. Tiraquel. De nobilit. c.37. num.68. & seqq. Menoch. lib. 2. casu 67. arb. iud. quaest. For the more excellent and outstanding the business or labours with which a man is occupied or at leisure, or the closer he comes to the dignity of a superior, or the nearer he is to outstanding persons, the more worthy and venerable he ought to be held. Esther c.1.14.15 c.6.7. Nehem.c.4.14.19.c.5.7.1.Reg.c.10.5. 2.Timoth.c.2.20. Roman. c.12.10. Philip. c.2.3. Matth.c.20.21.& seqq. 1. Corinth.c.10. Exod.c.11.8.c.8.3.31.c.7.13.23. Genes.cap.41.39.40.41.42. Est.c.10.3. Tiraquel. De nobil. c.5. c.6.7.& seqq. Pet. Gregor. de Repub. lib.4. c.3.4.10. Fernand. Vasq. lib.1. in praefat. num.26. & 126. & seqq. Chassan. part.11. confid.38. catal. glor. mundi.

units.la: Hinc recte quædam dignitas clara, præclara, inclyta, generosa, illustris, principalis, regia, imperialis, ex quibus quædam superior, quædam intermedia;& quaedam inferior vocatur,1. Pet. c. 2. 13. 14. Genef. c. 41. 40. & seqq. Dan. c. 5. 16. 17. Ester c. 8. 2. & seqq. Matth. c. 20. 21. 22. 23. 2. Sam. cap. 23. 8. Apud Romanos varii dignitatum gradus & ordines erant, de quibus in tit. C. de equest. dign. libr. 2. tit. C. de dignit. tit. de Decurion. tit. de prox. sacr. scrin. tit. C. ut ord. dign. feruet. & latius dixi lib. 11. Dicaeolog. & Pet. Greg. de Repub. lib. 4. cap. 10. & lib. 6. Syntag. cap. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. & Gloss. in §. 1. Nouel. 71. Vide Chassan. part. 4. §. 6. 7. & seqq. catalog. glor. mund. Inter dignitates seculares, Imperatoria primum locum obtinet. l. pen. C. de bon. quae lib. 1. quaeris. de natal. rest. vid. Chas. par. 5. cosid. 27. qui ideo corona triplici coronatur, ferrea, argentea, & aurea. Imperatore sequuntur reges, atq; hos Archiduces, hos vero Duces, quos sequitur principes, & hos Marchiones, quos Comites, atq; illos Barones, & deniq; hos nobiles sequuntur. late differt Chass. d. part. 5. consid. 44. & seqq. vbi videre licet.
units.tr: Hence some dignities are rightly called clear, distinguished, renowned, noble, illustrious, principal, royal, imperial; of these some are called superior, some intermediate, and some inferior. 1. Pet. c. 2. 13. 14. Genef. c. 41. 40. & seqq. Dan. c. 5. 16. 17. Ester c. 8. 2. & seqq. Matth. c. 20. 21. 22. 23. 2. Sam. cap. 23. Among the Romans there were various grades and orders of dignities, concerning which see tit. C. de equest. dign. libr. 2. tit. C. de dignit. tit. de Decurion. tit. de prox. sacr. scrin. tit. C. ut ord. dign. feruet. and I have spoken more fully in lib. 11 of the Dicaeologia; and Pet. Greg. de Repub. lib. 4. cap. 10 and lib. 6 Syntag. cap. 6-11, and the Gloss on §1 Novel. 71. See Chassan. part. 4. §6, 7 and following, catalog. glor. mund. Among secular dignities the imperial holds the first place, l. pen. C. de bon. quae lib. 1. quaeris. de natal. rest. see Chas. par. 5. consid. 27. and for this reason it is crowned with a triple crown: iron, silver and gold. The emperor is followed by kings, and these by archdukes, these by dukes, whom princes follow, and these by margraves, whom counts follow, and then barons, and finally these nobles follow. Chass. d. part. 5. consid. 44. & seqq., where one may see at length.

units.la: Huius loci sunt duae quaestiones sequentes; quarum prior est, An honor semper virtutem comitetur. Altera, inter plures honoratos concurrentes, qui alteri cedere vel praeferri debeat.
units.tr: Two questions follow from this place. The first is: Does honour always accompany virtue? The second: when several honoured persons meet, which of them ought to yield to or be preferred over another?

units.la: Ad priorem quaestionem, recte respondetur, quod virtutem non semper honor & gloria comitetur, aut coniuncta sit eodem gradu & splendore. Interdum enim antecedit honor & opinio, vel exististimatio virtutis perfectione; interdum coniunctus est honor cum virtute. Quandoque ex intervallo subsequitur. Interdum obscurior est, atq; interdum illustrior. Nam sicut Petr. Mart. aut, comes corporis est umbra, ita & virtutis comes gloria. Umbra corpus comitatur, sed non eodem modo. do. Nonnunquam enim praecedit, interdum iungitur à latere & quasi incedit vnà: interdum sequitur corpus, pro diuersa corporis theses & radiorum illapsu, vt docent Optici.
