Similli modo virtus quorundam vix inchoata, seu sub ipsis eius initiis habetur in honore. Aliorum vero non suspicitur & praedicatur, nisi cum aucta est & perfecta. Denique videas aliquot non ante honoratos, quam viuere desierint. Nescio enim quo pacto comparatum sit, vt ea, quae in manibus nostris posita sunt, oculisque quotidie obuersantur, sensim quasi obrepente satietate, fastidiamus, eorumq; nos tandem pertaedeat: vbi vero elapsa amissaque sunt, incredibile sui desiderium excitent, & animus multo ea ardentius, licet sero, requirat. Sicuti scite Horatius, Virtutem, inquit, incolumem odimus, Sublatam ex oculis requirimus inuidi. Goclenius Quaest. Ethic. c. 6. Flam. c. 11. d. honor.
units.tr: To the first question it is rightly answered that honour and glory do not always accompany virtue, nor are they joined to it at the same degree and splendour. For sometimes honour and opinion, or esteem of virtue, precede its perfection; sometimes honour is joined to virtue; sometimes it follows at an interval. Sometimes it is more obscure, and sometimes more illustrious. For, as Peter Martyr says, glory is the companion of virtue as the shadow is of the body. The shadow accompanies the body, but not in the same way. For sometimes it goes before, sometimes it is joined at the side and walks as it were together, and sometimes it follows the body, according to the different position of the body and the incidence of the rays, as the opticians teach. In the same way, the virtue of some people, scarcely begun or still at its very beginnings, is held in honour; but of others it is not esteemed and praised until it has grown and been perfected. Finally, you may see some who were not honoured until they had ceased to live. For I know not how it comes about that we grow weary of those things which are in our hands and daily before our eyes, as satiety creeps on unnoticed, and at last we are tired of them; but when they have slipped away and been lost, they arouse an incredible longing for themselves, and the mind seeks them much more eagerly, though too late. As Horace wisely says: "We hate virtue while it is unhurt; once it is taken from our eyes, we envious men seek it." Goclenius Quaest. Ethic. c. 6. Flam. c. 11. d. honor.

units.la: In altera quaestione, inter plures praestantes honoratior & dignior habetur is, in quem plures caussae dignitatis concurrunt, modo officii & muneris praestantia non sit tanta, quae primum locum & gradum dignitatis obtineat. Prauo hominum iudicio, diuitiarum praestantia & dignitas sapientiae praefertur. Ecclesiastic. cap. 9. 17. Adfuit in ciuitate vir indigus sapiens, qui liberauit ipse ciuitatem illam sua sapientia, nec tamen quisquam recordatus est viri indigi illius. 18. Dico autem ego, meliorem esse sapientiam robore, quamvis sapientia illius indigi despiciatur & verba eius no audiantur. 19. Verba submissorum sapientum audienda esse potius, quam clamorem dominantis cum stoli-
units.tr: In the second question, among several excellent persons, the one in whom several causes of dignity concur is held to be more honourable and worthy, provided the excellence of his office and function is not so great as to win the first place and degree of dignity. By the perverse judgment of men, the excellence and dignity of wealth is preferred to that of wisdom. Ecclesiastic. cap. 9. 17. "There was in the city a poor wise man, who by his wisdom alone delivered that city, yet no one remembered that poor man. 18. I say, then, that wisdom is better than strength, although the wisdom of that poor man is despised and his words are not heard. 19. The words of the humble wise men are rather to be heard than the shouting of a ruler among fools."

units.la: dissuis.20. Meliorem esse sapientiam armis bellicis, aberrantem vero unum perdere boni plurimum. 21. Ut muscarum mortuarum una efficit, ut foetorem eructet unguentum pigmentarii, similiter pretiosum nomen sapientiae & gloriae virum foetidum efficit stoliditatis parum. 22. Animus sapientis adest dexterae ipsius, animus vero stolidi sinistrae ipsius, & Ecclesiastic.c.13.26. Si humilis lapsus est, increpatur ipse; nunciauerit verbum intelligentiae, non tamen tribuitur ipsi locus. 27. Diuite loquente, omnes silent, etiam sermonem eius exaltauerunt ad nubes usque. 28. Pauper loquente, dixerunt, Quis iste est? & si offenderit, amplius subuertere solent ipsum. Sed haec ex prauo hominum iudicio & opinione. Sed in rei veritate sapientia & quaeuis virtutes longe diuitiis meliores & praestantiores sunt, Prou.c.8.11. Na melior est sapientia carbunculis, & omnia obiectamenta non possunt aquari ei.
units.tr: "...20. Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good. 21. As one dead fly makes the perfumer's ointment give off a stench, so a little folly outweighs a precious reputation for wisdom and glory. 22. The heart of the wise is at his right hand, but the heart of the fool at his left. And Ecclesiasticus 13:26. If a humble man has fallen, he is rebuked; if he has spoken words of understanding, yet no place is given to him. 27. When a rich man speaks, all are silent, and they exalt his speech to the clouds. 28. When a poor man speaks, they say, 'Who is this?' and if he stumbles, they are ready to push him down further."* But this is the judgment and opinion of perverse men. In the truth of the matter, however, wisdom and all virtues are far better and more excellent than riches. Prou. c.8.11. For wisdom is better than rubies, and nothing you desire can be compared with her.

units.la: Quod si filius publicam cum imperio, vel honore personam gerat, pater vero sit priuatus; hic in locis & actionibus publicis filii, pater debet cedere filio; in priuatis vero negotiis & conuentibus cessabit publica, & praevalebit paterna auctoritas: sicuti demonstrat exemplum Sempronii Gracchi consulis Romani. Hic enim ut dignitatem suam publice tueretur, cum obuiam ei factus esset pater Quintus Fab. Maxim. Proconsul, equo insidens, lictoribus ad eum missis, equo ut descenderet, imperauit. Pater, dicto audiens, imperata prompte fecit, filiumque collaudauit, quod dignitatem populi Romani imperio conuenientem, tueri noluerat, quae de re Val. Max. lib.2.c.2. Extat quoque exemplum in Salomone; qui etiamsi rex esset potentissimus, nihilominus tamen matri honoris & obsequii officia exhibuit. 1. Reg. c. 2. 19. Itaque cum venisset Bathsheba ad Regem Salomonem, ut loqueretur ei pro Adonia, assurgens Rex obuiam ei incuruauit se, honorem habens ei, & sedens in solio suo, apponi iussit solium matri Regis, quae sedit ad dexteram eius; sed tamen in publicis negotiis regni, contra cuius utilitatem mater petebat, Salomon illi non cessit, neque obediuit. d. c. 2. 20. 21. & seqq. Aliud extat Exod. c. 18. 7. Tum processit Mose obuiam socero suo, & incuruans se osculatus est eum; rogaruntque alter alterum de prosperitate. vbi Moses qui erat Rex populi Iudaici, socero suo, homini priuato honorem obuiam procedendo incuruandoque habuit. Sic fratres maiores natu Iosephi & parentes honore & obseruantia fratrem suum & filium prosecuti sunt. Genes. c. 37. & c. 42. & seqq. Refert Gellius lib. 2. cap. 2. noct. Attic. ad philosophum Taurum Athenas visendi cognoscendique gratia venisse patrem, personam priuatam, cum filio personam publicam gerente. Taurus, allata vna sella, mutauit patrem ut sederet. Atque ille pater ait, Sedeat hic potius qui pop. Romani magistratus est. Absque praeiudicio, inquit Taurus, tu interea sede, dum inspicimus quaerimusque vtrum conueniat tene potius sedere, qui pater es, an filium qui magistratus est. Et cum pater adsedisset, apposituque esset aliud filio quoque sedile, verba Taurus super ea re fecit ita: In publicis locis & muneribus atque actionibus patrum iura cum filiorum, qui in magistratu sunt, potestatibus collata, interquiescere paululum & conuenire. Sed cum extra Rempub. in domestica re atque vita sedeatur,ambuletur,in conuiuio discumbatur, tum inter filium magistratum & patrem priua-tum publicos honores cessare, naturales & ge-nuinos exoriri.Hæc Gellius, Fieri enim potest vt pa-ter vilis,abieƈta & sordida sit persona, cum contra fi-lius sit persona honesta,dignior & honorata.l.sed si v-nius.17.§.13.interdum.de iniur. Pet.Martyr Rom.c.12.& Genef.c.37.11.
units.tr: If the son holds a public person with authority or honour, while the father is a private individual, then in public places and public business the father should yield to the son; but in private affairs and gatherings the public standing will cease and paternal authority will prevail. The example of Sempronius Gracchus, a Roman consul, shows this. When he was going about to uphold his public dignity, his father Quintus Fabius Maximus, a proconsul, met him and, sitting on horseback, sent lictors to him ordering him to dismount. The father obeyed the command promptly and praised his son for refusing to lower the dignity of the Roman people, which befitted his office. Val. Max. lib.2.c.2. There is also an example in Solomon, who, although he was the most powerful king, nevertheless showed his mother the duties of honour and obedience. 1 Kings 2:19. When Bathsheba came to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah, the king rose to meet her, bowed down to her, honouring her, and then, seating himself on his throne, ordered a throne to be set for the king's mother, who sat at his right hand. Yet in the public affairs of the kingdom, against whose advantage his mother was asking, Solomon did not yield to her nor obey her. Ibid. 2:20, 21 and following. Another example is in Exodus 18:7. Then Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him, and they asked each other about their welfare; here Moses, who was king of the Jewish people, showed honour to his father-in-law, a private man, by going out to meet him and bowing. So too the elder brothers of Joseph and his parents showed honour and respect to their brother and son. Genesis 37 and 42 and following. Gellius relates in his Attic Nights, book 2, chapter 2, that a father, a private person, came to Athens to see and meet the philosopher Taurus, while his son held a public office. Taurus brought up a single chair and invited the father to sit. But the father said, "Let him rather sit who is a magistrate of the Roman people." "Without prejudice," said Taurus, "you sit meanwhile, while we consider and ask whether it is more fitting for you, who are the father, or for your son, who is the magistrate, to sit." And when the father had sat down, another seat was also set beside it for the son. Taurus then spoke on this matter as follows: "In public places, in offices and in official acts, the rights of fathers yield to the powers conferred on sons who are in magistracy, and they must rest a little and come together. But when we sit, walk or recline at table outside the commonwealth, in domestic affairs and private life, then the public honours cease between the magistrate son and the private father, and natural and genuine ones arise." These things are from Gellius. For it can happen that the father is a base, abject and squalid person, while the son is an honourable, more worthy and esteemed person. l. sed si unius 17 §13 interdum de iniur.; Petrus Martyr, Romans, c. 12 and Genesis c. 37.11.

Chas.confid.31.& in Aca-demia præstantiore creatus præferendus est ei qui est in Academia inferiori.Chas.cofid.32.d.par. 10.Deniq;Doctor vtriusq; iuris præfertur legum Doctori.Chas.confid.33.& plurium artium & fa-cultatum Doctor alii simplici præfertur.
units.tr: Among teachers, those who actually lecture are preferred as more worthy. l.2 C. ut dign. ordo serv.; lib. 12, l. unic. C. de profes.; Chassanaeus, part 10, consid. 10, who there sets out the requirements from the same law, the unique law: and among lecturers, those who have larger stipends. arg. l.1 (de agendis in rebus), lib. 12, l.1 C. de castrensi. And among several teachers, those who have published books and have been of service to the commonwealth by their writings are more worthy. Chassanaeus, ibid., part 10, consid. 28, and the older are preferred to the younger. l.1 de alb. scrib. Yet a younger man who is more excellent in learning is to be preferred to an older one. Chassanaeus, consid. 30. And one created by the emperor, or by his authority, is to be preferred to one created by any inferior. Chassanaeus, consid. 31. And one created in a more eminent academy is to be preferred to one who is in a lesser academy. Chassanaeus, consid. 32, part 10. Finally, a doctor of both laws is preferred to a doctor of law alone. Chassanaeus, consid. 33, and a doctor of several arts and faculties is preferred to a simple one.

units.la: Præterea inter honoratos officiarios plures honoratior& præstatior habetur, qui prior coo-ptatus in ordinem, honores & munera eadé ge-rentium.l.1. C.de confuI.& nö sparg.nu.l.1.l.2. C.de præfeƈt.prat.l.1.(de præpos.sacri cubic.l.1. de alb scri. vbi Goth.Tacit.li.4.Suet.in Claud.c.16.& in Nerone. c.10.c.1.de maior.& obedient. c.episcoporū etiā.74. dist.c.sin.75.dist Chassan.in libro Catalogi gloriæ mū-di.part,12.confid.99.& part.6.confid.5.
units.tr: Moreover, among honoured officials, the one who was earlier admitted into the order and holds the same honours and offices is regarded as more honoured and more distinguished than the others. l.1 C. de consulibus et non sparg. nu.; l.1, l.2 C. de praefectis praetorio; l.1 (de praepositis sacri cubiculi); l.1 de alb. scrib.; where Gothofredus; Tacitus, book 4; Suetonius, Claudius c.16 and Nero c.10; c.1 de maior. et obedient.; c. episcoporum etiam 74 dist.; c. sin 75 dist.; Chassanaeus in the Catalogue of the Glory of the World, part 12, consid. 99, and part 6, consid. 5.

units.la: Habentes dignitatem cum administratione praeferuntur iis, qui habent dignitatem sine administratione. Pet. Greg. lib. 4. c. 6. c. 10. de Repub. l. 2. C. ut ord. dign. feruet. Chassan. part. 6. confid. 4. & seqq. catal. glor. mundi. qui honorarius dicitur & nihilominus, omnib. aliis inferiorib. dignitatibus praefertur. Nouitius in ordine vltimum gradum obtinet, non quem defunctus vel antecessor habuit. l. si quis. 10. c. de profess. & medic. l. 7. vnicuiq;. C. de prox. sacr. scrin. lib. 12. tit. 19. l. 1. vbi Bartol. C. de consul. & nu. sparg. Chass. consid. 23. par. 4. & prius matriculatus praeferri debet posterius matriculato. l. vlt. ibi iuxta matriculae ordinem. C. de offic. praefect. vrb. Sed de dignitate maiori inter omnes status & ordines late Chassan. part. 3. 4. 5. 6. & seqq. catal. glor. mundi.
units.tr: Those who hold a dignity together with an administration are preferred to those who hold a dignity without administration. Petrus Gregorius, lib. 4, c. 6, c. 10, de Republica; l. 2 C. ut ord. dign. serv.; Chassanaeus, part 6, consid. 4 and following, Catalogue of the Glory of the World. The one called honorary, nevertheless, is preferred to all other lower dignities. A novice in an order holds the last rank, not the rank that the deceased or predecessor held. l. si quis 10 C. de profess. et medic.; l.7 unicuique C. de proximis sacrorum scriniis, lib. 12 tit. 19; l.1, where Bartolus; C. de consulibus et nu. sparg.; Chassanaeus, consid. 23, part 4. And one who was matriculated earlier should be preferred to one matriculated later. l. ult., where "according to the order of the matricula"; C. de officio praefecti urbi. But concerning greater dignity among all states and orders, see at length Chassanaeus, parts 3, 4, 5, 6 and following, Catalogue of the Glory of the World.

units.la: Supernumerarius, hoc est, qui vltra ordinarium statutumq; numerum adsumptus & cooptatus est, vltimum locum occupat. dict. l. 7. vnicuiq. l. 1. C. de collegiat. & charto. lib. 11. tit. 18. l. vlt. C. de apparit. magist. lib. 12. tit. 54. Qua de re pluribus egi in lib. 1. Dicaeologica, c. 38.
units.tr: A supernumerary, that is, one who has been admitted and co-opted beyond the ordinary and fixed number, occupies the last place. Said law 7 unicuique; l.1 C. de collegiatis et chartularis, lib. 11 tit. 18; l. ult. C. de apparitoribus magistratuum, lib. 12 tit. 54. I have treated this matter at more length in book 1 of the Dicaeologica, c. 38.

units.la: Qui princeps est collegii primicerius, Graecis vocatur reliqui primates ex ordine, secundocerius, tertiocerius, quartocerius, & sicde inceps, tot. ti. C. de primic. & secund. ocer. vbi Gu. Apud Iudaeos erant Archisynagogi, Nu. c. 4. 34. c. 16. 2. Matt. c. 9. 18. Luc. 8. 41. 47. Marc. c. 5. 22. 23. & principes tribuu & familiarum, ciuitatum, populi. de quib. latis. lib. 1. Dicaeol. c. 6. & Sigo lib. de Repub. Heb.
units.tr: The leader of a college is called the primicerius; the others who are the chief men in order are, in Greek, the secundocerius, tertiocerius, quartocerius, and so on in sequence. Title "de primicerio et secundocerio", where Gutierrez. Among the Jews there were archisynagogues, Num. 4:34; 16:2; Matt. 9:18; Luke 8:41, 47; Mark 5:22, 23, and the princes of tribes and families, of cities and of the people. On these matters see at length book 1 of the Dicaeologica, c. 6, and Sigonius, book on the Hebrew Commonwealth.

units.la: Apud Romanos populus ex praestantia & dignitate distribuebatur in tres ordines: Primus erat senatorum; secundus & intermedius equestris; tertius & infimus,erat plebeiorum. Sigon. de antiq.iur.ciu. Roman. & dixi lib. 1. Dicaeol. cap. 6.
units.tr: Among the Romans the people were divided by excellence and dignity into three orders: the first was that of the senators; the second and intermediate was the equestrian; the third and lowest was that of the plebeians. Sigonius, On the Ancient Civil Law of the Romans; and I have discussed it in book 1 of the Dicaeologica, chap. 6.

units.la: Inter Ecclesiasticos quoq; gradus dignitatis & honoris constituti. Alii enim ex hisce Apostoli fuerunt, alii prophetæ, alii Euangelistæ, alii pastores & doctores. Ephes. c. 4. In Papatu alii clerici, alii psalmistæ, alii ostiarii, lectores, exorcistæ, acolythi, subdiaconi, diaconi, presbyteri, Episcopi, Archiepiscopi, seu metropolitæ, patriarchæ & cardinales, & denique summus Pontifex. vid. Pet. Greg. lib. 15. Syntagm. c. 3. & in iure Canonico passim latissime Chassan. part. 3. & 4. catal. glor. mundi.
units.tr: Degrees of dignity and honour were also established among the ecclesiastical orders. For some of these were apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, others ministers and teachers. Eph. 4. In Papacy there are clerks, psalmists, doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, elders, bishops, archbishops or metropolitans, patriarchs and cardinals, and finally the supreme Pontiff. See Petrus Gregorius, lib. 15, Syntagma c. 3, and throughout the canon law, very fully, Chassanaeus, parts 3 and 4, Catalogue of the Glory of the World.

units.la: Sequitur de affectione mutua digniorum & viliorum inter se inuicem in ciuili conuersatione, ad quam vterq; se, quantum salua conscientia & pietate fieri potest, conformare debet, & se affectibus superioris honorati, adcommodare, adeo vt proprias affectiones non habeat inferior, sed praestantioris in seriis, iocosis, iucundis & tristibus sequatur. Obsequia enim amicos & gratiosos faciunt homines. Iuxta illud, Vitia & virtutes hominis, cum quo vivis, noueris, non oderis eundem, cuius errata æquo animo tuleris, Roman. c. 15. 1. Debemus autem nos, qui firmi sumus, imbecillitates infirmorum portare, ac non indulgere nobis ipsis, 2. Itaq; vnusquisq; nostrum proximo placeat in bonum, id est, ad eius ædificationem. Coloss. c. 3. 13. Tolerantes alii alios & condonantes vobis mutuo. Ephes. c. 4, 2. 32. arg. 1. Pet. c. 2. 18. Genes. c. 9. 22. 13. & Cato:
units.tr: There follows the matter of mutual affection between the more honoured and the less honoured in civil conversation, to which each should conform as far as a good conscience and piety allow, and should accommodate himself to the affections of the superior person, so that the inferior has no affections of his own, but follows those of the more distinguished in serious matters, jesting, pleasures and sorrows. For compliance makes men friends and agreeable. Accordingly, the faults and virtues of the man with whom you live you should know, but not hate him whose errors you have borne with an even mind, Romans 15:1. "We who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not please ourselves," 2 Cor. ... "Let each of us therefore please his neighbour for good, that is, for his edification." Colossians 3:13. "Bearing with one another and forgiving one another." Ephesians 4:2, 32; argument from 1 Peter 2:18; Genesis 9:22, 13; and Cato:

units.la: Vincere cum possis interdum, cede sodali:
units.tr: Since you can sometimes conquer, yield to your comrade:

units.la: Obsequio quoniam dulces retinentur amici.Quae superare potes, interdum vince ferendo:Maxima enim morum semper patientia virtus.
units.tr: For friends are kept sweet by compliance. Whatever you can overcome, sometimes overcome by bearing it, for patience is always the greatest virtue of character.

units.la: Viliores, inopes, tenuiores, humiles, seu inferiores, vtilitatem spectant, vt nimirum a diuitibus & honoratis consequantur commoda & vtilia, vt pecuniam, diuitias, dignitatem & officia; atque haec ab iis superioribus, quibus vitae suae vsuram locant & obsequia praestant, tanquam laborum suorum mercedem exspectant, & de iis solis sunt soliciti & anxii; tum quoque, vt ob imbecillitatem suam aduersus iniurias aliorum promotionem amicos, patronos & defensores sibi comparent.
units.tr: The lower sort, the poor, the needy, the humble, or those of inferior rank, look to their advantage: namely, that they may obtain from the rich and honoured what is useful and profitable to them, such as money, riches, dignity and offices. They expect these things from their superiors, to whom they hire out their life's labour and render their services, as the reward of their toil, and they are anxious and concerned about these alone. They also seek to win for themselves friends, patrons and defenders, so that, being weak, they may be protected against the injuries of others.

units.la: Digniores contrà & honoratiores, prout variis ex causis exstimationem & opinionem apud alios sibi comparararunt, ita & variis affectionibus & cupiditatibus sunt obnoxii, & existimant se πολυτιμότερους, id est, magnifieri debere ab iis, qui sunt inferiores. Ita enim comparatum, vt qua in re quis praestiterit, ea ipsa quoque se fieri magni debere, censeat. Contrà, graviter irascuntur & ferre nequaquam possunt, quando contemnuntur in eiusmodi rebus, quae proprie ad eos pertinent. Propter excellentiam enim, quam sibi ipsi imaginantur, quasi suo iure postulant honorem sibi deferri, quem si ab inferioribus non impetrant, ceu debito suo fraudari se indignantur. Existimant etiam conueniens esse, vt ab iis magni fiant & honorentur, a quibus sibi benefieri debere putant. Vnde fit, vt illi irascantur τὰς ἀλλυμένας inprimis, quando nihili nulliusque existimationis homines, eos parui faciunt, vel contemnunt. Contra vero leniessint τὸς πολυωφέλει. Aristot. lib. 2. Rhetor.
units.tr: The more worthy and honoured, on the other hand, having won esteem and reputation among others for various reasons, are subject to various passions and desires. They think themselves [πολυτιμότερους] (that is, they believe they ought to be held in greater honour) by those who are their inferiors. For it is the nature of things that a man thinks he ought to be valued all the more in that very matter in which he excels. Conversely, they grow bitterly angry and cannot bear it at all when they are despised in those matters which properly pertain to them. For on account of the excellence they imagine in themselves, they demand as though by right that honour be paid them, and if they do not obtain it from their inferiors, they are indignant at being cheated of what is their due. They also think it fitting that they be valued and honoured by those from whom they believe they ought to receive benefits. Hence it is that they are especially angry at [τὰς ἀλλυμένας] those who are of no worth or esteem when such men make little of them or despise them. But on the contrary they are gentler towards [τὸς πολυωφέλει] those who are of great benefit. Aristotle, Rhetoric book 2.

units.la: Sunt autem eiusmodi honoratiores & dignio-tes quidam diuites, quidam senes experientiâ & prudentiâ pollentes, quidam potentes, quidam genere nobiles, vel virtute aut eruditione excellentes. Ier. c. 9. 23. 1. Reg. c. 3. 9. 12. 13. Eccl. cap. 44. 1. 2. & seqq. c. 45. 1. 2. & seqq. & c. seqq. Eccles. c. 9. 13. & seqq. c. 5. 18. c. 8. 2.
units.tr: Such honoured and worthy persons are of various kinds: some are rich, some are old and strong in experience and prudence, some are powerful, some noble by birth, or excellent in virtue or learning. Jer. 9:23. 1 Kings 3:9, 12, 13. Ecclus. 44:1, 2 and following; 45:1, 2 and following; and the following chapters. Eccles. 9:13 and following; 5:18; 8:2.

units.la: Diuites quidem & locupletes bonis affluentes, nullum sequuntur emolumentum, sed id modo attendunt, quod eam sibi coniunctionem inferioris, ad splendorem dignitatis honorificam, ad victum autem cultumq; atque res gerendas, cum iucundam, tum vero multis sanè locis peroportunam esse intelligunt. Est enim locupletum natura & mos, ut superbia, insolentia & fastidio efferantur, & luxuria pene diffluant, propter delicias quas perpetuò sectantur, & quarum ostentatione beati videri volunt. Perinde enim affecti viuunt, quasi omnibus affluant bonis; & quia pecunia omnia venduntur & comparari possunt, ideo omnium rerum pretium penes se esse opinantur, ob id q; se beatos esse exi stimant. Ad hoc accedit, quod homines in re facienda & exaggeranda occupatos & diuitiis inhiantes videant. Quare possessione huius tanquam excellenti inter homines bono quodam, quod vnum expetunt, quodq; admirantur, omnes ipsi gloriantur, & reliquos despiciunt: quae insolentia & arrogantia augetur, quod multos multa locupletem rogare sit necesse, ideo dignos se domidominatu arbitrantur. Nam diuitiæ sua natura gloriosæ & insolentes sunt, atq; petulantiam su-perbiæ comitem habent, sicuti quoq; copiarum ostentationem, luxuriam & mollitiem. Vt recte Galatæus ex Aristotele lib. 2. Rhetor. disserit, & apparet ex Luc. c. 16. 19. & seqq. 1. Timoth. cap. 6. 17. 18. Matth. c. 6. 21. Eccles. c. 13. 1. 2. 3. 4. 21. & seqq. & c. 31. 3. 4. & seqq. c. 10 33. 34. 35. 25. 26. 27. c. 11. 14. 22. cap. 40. 1. Sam. c. 18. 18. 23. Iacob. cap. 2. 2. 3. Deut. c. 15. & passim alibi, vbi affectiones & studia diuitum & potentiorum describuntur. Vide Aristotelem lib. 2. Rhetor. & recte Horatius dicit:
units.tr: The rich and wealthy, abounding in goods, seek no advantage from this, but attend only to this: that they understand that a union with an inferior is honourable for the splendour of their dignity, and, for their livelihood, their cultivation and the conduct of affairs, both pleasant and in many places very convenient. For it is the nature and custom of the wealthy to be puffed up with pride, insolence and disdain, and to almost dissolve in luxury, on account of the pleasures they constantly pursue and by whose display they wish to be seen as blessed. For they live as though they abounded in every good; and because all things are bought and sold for money, they think the price of all things lies in their hands, and therefore they consider themselves blessed. Added to this is that men are seen to be busy in making and increasing wealth and to gape after riches. Therefore, possessing this as a certain excellent good among men, which alone they seek and admire, they all boast of it and despise the rest; and this insolence and arrogance grows, because many must ask much of the rich man, and so they think themselves worthy of lordship in their house. For riches are by their nature boastful and insolent, and they have petulance, the companion of pride, as well as the display of wealth, luxury and softness. As Galataeus rightly argues from Aristotle, Rhetoric book 2, and it appears from Luke 16:19 and following; 1 Timothy 6:17, 18; Matthew 6:21; Eccles. 13:1–4, 21 and following; 31:3, 4 and following; 10:33–35, 25–27; 11:14, 22; Ecclus. 40:1; 1 Sam. 18:18, 23; James 2:2, 3; Deut. 15, and passim elsewhere, where the dispositions and pursuits of the rich and powerful are described. See Aristotle, Rhetoric book 2, and Horace rightly says:

units.la: omnis enim res: Virtus, fama, decus, diuina humanaq; pulcris Diuitiis parent; quas qui construxerit, ille Clarus erit, fortis, iustus, sapiens etiam & rex, Et quidquid volet.
units.tr: For all things: virtue, fame, honour, and things divine and human, are won by beautiful riches; he who has built them up will be famous, brave, just, wise, even a king, and whatever he wishes.

units.la: Senectus quoq; venerabilis iuuenibus esse debet. Leu. c. 19. 32. 1. Timoth. c. 5. 1. 2. 3. 4. 17. Tit. c. 2. 1. 2. Prou. c. 10 29. Eccles. cap. 25. 7. 8. & seqq. 1. Pet. c. 5. 5. Iob c. 32 6. c. 12. 12. 1. Reg c. 12. 6. 7. 8. Ezech. c. 7. Deut. c. 21. 2. late Tiraquell. De iure primogenitorum, in præfat. n 80. & seqq. & latius dixi lib. 1. Dicæol. c. 6. Ouid. ç. Fastor.
units.tr: Old age also ought to be venerable to the young. Lev. 19:32. 1 Tim. 5:1–4, 17. Titus 2:1, 2. Prov. 10:29. Ecclus. 25:7, 8 and following. 1 Pet. 5:5. Job 32:6; 12:12. 1 Kings 12:6–8. Ezek. 7. Deut. 21:2. Widely Tiraquellus, On the right of firstborns, preface, n. 80 and following; and I have discussed it more fully in book 1, Dicaeol. ch. 6. Ovid, Fasti.

units.la: Magna fuit quondam capitis, reuerentia cani; Inq; suo pretio ruga senilis erat.
units.tr: Once there was great reverence for the grey head, and the wrinkle of old age was held in high esteem.

units.la: Maiores natu, inquit Gell lib. 2. cap. 15. a minoribus colebantur ad Deum prope & parentum vicem, atque in omni loco inq; omni specie honoris priores potiores habiti. & seqq. & Cic. lib. 1. Offic. Est, dicit, adolescentis, maiores natu vereri, & eu qui ætate nos anteit, tanquam superiore colere debemus. Porro senectutis naeui sunt, quod natura sua solcat senes esse suspiciosi, morosi, difficiles, queruli, austeri, aua-ri, tristes, in quas senectutis affectiones ne in-currat Ethicus, prudenter cauebit, vid. Aristot. lib. 2. Rhetor.
units.tr: Gellius, book 2, chapter 15, says: the elder men of old were honoured by the younger, nearly in the place of God and of parents, and in every place and in every kind of honour the elders were held first and most worthy. And so on. Cicero, On Duties, book 1: It is the duty of a young man, he says, to revere his elders, and to honour the one who surpasses us in age as our superior. Furthermore, old age has its faults, since by its nature old men tend to be suspicious, peevish, difficult, querulous, austere, avaricious and gloomy; the ethical man will prudently guard against falling into these affections of old age. See Aristotle, Rhetoric book 2.

units.la: Naturam & mores senum Scaliger in Idea Poetices, vt à Chytræo allegatur, describit hoc mo-do. Senilis, inquit, ætas ex parte maxima contra-ria est moribus adolescentiæ. Ergo quod diu vi-xerint, parum sperant, pauca moliuntur, præte-ritis gaudent, quæ sola probant præiis quæ præ-sentia sunt; quibus non adquiescunt. Nouarum rerum obtrectatores, semper habent quod obiiciant. Soliciti officiorum exactores, ad rem at-tenti, lenti ac difficiles, ad persuasiones cauti, at-que etiam suspiciosi. Multa enim indigne aut se, aut alios perpessos meminere. Ac quemad-modum adolescentes spe, ita senes memoria metiuntur omnia. Raro affirmant ea, quorum non habeant exemplum in memoria; rarius deiiciuntur de sententia, rarissimè sibi alias an-teferri patiuntur ætates. Meticulosi, pertinaci vlterioris vitæ exspectatione, queruli. Odia ho-stiliter exercent, atq; etiam conuicia. Garruli, tristes, importuni interpellatores: semper et-iam quippiam imminentis mali minitantur. Quamobrem exercet frequentissimas compa-rationes, &c.
units.tr: Scaliger, in his Poetics, as cited by Chytraeus, describes the nature and manners of old men in this way. "Old age," he says, "is for the most part contrary to the manners of youth. Therefore, since they have lived long, they hope little, undertake few things, rejoice in the past, and approve only what is past, not what is present, with which they are not content. They are detractors of new things and always have something to object." They are anxious exactors of duties, attentive to business, slow and difficult, cautious in being persuaded, and also suspicious. For they remember many things that they or others have suffered unworthily. And just as young men measure everything by hope, so old men measure everything by memory. They rarely affirm things of which they have no example in memory; they are more rarely turned from their opinion, and most rarely do they allow that the ages after them are preferred to their own. They are timid, querulous, and stubborn in their expectation of a further life. They pursue hatreds with hostility, and even with reproaches. They are talkative, gloomy, troublesome interrupters; they always also threaten some impending evil. Therefore they practise very frequent comparisons, and so on.

units.la: Contrà natura adolescentum alia est, quam idem Scaliger ita describit: Fertur atq; etiam im-pellitur, inquit, ætas prima hæc tum facilè, tum vehementer ad ea quæ concupiscit. Concupi-scit autem & statim & multa potita contemnit; ad alia animum appellit; præceps potius ani-mus, mus, quam magna voluens. Iram atque animum ipsum in fronte atque ore gerunt. Anteuertit impetus deliberationi, facta verbis, poenitentia perfectioni. Honoris atque praelationis exactores importuni potius, quam seduli vindicatores. Contemtus vltores; ipsi contemtores diuersorum à suis studiorum. Laudatoribus suis fauent, odere monitores. Potentiae studiosi; opum negligentes. Ipse enim aluntfiduciam sui. Liberalitatem exercent, ignari fortunae deterioris. Omnino simplicitatem & à se profitentur, & ab aliis exigunt. Parum suspicaces, credduli multum. Honesta vtilibus anteponunt; nondum acuit eos rerum experientia. Sibi ipsis lex sunt. Sodalitatum atque societatum studiosi, sibi ita viuunt, vt credi velint aliis quoque viuere. Denique nihil mediocre. Alienarum miseriarum pii obseruatores; suarum securi. In iocos soluti; verecundiae obnoxii in erroribus, elati in benefactis. Omnino autem iuuenis naturâ inter adolescentiae & senectutis tempora, vt media est, ita & particeps tum viriorum, tum virtutum, scilicet affectuum atque propensionum.
units.tr: On the other hand, the nature of young men is different, which the same Scaliger describes thus: "This first age," he says, "is carried along and also driven, both easily and vehemently, towards the things it desires. It desires at once, and having gained many things it despises them; it turns its mind to other things, a mind rash rather than pondering great matters. They bear anger and the mind itself openly in face and expression. Impulse anticipates deliberation, deeds come before words, and repentance before completion. They are troublesome demanders of honour and precedence rather than diligent avengers. They avenge contempt; they themselves despise those whose pursuits differ from theirs. They favour those who praise them, and hate those who advise them. They are zealous for power and negligent of wealth. For they nourish confidence in themselves. They practise liberality, ignorant of worse fortune. In general they both profess simplicity for themselves and demand it from others. They are little suspicious, very credulous. They put honourable things before useful ones; experience of affairs has not yet sharpened them. They are a law to themselves. Zealous for fellowships and societies, they live for themselves in such a way that they wish others to believe they live the same way. In short, nothing in them is moderate. They are pious observers of others' miseries and careless of their own. They are loose in jests, prone to shame at mistakes, and elated by benefits." In general, the young man by nature, lying between the times of youth and old age, is in the middle, and so shares in both the vices and the virtues, that is, in the passions and inclinations.

units.la: Potentum & honores seu munera gerentium natura, mores & affectio cum locupletum consuetudine & natura congruunt, & partim aliquanto etiam probiores sunt. Nam & honorum studium in hisce est, & animus virilis atque ad agendum promptus. Praebet enim potentia facultatem, & propter dignitatem grauitas inest. Nulla autem de re magis solliciti sunt potentes, quam vt ne cuipiam succumbere, aut quidquam cuiquam concedere videantur; austeri, tristes, duri, omnia summo iure seuerè agentes, atq; acerbè, qui si appellentur modo, continuo ad calculos abeunt, confestim sua & aliena metiuntur & rationem subducunt à quâ discedere nefas arbitrantur. Ideoq; quæuis sibi arrogant,& nemini cedere volunt; atq; ob potentiam suam videri & aliis præferri cupiunt: & sua perpetuo iactant & laudem quærunt. quas affectiones superbiæ videre licet in exemplis Dauidis, numerantis populum, 2.Sam.c.24. in Roboamo superbè populo suo respondente. 1.Reg.c.12.14.16. Ozia, sacerdotium ambiente, 2. Chron.c.26.19. Sennacherib. Esa.c.36.37. in Hamano, Esth.c.7.10. Nebucadnezare, Daniel.c.4.27. Herode, Act.c.12.23. & in exemplis superbissimorum hominum, Xerxis, Alexandri, Iulii Caesaris, Pompeii, Caligulae, & aliorum, vide Arist. lib.2. Rhetor.
units.tr: The nature, manners and disposition of the powerful and of those who hold honours or offices agree with the habits and character of the wealthy, and in some respects they are even somewhat more upright. For among them there is both a zeal for honours and a manly spirit ready for action. Power provides opportunity, and gravity goes with dignity. Yet no men are more anxious about anything than the powerful that they should not seem to give way to anyone or to concede anything to anyone. They are stern, gloomy, hard, and they carry everything out with the full rigour of the law and with harshness. If they are merely addressed, they at once go to reckoning, straightway measure their own affairs and those of others, and work out an account from which they think it wrong to depart. Therefore they claim everything for themselves and will yield to no one; because of their power they wish to be seen and preferred to others, they constantly boast of their own deeds and seek praise. These feelings of pride may be seen in the examples of David numbering the people, 2.Sam.c.24.; of Rehoboam answering his people arrogantly, 1.Reg.c.12.14.16.; of Uzziah, who aspired to the priesthood, 2. Chron.c.26.19.; of Sennacherib, Esa.c.36.37.; in Haman, Esth.c.7.10.; of Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel.c.4.27.; of Herod, Act.c.12.23.; and in the examples of the most proud men, Xerxes, Alexander, Julius Caesar, Pompey, Caligula and others: see Arist. lib.2. Rhetor.

units.la: Nobilium mores & natura fere cum praecedentibus eadem. Sunt enim honoris immodici appetentissimi, & aliorum contemptores, ideoque superbi, inimici popularium, gulosi, luxuriosi, libidinosi. De quibus nobilium nauis late Tiraquell. De nobilitat. cap.23. & Aristot. libr.2. Rhetor.
units.tr: The manners and nature of the nobles are almost the same as those of the preceding group. For they are greedy for immoderate honour and despisers of others, and therefore proud, hostile to the common people, gluttonous, luxurious and lustful. On these faults of the nobility see at length Tiraquell. De nobilitat. cap.23. and Aristot. libr.2. Rhetor.

units.la: Haec vitia etiam viris doctis virtutibusque praestantissimis cum superioribus sunt communia, vide Spinaum lib.2. in Ambit, vbi exemplis illustrat.
units.tr: These vices are common to learned men and to those most outstanding in virtue, as well as to the preceding groups: see Spinaus lib.2. in Ambit., where he illustrates them with examples.

units.la: Commune omnium & singulorum honoratorum vitium est, quod laudari cupiant & honorari, & quod superiorem vel parem vix ferre possint, qui in dignitate vel honore ipsis sit superior, vel par. Spinaus dict. libr. 2. in Ambit. id probat exemplo Iosephi & fratrum eiusdem, Genef. cap. 37. Saulis & Dauidis, 1. Sam. c. 17. Abfolomi & Dauidis, 2. Sam. c. 15. Solomonis & Ieroboami, 1. Reg. c. 11. & quam plurimis aliis profanis. Ad quas affectiones refrenandas & cohibendas videndus Ierem. cap. 9. 23. Sic ait Ieho-ua, Non gloriator sapiens in sapientia sua, neque gloriator potens in potentia sua, neque gloriator dives in divitiis suis, &c. 2. Corinth. c. 10. 17. & late Spinaus d. loco.
units.tr: It is a common vice of all and each of the honoured that they wish to be praised and honoured, and that they can hardly bear a man who is equal or superior to them in dignity or honour. Spinaus, in the book just cited, Ambit. lib.2., proves this by the example of Joseph and his brothers, Gen. cap. 37; of Saul and David, 1 Sam. c. 17. Absalom and David, 2 Sam. c. 15. Solomon and Jeroboam, 1 Kings c. 11, and very many other profane examples. To restrain and check these passions, see Jer. cap. 9. 23: Thus says the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man glory in his might, nor the rich man glory in his riches, etc.; 2 Cor. c. 10. 17, and at length Spinaus in the place cited.

units.la: Haec igitur affectiones, consuetudo & natura, studia & voluntates, & vitia honoratorum, superiorum vel digniorum, nota debent esse vilioribus, humilibus & inferioribus, ut ad ea se dirigere, & cum illis conuersari utiliter possint. Ut ergo iucunda & grata sit talis conuersatio, necesse est ut inferiores & humiles eiusmodi ad superiorum arbitrium, sensumque viuant, quo facta, dicta, motus & gestus referant, cum humilitate & reuerentia; ut sciant, quibus verbis gestibusque exhilarentur, quibusve offendantur. Plane haec sec-ta, inquit Galatus, beneficentia & suauitate capitur & iisdem retinetur; violentia vero & asperitate fugatur. Sic igitur animati erga potentes, pecuniosos, nobiles, senes, doctos; tenues humiles & plebeii esse debent, ut illorum incommoda, iniurias, ineptias, non modo facile perferant, sed amanter quoque tegant, eosque quoad fieri poterit, diligant, colant & omnibus in locis obseruent; de suo iure animo hilari & aequo discedat, & obsequio prompto eos semper demulceant, ita vt quæcunq; nos retrahunt ab obse-quio & cultu potentioris, locupletioris, nobilioris, honoratioris, illa fugiamus & omittamus. Nam huic obsequio & obseruantiæ nihil tam est aduersum, quam arrogantia, quæ sibi vindicat quæ in alio agnoscere, eiq; adscribere debebat. Atq; ideo à nobis diligi volunt superiores & honoratiores, quod existiment, à quibus amantur, iisdem etiam se probari. Difficile enim est, vt quem non probas, eundem diligas. Siquidem colimus & obseruamus, quos insigni aliqua re antecellere putamus, & quibus placere volumus.
units.tr: These dispositions, habits and inclinations, pursuits and wills, and the faults of the honoured, the superior or the more worthy, ought to be known to the lowlier, the humble and the inferior, so that they can usefully direct themselves to them and live with them. Therefore, if such intercourse is to be pleasant and agreeable, the inferior and the humble must live according to the judgement and feeling of their superiors, so that they may report their deeds, words, movements and gestures with humility and reverence, and know by what words and gestures they are cheered, or by what they are offended. Galatus says: this sort of people is won by kindness and courtesy and kept by them, but is driven off by violence and harshness. Thus, those who are humble and of lowly rank ought to be so disposed towards the powerful, the wealthy, the nobles, the aged and the learned that they not only readily bear their inconveniences, wrongs and follies, but also lovingly cover them over, and, as far as possible, love, cherish and honour them everywhere; they should give up their own right with a cheerful and fair mind, and always soothe them by ready deference, so that whatever draws us away from obedience and respect to the more powerful, wealthier, nobler or more honoured, we avoid and leave aside. For nothing is so opposed to this obedience and observance as arrogance, which claims for itself what it ought to recognise in another and ascribe to him. And so superiors and the more honoured want to be loved by us, because they think that those by whom they are loved also approve of them. For it is difficult to love one whom you do not approve. Indeed we cultivate and honour those whom we think to excel in some notable quality, and whom we wish to please.

units.la: Non omittendæ quoq; ab humilioribus & inferioribus sunt actiones illæ, quarum omissio eosdem de vitiis, inprimis de oligoria suspectos reddere possit. Sic enim, qui antea aliquem honorare est solitus, eiusq; curā habere, & id ipsum postea facere intermittit, de oligoria & contemptu suo indicium præbet alii.
units.tr: Nor should the lowly and inferior neglect those actions whose omission could make them suspected of vices, especially of disregard. For someone who was accustomed to honour another, and to look after him, and then stops doing so, shows to others a sign of disregard and contempt on his part.

units.la: Gratiam quoq; non referens, iram aliorum in se concitat & benefactoris contemptum præ se fert.
units.tr: Likewise, one who does not return a favour stirs up the anger of others against himself and displays contempt for his benefactor.

units.la: Præterea qui aliis omnibus benefacit, & vnum solum præterit, eiusdem iræ & contemtus suspicionem præbet: quasi scilicet non dignus sit beneficio vnus ille, quo omnes alios dignatur? Sic & obliuio alicuius est ὀλιγωρίας indicium, & incommodatio & comparatio cum inferioribus se.
units.tr: Moreover, one who does good to all others but passes over one alone gives rise to the suspicion of anger and contempt towards that one, as if he were not worthy of the benefit by which he favours all the others. So too forgetting someone is a sign of disregard [ὀλιγωρίας], and so is withholding help and comparing oneself with one's inferiors.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: De cultu, reuerentia & obsequio communi, quod honoratioribus & dignioribus sermone praestatur.
units.tr: On the worship, reverence and common deference that are shown in speech to the more honourable and worthy.

units.la: TAntum de primo requisito conuersationis & Ethicae propriae inter digniores & inferiores, seu tenuiores. Sequitur nunc de altero eiusdem requisito; officio nimirum eorundem inter se inuicem in ciuili conuersatione; quod consistit in vsu sermonis & habitus, seu gestus hisce personis conuenientium, quibus scilicet agnoscant dona quibus honorandi & excellentes homines sunt praediti, eosque ob ea, amore prosequantur. 1.Thess.c.5.12. Rogamus vos fratres, ut agnoscatis eos qui laborant inter vos, & vobis praesunt in Domino, & admonent vos. 13. & quam maxime charos ducatis propter opus ipsorum. Iob c.29.9.10.11. c.30.1.2, & seqq. Eccles.c.3.9. Opere & sermone honora patrem tuum. adde 2.Sam. c. 25.24. & seqq.2. Reg.6.13, 14.cap.2.12,c.6.21. 1.Timoth. c.5.4. Ioh. c.19.26.27.c.6.5.8. 1.Corinth.c.4.15. Eccles.c.4.7. Coram magnate demitte caput tuum. Iustitia enim vult, ut suum cuique tribuatur, etiam honos cui honor debetur. Rom.c.13.7. Malach.c.1.6. Filius honorat patrem & servus dominum suum. Quod si Pater vester sum, vbi est honor meus? & si Dominus sum, vbi reuerentia mei? 1.Pet.c.2.17. 1.Timoth.c.6. Roman.c.12.10. Philip.c.2.3. 1.Pet.cap.5.5. Coloss.c.2.23. 1.Samuel.cap.2.30. Iohan.cap.8. 49. 1.Timoth. cap.5.3.17.
units.tr: So much for the first requirement of conversation and of ethics proper between the more worthy and the inferior, or humbler. Now follows the second requirement of the same: namely, the duty of these people towards one another in civil conversation, which consists in the use of speech and of bearing or gesture fitting for such persons, by which they acknowledge the gifts with which the honourable and excellent are endowed, and so cherish them with affection. 1 Thess. 5:12. We beseech you, brothers, to acknowledge those who labour among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you. 13. And to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Job 29:9-11; 30:1-2, and following. Eccles. 3:9. Honour your father in deed and word. Add 2 Sam. 25:24ff. 2 Kings 6:13-14; 2:12; 6:21. 1 Tim. 5:4. John 19:26-27; 6:5, 8. 1 Cor. 4:15. Eccles. 4:7. Before a great man bow your head. For justice wills that each be given his due, and honour to whom honour is owed. Rom. 13:7. Mal. 1:6. A son honours his father and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honour? And if I am a lord, where is my reverence towards me? 1 Pet. 2:17. 1 Tim. 6. Rom. 12:10. Phil. 2:3. 1 Pet. 5:5. Col. 2:23. 1 Sam. 2:30. John 8:49. 1 Tim. 5:3, 17.

units.la: Officium ergo popularium, tenuiorum & inferiorum erga honoratiores & superiores, consistit in motibus reuerentialibus & obsequia-libus; hoc est, in vsu sermonis & gestus talium, qui superiori reuerentiam, obseruantiam, honorem & obsequium tribuunt, quibusque virtutes & dona superioris, quibus excellit, aut sane ornatus esse debebat, agnoscat, colat, exosculetur & admiretur, cum humilitate etiam suam agnoscens penuriam & indigentiam. Hisce igitur virtutibus & donis honorationis, congruenter loqui & agere & mores suos in sermone & actionibus suis conformare & adcommodare necesse habet; atq; omnia contraria hisce, inprimis contemptum, arrogantiam, vanitatem & futilitatem, atque scurrilitatem fugere debet. 1.Pet.c.3.1.2. Vbi speciarint cum reuerentia coniunctam castam conuersatione vestram, 1.Timoth.c.2.9.10.11.12. Cicero alibi de hoc ita: Venerationest virtus qua reuerentiam exhibemus maioribus in corporis humiliatione, gestu, nutu & verborum emissione. & idem alibi: Obseruantia est, per quam homines aliqua dignitate antecedentes, cultu quodam & honore veneramur. Reuerentia est honor qui exhibetur cum pauore inter maiores & minores. Chass. part. 1. confid. 71. cat. glor. mundi. & sic præstatur ratione potestatis & dignitatis.
units.tr: The duty of the common people, the humble and the inferior towards the more honourable and superiors, therefore consists in reverential and deferential movements, that is, in the use of speech and gesture of those who give to a superior reverence, respect, honour and deference, and who acknowledge, cherish, kiss, and admire the virtues and gifts by which the superior excels, or ought to be adorned, while also acknowledging with humility their own poverty and need. Therefore one must speak and act fittingly with these virtues and gifts of honour, and shape and adapt one's manners to them in speech and deeds; and above all one must flee everything contrary to these, namely contempt, arrogance, vanity, frivolity and buffoonery. 1 Pet. 3:1-2. When they have seen your chaste conduct joined with reverence. 1 Tim. 2:9-12. Cicero, elsewhere, says of this: Veneration is the virtue by which we show reverence to our elders in the bowing of the body, in bearing, in nod and in the utterance of words. And the same elsewhere: Observance is that by which we venerate, with a certain cult and honour, men who excel in some dignity. Reverence is the honour that is shown with awe between elders and juniors. Chass. part 1, consid. 71, On the glory of the world. And so it is rendered on account of power and dignity.

units.la: Sunt autem generaliter hic duæ regulæ inferioribus & humiliorib. in vsu sermonis & habitus reuerentialium erga superiores semper obseruandæ.
units.tr: Generally, there are two rules that inferiors and humbler persons must always observe in the use of speech and of reverential bearing towards superiors.

units.la: Prima est, vt debitus honor habita ratione dignitatis cuiusque, cuiq; digniori exhibeatur, ne quid in hoc peccetur in defectu, vel excessu.
units.tr: The first is that the honour due, with regard to the dignity of each, be paid to each more worthy person, so that nothing is sinned in this by defect or excess.

units.la: In excessu peccatur, quando in moribus hisce reuerentialibus prastandis, sunt exquisiti, superflui, nimii & prodigi. Hinc suæ vanitatis, leuitatis, adulationis & nugarum specimen eduñt, & suspicionem de se præbent superioribus & aliis. Honorationibus etiam isti palpatores suspicionem præbent de se; quem scilicet adeo stupidum, hebetem & simplicem esse existimant, vt hisce blanditiis inescari & capi posse opinentur. Et quid aliud est immodicus eiusmodi honor & obseruantia, quam irrisio & contemptus & iniustitia? Sic Iudæi Christo illudentes, summos honores, mores & habitus summissos præstiterunt. Matth. cap. 27. 28. 29. 30. 31. 32. Iniusti quoque tales prodigi & palpatores apparent, quod non suum cuique honorem, sed honorando alienum & non congruentem dignitatiq; eiusdem non responden-tem, vel maiorem, altiori & excellentiori debitum, præstent.
units.tr: Sin is committed by excess when, in paying these reverential courtesies, people are affected, superfluous, excessive and prodigal. Hence they display a specimen of their own vanity, levity, flattery and trifling, and give others and their superiors cause for suspicion about themselves. These flatterers also give cause for suspicion about themselves through their honours; for they think the one they fawn upon is so stupid, dull and simple that they suppose he can be caught and enticed by such blandishments. And what else is such immoderate honour and observance than mockery, contempt and injustice? Thus the Jews, mocking Christ, paid him the highest honours while their manners and bearing were submissive. Matt. 27:28-32. Such prodigal and flattering people also appear unjust, because they render not each his own honour, but honour that is foreign to the one honoured and does not fit his dignity, or honour greater than that due to a higher and more excellent man.

units.la: In defectu vero peccatur, quando in hisce moribus reuerentialibus exhibendis, inferior est nimis parcus & tenax, neque pro ratione honorandi cultum & obseruantiam & obsequia sua temperat & commensurat. Vnde arrogantia eius elucet, inuidia & iniustitia, quibus sibi multum tribuit & alteri suum detrahit: Hinc & contemptus siue despicientia & ὀλιγωρία oritur. In defectu etiam peccatur, quādo inter plures præsentes præstantiores inæquales, omnium præstantissimo, primo loco, mores reuerētiales iiq; maiores, non exhibentur, & is aliis presenti-bus, prout requirit eiusdē dignitas & existimatio, non præfert.
units.tr: Sin is committed by defect when, in showing these reverential courtesies, the inferior is too sparing and stingy, and does not moderate or proportion his worship, respect and deference to the measure of the one to be honoured. Hence his arrogance shines forth, with envy and injustice, by which he attributes much to himself and takes away what is another's. From this also arise contempt, or scorn, and disdain [ὀλιγωρία]. Sin is also committed by defect when, among several present who are of unequal excellence, the most excellent is not given the first place and the greater reverential courtesies, and this man is not preferred to the others present, as his dignity and reputation require.

units.la: Qui medium inter hosce tenent, vocantur elegantes & urbani vt tamen in honore præftan-do vitetur nimia segnities & nimia festinatio. Illa, qua somniculose, pigre, lente, oficitanter, nulla cum animi alacritate: hæc, qua concitatè, festinanter, turbulenter omnia fiunt.
units.tr: Those who hold the middle course between these are called elegant and courteous; yet in paying honour one must avoid both excessive sluggishness and excessive haste. The former is when everything is done drowsily, lazily, slowly, carelessly and without any liveliness of spirit; the latter is when everything is done hastily, rashly and in confusion.

units.la: Altera regula est, vt tempestiue tribuatur honor debitus, ratioq; habeatur conditionis, cum illius apud quem vtimur obsequio, tum etiam nostræ conditionis.
units.tr: The second rule is that the honour due be paid in good time, and that account be taken of the condition both of the one whose deference we use and of our own condition.

units.la: Apud homines qui occupationibus distinentur, plane mores hosce reuerentiales abrumpere, aut certe quantum fieri potest, imminuere & significatione potius eas indicare, quam reipfa exprimere conuenit, ne aliis rebus peragendis sint impedimento.
units.tr: Among people who are distracted by occupations, it is fitting that these reverential courtesies be broken off altogether, or at least, as far as possible, reduced, and that they be indicated by signs rather than actually expressed, lest they hinder others in carrying out their business.

units.la: Opifices quoq; & infimæ fortis homines operam non dabunt, vt erga superiores suos multis moribus reuerentialibus vtantur. Hi enim illis aduersantur & conditionem præstantis non decent. Nam ab hoc hominum genere potius obedientiam, quam honorum ceremonias honoratiores hi atque superiores requirunt & expectant.
units.tr: Craftsmen too, and men of the lowest sort, will not take care to use many reverential courtesies towards their superiors. For these things are contrary to them and do not suit the condition of their betters. For the more honourable and superiors demand and expect from this class of men obedience rather than the ceremonies of honour.

units.la: Mores reuerentiales rursum sunt communes & conuenientes omnibus honoratioribus & dignioribus; vel quibusdam ex iis proprii & singulares.
units.tr: Again, reverential courtesies are either common and suitable to all the more honourable and worthy, or proper and particular to some of them.

units.la: Communes, & quibusvis honoratioribus conuenientes dicuntur, qui indistincte omnibus honoratioribus honoris & reuerentiæ ergo præstantur. arg. 1. Sam. c. 24. 7. c. 26. 9. 10. 11. 2. Sam. c. 1, 11. & seqq. c. 4. 9. 1. Timoth. c. 6. 1. Deut. c. 34. 8. 1. Timoth. Timoth.2.2.Eccles.c.3.1,2.&feqq.1.Sam.c.28.3.Ec-clef.c.34.17.18.22.c.44.c.45. Pet.c.2.17. Malach.c. 1.6. Rom.c.13.7.1. Chron.c.29.11,12.28. 2.Chron.c.1. 12.13. Hic fugienda quæcunq; præbent indici-um contemptus, incommodationis, contume-liæ & impediendi conatus honorationis.
units.tr: Those are called common, and suitable to any of the more honourable, which are paid without distinction to all the honourable for the sake of honour and reverence. Compare 1 Sam. 24:7; 26:9-11. 2 Sam. 1:11ff.; 4:9. 1 Tim. 6. Deut. 34:8. 1 Tim. 2:2. Eccles. 3:1-2ff. 1 Sam. 28:3. Ecclus. 34:17-18, 22; 44; 45. 1 Pet. 2:17. Mal. 1:6. Rom. 13:7. 1 Chron. 29:11-12, 28. 2 Chron. 1:12-13. Here one must avoid whatever gives signs of contempt, disrespect, insult, and an attempt to hinder honour.

units.la: Communes eisdem mores reuerentiales, ex-hibentur sermone, vel gestu habituve.
units.tr: Common reverential courtesies of this kind are shown by speech, or by gesture and bearing.

units.la: In sermone, quando conuersatur cum supe-riore & honoratiore, humilis seu inferior, adhi-bebit non modo verecundiam, modestiam & comitatem, sed etiam suauitatem, cum significa-tione reuerentiæ & amoris, pudoris & verecundiæ, ita vt oratio & sermo omnis ad voluntatem & nutum illius attemperetur verbis placidis & benignis, sed ita tamen, vt in hisce euitetur omnis suspicio assentationis & tristitiæ; deinde nimia taciturnitas & loquacitas. Omnis assentatio vitanda ideo, quod de pessimis animi affectionibus in superiorem honorantem suspectum reddit, vt dixi sup.cap.2. De adulatione.
units.tr: In speech, when a humble or inferior person converses with a superior and more honourable one, he should use not only modesty, moderation and courtesy, but also gentleness, with signs of reverence and love, of shame and bashfulness; so that all his speech and discourse is adapted to the will and nod of the other, with gentle and kindly words; yet in such a way that every suspicion of flattery and of sadness is avoided here, and also excessive silence and loquacity. All flattery is to be avoided, because it makes the superior who is honoured suspect of the worst feelings of mind, as I said above, chap. 2, On flattery.

units.la: Nimia tristitia & taciturnitas superiores honorariores minime amabiles inferioribus reddit, & plerunq; inuisos & suspectos, qui nimirum non satisfieri a se inferioribus inde suspicantur Eccles.c.8.2. Neperturbatè a facie eius abito, &c. 1. Timoth.c.2.9. cum verecundia & modestia se ornare, &c. Loquacitas ideo fugienda, quod reuerentiæ omnino contraria, vt dixi cap.4. in fine fere. Syracid. c.32.12: Inter magnates æqualem ne præbeas te, & vbi senes sunt, ne multa effutias, & c.7.13. Ne verbosus sis in multitudine seniorum, sed eosdem potius audias, Eccles.cap.6.34.35. cap.8.9.10.11.12.
units.tr: Excessive sadness and silence make superiors who are honoured less lovable to their inferiors, and generally hateful and suspect, since the inferiors suspect that they are not satisfied with them. Eccles. 8:2. Do not hurry away from his face, etc. 1 Tim. 2:9: to adorn oneself with modesty and moderation, etc. Loquacity is to be avoided because it is wholly contrary to reverence, as I said in chap. 4, near the end. Ecclus. 32:12: Among great men do not make yourself their equal, and where there are elders, do not chatter much, etc.; and 7:13: Do not be wordy in the company of elders, but rather listen to them. Eccles. 6:34-35; 8:9-12.

units.la: Iob c.32.6. Eccles. c.7.5. 1 Timoth. d.c.2.11. Mulier cum silentio discito, cum omni submissione. 12. Mulierem enim docere non permitto, neque auctoritatem vsurpare in virum: sed mando vt sit in silentio. Neque si adsunt seniores, vel quos reuereri aequum est, rendum est; nisi forte ipsi quoque vt nos exhilarent, vt bane aliquid & lepide dixerint. Clemens Alex. lib.2. Paedag. c.5.
units.tr: Job 32:6. Eccles. 7:5. 1 Tim. 2:11: Let a woman learn in silence, with all submission. 12: For I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over a man, but I command that she be in silence. Nor, if elders are present, or those whom it is right to revere, should one speak, unless perhaps they themselves, to cheer us, have said something witty and pleasant. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, bk. 2, chap. 5.

units.la: Sermonem tenuiores & inferiores priores non inducant, nisi forte à superioribus iussi aliquid proponant. Ergo loquendi & decernendi facultatem priorem relinquere debent digniori & honoratiori, l.1. quisquis, Cod. de praefect. prator, l.12. tit.4. l.1. l.2. C. de praepos. fac. cub. l.1. de alb. scribend. Tiraquell. de iure primogen. in praefatione, num.112. & seqq. & num.123. & seqq. Iob cap.32.6. Minimus sum aetate, vos autem decrepiti; idcirco veritus sum ac timui offendere sententiam meam vobis. 7. Dicebam, prouecti aetate loquentur, & annosi notam facient sapientiam, & vers.16. 17. & c.29.21 Mihi auscultantes exspectabant & consilicescebant ad consilium meum. 21. Post verbum meum non iterabant, itasuper eos stillabat sermo meus. 23. Exspectabant enim tanquam pluviam me, & os suum distendebant, & seqq. Ecclesiast. cap.32.9. Loquere adolescens, vix si opus erit tibi, si bis interrogatus fueris. 10. Summatim sermonem contrahe, paucis multa. 11. Esto tanquam is qui nouit & silet tamen, 12. Inter magnates aequalem te ne praebeas, & vbi senes sunt, ne multa effutias, & c.7.13. cap.6.34-35. & c.8.9.10.11.12. 1 Timoth. cap.2.11.12. Pertinet enim ad superiores & digniores, quapotissimum de re velint audire; quod sibi arrogare, & te, & praeminentiam atq; excellentiam quandam sibi adfectare praesumitur, qui praefatinat loqui & sermonis exordium facit in praesentia praestantioris. Sic & sanctos homines coram excellentioribus loquendi facultatem petiisse legimus, & non nisi iussos sermonem instituisse,2. Sam.c.14.13. Tum dixit mulier illa, Eloquatur, quaeso, ancilla tua apud Dominum meum Regem aliquid, quo dicente eloquere, dixit mulier. Et 1. Sam. c.25.24. Quumq; procidisset ad pedes eius, dixit, In me, me inquam, Domine mi, sit hoc inquitas: sed loquatur, quaeso, ancilla tua, ad aures tuas & audi verba ancillae tuae, & 1. Sam.c.15.16. Tum dixit Samuel Schauli, Desine ut renuntiem tibi, quod elocutus est mihi Iehova, Genes.c.44.18. Sed accedens ad eum Iuda, dixit. Attende ad me domine mi, loquatur quaeso servus tuus verbum audiente domino meo; nec accendatur ira tua in servum tuum; na tu perinde es ac Pharao. 1. Sam.c.16.19. Nunc ergo audiat quaeso dominus meus Rex verba servi sui. Et Dauid ad Saulem dixit, &c. 1. Reg.c.1.15.16. & seqq. Act.c.24.10. Actor. cap. 26.1. Agrippa vero Paulo dixit, Permittitur tibi pro te ipso dicere. Tunc Paulus extenta manu, hac defensione usus est, &c.24.10. Respondit autem Paulus cum innuisset ei praeses ut loqueretur, &c. Genes.cap.18.27. Abraham vero subiecit, dicens: Ecce nunc cuperem alloqui Dominum tametsi ego sim pulvis & cinis, 30. Quaeso ne accendatur ira tua, Domine, si loquar, &c.31. Ecce nunc cuperem alloqui Dominum, &c.32. Ne quaeso accedatur ira Domini, si loquar tantum hac vice, &c. &c.44.18. Iob c.29.8.9. Exempla huius extant plura Act.c.5.34. Matt. c.11,13.24.27. 2. Sam. c.20,17.18. Plutarch.
units.tr: Earlier speakers should not bring forward a lower or humbler speech unless their superiors have ordered them to put something forward. So they ought to leave the power of speaking and deciding to the worthier and more honourable, law "quisquis," Cod. de praefect. praetor., law 12 tit. 4; laws 1 and 2, C. de praepos. fac. cub.; law 1, de alb. scribend.; Tiraquell., de iure primogen., preface, nos. 112 ff. and 123 ff.; Job 32:6, "I am younger in years, and you are aged; therefore I was afraid and feared to declare my opinion to you." 7. "I said, Let those advanced in years speak, and let the aged make known wisdom," and verse 16. 17. and 29:21, "They listened to me and waited, and kept silence at my counsel." 21. "After my words they did not speak again, and my speech dropped upon them." 23. "They waited for me as for the rain, and opened their mouths wide," and following; Ecclesiasticus 32:9, "Speak, young man, only if there is need for you, if you are asked twice." 10. "Sum up your speech briefly, say much in few words." 11. "Be like one who knows and yet keeps silent." 12. "Do not put yourself on an equal footing with the great, and where there are elders, do not chatter," and 7:13; Job 6:34-35; ch. 8:9-12; 1 Timothy 2:11-12. For it belongs to superiors and worthier men, above all, to wish to hear what is concerning the matter; and it is presumed that someone who hurries to speak and begins his address in the presence of a more eminent person claims for himself that privilege, and aims at some preeminence and excellence over him. So we read that holy men too asked leave to speak before more excellent persons, and began to speak only when ordered: 2 Sam. 14:13, "Then that woman said, Let your handmaid, I beg, speak something to my lord the king. And when she had spoken, she said..." And 1 Sam. 25:24, "When she had fallen at his feet, she said, Upon me, I say, my lord, let this iniquity be; but let your handmaid, I beg, speak in your ears and hear the words of your handmaid," and 1 Sam. 15:16, "Then Samuel said to Saul, Stop, that I may tell you what Jehovah has said to me." Genesis 44:18, "But Judah came near to him and said, Hear me, my lord, let your servant, I beg, speak a word in my lord's hearing, and let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are even as Pharaoh." 1 Sam. 16:19, "Now therefore let my lord the king hear the words of his servant." And David said to Saul, etc.; 1 Kings 1:15-16 and following. Acts 24:10; Acts 26:1, "Agrippa said to Paul, You are permitted to speak for yourself. Then Paul, stretching out his hand, made his defence," etc. Acts 24:10, "Paul answered when the governor had motioned to him to speak," etc. Genesis 18:27, "Abraham answered and said, Behold now, I have ventured to speak to the Lord, though I am dust and ashes;" 30, "I beg, let not the Lord be angry if I speak," 31, "Behold now, I have ventured to speak to the Lord," 32, "I beg, let not the anger of the Lord be kindled if I speak only this once," etc.; Genesis 44:18; Job 29:8-9. Many examples of this are found in Acts 5:34; Matt. 11:13, 24, 27; 2 Sam. 20:17-18. Plutarch.

units.la: De liber.educ. Dum alius inquit, loquitur, obticescere conuenit, locum cedere & orationem & primas sedilia concedere, & primas dicendi partes dare. Maximum enim honoris est signum habere primam vocem. Chassan.consid.19.part.1. & part.10.consid.29.cat.glor.mundi.
units.tr: In his book on the education of children: "While another is speaking, it is fitting to be silent, to give way in place and in speech, and to yield the front seats and the first parts of speaking." For to have the first voice is a great sign of honour. Chassanaeus, consil. 19, part 1, and part 10, consil. 29; Catal. glor. mundi.

units.la: Pronuntiatio inferioris, tenuioris, coram superiore, digniore, reuerentialis conuenit esse summissa & prope abiecta, ex caussis quas retuli lisup.c.5. Insuper & blanda, suauis & benigna, pro natura negotii, de quo agitur, vt non omnia semper ad voluntatem loquamur, neque petulanter, vel imperiosè, vel austerè, vel iracundè. Itaque pronuntiatio eiusmodi cum verecundia & prudentia fieri debet. Petulantia enim securitatem præ se fert; iracundia & austeritas imperandi affectationem indicat. De qua prudentia adi loquentem Apostolum, 1.Timoth.cap.5.1. Seniorem ne increpato, sed hortare, vt patrem, iuniores vt fratres.2. Mulieres natu grandiores, vt sorores cum omni castitate.3. Viduas honora, quae verè viduae sunt. Late vide Ecclesiasticis c.10.1.2. & seqq. vbi Iun.Prou. c.15.15. & exemplum 1.Sam.c.1.14.15. & cap.25.16. & seqq.
units.tr: The delivery of an inferior or humbler person before a superior or worthier one ought to be submissive and nearly abject, for the reasons I have given, see above, c. 5. Besides, it should be gentle, pleasant and kind, suited to the nature of the business under discussion, so that we do not always speak according to our own will, nor wantonly, nor imperiously, nor harshly, nor angrily. Such delivery must therefore be made with modesty and prudence. For pertness shows over-confidence; anger and harshness indicate a desire to command. On this prudence, hear the Apostle: 1 Timothy 5:1-3, "Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, with all purity; honour widows who are truly widows." Look widely at Ecclesiasticus 10:1-2 and following, where Junius on Proverbs 15:15; and the example of 1 Sam. 1:14-15; and 25:16 and following.

units.la: Memoria & mentio de superiore honorifica sit, Ecclesiast.c.38.17.18.22. c.44. per tot. & c.45. & seqq.2.Sam.c.23.8. & seqq.Eccles.c.10.17. Nequidem in conscientia tua regi maledicito & in conclavibus cubilis tui ne maledicito diuiti; nam vel auis caelorum perferret vocem istam, & alis indicaret verbum, etiam de inimico & malo, arg.Rom.c.12.20. & v.14. Benedicite iis qui vos infestantur, benedicite, inquâ, & ne imprecamini.
units.tr: Mention and remembrance of a superior should be honourable: Ecclesiasticus 38:17-18, 22; ch. 44 throughout, and ch. 45 ff.; 2 Sam. 23:8 ff.; Eccles. 10:17. "Do not curse the king, not even in your thoughts, and do not curse the rich in the rooms of your bed; for a bird of the air might carry that voice, and a winged creature might report the word," even about an enemy and an evil man; compare Rom. 12:20 and verse 14: "Bless those who persecute you; bless, I say, and do not curse."

units.la: Quæ probanda in superiore sunt, pleniore ore laudanda, & contra næui tegendi & dissi-mulandi, Genef.cap.9.23. Tum accepit Schem cum Iepheto pallium eius, quod imposuerunt suo ambo-rum humero; & accedentes retrorsum texerunt eo nu-ditatem patris sui, facie sua, inquam, retrorsum, adeo ut nuditatem patris sui non respexerint. Nam qui tegit defectionem, quærit dilectionem, Prouerb.c.17.9.10. & omnes defectiones charitas tegit, Prouerb.cap.10.12.hoc est, ut Iunius ibidem explicat, non promul-gat, sed aut dissimulat, quidquid bona fide & conscientia potest, aut ex συμπαθείᾳ corrigit, Leu.c.19.7.ad-de Matth. c.1.19. Ioseph vir eius cum esset iustus, & nollet eam ignominia exponere, voluit eam clam dimittere, vide 1.Cor.c.13.4.5.6.7.8. 1.Pet.c.4.8. & Ante omnia vero charitatem alii in alios intensam habentes. Charitas operiet multitudinem peccatorum. Rom.c.15.1.2.3. Coloss.c.3.13. Ephes.c.4.2.32. Exemplum notabile extat in Danide, 1.Sam.c.24.9.10. 11.c.26.9.10.2.Sam.c.4.9.10.11,c.1.11. & feqq. & Act. c.24.10.3,c.26.2.3.4.7.25.
units.tr: What is commendable in a superior should be praised with a full voice, and what is a blemish should be covered and overlooked. Genesis 9:23, "Then Shem and Japheth took a garment and laid it on their shoulders, and going backwards covered the nakedness of their father; with their faces turned away, they did not see their father's nakedness." For he who covers a fault seeks love, Prov. 17:9-10; and "love covers all faults," Prov. 10:12, that is, as Junius explains there, it does not publish but either overlooks whatever it can in good faith and conscience, or corrects it in a spirit of sympathy (συμπάθεια), Lev. 19:17. Add Matt. 1:19: Joseph, her husband, being a just man and unwilling to expose her to shame, planned to put her away quietly. See 1 Cor. 13:4-8; 1 Pet. 4:8. And above all, having a fervent love for one another; "love covers a multitude of sins." Rom. 15:1-3; Col. 3:13; Eph. 4:2, 32. A notable example is found in David, 1 Sam. 24:9-11; 26:9-10; 2 Sam. 4:9-11; 1:11 and following; and Acts 24:10; 26:2-4, 7, 25.

units.la: Ergo in commendatione & prædicatione virtutis excellentioris, quandoq; occupari inferiorem conuenit. nam umbra virtutis, ut Seneca ait, est gloria. Prou.c.12.7. Pro ratione intellectus sui laudabitur vir, &c. Act.c.23.12. & Ananias quidam vir pius secundum legem, testimonio ornatus omnium illic habitantium Iudæorum c.9.22. Cornelius centurio vir iustus & timens Deum, & ornatus testimonio totius gentis Iudæorum, c.16.2. Huic dabant testimonium fratres, qui Lystris erant & Iconii, Rom.c.1.8. 2.Chronic.c.25.2.c.27.2. Paulus commendat & laudat dona Iudæorum. Rom.c.9.3.
units.tr: Therefore, in commending and proclaiming an excellent virtue, it is sometimes fitting for an inferior to be employed. For the shadow of virtue, as Seneca says, is glory. Prov. 12:7, "A man will be praised according to his understanding," etc.; Acts 23:12. Ananias, a pious man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, Acts 22:12; Cornelius the centurion, a just man who feared God and was well reported of by the whole nation of the Jews, Acts 10:22; "The brethren who were at Lystra and Iconium gave testimony to him," Acts 16:2; Rom. 1:8; 2 Chron. 25:2; 27:2. Paul commends and praises the gifts of the Jews, Rom. 9:3.

units.la: 4. s. c. 10. 1. 2. c. 16. 1. 2. 3. Marc. c. 14. 9. Vbicunque praedicatum fuerit Euangelium hoc in toto mundo, etiam id quod ista fecit, dicetur in memoriam ipsius. 2. Cor. c. 8 22. Misimus autem cum eo fratrem nostrum, quem saepe in multis probavimus studiosum, nunc autem multo studiosiorem ob multam meam fiduciam in vobis, 1. Timoth. c 3 7. Oportet autem habere etiam bonum testimonium ab extraneis. Rom. c. 16. 1 2. & seqq. Iob c. 19. 9. & seqq. 1. Cor. c. 8. 11. 23. Ephes. c. 6. 21. Philemon. c. 1. v. 6. 7. 1. Timoth. c 5. 17. 1. Sam. c. 1. 19. 20. & seqq. c. 3 33. & seqq. Iudic. cap. 5. 9. & seqq. Ruth. c. 2. 0. & seq. 7. Psalm. 8. & 21. & 68. & 65. adde l. iussimus. C. de offic. rect. prounc. l. unic. C. de quaest. l. si in aliquam. de offic. proconf. & leg. Chasfan confil. 32. part. 1. catal. glor. mundi.
units.tr: Mark 14:9, "Wherever the gospel is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be told in memory of her." 2 Cor. 8:22, "We have sent with him our brother, whom we have often proved to be diligent in many things, but now much more diligent because of my great confidence in you." 1 Tim. 3:7, "Moreover he must have a good testimony from those outside." Rom. 16:1-2; Job 19:9 and following; 1 Cor. 8:11, 23; Eph. 6:21; Philemon 1:6-7; 1 Tim. 5:17; 1 Sam. 1:19-20 and following; 3:33 and following; Judges 5:9 and following; Ruth 2:10 and following; Ps. 8, 21, 68, 65. Add law "iussimus," C. de offic. rect. prounc.; law "unic.," C. de quaest.; law "si in aliquam," de offic. proconsul. and legate; Chassanaeus, consil. 32, part 1; Catal. glor. mundi.

units.la: Ratio est, quod commendatione virtutis apud alios, eiusdem desiderium & studium excitetur, & apud laudatum virtus crescat & foveatur, & veritati testimonium detur, donaque Dei in ministris ipsius agnoscatur, atque honor tribuatur, cui honor debetur. Talis tamen commendatio in absentia laudati fieri debet, ut dixi supra, cap. 3. in Commendatione.
units.tr: The reason is that when virtue is commended to others, the desire for it and zeal after it are stirred up, the virtue of the one praised grows and is nurtured, testimony is given to the truth, the gifts of God in his ministers are acknowledged, and honour is paid to whom honour is due. Such commendation, however, must be made in the absence of the one praised, as I said above in chapter 3, under Commendation.

units.la: Hisce addo, quod talium honoratarum & excellentium personarum memoria, etiam post mortem earundem viuat & maneat sancta & venerabilis. Ecclesiast. c. 44. 13. In seculum manet eorum semen, neque deletur eorum gloria, 14. Sunt quidem corpora eorum sepulta in pace, sed nomen eorum viuit in generationem quamque, 15. Sapientiam eorum narrant populi & laudem eorum enunciat Ecclesia, & vers. seqq. ubi exemplorum inductione & cap.seqq.probat & c. 41.16. Vita bona numerantur quidem dies sed bonum nomen in seculum permanet, Prouer. c. 10.7. Memoria iusti benedicta, grata & suauis, contra vero impii nomen exosum, Proverb. d.c.10.7. Hinc ignominiae & infamiae loco habetur, defuncti memoriae condemnatio & abolitio, Eccles.23.32 33. c.8.9.cap 41.14. Deut. cap. 32.26.Exod. cap.17.14.Iosc.6.29. c.7.25. & Prou. c.10.6. Benedictiones sunt super caput iusti: os impiorum operiet violentia, 7. Memoria iusti erit in benedictione,& 8. & Psalm. 112. In memoria aeterna erit iustus,& Psalm.34. & Iob. cap, 13. Esaia 26. & Psal. 09.13.14.15.l.s. vbi Dd. C. ad l. Iulia, Maiestatis.
units.tr: To this I add that the memory of such honoured and excellent persons lives on, and remains holy and venerable, even after their death. Ecclesiasticus 44.13-15: "Their seed remains for ever, and their glory is not blotted out. Their bodies are buried in peace, but their name lives from generation to generation. The peoples declare their wisdom, and the Church proclaims their praise." Verses following, and chapter 41.16, where by the citation of examples the author proves this: "A good life is counted in days, but a good name remains for ever." Proverbs 10.7: "The memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked will rot." Hence the condemnation and abolition of a dead person's memory is held to be a mark of disgrace and infamy: Ecclesiastes 23.32-33; 8.9; 41.14; Deuteronomy 32.26; Exodus 17.14; Joshua 6.29; 7.25; Proverbs 10.6: "Blessings are upon the head of the just; violence covers the mouth of the wicked." Verse 7: "The memory of the just shall be in blessing." Verse 8; Psalm 112: "The just shall be in everlasting remembrance." Psalm 34; Job 13; Isaiah 26; Psalm 9.13-15, and elsewhere, where the doctors on C. ad l. Iulia maiestatis.
