units.la: Praeterea in colloquio digniores & excellentiores cohonestandi sunt titulis & cognomentis honorem venerationemque praefe-rentibus, ex quibus submissio loquentis apparet. Itaque decorum est vt cognomentum & compellationem domini honoratiori inferior, & sibi serui attribuat, vti ex pluribus constat exemplis sanctorum hominum. Genef.cap.23.6. Audi nos, dom ne mi, princeps Dei, &c. & verf. 11.15.17.cap 24.18. & illa, Bibe, inquit domine mi, 27.1. Pet. c.3 6.sicut Sara obediuit Abrahamo, dominum eum vocans; 2. Reg. cap. 6.21. Percutiamne pater mi.c.5.13.c.12. 2. Marc.c.10.17.18.2.Iohan.c.1. 1.1.Sam. c.1.14.15.Genef.c.42.10.11.c.43.20.28.cap. 44.16.17.18.19.20.21.22.23.24.32.cap.45.8.9.cap. 27.c.24.42.14.18.27.35.36. &seqq.c.19.18. c.23.6. 17.15.c.16.14.4.8.cap.33.13.c.47.3.4. 1.Sam.cap.25. 24.&seqq.Actor. c.25.26.1.Sam. c.16.16. Luc.cap. 22.25.1.Reg. c.18.7. Iohan. c.12.21. c.20.15. 2.Sam. c.25.8.24 25.26.27.28.29.30.31.1.Reg.c.1.2.17. & seqq.per tot.2.Sam. cap.14.6.7.8.10.13.16.cap.19.28. c.13 32. c.24.21.22. Profana exempla refert Alex. ab Alex.Genial.dier.lib.2.c.19. Atque hic nomen officii & muneris quod honoratus gerit exprimere,ciuile & decorum est.1.Reg.c.1.17.18.24.25.26.27.31.Matth.c.23.7. & in foris salutationes, & vocari ab hominibus Rabbi.8.9. 1.Sam.cap.10.24.25.Genef.c.41.9.10.11.16.25.32.33.34. & seqq. Est.c.5.c.6.2.Sam.c.15.5.6. cap.24.20.21. Marc.cap.12.14.15.19.32.c.11.21.Luc.c.22.25.Ipse vero dixit, Reges gentium dominantur eis, & qui habent in eas potestatem,benefici vocantur.vbi Beza notat.Marc.c.10.17. Praeceptor bone,quid faciam vt vitam aeternam possideam?18.20.Act.c.26.25.Tum ille, Non insania, praestantissime Feste, &c. & verf.26. Scit enim Rex apud quem libere loquor, & seqq. & cap.24.2. cap.25.13. Exemplum elegans extat 2.Sam.c.19.28.cap.24.21. 22.c.14.21.22. Iudic. c.6.12. Cumque appareret ei angelus Iehova, dixit ei, Iehova est tecum, valentissime robore. Quam ob causam leguntur veteres habuisse suos nomenclatores, qui salutantibus nomina eorum,qui salutandi erant, suggerebat. &,si nomen alicuius incognitum erat, eum honoris causa dominum vocabant. Alexand.ab Alexand.lib.2.Genial.dier. c.19.Senec. lib.1. De benefic. c.3. Ex senatus decreto imperatori Traiano hic honos habitus fuit, vt optimus nuncuparetur, vt referunt historici. Elogium Flauio Claudio imperatori a Senatu hoc tributum, vt Augustus, frater, amicus, bonus senator & vere bonus princeps diceretur. Senes in tanto honore fuerunt apud Romanos, vt parentes a iunioribus fuerint appellati honoris ergo.
units.tr: Also, in conversation the more worthy and excellent are to be honoured with titles and cognomens that express honour and reverence, by which the speaker's submission becomes apparent. So it is fitting that an inferior should address a more honoured person with the cognomen and form of address "lord", and call himself the servant, as is clear from many examples of holy men: Genesis 23.6, "Hear us, my lord, prince of God," etc.; verses 11, 15, 17; 24.18; and "Drink, my lord," she said, Genesis 24.27; 1 Peter 3.6: "as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord." 2 Kings 6.21: "Shall I strike them, my father?" 5.13; 12; Mark 10.17-18; John 1.1; 1 Samuel 1.14-15; Genesis 42.10-11; 43.20, 28; 44.16-24, 32; 45.8-9; 27; 24.42; 14.18, 27, 35-36, and following; 19.18; 23.6; 17.15; 16.14; 4.8; 33.13; 47.3-4; 1 Samuel 25.24 and following; Acts 25.26; 1 Samuel 16.16; Luke 22.25; 1 Kings 18.7; John 12.21; 20.15; 2 Samuel 25.8, 24-31; 1 Kings 1.2, 17 and following; throughout 2 Samuel 14.6-10, 13, 16; 19.28; 13.32; 24.21-22. Profane examples are given by Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial. dier. 2.19. And here it is civil and proper to name the office and function that the honoured person holds: 1 Kings 1.17-18, 24-27, 31; Matthew 23.7, "greetings in the marketplaces, and to be called Rabbi by men"; 23.8-9; 1 Samuel 10.24-25; Genesis 41.9-11, 16, 25, 32-34, and following; Esther 5; 6; 2 Samuel 15.5-6; 24.20-21; Mark 12.14-15, 19, 32; 11.21; Luke 22.25. But he himself said, "The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors," where Beza notes it. Mark 10.17: "Good teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" 10.18, 20; Acts 26.25: "Then he said, 'I am not mad, most excellent Festus,' etc."; verse 26: "For the king, before whom I speak freely, knows these things," and following; 24.2; 25.13. There is a fine example in 2 Samuel 19.28; 24.21-22; 14.21-22; Judges 6.12: "When the angel of Jehovah appeared to him, he said to him, 'Jehovah is with you, mighty man of valour.'" For this reason the ancients are said to have had their nomenclators, who suggested to those greeting the names of those who were to be greeted; and if the name of someone was unknown, they called him "lord" as a mark of honour. Alexander ab Alexandro, lib. 2, Genial. dier. c. 19; Seneca, De beneficiis 1.3. By decree of the senate the emperor Trajan was given the honour of being called "Optimus," as the historians report. The title granted by the Senate to the emperor Flavius Claudius was that he should be called Augustus, brother, friend, good senator and truly good prince. Among the Romans the elderly held such honour that parents were addressed by their juniors as a mark of honour.

units.la: In relatione quoque & pronunciatione honoris & reuerentiæ ergo nomen honorationis & dignioris aliorum minus honoratorum nominibus præponere solemus. Chassan.part.1.consid.17. catal.glor.mundi. Genes.c.48.20.21. quod tamen Iudæi non semper obseruarunt.
units.tr: Also in relating and naming people, out of honour and reverence, we customarily place the name of the more honoured and worthier person before the names of those less honoured. Chassanaeus, part 1, consid. 17; Catal. glor. mundi; Genesis 48.20-21; though the Jews did not always observe this.

units.la: Ex eiusmodi honore & reuerentia est etiam quod pro incolumitate & prosperitate superiorum honoratorum, preces ad Deum inferiores fundere iubentur. Ephes.c.6.19.20.1. Timoth. cap.2.2. Proregibus & quibusuis in eminentia constitutis, fiant deprecationes, preces, postulationes & gratiarum actiones, &c. Ierem.c.29.7. Baruch.c.1.11. & seqq.1.Reg.c.1.47.48.c.13.7. Daniel.cap.6.6.21, 2.Reg.c.11.12.
units.tr: From this same honour and reverence it is also commanded that inferiors pour out prayers to God for the safety and prosperity of their honoured superiors. Ephesians 6.19-20; 1 Timothy 2.2: "For kings and all who are placed in high authority, let entreaties, prayers, petitions and thanksgivings be made," etc.; Jeremiah 29.7; Baruch 1.11 and following; 1 Kings 1.47-48; 13.7; Daniel 6.6, 21; 2 Kings 11.12.

units.la: Huc pertinent quoque salutationes & consolationes quæ honoris causâ fiunt, quibus nostram charitatem, beneuolentiam & obseruantiam erga alios testificamur, 1.Sam.c.25.5. Misit Dauid decem pueros, edixitque Dauid pueris illis, Ascendite Carmelum, & ingressi ad Nabalem, interrogabitis eum nomine meo de prosperitate. 6. Ac ita dicetis ei, si incolumis es & tu pace, & domus tua pace, & quidquid est tibi, pace fruitur, & 2.Samuel. cap.10,2.Dixit Dauid, exercebo benignitatem erga Chanunem filium Nachaschi, quemadmodum exercuit pater eius erga me benignitatem, & misit Dauid consolatum eum per seruos suos de patre eius, venerunt, serui Dauidis in regionem Hammonitarum.
units.tr: To this belong also the greetings and condolences that are made out of honour, by which we testify our love, goodwill and respect toward others. 1 Samuel 25.5-6: "David sent ten young men, and David said to them, 'Go up to Carmel, and when you come to Nabal, you shall greet him in my name concerning his prosperity. And thus you shall say to him: Peace be to you, and peace to your house, and peace to all that is yours.'" And 2 Samuel 10.2: "David said, 'I will show kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to me.' So David sent servants to comfort him concerning his father. The servants of David came into the land of the Ammonites."

units.la: 3.Dicentibus autem Principibus Hammonitarum Chanuni domino suo: Dauidne honore afficere patrem tuum in oculis tuis videtur, quia misit tibi consolatores? &c. late Chassan, consid.26. part.1, catal.glor. mundi. l. sin (de offic. div. ind. l. peculium, (de pros. sacri scrinii.
units.tr: 3. "But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, 'Does David seem to you to honour your father, because he has sent comforters to you?'" etc. See Chassanaeus, consid. 26, part 1, Catal. glor. mundi; the laws cited.

units.la: Salutatio autem hæc verbalis, Græcis dicta ἀσπασμὸς & ἀσπαστικὸς, consistit in nomi-nibus atque titulis honorificis, vel etiam quan-doque in certis formulis & phrasibus. Nomi-na illa quibus vtimur in salutationibus, vel sunt propria, vel appellatiua; eaque naturæ vel san-guinis; vt nomen matris, patris, filii, &c. vel sortis atque conditionis, seu cuiuscunque con-iunctionis; vt sunt nomina domini, serui, præ-ceptoris, discipuli, clientis, patroni, tutoris, pupilli, collegæ. Apud veteres honorificum & præstantissimum fuit, suis nominibus quemque venerari & salutare, vel salutantibus reddere salutem. Alexan. ab Alex. Genial. dier. c. 19. lib. 2.
units.tr: This verbal greeting, called by the Greeks aspasmos [ἀσπασμὸς] and aspastikos [ἀσπαστικὸς], consists in honorific names and titles, or sometimes in fixed formulas and phrases. The names we use in greetings are either proper or common nouns, and these denote either natural or blood relationship, such as the names of mother, father, son, etc., or status and condition, or any other connection, such as the names of master, servant, teacher, disciple, client, patron, guardian, ward, colleague. Among the ancients it was regarded as honourable and most excellent to honour and greet each person by his own name, or to return a greeting to those who greeted.

units.la: Officii nomine, aut muneris quod quisq; gerit, salutare, iudicatur esse religiosius & ciuilius. De formulis salutandi vid. Ioh. Guil. Stuckium lib. 2. conuiuial. antiquit. c. 31. & Guil. Perkinsum de vsu linguæ. & sup. dixi.
units.tr: To greet someone by the title of the office or function that he holds is judged more religious and more civil. On the forms of greeting see Johann Wilhelm Stuck, lib. 2, Conviv. antiquit., c. 31, and Guilielmus Perkinsus, On the Use of Language, and what I said above.

units.la: Quod si qua in re repugnandum forte fue-rit honorationi & excellentiori, videndum vt illud à tenuioribus fiat timidè, pedetentim, & raro: neque nisi necessario; non est enim obse-quentis aduersari. 2. Sam. c. 24. 3. Et quamuis diceret Ioab regi, at Iehoua Deus tuus adiciat ad popu-lum quotquot sunt, centuplum, idque oculis domini mei regis videntibus: dominus autem meus rex quare deleclaretur rem illa? tamen confirmatum est verbum regis. Quod expressius habetur 1. Chron. c. 21. 1. 2. 3. 4. & quamuis diceret Ioab, Adiciat Iehoua populo suo, quotquot sunt, centuplum: an non omnes, domine domine mi Rex, sunt domino meo serui? cur quaereb ut istud dominus meus? cur esset ad dandum reatum Israeli? 2. Sam. c. 12. 18. Fuit autem die septimo ut moreretur infans. Quapropter timuerunt serui Dauidis nunciare ei mortuum esse infantem. Dicebant enim, Ecce cum esset infans viuus alloquebamur eum, sed non auscultabat voci nostrae; quomodo ergo dicentibus nobis ei, Mortuus est infans, id afficiet eum malo? 19 Sed videns Dauid seruos suos inter se mussitantes, intellexit mortuum esse infantem. 2. Sam. c. 14. vbi famina afluta Tecoita colloquium cum rege Dauide repugnante & contradicente eidem, describitur, quod prudenter illa vsa est ad regis animum flectendum. Sic & Abigail in deprecanda culpa a marito commissa, timide & reuerenter locuta legitur cum Dauide: vt hoc colloquium describitur 1. Sam. c. 25. 23. 24. & seqq. & sic sapiens mulier quadam se Ioabo opponebat 2. Sam. c. 20. 16. 17. 18. 19. sic Dauid Sauli se opponebat, & eundem cum omni lenitate admonebat. 1. Sam. c. 14. 9. 10. 11. & seqq. c. 16, 18. 19. & seqq. sic serui suum dominum. 2. Reg. c. 5. 13. Accedentes vero serui eius allocuti sunt eum ac dixerunt; Pater mi, si rem magnam ipse propheta edixisset tibi, an non facturus fuisses? Ita Apostolus cum senioribus conuersari iubet. 1. Timoth. c. 5. Ita eleganter & graviter Ecclesiastes c. 10. 1. Cum spiritus eius qui dominatur, se effert contra te, locum tuum ne deserito. nam vir sanans sedat peccata magna. vbi Iunius id summatim contrahit ad modestiam & animi summissionem apud honoratos colendam. & vers. seqq. & c. 8. 2. Ne pertur-bate a facie eius abito, ne persistito in re mala, nam quidquid volet, facturus est. & vers seqq. Atque huc pertinet generalia illa quae in reprehensione & increpatione monui sup. c.4. & Colos. c.4.6. Gal.6.1.2. in quibus Ioab peccauit 2.Sam. c.19.6.7. & seqq. & Roboam, 1.Reg.c.12.
units.tr: But if in some matter it should happen that one must oppose the more honoured and excellent person, one should see to it that the lesser person does so timidly, step by step, and rarely, and only when necessary; for it is not the mark of a compliant person to oppose. 2 Samuel 24.3-4: "Joab said to the king, 'May the LORD your God add to the people, however many they are, a hundredfold, and may my lord the king see it with his own eyes; but why does my lord the king delight in this thing?' Yet the word of the king prevailed." This is stated more fully in 1 Chronicles 21.1-4: "Joab said, 'May Jehovah add to his people, however many they are, a hundredfold. Are they not all, my lord the king, servants of my lord? Why does my lord seek this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?'" 2 Samuel 12.18-19: "On the seventh day the child died. The servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, 'Behold, while the child was alive we spoke to him, but he did not listen to our voice; how then will we tell him that the child is dead, and will it not grieve him badly?' But David, seeing his servants whispering among themselves, understood that the child was dead." 2 Samuel 14, where the wise woman of Tekoa is described speaking with King David, who resisted and contradicted her, and it is recorded that she prudently managed to bend the king's mind. So too Abigail, in pleading for pardon for the fault committed by her husband, is read to have spoken timidly and reverently to David, as this conversation is described in 1 Samuel 25.23-24 and following. So too a wise woman opposed Joab, 2 Samuel 20.16-19; David opposed Saul and admonished him with all gentleness, 1 Samuel 24.9-11 and following; 26.18-19 and following; servants addressed their master, 2 Kings 5.13: "But his servants came near and spoke to him and said, 'My father, if the prophet had bidden you do some great thing, would you not have done it?'" So the Apostle bids us live among the elders, 1 Timothy 5. So elegantly and gravely Ecclesiastes 10.4: "If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for gentleness lays to rest great offences," where Junius summarises this as the cultivation of modesty and humility of mind before the honoured. And verses following; and 8.3: "Do not be alarmed; withdraw from his presence; do not persist in an evil thing, for he will do whatever he wills." To this belongs also that general teaching which I warned of above in chapter 4, and Colossians 4.6; Galatians 6.1-2, in which Joab sinned, 2 Samuel 19.6-7 and following, and Rehoboam, 1 Kings 12.

units.la: In congressionibus & conuiuiis, non sermo hisce abrumpendus, non obloquendum, neque interturbandi illi, multo minus pertinaciter hisce resistendum, neque iidem redarguendi & acerbe atq; acriter reprehendendi, vel cum iis contendendum. quæ omnia indubitata signa sunt denegati obsequii & reuerentiæ, & stomachum concitant, vide Genes. cap.18. 2.Sam.c.14. 12.13.14. & seqq. Contrà potius cum patientia, humili & alacri animo, omnia suscipienda, nihil siniftre accipiendum; & crudelitas, obstinatio, intractabilitas, morositas, inhumanitas & ferocia superioris, humilitate, patientia & benignitate vincenda; & vociferatio atque exclamatio silentio & lenitate excipienda. Quapropter si contentio quædam inter honoratum dignio-rem & tenuiorem humilem oboriatur, quæ tamen cauenda erat, hic illi cedet. Nam & victi oderunt; & pares cum discedunt, tamen vinci se putant. Quam ob causam homini docto hac in re suis viribus non vtendum, sed ratio habenda potentioris præsentis, cum quo luctatur. Scitum enim est in loco cedere aut succumbere, in ea etiam arte, quam profiteris: cum victoria sæpe perniciem habeat. Ecclesiastic.c.10.29. Ne sapien-tem age in opere tuo faciendo, neque gloriosum tempore angustiæ tuæ. c.32.6. in tempestate ne agas sapien-tem, & c.7.5. ne iustitiam tibi adseras coram Domino, neq; coram Rege sapientiam. & Senec.lib.7. De benefic.c.31. vincit malos bonitas.
units.tr: In meetings and at banquets one must not cut off another's speech, contradict, interrupt, or, much less, stubbornly resist, nor rebuke or harshly and sharply reprove the same people, or contend with them. All these are unmistakable signs of refused deference and respect, and they stir up anger. See Gen. 18; 2 Sam. 14:12-14 and following. On the contrary, everything should be borne with patience and a humble, cheerful spirit, and nothing taken amiss. The cruelty, obstinacy, intractability, peevishness, inhumanity and ferocity of a superior are to be overcome by humility, patience and kindness, and shouting and outcry are to be met with silence and gentleness. Therefore, if some contention arises between an honoured, more worthy person and a humbler, lesser one, which nevertheless ought to have been avoided, the lesser one shall give way. For even the defeated hate, and even equals, when they part, think they have been beaten. For this reason the learned man should not use his own strength in this matter, but take account of the more powerful person present with whom he struggles. It is a known rule to yield in a place or give way, even in the art you profess, since victory often brings ruin. Ecclesiasticus 10:29: Do not be wise in your own works, nor glorious in the time of your distress. 32:6: In a storm do not play the wise man; and 7:5: Do not claim justice for yourself before the Lord, nor wisdom before the King. And Seneca, On Benefits, book 7, ch. 31: goodness conquers the wicked.

units.la: A potentiore quoq;,vel honoratiore,aliquid acerbè exigere, vel flagitare non licet; sed tantùm admonere & verecundè rogare.
units.tr: It is also not permitted to demand or press anything harshly from a more powerful or more honoured person; one may only admonish and ask respectfully.

units.la: Iocari cum potente, vel honoratiore & digniore,inferior humilis omnino non debet, nisi esset ab illis prouocatus,iussus & inuitatus.Inest enim in ioco,sicuti etiam in ludo,æqualitatis significatio,& securitas quædam, quâ superbia irritatur.
units.tr: A lowly inferior ought not at all to joke with a powerful, honoured and more worthy person, unless he has been provoked, bidden and invited by them. For in joking, as in play, there is an expression of equality and a certain security, by which pride is roused.

units.la: Cauillationem autem & in iocando licentiam,etiam immoderatam præstantioris & excellentioris,quamuis aculeum & contumeliam præse ferat, cum hilaritate & lepore in partem bonam inferioribus excipere conuenit, ita vt inprimis iracundiam, nequa forte erumpat, (efferuescet enim illa quidem) quam diligentissime poterunt,comprimant; adeo vt licèt acrius superior pupugerit, nihil quidquam mordeant. Omnia hæc vindictæ signa & metum præbent, & obsequio atque obseruantiæ contraria sunt,cum non dicatur obedire qui doloris sui pœnas persequitur. Et suprà dictum,infirmitates, næuosque honorandorum, æquo animo tolerandos, Rom.c.15.1.2.3. Coloss.3.13. Ephes. c.4.2.3.2. & ob eos de obedientia, humilitate,reuerentia & obsequio, nihil detrahendũ, 1.Pet. c.2.18.19.20. Exemplo Dauidis, qui Regi impio & Tyranno Sauli nihilominus hæc præstitit, 1.Sam.c.26.8.9.10.11.15.16. & seqq. 1.Pet.c.2. 17. & seqq. Ergo sequere consilium Catonis:
units.tr: But raillery and licence in joking, even immoderate, from a superior and eminent person, although it carries a sting and an insult, should be received by inferiors in good part, with cheerfulness and wit. Above all, they should check their anger as carefully as they can, lest it burst out (for it will indeed boil up), so that even if the superior has stung more sharply, they bite back nothing at all. All these are signs of vengeance and fear, and they are contrary to obedience and observance, since one who pursues the penalty of his own pain is not said to obey. And it was said above that the infirmities and blemishes of those to be honoured are to be borne with an even mind: Rom. 15:1-3; Col. 3:13; Eph. 4:2-3; and on account of them nothing is to be taken away from obedience, humility, reverence and deference: 1 Pet. 2:18-20. Example: David, who nevertheless showed these things to the impious king and tyrant Saul: 1 Sam. 26:8-11, 15-16 and following; 1 Pet. 2:17 and following. Therefore follow the counsel of Cato:

units.la: Cede locum, lasus, fortunæ; cede potenti:
units.tr: Yield your place to the injured, yield to fortune, yield to the powerful.

units.la: Cedere qui potuit, prodesse aliquando valebit. Proverb,c.14. Qui patiens est, multa gubernatur sapientia: qui autem impatiens est, exaltat stultitiam suam. Et Cicero: Tempori cedere, id est, necessitati parere semper sapientis est habitum. Senec. lib. 2. De ira: Potentiorum iniurias hilari vultu, non patienter tantum ferenda sunt, & Cicer. ad Attic. Temporibus parere omnes politici praecipiunt. Est enim non modo liberale, paululum nonnunquam de suo iure cedere, sed interdum etiam fructuosum, Cicer. libr. 2. Offic.
units.tr: He who has been able to yield will sometimes be able to profit. Prov. 14: He who is patient is governed by much wisdom, but he who is impatient exalts his folly. And Cicero: to yield to the times, that is, always to obey necessity, has been regarded as the mark of the wise man. Seneca, book 2 On Anger: The injuries of the more powerful are to be borne with a cheerful countenance, and not merely patiently. And Cicero to Atticus: All political writers teach us to yield to the times. For it is not only generous to give up a little of one's right now and then, but sometimes even profitable. Cicero, book 2 On Duties.

units.la: CAP. III. De gestu & habitu reuerentiali communi.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. On common reverential gesture and bearing.

units.la: DE Reuerentiali sermone hactenus. Sequitur de gestu & habitu reuerentiali.
units.tr: So far on reverential speech. Next comes reverential gesture and bearing.

units.la: Iurisconsulti vocant operas obsequiales & officiales. l. 6. l. 9. De oper. libert. tot. tit. De obseq. parent. & pat. praestand. quae verecundiae causa & honoris ergo praestantur, l. 4. 1. libertus, De oper. liber. l. 1. & seqq. D. de obseq. parent. & patron.
units.tr: The jurists call these obsequial and official services (operae obsequiales et officiales), which are rendered out of modesty and for the sake of honour: Code, bk. 6 and bk. 9, On services of freedmen, the whole title, On rendering obsequies to parents and patrons; Digest, bk. 4, §1 (libertus), On services of freedmen; Digest, bk. 1 and following, On obsequies to parents and patrons.

units.la: Hic imprimis curandum inferiori, vt gestus, motus, incessus, status, sessio, accubatio, manus, oculi, vox, ineptiis vacent, nec non contemptu & vilipendio, sed reuerentiam potius & obsequia erga superiorem ostendant.
units.tr: Here the inferior must above all take care that his gestures, movements, gait, posture, sitting, reclining, hands, eyes and voice are free of silliness, and likewise free of contempt and disparagement, but rather show reverence and deference towards his superior.

units.la: Locus & sedes conspectior & superior digniori ab inferiore tributus, reuerentiae, obseruantiaeque declaratio esse existimatur, 1. Sam. cap. 9. 22. Adsumpsit tamen Samuel Saulem & puerum eius, quos introduxit in cœnaculum, deducens eis locum in summo innitatorum, &c. Genef. cap. 43. 33. Sederunt autem coram eo secundum primogenita sua & ætatem, &c. 34. Matth. c. 23. 6. 12. Marc. c. 12. 39. Luc.c.20.46.c.14.7.8. (um vocatus fueris ab aliquo ad nuptias,ne accumbito primo loco,ne forte honoratior te sit vocatus abeo,9. & is qui te & illum vocauit,veniens dicat tibi,Da huic locum, & tunc incipias cum pudore ultimum locum obtinere,10.Sed cum vocatus fueris,vade discubitum in ultimum locu, vt quum venerit qui te vocauit,dicat tibi,Amice, ascende superius,tunc erit tibi gloria in conspectu eorū,qui tecū discumbunt.Iob.c.29.25.Si eligebam viam eorum,, primarius sedebam,deniq; habitabam, sicut Rex inter turmarios suos,Prou.c.25.7. Est.c.3.1.c.1.14.15. 1.Reg.c.2.19.Genes.c.43.33.34. 1.Sam.cap.20.25. Iacob.c.2.3.4.Prouerb.cap.25.6.7. nam melius est tibi dici, Ascende huc, quam deprimi coram ingenuo.Drusus lib.12.Obseruat.c.25.Tiraquel. De nobilit.c.20.num.51.& seqq.& de iure primogen.in praefat.num.115.& seqq.Valer.Maxim.lib.2. c.1.l.2. l.3. C. de offic.ciuil.iudic.l.3.§.sedendi, vbi gloss.C. vbi Senat.vel clariss.l.vlt. C.de tyronibus.Seneca lib. 6.De benefic.Est proprium superbia,magno aestimare introitum,ac taclum sui liminis pro honore dare, vt ostio suo propius assideas, vt gradum prior intra domu ponas,&c.
units.tr: A place and seat more conspicuous and higher, given by the inferior to the more worthy, is considered a declaration of reverence and esteem. 1 Sam. 9:22: "Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the parlour, and made them sit in the chief place among those who were bidden, about thirty persons." Gen. 43:33: "And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth." Matt. 23:6, 12; Mark 12:39; Luke 20:46; Luke 14:7–10: "When you are invited to a wedding, do not sit down in the best place, lest a more honourable man than you be invited by him, and he who invited you and him come and say to you, 'Give this man place,' and then you begin with shame to take the lowest place. But when you are invited, go and sit down in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you, 'Friend, go up higher'; then you will have glory in the sight of those who sit at table with you." Job 29:25: "I chose out their way and sat chief, and dwelt as a king in the army." Prov. 25:6–7; Esth. 3:1; 1 Kings 2:19; Gen. 43:33–34; 1 Sam. 20:25; James 2:3–4; Prov. 25:6–7, for it is better that you be told, "Come up here," than that you be humbled before a noble. Drusius, Observations, bk. 12, ch. 25; Tiraquellus, On nobility, ch. 20, nn. 51ff., and On the right of primogeniture, preface, nn. 115ff.; Valerius Maximus, bk. 2, ch. 1; Code, bk. 2, 3; Code, On the duties of civil judges, law 3, §sedendi, with the gloss; Code, Where the Senate, or the most illustrious; Code, last law, On recruits; Seneca, On benefits, bk. 6: "It is the mark of pride to value highly entry into a house and to regard the touch of its threshold as an honour, to sit closer to a door, to place one's foot first within a house," etc.

units.la: Equitibus etiam apud Romanos locus & sedes honoris causa dabatur,Senec.lib.7. De benefic.Cicer.Philip.2.& senatoribus primus ordo subselliorum obsignatus.Sueton.in Augusti. cap.44. Tacit.lib.16.Annal. Aliquando tamen pro ratione dignitatis etiam locus intermedius tribuitur.l.1. l.2.C.vt ord.dign.seruet.lib.12.Tiraquell.d.loco. secundum loci cuiusque consuetudinem, l. non tantum, C.de Decurion.lib.10. Tiraquell.d.loc.Daniel.cap.13.50.Dixerunt Danieli seniores, adesdumiam, sede in medio nostrum, & renuncia nobis, &c. Luc.c.2.46.Et factum est triduo post, ut invenerunt eum in templo sedentem in medio Doctorum & audientem eos & interrogantem, vid. Joh. Guil. Stuckiu, lib.2.conuiuial. antiquit. c.35. in sin. varias diversorum populorum opiniones & mores de loco supremo, medio & infimo referentem, & Iustum Lipf. Antiq. lection.lib.3. & Cal. Rhodigin. lib.10. c.15. Pet.Greg. lib.4.de Repub. c.10.num.12.13.
units.tr: Among the Romans too, the knights were given a place and seat as a mark of honour (Seneca, On benefits, bk. 7; Cicero, Philippics, bk. 2), and the senators were given the first row of benches, reserved for them (Suetonius, Augustus, ch. 44; Tacitus, Annals, bk. 16). Sometimes, however, according to the rank of the person, a middle place is also assigned (Code, laws 1 and 2, On keeping the order of dignity; Tiraquellus, bk. 12, loc. cit.), according to the custom of each place (Code, law "non tantum," On decurions; Tiraquellus, bk. 10, loc. cit.). Daniel 13:50: "The elders said to Daniel, 'Come, sit down in the midst of us and inform us,' etc." Luke 2:46: "And it came to pass, after three days, that they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the teachers, both hearing them and asking them questions." See Johann Wilhelm Stuck, Banquet antiquities, bk. 2, ch. 35, near the end, who records the varied opinions and customs of different peoples concerning the highest, middle and lowest place; and Justus Lipsius, Antique lectures, bk. 3; and Caelius Rhodiginus, bk. 10, ch. 15; Peter Gregorius, On the Republic, bk. 4, ch. 10, nn. 12–13.

units.la: Locus vero a dexteris adsignatus, vel occupatus, dignitatis & honoris esse dicitur. Matth.c. 20.21.& seqq.c.25.33.34. Luc.c.22.20. Coloss cap 3. 1. Marc.c.16.19. 1. Reg. c.2.19. Et sedens in ssolio suo (Salomo) apponi iussit solium matri Regis, quae sedit ad dexteram eius. & Psalm.45.10. & Psalm.110.1. vbi Iunius. Genes. c.48.13.14.17.18. Alex.ab Alex. lib.2.Genial. dier.c.19. Gell.lib.2.c.2. Tiraquellus de iur.primogen.in praefat.num.13.& seqq. Petr. Greg. de Repub.lib.4.c.10.num.10.12. & seqq.libr.6. Syntagm.c.6.7.8.& seqq. vel sessio prope digniorem. Chassan.consid.12 par.1.2.Esd.c.3.
units.tr: A place assigned or occupied at the right hand, however, is said to be a mark of dignity and honour. Matt. 20:21ff.; 25:33–34; Luke 22:20 [sic]; Col. 3:1; Mark 16:19; 1 Kings 2:19: "And the king sat on his throne and had a seat placed for the king's mother, and she sat at his right hand." Psalm 45:10; Psalm 110:1, where Junius; Gen. 48:13–14, 17–18. Alexander ab Alexandro, bk. 2, Genial days, ch. 19; Gellius, bk. 2, ch. 2; Tiraquellus, On primogeniture, preface, nn. 13ff.; Peter Gregorius, On the Republic, bk. 4, ch. 10, nn. 10–12ff.; bk. 6, Syntagma, chs. 6–8ff. Or a seat near the more worthy man: Chassanaeus, Considerations, 12, part 1; 2; Esdras 3.

units.la: Sedenti praestantiori & honoratiori adstare, honoris & reverentiae argumentum esse dicitur. Genes.c.18.8. Et ipse (Abraham) adstabat eis sub arbore illa comedentibus. Exod.c.18.13 Fuit autem alterodie, sedente Mose ad iudicandum populum, cum adstaret populus ipse Mosi, a mane illius diei usque ad vesperam.& 1.Reg.c.1.28.c.8.14. Tota congregatione Israelis stante, Rex benedixit,&c & verf. 55.1.Sam.c.22.6.9.Genes.c.47.31. c.49.33. vbi Iunius notat.& ad idem allegat Num.c.23.22.Iudic.c. 3.20.2.Reg. c.23.2. 2.Chronic.c.34.31. Nehem.c.8. 6.Iacob.c.2.3.4.Luc.c.22.25,26.Iob c.29.8.9.2.Reg. c.23. c.23. Est.c.5.9. Act.c.23.3. Tu sedens iudicas me, &c. & vers.4. Tum qui adstabant, dixerunt, &c. Gell. lib.2.c.2. Alexand ab Alex.lib.2. Gen.dier.cap.19.l. quisquis, §.vlt. (de postul. Sedere enim proprium est dignior um. Psalm.119.23. Psalm.80. 2.Psal.47. 9. Matt.c.23.2.c.26.55. Marc.c.3.32. Luc.c.10.39. Vid.Chassan.part.1.consid.11.catal.glor.mundi.
units.tr: To stand beside a more excellent and honourable person who is seated is said to be a sign of honour and reverence. Gen. 18:8: "And he (Abraham) stood by them under the tree while they ate." Exod. 18:13: "On the next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood before Moses from morning until evening." 1 Kings 1:28; 8:14: "While all the congregation of Israel stood, the king blessed," etc., and verse 55; 1 Sam. 22:6, 9; Gen. 47:31; 49:33, where Junius notes this, and for the same point cites Num. 23:22; Judg. 3:20; 2 Kings 23:2; 2 Chron. 34:31; Neh. 8:6; James 2:3–4; Luke 22:25–26; Job 29:8–9; 2 Kings 23. Esther 5:9; Acts 23:3: "You sit to judge me," etc., and verse 4: "Then those who stood by said," etc. Gellius, bk. 2, ch. 2; Alexander ab Alexandro, bk. 2, Genial days, ch. 19; Digest, "quisquis," last §, On demands. For to sit belongs to the more worthy: Psalm 119:23; Psalm 80:2; Psalm 47:9; Matt. 23:2; 26:55; Mark 3:32; Luke 10:39. See Chassanaeus, part 1, consideration 11; Catalogue of the glory of the world.

units.la: In eundo etiam, gestu & habitu, honor, reuerentia, cultus & obsequium digniori & honoratiori præstari potest ab inferiore, quando primus locus in eundo seu præitio & præcessio illi conceditur. Tiraquel.de iur.primigen. in prafation.num.118. & illi ceditur. Tiraquel. d.loc.num.80. &feqq. Luc.c.14.7.8.9.10. vel eundem comitatur inferior, deducit, exspectat, vel sequitur. l.15.item.§.23.de iniur. Gell.lib.2.c.14. Valer.Max. lib.2.c.1.in sin.&c.2. Act.c.21.5.6. Sed peractis illis, abiimus, omnibus deducentibus nos cum vxoribus & liberis extra vrbem vsque. 2.Sam.c.19.32. Barzillai quoq; Gilhadita descenderat Roglinis, quare traiecit cum rege Iordanem, prosequendo eum Iordanem, & vers.10.11.12. Quare essetis postremi, ad reducendum regem domum suam. 1.Sam.c.10.26. Comitantibus eum copiis quorum tetigerat Deus animos. 2.Sam.c.15.ibi vniuersi serui eius ambulabant iuxta eum. Genef.c.26.31. Surgentes mane iurauerunt alter alteri, deduxitq; eos Isaac, & abierunt ab eo cum pace. Act.c.20.38. & deduxerunt eum ad nauim. Sic & Abraham Angelos illos comitatus est. Genef.c.18. & 1.Sam.c.9.26.27. Unde sequi tergum, est obsequium declarare, Esai.c.59.13.1.Sam.cap.12.22. & seqq.c.10.26.Luc.c.2.51. adde Actor.c.10.23. Postridie vero Petrus abiit cum eis, & quidam ex fratribus Ioppensibus comitati sunt eum. Et referri Gellius libr. 2. cap. 15. seniores à minoribus domum reductos fuisse honoris ergô.
units.tr: In going, too, honour, reverence, respect and deference can be shown by the inferior to the more worthy and more honourable, through gesture and bearing, when the first place in going, that is, leading the way and going before, is granted to him. Tiraquellus, On primogeniture, preface, n. 118, and that place is yielded to him: Tiraquellus, loc. cit., nn. 80ff.; Luke 14:7–10. Or the inferior accompanies him, escorts him, waits for him, or follows him: Digest, law 15, also §23, On injuries; Gellius, bk. 2, ch. 14; Valerius Maximus, bk. 2, ch. 1, near the end, and ch. 2. Acts 21:5–6: "But when those days were over, we departed, and all of them, with wives and children, brought us out of the city." 2 Sam. 19:32: "Barzillai the Gileadite also had come down from Rogelim, and he went over the Jordan with the king, to send him on his way over the Jordan"; verses 10–12: "Why are you the last to bring back the king to his house?" 1 Sam. 10:26: "With him went men whose hearts God had touched." 2 Sam. 15: "There all his servants went along beside him." Gen. 26:31: "They rose early in the morning and swore to one another, and Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace." Acts 20:38: "And they brought him to the ship." So Abraham also accompanied those angels, Gen. 18; 1 Sam. 9:26–27. Hence to follow someone at the back is to declare obedience: Isa. 59:13; 1 Sam. 12:22ff.; 10:26; Luke 2:51; add Acts 10:23: "On the next day Peter went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa went with him." And Gellius, bk. 2, ch. 15, is cited as reporting that elders were escorted home by younger men as a mark of honour.

units.la: Prætereunti honoratiori & digniori adsurrectio à sedente honoris ergô præstari solet ab inferiore, Levit. c. 19. 32. Coram canitie assurgito, ut honorem habeas faciei, senis: & timebis à Deo tuo. Genes. c. 23. 7. Tum adsurgens Abraham, incurvauit se coram populo eius regionis, honorem exhibens filiis Cheti. Exod. c. 33. 8. 9. 10. & 1. Reg. cap. 2. 19. Itaque cum venisset Bathsebah ad Regem Salomonem, ut loqueretur ei pro Adonia, adsurgens Rex obviam ei incurvauit se, &c. Iob c. 29. 8. etiam decrepiti adsurgentes stabant, Genes. c. 42. 6. Esther. cap. 8. 4. Unde stare ante Deum, erat eidem ministrare. Ierem. c. 23. 21. Zachar. c. 3. 7. Esther. cap. 5. 9. Sed cum videret Haman Mordecaium in porta Regis, ut neq; adsurgebat, neque movebat se propter ipsum, &c. 2. Chron. 7. 6. Esa. c. 6. ibi vidi Dominum sedentem & postea Seraphin stabant, &c. Chassan. part. 1. consid. 10. catal. glor. mundi. l. sin. C. de offic. diu. iud. & paulo ante pluribus confirmat. Cuius Athenienses senex in theatrum veniens occupatis sedibus locum quærebat, nec erat ex Atheniensibus qui vellet cedere. Delatus ad Lacedæmonios, simul omnes adsurrexerunt & senem sessum receperunt. Quam observantiam populus videns, commendauit hoc encomio quod in sola Sparta iuuet consenescere. Athenienses vero hoc dicto notati sunt: Scire quidem eos quid honestum sit, sed non facere. Virgilio in theatrum ingredienti & carmina sua recitaturo, populus Romanus adsurrexit ac si ipse imperator esset, adde Gell. lib. 2. c. 15.
units.tr: To a passing man of rank and dignity, the inferior commonly shows respect by rising from his seat, as a mark of honour. Lev. 19:32: "You shall rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of an old man, and fear your God." Gen. 23:7: "Then Abraham rose and bowed himself before the people of that land, the sons of Heth." Exod. 33:8–10; 1 Kings 2:19: "So when Bathsheba came to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah, the king rose to meet her and bowed down to her," etc. Job 29:8: "Even the old men rose and stood." Gen. 42:6; Esther 8:4. Hence to stand before God meant to minister to him: Jer. 23:21; Zech. 3:7; Esther 5:9: "But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor moved for him," etc. 2 Chron. 7:6; Isa. 6: "I saw the Lord sitting, and afterwards the seraphim stood," etc. Chassanaeus, part 1, consideration 10; Catalogue of the glory of the world; last law, Code, On the duties of divine judges, and above he confirms it at greater length. When an old Athenian came into the theatre and, finding all the seats taken, looked for a place, none of the Athenians was willing to give up his seat. When he was brought before the Lacedaemonians, they all rose together and received the old man as he sat. The people, seeing this respect, praised it with the saying that only in Sparta is it a pleasure to grow old. The Athenians, however, were rebuked by this saying: they know what is honourable, but do not do it. When Virgil entered the theatre to recite his poems, the Roman people rose as if he were the emperor himself; add Gellius, bk. 2, ch. 15.

units.la: Processus obuiam factus venieti, honoris & reverentiae signum esse iudicatur. 1. Reg. cap. 2. 19. Genes. c. 18. 2. Quos videns, accurrit obuiam eis ex osiorentoru fui, & seqq. c. 47. 7. & 1. Reg. d. cap. 2. 19. Exod. c. 18. 7. Tunc processit Moses obuiam socero suo, & incurvans se osculatus eum est. 2. Sam. c. 19. 26. Fuit q3 obuius regi, cum rediret Rex Ierusalem, & vers. 16. 17. 18. 21. Genes. c. 46. 29. 30. 1. Sam. c. 13. 10. Et exiuit Saul obuiam Samuel ad benedicendum ei, cap. 16. 4. 5. Cum itaq3 Samuel aduenisset Bethlehemum, trepidi accurrerunt seniores ciuitatis obuiam ei, & dicebat quisq3 profecto aduenis? cap. 18. 5. Genes. c. 14. 17. Quare egressus est Rex Sedomi obuiam Abrahamo postquam reduit a cade, &c. Ita Iacobus cum tota familia sua f atri suo Esau obuiam venit, quo ut placato uti posset muneribus & obseruantia delinitum sibi reconciliauit. Atq3 ut actus esset splendidior, primo ancilla cum liberis suis accedunt; deinde Lea cum suis liberis: tandem Rahel cum Iosepho, vid. Genes. c. 32. 2. Sam. c. 9. 16. Iehuda autem venit Gilgalem, ut iret obuiam Regi, ad traducendum Regem, cis Iordanem, & 17. 18 & seqq. 2 Reg. c. 2. 15. Quare venientes obuiam ei, incurvaruntse in terram vsq3, honorem exhibentes, & 1. Reg. c. 2. 19. ibi adsurgens Rex obuiam ei, &c.
units.tr: To go out to meet someone who is coming is judged to be a sign of honour and reverence. 1 Kings 2:19; Gen. 18:2: "When he saw them, he ran from the door of his tent to meet them," and following; Gen. 47:7; 1 Kings 2:19 as above; Exod. 18:7: "Then Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, and bowed down and kissed him." 2 Sam. 19:26: "He also came to meet the king when the king returned to Jerusalem," and verses 16–18, 21; Gen. 46:29–30; 1 Sam. 13:10: "And Saul went out to meet Samuel, to bless him"; 16:4–5: "When Samuel came to Bethlehem, the elders of the city came trembling to meet him, and said, 'Do you come peaceably?'"; 18:5; Gen. 14:17: "The king of Sodom went out to meet Abraham after his return from the slaughter," etc. So Jacob came with his whole household to meet his brother Esau, and by gifts and respect he sought to win him over and reconcile him, so that he might be placated. And to make the act more splendid, first the maidservants came forward with their children, then Leah with her children, and at last Rachel with Joseph; see Gen. 32; 2 Sam. 9:16. Judah went to Gilgal to meet the king, to bring the king across the Jordan, and verses 17–18ff.; 2 Kings 2:15. Hence those coming to meet him bowed themselves to the ground, showing honour; and 1 Kings 2:19: there the king rose to meet her, etc.

units.la: Eiusdem generis & significationis est descensio è via, quae honoris ergo fieri solet, occurrenti honoratiori. Alex. ab Alex. Gen. dier. lib. 2. c. 19.
units.tr: Of the same kind and meaning is dismounting from the road, which is customarily done out of honour when one meets a more honourable person. Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, book 2, chapter 19.

units.la: Similiter & descensus de equo vel curru, honoratiore se obuiam offerete. Iudic. c. 1. 14. Quare ea desiliit de asino. Cui dixit Caleb, quid tibi est? vbi Petr. Martyr Genes. c. 24. 64. Ribba vero sublatis oculis suis, quum videret Iuzhakum, descendit se de camelo.& verf.65. & accepto peplo operuit fe, &c. 20.16.vbi Iun.Senec.lib.8. epist.65. Si consulem, in-quit,videro,aut pratorem omnia quibus honor haberi solet,faciam,equo desiliam,caput aperiam. Ex hac caussa Fabius pater proconsul a filio suo consule equo descendere iussus fuit.vid. Gell.lib.2.c.2.in sin.
units.tr: Similarly, getting down from a horse or chariot when presenting oneself to a more honourable person. Judges 1:14: "Therefore she got off her donkey." To her Caleb said, "What is the matter with you?" See Peter Martyr. Genesis 24:64: "Rebekah, lifting up her eyes and seeing Isaac, got down from the camel." Verse 65: "And taking a veil, she covered herself," etc. 20:16, where Junius. Seneca, book 8, letter 65: "If I see a consul or a praetor, I will do everything by which honour is customarily shown: I will dismount from my horse and uncover my head." For this reason Fabius the father, a proconsul, was ordered by his son, the consul, to dismount from his horse. See Gellius, book 2, chapter 2, at the end.

units.la: Huc etiam refero, quod in itinere faciendo digniores & honoratiores rheda vrantur, vel e-quo,quibus vehuntur.Genef.c.41.43. Et iussit eum infidere currui secundani, &c.t.46.29. Est.c.6.6.7. 8.Et equo cui Rex insidet adductio,quum impositum fuerit Diadema regum caput eius, 9.10. & seqq.vid. Ierem.c.17.Huc facit Zach.c.9.9. Matth.c.21.3. Dionysius Tyrannus Platoni in Siciliam venienti, nauem pulcherrime exornatam misit qua vehereturi, & egredientem e naue, currui impositu, quem quatuor albiequi trahebant.Et Iosephpatri currum misit. vide Tiraquel.de nobil.c.20.n.77.& seqq. Vel etiam gestantur lectica a lecticariis & gerulis. Sen.lib. 7.epist.56. & De vita breuit. l. item, 49. de legat.3. Sueton.in Caligul.c.43. Martia. Apuleius 2. Apo-log. & cibis delicatis vescantur & vestibus pre-tiofis vtantur, vt dicit Chass.part.1.glor.mundi.
units.tr: I also refer here to the fact that, when travelling, the more worthy and honourable use a carriage or the horse they ride. Genesis 41:43: "And he made him ride in the second chariot," etc. 46:29. Esther 6:6-8. And the horse on which the king rides is led, when the royal diadem has been placed on his head, 9-10 and following. See Jeremiah 17. Zechariah 9:9 and Matthew 21:3 apply here. Dionysius the tyrant, when Plato came to Sicily, sent him a most beautifully decorated ship in which to be carried, and, as he came off the ship, a chariot drawn by four white horses. He also sent a chariot to Joseph's father. See Tiraquellus, On Nobility, chapter 20, nn. 77 ff. Or they are carried in litters by litter-bearers and porters. Seneca, book 7, letter 56; and On the Shortness of Life; also, book 4 on Benefits (?); Suetonius, Caligula, chapter 43; Martial; Apuleius, Apology 2; and they eat delicate foods and use precious clothing, as Chassanaeus says, part 1, Glory of the World.

units.la: Honoris quoque ergo honoratioris & di-gnioris aedes seu domum in negotiis etiam di-gnioris,adit infetior.l.pen. §. vlti. de condit. & de-monst. Luc. c.1.43. c.7.6. Misit ad eum centurio amicos,dicens ei, Domine non sum dignus, vt tectum meum subeas, 7. Ideo ne me ipsum quidem sum dignum arbitratus, qui venirem ad te.&c. Luc.cap.1. 43. Unde hoc mihi, vt veniat ad me mater Domi-ni.&c. Act.c.21.s. Tiraquel.de nobilit.c.num.46. & seqq. sed adit non subito & inopinato, sed praepræmonitione facta & quasi venia petita,&adi- tu impetrato accedit. Exod.c.18.6: Dixitq; Mosi, ego socer tuus Iethro, venio ad te, &c. Tunc processit Mose obuiam ei. Ester. c.4.11.16.c.5.2. c.2. in sin. & Genes.c.42.17. &seqq.
units.tr: Also, for the sake of honour, the inferior approaches the house or dwelling of a more honourable and worthier person, even on business of a more worthy person. Digest, last law, last paragraph, On Conditions and Demonstrations. Luke 1:43; 7:6: "The centurion sent friends to him, saying: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; 7: therefore I did not even think myself worthy to come to you," etc. Luke 1:43: "Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Acts 21:5. Tiraquellus, On Nobility, chapter, number 46 ff. But he does not approach suddenly and unexpectedly; he gives notice beforehand and, as it were, asks leave, and having obtained permission he comes in. Exodus 18:6: "And he said to Moses, I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you," etc. "Then Moses went out to meet him." Esther 4:11, 16; 5:2; chapter 2, at the end; and Genesis 42:17 ff.

units.la: Vocato humiliori ad honoratiorem vel excellentiorem, non abeundum est, nisi veniam præferatur, aut dimissus sit.
units.tr: When a humbler person is summoned to a more honourable or excellent one, he must not withdraw unless leave has first been given or he has been dismissed.

units.la: Reuerentiæ quoq; & honoris ergo sella, vel ledes ad sedendum, seu sessum capiendum, digniori & honoratiori ponitur.1.Reg.c.2.19. Et sedens in solio suo, apponi iussit solium matri Regis, quæ sedit ad dexteram eius. Refert etiam Iob d.c.29 8 pueros, honoris ergo, se visò, se occultasse. Gellius lib.2.c.2. historiam refert de Philosopho sellam patri & filio honoris ergo ponenti.
units.tr: For the sake of reverence and honour, a chair or seat is placed for the worthier and more honourable person to sit down or take a place. 1 Kings 2:19: "And sitting on his throne, he ordered a throne to be set for the king's mother, and she sat at his right hand." Job 29:8 also relates that the young men, when they saw him, hid themselves out of respect. Gellius, book 2, chapter 2, relates the story of a philosopher who out of honour placed a chair for a father and his son.

units.la: Gestu & habitu singulorum membrorum corporis inferior honorem præstare potest superiori, honoratiori & præstantiori, vti genuum inflexione, corporis terram versus inclinatione & incuruatione, quo habitu sancti quoq; viri in honoris signum vsi sunt, vt constat exemplis pluribus. Marc.c.10.17. Psalm.72.9. vbi sun. Genes.c.43.26.27.28. c 33,3. & seqq. c 37.7.9.10. & text.notab. Genes.c.32.c.47.31.c.18.2 c.19.cap.23.12. c.41.43.c.48.12.c.27.31.c.42. 6. Num.c.22.31.2. Sam.c.24.20.22.1. Reg.c.1.16.23.24.31.53. Exod. cap.12.27.43 45.48 cap.18.7. cap.20.5.c 33.10.cap. 34.8.2. Chronic.c.24.17 c.6.13.c.7.3. 1.Reg.c.19 18. Luc.c.24.5. Actor.c.16.29. 2.Sam.c.25.10. & seqq. Daniel.c.2.in sin. Marc.c.10.17. Roman. c.14.11.Est. c.3.5.2.c.5.9.2. Samuel.c.15.5.6.c.14.23.4.5. c.18. 20.18.c.19.18. & passim alibi.vid.Alex.ab Alex.Genial.diet. lib.2.c.19.
units.tr: By the gesture and bearing of the individual parts of the body, an inferior can show honour to a superior, more honourable and excellent person, such as by bending the knees and by inclining and bowing the body towards the ground. Holy men also used this posture as a sign of honour, as many examples show. Mark 10:17; Psalm 72:9, see there. Genesis 43:26-28; 33:3 ff.; 37:7, 9, 10, and the notable text there. Genesis 32; 47:31; 18:2; 19:1; 23:12; 41:43; 48:12; 27:31; 42:6. Numbers 22:31. 2 Samuel 24:20, 22. 1 Kings 1:16, 23, 24, 31, 53. Exodus 12:27, 43, 45, 48; 18:7; 20:5; 33:10; 34:8. 2 Chronicles 24:17; 6:13; 7:3. 1 Kings 19:18. Luke 24:5. Acts 16:29. 2 Samuel 25:10 ff. Daniel 2, at the end. Mark 10:17. Romans 14:11. Esther 3:5; 2:2; 5:9. 1 Samuel 15:5-6; 14:23; 4:5; 18:20; 18; 19:18; and in many other places. See Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, book 2, chapter 19.

units.la: Hodie in corporis incuruatione, alii vtrumque genu pariter inflectunt, idq; rursus alii recto corpore, alii nonnihil incuruato. Quidam, erecto corpore primum dexterum incuruant genu, mox sinistrum. Alii, modulato corporis circumactu, dextrum duntaxat inflectunt genu, vt Erasmus ait.
units.tr: Today, in bowing the body, some bend both knees together, others again bend them with the body upright, and others with the body somewhat bent. Some, with the body erect, first bend the right knee, then the left. Others, with a graceful turning of the body, bend only the right knee, as Erasmus says.

units.la: Honoratur etiam praestantior & dignior humili inferioris submissione, qua eiusdem ministerio & vtibus se suamque operam & studium offert, 1. Sam. c. 25 24. & seqq. 2. Sam. c. 16. 15. Dicentibus ergo Regi serui regis, omnino prout elegerit dominus meus Rex, ecce serui tui, 21. In loco vbi erit dominus meus Rex, siue ad mortem, siue ad vitam, ibi futurus est seruus tuus. & verf. 32. & seqq. Gen. c. 45. 9. 10. 11. & seqq. Iob c. 29. 2. Sam. c. 24. 20. & seqq. c. 17. 27. 28. 29.
units.tr: The more excellent and worthier person is also honoured by the humble submission of the inferior, by which the inferior offers his service, his effort and his zeal for the other's use. 1 Samuel 25:24 ff.; 2 Samuel 16:15: "And the king's servants said to the king, Behold, your servants will do whatever my lord the king has chosen." 21: "In whatever place my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there your servant will be." And verse 32 ff. Genesis 45:9-11 ff. Job 29:2. 2 Samuel 24:20 ff.; 17:27-29.

units.la: Atq; hinc lotio pedum, quae in signum ministerii & seruitii alii fit. Iohan. c. 13. 14. & seqq. Luc. c. 7. 38. Solutio corrigiarum solearum, Iob. c. 1. 27. Hic ille est qui pone me venit, qui mihi antepositus est, cuius soleárum ego non sum dignus, qui soluam corrigiam. Pedum excalceatio Suet. in Vitell. c. 2. vid. Ioh. Guil. Stuckium lib. 2. antiq. conuiuial. c. 27. Ministerii ad mensam praestatio, Luc. c. 17. 8. Imonone dicet ei (seruo suo) para quod canem & praecinctus ministra mihi vsque dum edero ac bibero, & postea edito tu & bibito, Iob. c. 12. 2. 3.
units.tr: Hence comes the washing of feet, which some do as a sign of ministry and service. John 13:14 ff.; Luke 7:38. The loosing of the thongs of sandals: John 1:27: "He it is who comes after me, who is preferred before me, whose sandal thong I am not worthy to loosen." The removing of shoes: Suetonius, Vitellius, chapter 2; see John Wilhelm Stuck, book 2 of Antiquities of Banquets, chapter 27. The rendering of service at table: Luke 17:8: "Will he not rather say to him: prepare what I may eat, and gird yourself and serve me until I have eaten and drunk, and afterwards you shall eat and drink." Job 12:2-3.

units.la: Capitis nudatione honoratiores & praestantiores honorare solemus, qua omnia nostra patefacere nos velle declaramus, & subiectionem arq; submissionem nostram patefacimus, arg. 1. Corinth. cap. 11, 4. & seqq. Genes. cap. 20. 16. vbi Iun. Iun. c. 24. 65. c. 20. 16. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 2. c. 19. Gen. dier. & Seneca lib. 8. epist. 65. Plutar. in problem. 10. Polydor. Virgil. lib. 4. cap. 13. Guil. Stuck. lib. 2. cap. 28. antiqu. convivial. Seneca in epistolis. Si consulem video aut praetorem, omnia quibus honor haberi solet, faciam, equo descendam, caput adaperiam, semitâ cedam.
units.tr: We customarily honour the more honourable and excellent by uncovering the head, by which we declare that we wish to lay open all that is ours and reveal our subjection and submission. Argument from 1 Corinthians 11:4 ff.; Genesis 20:16, see there, Junius; 24:65; 20:16; Alexander ab Alexandro, book 2, chapter 19, Genial Days; and Seneca, book 8, letter 65; Plutarch, in Problems 10; Polydore Vergil, book 4, chapter 13; Guillaume Stuck, book 2, chapter 28, Antiquities of Banquets. Seneca in his letters: "If I see a consul or a praetor, I will do everything by which honour is customarily shown: I will dismount, uncover my head, and give way on the path."

units.la: Huius generis est etiam civilis adoratio quaedam honoris causâ praestita Est. c. 3. 2. Drusius lib. 12. Obs. c. 11. hanc Persis familiarem fuisse adserit, quae adoratio manu ori admota, fieri solet. Ita Drusius lib. 1. Obs. c. 20. per alleg. ibidem & Iob c. 31. 27. vbi Iun. Vel manus aut pedis dignioris deosculatione, Genes. c. 41. 40. Tu praeerit domui meae, & ad os te osculabitur universus populus meus. vbi Iun. quem sequitur Drus. libr. 2. Obs. cap. 15. & cap. 16. Psalm. 2. 12. Osculamini filium, &c. Hosea c. 13. 2. Homines qui sacrificant vitulos osculantur, 1. Reg. cap. 19. 18. Reliquos feci ex Israele septem mille, quorum omnium genua non curvarunt se Baali, & quorum omnium os non osculatum est illum, 1. Sam. c. 10. 1. Tunc accepta Schemuel lenticula olei, perfundens caput eius osculatus est eum, & dixit, &c. Prov. c 14. 26. Labia osculabitur eius qui respondet verba recta. vbi Iun. Luc c. 7. 38. Et stans apud pedes eius retro, flens coepit lachrymis pedes eius rigare & capillis capitis sui extergebat, & deosculabatur pedes ipsius & unguento unguebat, & 45. Non intermisit deosculari pedes meos, Ecclesiast. c. 29. 5. &c. 7. dixi latius de osculi varia significatione, quae erat rei charissima nota. Hodie filius perditionis, pedes suos ad malefaciendum veloces, potentissimis etiam Monarchis osculandos praebere solet, ut hoc ipso quoq; testetur se super omnia se extulisse. Sen. lib. 2. De benef. c.12. Cæsar Pompeio Pano absoluto & agenti gratias porrexit osculandum sinistrum pedem. Qui excusant, negant id insolentia causa factum, & aiunt soccului auratum, imo aureum, margaritis distinctum ostendere eum voluisse, vid. Polydor. Virg. lib. 4. c. 13. Platin. in vitis Pontif. Persæ olim quos sibi pares colebant, osculo impartiebantur; potentiorum vero genua inferiores manu tangebant; & non-nunquam pedes, sicuti & aliæ gentes osculabantur. Alex ab Alex. lib. 2. Gen. dier. c. 19. atque eodem cultu & reverentia honestatum & exceptum fuisse Scipionem a quibusdam, refert Val. Max. lib. 2. c. 10. & latius Seneca lib. 6. epist. 47. Suet. in Caligul. c. 56. & in Domit. c. 11.
units.tr: Of this kind also is a certain civil adoration performed out of honour. Esther 3:2. Drusius, book 12 of Observations, chapter 11, asserts that this was a custom of the Persians. This adoration is usually done by bringing the hand to the mouth. So Drusius, book 1 of Observations, chapter 20, by allegory there; and Job 31:27, see Junius. Or by kissing the hand or foot of a more worthy person. Genesis 41:40: "You shall be over my house, and all my people shall kiss you on the mouth." See Junius, whom Drusius follows, book 2 of Observations, chapter 15, and chapter 16. Psalm 2:12: "Kiss the Son," etc. Hosea 13:2: "Men who sacrifice kiss calves." 1 Kings 19:18: "I have left seven thousand in Israel, all of whose knees have not bowed to Baal, and all of whose mouths have not kissed him." 1 Samuel 10:1: "Then Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it on his head, kissed him and said," etc. Proverbs 24:26: "He will kiss the lips of him who answers with right words." See Junius. Luke 7:38: "And standing behind at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head, and kissed his feet and anointed them with ointment." 45: "She has not ceased to kiss my feet." Ecclesiasticus 29:5, etc. I have spoken more fully, in chapter 7, on the various meanings of the kiss, which was a most familiar sign of affection. Today the son of perdition, swift to do evil, is accustomed to offer his feet to be kissed even by the most powerful monarchs, so that by this too he may show that he has exalted himself above all. Seneca, book 2 On Benefits, chapter 12: "When Caesar had acquitted Pompeius Pano and he was giving thanks, Caesar offered his left foot to be kissed." Those who excuse it deny that it was done out of insolence, and say that he wished to show a gilded, indeed golden, sandal set with pearls. See Polydore Vergil, book 4, chapter 13; Platina, in the Lives of the Popes. The Persians once gave the kiss to those they regarded as their equals; to the knees of the more powerful they gave a touch with the hand, and sometimes they kissed their feet, as other nations also did. Alexander ab Alexandro, book 2, Genial Days, chapter 19. And Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 10, relates that Scipio was honoured and received by some with the same worship and reverence; and more fully Seneca, book 6, letter 47; Suetonius, Caligula, chapter 56, and Domitian, chapter 11.

units.la: Honestatur etiam dignior & præstantior ab illo qui silentium præstat, & ad sermones loquentis attendit. Iob c. 29. 9. Principes continebant sermones, & manum imponebant ori suo, 10. Eloquentes antecessores occultabant se, eorumque lingua palato eorum adhærebat, & verf. 21. Mihi auscultantes, exspectabant: & conticescebant ad consilium meum, 22. Post verbum meum non iterabant; ita super eos stillabat sermo meus, 23. Exspectabant enim tanquam pluviam me, & os suum distendebant. Marc. c. 9. 32. 34. Luc. c. 9. 45. Actor. c. 5. 13. Diuite loquente, omnes silent, &c. Paupere loquente dixerunt, quis est iste? Eccl. c. 9. 17. & seqq. Chassan part. 1. consid. 10. catal. glor. mundi.
units.tr: A more worthy and distinguished person is also honoured by one who keeps silence and attends to the words of the speaker. Job 29:9, 10, 21-23: "The princes refrained from speaking and laid their hand on their mouth; the nobles held their tongues, and their tongue clave to their palate. They listened to me and waited, and kept silent for my counsel. After my word they did not speak again, for my speech dropped upon them. They waited for me as for the rain, and opened their mouth wide." Mark 9:32, 34; Luke 9:45; Acts 5:13. When the rich man speaks, all are silent; when the poor man speaks, they say, "Who is this?" Eccl. 9:17 ff. Chassan, part 1, consid. 10, catal. glor. mundi.

units.la: Hinc reuerentiæ & cohonestationis significatio est, quando quis iudicio & sententiæ dignioris adquiescit, vti apparet ex Iob cap. 29. 21. 22. 24. 25. vbi Iunius. sicuti & quando monitis & præceptis præstantioris obedientiam præstat,
units.tr: Hence the sign of reverence and honour is when someone yields to the judgment and opinion of a more worthy person, as appears from Job 29:21, 22, 24, 25, where Junius (translates this passage). It is likewise when someone shows obedience to the admonitions and commands of a more eminent person.

units.la: 1.Timoth.c.6.1.2.3.4.Hebr.c.13.17. Ephef.c.6.5.6.1. Pet.c.2.18. Coloss.c.3.20.22. Ierem. c 35.6.14.18.19. quæ obedientia sub honore comprehenditur iuxta præceptum, Honora patrem & matrem tuam,1.Sam.c.15.30.c.2.30. Rom.c.13.7. Ioh.cap.8. 49.Matth.c.15.4.5.Ephef.c.6.2.1.Timoth.c.5.3.17. 1.Pet.c.2.17.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 6:1-4; Heb. 13:17; Eph. 6:5-6; 1 Pet. 2:18; Col. 3:20-22; Jer. 35:6, 14, 18, 19. This obedience is included under honour, according to the precept, "Honour your father and your mother" (1 Sam. 15:30; 2:30; Rom. 13:7; John 8:49; Matt. 15:4-5; Eph. 6:2; 1 Tim. 5:3, 17; 1 Pet. 2:17).

units.la: Quandoq; honoratior præstantiorq; etiam munusculi, seu honorarii oblatione honoratur. De quare vide exempla Genef.c.32.13.18. c.33.8.10. 15.c.43.11. Num.c.24.constitueram te honorare,&c. Dan.c.2.48.1.Sam.c.10.4.5.c.9.23.24.2. &c.8.12. 23.1.Timoth c.5.17.1.Reg c.10.10.13. Ierem.c.40.5. Matth.cap.11. Iudith c.13. Judic. c.3.17. Helius Adrianus Imperator liberalitatis & obseruantiæ ergo emeritos professores Romæ honoribus & congiariis auxit, ut honestè quod reliquum vitæ esset, transigerent. Vel etiam honoris & delectationis gratiâ, conuiuio excipitur, Luc.c.5.29. Et fecit ei Leui epulum magnum domi suæ, Ioh.c.12.2. Fecerunt igitur ei cœnam illic, & Martha ministrabat; Lazarus vero erat unus ex discumbentibus cum eo. Iob c.1. Luc.c.14.7.&seqq. Genef.cap.43.16.33.34.1. Samuel.9.23.24.c.1.5. Vide Athenaum lib.1. Dipnosoph.& Ioh.Guil.Stuckius.lib.1.De conuiu.& Exod.18. 12.&infra.
units.tr: Sometimes the more honoured and eminent person is also honoured by the offering of a small gift or fee. For examples of this see Gen. 32:13-18; 33:8, 10, 15; 43:11; Num. 24 ("I had intended to honour you," etc.); Dan. 2:48; 1 Sam. 10:4-5; 9:23-24; 2 Sam. 8:12; 23; 1 Tim. 5:17; 1 Kings 10:10, 13; Jer. 40:5; Matt. 11; Judith 13; Judg. 3:17. The emperor Hadrian, out of generosity and esteem, increased the honours and gifts of retired professors at Rome, so that they might spend honourably the rest of their lives. Or someone is also received at a banquet for the sake of honour and pleasure: Luke 5:29, "And Levi made him a great feast in his house"; John 12:2, "So they made him a supper there, and Martha served; but Lazarus was one of those who sat at table with him." Job 1; Luke 14:7 ff.; Gen. 43:16, 33-34; 1 Sam. 9:23-24; 1 Sam. 1:5. See Athenaeus, book 1 of the Deipnosophists, and Johann Wilhelm Stuckius, book 1 De conviviis; and Exod. 18:12 and following.

units.la: Honoris quoq; & reuerentiæ ergo præstantiores & digniores homines pro charissimis à nobis sunt agnoscendi. 1.Thess.c.5.12. Rogamus autem vos fratres, ut agnoscatis eos qui laborant inter vos & præsunt vobis in Domino & admonent vos, 13. Et quam maxime charos ducatis propter opus ipsorum. quibus adde 1. Macch. cap.14.43.44.c.15.32.8.9.Rom.cap.16.1.2.& seqq. adeo vt quandoq; patris loco reuerentiæ ergo habeantur. Iob c.19.16. Pater eram egentibus, & seqq.2.Reg.c.13.14. c.2.12. 1.Timoth.cap.5.2.3. Ioh. cap.19.26.27. c.6 58. 1.(or.cap.4.15. ita vt non solum ipsi honoratiores & digniores tali amore & dilectione sint afficiendi,sed & eorundem amici & fautores,& cognati & quoscunq; amât illi,& contra eorundem inimici fugiendi. Adde his quod & insignibus quibusdam priuilegiis & immunitatibus gaudeant & honestentur. De quibus l.5.&seqq.tit. C.de dig. tit. De vacat. & immu.mun.Tiraquell.De nobilit.c.20. & De iure primog.in præfatio.num.108.&seqq. & Horat. Lucius de priuileg.studios.
units.tr: For the sake of honour and reverence, the more distinguished and worthy men are also to be acknowledged by us as most dear. 1 Thess. 5:12-13: "We beseech you, brethren, to acknowledge those who labour among you and preside over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work." To these add 1 Macc. 14:43-44; 15:32; 8:9; Rom. 16:1-2 and following. So much so that sometimes they are held in the place of a father, for the sake of reverence: Job 19:16; "I was a father to the needy," etc.; 2 Kings 13:14; 2:12; 1 Tim. 5:2-3; John 19:26-27; 6:58; 1 Cor. 4:15. Thus not only should such more honoured and worthy men be regarded with this love and affection, but also their friends and supporters, their relatives, and whoever they love; and conversely, their enemies are to be shunned. Add to these that they enjoy certain special privileges and immunities and are honoured by them. On these see the law of the Code, title On dignities, and title On exemptions and immunities; Tiraquell, On nobility, c. 20, and On the right of primogeniture, preface, nn. 108 ff.; and Horatius Lucius, On the privileges of students.

units.la: Deniq; gestus & habitus conuersationis cum præstantiore & honoratiore ita instituendi, vt omnia quæ vel vmbram suspicionis cuiusdam malæ, sinistræ, molestæ, vel abominationis, aut odii superioris generare possunt, fugiat inferior & omittat. Contra vero elaborandum inferiori & viliori, vt quibuscunque modis licitis & honestis præstantiori placeat; 1. Corinth. c.7.33.34. Ecclesiastic. c.8. Quapropter moribus & voluntati illius gratiose humilis obsecundare poterit,& illius affectibus se adcommodare in iocosis, seriis, iucundis, vel tristibus, ne morum diuersitas tacitum odium & dissidium pariat.
units.tr: Finally, the gestures and demeanour in conversation with a more eminent and honoured person are to be so arranged that the inferior avoids and omits everything which can give rise even to a shadow of some bad, sinister, troublesome or abominable suspicion, or of hatred towards the superior. On the contrary, the inferior and lowlier person must take pains to please the superior by whatever lawful and honest means: 1 Cor. 7:33-34; Ecclus. 8. Therefore he can graciously humble himself and comply with the superior's manners and will, and adapt himself to the superior's moods, whether in jests, serious matters, pleasant or sad circumstances, lest the difference in manners produce silent hatred and discord.

units.la: Dignior etiam eiusmodi & excellentior honorifice sepelitur, reuerentiæ & honoris ergo, vt constat exemplis Genes.cap.25.8.cap.49.29. & seqq.c.50.1.2.3.24.25.26, Iosu. cap.24.32.33. Iudic. c.12. c.12.7.c.16.1.Reg.c.2.10.34. cap.11.43. Num.cap. 20.28.Deut.c.34.f.6.Psal.88.Genes.c.50.2.Sam.c.2. ibi benedicti vos qui Saulem sepeliuistis. Val.Max. lib.5.c.de human. & passim alibi. & latissime probat Tiraquell. De nobilitat. cap.20.numer.150. & seqq. & ab omnibus publice lugetur. Deut. cap. 34.8. Et defleuerant filii Israelis Moysen in campestribus Moabitarum triginta diebus, quibus absoluti sunt dies luctus Moysi, Genes.c.vlt. 1.Sam. c.28.3. Samuel autem mortuus est & planxerunt eum omnes Israelitae, quum sepeliuissent eum Rama. &c. 2.Sam. c.1.11,12.17.c 3.31. & seqq. vbi Dauid & totus populus mortem Abneri lugent & honorifice sepeliunt. Esaia.c.11. ibi & erit sepulcrum eius gloriosum. vid. Chaffan.part.2.confid.5.catal.glor.mundi.
units.tr: A more worthy and excellent person is also buried with honour, for the sake of reverence and esteem, as the examples show: Gen. 25:8; 49:29 ff.; 50:1-3, 24-26; Josh. 24:32-33; Judg. 12; 12:7; 16:1; 1 Kings 2:10, 34; 11:43; Num. 20:28; Deut. 34:6; Ps. 88; Gen. 50:2; 2 Sam. 2, where it is said: "blessed are you who buried Saul." Valerius Maximus, book 5, On human matters, and passim elsewhere. Tiraquell, On nobility, c. 20, n. 150 ff., proves this most fully. And he is publicly mourned by all: Deut. 34:8: "And the children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, until the days of mourning for Moses were ended." Gen. last chapter; 1 Sam. 28:3: "Now Samuel was dead, and all Israel lamented him and buried him in Ramah," etc.; 2 Sam. 1:11-12, 17; 3:31 ff., where David and the whole people mourn the death of Abner and bury him honourably. Isa. 11: "and his tomb shall be glorious." See Chassan, part 2, consid. 5, catal. glor. mundi.

units.la: Sepultura eiusmodi & pompa lugubris reditur honorificentior vestitu lugubri & pullato, epicediis, lamentationibus, orationeve aut carminibus funebribus, virtutes & facta laudabilia defuncti cantantibus & praedicantibus, 2.Sam.cap.1.17. & seqq. & c.3.31.32. & seqq. vide Lament.Ierem.vid. Alex ab Alexand.lib.3 Genial. dier.c.7.Genes.c.50.Deut.c.34. Chaffan. d.loc.refert varias lugendi consuetudines. Feretrum solebant honoratissimi ferre, Alexand. ab Alex. d.cap.7. Actor.c.8,2.Et Stephanum viri religiosi extulerunt, & fecerunt planctum super eum. Funus etiam, & exequias clarissimorum & honoratissimorum virorum praesentia & deductio exornare solet, vti factum in funere Abneri.2.Sam,c.3.31.32. & Iacobi Patriarchae, Genes.c.50.7.8. & seqq. Tiraquell.De nobilitate,c.20.num.150. & seqq. Solebat quoque Romani honoris gratia, insignia honorum, quos defunctus gessit, præferre funeri & exequiis defuncti, vti fasces, secures, lictores, arma, dona militaria, coronas omnis generis, quas in vita meruisset, & similia plura magno cum apparatu; Quandoque etiam vniuersus senatus & magistratus cum vexillis, vel equitum turmis, funus comitabantur, quod præcedebat, & quod illi tanquam paulo post morituri, sequebantur. In sepultura viri militaris honoratissimi, ea fuit pompa, vt armatæ instructæque legiones in turmas & centurias cum vexillis militaribus inuersis, aut abiectis militiæ insignibus, defunctum comitentur, phalerasque equis detrahebant, ensium mucrones & lancearum cuspides humi deiectas ferebant & rogum lustrabant. Vid. Alexand. ab Alexand. lib. 3. Genial. dier. cap. 7. & Euseb. lib. 4. cap. 65. & seqq. in exequiis Constantini. De pompa funerali late disserit Chassan. d. loc. confid. 6. In sepulchrum defuncti, ea quæ charissima in vita habuit defunctus, iniiciebantur, d. cap. 7. vbi etiam refert gentium diuersarum mores in condendis humandisque corporibus defunctorum, & idem Alex. ab Alex. lib. 3. cap. 2. Monumenta quoque & sepulchra præclarorum & honoratorum virorum à plebeiorum sepulchris distinguebantur. vid. Ierem. cap. 26. 23. Abiecitsque cadaver in sepulchra popularium, 2. Reg. c. 23. 6. Et proiecit pulverem eius super sepulchrum illorum popularium. 2. Chron. cap. 26. 23. Tiraquell. d. loc. de Christi honorifica sepultura Iohan. cap. 19. Plane in sacris literis sepultura carere vel assimi sepultura sepeliri, ignominia & infamia tributur, Ierem. c. 22. 19. vbi jun. 2. Reg. cap. 9. 33. 2. Chron. c. 21. 19. 1. Reg. 19.1.Reg.c.13.23.c.16.s.6.7.8.cap.21.24. Esa.c.14. 19.20. Scipio Africanus tanti fecit Ennium Poetam, ut honoris ergo columnam in sepulchro illius erigi curauerit.
units.tr: Burial of this kind and mournful pomp is made more honourable by mourning dress and black clothing, by funeral songs, lamentations, funeral orations or poems, praising and proclaiming the virtues and laudable deeds of the deceased: 2 Sam. 1:17 ff.; 3:31-32 ff.; see Lamentations of Jeremiah. See Alexander ab Alexandro, book 3, Genial days, c. 7; Gen. 50; Deut. 34; Chassan, loc. cit., who relates the various customs of mourning. The most honoured men used to carry the bier: Alexander ab Alexandro, loc. cit. c. 7; Acts 8:2: "And devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him." The funeral and obsequies of the most illustrious and honoured men are also usually adorned by the presence and escort of others, as happened at the funeral of Abner (2 Sam. 3:31-32) and of the patriarch Jacob (Gen. 50:7-8 ff.). See Tiraquell, On nobility, c. 20, n. 150 ff. The Romans also used, for the sake of honour, to carry before the funeral and obsequies of the deceased the insignia of the offices which he had held: fasces, axes, lictors, weapons, military gifts, and crowns of every kind which he had earned in life, and many similar things, with great display. Sometimes the whole senate and the magistrates accompanied the funeral with standards or troops of horsemen, and these went before it, while those who were to die shortly afterwards followed it. At the burial of a most honoured military man the pomp was such that armed and drawn-up legions, in troops and centuries, with military standards reversed, or with the insignia of the army cast down, accompanied the dead man; they stripped the trappings from the horses, carried the points of the swords and the tips of the lances lowered to the ground, and circled the pyre. See Alexander ab Alexandro, book 3, Genial days, c. 7; and Eusebius, book 4, c. 65 ff., on the funeral of Constantine. Chassan, loc. cit., consid. 6, discusses the funeral pomp at length. Into the tomb of the deceased were placed those things which the deceased held most dear in life: loc. cit. c. 7, where he also relates the customs of various peoples in burying and interring the bodies of the dead; and the same Alexander ab Alexandro, book 3, c. 2. The monuments and tombs of illustrious and honoured men were also distinguished from the graves of commoners: see Jer. 26:23, "and cast his body into the graves of the common people"; 2 Kings 23:6, "and strewed its dust upon the graves of the common people"; 2 Chron. 26:23. Tiraquell, loc. cit. On the honourable burial of Christ, John 19. Plainly, in the sacred letters, to lack burial, or to be buried like an animal, is counted a sign of disgrace and infamy: Jer. 22:19; see Junius; 2 Kings 9:33; 2 Chron. 21:19; 1 Kings 13:23; 16:6-8; 21:24; Isa. 14:19-20. Scipio Africanus esteemed the poet Ennius so highly that, out of honour, he had a column erected on his tomb.

units.la: Huc pertinet quoque memoria atq; nomen eorum honoratorum, quod post mortem honorati manet & viuit apud superstites. Eccles.c. 44.13. In seculum manet eorum semen, neq; deletur eorum gloria, 14. Sunt quidem eorum corpora in pace, sed nomen eorum viuit in generationem quamque, 15. Sapientiam eorum narrant populi & laudem eorum enunciat Ecclesiast.cap.45.1.2. & seqq. c.46. & seqq.
units.tr: To this also belongs the memory and name of honoured persons, which remains and lives on among the survivors after death: Eccl. 44:13-15, "Their seed remains for ever, and their glory is not blotted out. Their bodies are buried in peace, but their name lives for generation after generation. Peoples tell of their wisdom, and the assembly proclaims their praise." Ecclus. 45:1-2 ff.; 46 ff.

units.la: Iurisconsulti de operis obsequialibus & officialibus quas liberti suis patronis, & liberi suis parentibus, & serui suis dominis praestare tenentur, agunt in tit. De oper.libert. & tit. De obsequiis parent. & patron. praestand. quae consistunt in faciendo vel omittendo.
units.tr: The jurists treat of the services of obedience and duty which freedmen are bound to render to their patrons, children to their parents, and slaves to their masters, under the title On the services of freedmen and the title On the services to be rendered to parents and patrons, which consist in doing or omitting something.

units.la: In faciendo consistentes sunt, seruire & famulari in mensa, camera, peregrè proficiscentem comitari & cum eodem morari & eius negotium exercere. l.38.hæ demum, in sin. l 23. §.1.l. 20.§.1.de op.libert. Zaf.lib.1.c.3. intellect. singul. dictis factisque eum obseruare, reuereri ita, ut persona patris, patroni & domini semper illis honesta & sancta sit, l. liberto.9. De obseq. parent. & patron.praest.l.1.d.t.l.6.de in ius voc. Ephes.c.6.s.& seqq. monentem & iubentem audiant, l.1. De obsequi.l.7.§.2.de iniur. ei adsurgant & de via decedant, argument.l.1.l.9.de obsequi.par. praestent illa quae amicus amico praestare solet, arg.l.3.4.C.de libert.& eor.lib.& tit.C.de ingrat.lib. egetem alant,
units.tr: They consist in doing: serving and waiting at table and in the bedchamber, accompanying a man who sets out on a journey abroad, staying with him, and carrying out his business. l.38.hæ demum, in sin. l 23. §.1.l. 20.§.1.de op.libert. Zaf.lib.1.c.3. intellect. singul. Observing him in words and deeds, and showing him reverence, so that the person of father, patron and master is always honourable and sacred to them, l. liberto.9. De obseq. parent. & patron.praest.l.1.d.t.l.6.de in ius voc. Ephes.c.6.s.& seqq. They listen to him when he advises and commands, l.1. De obsequi.l.7.§.2.de iniur. They rise for him and step aside from the road, argument.l.1.l.9.de obsequi.par. They render what a friend customarily renders to a friend, arg.l.3.4.C.de libert.& eor.lib.& tit.C.de ingrat.lib. and they feed the needy,

units.la: 2 l. 5.l.6.de lib.agnof.& alend. defendant corpus, fa-mam, vitam & bona eiusdem, arg.l.1.de iur.patronat.& d.l.9.de obsequiis. l.1. C.d.t.l.unic.C.de ingrat.lib.
units.tr: 2 l. 5.l.6.de lib.agnof.& alend. they defend the body, reputation, life and goods of the same, arg.l.1.de iur.patronat.& d.l.9.de obsequiis. l.1. C.d.t.l.unic.C.de ingrat.lib.

units.la: In omittendo, ne dominos, patronos patres-ve suos laedant vel iniuria afficiant, l.7.§.2.l.15.item, §.44.45.de iniur.l.1.l.2.C.de libert.& liber.eor. l.1. de obsequiis parent. & pat. vel paupertate aut corporis valetudine laborantes, deserant, l.5.l.6. De liber. agnosc. & alend. aut quidquid faciant, quod existimationem, vitam, bona vel corpus eorum laedit, l.1.de iur.patron.d.l.7. §.2.l.15. §.44.45.de iniur.l.6.de ius voc.l.1.de obseq.l.unic. (C.de lib. ingrat. Novel.115.c.3. Colerus de proceff.executiu.par. 1.c.9.& Zaf.d.loc.
units.tr: In omitting, they must not injure or insult their masters, patrons or fathers, l.7.§.2.l.15.item, §.44.45.de iniur.l.1.l.2.C.de libert.& liber.eor. l.1. de obsequiis parent. & pat. nor desert them when they are in want or suffering from ill health, l.5.l.6. De liber. agnosc. & alend. nor do anything that harms their reputation, life, goods or body, l.1.de iur.patron.d.l.7. §.2.l.15. §.44.45.de iniur.l.6.de ius voc.l.1.de obseq.l.unic. (C.de lib. ingrat. Novel.115.c.3. Colerus de proceff.executiu.par. 1.c.9.& Zaf.d.loc.

units.la: Vestitus popularium conuersantium & a-gentium cum dignioribus & honoratioribus, debet reuerentiae ergo esse elegans, mundus & honestus, Genef.c.41.14. Ioseph cum abrasisset caput & mutasset vestes, venit ad Pharaonem, & c.50.4.vbi Iun. Daniel. c.1.4.5.& seqq. Luc.c.7.25. Ecce qui vestitu magnifico vtuntur, sunt in palatiis regum, Esth.c.4.2.& seqq. vid. Alex. ab Alex. Gen. dier.c.19.
units.tr: The clothing of commoners who associate and deal with the more distinguished and honourable should, out of respect, be elegant, neat and decent. Genef.c.41.14. Joseph, when he had shaved his head and changed his clothes, came to Pharaoh, & c.50.4. where see Junius and Daniel. c.1.4.5.& seqq. Luke c.7.25. Behold, those who wear splendid clothing are in the palaces of kings. Esth.c.4.2.& seqq. see Alexander ab Alexandro, Gen. dier. c.19.

units.la: Conuersatio popularium cum honoratio-ribus, temperata, parca, rara, esse debet: non frequens, assidua, crebra, iuxta vulgatum, Procul a fulmine & loue, & Prouerb.c.25.17. Studio-se contine pedem tuum a domo proximi tui, ne satura-tus tui odio habeat te. Quam ob causam conuer-satione superiorum, tanquam igne vrendum, a quo si longius recesseris, minus caloris perci-pies; si propius accesseris, plus caloris quo ab-sumeris. fumeris.Eccles. c. 13. 11. Accersente te potentiore, esto ut qui subducit se, & eo magis perget te accersere, 12. Ne irrumpas, ne detrudaris, ne longe absistas, ne tradaris oblitioni. vid. d. c. 13. per tot. & c. 32. 12. Inter magnates ne æqualem te præbeas. Nam multum & frequenter conuersari & communicare cum potentioribus & superioribus te, periculosum, vt late & eleganter explicat Ecclesiasticus cap. 13. per tot. Nam humili & paupere labente omnes increpant; & eodem loquente scientiam, non tribuitur illi locus. Eccles. d. c. 13. 26. Contra fit in diuitibus & potentioribus, d. c. 13. 14. 25. 26. 27. 28. & Eccles. c. 9. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21. 22. Iacob c. 2. 2. 3. 4. & Seneca De prouident.
