Inimicitiæ potentum sunt graues. & lib. 2. epist. 14. Sapiens nunquam potentium iras prouocat; imo declinat, non aliter quam in nanigando procellam. Eccl. c. 9. 16. Longe absiste ab homine qui potestatem habet occidendi, vt minime suspiceris timorem mortis. & seqq.
units.tr: The association of commoners with the honourable should be moderate, sparing and infrequent: not frequent, constant or repeated, as the common saying has it, Far from the thunderbolt and Jove. And Prov. c.25.17. Take care to keep your foot out of your neighbour's house, lest he become sated with you and hate you. For this reason dealings with superiors are to be treated as a fire that must be kept at a distance: if you withdraw farther from it, you will feel less heat; if you approach nearer, you will feel more heat, by which you will be consumed. Eccles. c.13.11. When a more powerful man invites you, be like one who draws back, and he will all the more persist in inviting you, 12. Do not force your way in, do not be pushed away, do not stand too far off, do not be forgotten. See the same chapter 13 throughout, and c.32.12. Among great men do not present yourself as their equal. For to associate and communicate often and at length with the more powerful and superiors is dangerous, as Ecclesiasticus explains broadly and elegantly in chapter 13 throughout. For when a humble and poor man falls, everyone reproaches him; and when he speaks sense, no place is given to him. Eccles. ibid. 13.26. The opposite happens with the rich and the powerful, ibid. 13.14. 25. 26. 27. 28, and Eccles. c.9.17. 18. 19. 20. 21. 22. James c.2.2. 3. 4, and Seneca, De providentia: The enmities of the powerful are grave; and Book 2, Letter 14: The wise man never provokes the anger of the powerful; rather he avoids it, just as in sailing one avoids a storm. Eccl. c.9.16. Keep far from the man who has power to kill, so that you do not fear the dread of death, and so on.

units.la: CAP. IV. De caussa morum reuerentialium, qui præeminentibus splendore & gloria fulgentibus præstantur.
units.tr: CHAP. IV. On the cause of the reverential customs shown to those eminent persons who shine with splendour and glory.

units.la: DE moribus & conuersatione reuerentiali & obsequiali omnibus honoratioribus communi, huc vsque dictum esto; sequitur nunc de moribus reuerentialibus, quæ singularibus & quibusdam, imperio scilicet & potestate propria præditis & præeminentibus personis, præstantur.
units.tr: Thus far has been said about the conduct, reverence and deference common to all men of rank. Now follow the reverential customs, which are owed to singular persons, namely those endowed with command and power of their own and set above others.

units.la: Dignitas hæc superior, cui hi mores obsequiales debentur & competunt, est, quæ comitatur eum, qui suo iure in subditos imperium exercet cum potestate puniendi, coercendi, animaduertendi in facinorosos & bonos praemiis afficiendi.
units.tr: This higher dignity, to which these deferential customs are owed and belong, is the dignity that accompanies one who by his own right exercises authority over subjects, with the power to punish, restrain, and take vengeance on wrongdoers, and to reward the good.

units.la: Haec dignitas suos etiam habet gradus, pro ratione potestatis & magistratus, quem comitatur. Est enim quaedam suprema & maxima, quae dam ab hac immediate pendens. 1 Pet. c 3. 13. 14. Subiecti estote cuiuis humanae ordinationi propter Dominum; sive Regi, ut qui superemineat. 14. Sive praesidibus, ut qui per eum mittantur, tum ad vltionem maleficiorum, tum ad laudem rectè agentium, Rom. c. 13. 1. 2. 3. 4. Exempla huius extant Genes. cap. 41. 38. & seqq. Esth. c. 3. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. cap. 8. 1. 2. & seqq. Daniel. c. 6.
units.tr: This dignity also has its own degrees, according to the extent of the power and the magistracy that accompanies it. For there is one that is supreme and greatest, while others depend immediately upon it. 1 Pet. c 3. 13. 14. "Be subject to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake, whether to the king, as the one who is supreme, or to governors, as those sent by him, both for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of those who do well." Rom. c. 13. 1. 2. 3. 4. Examples of this are found in Gen. ch. 41. 38. ff.; Esth. ch. 3. 1. 2. 3. ff.; ch. 8. 1. 2. ff.; Dan. ch. 6.

units.la: Quo maiorem in genus humanum quis habet administrationem & potestatem eo dignior & sublimior fede, loco, gloria & honore dicitur. l. 2. vbi Lucas de penna. C. ut ord. dign. feru. l. vlt. C. de Decur. Fernand. Vasquius lib. 1. in praefat. num. 126. & seqq. illust. cont. Chassan. part. 5. catal. glor. mundi.
units.tr: The greater the administration and power that someone has over the human race, the more worthy and exalted he is said to be in rank, place, glory and honour. l. 2. where Lucas de Penna; C. ut ord. dign. feru.; l. vlt. C. de Decur.; Fernand. Vasquius lib. 1, in praefat. num. 126 ff.; illust. cont. Chassan. part. 5, catal. glor. mundi.

units.la: Supremae dignitati, quae nullum alium quam Deum, agnoscit superiorem, debetur omnis reuerentia, honor & obsequia, quae in hominem post Deum cadere possunt, vid. Eccles. c. 8. 1. 2. 3 & seqq. vbi Iun. Nam cum hic maximam curam, solicitudinem & studium ponat defendendorum & protegendorum subditorum, contra quasuis iniurias aliorum; & potestatem ordinandorum eorum quae ad salutem subditorum & vitam pie & tranquille ducendam pertinent, habeat; & aliis inferuiedo seipsum quasi consumat, ideo hæc cura, protectio, prouidentia, gubernatio & officium merito honorandum est. Qua de re eleganter Sen lib. ad Polybium: Cæsari, inquit, ipsi cui omnia licent, multa non licent; omnium domos illius vigilia defendit; omnium otium illius labor, omnium delicias, illius industria; omnium vacationem illius occupatio. Ex quo se Cæsar orbi terrarum dedicauit, sibi eripuit, & syderum modo (quæ irrequieta semper cursus suos explicant) nunquam illi licet nec subsistere, neq; quicquam suum facere. Deinde negari non potest, Magistratum dominum & defensorem esse subditorum corporum, vitæ, bonorum, famæ & existimationis & pudicitiæ defensorem & maleficiorum vltorem; quæ dona à Deo in ipsum collata, agnoscenda sunt. Gerit enim in his quasi typum Diuinæ potentiæ, maiestatis, gloriæ, imperii, clementiæ, prouidentiæ, curæ, protectionis, gubernationis & bonitatis, quod potissimum apparet ex illis quæ huius officio commissa sunt. Habet enim hic Magistratus, imperium perpetuum, nullis legibus, tempore, loco, vel caussis definitum, vt Iurisconsulti definiunt, & exemplis piorum magistratuum probatur, Deut. c. 17. 20. Genes. c. 49. 10. & dixi latius in Dicæolog. lib. 1. c. 32. De summo imperio. Chassan. late d. part. 5.
units.tr: To the supreme dignity, which acknowledges no superior other than God, is owed all the reverence, honour and deference that can be paid to a man after God. See Eccles. ch. 8. 1. 2. 3 ff., where Junius. For since he bears the greatest care, concern and zeal in defending and protecting his subjects against any injuries from others, and has the power of ordering those things which pertain to the safety of the subjects and to leading a pious and tranquil life, and since he almost wears himself out in serving others, this care, protection, foresight, government and office deserve to be honoured. On this matter Seneca writes elegantly in his letter to Polybius: "To Caesar himself, to whom all things are permitted, many things are not permitted. His vigilance defends the homes of all; his labour is the leisure of all, his industry the delights of all, his occupation the rest of all. From the time Caesar dedicated himself to the world, he took himself away from himself, and like the stars (which always unfold their courses without rest), it is never permitted him to stand still or to do anything of his own." Next, it cannot be denied that the magistrate is the lord and defender of the subjects' bodies, life, goods, reputation, esteem and chastity, and the avenger of wrongdoers; these gifts, bestowed by God upon him, must be acknowledged. For in these things he bears, as it were, a type of the divine power, majesty, glory, authority, clemency, foresight, care, protection, government and goodness, which appears chiefly from those things committed to his office. For this magistrate has a perpetual authority, not limited by laws, time, place or causes, as the jurists define it, and this is proved by the examples of pious magistrates. Deut. ch. 17. 20. Gen. ch. 49. 10. And I have spoken more fully in the Dicaeologia, book 1, ch. 32, On supreme authority. Chassan. at length, loc. cit., part 5.

units.la: Habet quoque potestatem per ministros verbi Religionis exercendæ, introducendæ, promulgandæ, secundum verbum Dei in territorio suo. vid. 2. Chronic. c. 33. 16, c. 34. 8. 33. & seqq. 2. Reg. c. 10. 1. Sam. c. 8. Daniel. c. 3. c. 6. 26. Pet. Martyr 1. Sam. c. 28. Eusebius in vita Constantini, lib. 4. Socrates lib. 11. c. 9. histor. ecclesiast. Theodoret. lib. 5. c. 2. lib.4.c.5 Ruffin.lib.2. c.1. & ad veram religionem & externam disciplinam suos subditos cogendi, 2.Chron. c.15.12.13.14. c.34.35. c.17. c.33. 16. Nehem. c.10. Luc.c.14. 23. vt latius differt lib.1. Dicaeol. Habet etiam ius concilii vniuersalis indicendi & conuocandi. Iudic. c.20.2.Chron. c.1.2.3.5.15.9. 10.11.c.10.1. c.32.6.7. cap.34.19. Ius publicae securitatis, seu salui conductus, per territorium impsius eundi, sine vlla alterius offensione, laesione, aut impedimento, qui dicitur commeatus & remeatus, l. 22.filii, §. pen. ad municip. l.relegati, de pœn.de quo etiam Genef.cap.33.15. cap.26.16.17.27. cap.12 17.cap.18.16. Numer.cap.21.22. Iudic.cap. 11.19.20.21.22. & 1.Samuel.cap.27.5.6. Deut.cap. 2.27.28. Numer.cap.20.21.22.16.17. Exod. cap. 18.27.1.Samuel.c.22.23. 2.Sam. cap.14.9.10. Habet etiam ius commerciorum, in territorio suo agitandorum & excercendorum. tit. C. de commerc. & mercat.Genef.c.34.21. & seqq. cap. 42. 34. Ius monetae percutiendae & signandae cum certo pondere, valore & publica functione, c.1.quae sunt reg.in vsib.feud.1. Macchab.c.15.5.6.7. Matt. cap.22.17.18.20. Ius belli indicendi, vel pacis ineundae, tit. Cod.vt arm.vf. inscio princ. libr. 11. Nouell.85.& 1.Samuel. cap.13.19. c.11.6.7. & seqq. 2.Sam. cap. 5. 2. ibi, Tu educebas & introducebas, &c.Exod.cap.17.Iudic. cap.5.9.23.cap.21.c.11. Leuit.cap 27. Num.c. 21.Iosc.c.15.c.8. Deut.cap.17.16. 17. Ius magistratus intermedii constituendi, 1.Pet.c.3.13.14.15.Exod.c.18 21.22.23.25.26.Deut. cap.1.15.c.16.18.2.Chron.cap.19.Ius extremae provocationis, Bodin.de Repub.lib.2. c.10. Pet.Gregor. & Repub.li.9. c.1.n.36. &seqq.Exod. c.18.19.22.26.
units.tr: He also has the power, through the ministers of the Word, to exercise, introduce and promulgate the religion according to the Word of God in his territory. See 2 Chron. ch. 33. 16, ch. 34. 8. 33 ff.; 2 Kings ch. 10; 1 Sam. ch. 8; Dan. ch. 3, ch. 6. 26; Pet. Martyr on 1 Sam. ch. 28; Eusebius in the Life of Constantine, book 4; Socrates, book 1, ch. 9 of the Ecclesiastical History; Theodoret, book 5, ch. 2. book 4, ch. 5; Rufinus, book 2, ch. 1. And he has the power to compel his subjects to the true religion and to external discipline, 2 Chron. 15. 12. 13. 14; ch. 34. 35; ch. 17; ch. 33. 16; Neh. ch. 10; Luke ch. 14. 23, as is discussed more fully in the Dicaeologia, book 1. He also has the right to announce and convene a general council. Judg. ch. 20. 2; Chron. ch. 1. 2. 3. 5. 15. 9. 10. 11; ch. 10. 1; ch. 32. 6. 7; ch. 34. 19. The right of public security, or safe-conduct, to go through his territory without any offence, injury or hindrance, which is called passage and return: Lib. 22, "Filii," §. pen. ad municip.; l. "relegati," de poen., concerning which also Gen. ch. 33. 15; ch. 26. 16. 17. 27; ch. 12. 17; ch. 18. 16; Num. ch. 21. 22; Judg. ch. 11. 19. 20. 21. 22; 1 Sam. ch. 27. 5. 6; Deut. ch. 2. 27. 28; Num. ch. 20. 21. 22. 16. 17; Exod. ch. 18. 27; 1 Sam. ch. 22. 23; 2 Sam. ch. 14. 9. 10. He also has the right of trade, to be conducted and carried on in his territory. Title C. de commerciis et mercatoribus; Gen. ch. 34. 21 ff.; ch. 42. 34. The right to strike and stamp money with a fixed weight, value and public function: c. 1, "quae sunt regalia" in the Libri feudorum; 1 Macc. ch. 15. 5. 6. 7; Matt. ch. 22. 17. 18. 20. The right to declare war or to make peace: Title C. ut armorum usus; Novel 85; 1 Sam. ch. 13. 19; ch. 11. 6. 7 ff.; 2 Sam. ch. 5. 2, where "you used to lead out and bring in," etc.; Exod. ch. 17; Judg. ch. 5. 9. 23; ch. 21; ch. 11; Lev. ch. 27; Num. ch. 21; Josh. ch. 15; ch. 8; Deut. ch. 17. 16. 17. The right to appoint intermediate magistrates: 1 Pet. ch. 3. 13. 14. 15; Exod. ch. 18. 21. 22. 23. 25. 26; Deut. ch. 1. 15; ch. 16. 18; 2 Chron. ch. 19. The right of final appeal: Bodin, On the Commonwealth, book 2, ch. 10; Pet. Gregor., and On the Commonwealth, book 9, ch. 1, n. 36 ff.; Exod. ch. 18. 19. 22. 26.

units.la: Aff. Act.c.25.11.12.13.c.26.32.Ius vitæ & necis. Iohan. c.19.10.11.&seqq. Eccles.cap.8.c.9. Roman.cap.13. Prouer.c.16.14. c.19.12.1.Sam. c.22.8. &seqq. Daniel.c.2.5.12.Senec.lib.1.De clement.c.1. Habet denique ius & officium ordinandi, constituendi, defendendi,conseruandi ea, quæ ad salutem & tranquillam, honestam ac piam vitam pertinent;ius gubernandi & regendi subditos, pœnas maleficis infligendi & præmio bonos afficiendi. Ideo custodiam & curam suorum subditorum gerit,ne eorum corpora,bona,fama,pudicitia, & existimatio, atque honor ab aliis lædantur impunè, vel iniuriâ quouis modo afficiantur.Et hinc est,quod honorificis titulis & cognominib. ornetur Magistratus. Vocatur enim Regia maiestas,pater patriæ, Senec.lib.1. De clement.c.14.l.19.de interd. & relegat. Genef.c.41.42. 43.&seqq.c.45.8.9.Iudic.cap.5.7. vbi Petr.Martyr & Iun. & verf.13. 1.Samuel, c.24.12. Lucerna Reipubl.2.Sam.c.21.17.1.Reg cap.11.36. & Psalm. 132.17. vbi Iun. Dux & pastor populi & subditorum suorum, 1.Sam. cap.5.2.Esai.c.44.Ierem. cap.10.cap.50.6.Ezech.cap.34. Nahum.c.3.Psalm. 78. in fine. Cor populi, anima Imperii & spiritus vitalis,Senec.lib.1.De clement.c.4.5.Esa.cap.1.5. 6.vbi Iun. caput Reipub. Iudic.cap.11.2.10.11.13. 19.21.c.5.7.2.Sam.c.22.44. 1.Sam. c.15.17.18.Esa. cap.5.7 vbi Iun. & verf.13.c.14.15.Psalm.18.44. arg.1.ad Corinth.c.11.10.Esa.c.7.cap.9.Deut.cap.28. Ierem.c.48.Regni anima.Lipsius lib.2. Polit. c.16. & lib.4. c.9.Senec.lib.1. De clem. c.4.cap.5. statu s publici tutor, Senec.lib.1. De clem. c.4.l.3.de offic. præfect.vig.& instar plurimorum esse.2.Sam,cap. Lex viua subditorum. Nouell. 105. §.1. vid. Pet.Gregor.de Repub.lib.6. & lib.4. & Magistratus ideo Diuus vocatur, l.Diuus,de bon.damnat. §.39. thesauros,Inst.de rerum diuif.§ 3. Justit. de donat. & passim alibi in iure ciuili,praesertim in Codice & Nouell, Semideus in terris, Psalm.82.6. Exod.c.7.12.9.10.18. Ioh.c.10.34.35. Dan.cap.2.37.38.39.40. Senec.lib.1. De clement.c.1.c.19. sanctissimus & nobilissimus dicitur in l.quaeris. de natal.restit. supremus omnium. l.pen.(de bon.qua.lib.vide Chassan. part.5.confid.27.catal.glor.mundi. l.celsissimus l.sin. C.de consul. lib.12. Apud Germanos eiusmodi summi Magistratus vocantur Caesares, Imperatores, Reges, Principes, Duces, Marchiones, Comites, Marcgraui, Pfaltzgraui, Rheingraui, Barones, & pluribus aliis nominibus. Apud Aegyptios, Pharaones appellabantur. Apud Turcos hodie Sultani. Apud Iudaeos, modo Reges, 1.Sam.c.8. & 1. & 2.Reg. quandoque antecessores & ductores, 1.Sam.c.9.16.c.10.1.c.8.20.19.c.12.4.c.13.14.1.Chro. c.11.2.c.17.7.8.Esa.cap.3.8.13.15. In sacris literis vero ευεργέται munifici, liberales appellantur, vt in Psalm.146.3. vbi Iun. Psalm.113.8. vbi Iun. Prouer. c.8.16.c.19.6.c.25.7.Esa.c.13.2.1.Sam.c.2.8. Job c.30.15.c.29. Filii excelsi, Psal.82.6. & Dii, Ioh. c.10. 34.35.d.Psal.82.6. ideo quod Dei sermo ad eos factus est, vt Christus docet, Ioh.d.c.10.35. beneficii & magnates, Luc.c.22.25. Mat.c.20.25. Mar. cap.10.42.
units.tr: Aff. Acts ch. 25. 11. 12. 13; ch. 26. 32. The right of life and death. John ch. 19. 10. 11 ff.; Eccles. ch. 8; ch. 9; Rom. ch. 13; Prov. ch. 16. 14; ch. 19. 12; 1 Sam. ch. 22. 8 ff.; Dan. ch. 2. 5. 12; Seneca, On Clemency, book 1, ch. 1. Finally, he has the right and duty to order, establish, defend and preserve those things which pertain to the safety and to a tranquil, honest and pious life; the right to govern and rule the subjects, to inflict punishments on wrongdoers and to reward the good. Therefore he keeps watch over and cares for his subjects, so that their bodies, goods, reputation, chastity and esteem, and their honour, are not harmed with impunity by others, or injured in any way. And hence it is that the magistrate is adorned with honourable titles and surnames. For he is called "royal majesty," "father of the country," Seneca, On Clemency, book 1, ch. 14; l. 19, de interd. et relegat.; Gen. ch. 41. 42. 43 ff.; ch. 45. 8. 9; Judg. ch. 5. 7, where Peter Martyr and Junius; and verse 13; 1 Sam. ch. 24. 12. "lamp of the commonwealth," 2 Sam. ch. 21. 17; 1 Kings ch. 11. 36; and Psalm 132. 17, where Junius. "leader and shepherd of the people and of his subjects," 1 Sam. ch. 5. 2; Isa. ch. 44; Jer. ch. 10; ch. 50. 6; Ezek. ch. 34; Nahum ch. 3; Psalm 78, at the end. "heart of the people," "soul of the empire and vital spirit," Seneca, On Clemency, book 1, ch. 4. 5; Isa. ch. 1. 5. 6, where Junius. "head of the commonwealth," Judg. ch. 11. 2. 10. 11. 13. 19. 21; ch. 5. 7; 2 Sam. ch. 22. 44; 1 Sam. ch. 15. 17. 18; Isa. ch. 5. 7, where Junius, and verse 13; ch. 14. 15; Psalm 18. 44; argument to 1 Cor. ch. 11. 10; Isa. ch. 7; ch. 9; Deut. ch. 28; Jer. ch. 48. "soul of the kingdom," Lipsius, Politics, book 2, ch. 16, and book 4, ch. 9; Seneca, On Clemency, book 1, ch. 4, ch. 5. "guardian of the public state," Seneca, On Clemency, book 1, ch. 4; l. 3, de officio praefecti vigilum. and "to be like many," 2 Sam. ch. ... "living law of the subjects," Novel 105, §. 1. See Peter Gregor., On the Commonwealth, book 6 and book 4. And the magistrate is therefore called "divine," l. "Divus," de bonis damnatorum, §. 39; "thesauros," Inst. de rerum divisione, §. 3; Justinian, de donationibus; and elsewhere throughout the civil law, especially in the Code and the Novels; "demigod on earth," Psalm 82. 6; Exod. ch. 7. 12; 9. 10. 18; John ch. 10. 34. 35; Dan. ch. 2. 37. 38. 39. 40; Seneca, On Clemency, book 1, ch. 1, ch. 19. He is called "most holy and most noble," in l. "Quaeris," de natalibus restituendis; "supreme over all," l. pen. (de bonis quae liberis); see Chassan. part 5, consid. 27, catal. glor. mundi; l. "Celsissimus"; l. "Sin," C. de consulibus, book 12. Among the Germans such supreme magistrates are called Caesars, Emperors, Kings, Princes, Dukes, Margraves, Counts, Markgraves, Palsgraves, Rhinegraves, Barons, and by many other names. Among the Egyptians they were called Pharaohs; among the Turks today, Sultans. Among the Jews, formerly kings, 1 Sam. ch. 8; 1 and 2 Kings, and sometimes forerunners and leaders, 1 Sam. ch. 9. 16; ch. 10. 1; ch. 8. 20; ch. 19; ch. 12. 4; ch. 13. 14; 1 Chron. ch. 11. 2; ch. 17. 7. 8; Isa. ch. 3. 8. 13. 15. In the sacred writings they are called εὐεργέται [benefactors], munificent and liberal, as in Psalm 146. 3, where Junius; Psalm 113. 8, where Junius; Prov. ch. 8. 16; ch. 19. 6; ch. 25. 7; Isa. ch. 13. 2; 1 Sam. ch. 2. 8; Job ch. 30. 15; ch. 29. "sons of the Most High," Psalm 82. 6; and "gods," John ch. 10. 34. 35; and Psalm 82. 6, because the word of God was addressed to them, as Christ teaches, John ch. 10. 35. "benefactors and magnates," Luke ch. 22. 25; Matt. ch. 20. 25; Mark ch. 10. 42.

units.la: Huic praedictae causae summae reverentiae, honoris & obsequiorum Magistratui summo praestandorum, accedit, quod Deus illi notas maiestatis cuiusdam impressit; & Diuinae suae potentiae, tentiæ, maiestatis, gloriæ, imperii, clementiæ, bonitatis, defensionis, prouidentiæ, curæ, gubernationis & pœnæ infligendæ signa, impressit & indidit, vt patet ex exemplis. Num.c.27.18. Edixit vero Iehoua ad Mosi, Sume tecum Iosuam filium Nunis, virum in quo est spiritus meus, vt imponens manum tuam illi, 19. Sistensq; illum coram Eleazare sacerdote, & coram toto cœtu, mandatis instruas illum, ante oculos eorum, 20. Et impertiaris ei de gloria tua, vt auscultent ei totus cœtus filiorum Israelis, & seqq. Psal.51.14. Redde mihi gaudium salutis tuæ & spiritu ingenuitatis sustentato me, 1. Chron. c.29.25. Magnificabat enim Iehoua Salomonem ante oculos totius Israelis, indensei maiestatem regiam, qualis non fuerat in vllo regum ante ipsum super Israelem, & c. 14.17. Sic abiit fama Dauidis per omnes regiones; & Iehoua indidit metu eius omnib. gentibus, Iud. c.3.10. Cui cum insideret spiritus Dei, vindicauit Israel, & v. 15. Iosu. c.4.14. Die isto magnificauit Iehoua Iosuam ante oculos omnium Israelitarum, vt reuerentur eum quemadmodum erant veriti Mosen omnibus diebus vitæ eius. Deut.c.vlt.9. Erat autem Iosua filius Nunis plenus spiritu sapientiæ, cum imposuisset Moses manus suas ei: quapropter auscultantes ei filii Israelis, fecerunt quemadmodum præceperat Iehoua per Mosen. Exod.cap.19.9.10. Haggæ.c.1.14. Concitauitque Iehoua spiritum Zerubabelis, ducis Iehudæ & spiritum Iehosuæ. & seqq. Tantam etiam Mosi maiestatem Deus indidit, vt nunquam Pharao in eum manum mittere ausus sit. Et sic Gedion, Iudic. c.6. adde 2. Samuel.c.19.28. & c.14.21. & Exod.c.34.29. & seqq. vbi Mosen ex monte Sinai redeuntem & facie splendentem populus timebat accedere. Num.c.11.17. Tum descendens loquar tecum ibi: & seponam de spiritu qui est super te, ponamque in eis, sic portabunt tecum onus populi, neque portabis tu solus. & verf. 25. Tum descendens Iehoua in nube illa, allocutus est eum: & seponens de illo spiritu qui erat super eum, indidit septuaginta illis viris senioribus. Fuitque cum resideret super eos spiritus ille, &c. & verf. 26. 27. 28. 29. 1. Sam. cap 10. 6. Irruetque super te spiritus Iehoua ut prophetes cum eis: & mutaberis in virum alium. & verf. 9. 26. & c. 11. 6. & seqq. & c. 16. 14. Samuel itaque accepto cornu olei, unxit eum in medio fratrum eius, & irruens spiritus Iehoua in Dauidem, egt eum a die illo & deinceps. Exod. cap. 4. 16. Iudic. c. 6. 34. Sed spiritus Iehoua induit Gedeonem, qui vbi clanxisset buccina, conuocati Abihezerita eum secuti sunt. 1. Re. c. 8. c. 9. Maiestatis huius Magistratui impressae exempla refert. Valer. Maxim. lib. 2. c. 10. & Plutarc. in vita Marii. & Sueton. Tranquill. in vita Vespasiani. c. 7.
units.tr: To the aforesaid reasons for the highest reverence, honour and obedience owed to the supreme magistrate, there is added this: God has stamped upon him certain marks of majesty, and has impressed and placed upon him the signs of his divine power, majesty, glory, dominion, clemency, goodness, defence, providence, care, government and the punishment to be inflicted, as the examples show. Num. 27:18. The LORD said to Moses, Take Joshua the son of Nun with you, a man in whom is the spirit, and lay your hand upon him, 19. and set him before Eleazar the priest and before all the congregation, and charge him in their sight, 20. and give him some of your honour, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey him, and following. Ps. 51:14. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit, 1 Chron. 29:25. For the LORD magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, and bestowed upon him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel, and 14:17. So the fame of David went out into all lands, and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations, Judg. 3:10. The Spirit of God came upon him, and he judged Israel, and v. 15. Josh. 4:14. On that day the LORD magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel, so that they revered him as they had revered Moses all the days of his life. Deut. last ch. 9. Now Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands upon him; so the children of Israel obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses. Exod. 19:9, 10. Hag. 1:14. The LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua, and following. God also bestowed such majesty upon Moses that Pharaoh never dared to lay hands on him. So also Gideon, Judg. 6; add 2 Sam. 19:28; 14:21; and Exod. 34:29ff., where the people, seeing Moses coming down from Mount Sinai with his face shining, were afraid to approach him. Num. 11:17. I will come down and speak with you there, and I will take some of the spirit that is upon you and put it upon them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you will not bear it alone. And v. 25. Then the LORD came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and took some of the spirit that was upon him and gave it to the seventy elders. And when the spirit rested upon them, etc.; and vv. 26, 27, 28, 29. 1 Sam. 10:6. The Spirit of the LORD will come upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man, and vv. 9, 26; and 11:6ff.; and 16:14. So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward. Exod. 4:16. Judg. 6:34. But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, who, when he had blown the trumpet, the Abiezrites were gathered and followed him. 1 Kings 8; 9. Examples of this majesty impressed upon the magistrate are given by Valerius Maximus, book 2, ch. 10; Plutarch in the Life of Marius; and Suetonius Tranquillus in the Life of Vespasian, ch. 7.

units.la: Praeterea in veneratione hac Magistratus, non tam persona ipsius Magistratus, qui instar Dei legati est, quam ipsius Dei delegantis, Rom. cap. 13. 4. 6. 1. 2. 3. 2. Chronic. c. 19. 6. Hebr. cap. 13. 17. Exod. cap. 4. 15. 16. c. 5. cap 6. 9. Daniel. cap. 2. 37. & seqq. Eccles. c. 6. 5. & seqq. c. 13. 11. & seqq. cuius vicem magistratus gerit, cum timore agnoscenda est, arg. Luc. c. 10. 16. Qui vos audit, me audit & honorat. c. 10. atque arg. Matt. c. 23. 2 3. 4. Vt tamen Deo ipsi in omnibus non assimiletur, Act. c. 14. 14, 15. c. 12. 21. & seqq. c. 10. 25. 26. Quia honorem suum Deus, alii non vult dare, Esa c. 42. Matth. c. 4. 10. Quamuis quidam ita stulti fuerunt, ut sibi honores diuinos tribui voluerint & superbiae atque atq; vanitatis intolerabiles titulos sibi vsurpa-rint, obliti se homines esse. Daniel. cap. 6, 8, 9. & Dii dici & haberi, & Domini dominantium. vide de hisce Pet. Greg. lib. 6. c. 10. c. 11. c. 12. de Repub. Iudith. c. 3. c. 5. 29. c. 6. Act. c. 12. Daniel. c. 2 c. 3. c. 6. 8. 9. c. 4. 2. Chron. c. 32. 13. & seqq. 2. Reg. cap. 18. c. 19. 2. Macchab. c. 9. 8. 13. c. 11. 23. 24.
units.tr: Moreover, this reverence is owed to the magistrate not so much for his own person, though he is God's envoy, as for the God who sent him. Rom. 13:4, 6, 1, 2, 3; 2 Chron. 19:6; Heb. 13:17; Exod. 4:15, 16; 5; 6:9; Dan. 2:37ff.; Eccles. 6:5ff.; 13:11ff. Whose place the magistrate holds, and so he is to be acknowledged with fear, by argument from Luke 10:16, He who hears you hears me and honours me; ch. 10; and by argument from Matt. 23:2, 3, 4. Yet he is not to be likened to God himself in all things, Acts 14:14, 15; 12:21ff.; 10:25, 26, because God does not wish to give his honour to another, Isa. 42; Matt. 4:10. Although some have been so foolish as to want divine honours paid to them, and have assumed to themselves intolerable titles of pride and vanity, forgetting that they are men, Dan. 6, 8, 9; and to be called and held gods, and lords of lords. On these matters see Peter Gregory, book 6, chs. 10, 11, 12, On the Republic; Judith 3; 5:29; 6; Acts 12; Dan. 2; 3; 6; 8; 9; 4:2; 2 Chron. 32:13ff.; 2 Kings 18; 19; 2 Macc. 9:8, 13; 11:23, 24.

units.la: Denique & exempla huius venerationis passim occurrunt. 2. Sam. c. 19. 28. Dominus meus sicut Angelus Dei. cap. 14. 21. Dominus meus sapiens est quasi sapientia angeli ad cognoscendum, quidquid fit in hac terra. Sic Dauid Saulem etiam impium pro Christo Domini agnouit. 1. Samuel. cap. 24. 5. 6. 7. cap. 26. 9. & Abisai Dauidem. 2. Samuel. cap. 19. 21. 26, 27. & Adonias. 1. Reg. c. 2. 15. & Israel. cap. 3. 28. & alii 2. Sam. cap. 14. 21. 1. Sam. cap. 25. 28. & seqq. Est enim ira & indignatio huius, nuntius mortis. Ecclesiastes c. 16. 14. c. 19. 12. c. 20. 2. Chron. c. 24. 21. 22. Daniel. c. 2. 5. 12. & Actor. cap. 23. 3. 4. 5. Exod. cap. 22. 28. vide Chassan. part. 5. catal. glor. mundi.
units.tr: Finally, examples of this reverence occur everywhere. 2 Sam. 19:28, My lord is like the angel of God. 14:21, My lord is wise, with the wisdom of an angel of God, to know whatever happens on this earth. Thus David acknowledged Saul, even though impious, as the anointed of the LORD. 1 Sam. 24:5, 6, 7; 26:9. And Abishai (acknowledged) David, 2 Sam. 19:21, 26, 27; and Adonijah, 1 Kings 2:15; and Israel, Gen. 3:28; and others, 2 Sam. 14:21; 1 Sam. 25:28ff. For the anger and indignation of such a man is the messenger of death. Eccles. 16:14; 19:12; 20:2; 2 Chron. 24:21, 22; Dan. 2:5, 12; Acts 23:3, 4, 5; Exod. 22:28. See Chassanaeus, part 5, Catalogue of Worldly Glory.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: De summa reuerentia & veneratione, qua gestu & sermone praestatur.
units.tr: On the greatest reverence and veneration, which is shown by gesture and speech.

units.la: DE cautiis summae venerationis huc vsque: sequitur vt videamus, quibus sermonibus & gestibus reuerentialibus illa praestetur.
units.tr: So far I have treated the cautions of the highest veneration. Next we shall see by what words and reverent gestures it is shown.

units.la: Eiusmodi igitur mores & conuersatio in sermone consistens, est deprecatio pro salute summi magistratus facienda, 1. Timoth. c. 2. 2. Pro regibus & quibusuis in eminentia constitutis, fiant deprecationes, preces, postulationes, & gratiarum actiones, vt tranquillam, & quietam vitam degamus, cum omni pietate & honestate. Ierem. c. 29. 7. Denique quaerite prosperitatem illius ciuitatis, quo deportauì vos: & orate pro ea Iehouam. nam in prosperitate eius futura est vobis prosperitas. Baruch. c. 1. 11. Orate pro vita Nebucadnezaris Regis Babylonis, & pro vita Belschatzaris filii eius, & seq. 12. 13. 1. Reg. c. 1. 47. 48. c. 13. 7. 2. Chron. c. 22. 12. 1. Sam. c. 10. 24. 2. Reg. c. 11. 12. Daniel. c. 3. 9. c. 6. 6. 21. & vota pro salute illius facienda. l. vnic. C. de oblat. vot. l. si caluitur. 233. §. 1. de verb. sign. Senec. ad Polyb. 31. eiusmodi vota & deprecationes pro Rege describit, & Polybius in Panegyrico Traiani, & lib. 10. epist. ad Traian. Alexand. ab Alex. lib. 3. c. 22. Gen. dier.
units.tr: Such manners and conduct, consisting in speech, are the prayer to be made for the safety of the highest magistrate: 1 Timothy 2:2: "Prayers, supplications, intercessions and thanksgivings be made for kings and all who are in high place, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty." Jeremiah 29:7: "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace shall you have peace." Baruch 1:11–12: "Pray for the life of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and for the life of Belshazzar his son," and so on. 1 Kings 1:47–48; 1 Kings 13:7; 2 Chronicles 22:12; 1 Samuel 10:24; 2 Kings 11:12; Daniel 3:9; Daniel 6:6, 21. and vows are to be made for his safety. Cod. 'l. unic. C. de oblat. vot.'; 'l. si quis' 233, §1, de verb. sign.; Seneca to Polybius, 31: he describes such vows and prayers for the king; and Polybius in the Panegyric of Trajan, and book 10, letter to Trajan; Alexander ab Alexandro, book 3, ch. 22; Gen. dier.

units.la: Deinde semper de hisce Magistratibus & vbicunque bene & honorifice loquendum & iudicandum. Nihil enim fit vel dicitur, quod ipsos lateat, quodq; non ad ipsos deferatur. ideoque longas manus & longas aures habere, hoc est, magnae scientiae & potentiae esse dicuntur. Ecclesiastis c. 10. 17. Nequidem in conscientia tua Regi maledicito, & in conclavibus cubilis tui, ne maledicito diuiti nam vel auis caelorum perferret vocem illam, & alis indicaret verbum. Ratio sumitur ex verf. 4. & seqq. d. c. 10. & c. 8. Ecclesiastis 2. Sam. c. 18. 13. Aut si commisero ex memetipso falsitatem, cum nulla res possit a Rege celari, an tu futurus es te ex aduerso? Genes. c. 44. 5. 15. argum. Act. c. 23. 4. 5. Exod. c. 22. 28. Eccl. c. 44. & seqq. 2. Sam. c. 16. 9.
units.tr: Next, one must always speak and judge well and honourably of these magistrates, wherever one is. For nothing is done or said that does not reach their ears and is not reported to them. Hence they are said to have long hands and long ears, that is, to have great knowledge and power. Ecclesiastes 10:20: "Curse not the king, no, not in your thought, and curse not the rich in your bedchamber; for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which has wings shall tell the matter." The reason is taken from verse 4 and following of the same chapter 10, and chapter 8. Ecclesiastes 2. Samuel 18:13: "Otherwise, if I had dealt falsely against my own life (for there is no matter hidden from the king), would you yourself have stood aloof?" Genesis 44:5, 15, argument; Acts 23:4–5; Exodus 22:28; Ecclesiasticus 44 and following; 2 Samuel 16:9.

units.la: Ciuile quoque est, honorificis cognominibus & titulis ab officio, vel aliis adiunctis, cohonestare Magistratus: cum etiam in Scriptura saepius vocentur benefici, ingenui, Dii, & ab aliis clementes, mentes, patres, magni, felices, caput & anima Reipub. de quibus supra dixi & in Sueton. in August. c. 58. & 7. Sen. lib. 1. De clement. c. 14. vid. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 2. c. 19. Sic discipuli Christum non Iesum, sed magistrū vocabant & dominum suum.
units.tr: It is also a civil duty to honour the magistrates with respectful titles drawn from their office or other attributes, since in Scripture they are often called benefactors, noble, gods, and by others merciful, mighty, fathers, great, fortunate, head and soul of the commonwealth, about which I have spoken above; and see Suetonius, Augustus 58 and 7; Seneca, On Clemency, book 1, ch. 14; see Alexander ab Alexandro, book 2, ch. 19. So the disciples called Christ not Jesus but their teacher and their lord.

units.la: Huc etiam pertinet admonitio & consilium de vtilitate, salute & commodo, vel incommodo & periculo futuro Magistratus, quam subditus facere tenetur, Jerem. c. 29. 7. Quaerite prosperitatem istius ciuitatis, &c. & 2. Reg. c. 5. 13. & seqq. vbi notabile exemplum extat, & 2. Sam. c. 17. 15. 16. 17. 18. & seqq. c. 21. 17. 18. c. 18. 3. 4. 5. c. 15. per tot. c. 19. 6, 7. 8, 9. Ephes. c. 19. 20.
units.tr: To this also belongs the admonition and counsel concerning the advantage, safety and welfare, or the harm and future danger, of the magistrate, which the subject is bound to give: Jeremiah 29:7: "Seek the peace of that city," etc.; and 2 Kings 5:13 and following, where a notable example stands; 2 Samuel 17:15–18 and following; 2 Samuel 21:17–18; 2 Samuel 18:3–5; 2 Samuel 15 throughout; 2 Samuel 19:6–9; Ephesians 19–20.

units.la: Huc quoq; benedictio, quae fit Magistratui a subditis inferioribus. 1. Reg. c. 1. 31. 47. 48. 2. Sam. c. 14. 23. Daniel. c. 6. 22. c. 4. 19. 2. Reg. c. 11. 12. 1. Sam. cap. 10. 24. Genes. 47. 7. 10. cum professione obedientiae & seruitutis debitae, 1. Reg. c. 1. 17. & seqq. 2. Sam. c. 14. 6. 7. & seqq. c. 13. 32. c. 24. 21. 22. Genes. c. 44. 16. & seqq. 1. Sam. cap. 24. 25. & seqq. & supra cap. 11, ita vt humilitate & submissione suam indigentiam subditus declaret. Eccles. c. 7. 5. Ne iustitiam tibi adseras coram Domino, neq; coram Rege sapientiam. & c. 10. 29. Ne sapientiam age in opere tuo faciendo, neq; gloriosum tempore angustia tua, & c. 32. 6. 12. Inter magnates, ne aequalem te prabeas. & c. 13. 10. & seqq. Ecclesiastis cap. 9. 17. & seqq. & Prou. c. 25. 6. Ne arrogato tibi decorem coram Rege, & in loco magnatum ne stato. 7. Nam melius est tibi dici, Ascende huc, quam deprimi te coram ingenuo: quod vident oculi tui, & cap. 23. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. & c. 11. 2. Ex qua causa humilis coram Magistratu non sibi sumet loquendi licentiam, non prius potestate dicendi impetrata, vel data, Genef.c.44.18. c.18. 27.30.31.32. 2.Sam.cap.14.13.cap.20.17.18.& 1.Samuel.c.15.16.c.25.24.Actor.c.26.1.2.3.cap.24.10. Iob.c.29.8.9. cap.32. 6.7.16.17.21.23. & dixi supra cap.12.
units.tr: To this also belongs the blessing which lower subjects pronounce upon the magistrate: 1 Kings 1:31, 47–48; 2 Samuel 14:23; Daniel 6:22; Daniel 4:19; 2 Kings 11:12; 1 Samuel 10:24; Genesis 47:7, 10. together with a profession of obedience and of the service owed, 1 Kings 1:17 and following; 2 Samuel 14:6–7 and following; 2 Samuel 13:32; 2 Samuel 24:21–22; Genesis 44:16 and following; 1 Samuel 24–25 and following; and above, chapter 11, so that by humility and submission the subject declares his need. Ecclesiastes 7:5: "Do not claim righteousness for yourself before the Lord, nor wisdom before the king." And 10:29: "Do not act wisely in your work of doing, nor glory in your time of distress." And 32:6, 12: "Among great men, do not make yourself equal." And 13:10 and following; Ecclesiastes 9:17 and following; and Proverbs 25:6–7: "Do not claim honour for yourself before the king, nor stand in the place of great men; for it is better that it be said to you, 'Come up here,' than that you be humbled before a noble, which your eyes have seen." And 23:1–3 and following; and 11:2. For this reason the humble man before the magistrate will not take to himself the liberty of speaking, unless the power to speak has first been obtained or granted. Genesis 44:18; 18:27, 30–32; 2 Samuel 14:13; 20:17–18; 1 Samuel 15:16; 25:24; Acts 26:1–3; Acts 24:10; Job 29:8–9; Job 32:6–7, 16–17, 21, 23; and I have said above in chapter 12.

units.la: Verborum & sermonis pronunciatione vti debet molli cum longanimitate.Prouerb.c.15.15. cuius rei exemplum extat Iudic.c.8.1.2.3.4.5.1.Sam. c.15.23. & seqq. Ita adcommodata, vt iram & indignationem superioris Magistrat,sanet, mitiget,leniat:& affectus turbatos sedet. Eccl.c.10. 1. Cum spiritus eius qui dominatur, se effert contra te,locum tuum ne deserito, (hoc est, vti Iunius explicat,modeste te contineto, ne rebellato,) nam vir sapiens sedat peccata, 2.Est malum quod vidi sub sole secundum errorem, qui procedit a facie imperantis, & verf.seqq. vbi mala enumerat quae alias ipsi subdito secus facienti sint eventura,vbi omnino vide Iun. & Colos.cap.4.6. Prouerb.cap.16.14. Nuncii excandescentia regis, sunt nuncii mortis; sed vir sapiens expiabit eam. Senec. Suasor. 1. Apud Reges ea quae prosunt,suadenda sunt ita,vt delectent. Et ideo iniuria eorum,etiam hilarivultu patienter ferenda sunt, Seneca lib.2. De ira,sol.34. Ecclesiast.cap. 16.14. cap.19.12.cap.20.2.2. Chron.cap.24.21.22. Daniel, cap.2.5.12. Rom.c.13.7.8. Lipf.lib.4. & c.9.& ira Regis metuenda & declinanda, 1.Sam.c.20.1.& c.25.24.Prou.c.16.14.c.20.2. & placanda,Prouer. c.25.15.
units.tr: One must use a gentle manner of speech and pronunciation, with long-suffering. Proverbs 15:15; an example of this stands in Judges 8:1–5; 1 Samuel 15:23 and following. One's words must be so fitted that they soothe, mitigate and lighten the anger and indignation of the superior magistrate, and calm his disturbed passions. Ecclesiastes 10:4: "If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place" (that is, as Junius explains, restrain yourself modestly and do not rebel), "for a wise man quiets great offences." 10:5: "There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, as an error which proceeds from the face of the ruler," and the following verses, where he lists the evils that would otherwise befall the subject who acts differently; see Junius thoroughly. Colossians 4:6. Proverbs 16:14: "The anger of a king is the messenger of death; but a wise man will appease it." Seneca, On Providence 1: "Before kings, what is useful must be urged in such a way that it also pleases." And therefore their injuries must be borne patiently, even with a cheerful face; Seneca, On Anger, book 2, ch. 34. Ecclesiasticus 16:14; 19:12; 20:2. 2 Chronicles 24:21–22. Daniel 2:5, 12. Romans 13:7–8. Lipsius, book 4, and ch. 9. The anger of the king is to be feared and avoided: 1 Samuel 20:1; 25:24; Proverbs 16:14; 20:2; and it is to be appeased: Proverbs 25:15.

units.la: Gestus & habitus reuerentialis hic est, quo honor, obsequia & obseruantia, reuerentia & veneratio erga Magistrum hunc summum,cum timore,amore,modestia, tempestiue, cum τιμὴ & tolerantia præstantia, de quibus singulis ordine videbimus.
units.tr: The reverent gesture and bearing is that by which honour, obedience and observance, reverence and veneration are shown to this highest magistrate: with fear, with love, with modesty, in good time, with honour [τιμὴ], and with forbearance and excellence. We shall consider each of these in order.

units.la: Cum timore obsequia, honorem & venerationem exhibere debemus. 1. Pet. c. 2. 17. Deum timete, Regem honorate, 18. Famuli, subditi estote cum omni timore dominis non solum bonis & æquis, sed etiam prauis. 2. Sam. cap. 11. 17. 18. & seqq. Rom. cap. 13. 4. 7. Ephes. c. 6. 5. Serui auscultate iis qui veštri domini sunt secundum carnem, cum timore & tremore, cum simplicitate cordis veštri, vt Christo, 7. cum benevolentia seruientes, &c. Est enim ira & indignatio huius nuntius mortis, Eccles. c. 16. 14. c. 19. 12. c. 20. 2. 2. Chron. c. 24. 21. 22. Dan. cap. 2. 5. 12. Malach. cap. 1. 6. Filius honorat patrem, & seruus dominum suum. quod si pater, vbi honor meus? & si dominus sum, vbi reuerentia mei? 2. Chronic. c. 1. 12. 13. Rom. c. 13. 7. Est. c. 1. 3. 4. 5. & seqq. cum amore, fauore & benevolentia, 2. Sam. cap. 15. 20. 21. & seqq. c. 19. 32. 33. c. 24. 20. & seqq. Colos. c. 3. 22. Ephes. c. 6. 6. Tit. c. 2. 9. 10. Daniel. cap. 6. 22. 2. Samuel. c. 14. 23. 1. Reg. cap. 1. 47. 48. quia minister Dei & pater subditorum suorum. Dixi etiam, cum modestia & submissione, Ecclesiastis c. 10. 1. 2. & seqq. sine murmuratione, vel perturbatione, Ecclesiastis c. 8. 1. 2. 3. Tit. c. 2. 9. 10. Ephes. cap. 6. 6. idque tempestiue, vt nimirum rationem obsequendi, tempus modumq; observet, Eccles. cap. 8. 3. Vbicunque verbum Regis est, ibi dominatio, ecquis dicat ei, quid facis? 4. qui obseruat præceptum, non experitur rem malam: tempus enim ac rationem nouit animus sapientis, (hoc est, vt Iunius explicat, tum obsequendi, tum dissimulandi, tum ab obsequio desistendi,) 5. nā cuiq; voluntati, est tempus & ratio, sed malum hominis, multum incumbit ei, & seqq. vbi Iun. Facit huc ad Coloss. c. 4. 6. Ecclesiastes c. 10. 1, 2. & seqq. Cuius affectibus ita obsequia sua adcommodare debet, quo omnibus modis iram & indignationem superioris lenire, sedare, & affectus turbatos sanare possit: & quo a malo & peccatis superior revocetur, gratia eiusdem incatur, conseruetur, vel amissa recuperetur, dicto cap. 10. vbi Iunius. Cuius rei elegans extat exemplum in Abigail, qua hoc modo animum Dauidis iratum & commotum ad lenitatem traduxit, & ab homicidio & peccatis revocauit. vide 1. Samuel. cap. 25. per tot. & aliud in muliere Tecoensi, de qua 2. Samuel. c. 14. per tot. & aliud 2. Samuel. c. 20. 16. & seqq. & aliud Genes. c. 18. 23. & seqq per tot. Ratio huius petenda ex Rom. cap. 15. 2. Itaque vnusquisq; nostrum placeat proximo in bonum, id est, ad eius aedificationem. Plures adfert Sapiens in d. c. 10. & c. 8. 4. 5. 6. 8. Proverb. cap. 16. 14. c. 19. 12. & quod charitas defectionem tegat & dissimulet. Proverb. c. 17. 9. 10. c. 10. 12. Quam ob causam recte tales politici & prudentes alibi commendantur, 1. Chron. c. 12. 32. & e filiis Issachar noscentes scite tempora, ut nosceret Israelita quid sibi faciendum esset. Esther c. 1. 13.
units.tr: We must show obedience, honour and veneration with fear. 1 Peter 2:17–18: "Fear God, honour the king. Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward." 2 Samuel 11:17–18 and following; Romans 13:4, 7; Ephesians 6:5, 7: "Servants, be obedient to those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of heart, as to Christ; serving with goodwill," etc. For the anger and indignation of the magistrate is a messenger of death: Ecclesiastes 16:14; 19:12; 20:2; 2 Chronicles 24:21–22; Daniel 2:5, 12; Malachi 1:6: "A son honours his father, and a servant his master. If then I am a father, where is my honour? And if I am a master, where is my reverence?" 2 Chronicles 1:12–13; Romans 13:7; Esther 1:3–5 and following. We must show love, favour and goodwill: 2 Samuel 15:20–21 and following; 19:32–33; 24:20 and following; Colossians 3:22; Ephesians 6:6; Titus 2:9–10; Daniel 6:22; 2 Samuel 14:23; 1 Kings 1:47–48, because the magistrate is God's minister and the father of his subjects. I have also said that it must be with modesty and submission: Ecclesiastes 10:1–2 and following; without murmuring or disturbance: Ecclesiastes 8:1–3; Titus 2:9–10; Ephesians 6:6. And this must be done in good time, so that one observes the manner, time and measure of obeying: Ecclesiastes 8:3: "Where the word of the king is, there is power; who will say to him, What are you doing?" 8:4: "He who keeps the commandment shall experience no evil thing; for the heart of the wise knows time and manner" (that is, as Junius explains, of obeying, of dissembling, and of ceasing to obey). 8:5: "For every will has its time and manner, but the evil of man lies heavy upon him," and following, where Junius. Relevant here is Colossians 4:6; Ecclesiastes 10:1–2 and following. One must fit one's obedience to the passions of the superior in such a way that one can, in every way, soften and calm his anger and indignation and heal his disturbed passions; and so that the superior is called back from evil and sin, his favour is won and kept, or, if lost, is recovered, as in chapter 10 above, where Junius. A fine example of this stands in Abigail, who in this way brought David's angry and stirred spirit to gentleness, and called him back from homicide and sin. See 1 Samuel 25 throughout; and another in the woman of Tekoa, of whom 2 Samuel 14 throughout; and another, 2 Samuel 20:16 and following; and another, Genesis 18:23 and following throughout. The reason for this is to be sought in Romans 15:2: "Let each of us please his neighbour for good, that is, for his edification." The Wise Man brings more in the same chapter 10, and chapter 8:4–6, 8; Proverbs 16:14; 19:12; and that love covers and hides defection: Proverbs 17:9–10; 10:12. For this reason such men, politic and prudent, are rightly commended elsewhere: 1 Chronicles 12:32, "and of the sons of Issachar, who knew well the times, so that Israel might know what it ought to do"; Esther 1:13.

units.la: Cum συμπαθεια honor debitus praestatur, quando lugente & dolente superiore, subditus quoque luget, vel contra, 2. Sam. cap. 19. 2. 3. 4. & seqq. cap. 15. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. & seqq. cap 3. 31. & seqq. c. 14. 16, 17. & seqq. 2. Pet. cap. 3. 8. Nam ira concitamur in eos qui aut nostro infortunio gaudent, aut saltem in rebus nostris aduersis bono sunt animo. Hoc enim parui facientis; illud, plane hostis est. Immo iis etiam irascimur, qui patienter audiunt mala nostra, aut qui nostranostrarum miseriarum spectatores esse possunt. illud enim oligoria; hoc, inimicitia indicium est.
units.tr: When honour is paid through sympathy [συμπάθεια], the subject also mourns when the superior mourns and grieves, or the reverse (2 Sam. 19:2-4 and following; 2 Sam. 15:14-18 and following; 2 Sam. 3:31 and following; 2 Sam. 14:16-17 and following; 2 Pet. 3:8). For we are roused to anger against those who rejoice at our misfortune, or at least are glad of our adversities. The first is the mark of someone who cares little for us; the second is plainly that of an enemy. Indeed we are angry even with those who listen calmly to our troubles, or who can be spectators of our miseries. For the former is a sign of contempt (oligoria); the latter, of enmity.

units.la: Tolerantia denique magistratus sui næuos, lapsus & infirmitatem, errata & iniurias, æquo animo ferre, & ab hosce defectus in officio faciendo nihil remittere debet, exemplo Dauidis ferentis Saulis iniquitatem. 1. Sam. cap. 26, §. 9, 10. 11. Roman. cap. 15. 1. 2. 3. Colos. c. 3. 13. Ephef. c. 4. 2. 32. 2. Sam. 4. 9. 10. 11. c. 1, 11, & seqq. Senec. libr. 2. De ira, cum impiis etiam magistratibus obedientia & honor debeatur, 1. Petr. c. 2, 18. Ierem. c. 29, 7. c. 27. 7. & passim alibi. Sed tamen ob hanc toleran- tiam erranti obsequium non adcommodabit, aut non probanda probabit, ne aliena vitia & peccata sua faciat; licet etiam pœnas iniustè illa- tas, æquo animo ferre debeat, donec remedium legitimum habeat, 1. Petr. c. 2. 19. Hoc enim gratum est, si quis propter conscientiam Dei, suffert molestias iniquè afflictus, 20. Qua enim laus est, si cum peccan- tes colaphis cædimini, toleratis? sed si cum benefacitis, tamen affliƈti toleratis, hoc est gratum apud Deum, Genef. c. 16. 6. 9.
units.tr: Finally, the subject must bear with equanimity the blemishes, lapses and weaknesses, the faults and injuries of his magistrate, and must not on that account relax anything in discharging his duty, following the example of David bearing the wickedness of Saul (1 Sam. 26:9-11; Rom. 15:1-3; Col. 3:13; Eph. 4:2, 32; 2 Sam. 4:9-11; 2 Sam. 1:11 and following; Seneca, On Anger book 2). Obedience is owed even to ungodly magistrates (1 Pet. 2:18; Jer. 29:7; Jer. 27:7; and elsewhere passim). Yet by this tolerance he will not accommodate himself to the one who errs, nor approve what ought not to be approved, lest he make other people's vices and sins his own. He must also bear with equanimity punishments unjustly inflicted, until he has a lawful remedy (1 Pet. 2:19-20: "For this is pleasing, if someone for conscience toward God endures grief, suffering unjustly. For what glory is there if, when you sin and are beaten, you endure it? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure it, this is pleasing before God"; Gen. 16:6, 9).

units.la: Porrò hi gestus & habitus reuerentiales con- sistunt in obsequio, vel operis. Obsequium, est gestus & habitus, quo Magistratus amplitudo, dignitas & auctoritas, maiestas & excellentia, existimatio, splendor & gloria atq; magnifcen- tia agnoscitur & approbatur.
units.tr: Moreover, these reverential attitudes and habits consist either in deference or in outward service. Deference is the bearing and habit by which the greatness, dignity and authority, the majesty and excellence, the reputation, splendour and glory and magnificence of the magistrate are acknowledged and approved.

units.la: Obsequium eiusmodi exhibetur & præstatur Magistratui in aditu, vestitu, obedientia, studio & beneuolentia subditi erga Magistratum, & ci- uili adoratione.
units.tr: Such deference is shown and paid to the magistrate in approach, dress, obedience, eagerness and goodwill of the subject towards the magistrate, and in civil reverence.

units.la: In aditu inferior subditus, non nisi venia & potestate seu licentia impetrata superiorem accedat, vel in conspectum eius veniat. Esther c. 4.11. Omnes serui Regis sciunt, quicunque vir, aut mulier ingressus fuerit ad Regem in atrium interius, qui non fuerit vocatus, vnum esse eius de eo morte afficiendo, præterquam cui extenderit rex sceptrum aureum, eum viuere. Ego vero non sui vocata, vt ingrederer ad Regem, & vers.16. & cap.5.2.c.2. in sin. Pet.Gregor. de Repub. lib.22. c.11. Genes.cap.41.14. exceptis intimis consiliariis & principibus, qui faciem Regis quotidie vident. Est. c.1.10.14. Septem principibus Persidis & Medis videntibus faciem Regis, sedentibus primis in regno. & c.8.1.2. Hesra c.7.14. ob quam causam, vt nimirum non cuiuis ad Magistratum aditus concedatur. Reges aliique summa potestate præditi principes, suos habent ministros, famulos, satellites, perpetuo eosdem comitantes, ⲥⲱⲣⲁⲡⲉⲩⲁⲥ, 1. Regum, cap.1.21.22. & seqq.c.10.8. Esther c.13.14. 1.Samuel. cap.16.17. Luc.cap.7.6.8.9. Matth.cap.8.3. & seqq. Daniel.cap.14.19.20. Exod.cap.11.8. cap.8.3.31. cap.7.13.23. Jerem.c.21.5.6.c.34.19. 2.Sam.1. cap.8. in sin.vbi Pet. Martyr.c.19.33. & seqq. cap.12.17.18. 19.10.21.c.15.14.16. & seqq.c.9.4. vbi Iun. quales officiarii numerantur 1.Chronic.cap.27. & c.28. & 2.Chro.c.17.14. Nam quia eiusmodi Magistratus, multis periculis & insidiis sunt expositi, ideo expedit, imo necessarium est, vt ad sui defensionem & corporis custodiam, habeant ministros, non quosuis promiscue ad eos admittetes, vid. Pet. Gregor. lib.22. c.11. de Repubi. vbi exemplis & historiis hoc illustrat. Hisce præfectus, apud Romanos vocabatur præfectus palatio cubiculo biculo principis, vel prætorio. Præpositi admissionalis& magister admissionum, qui aditum impetrabat & introducebat, & qui solus ad superiorem seu Regem aditum liberum habet. Dan.c.2.49. Daniel vero præerat porta Regis, vbi Iun.notat. Apud Romanos quoq; valentissimi serui catenis religati, pro ostio aditum custodiebant, ne non vocati admitterentur. Sæpè etiam interiores aulici scrutabantur & sinum accedentium pertentabant, ne quis cum telo esset. Alex.ab Alexand. lib.5. Genial.dier. cap.24. Tales ianuæ custodes habebant potestatem aperiendi & claudendi, homines intromittendi & educendi; canes, fures, mendicos, abigendi, & liminarcha dicebantur. vid. Ael. Lampr.id. in vita Seuer. Imperat. & Sueton. in Vespasian. Apud Romanos quoque non modica laus erat, plurimos habere clientes, cateruas togatorum, imo & tenuiores amicos, à quibus obseruarentur quotidie & colerentur, cumq; his ad forum deducerentur, frequenti comitatu. Nam maximi decoris erat, amplos viros illustresq; etiam ab infima plebe, quotidie salutari, experti, deducci, reduci, consuli, eisque decedi & adsurgi. vid. Alexand. ab Alexand. libr. 5. Genial. dier. cap.24.
units.tr: In approach, the inferior subject should not come before a superior, or into his presence, except with permission and authority, or licence, obtained. Esther 4:11: "All the king's servants know, and the people of the king's provinces know, that whoever, man or woman, comes to the king into the inner court without being called, there is one law for him, that he be put to death, except those to whom the king holds out the golden sceptre, that they may live. But I have not been called to come in to the king"; verse 16; chapter 5:2; chapter 2, at the end; Peter Gregorius, On the Commonwealth, book 22, chapter 11; Gen. 41:14, except for the closest counsellors and princes who see the king's face every day (Esther 1:10, 14: the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom; Esther 8:1-2; Ezra 7:14). The reason is, of course, that access to the magistrate is not granted to just anyone. Kings and other princes endowed with supreme power have their own ministers, servants and guards, always attending them (1 Kings 1:21-22 and following; 1 Kings 10:8; Esther 13-14; 1 Sam. 16:17; Luke 7:6-9; Matt. 8:3 and following; Dan. 14:19-20; Exod. 11:8; 8:3, 31; 7:13, 23; Jer. 21:5-6; 34:19; 2 Sam. 1, chapter 8 at the end, where Peter Martyr; 19:33 and following; 12:17-18; 19:10, 21; 15:14, 16 and following; 9:4, where Junius), such as the officials listed in 1 Chron. 27 and 28 and 2 Chron. 17:14. For since such magistrates are exposed to many dangers and plots, it is expedient, indeed necessary, that for their defence and the protection of their person they have ministers, who do not admit just anyone to them indiscriminately; see Peter Gregorius, book 22, chapter 11, On the Commonwealth, where he illustrates this with examples and histories. Over these the Romans appointed a prefect, called the prefect of the palace, of the chamber, or of the praetorium. There was also the master of admissions, who obtained access and introduced people, and who alone had free access to the superior or king. Dan. 2:49; Daniel indeed presided over the king's gate, where Junius notes it. Among the Romans, too, the strongest slaves, bound with chains, guarded the entrance at the door, lest anyone not called should be admitted. Often the inner courtiers also searched and felt the clothing of those approaching, lest anyone have a weapon: Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, book 5, chapter 24. Such doorkeepers had the power to open and shut, to admit and to send out people; they drove off dogs, thieves and beggars, and were called doorkeepers (liminarchae). See Aelius Lampridius, in the life of Severus Emperor, and Suetonius, in Vespasian. Among the Romans it was also no small honour to have many clients, troops of men in togas, and even humbler friends who would wait on them and honour them daily, and who escorted them to the forum with a large retinue. For it was a great mark of distinction for distinguished and notable men to be greeted daily, escorted, accompanied home, consulted, and to be given way to and stood up for even by the lowest of the common people. See Alexander ab Alexandro, book 5, Genial Days, chapter 24.

units.la: De officiariis aulæ Gallicæ vid.Chassan.part.6. conf.6. Aulicorum officiariorum & munerum tres ordines constituuntur, administrantium, vacantium & honoratiorū.Quidā ex his gerunt curā palatii quidam cubiculi, quidam victualiorum, quidam medicamentorum,quidam stabuli. vid. tit. C. de comitib. scholar. lib. 12. tit. C. de propos. sacri. cubic. lib. 12. tit. C. de stratorib. tit. C. de comitib. & archiat. sacr. palat. lib. 12.
units.tr: On the officials of the French court, see Chassanaeus, part 6, consideration 6. Three orders of court officials and offices are established: those who administer, those who are attendants, and those who are honorary. Some of them have charge of the palace, some of the chamber, some of the provisions, some of the medicines, some of the stables. See the title "On the counts of the schools", book 12; the title "On the proposals of the sacred chamber", book 12; the title "On the equerries", book 12; the title "On the counts and archiater of the sacred palace", book 12.

units.la: Admissus autem in superioris Principis conspectum, induitus sit vestibus elegantibus, non sordidis, incultis, vel luctuosis, de qua re extant exempla Genes. cap. 41. 14. Mittens itaque Pharao accersiuit Iosephum, qui celeriter eductus est ex illa fovea, postquam abrasisset caput, & mutasset vestes suas, venit ad Pharaonem, Luc. cap. 7. 25. Ecce, qui vestitu magnifico vtuntur, sunt in palatiis regum. Ester cap. 4. 2. Non enim erat ingrediendum in portam Regis cum indumento cilicii, 4. & seqq. Genes. c. 50. 4. vbi Iun. vid. Daniel. cap. 1. 4. 5. & seqq. Conuenit etiam, vt inferior Principem ob dignitatem eiusdem per epistolam adeat, vt vult Durus de Pascolo. Vel per alium, cum quo Principi maior est conuersatio, exponat.
units.tr: When admitted into the sight of a superior prince, one should be dressed in elegant clothes, not dirty, unkempt or in mourning. Examples of this matter are in Gen. 41:14: "Pharaoh therefore sent and called Joseph, who was quickly brought out of that pit, after he had shaved his head and changed his garments, and came to Pharaoh"; Luke 7:25: "Behold, those who wear splendid clothing are in the palaces of kings"; Esther 4:2: "For no one was to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth"; 4 and following; Gen. 50:4, where Junius; see Dan. 1:4-5 and following. It is also fitting that an inferior, because of the prince's dignity, approach him by letter, as Durus de Pascolo says, or present his case through another person who is more intimate with the prince.

units.la: Audire autem loquentem superiorem magistratum debet stans. Num. c. 23. 22. vbi Iunius, Genes. cap. 49. 33. Iudic. c. 3. 20. 2. Chron. cap. 34. 31. 2. Reg. c. 47. Nehem. c. 8. 6. 1. Reg. c. 1. 28. Est enim famulantium & inseruientium proprium, stare: & superiorum dignorum sedere, 1. Sam. c. 26. 15. 1. Reg. c. 19. 8. Beati homines tui, beati serui tui isti, qui stantes coram te, iugiter audiunt sapientiam tuam. Deut. cap. 10. 8. Tempore illo separauit Iehoua tribum Leuiticam ad portandum arcam foederis Iehouae, ad standum coram Iehoua, vt ministraret ipsi, 1. Sam. c. 22. 6. 7. Act. c. 23. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Tu sedes iudicas me, &c. tunc qui adstabant dixerunt, & Exod. cap.18.14.15. &sfeqq.
units.tr: A superior magistrate, when he is speaking, should be listened to standing. Num. 23:22, where Junius; Gen. 49:33; Judg. 3:20; 2 Chron. 34:31; 2 Kings 4:7; Neh. 8:6; 1 Kings 1:28. For it is the proper attitude of servants and attendants to stand, and of the worthy superiors to sit: 1 Sam. 26:15; 1 Kings 19:8; "Happy are your men, happy are these your servants, who stand before you and constantly hear your wisdom"; Deut. 10:8: "At that time the LORD separated the tribe of Levi to bear the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to stand before the LORD, to minister to him"; 1 Sam. 22:6-7; Acts 23:1-5; "You sit to judge me," etc.; then those who stood by said; Exod. 18:14-15 and following.

units.la: Obedientia est, quæ æquis superioris imperantis mandatis est præstanda exactè, & ad a-muffim, vt neque ei addatur neque detrahatur quid,Roman. cap.13.v.1. Omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subiecta esto. Non enim est potestas nisi à Deo. & quæ sunt potestates, à Deo sunt ordinatæ,& verf.2. Itaque quisquis se opponit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit; qui autem resistunt, ipsi sibi condemnationem auferent,& verf.seq. Tit. c.3.1. Suggere ipsis, vt sese subiiciant principatib. vt obtemperent,&c. 1.Coloss.c.3.23.1.Timoth.c.2.2. 1.Pet.c.2.13.14. Exod.c.22.28.1. Chron. c.30.23. &seqq. Obedientia exempla vide Genef.cap.24.2.3.10.11.12.33, cap.16. 6.9.2.Sam.c.15.13.14.1.Sam.c.11.14.15.c.14.24.cap. 16.17.18.1.Reg.c.2.15.2.Reg.c.10.25.Ecclesiast.ca.8. 1.2.3.Ierem.c.29.7. &c.38. Daniel.c.3.c.6. &passim alibi, quæ obedientia etiam impio & scelerato Magistratui præstanda, etiam in pœnis iniuste infligendis perferendis, 1.Pet.c.2.18.19.Ierem.cap.29.7.c.27.7.c.38.arg.Matth. c.23.2. In cathedra Mosis sedent Scribæ & Pharisæi, 3. omnia ergo, quæ dixerint vobis vt seruetis, seruate & facite, sed secundum opera eorum ne facite, 1.Sam.c.15.c.26.9. c.24. 7.8.13.14.cap.31.11.cap.36.9. Actor. c.25.f. 2.Sam. c.4.9.10.11. c.1.11.&seqq. Neque enim scelerata Magistratus vita priuata regiam dignitatem illi abrogat. 1.Sam.c.15.31. Ester c.1.11.12. atque hanc obedientiam subditi suo magistratui in principio sui imperii spondere solent.Iof.c.1.16.17.18.2. Chron.c.23.16.c.34.31.32. Studium & beneuolentia subditi erga magistratum consistit primo in defendenda, amplí-ficanda, excellentia, atque authoritate Magi-stratus; & cura, ne illa contemnatur, vel vilescat. 1. Sam. cap. 16. 7. 8. 9. Tum dicente Abischaio filio Tzeruia regi, quare malediceret canis iste mortuus domino meo regi? Transeam quaeso, vt auferam caput eius. 1. Sam. cap. 11. 12. Tum dixit populus Samueli, Quis est qui dicebat, Saul ne regnaret super nos? date ipsos homines vt mortí tradamus eos. Act. c. 23. 4. 5. Iudic. cap. 1. 8. Exemplum extat 1. Sam. cap. 10. 26. 27. cap. 11. 12. 13. 2. Sam. cap. 15. 35. 36. cap. 19. 29. 30. 31. 32. 33. & vers. 7. 8. Petr. Gregor. lib. 8. cap. 3. de Repub.
units.tr: Obedience is the duty to carry out exactly, and to the last detail, the lawful commands of a superior who rules, adding nothing to them and taking nothing away. Rom. 13:1: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power but of God, and the powers that exist are ordained of God; and v. 2: therefore whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God, and those who resist will bring judgment on themselves; and the following verses. Titus 3:1: Remind them to be subject to principalities, to obey, etc. Col. 3:23; 1 Tim. 2:2; 1 Pet. 2:13–14; Exod. 22:28; 2 Chron. 30:23 and following. For examples of obedience see Gen. 24:2–3, 10–12, 33; 16:6, 9; 2 Sam. 15:13–14; 1 Sam. 11:14–15; 14:24; 16–18; 1 Kings 2:15; 2 Kings 10:25; Eccles. 8:1–3; Jer. 29:7; 38; Dan. 3; 6; and passim elsewhere. This obedience is to be rendered even to an impious and wicked magistrate, and even when unjust punishments are inflicted: 1 Pet. 2:18–19; Jer. 29:7; 27:7; 38, argument; Matt. 23:2–3: The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; therefore all that they tell you to observe, observe and do, but do not do according to their works; 1 Sam. 15; 26:9; 24:7–8, 13–14; 31:11; 36:9; Acts 25; 2 Sam. 4:9–11; 1:11 and following. For a wicked magistrate's private life does not strip him of royal dignity: 1 Sam. 15:31; Esther 1:11–12; and subjects are wont to pledge this obedience to their magistrate at the beginning of his rule: Josh. 1:16–18; 2 Chron. 23:16; 34:31–32. The zeal and goodwill of a subject towards the magistrate consist, first, in defending, enhancing and esteeming the excellence and authority of the magistrate, and in taking care that it is not despised or cheapened: 1 Sam. 16:7–9. Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me, I beg you, go over and take off his head." 1 Sam. 11:12. Then the people said to Samuel, "Who is it that said, Shall Saul reign over us? Bring the men, that we may put them to death." Acts 23:4–5; Judg. 1:8. An example is found in 1 Sam. 10:26–27; 11:12–13; 2 Sam. 15:35–36; 19:29–33, and v. 7–8. Petrus Gregorius, Book 8, ch. 3, On the Commonwealth.

units.la: Secundo consistit etiam in prosperitate, sa-lute & commodo Magistratus promouendo & quaerendo. Ierem. c. 9. 7. Baruch. cap. 1. 11. 12. 2. Reg. c. 5. 13. 14. & seqq. 2. Sam. cap. 17. 18. & seqq. cap. 21. 17. 18. cap. 18. 3. 4. 5. c. 19. 6. 7. 8. 9. cap. 15. 27. 28. & seqq. c. 16. ita vt salutem & commodum Magistratus proprio anteponat. 2. Sam. c. 19. 31. Dixit vero Mephiboseth Regi, vel omnia accipiat, postquam venit Dominus meus rex cum pace domum suam, c. 15. 21. Respondens vero Ithai regi dixit, vt viuit Iehoua & viuit Dominus meus Rex, tantum modo in loco vbi erit Dominus meus rex, siue ad mortem siue ad vitam, ibi futurus est seruus tuus. & 1. Sam. cap. 16. 15. 16. 17. 2. Sam. c. 18. 3. 4. c. 21. 17. 2. Sam. c. 2. 24. 20. & seqq. c. 1. 14. 16. Genef. c. 45. 9. 10. 11. & sustenta-bo te ibi, ne pauperiate consumaris tu & familia tua, & omnia quae sunt tibi: & 1. Chronic. c. 12. 39. Hi fue-runt cum Dauide tribus diebus, comedentes & bibentes, quia praparauerant eis fratres eorum. 40. Atque etiam propinqui ipsorum ab Issachare & Zebulone & Na& Napthali, aduehebant panes asinis, camelis & mulis & bobus, cibum, farinam, palathas & uuas passas, vinumq; & oleum, boues pecudesque copiose. arg. Roman.c.16.4. Qui pro anima mea suam ipsorum cervicem supposuerunt. Galat.c.4.15. Testimonium enim reddo vobis, vos si fieri potuisset, oculos vestros effosos daturos mihi fuisse.
units.tr: Second, it also consists in promoting and seeking the prosperity, safety and advantage of the magistrate, Jer. 9:7; Bar. 1:11–12; 2 Kings 5:13–14 and following; 2 Sam. 17–18 and following; 21:17–18; 18:3–5; 19:6–9; 15:27–28 and following; 16. so that the safety and advantage of the magistrate are put before one's own. 2 Sam. 19:31: But Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him take everything, since my lord the king has come home in peace." 15:21: And Ittai answered the king and said, "As Jehovah lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether in death or in life, there will your servant be." Also 1 Sam. 16:15–17; 2 Sam. 18:3–4; 21:17; 2 Sam. 2:24; 20 and following; 1:14, 16. Gen. 45:9–11: "And I will provide for you there, lest you and your household and all that you have come to poverty." And 1 Chron. 12:39–40: They were with David three days, eating and drinking, for their brothers had made provision for them. Moreover their neighbours from Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali brought bread on asses, camels, mules and oxen: food, flour, cakes, raisins, wine and oil, and oxen and sheep in abundance. Argument from Rom. 16:4: who for my life laid down their own necks; Gal. 4:15: For I bear you witness that, if it had been possible, you would have plucked out your own eyes and given them to me.

units.la: Tertio in eo quoque, vt affectibus Magistratus studia & actiones suas ita adcommodet, quo illi turbati sanentur, & a malo & peccatis reuocentur, gratia eiusdem ineatur, conseruetur, vel amissa recuperetur. Ecclesiastis cap. 10. 1.2.3 & seqq. vbi eleganter docet Iunius. & cap.8.1. 2.3.& seqq. Exemplum eius extat 1.Sam. cap.25. 2. Sam. cap. 20. 16. & seqq. Genef.cap.18.23. & seqq. quo pertinet etiam generale id praeceptum Galat.cap. 6.1. Fratres etiamsi praeoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo lapsu, vos spirituales, instaurate huiusmodi hominem cum spiritu mansuetudinis, &c. & Colos. cap. 4.6. quod infirmitates Magistratus aequo animo sint ferenda. 1.Pet. c.2.17.18.19. Roman.cap.15.1.2 3. Colos.cap.3.13. Ephes.c.4.2.23. Exemplo Dauidis. 1.Sa. c.24.9.10.11.c.26.9.10. 2.Sam.c.4.9.10.11. cap.1.11. & seqq.
units.tr: Third, it also consists in this: that a subject so adapts his zeal and actions to the emotions of the magistrate that the magistrate, when troubled, is healed and recalled from evil and sins, and that the magistrate's favour is gained, kept, or, if lost, recovered. Eccles. 10:1–3 and following, where Junius teaches elegantly; and 8:1–3 and following. An example of this is found in 1 Sam. 25; 2 Sam. 20:16 and following; Gen. 18:23 and following, to which also belongs the general precept of Gal. 6:1: Brothers, even if a man has been overtaken in some fault, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, etc.; and Col. 4:6, that the weaknesses of the magistrate are to be borne with an even mind. 1 Pet. 2:17–19; Rom. 15:1–3; Col. 3:13; Eph. 4:2, 23. By the example of David: 1 Sam. 24:9–11; 26:9–10; 2 Sam. 4:9–11; 1:11 and following.

units.la: Conuenit igitur commotum & vociferante Magistratum silentio, silentem vero & tristem alloquio excipere.
units.tr: It is therefore fitting to meet a magistrate who is agitated and loud with silence, and a silent and sad one with conversation.

units.la: Quarto, consistit haec beneuolentia in muneris oblatione, cuius rei exempla extant 1.Sam. c.10.27. 2.Chron.c.17.5.c.12.39.40.c.26.8. cap.27.5. 1.Reg.cap.10.10.25.2.Sam.c.16.1.2 3.c.19.33. cap.17. 27.28.29. Iudic.c.4.15.16.17. Senec.lib.2.epist.c.17. l.vnic, C.de oblat.vot.lib.12. vbi Dd.
units.tr: Fourth, this goodwill consists in offering gifts. Examples of this are found in 1 Sam. 10:27; 2 Chron. 17:5; 12:39–40; 26:8; 27:5; 1 Kings 10:10, 25; 2 Sam. 16:1–3; 19:33; 17:27–29; Judg. 4:15–17; Seneca, Letters, Book 2, letter 17; Code, the single law, On votive offerings; Book 12, where the doctors.

units.la: Quinto, apud Romanos etiam feriæ in honorem principis constitutæ, celebrabantur.l. 7. C. de fer. Liu. lib. 1. & 2. & 5. & 7. & 33. & 38. Statuę quoque & imagines in memoriam posteritatis & reuerentiam Principis honorificam erigebantur;Alex. ab Alexand. lib. 3. Gen. dier. c. 7. Sueton. in Tiberio. c. 26. l. 1. l. 2. C. de statu. & imag. l. 2. C. de loc. public. l. 6. toties. §. vlt. de pollicitat. l. 5. & seqq. adl. Iud. maiest. l. 28. capitalium, §. 7. ad statuas. de pœn. l. 1. C. de his qui ad stat. Dion. lib. 54. & 57. Seneca ad Polyb. Chassan. consider. 35. part. 1. catal. glor. mundi refert plures quorum memoria statuis honorata fuit. Ludi quoque in eiusdem honorem exhibebantur & spectacula, comœdiæ & Tragœdiæ, item gymnastica palæstræ certamina virtutis exercendæ caussa: similiter ludi theatrales, circenses, equestres, scenici, & id genus alii, de quibus Pet. Gregor. li. 39. Syntag. c. 5. Isidor. lib. 18. c. 13. & seqq. Senec. lib. 10 epist. 71. & lib. 1, epist. 7. Sueton. in Claudio, c. 34. c. 21. in Tito c. 8. in Domitian. c. 10. in Neron. cap. 12. in Galba c. 6. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 3. Gen. dier. c. 7. & dixi latius lib. 1. Dicaolog. cap. de alien. inualida. Vsus ciborum & vestimentorum pretiosissimorum, insignium & armorum in argumentum honoris & eminentiæ hisce conueniit. vid. Chass. part. 1. confid. 38. & seqq. catal. glor. mundi, vbi regum principum & nobilium quorundam insignia describit & aliorum excellentium & honoratissimorum virorum, ad denotandam excellentiam & dignitatem officii & muneris quo vuntur. De magnificentia Salomonis in cibo & ministris aulicis vide. 1. Reg. c. 4. per tot. Sexto studium hoc, benevolentia, fauor amor erga Magistratum declaratur, quando calamitatibus & necessitati ipsius subditus succurrit & cum συμπαθεία sibi applicat, atque in persona sui magistratus ipse patitur. (Cuius exempla extant 1.Sam.c.17,27,28.29.c.19.per tot. cap.1s. 2i.&seqq.1.Chron.c.13.per tot.2.Sam.c.19.31.cap.1s. 2i.c.24.20. &seqq.
units.tr: Fifth, among the Romans holidays were also established and celebrated in honour of the prince: Code, law 7, On holidays; Livy, books 1, 2, 5, 7, 33, 38. Statues and images were also erected in memory for posterity and as an honourable mark of reverence for the prince: Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 3, Genial Days, ch. 7; Suetonius, Tiberius, ch. 26; Code, laws 1 and 2 On statues and images; Code, law 2 On public places; Digest, law 6, On promises, §last; Digest, law 5 and following on the law of majesty; Digest, law 28 On capital crimes, §7 On statues, On punishments; Code, law 1 On those who are on statues; Dio, Books 54 and 57; Seneca to Polybius; Chassanaeus, Consideration 35, part 1, Catalogue of the Glory of the World, relates several whose memory was honoured by statues. Games and spectacles were also staged in his honour, comedies and tragedies, likewise gymnastic wrestling contests for the exercise of virtue; similarly theatrical, circus, equestrian, stage games and others of that kind, concerning which Petrus Gregorius, Book 39, Syntagma, ch. 5; Isidore, Book 18, ch. 13 and following; Seneca, Letters, Book 10, letter 71, and Book 1, letter 7; Suetonius, Claudius ch. 34; ch. 21; Titus ch. 8; Domitian ch. 10; Nero ch. 12; Galba ch. 6; Alexander ab Alexandro, Book 3, Genial Days, ch. 7; and I have spoken more fully in Book 1, Dicaeologia, chapter on alienation and invalidity. The use of the most precious foods and garments, and of insignia and arms, is fitting for this, as a sign of honour and eminence. See Chassanaeus, part 1, consideration 38 and following, Catalogue of the Glory of the World, where he describes the insignia of kings, princes and certain nobles, and of other excellent and most honoured men, to denote the excellence and dignity of the office and function they hold. On the magnificence of Solomon in food and court servants, see 1 Kings 4, throughout. Sixth, this zeal, goodwill, favour and love towards the magistrate is shown when a subject comes to the aid of the magistrate's calamities and needs and shares them with sympathy [συμπάθεια], and suffers in the person of his magistrate. (Examples of this are found in 1 Sam. 17:27–29; 19 throughout; 1 Chron. 13 throughout; 2 Sam. 19:31; 1:14–15; 24:20 and following.)

units.la: Ciuilis adoratio Magistratus est, qua verticis & corporis terram versus inclinatione & incurvatione nos eiusdem imperio ac potestati humiliter submittimus, eumque dominum nostrum & nos seruos agnoscimus & profitemur; quod etiam a sanctis viris & personis obseruatum & factum legimus, 2.Sam.c.14.s.6. &seqq. c.1s.s.6.c.9.6.10.11.12.c.18.28. c.19.19. c.24.20.21. 22.c.1.2.c.14.23.c.16.4.1.Reg.c.1.16.23.24.25.31.s3. 2.Reg.c.2.1s.1.Sam.c.24.9. &seqq.c.23.24.2s.Est. c.10.3.c.3.2.c.7.3.Genes.c.23.12.c.42.6.cap.43.26. 28.c.44.14.1s.cap.so.18. Num.c.22.31 vid Alex. ab Alexan. Genial.dier.lib.2.c.19.l.4.sancimus.ibi, adoranda nostra purpura. (de confulib.&non sparg. lib.12.l.1.C.de apparitorib.praefect.prator.lib.12.l.1.C. de apparitor.praefect.vrb.l.1. C.de prapof.sacri cubici &pass.alibi dixi in Dicaeolog.lib.1.c.36. cui incurvationi accedit exosculatio, quae & olim in signum subiectionis fiebat. 1.Sā.c.10.1.Genes.c.48. 49.vbi Jun.1.Reg.c.21.22.18.19.Hos.c.13. Psalm.2. 12.l.1.vbi Gothofred.C.de domest.&protect.lib.12. de cuius osculi significatione etiam alia quadam supra dixi.
units.tr: Civil adoration of the magistrate is the act by which we humbly submit ourselves to his command and power, bowing and inclining the head and body toward the earth, and acknowledge and profess him as our lord and ourselves as his servants. We read that holy men and persons also observed and did this: 2 Sam. 14.6 ff.; 15.6 ff.; 9.6, 10, 11, 12; 18.28; 19.19; 24.20, 21, 22; 1 Kings 1.16, 23, 24, 25, 31; 2 Kings 2.1 ff.; 1 Sam. 24.9 ff.; 23.24, 25; Esther 10.3; 3.2; 7.3; Gen. 23.12; 42.6; 43.26, 28; 44.14; 50.18; Num. 22.31; see Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial. dier. bk. 2 c. 19 and bk. 4, where he decrees there, "our purple is to be adored." (On this see de conviviis and non sparg. bk. 12 l. 1 C.; de apparitoribus praefecti praetorio bk. 12 l. 1 C.; de apparitoribus praefecti urbi l. 1 C.; de praepositis sacri cubiculi, and I have said this elsewhere in Dicaeologica bk. 1 c. 36.) To this bowing there is added the kiss, which was also done of old as a sign of subjection: 1 Sam. 10.1; Gen. 48, 49; see Junius; 1 Kings 21.22; 18.19; Hos. 13; Ps. 2.12; l. 1 (see Gothofredus), C. de domesticis et protectoribus, bk. 12; of the meaning of this kiss I have also said something elsewhere above.

units.la: Palatinis conuenit vt sint obsequiosi. nam quanto quis apud principem obsequio promptior, tanto honoribus & opibus extollitur.
units.tr: It befits courtiers to be obsequious. For the more ready someone is in obsequiousness before the prince, the more he is raised up with honours and wealth.

units.la: Tacit.lib. 1. annal. Deinde vt sint vtibiles, ne tinea & lorices palatii dicantur. 3. vt modesti. 4. quieti. 5. vt virtutum simulatores, vt inuidia vitetur. 6. vt omnia referant ad suum principem, atque huic, non ubi praeclara cuncta adscribant, tanquam illius ministri. Haec enim est regum conditio, vt casus tantum aduersos hominibus tribuant, secundos vero suae fortunae & felicitati. Itaque labores aulicus sibi sumet, gloriam vero principi, seu superiori suo tribuat. 7. vt sint patientes. Senec. lib. 2. de ira interrogatus, quomodo rem rarissimam in aulis consecutus est: iniurias, respondit, ferendo & gratias referendo. 8. vt caute ambulent in aula in actionibus & sermonibus suis. Fraudis enim sedes est aula: potentia lubrica, & principes mutabiles.
units.tr: Tacit. lib. 1 annal. Next, they should be useful, lest they be called the moths and corslets of the palace. (3) They should be modest. (4) Quiet. (5) They should not be pretenders to virtue, so that envy is avoided. (6) They should refer everything to their prince, and to him, not claim all the brilliant deeds for themselves as if they were his ministers. For this is the condition of kings: they attribute only adverse events to men, but successes to their own fortune and luck. So the courtier takes the labours upon himself, but gives the glory to the prince or his superior. (7) They should be patient. Seneca, On Anger bk. 2, when asked how he had attained what is very rare in courts, answered: by enduring injuries and returning thanks. (8) They should walk cautiously in court in their deeds and words. For the court is the seat of fraud: power is slippery and princes are changeable.

units.la: Actiones seu gestus consistentes in operis inferioris subditi, sunt seruitia & ministeria corporalia & officia quaeuis, pro magistratus defensione & protectione, salute & incolumitate, praestanda prompto & summisso animo. 2.Sam. c.15.21.22. c.17.27.28.29. c.19.per tot. quo pertinent omnia illa commoda, quae subditi suo magistratui praestant, ad onera imperii ferenda & sumptus necessarios & utiles Reipub. & Imperii causa faciendos, necnon ad compensationem & praemium immensi laboris, item ad maiestatem & dignitatem imperii conseruandam, ad Rom.c.13. 1.Sam.c.8.
