Nehem.c.9.37. c.4.13.14.15. vti sunt muneris iniuncti a superiore suscepcio, praestatio tributorum, indictionum, num, vectigalium, canonis iniuncti stipendii, census, angariorum & parangariorum, collectarum, contributionum extraordinariarum, capitationum. De quibus 1. Chro. c. 7. §. 9. 40. Num. c. 3. 47. 44. & seqq. 2. Chron. c. 24. 2. Reg. c. 12. c. 15. 20. Exod. c. 30. 1. Reg. c. 9. c. 10. 14. & passim alibi in locis pluribus iura civilia latissime tradunt in tot. libr. 10. 11. & 12. Codicis, & dixi libr. 1. Dicaeologica, c. 40. & seqq. quae officia omnia magistratus necessitate & utilitate Reip. postulante a suis subditis exigere potest, & hi etiam praestare coguntur. Pet. Greg. li. 9. c. 1. de Rep. & lib. 7. c. 20. per tot. 1. Sa. c. 8. 2. Sam. c. 17. 27. 28. 29. c. 16. c. 19. 33. & Nehem. c. 9. 37. & dixi d. lib. 1. c. 36.
units.tr: Actions or gestures consisting in the work of an inferior subject are bodily services and ministries and any duties whatever, to be rendered with a ready and humble spirit for the defence and protection, safety and well-being of the magistrate. 2 Sam. 15.21, 22; 17.27, 28, 29; 19 throughout. To this belong all those benefits which subjects render to their magistrate: for bearing the burdens of government, for making the necessary expenses for the good and advantage of the commonwealth and empire, as well as for compensation and reward for immense labour, and likewise for preserving the majesty and dignity of the empire. Rom. 13; 1 Sam. 8; Neh. 9.37; 4.13, 14, 15. Such are the performance of duties laid upon one by a superior, the payment of tributes, levies, excises, tolls, the imposed rent, the stipend, the census, angary and parangary, collections, extraordinary contributions, and poll taxes. On these see 1 Chr. 7.9, 40; Num. 3.47, 44 ff.; 2 Chr. 24; 2 Kings 12; 15; 20; Exod. 30; 1 Kings 9; 10; 14, and elsewhere in many places; the civil laws teach these matters at great length throughout bks. 10, 11 and 12 of the Code, and I have said so in Dicaeologica bk. 1 cc. 40 ff. All these duties the magistrate can demand from his subjects as the necessity and utility of the commonwealth require, and these subjects are also compelled to render them. Pet. Greg. bk. 9 c. 1, de Republica, and bk. 7 c. 20 throughout; 1 Sam. 8; 2 Sam. 17.27, 28, 29; 16; 19; 33; Neh. 9.37; and I have said this in the same Dicaeologica bk. 1 c. 36.

units.la: Obseruandum hic conuersanti in aulis, plenas eas esse fallacibus amicis, occultisque insidiis, quae latent in simulatione officii, aut aliquo necessitudinis vinculo. Imo sub quouis lapide scorpionem latere existimandum est. In aulis in occulto stat invidia & avaritia: in aperto vero, adulatio & ambitio.
units.tr: One who lives at court should observe that courts are full of deceitful friends and hidden snares, which lie concealed under the pretence of duty or under some bond of kinship. Indeed, one should think that a scorpion lurks under every stone. In courts envy and avarice stand in secret; in the open, flattery and ambition.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: De officio communi infermone & gestu dignio-rum & excellentiorum erga populares & inferiores.
units.tr: On the common manner of speech and bearing of the dignified and eminent toward the common people and their inferiors.

units.la: HActenus de officio popularium, tenuio-rum, aut inferiorum erga superiores, digniores & excellentiores. Sequitur nunc de officio horum erga populares inferiores.
units.tr: So far I have discussed the duty of the common people, the humble, or inferiors toward their superiors, the more dignified and eminent. Now follows the duty of these superiors toward common and inferior people.

units.la: Officium ergo superiorum & excellentiorum erga inferiores populares est, quod mores reuerentiales praestantibus, illi sermone & geftu exhibere tenentur in ciuili conuersatione. Hoc Senec. lib.1. De clem.c.2. paucis comprehendit, dum ait, Principem fe talem ciuibus, quantum potest, exhibeat, qualem sibi Deum esse velit.
units.tr: The duty of superiors and the eminent toward inferior common people is that those in authority are bound to show them respectful conduct in word and bearing in civil life. Seneca, On Clemency, book 1, chapter 2, sums this up briefly when he says: the prince should show himself to his citizens as he would wish God to show himself to him, as far as he can.

units.la: Est autem hoc officium duplex: vnum, commune omnibus superioribus & excellentioribus: alterum quibusdam peculiare & singulare.
units.tr: This duty is twofold: one part is common to all superiors and the eminent, the other is peculiar and specific to certain persons.

units.la: Commune officium consistit in faciendis & omittendis.
units.tr: The common duty consists in what is to be done and what is to be left undone.

units.la: Facienda quę sunt, confirmunt in vsu legitimo morum reuerentialium, & in defensione dignitatis & status.
units.tr: What is to be done is to maintain the lawful practice of respectful conduct and to defend dignity and rank.

units.la: Vsus eiusmodi rursum consistit in obsequiorum susceptione & conuersatione dignioris & excellentioris.
units.tr: This practice in turn consists in receiving courtesies and in conversing with those who are lesser and more eminent.

units.la: Susceptio talis comparata esse debet ita, vt primo obsequia, reuerentiam & honores congruentes sibi delatos & præstitos, superior, dignior, excellentior benignè & humaniter sermone & gestu decentibus excipiat, non rigidè vel acerbè exigat, vel ad amussim requirat. Et cogitet Deum, non homines in bonis operibus esse glorificandum, vt videntes nostra opera bona homines Patrem Deum nostrum glorificent. Deinde non plus honoris exigat quam sua merita & virtutes postulent. Tertio, honores non extorqueat, vt Abimelechus Iudic.c.9. vt ibid. notat Martyr. vid. tit. ad l. Jul. de ambit. Ex hoc enim intelligunt inferiores populares, fe non feruiliter tractari & fe digniori & honorato acceptos & gratos esse.
units.tr: Such reception ought to be arranged so that, first, the superior, the more dignified and eminent, receives with kindness and good humour, in fitting word and bearing, the courtesies, reverence and honours that are fittingly offered and paid to him. He should not demand them harshly or sharply, or exact them to the last detail. He should remember that God, not men, is to be glorified in good works, so that men, seeing our good works, may glorify our Father God. Second, he should not demand more honour than his merits and virtues warrant. Third, he should not extort honours, as Abimelech did (Judg. 9), as Martyr notes there; see the title on the Julian law on ambition. For from this the common people among the inferiors understand that they are not treated like slaves, and that they are welcomed and valued by the dignified and honoured man.

units.la: Deinde, id quod beneuolentiæ causâ & officiose ficiose praestatur ab alio, reiicere & auersari, vel placide alios non intueri, est hominis barbari. Et qui grate beneficium oblatum accipit, primam eius penstonem soluere dicitur, vt ait Senec. lib. 2. c. 22. De benefic. Denique hoc ipsum facit ad authoritatem status sui conseruandā, vti Quintus Fabius Maximus filio suo consuli sibi imperanti vt equo descenderet, respondit, vid. Valerium Maximum lib. 2. c. 2.
units.tr: Next, to reject or shun a kindness offered by another out of goodwill and courtesy, or to look calmly away from others, is the mark of a barbarian. Seneca, On Benefits, book 2, chapter 22, says that the one who gladly accepts an offered favour is said to pay its first instalment. Finally, this very thing serves to preserve the authority of one's rank, as Quintus Fabius Maximus, when his son, a consul, ordered him to dismount from his horse, replied; see Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 2.

units.la: Ad amussim non exigit tum, quando si aliquid ab inferiori offensum, vel si quid repertum in natura, vel moribus forte sit vitii, aequo animo tolerat. Si quid in quotidiano ministerio & obsequiis minus apte, minusque eleganter ceciderit, aut in rebus mandatis gerendis non exquisitam quandam solertiam, industriam, diligentiam, celeritatem, praestiterint tenues, non continuo excandescit, sed dissimulat. arg. Rom. c. 15. 1. 2. 3. Coloss. c. 3. 13. Prou. c. 17 9 10. Ephes. c. 4. 2. 32. vel cum lenitate & manuetudine corrigit, Galat. c. 6. 1. 1. Thess. c. 5. 14. Senec. De quat. virtut. In reddenda, inquit, officiositate, neq; negligens, neq; exactor appareas.
units.tr: He does not demand strict accuracy when, if something offensive from an inferior, or some fault of nature or manners, is present, he bears it with an even mind. If in daily service and attendance something has fallen out less aptly or less elegantly, or if humble men have shown less than exquisite skill, industry, diligence or speed in carrying out commissions, he does not flare up at once but overlooks it, cf. Romans 15:1–3; Colossians 3:13; Proverbs 17:9–10; Ephesians 4:2, 32, or corrects it with gentleness and meekness, Galatians 6:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:14; Seneca, On the Four Virtues: in rendering service, he says, you should appear neither careless nor an exacting taskmaster.

units.la: Conuersatio honoratorum cum honorantibus inferioribus popularibus talis esse debet, qualis beneuolentiam & amorem illorum conciliare possit. Nam, vt ait Seneca lib. 1. De clement. c. 1. vnum inexpugnabile munimentum, amor ciuium. Qui autem amari volet, prius amet ipse necesse est. Amat vero, qui Dei minister est ad commodum subditorum, vel popularium, Rom. cap. 13. 4. Ierem. c. 49. 23.
units.tr: The conversation of the honoured with their inferior, common, honouring people ought to be such as can win their goodwill and love. For, as Seneca says, book 1, On Clemency, chapter 1, the citizens' love is one impregnable fortification. But whoever wishes to be loved must first love himself. He loves who is God's minister for the good of his subjects or common people, Romans 13:4; Jeremiah 49:23.

units.la: Temperata autem & condita debet esse haec conuersatio honoratorum cum popularibus, grauitate & iustitia, quibus pro dignitatis conditione&personæ vilioris qualitate,illa conuersatio temperatur. Nam neq; par est omnium superiorum præstantia, neq; par & eadem omnium popularium tenuitas & vilitas. Varian-tur etiam obsequia & officia personis, temporibus,ætate, rerum natura, locorum consuetudine,& aliis rebus pluribus.
units.tr: This conversation of the honoured with the common people ought to be tempered and seasoned with gravity and justice, by which that conversation is moderated according to the condition of dignity and the lowly quality of the person. For the eminence of all superiors is not equal, nor is the humbleness and lowliness of all common people equal and the same. Courtesies and duties also vary according to persons, times, age, the nature of things, local custom, and many other circumstances.

units.la: Grauitas constat requisitis quinque. Primum est, vt parca & rara dignioris & honoratioris sit conuersatio cum inferiore populari & viliori. Quæ enim incognita habemus & intacta,ea maiora plerunque animo nobis fingimus, vel esse suspicamur; iuxta Apologum de vulpecula, quæ primo, secundo & tertio Leonem viderat. Lib.obseruandum. De offic. præsid. l.1. De postliminio. l.9. nec. §. 2. de offic. proconsul. Deinde,in conuersatione hac modus seruetur, quo nimirum arcana,intima,ardua,aliaq; ad personam dignioris honorati pertinentia, & imprimis arcana, lapsus, infirmitates & alia quæ ad minuendam & extenuandam eiusdem dignitatem faciunt, aut scandalum parere possunt, tegantur & celentur.
units.tr: Gravity consists of five requisites. The first is that the conversation of the more dignified and honoured man with an inferior, common and lowlier person be sparing and infrequent. For we usually imagine or suspect things greater than we have not known or handled, in accordance with the fable of the little fox, who had seen the lion first, second and third time. Cf. the law "Observandum," On the Duties of the Governor, book 1; the law "De postliminio," 9; and §2 of the law "De officio proconsulis." Next, in this conversation a measure should be kept, so that secrets, private matters, difficult affairs and whatever else pertains to the person of the dignified and honoured man, and above all secrets, lapses, weaknesses, and anything that tends to diminish and lessen his dignity or may give offence, are covered and concealed.

units.la: Secundum grauitatis requisitum est, vt rigidè & seuerè conuersationem suam honoratior dirigat & conformet ad honestatis, pietatis, iustitiæ, aliarumque virtutum exercitium. Actor.cap.14. 14.15.16. Matth. cap.5. 16. Splendeat lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant vestra bona opera, & glorificent patrem vestrum qui est in cœlis. Et statu conditioneque sua digne secundum eundum communis Ethicæ præcepta viuat. Galat.c.6.4.Ephes.cap.4.Pretor vos ut incedatis ita, ut dignum est vocatione, qua vocati estis & seqq. 2. Corinth.c.6.3.Philip.cap.3.17. 2.Pet.c.3 7 & seqq. Tit.cap.2.7. Per omnia teipsum prabens exemplar bonorum operum, in doctrina integritatem, gravitatem.& verf.2. Vt senes sobrii sint, venerandi, temperantes, sani fide, charitate, tolerantia 3. Anus itidem vt habitus sint qui sanctimoniam deceat, &c. 1. Pet.cap.4.10. Vt quisque accepit donum, ita alius in alium illud subministrantes, vt boni dispensatores varia Dei gratia, & seqq.1.Timoth.cap.4.12.Nemo tuam iuuentutem despiciat, sed esto exemplar fidelium in sermone, in conuersatione, &c. Galat.cap.6.3.
units.tr: The second requisite of gravity is that the more honoured man direct and shape his conversation strictly and severely toward the exercise of honesty, piety, justice and the other virtues. Acts 14:14–16; Matthew 5:16: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." He should also live worthily of his station and condition, according to the precepts of common ethics. Galatians 6:4; Ephesians 4:1: "I beseech you to walk worthy of the calling with which you have been called"; 2 Corinthians 6:3; Philippians 3:17; 2 Peter 3:7ff.; Titus 2:7: "In all things showing yourself a pattern of good works, in doctrine integrity, gravity"; and verse 2: "that the aged men be sober, reverent, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience"; 3: "likewise the aged women, that they be in holy behaviour, as becomes holiness," etc.; 1 Peter 4:10: "As every man has received the gift, so let him minister it one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God," etc.; 1 Timothy 4:12: "Let no man despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, in conversation," etc.; Galatians 6:3.

units.la: Tertium requisitum est, vt omnem humiliorum, popularium, tenuiorum leuitatem, stultitiam, excessus, defectus, errata & delicta, cum lenitate corrigat, emendet, & omnes nævos, quantum fieri poterit, tollat tanquam fidelis & vigilans morum inspector, qui etiam solo nutu aliquo graui delinquentibus & errantibus pudorem incutere possit & cum authoritate monere.Marc.cap.1.12.Tit.cap.2.15.
units.tr: The third requisite is that he correct and amend, with gentleness, all the lightness, folly, excesses, defects, errors and faults of the humbler, common and lowly people, and as a faithful and watchful inspector of morals remove all blemishes so far as it can be done. He should be able, even by a single serious nod, to instil shame into those who offend and err, and to admonish them with authority. Mark 1:12; Titus 2:15.

units.la: Hæc loquere, exhortare & argue cum omni imperio, nemo te despiciat. Matth.cap.7.29. Docebat enim eos vt habens authoritatem, non autem vt Scriba, Luc.c.4 31. Huic admonitioni, vel reprehensioni vtile est addere spem honoris & metu poenæ; quæ duo sunt elementa virtutis; illa ad virtutes stimulat; hic, à vitiis auocat. Sic itaque alternis vicib9 increpationes & collaudationes vsurpandæ & adhibendæ, vt cum exultant animi, reprehensionibus ad pudorem redigantur: Et cum deiecti sunt, rursum laudibus erigatur. Nimiis laudibus inflare eos & ad superbiam extollere, non decet. Unde luxuria & vanitas. Plutarch. de lib. educat.
units.tr: "Speak these things, exhort and rebuke with all authority; let no man despise you." Matthew 7:29: for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. Luke 4:31. It is useful to add to this admonition or reproof the hope of honour and the fear of punishment, which are two elements of virtue: the one stirs us to virtues, the other turns us away from vices. So rebukes and words of praise are to be used and applied in turn, so that when minds are elated they may be brought back to shame by reproofs, and when they are cast down they may again be raised up by praise. It is not fitting to puff them up with excessive praise and lift them to pride, whence come luxury and vanity. Plutarch, On the Education of Children.

units.la: Atque haec potestas & cura obiurgandi, monendi & corrigendi, digniori & honorationi incumbit. Iob. cap. 32. 6. 7. Minimus sum aetate, vos autem decrepiti. Idcirco veritus sum ac timui ostendere sententiam meam vobis. Dicebam, provectii aetate loquentur, & annosi notam facient sapientiam, &c. & verf. 16. 17. c. 29. 21. 22. 2. Pet. c. 1. 13. Iustum autem arbitror, quandiu sum in hoc tabernaculo, excitare vos per commonefactionem. & 2. Timoth. cap. 4. 2. Tit. c. 2. 2. 3. & seqq. 1. Timoth. cap. 5. cap. 6. 1. Thess. cap. 5. 14. c. 4. 18. Act. c. 3. 12. c. 7. 51. cap. 8. 20. c. 13. 10. Et sic maiores natu, minorum curam habere iubentur: & monere, ut fugiant iuveniles cupiditates & rectum inuita cursum teneant. Vide Num. c. 8. 26. Genes. c. 4. 7. 9. c. 27. 31. 39. 42. Ruth. c. 3. 1. 5. Exod. c. 18. 17. 19. 24. Tit. c. 2. c. 3. 1. Timoth. c. 5. c. 3. Prov. c. 23. 13. 14. 1. Pet. c. 5. 5. Similiter iuniores subiecti estote senioribus, & omnes vicissim subiicimini. Levit. c. 19. 17. Ne odio habeto fratrem tuum in corde tuo, libere corripito proximum tuum, neq; ferto in eo peccatum. Heb. c. 10. 24. Et obseruemus alii alios, ut nos acuamus ad charitatem & bona opera. 1. Thess. c. 5. 14. Hinc censura & iudicia seniorum, quae apud Iudaeos erant. Num. c. 11. 16. & seqq. Deut. c. 21. 2. c. 13. 9. Hinc seniores patres & iuniores filii saepe appellantur, 1. Timoth. c. 5. 1. 2. 3. 4. c. 1. 18. & 1. Cor. c. 14. 15. c. 4. 14. Joh. c. 19. 26. 27. c. 6. 58. 1. Joh. c. 2. 2. Reg. c. 13. 14. c. 2. 12. Tit. c. 2 2. 3. 4. Inprimis vero
units.tr: This power and care of rebuking, admonishing and correcting falls upon the more dignified and honoured man. Job 32:6–7: "I am young in years, and you are aged. Therefore I was afraid and feared to show you my opinion. I said, let those advanced in age speak, and let the aged make known wisdom," etc.; verses 16–17; 29:21–22; 2 Peter 1:13: "I think it right, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by reminding you"; 2 Timothy 4:2; Titus 2:2–3ff.; 1 Timothy 5; 6; 1 Thessalonians 5:14; 4:18; Acts 3:12; 7:51; 8:20; 13:10. And so the older men are bidden to take care of the younger, and to admonish them to flee youthful desires and keep to the straight course. See Numbers 8:26; Genesis 4:7, 9; 27:31, 39; 42; Ruth 3:1, 5; Exodus 18:17, 19, 24; Titus 2; 3:1; 1 Timothy 5; 3; Proverbs 23:13–14; 1 Peter 5:5: "Likewise, you younger, be subject to the elders, and all of you be subject one to another." Leviticus 19:17: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall freely rebuke your neighbour, and not bear sin on account of him." Hebrews 10:24: "And let us consider one another, to stir up one another to charity and good works." 1 Thessalonians 5:14. Hence the censure and judgments of the elders, which existed among the Jews. Numbers 11:16ff.; Deuteronomy 21:2; 13:9. Hence elders are often called fathers and the younger sons, 1 Timothy 5:1–4; 1:18; 1 Corinthians 14:15; 4:14; John 19:26–27; 6:58; 1 John 2:2; 1 Kings 13:14; 2:12; Titus 2:2–4. Above all, however,

units.la: hæc monendi cura & morum inspectio perti- net ad Præceptorem, Rectorem, Doctorem, Pa- ftorem, patrem & dominum, quorum difcipline & institutioni alii sunt commissi, quorum pi- gritia excitanda, vagiq; ætatis impetus reprimē- di, Tit.c.1.9.& feqq.c.2.2.3. & feqq. 2.Timoth.c.4. Num.c.8.26.1.Cor,c.4.19. & feqq. Prou.c.13.24. c. 22.15.c.23.13.c.19.18.Hebr.c.12.7. Menoch.libr.2. arb.iud.quaft.caf.364. Ruth.c.3. 1.2.3. tot.tit. C.de emendat.propinq. Eccl. c.10.1. Iudex sapiens erudit populum suum.
units.tr: This care to admonish and to oversee morals belongs to the teacher, the tutor, the doctor, the minister, the father and the master, to whose discipline and instruction others have been entrusted, whose sloth must be roused and whose youthful impulses must be restrained: Tit. c. 1. 9. and following; c. 2. 2. 3. and following; 2 Tim. c. 4; Num. c. 8. 26; 1 Cor. c. 4. 19 and following; Prov. c. 13. 24; c. 22. 15; c. 23. 13; c. 19. 18; Heb. c. 12. 7; Menoch. lib. 2, arb. iud., quaest. cas. 364; Ruth c. 3. 1. 2. 3, the whole title; C. de emendat. propinq.; Eccl. c. 10. 1. A wise judge instructs his people.

units.la: Quartum requisitum est, vt dignior & ho- noratior opinioni de se conceptæ, congruenter loquatur & agat; nec seipsum nimium deiiciat & submittat, neq; vltra modum efferat, vel fa- ciat quæ non decent statum & conditionem suam, vid.quasup.dixi cap.3. De σεμνολογία. Non tractet leuia vilia sordida abiecta, quæ contem- ptum pariunt, sed præclara magna plus facto ipso præstet quam promisit. In sermone vtatur voce tardâ, in incessu gradu lento; inquibus gra- uitas quædam. Nam vt recte Seneca in epistol.dicit, Sapienti viro incessus modestior convenit, & oratio pressa, non audax. vbi enim loquentiæ multum, ibi sapientiæ parum. Decorum est sermo lenis, quietus & remissus, facitq; persepe sibi audien- tiam diserti lenis compta oratio & mitis. Cato maior. Idem Cicero cum Pisone genere eius mollius incederet, fi- lia autem concitatius, aut genero, Ambula tanquam fæmina: & filia, ambula tamquam vir. Silentium & arcanorum custodia decet principes & ho- mines suspensos detinet vt cupide euentum & exitum exspectent.
units.tr: The fourth requirement is that a man who is more honoured than others, in keeping with the opinion conceived of him, should speak and act fittingly. He should neither belittle and humble himself too much, nor exalt himself beyond measure, nor do what does not befit his rank and condition; see what I said above in chapter 3 on σεμνολογία. He should not handle trivial, base, filthy or abject matters, which breed contempt, but should excel in what is distinguished and great, and should perform more than he promised. In speech he should use a slow voice, and in gait a measured step, in which there is a certain gravity. For, as Seneca rightly says in his epistles, a modest gait suits a wise man, and restrained speech, not bold. Where there is much talk, there is little wisdom. Gentle, quiet and relaxed speech is becoming, and a polished and mild oration often wins a hearing for the eloquent man. Cato the Elder. Cicero too, when his son-in-law Piso walked more softly and his daughter more briskly, said to the son-in-law, "Walk like a woman," and to the daughter, "walk like a man." Silence and the keeping of secrets become princes and men of standing, and they keep others in suspense so that they eagerly await the outcome and the result.

units.la: S
units.tr: S

units.la: Quintum grauitatis requisitum est in defen- denda bona fama, existimatione, dignitate & statu suo; quod in tribus potissimum consistit. Primò, in assertione illius contra lædentes, auferentes, vel minuentes existimationem, integritatem & famam honestam. Secundo, in vita integra atq; omni turpitudine carente. Tertiò, in vestitu eleganti & decenti.
units.tr: The fifth requirement of gravity lies in defending one's good name, reputation, dignity and status. This consists chiefly in three things. First, in asserting it against those who harm, take away or diminish one's reputation, integrity and honest fame. Second, in a life that is upright and free of all baseness. Third, in elegant and decent dress.

units.la: Defensio existimationis, dignitatis, authoritatis & integritatis ideo licita & ciuilis est, vt reprimantur iniuriæ, in gratiam eius qui eas facit vt peccare se agnoscat, & desinat, argum. Galat.cap.6.1.2.3.Proverb.cap.26.s.6. Deinde, in aliorum gratiam qui impetuntur. Et denique, nostrâ causâ, ne authoritatem nostram quæ Reipub.vel ecclesiæ vtilis esse potest, amitta- mus, & magistratus superior, vel ipse Deus, quorum negotia gerimus & administramus, & vices sustinemus, per nos contemnatur, nisi fortè defensione tua iniurians deterior fieret.& maius malum secuturum esset.arg. 2. Reg.c.18.36. vel quando sentis, te commotum & in defen- dendo fines excessurum.Proverb. cap. 26. 4. Itaque quando aliter non possumus, iniuria seren- da & mussitanda est,1.Petri cap. 2. 16. &seqq. 2. Samuel.cap.16.5.6.9.10.11. Matth. cap.5.39.40. Petr.Martyr.in d. c.16.2. Samuel. Exempla fa- ctæ huius defensionis, authoritatis, existima- tionis, passim in sacris literis videre licet. Sic enim Samuel existimationem suam vindicasse legitur, 1.Samuel.c.12.3.4. &seqq. Sic Christus suam innocentiam & integritatem contra im- probos & diffamantes asseruit.Johan.c.8.46.47.
units.tr: Defence of one's reputation, dignity, authority and integrity is lawful and civil for three reasons: that injuries may be restrained, for the benefit of the one who commits them, so that he may recognise his fault and cease, argument from Gal. c. 6. 1. 2. 3; Prov. c. 26. 6. Then, for the benefit of those who are attacked. And finally, for our own sake, lest we lose our authority, which can be useful to the commonwealth or the Church, and lest the superior magistrate, or God himself, whose affairs we conduct and administer and whose place we hold, be despised through us; unless perhaps by our defence the wrongdoer would become worse and a greater evil would follow, argument from 2 Kings c. 18. 36; or when you feel you are stirred and would go beyond due bounds in defending yourself, Prov. c. 26. 4. Therefore, when we cannot do otherwise, an injury must be borne and kept silent, 1 Pet. c. 2. 16 and following; 2 Sam. c. 16. 5. 6. 9. 10. 11; Matt. c. 5. 39. 40; Peter Martyr on the same chapter, 16. 2; Samuel. Examples of this kind of defence of authority and reputation may be seen everywhere in the Holy Scriptures. Thus Samuel is read to have vindicated his reputation, 1 Sam. c. 12. 3. 4 and following. Thus Christ asserted his innocence and integrity against wicked men who defamed him, John c. 8. 46. 47.

units.la: & &seqq. cap.18.21.23.24. Sic Paulus quoque, vt pater 1.Thessalon.cap.2. Actorum cap.28.17.18. cap. 22.25. &seqq. cap. 26.25.26. cap. 23.3.6.7.10. & seqq.cap.25.7. &seqq. Sic & plures alii sancti homines. Actor. cap. 2, 15. 16. cap.7. 2.8. & Genes. cap.31.36. &seqq. Num.cap.16.28. &seqq. Matth. cap.22.6.7.8.1.Sam.c.1.14. 5.16.17. & c.24.9.10.11. 1.Reg.cap.18.18.19.20. Ierem.cap.37.13. Iof.cap. 22. 21. &seqq.2.Sam.cap.16. vbi Petr.Martyr. Huic defensioni adfinis, vel potius eius speciesest, suspicionis malae de se conceptae purgatio & innocentiae probatio, cuius exempla vid. Iof.cap. 22.22. 1.Sam.cap.1.14. & cap.12.3. 1.Reg. cap.18. 17.Iere.c.37.12. Act c.2.14.cap.6.14. c.7.2. c.28.27.
units.tr: and following, c. 18. 21. 23. 24. So Paul too, as a father, 1 Thess. c. 2; Acts c. 28. 17. 18; c. 22. 25 and following; c. 26. 25. 26; c. 23. 3. 6. 7. 10 and following; c. 25. 7 and following. So also several other holy men, Acts c. 2. 15. 16; c. 7. 2. 8; Gen. c. 31. 36 and following; Num. c. 16. 28 and following; Matt. c. 22. 6. 7. 8; 1 Sam. c. 1. 14; c. 5. 16. 17; and c. 24. 9. 10. 11; 1 Kings c. 18. 18. 19. 20; Jer. c. 37. 13; Josh. c. 22. 21 and following; 2 Sam. c. 16, where Peter Martyr. Closely related to this defence, or rather a species of it, is the purging of an evil suspicion conceived about oneself and the proof of one's innocence. Examples of this may be seen in Josh. c. 22. 22; 1 Sam. c. 1. 14; c. 12. 3; 1 Kings c. 18. 17; Jer. c. 37. 12; Acts c. 2. 14; c. 6. 14; c. 7. 2; c. 28. 27.

units.la: Secundo omnino etiam ad existimationem & famam bonam necessaria est vita integra, honesta & pia.2.Sam. c.13.3. qui dominatur hominibus iustis, iustus esto, dominans in timore Dei. Tit.c.2. 7.Per omnia te ipsum praebens exemplar bonorum operum,in doctrina integritatem,gravitatem, 15. Nemo te despiciat, 1.Timoth. c.4.12. Nemo iuventutem tuam despiciat, sed esto exemplar fidelium in sermone,conversatione, &c.1.Timoth.cap.3.7. Oportet eum etiam bonum habere testimonium ab extraneis, ne in probrum incidat. Philip. c.4.8. Quod reliquum est, fratres, quaecunque sunt vera, quaecunque veneranda quaecunque iusta, quaecunque pura, quaecunque amabilia, quaecunque boni nominis, si qua virtus, & si qua laus est. haec cogitate, quae fama & existimatio omnibus diuitius melior. Prov.c.22.1. Eccles.cap.7.2.c.41. 15.16.cap.44.8. & seqq. Psal.112. 4.5. &seqq. vide quae suprac.13.in commendatione virtutis dixi & allegavi. Ergo bona fama, opinio & existimatio & authoritas studio virtutis & recte factis confer-uatur, fouetur continuatur & propagatur, 1. Timoth. cap. 4. 12. 1. Macchab. cap. 13. 3. & seqq. cap. 16. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. Iob. c. 29. 8. Eccles. cap. 32. 12. & seqq. Matth. c. 23. 13. 14. Tiraquel. De nobilit. c. 37. nu. 40. & seqq.
units.tr: Second, a life that is whole, honest and pious is absolutely necessary for a good name and fame. 2 Sam. c. 13. 3; he who rules over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God; Titus c. 2. 7: in all things showing yourself a pattern of good works, in doctrine integrity and gravity; 15: let no one despise you; 1 Tim. c. 4. 12: let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in speech, conduct, etc.; 1 Tim. c. 3. 7: he must also have a good testimony from outsiders, lest he fall into reproach. Phil. c. 4. 8: Finally, brethren, whatever is true, whatever is honourable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is of good report; if there is any virtue and any praise, think on these things, for good fame and esteem is better than all riches, Prov. c. 22. 1; Eccl. c. 7. 2; c. 41. 15. 16; c. 44. 8 and following; Ps. 112. 4. 5 and following. See what I said and cited above, chapter 13, in commendation of virtue. Therefore good fame, opinion, esteem and authority are preserved, fostered, continued and propagated by the pursuit of virtue and right conduct, 1 Tim. c. 4. 12; 1 Macc. c. 13. 3 and following; c. 16. 1. 2. 3 and following; Job c. 29. 8; Eccl. c. 32. 12 and following; Matt. c. 23. 13. 14; Tiraquellus, De nobilitate, c. 37, n. 40 and following.

units.la: Tertio, vestitus honoratorum, excellentio-rumq; hominum sit nec exquisitus, neq; sordidus, sed elegans & decorus, statui & conditioni quam profitentur, respondens. De quo vid. Tiraquell. De legib. connubial. lege 3. & de nobilit. cap. 10. num. 143. & seqq. Ordinat. imper. de anno 38. 77. Petrum Gregor. lib. 9. Syntagm. c. 19. & licet videre exempla Daniel. c. 5. 7. 29. Esther c. 6. 6. & seqq. Genes. cap. 41. 40. 41. & seqq. 2. Samuel. cap. 13. 18. vbi Martyr. Iacob. c. 2. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. 1. Macchab. c. 10. 20. 21. 22. 64. 65. 66. 68. c. 11. 58. cap. 14. 43. 44. Marc. c. 12. 38. Matth. c. 22. 11. c. 11. 8. Luc. c. 7. 25. 26. tit. C. De vestitu holosericis. Isidor. lib. 19. Etymol. c. 21. & seqq. Exod. c. 28. Num. c. 27. 29. & seqq. & Baptisum de re vestiaria, c. 9. Pet. Greg. lib. 9. Syntag. c. 19.
units.tr: Third, the clothing of honoured and eminent men should be neither exquisite nor squalid, but elegant and decorous, corresponding to the station and condition they profess. On this see Tiraquellus, De legibus connubialibus, lex 3, and De nobilitate c. 10, n. 143 and following; the imperial ordinance of the year 38, 77; Peter Gregory, Syntagma lib. 9, c. 19. And examples may be seen at Dan. c. 5. 7. 29; Esther c. 6. 6 and following; Gen. c. 41. 40. 41 and following; 2 Sam. c. 13. 18, where Martyr. James c. 2. 1. 2. 3 and following; 1 Macc. c. 10. 20. 21. 22. 64. 65. 66. 68; c. 11. 58; c. 14. 43. 44; Mark c. 12. 38; Matt. c. 22. 11; c. 11. 8; Luke c. 7. 25. 26; the title C. De vestitu holosericis; Isidore, Etymologiae lib. 19, c. 21 and following; Exod. c. 28; Num. c. 27. 29 and following; and Baptista on the matter of clothing, c. 9; Peter Gregory, Syntagma lib. 9, c. 19.

units.la: Erogationes honestae & sumptus atque liberalitas, nonnunquam etiam honoratiorem decet, pro ratione facultatum & conditionis & status sui. l. 4. vbi pupill. educ. l. 12. cum plures, §. 2. De adm. tut. Vetus mos fuit, vt pro introitu, seu ingressu dignitatis & officii eiusdem collegii sociis & collegis aliquid praestaretur, l. pen. §. pen. & vlt. De legat. 3. & l. 7. vnicuiq;, C. de prox. sacro scrin. & l. vlt. C. d. tit. & conuiuia in principio administrationis inceptae, apud Iudaeos vsitata fuerunt, 1. Sam. c. 9. 19. 25. 26. Est. c. 1. 1. Reg. c. 3. 15. 1. Chron. c. 12. 38. 39. 40. c. 29. 22.
units.tr: Honest expenditure, outlay and liberality also sometimes befit a more honoured person, in proportion to his means, condition and status: L. 4, where pupils are educated; L. 12, cum plures, §2, De administratione tutorum. It was an old custom that on the entry into a dignity or office something was provided for the associates and colleagues of the same college, L. pen., §pen. and ult., De legatis 3; L. 7, unicuique, C. de proximis sacri scrinii; L. ult., C., the same title; and banquets at the beginning of an administration undertaken were customary among the Jews: 1 Sam. c. 9. 19. 25. 26; Esther c. 1. 1; 1 Kings c. 3. 15; 1 Chron. c. 12. 38. 39. 40; c. 29. 22.

units.la: Sequitur de iustitia, qua conuersatio honoratorum & praestantiorum cum popularibus, temperatur & peragitur iustè & moderatè; vt ex ea inferiorum beneuolentiam, amorem & studium sibi comparet, ita vt reuerentiam non terrore nec amorem humilitate captet. Hæc consistit potissimum in mutuo amore, inadsignatione minisseriorum, patrocinio & compensatione obsequiorum.
units.tr: There follows justice, by which the conduct of the honoured and eminent towards the common people is tempered and carried out justly and moderately, so that from it they win the goodwill, love and zeal of their inferiors, and seek reverence not by terror nor affection by humility. This consists chiefly in mutual love, in the assignment of duties, in patronage and in the requital of services.

units.la: In mutuo amore: quia amamus eos, apud quos in pretio & honore esse cupimus; & amici illis esse volumus, quos nostri admiratores & quasi æmulos, & imitatores esse cupimus. Ideoque etiam orare conuenit superioribus pro inferioribus. Sic Moses pro gente sua Deo supplicabat: Abraham, pro Sodomis: Samuel, pro Saule: Ieremias, pro populo: & Paulus, pro suis auditoribus & ecclesiis.
units.tr: Mutual love: because we love those among whom we wish to be prized and honoured, and we want to be friends to those whom we wish to be our admirers, as it were our rivals and imitators. Hence it is also fitting for superiors to pray for inferiors. Thus Moses prayed to God for his people; Abraham for Sodom; Samuel for Saul; Jeremiah for the people; and Paul for his hearers and churches.

units.la: In officiis & ministeriis adsignandis, personarum ratio & delectus habendus, vt si quid sordidius tractandum inciderit, illud vilissimo cuique mandetur: laboriosa robustis, leuia imbecillis & natu grandioribus iniungantur, pro ut iustitia distributiua exigit; ne intempestiue vltra modum obsequia debita exigantur; neq; rigidè, seuerè & exacte & exquisite; sed humaniter, leniter, clarè, distinctè, placide & amanter. Coloss. c. 4. Philem. v. 13. & seqq. Senec. lib. 6. Epist. 42. & Epist. 46. & lib. 6. c. 4. de benefic. Nam vt Dion ait lib. 43 potentia mediocriter exercita, omnia quaesita conseruat. Et qui impudenter & passim in omnibus potentia abutitur, is neq; veram beneuolentiam, neq; firmam securitatem inuenit.
units.tr: In assigning duties and ministries, regard must be paid to each person's circumstances and suitability, so that if some dirtier task has to be done, it is handed to the lowliest person. Laborious tasks are to be given to the strong, and light ones to the weak and the older. This is what distributive justice requires. Services due are not to be demanded untimely or beyond measure, nor rigidly, harshly, strictly, exactingly and punctiliously, but humanely, gently, clearly, distinctly, calmly and lovingly. Col. 4. Philem. 13 and following. Sen. Epist. 42 and 46, and De benef. 6.4. For, as Dio says in book 43, power used with moderation preserves everything that has been gained. And whoever shamelessly abuses his power on every occasion finds neither true goodwill nor firm security.

units.la: Hucetiam pertinet, quod ciusmodi superior & praestantior in conuersatione cum humiliori verbis factisque benignis se amabilem, lenem & humanum praebere debeat, qui etiam inferiori se suum honorem tribuat, 1. Pet. cap. 3. 7. Viri similiter una versentur ut scientes decet, vasi muliebri, ut infirmiori, tribuentes honorem, utpote cum una etiam haeredes sitis gratiae vitae, ne interrumpantur preces vestrae, & Senec. libr. 6. epist. 42. & 46. Serui sunt, inquit, imo homines, imo contubernales, imo humiles amici, imo conserui, si cogitaueris tantundem in utrofq; lucere fortuna. Ideo rideo istos, qui putant turpe cum feruis suis coenare. Quare? nisi quia superbissima consuetudo tanantem dominum stantium seruorum turba circumdedit, & late epist. 47.
units.tr: To this also belongs the fact that a superior and more distinguished person, in dealing with a humbler one, ought to show himself lovable, gentle and kind in word and deed. He should also grant the inferior his due honour. 1 Pet. 3:7: "Husbands, likewise, dwell with your wives according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered." Also Seneca, Epist. 42 and 46: "They are slaves, but no, they are men; they are companions; they are humble friends; they are fellow-slaves, if you consider that fortune shines equally upon both. So I laugh at those who think it shameful to dine with their slaves. Why? Only because a most arrogant custom has surrounded the master with a crowd of standing slaves." And at length in Epist. 47.

units.la: Sic Dauid victo & profligato Goliatho a Saule ad conuiuium & mensam inuitatus legitur honoris ergo. Et Dauid honoris causa Mephibosetih in mensa sua edere voluit. 2. Samuel. c. 9. 1 r. 16. 17. & Rex Babyloniae captum regem Iudae. 2. Reg. c. 25. 31. 32. 33. & Dauid filium Barzillai. 2. Sam. c. 19. 34. & seqq. quamuis alias inferiores & humiliores ministeria ad mensam praestare teneantur. Luc. c. 17. 8. Iob. cap. 12. 2. 5. vide Sueton. in Caligul. Val. Max. lib. 5, c. 1, Lipsi. lib. 4. Plut. c. 8.
units.tr: So David, after Goliath had been conquered and overthrown, is read as having been invited by Saul to a feast and table, for the sake of honour. And David, for the sake of honour, wished Mephibosheth to eat at his own table. 2 Sam. 9; 1 Kings 16, 17. And the king of Babylon (honoured) the captive king of Judah. 2 Kings 25:31–33. And David (honoured) the son of Barzillai. 2 Sam. 19:34 and following, although otherwise inferiors and humbler persons are bound to provide services at the table. Luke 17:8. Job 12:2, 5. See Suetonius in Caligula; Valerius Maximus book 5, chapter 1; Lipsius book 4; Plutarch chapter 8.

units.la: Patrocinium suum, protectionem, auxilium & consilium, honoratior atq; praestantior, humiliori populari, tenuiori clientulo, sponte, non rogatus, praestare, & exhibere debet. Apud Romanos, plebei singulos patronos, ex patribus legebant, quorum consilio & auctoritate veretur aduersus aliorum iniurias. vid. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 5. Genial. dier. c. 24.
units.tr: A more honoured and distinguished person ought to offer and provide his patronage, protection, aid and counsel freely, without being asked, to a humbler commoner or a poorer client. Among the Romans, the plebeians each chose a patron from among the patricians, by whose counsel and authority they were protected against the injuries of others. See Alexander ab Alexandro, book 5, Genial Days, chapter 24.

units.la: Compensatio obsequiorum iusta est, ex qua tenuiores intelligant, peccare esse inutile & perniciosum; recte vero facere, fructuosum. Hic itaque superiores & praestantiores, quantum possunt, imitari debet agros fertiles, vel terrae consuetudinem, quae a quibus diligentius & laboriosius colitur, iis veriores ferunt fructus. Ideo recte Senec. de benef. vit., Melius beneficiis imperium custoditur, quam armis. Videndum igitur & laborandum est inprimis hisce dignioribus & honorationibus, ut exspectationi inferiorum & tenuiorum satisfaciant, in eoque non haesitent, vel cunctentur donec a tenuibus admoneantur. Si quidem bis gratum est, quod vltro offertur. Et beneficium fero dedit, qui roganti dedit. Senec. libr. 2. De benefic. cap. 2. & libr. 1. De clement. cap. 3. & Prov. cap. 3. 28. Reuertere, cras sum daturus tibi, &c.
units.tr: Reciprocity of services is just, and from it the poorer understand that sinning is useless and harmful, while doing right is fruitful. Therefore the superior and more distinguished should, as far as they can, imitate fertile fields or the custom of the land, which bear truer fruits for those who cultivate them more diligently and with more labour. Hence Seneca rightly says in De beneficiis: Rule is better preserved by benefits than by arms. So these more worthy and honoured persons must above all take care and labour to satisfy the expectations of their inferiors and poorer folk. In this they should not hesitate or delay until they are reminded by the lowly. For what is offered unasked is doubly welcome, and he has given a benefit who gave it to one who asked. Seneca, De benef. 2.2; De clem. 1.3; and Prov. 3:28: "Go and come again; tomorrow I will give it thee," etc.

units.la: Hoc facto superiores tenuiorum & inferiorum studia & voluntatem in se excitabunt, ut summa alacritate, promptitudine & contentione impositorum obsequia praestent, ut vius obtemperantium fructuosior & iucundior illis reddatur: & semper alacres & bonae spei plenos suique amantes & vltro obsequentes humiliores populares experientur, qui ipsos tanquam parentes diligent, non ut tyrannos, vel auaros metuent. Atque eiusmodi liberalitas, hominibus etiam maximè commendatur. Prouerb. cap. 11. 26. cap. 28. 16. Tit. cap. 3. 13. 1. Samuelis cap. 30. 26. 2. Samuelis cap. 9. 7. Apud Romanos Imperatores saepè maximas largitiones in populum faciebant. De quibus vide Alexand. ab Alexan.lib.5.c.24. Genial.dier. Et Seneca lib.3. De benefic cap.15. elegantèr dicit, Generosi animi est & magnifici, iuuare & prodesse, & in lib. De moribus. Generosi animi est, vires suas beneficiis potius, quam iniuriis manifestare. Item: Multi sunt obligandi, pauci offendedi. Nam memoria beneficiorum facilis est, iniuriarum tenax. Qua de causa honoratiores etiam populares & humiliores ad conuiuia sua solebant vocare, vt dixi, 2.Sam.c.9.11.15.17. Luc.c.14.7.& seqq.2.Sam.c.3.10.c.13.25.28.1.Reg.c.1.9.cap.3.15. Luc.c.22.Ruth.c.2.14. Luc.c.5.19. Genes.c.43.16. 31.& seqq.c.21.8.c.26.30. c.29.22.c.40.20. Iob c.1. 2.Reg.c.25.31.32.33. Sueton. in Augusto, & Vespasiano & in Caligula, Valer. Max.lib.5. c.1. Stuck. libr.2 conuiuial. antiquit. cap.1. Quod si nulla beneficia tenuioribus praestare possunt, saltem beneuolentiae, fauoris & gratiae argumentum praebeant, seq; affabiles, humanos & amabiles praestent.
units.tr: By doing this, superiors will stir up in their poorer and lesser people the desire and goodwill toward themselves, so that they will render the services imposed upon them with the utmost eagerness, readiness and zeal. The yoke of those who obey will thus become more fruitful and more pleasant for them. The humbler commoners will always find them cheerful, full of good hope, loving them and serving them willingly. They will love them as parents, not fear them as tyrants or misers. Such liberality also commends a man very highly among men. Prov. 11:26; 28:16; Titus 3:13; 1 Sam. 30:26; 2 Sam. 9:7. Among the Romans, emperors often made very large donations to the people. On these see Alexander ab Alexandro, book 5, chapter 24, Genial Days. Seneca in De beneficiis book 3, chapter 15, elegantly says: It is the mark of a generous and magnificent spirit to help and to benefit. And in De moribus: It is the mark of a generous spirit to show one's strength by benefits rather than by injuries. Likewise: Many are to be bound to us, few offended. For the memory of benefits is easy to keep, but the memory of injuries is tenacious. For this reason the more honoured also used to invite commoners and humbler persons to their banquets, as I said. 2 Sam. 9:11, 15, 17; Luke 14:7 and following; 2 Sam. 3:10; 13:25, 28; 1 Kings 1:9; 3:15; Luke 22; Ruth 2:14; Luke 5:19; Gen. 43:16, 31 and following; 21:8; 26:30; 29:22; 40:20; Job 1; 2 Kings 25:31–33. See Suetonius in Augustus, Vespasian and Caligula; Valerius Maximus book 5, chapter 1; Stuck, Banquets of the Ancients, book 2, chapter 1. But if they cannot grant any benefits to the poorer, they should at least give proof of goodwill, favour and kindness, and show themselves affable, humane and lovable.

units.la: Sequitur de omittendis, quae fugere & euitare debet honoratior in conuersatione cum vilibus popularibusq; personis, quae è regione respondent illis, quae illi facienda esse diximus.
units.tr: Next follows what the more honoured person must omit and avoid in dealing with base and common persons. These are the opposites of what we said he should do for them.

units.la: Primum itaque in delato honore acceptando, fugere decet, ne honores competentes & obsequia debita recusat, quadam humilitatis simulatione, quae (vt dixi fuprac.2.) duplex est superbia, & praesumptionem contempti honoris facit & praemii reiecti, vid.Prov.c.13.7.Eccles. c.10.32.c.14. 4.5. Vnde etiam extenuatio suae conditionis & status homini Ethico & politico prohibita, vt dixi: supra cap.2.in ἀξιαυθλοχίᾳ. Qui contra autem supra quem decet ceremoniarum vsu delectatur, id ipsum ex quadam leuitate & vanitate facere dicitur, tanquam homo nullius precii.
units.tr: First, then, in accepting an honour offered, he ought to take care not to refuse the honours due to him and the services owed, by a certain pretended humility. As I said above (chapter 2), this is a double pride. It makes a presumption of rejecting the honour and the reward that is offered. See Prov. 13:7; Eccles. 10:32; 14:4, 5. Hence also the belittling of one's own rank and station is forbidden to an ethical and political man, as I said above in chapter 2, in the vice of self-depreciation [ἀξιαυθλοχίᾳ]. On the other hand, one who delights in ceremonies beyond what is fitting is said to do this out of a certain levity and vanity, as if he were a man of no worth.

units.la: Vsus obsequiorum fit abusus propter excessum, vel defectum. Ob excessum, quando superior honoratior acerbe obsequia exigit, inhumaniter, insolenter, tyrannice & iniuste; aut superbe, tanquam seruitio coacto & seruili, vel cum minis, iniuriis, aut acerbis sermonibus. Philemon. 1. 13. Quem ego cupiebam apud me retinere, ut pro te mihi ministraret, 14. Sed absque tua sententia nolui facere, ut non veluti ex necessitate sit beneficium tuum, sed voluntarium, & vers. 19. 20. 21. ibidem.
units.tr: The use of services becomes abuse through excess or deficiency. Through excess, when a superior and more honoured person demands services harshly, inhumanly, insolently, tyrannically and unjustly, or proudly, as if the service were forced and servile, or with threats, injuries or harsh words. Philemon 1:13: "Whom I would fain have retained with me, that in thy stead he might have ministered unto me in the bonds of the gospel." 14: "But without thy mind would I do nothing; that thy benefit should not be as it were of necessity, but willingly." And verses 19–21 of the same chapter.

units.la: Peccatur igitur hic, quando ad famulatum vsque viles & humiles a superioribus deprimuntur. Vti quando in Xysto diu inambulantem honoratiorem tenuis, popularis, aperto capite respicere cogitur; vel ille contumeliis, conuitiis, clamoribus, vel minis honestos homines, etiam in publico consectari delectatur, vel sordida ministeria exigit, vel iniqua iniungit & non congruentia, vel non debita; item, quando semel atque iterum in obsequiis & obseruantia cessantibus, atrociter succenser & se implacabilem & inexorabilem praebet; aut amarum, difficilem, morosum, durum, austerum, rigidum & asperu. Hoc modo honoratiores naturalem libertatem tenuiorum & popularium, constringunt: & odiosi, inuisique redduntur, aliisque spectantib. vel audientib. ridiculi, atque ita depressi illis nimiu vilescunt. Deut. c. 25. 3. Vide ne pergat plaga numerosiore his cadere eum, & frater tuus vilescat in oculis tuis. Coloss. c. 3. 21. Patres, ne irritate liberos, ne despondeant animum, 19. Viri diligite uxores & ne efiote aduersus eas amarulenti, Colof.cap. 4. Domini aequitatem & aequabilitatem feruis exhibete, ut quisciatis vos quoque dominum habere in calis, Ephef.c.6.4. Et vos patres, ne provocate ad iram liberos vestros, sed enutrite eos in doctrina & monitis Domini, & verf.9. Et vos domini eadem facite erga seruos remissis minis, scientes, vestrum etiam ipsorum Dominum esse in calis, nec personae respectum apud eum esse. adde Genef.c.30.14. Senec. libr. 6. Epistol. 42. & 46. & 47. neque enim debemus esse importuni exactores & imperiosi eorum, quae nobis praestantur ex charitate Chariftiana. Philemon.1.13.14. & seqq. imo & eorum quae iure nobis debentur, 1.Cor.c.9.15. & seqq. vid. Sen. lib.6. c.4. De benef.
units.tr: Sin is committed here when superiors lower the vile and humble to the level of servants. For example, when a more honoured person, walking up and down for a long time in the Xystus, forces a humble commoner to look up to him with his head uncovered. Or when he takes delight in pursuing honest men with insults, abuse, shouting or threats, even in public, or demands sordid services, or imposes unfair, unsuitable or undue tasks. Or when, once or twice, he flares up savagely against those who cease to show deference and obedience, and makes himself implacable and unrelenting. Or when he shows himself bitter, difficult, morose, hard, severe, stern and harsh. In this way the more honoured constrain the natural liberty of the poorer and common people. They become hateful and odious, ridiculous to onlookers and listeners, and so, by being oppressed, they become far too cheap. Deut. 25:3: "Lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee." Col. 3:21: "Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged." 19: "Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them." Col. 4:1: "Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal, knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven." Eph. 6:4: "And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath, but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord." Verse 9: "And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him." Add Gen. 30:14; Seneca book 6, Epistles 42, 46 and 47. For we ought not to be importunate exactors or domineering over those things which are rendered to us out of Christian charity. Philemon 1:13, 14 and following, indeed not even over those things which are due to us by right. 1 Cor. 9:15 and following. See Seneca, De benef. 6.4.

units.la: Ob defectum obsequio abutitur honoratior atq; praestantior, quando tenuiores & humiliores spe inanilactat, neque obsequia sibi praestita compensat; sed clementiae & bonitatis simulatione producit spem, & bonitatis praetextu frustrat.
units.tr: A more honourable and superior man also abuses the deference of others when he dangles empty hopes before the humbler and poorer, and does not repay the services they have rendered him. Under a pretence of mercy and goodness he holds out hope, and he cheats them under the cover of kindness.

units.la: Praeterea in primo requisito grauitatis, honoratiori fugiendum omnino est; primo, ne tenuiori populari se reddar familiarem, illiqueque se suaque nudet & patefaciat. Nimia enim familiaritas, ut habet prouerbium, parit contemptum. qua de re eleganter Calliftratus libr. 1. De cognitionibus: Obseruandum est, (inquit) ius reddenti, ut in adeundo quidem facilem se praebeat, sed contemni se non patiatur; unde mandatis adducitur, ne praesides prouinciarum in ulteriorem familiaritatem, prouinciales admittant. nam ex conuersatione aequali aequali contemptio dignitatis nascitur. Conspicien- dum se non praebeat facile cuiuis ex leui causa, vel saepius, sed tantum ob arduam causam, idque cum gravitate quadam. Sed & in cognoscendo, neque exandescere adversus eos quos malos putat, neque precibus calamitosorum illacrymari oportet; idenim non est constantis & recti iudicis, cuius animi motum vultus detegit, & summatim ita ut reddi debet, ut auctoritatem dignitatis ingenio suo augeat. hac in l. 19. observandum, De offic. praesid. quibus adde Nanell. 17. c. 2. in sin. l. 1. in sin. princ. de postuland. l. 1. §. sed etsi, 11. de vent. inspiciend. l. 9. nec, §. 2. De offic. proconsf. Proverb. c. 25. 17. & Senec. ad Polyb. & Livius lib. 35. Continuus aspectus minus verendos magnos homines ipsa familiaritate facit. Et ut Tacit. 1. Annal. ait, maiestati maior ex longinquo reverentia. Sed tamen hic contemptus in patria & inter cognatos difficulter praecaveri potest, Christo docere, Marc. c. 6. 3. 4. 5. Luc. c. 4. 24.
units.tr: Next, under the first requirement of gravity, the more honourable man must altogether avoid becoming too familiar with the lower sort of people, and must not expose himself and his affairs to them. For excessive familiarity, as the proverb says, breeds contempt. On this point Callistratus writes neatly in the first book of his De cognitionibus: "The one who renders justice must be observed; he should show himself accessible when people approach him, but he should not allow himself to be despised. Hence by mandate governors of provinces are forbidden to admit provincials into closer intimacy, for contempt for authority arises from equal familiarity." He should not let himself be seen readily by anyone for a slight cause, or too often, but only for a weighty matter and with a certain dignity. Likewise, in hearing cases, he should neither flare up against those whom he thinks wicked, nor should he weep at the entreaties of the afflicted; for it is not the mark of a steady and upright judge when his face betrays the movement of his mind. In short, he should pronounce judgment as is due, so that he increases the authority of his office by his character. On this see the 19th law, On the duties of the governor; add also Nanellus 17 c. 2 in fine; l. 1 in fine princ. de postulando; l. 1 §. sed etsi, 11, de ventre inspiciendo; l. 9 nec, §. 2, De officio proconsulis; Proverbs 25:17; and Seneca to Polybius; and Livy, book 35: "Constant exposure makes great men less revered, through familiarity itself." And as Tacitus says in the first book of the Annals: "Reverence for majesty is greater from a distance." Yet this contempt is hard to guard against among one's own countrymen and kinsmen, as Christ taught: Mark 6:3, 4, 5; Luke 4:24.

units.la: Caucebit quoq; vt alii non intelligant sealiorum consilijs instructum esse. Hinc enim contemptus & praesumptio insicitiae & propriae imbecillitatis.
units.tr: He must also take care that others do not understand that he is guided by the counsels of others. For from this come contempt, and the presumption of ignorance and of his own weakness.

units.la: In secundo requisito gravitatis omittenda & fugienda sunt honorationi illa quibus contemnitur & vilis habetur, ne scilicet sit obnoxius criminibus, vel culpabilis malum ab aliis habens testimonium. Nam ut Seneca libro 5. epist. 7. & 8. dicit, unum exemplar luxuriae, aut avaritiae, multum facit mali. 2. Corint. c. 6. 3. Nullam villam reprobantes offensionem, ne vituperetur ministerium. 4. sed in omnibus nos approbantes ut Dei ministri, &c. 1. ad Timo. c. 5. 14. Nullam occasionem date ad maledicendum, Tit. c.1.6.7.8.9. Philip. c.4.8.1. Timoth. cap.4.12. 2.Cor.cap.6.3.4. & seqq. Matth.c.23.13. & seqq. Tiraquel. de nobilit. cap.37. num.40. & seqq. Nam peruersus animo erit contemptui. Vir bonus vero laudabitur, ait Salomo Prouer.c.12.7.8. Ecclesiast.c.10.1. Ut muscarum mortuarum una efficit ut fœtorem eructet unguentum pigmentarii, similiter pretiosum nomine sapientiæ & gloria virum ut fœtidum officit stoliditatis parum. Nam & Iurisconsulti, per turpitudinem vitæ omnem dignitatem, nobilitatem & auctoritatem plerunque amittistatuunt, Tiraq. de nobilit. c.23.
units.tr: Under the second requirement of gravity, those things must be omitted and avoided by which a man is held in contempt and regarded as cheap, lest he be exposed to charges or be blamed, having a bad reputation among others. For as Seneca says in his fifth book of Letters, nos. 7 and 8, one example of luxury or greed does much harm. 2 Corinthians 6:3: "Giving no offence in anything, that the ministry be not blamed; but in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God," etc. 1 Timothy 5:14: "Give no occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully." Titus 1:6, 7, 8, 9; Philippians 4:8; 1 Timothy 4:12; 2 Corinthians 6:3, 4 and following; Matthew 23:13 and following; Tiraquellus, On nobility, c. 37, n. 40 and following. For a man who is perverse in mind will be despised, but a good man will be praised, says Solomon, Proverbs 12:7, 8. Ecclesiastes 10:1: as dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honour. For the jurists also hold that by a disgraceful life a man for the most part loses all dignity, nobility and authority; Tiraquellus, On nobility, c. 23.

units.la: Deinde etiam superbia omnino & gloriæ atque honoris cupiditas fugienda. Matth.cap.20. 26. & seqq. Rom.c.12.16. Eodem animo inter vos mutuo affecti, non elate de vobis ipsis sentientes, sed humilibus obsecundantes. Ne estote prudentes apud vosmet ipsos. 1. Corinth.c.13.4.5.6.7.8. Prouer.c.11. Vbi superbia, ibi & contumelia; vbi autem humilitas, ibi & sapientia. & c.16. Melius est humiliari cum mitib. & c. & c.29. Superbia enim Deo & hominibus exosa est, Eccles.c.10.7.8. & seqq.c.3.19. Quo maior es, eo magis te ipsum abiice; & coram Domino consequeris gratiam. 20. Multi excelsi & gloriosi sunt supra modum, sed mansuetis revelantur arcana, Marc. c.9 35. Si quis in vobis maior sit, fiat tanquam minimus. Deut.c.17.12. & seqq.20. Ne efferatur animus eius pra fratribus suis, & ne recedat ab hoc præcepto, & c.1.Reg.c.5.13.14. Iob c.31, 13. vid. Pet. Greg. lib.4 c.10.num.10. de Repub.
units.tr: Furthermore, pride and the desire for glory and honour must be altogether avoided. Matthew 20:26 and following; Romans 12:16; "Being of the same mind toward one another, not minded to high things, but condescending to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits." 1 Corinthians 13:4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Proverbs 11: "Where pride is, there also is shame; but with the humble is wisdom." Chapter 16: "It is better to be humble with the meek," etc.; chapter 29. For pride is hateful to God and to men, Ecclesiastes 10:7, 8 and following; 3:19: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find grace before the Lord." 20: "Many who are high and glorious are beyond measure, but secrets are revealed to the meek." Mark 9:35: "If anyone among you would be first, let him be last of all." Deuteronomy 17:12 and following, 20: "That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and that he turn not from this commandment," etc.; 1 Kings 5:13, 14; Job 31:13; see Petrus Gregorius, book 4, c. 10, n. 10, On the commonwealth.

units.la: Tertio etiam fugiendum exercitium artis sordidæ, vilis & abiectæ. Tiraquel. de nobilit. c.27. & seqq. Vid. Eccles. c.38.26. Qua in re efficeretur sapiens? piens? qui tenet aratrum & gloriatur de hastili stimulo boves agit, & nutritur inter opera eorum & cuius narratio est de taurorum fœtibus.27. & seqq. verfic. vbi late sordida manualia artificia describit, qua minus suis cultoribus honorifica & Reipub. non tantum utilitatis praebent, quantum honorifica alia nobilia officia, ex quibus dignitas & auctoritas & honor venit & adquiritur; sed proh dolor! hodie multis in locis Vespasianus cum suo lotio generosis & magnis familiis nobilibus se immiscet. Huc etiam pertinet, ne eiusmodi dignior cum inquinatissimis hominibus conuicio decertet, neque in maledictis adversus impudentes & improbos velitet, ut loquitur Gell. libr. 6. cap. 11. quia tantisper similis & compar eorum fit, dum paria & similia dicit.
units.tr: Thirdly, the practice of a dirty, base and abject trade must also be avoided. Tiraquellus, On nobility, c. 27 and following. See Ecclesiasticus 38:26: "In what way will he become wise who holds the plough and glories in the goad, who drives oxen and is occupied with their work and whose talk is of the young of bulls," 27 and following, where he describes at length the sordid manual crafts, which bring less honour to their practitioners and less benefit to the commonwealth than the honourable and noble offices, from which dignity, authority and honour come and are acquired; but alas! today in many places Vespasian, with his urine tax, mixes himself with well-born and great noble families. To this also belongs the rule that such a man of higher rank should not contend in insults with the most filthy men, nor skirmish in abuse against the shameless and wicked, as Gellius says in book 6, chapter 11, for so long as he says the same things, he becomes like and equal to them.

units.la: Quarto etiam arcana tenuioribus non sunt communicanda, ita enim honoratior prodit suam inopiam & stultitiam & iacturam opinionis de se conceptæ facit. Vid. Ecclesiast. cap. 6. 6. 13. cap. 32. 23. cap. 37. 7. 11. cap. 11. 30. cap. 13. 2. 3. 5. 6. 7. 8.
units.tr: Fourthly, secrets must not be communicated to the humbler sort, for in this way the more honourable man reveals his poverty and folly and brings loss to the opinion conceived of him. See Ecclesiastes 6:6, 13; 32:23; 37:7, 11; 11:30; 13:2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8.

units.la: In tertio grauitatis requisito, fugienda est negligentia, dissimulatio, incuria & oscitantia, indulgentia in monendo, instituendo, corrigendo & reprehendendo, reprimendo, cohibendo & puniendo. Nam non succensere delinquentibus, est indicium animi ad similia propensi. Similis enim simili gaudet. Addo, quod negligens se delictorum admissorum suo silentio participem facit & vilem se reddit humilioribus, & virtutis amorem & studium languefacit. Prov. c. 13. 24. 1. Sam. c. 2. 22. 29. c. 3. 13. 14. & 1. Reg. c. 1. 5. 6. vid. 1. Sam. c. 2, 12. 13. & seqq. c. 3. 13. & seqq. Ephes. c. 5. 7.11.1.Timoth.c.5.21. Prouerb.cap.29.24. vide exempla.Esa.c.1,23. Matth. c.14.4. 2.Sam.cap.12.7. cap.24.13.2.Chronic.c.19.2.2.Reg.c.3.13.cap.21.10. Exod.cap.31.21.1.Sam. c.2.23.27.28.cap.12.12,13. Num.c.20.12.Latius dixi in cap. de Seductione in maleficiis.
units.tr: Under the third requirement of gravity, negligence, dissimulation, carelessness and sloth must be avoided, as well as indulgence in admonishing, instructing, correcting and rebuking, restraining, checking and punishing. For not to be angry with wrongdoers is a sign of a mind inclined to similar things, for like delights in like. I add that the negligent man, by his silence, makes himself a partner in the offences committed and renders himself cheap to his inferiors, and he weakens the love and zeal for virtue. Proverbs 13:24; 1 Samuel 2:22, 29; 3:13, 14; 1 Kings 1:5, 6. See 1 Samuel 2:12, 13 and following; 3:13 and following; Ephesians 5:7, 11; 1 Timothy 5:21; Proverbs 29:24. See examples: Isaiah 1:23; Matthew 14:4; 2 Samuel 12:7; 24:13; 2 Chronicles 19:2; 2 Kings 3:13; 21:10; Exodus 31:21; 1 Samuel 2:23, 27, 28; 12:12, 13; Numbers 20:12. I have spoken more fully in the chapter on Seduction in crimes.

units.la: Huc etiam pertinet negligentia & cessatio in officio, de qua grauiter Esa.cap.1.23.24.17. 18 cap.3. Ezech.c.34.4. & nimia indulgentia & licentia. Prouerb. cap.13.24. 1. Reg. cap.1. 5. 6. quâ deteriores viliores fieri patitur. Sed tamen hic naturales quosdam exiguos naevos inferiorum, superiorem æquo animo ferre decet, quod scilicet illi sint urbani, indiscreti, stolidi, incurii, obliuiosi, queruli, auidi, iracundi, impotentes, importuni, vel aliis defectibus laborrent.
units.tr: To this also belongs negligence and neglect of duty, about which Isaiah speaks severely: Isaiah 1:23, 24; 17:18; 3:... Ezekiel 34:4; and excessive indulgence and licence, Proverbs 13:24; 1 Kings 1:5, 6, by which he allows his inferiors to become worse and more base. Yet here a superior should bear with an even mind the small natural blemishes of his inferiors, namely that they are rude, indiscreet, foolish, careless, forgetful, querulous, greedy, irascible, intemperate, importunate, or troubled by other defects.

units.la: Quarto requisito grauitatis contraria est sui ipsius extenuatio, de qua sup.c.2. & non vita, mores & gestus statum & grauitatem non decentes. vbi inprimis vanitatem, temeritatem, futilitatem, leuitatem & falsum fugere conuenit, ne ob dignitatem & authoritatem suam alios contemnat, vel altiorem gradum affectet. Gal. c.6.3. Roman.c.12 3. vel dictis & factis suis hominum, nō Dei gloriam quaerat, 1.Thess.c.2 6. Mat. c.23.5.&feqq. c.6.1. & supra quam par est sapere velit. Rom.c.12.3.cap.11.20. & suis viribus, vel prudentiae cuncta adscribat. Galat. cap.6.13. Iacob. cap.3.14. Esa.cap.2.9.&feqq. atque inferiores opprimat, laedat. vid. Eccles.cap.13.per tot. Ef. cap.3.4. &feqq.
units.tr: The opposite of the fourth requirement of gravity is self-belittling, of which above, chapter 2, and a life, manners and bearing that do not suit one's rank and gravity. Here above all one must avoid vanity, rashness, frivolity, levity and falsehood, lest because of his dignity and authority he despise others or aspire to a higher rank; Galatians 6:3; Romans 12:3, or lest by his words and deeds he seek the glory of men rather than of God, 1 Thessalonians 2:6; Matthew 23:5 and following; 6:1, and wish to be wise beyond what is fitting, Romans 12:3; 11:20, and ascribe everything to his own strength or prudence, Galatians 6:13; James 3:14; Isaiah 2:9 and following, and oppress and harm his inferiors. See Ecclesiasticus 13 throughout; Ephesians 3:4 and following.

units.la: Quinto requisito grauitatis contraria est leuitas in dictis & factis quæ non habet rationem retinendi & defendendi famam, existimationemque decentem statui suo; Galat. cap. 6.4. Tit. c. 2.7. Per omnia temet ipsum exemplum bonorum operum præbens, in doctrina integritatem, gravitatem. Ephes. cap. 5.4. Et obscænitas & stultiloquium, & scurrilitas quæ non conveniunt. Prover. c. 15.23. c.13.3. cap.20.1 5. Iacob. c.1.19. vid. quæ dixi. c. 2. 3. sup.
units.tr: Fifth, the opposite of gravity is levity in words and deeds, which does not take care to keep and defend a reputation and esteem fitting to one's station: Galatians 6:4; Titus 2:7, "In all things showing yourself a pattern of good works, and in your teaching showing integrity and gravity"; Ephesians 5:4, "Let there be no obscenity, nor foolish talk, nor coarse jesting, which are not fitting"; Proverbs 15:23; 13:3; 20:15; James 1:19; see what I said above, chap. 2, sec. 3.

units.la: Huic requisito etiam contrarius vestitus sordidus, inconveniens, avaritia, sordes. Vid. 1. Sam. cap. 2.13.14. & seqq. 1. Sam. cap. 25. 10.11.17. 25. 26.
units.tr: Also contrary to this requirement are squalid and unbecoming clothing, avarice and meanness. See 1 Sam. 2:13, 14 ff.; 1 Sam. 25:10, 11, 17, 25, 26.

units.la: Ne contra iustitiam committat, fugiendum honoratiori & cauendū ne incongruentia ministeria, turpia, vel inhonesta præcipiat obsequia, ne nimia sævitia, austeritate & severitate obsequiis vtatur iniquè, humiliores & inferiores exagitet, irritet, Coloss. c. 3.21.19. Ephes. c. 6.4.9. Coloss. c. 4.1. vel illicitas aut non necessarias operas exigat, vel patrocinium & defensionem contra lædentes præstare cesset, vel uno momento tria, vel quatuor simul præstari sibi exigat, vel nullo modo sibi satisfieri patiatur, vel citius fieri quā iniungi postulet.
units.tr: He must not commit injustice. The superior should avoid honouring the more distinguished, and beware of ordering incongruous, base or dishonourable services. He must not use his servants harshly, with excessive cruelty, austerity and severity, nor harass and provoke the humbler and inferior, Colossians 3:21, 19; Ephesians 6:4, 9; Colossians 4:1. Nor may he demand unlawful or unnecessary labours, cease to provide protection and defence against those who harm them, demand that three or four things be done for him at the same moment, refuse to let himself be satisfied in any way, or demand that things be done more quickly than they are ordered.

units.la: Compensatio obsequiorum neglecta & beneficentiæ omissio, gratiam & beneuolentiam collectam dissipat & dilabi patitur, quam tamen comparatam habere valde, dignitatem & authoritatem confirmat & auger, in qua cessans honoratior opinionem auaritiæ, sordium ve de se excitat & voces in se contumeliosas irritat. Nequaquam igitur tenuiores spe inani clementiæ, vel benignitatis & beneficentiæ læſtandi & simulatione quadam obsequiorum præmio fraudandi.
units.tr: Neglect of repaying services and omission of kindness dissipate the favour and goodwill that has been gathered, and allow it to slip away. Yet to have it secured greatly confirms and increases dignity and authority. A superior who fails in this brings on himself an opinion of avarice or meanness, and provokes insulting words against himself. Therefore the humbler should by no means be defrauded of the hope of empty clemency, or of kindness and beneficence, and of the reward of their service under some pretence of obedience.

units.la: CAP. VII. De officio peculiari in sermone & habitu, splendore & gloria præfulgentium erga inferiores populares.
units.tr: CAP. VII. On the particular duty, in speech and bearing, of those who stand out in splendour and glory toward the lowly common people.

units.la: DE officio communi excellentiorum & præstantium erga inferiores populares & tenuiores, dictum est. Sequitur de peculiari officio, quod excellentiores gloria & splendore præeminentes, erga inferiores præstare debent sermone & gestu.
units.tr: We have spoken of the general duty of the more eminent and distinguished toward the lowly common people and the humbler sort. Next comes the particular duty that those who excel in glory and splendour ought to show toward their inferiors in speech and demeanour.

units.la: Quoad sermonem, hisce superioribus ad amplitudinem, magnificentiam & maiestatem suam tuendam & conseruandam, per alios, nimirum ministros suos præstantes, loqui & sermonem habere conuenit, exemplo Moßs, Exod. c. 4. 16. Nam alloquetur ipse (Aaron) pro te populum: fietq; vt ipse sit tibi vice oris, tu vero sis ei vice Dei, & c. 7. 4. Tum dixit Iehoua Moßi, Vide constitueram te vice Dei Pharaoni. Aaronem vero fratrem tuum, vt esset interpres tuus, s. tu loquitor quæcunque præcepero tibi. Aaron vero frater tuus, alloquitor Pharaonem, vt dimittat filios Israelis è terra sua. Qua in re etiam imaginem aliquam Dei exprimunt, qui nobiscum ore & sermone ministrorum suorum loquitur. Exod. c. 7. 19. c. 19. c. 20. 19. Dixerunt itaque Moßi: Loquere tu nobiscum & audiemus te, sed ne loquatur nobiscum Deus, vt non moriamur.
units.tr: As to speech: to keep up and preserve their dignity, magnificence and majesty, those in high place should speak and give their address through others, namely their own eminent ministers, after the example of Moses. Exod. 4:16. "He shall speak for you to the people, and it shall be that he shall be to you in place of a mouth, and you shall be to him in place of God." 7:1-2. Then the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you as God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh that he let the children of Israel go out of his land." In this they also portray a certain image of God, who speaks with us through the mouth and speech of his ministers. Exod. 7:19; 19:19; 20:19. "So they said to Moses, 'You speak with us and we will hear; but let not God speak with us, lest we die.'"

units.la: Summo eiusmodi Magistratui vociferatio etiam verborumq; intemperantia, non ex ma-jestate est. Senec. lib. 1. Declam. 7. in sin.
units.tr: Shouting and intemperance of words are not becoming to a supreme magistrate of this kind; they do not belong to majesty. Seneca, Declamations 1, Declamation 7, at the end.

units.la: Gestus & habitus, quo summi huius Magistratus splendor gloria, magnificentia & maiestas ostenditur, consistit partim in ministerio inseruientium, partim in victu & amictu, partim quoq; in gubernatione Reipub.
units.tr: The bearing and style by which the splendour, glory, magnificence and majesty of this supreme magistracy are displayed consist partly in the service of attendants, partly in food and dress, and partly also in the government of the commonwealth.

units.la: Ministerium ad nutum huius summi magistratus praestant ministri, famuli, cursores, satellites & πωμφ & αυλαρχω perpetuo comitantes & adstantes eidem. Cuius rei exempla vid. in Salomone 1. Reg. c. 10. f. 6. 8. vbi Jun. cap. 4. Mat; c. 8 3. & seqq. in Saule 1. Sam. c. 16. 17. 18. in Dauide, 2. Sam. c. 8. in sin. vbi Pet. Martyr, & c. 19. 33. & seqq, & pluribus aliis. Ester c. 1. 13 14. Daniel. c. 1. 4. 19. 20, Exod c. 11. 8 c. 8 3. 31. c. 7. 13. 23. Ierem. cap. 22. f. 6. 7, c. 17. 25. c 34. 9. 2. Chronic. c. 9. 25, & Judic. cap. 24. 25. 2. Sam c. 12. 17. 19. 20, 21. cap. 15. 14. 16. & seqq. c. 9. 4 vbi Iun. & 2. Reg. cap. 11. 4 f. 6. & seqq, cap. 14. 14. 17. 1. Reg. cap. 14. 28. 1. Chronic. cap. 18. 17. cap. 29, 1. 2. 3. 2. Chronic cap. 17. 14. vsque ad finem. 1. Sam. c. 22. 6. 7, cap. 26. 15. 16. quales Regis officiarii numerantur, 1. Chron. cap. 27. c. 28. cap. 29. & 2. Reg. c. 11. c 24. Sumebantur tales ministri apud Iudaeos, ut plurimum, ad latera Regis, ex Cheretis & Pelethis, & filiis vel cognatis Regis. 2. Sam. c. 15. 18. 19. cap. 9. 4. vbi Iun, aliis est cap. 8. in sin. vbi & Pet. Martyr notat, 1. Chronic. cap. 18. 17. Genes. c. 41, 45 vbi Iun. Horum ministrorum officium erat neminem ad Regem admittere, sine eiusdem venia & mandato. Ester cap. 4. 11, 12. cap. 5. 1, 2. c. 2. 21. c. 8, 1. 2, & ad nutum atque voluntatem Regis inseruire & ministeria praestare, eiusque corpus & vitam contra pericula & iniurias aliorum defendere, vt patet ex locis supra adductis: & ex prophanis etiam probat Petr. Gregor. de Repub. lib. 22. cap. 11. & patet ex tit. C. de apparitor. praefect. praetor. l 8. Cod. de off. rector. provinc. & tit. C. de officio Magist. off. vbi Iuiac, adde Lipf. Polit. libr. 4. cap. 6. & 7.
units.tr: At the nod of this supreme magistrate, ministers, servants, couriers and guards, and the πωμφ and αυλαρχω [αὐλάρχης, court steward], attend him constantly and stand beside him. Examples of this may be seen in Solomon, 1 Kings 10:6-8, where Junius; Matt. 8:3 and following; in Saul, 1 Sam. 16-18; in David, 2 Sam. 8 at the end, where Peter Martyr; and 19:33 and following, and in many others. Esther 1:13-14; Daniel 1:4, 19-20; Exod. 11:8; 8:3, 31; 7:13, 23; Jer. 22:6-7; 17:25; 34:9; 2 Chron. 9:25; Judges 24-25; 2 Sam. 12, 17, 19, 20, 21; 15:14, 16 and following; 9:4, where Junius; 2 Kings 11:4, 6 and following; 14:14, 17; 1 Kings 14:28; 1 Chron. 18:17; 29:1-3; 2 Chron. 17:14 to the end; 1 Sam. 22:6-7; 26:15-16. Such are the royal officers listed in 1 Chron. 27; 28; 29, and 2 Kings 11; 24. Among the Jews such attendants were usually taken from the king's side, from the Cherethites and Pelethites, and from the sons or kinsmen of the king. 2 Sam. 15:18-19; 9:4, where Junius; others at 8, at the end, where Peter Martyr also notes; 1 Chron. 18:17; Genesis 41:45, where Junius. The duty of these ministers was to admit no one to the king without his leave and command. Esther 4:11-12; 5:1-2; 2:21; 8:1-2. They were to serve at the king's nod and will, to render services, and to defend his body and life against the dangers and injuries of others, as is clear from the passages cited above. Profane authors also prove this: Peter Gregorius, On the Commonwealth, book 22, chapter 11; and it is clear from the title of the Code, On the apparitors of the praetorian prefect, law 8 of the Code, On the duties of the governors of provinces; and the title of the Code, On the office of the Master of Offices, where Cujas; add Lipsius, Politics, book 4, chapters 6 and 7.

units.la: Officiarii principis, aut Chaff. sunt vel circa personam principis, vel circa aerarium illius, vel circa iustitiam administrandam, vel circa militiam.
units.tr: The officials of the prince, or Chassanaeus, are either attached to the prince's person, or to his treasury, or to the administration of justice, or to the military.

units.la: Circa personam principis versantur palatini, praepositi cubiculo principis, l. vnic. C. de comit. schol. lib. 12. tit. C. de praepos. sac. cubic. lib. 12. vel stabulo principis d. l. vnic. vel praefecti ornatui, cultui, vestibus, supellectili domus vel medicamentis: vel praepositi comitatui principis, vt sunt custodes protectores personae illius qui procedit & sequuntur eundem egredientem: quidam etiam nocturni custodes, qui dicuntur agentes in rebus. vid. tit. C. de domestic. & protect. lib. 12. De Salomonis ministris aulicis vid. 1. Reg. c. 4. per tot. & c. 10.
units.tr: About the prince's person are the palatines, the overseers of the prince's bedchamber, Code, On the counts of the schola, book 12; title On the chamberlains, book 12, or of the prince's stables, ibid., or the prefects of his ornaments, dress, clothing, household furniture or medicines; or the overseers of the prince's retinue, such as the guards and protectors of his person, who go before him when he goes out and follow him. There are also night guards, called agents in affairs. See the title of the Code, On the domestics and protectors, book 12. On Solomon's court ministers see 1 Kings 4 throughout and chapter 10.

units.la: De quaestoribus & praefectis aerario, vide titt. C. de palat. sacr. largit. libr. 11. C. de offic. rer. privat. tit. C. de offic. Comit. sacrar. largit. vide Chassan. part. 6. catal. glor. mundi. De officialibus iustitiae administrandae idem Chassan. part. 7. & passim in Codice Iustiniani. De talibus vide 1. Reg. c. 4. 10. & 2. Chron. c. 19. 5. & seqq.
units.tr: On the quaestors and prefects of the treasury, see the titles of the Code, On the sacred largesses of the palace, book 11; On the officials of private property; title On the office of the count of the sacred largesses. See Chassanaeus, part 6, Catalogue of the Glory of the World. On the officials for administering justice the same Chassanaeus, part 7, and throughout the Code of Justinian. On such officials see 1 Kings 4; 10; and 2 Chron. 19:5 and following.

units.la: Vt vero ministris debet princeps, praeclaris egregiis virtute & prosapia excellentibus non sordidis, leuibus, plebeis, imperitis. Illis auctoritatem ritatem suam conseruat.
