Hos vero contemptui aliis exponit. Alexander Magnus non nisi ab Apelle pingi voluit. Augustus Caesar non nisi ab insigni historico vitam & res suas gestas describi voluit. Ludovicus undecimus Rex Galliæ contemptui aliorum se exposuit, quod tonsore pro legato vteretur, & medico pro cancellario, vt refert Comminæus.
units.tr: Yet the prince ought to use as ministers men who are distinguished, outstanding in virtue and lineage, not base, frivolous, plebeian or unskilled. By such he keeps his own authority; those he exposes to the contempt of others. Alexander the Great wished to be painted only by Apelles. Augustus Caesar wished his life and deeds to be described only by a distinguished historian. King Louis XI of France exposed himself to the contempt of others, since he used a barber as ambassador and a physician as chancellor, as Commines reports.

units.la: Huc pertinet etiam equitatus, qui iisdem de caussis huic summo Magistratui attribuitur. Iudic.c.f.10.11.cap.10.4. cap.12.14.2.Sam.c.15.1.2, 3.1. Reg.cap.4.26.2.Chronic.cap.9.25. Ierem.cap. 17.25.cap.12.4. Item, Magistratus intermedios à superiore constitutos & ordinatos huc refero, de quibus supra dixi, nec non consiliarios, sapientia & scientia præstantes, scientes ius, iudicia & tempora. 1.Chron c.12.32. Esther c.1.13. 1. Chron. cap.27.32.33.34. 2.Chron.c.30. cap.31.8. quos imprimis in rebus dubiis & arduis consulere possit. Deut.cap.17.8.9.10.c.19.17.18. Exod.c.18.19.22, 27.1.Sam.cap.9.6.&seqq.2.Sam.c.15.37.38.34.c. 16.16.17. Prov. cap.11.14. vbi non sunt prudentia consilia, corruit populus: Saulus autem est in amplitudine consiliarii. vid. Senec.lib.3.De ira.c. 17.23.lib.2.De benefic.
units.tr: To this belongs also the cavalry, which for the same reasons is assigned to this supreme magistrate. Judges 10:4; 12:14; 2 Sam. 15:1-3; 1 Kings 4:26; 2 Chron. 9:25; Jer. 17:25; 12:4. Likewise I refer here the intermediate magistrates appointed and ordained by the superior, of whom I spoke above, and also counsellors, who excel in wisdom and learning, knowing law, judgements and times, 1 Chron. 12:32; Esther 1:13; 1 Chron. 27:32-34; 2 Chron. 30; 31:8, whom above all the prince can consult in doubtful and difficult matters. Deut. 17:8-10; 19:17-18; Exod. 18:19, 22, 27; 1 Sam. 9:6 and following; 2 Sam. 15:37-38; 34; 16:16-17; Prov. 11:14, where there is no wise counsel, the people falls; but Saul is in the abundance of counsellors. See Seneca, On Anger, book 3, chapters 17 and 23; On Benefits, book 2.

units.la: Hisce addo hostiarios, cubicularios, nomenclatores. Senec. insapient.non cad. iniur. trossulos, cursores, & plures similes. Item cantores, musicos quibus summus Magistratus ad lætitiam & hilaritatem, vel ad laudes Dei celebrandas vitur.2.Sam.c.19.35.&seqq.Nehem.c.7.67.1.Chron. c.25.&c.seq.& gynæceum.Est.c.2.3.8.11.13.14.
units.tr: To these I add doorkeepers, chamberlains, announcers. Seneca, That the Wise Man Is Not Harmed by Injury. Jesters, couriers, and many similar: likewise singers and musicians, by whom the supreme magistrate seeks joy and cheerfulness, or the celebration of God's praises. 2 Sam. 19:35 and following; Neh. 7:67; 1 Chron. 25 and following. And the women's quarters. Esther 2:3, 8, 11, 13-14.

units.la: Victus huius summi Magistratus consistit in splendidis & exquisitissimis epulis & cibo potuque laudatis. Amictus similiter magnificus, sumptuosus & splendidus esse solet. De hoc victu & amictu vid. exempla 1. Reg. c. 4. 22. 23. & seqq. c. 7. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. c. 10. 25. 8. & seqq. 15. 16. 17. 18. & seqq. 2. Chron. c. 9. Matth. c. 6. 29. Ester cap. 1. 4. & seqq. 2. Sam. cap. 19. 33. & seqq. 1. Macchab. cap. 10. 20. 21. 22. 64. 65. 88. 66. c. 11. 58. cap. 14. 43. 44. Petr. Gregor. lib. 6. c. 5. lib. 8. & lib. 22. c. 5. de Repub. & lib. 9. Syntag. c. 19. Pet. Martyr. Judic. c. 9. Deut. c. 28. 56. Menoch. lib. 4. praf. 161. Dd. in l. vestis, §. 2. de auro & arg. legat. & in l. vestis, 127. de verb. signif. De vestitu regio dixi etiam supra c. 8. & Isidor. lib. 19. cap. 22. & seqq. Bayfius de re vestiaria, c. 9. Tiraquell. de nobilit. cap. 20. num. 143. & seqq. & De legib. connub. leg. 3. & tit. (C. de vest. holosericis & aurat. lib. 11. tit. C. nulli licer. in fren. equi. & c. lib. 11. de paragaanda veste serica, purpurea, item frenis equestribus, sellis & baltheis, smaragdis, hyacinthis, margaritis, ornatis, vid. l. 1. l. 2. vbi Cuiac. C. de vestibus holosericis & aurat. & d. tit. C. nulli licer. in fren. equestr. sell. balt. aptar. smaragd. lib. 11.
units.tr: The food of this supreme magistrate consists in splendid and most exquisite feasts, and in food and drink praised for their quality. His clothing is likewise usually magnificent, costly and splendid. On this food and clothing see the examples in 1 Kings 4:22-23 and following; 7:1-3 and following; 10:25; 8 and following; 15-18 and following; 2 Chron. 9; Matt. 6:29; Esther 1:4 and following; 2 Sam. 19:33 and following; 1 Macc. 10:20-22, 64-65, 88, 66; 11:58; 14:43-44. Peter Gregorius, book 6, chapter 5; book 8 and book 22, chapter 5, On the Commonwealth; and book 9, Syntagma, chapter 19. Peter Martyr. Judges 9. Deut. 28:56. Menochius, book 4, presumption 161. The jurists on the law "Vestis," §2, On gold and silver legacies; and on the law "Vestis" 127, On the meaning of words. On royal dress I have also spoken above in chapter 8; and Isidore, book 19, chapters 22 and following. Baïf, On clothing, chapter 9. Tiraqueau, On nobility, chapter 20, number 143 and following; and On the laws of marriage, law 3. Code, On silk and gold-embroidered garments, book 11. Code, that no one may be permitted to wear silk, purple cloth, or horse-bridles, saddles and belts set with emeralds, hyacinths, pearls and ornaments; see laws 1 and 2, where Cujas, Code, On silk and gold-embroidered garments, and the said title, Code, that no one may be permitted to adorn bridles, saddles, belts with emeralds, book 11.

units.la: Gubernatio Reipub. ad utilitatem subditorum referenda est, ita ut hanc, propria vita chariorem habeat, arg. eius quod pie de se scribit Apostolus 1. Thessal. c. 2. 8. 9. 10. 11. & pro subditorum commodis promouendis & incommodis auertendis laborer. exemplo Samuelis, 1. Sam. c. 12. 25. & aliorum. 1. Macchab. c. 14. 4. 5. 14. 35. 36. Cic. lib. 1. Offic. Exod. c. 32. 11. 12. cap. 33. 6. 7. 8. 9. & Num. c. 14. 19. & illis tanquam animus corpori imperet, ut vere pater patriae dici & haberi possit, fit, Genef. c. 41. 42. 43. & seqq. c. 45. 8. 9. Psalm. 105. 21. 22. & amorem & beneuolentiam ciuium sibi conciliare possit, Senec. lib. 1. De clement. 1. lib. cap. 19. c. 3. Illius demum, inquit, magnitudo stabilis est, fundataq; quem omnes tam supra se, quam prose, sciunt, cuius curam excubare profalute singulorum, atque vniuersorum quotidie experimur; quo procedente, non tanquam malum ac noxium animal e cubili prosiliret, diffugiunt. sed tanquam ad clarum & beneficum sidus adnolant. & idem ad Polyb. latissime & grauissime describit, & Apostol. ad Rom. c. 13. 2. Dei enim minister est tuo bono, &c.
units.tr: The government of a commonwealth ought to be directed to the good of its subjects, so that the ruler holds this dearer than his own life. This is shown by the example of the Apostle, who writes of himself piously (1 Thess. 2:8, 9, 10, 11), and by his labouring to advance the welfare of his subjects and avert their harm. The same is seen in Samuel (1 Sam. 12:25) and others (1 Macc. 14:4, 5, 14, 35, 36; Cicero, De officiis 1; Exod. 32:11, 12; Exod. 33:6, 7, 8, 9; Num. 14:19). He should rule his people as the mind rules the body, so that he may truly be called and held the father of his country. This happens through the example of Joseph (Gen. 41:42, 43 and following; Gen. 45:8, 9; Ps. 105:21, 22), and so he can win the love and goodwill of the citizens. Seneca, De clementia 1, 19, 3, says: "Finally, his greatness is stable and well founded, since everyone knows him to be above them and for them; we daily experience that his care watches over the safety of each and of all. As he advances, men do not flee from him as from a harmful beast that leaps out of its den, but they flock to him as to a clear and beneficent star." Seneca also describes the same thing very fully and weightily in his letter to Polybius. The Apostle likewise says, Rom. 13:2: "For he is God's minister for your good," etc.

units.la: Porro in hac gubernatione, se ipsum praestare debet pium, sobrium, strenuum, prudentem, magnanimum, fortem, iustum, sapientem, veritatis amantem, Deut. c. 1. 13. 15. Praeteritorum memorem, praesentia prudenter ordinantem & in futurum cautum, Petr. Gregor. lib. 24. c. 2. & lib. 10. c. 4. De Repub. per Deuteron. c. 32. Proverb. c. 14. c. 16. Nam perfecta prudentia consistit in sapientia ex praeteritis, intelligentia de praesentibus, & prouidentia de futuris. arg. Deut. d. c. 32. Iob. c. 12. quam sapientiam imprimis ad Reipub. gubernationem necessariam & vtilem iudicauit sapientissimus Rex Salomon, 1. Reg. cap. 3. 9. & seqq. Proverb. c. 11. 14. ex qua subditorum timor & metus, 1. Reg. c. 3. 28. & Magistratus apud alios summa authoritas & fama, 1. Reg. c. 10. per tot. qui nihil aut suscipiat aut agat, nisi lente & circumspecte & cum consilio.
units.tr: Furthermore, in this government the ruler himself ought to show himself pious, sober, vigorous, prudent, magnanimous, brave, just, wise, and a lover of truth (Deut. 1:13, 15); mindful of the past, prudently ordering the present, and careful for the future (Petrus Gregorius, Syntagma 24, 2 and 10, 4; De republica on Deuteronomy 32; Prov. 14, 16). For perfect prudence consists of wisdom concerning the past, understanding of the present, and foresight of the future (cf. Deut. 32 above; Job 12). The wisest king Solomon judged this wisdom especially necessary and useful for the government of the commonwealth (1 Kings 3:9 and following; Prov. 11, 14). From it come the fear and awe of the subjects (1 Kings 3:28), and among others the highest authority and reputation of the magistrate (1 Kings 10, throughout). Such a ruler undertakes and does nothing except slowly, cautiously, and with counsel.

units.la: Strenuus inprimis apparet ex censura vitae & morum. Psalm. 101. & 119. 2. Reg. cap. 10. cap. 23. & quando prouinciam suam malis hominibus purgat. l.13.congruit. l. 6. de offic. praefid. Proverb. cap. 20.26.30. Iof. cap. 7. 19. 20. 25. 2. Chronic. cap. 14. 3. 5. 6. Senec. libr. 1. de ira. cap. 5. Legum praesidem ciuitatisque rectorem decet quandiu potest, verbis & his mollibus ingenia curare, vt facienda suadeat, cupiditatemque honesti & æqui animis concilier, faciatque vitiorum odium, pretium virtutis. Transeat vero deinde ad orationem tristiorem, quæ moneat adhuc & exprobret; nouissime ad pœnas, & has adhuc leues & revocabiles decurrat; vltima supplicia sceleribus vltimis ponat, vt nemo pereat, nisi quem perire etiam pereuntis interfit.Contraria huic virtuti in excessu tyrannis, & in defectu licentia & indulgentia nimia & ignauia. Vnde illud vulgatum: Malum est cum imperare sub quo nemini quidpiam concessum est; sed longe pejus viuere sub eo, sub quo maxime liceat quidvis.
units.tr: Vigour appears first of all in the censure of life and morals (Ps. 101 and 119:2; 2 Kings 10; 2 Kings 23), and when he purges his province of wicked men (Dig. 1.13 congruit; Dig. 6, de officio praesidis; Prov. 20:26, 30; Josh. 7:19, 20, 25; 2 Chron. 14:3, 5, 6; Seneca, De ira 1, 5). It becomes the governor of laws and ruler of the state, as long as he can, to cure minds with gentle words, to persuade them to do what should be done, to win over their hearts to a desire for what is honourable and just, and to make men hate vices and value virtue. Then he should move on to a sterner speech, which admonishes still and reproves; last of all he should resort to punishments, and even these should be light and reversible at first, reserving the extreme penalties for the extreme crimes, so that no one perishes except one whom it is also in the interest of the perishing to perish. The vices contrary to this virtue are tyranny in excess, and in defect, licence, excessive indulgence, and sloth. Hence the common saying: "It is bad when the ruler is one under whom nothing is granted to anyone; but it is far worse to live under one under whom anything whatever is permitted."

units.la: Hic tempestiue annectitur quæstio, An & quatenus Magistratus conuersationem fidelium cum infidelibus in sua Dioecesi ferre possit? Quod ipsi Pet. Martyr. Iudic. cap. 1. 36. concedit sub sequentibus conditionibus. Primo, quando infideles illi fideles non adigunt ad cultus impios. Deinde, quando infidelibus Magistratus non concedit prauos ritus & ceremonias impias in sua regione; vti fecit Salomo suis vxoribus & concubinis infidelibus. Tertio, quando eos infideles curat assidue & diligenter erudiri in sua dioecesi. Quarto, quando diu instructos & doctos ad sanos & puros cultus adigit tandem. Sub hisce conditionib. olim licuit populo Israelitico litico cum gentib. Idololatris coüersari. Deut. c. 7. ver. 25. C. de inud. & calib. dixi late in politic. Peregrinis merces importantibus vel exportantibus nulla vis inferenda.
units.tr: Here a question is aptly added: Whether and how far the magistrate can tolerate the association of believers with unbelievers in his dominion? Peter Martyr himself grants this (Judges 1:36) under the following conditions. First, when those unbelievers do not compel the believers to impious worship. Second, when the magistrate does not allow the unbelievers to have their depraved rites and impious ceremonies in his region, as Solomon did for his unbelieving wives and concubines. Third, when he takes care that those unbelievers are constantly and diligently instructed in his dominion. Fourth, when, after they have been instructed and taught for a long time, he finally compels them to pure and sound worship. Under these conditions the Israelite people was once permitted to associate with the idolatrous Gentiles (Deut. 7:25; C. de Iudaeis et caelicolis; I have discussed this at length in my Politica). No violence is to be done to foreigners who bring in or carry out merchandise.

units.la: Intermedius Magistratus alium superiorem recognoscens multo minus habet ius homines ad impias religiones adigendi, neque illas infidelibus etiam ex iussu sui superioris concedendi, quibus gratificari non debet in iis, quae pugnant cum verbo Dei, exemplo Ezechiae 2. Reg. c. 18. sed potius ex officio se opponere debent in negotiis impiis, non iis quae cum iactura bonorum fiunt. 1. Pet. c 2. vide quae differunt Dicaeolog. c. de abusu potest publicae. & Vrsin. lib. 2. Dispos. 42. & seqq. & Pet. Mart. d. loc.
units.tr: A middle magistrate, who acknowledges another superior, has much less right to compel men to impious religions, or to grant those religions to unbelievers even by order of his superior. He must not gratify them in matters that conflict with the Word of God, following the example of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18). Rather, he ought to oppose impious undertakings by virtue of his office, though not those which are done at the cost of goods (1 Pet. 2). See what is discussed in the Dicaeologica, the chapter on the abuse of public power, and Ursinus, Dispositiones 2, 42 and following, and Peter Martyr in the passage cited.

units.la: Iudaeos quoq; in consortio & conuersatione Christianorum tolerandos putat. Mart. d. loc. cum Aug. De ciuitate Dei, lib. 4. c. 18. & super Ps. 58. & primo quidem ob propheriam Rom. c. 11. 25. 26. Luc. c. 21. 24. Deinde, quod signa & instituta a Deo retineant, quae Deus in illis posuit, vt in Caino, ne interficiantur. Tertio, quod horum conuersatio Christianis vtilis admonitio. Ro. c. 11. 16. 17. & seqq. Quarto, quia Biblia seruant & legunt, & inuiti testes fidei nostrae sunt. Sed videndum & curandum a Magistratu vt conuiciis & blasphemiis in Deum abstineant, & habitu & notis quibusdam a Christianis discernantur.
units.tr: He also thinks that Jews should be tolerated in the company and association of Christians. See Martyr in the same place, with Augustine, De civitate Dei 4, 18, and on Psalm 58. This is first because of the prophecy (Rom. 11:25, 26; Luke 21:24). Second, because they keep the signs and institutions that God placed among them, as with Cain, so that they are not killed. Third, because their association is a useful admonition to Christians (Rom. 11:16, 17 and following). Fourth, because they preserve and read the Bibles, and are unwilling witnesses of our faith. But the magistrate must see to it and take care that they abstain from insults and blasphemies against God, and that they are distinguished from Christians by their dress and certain marks.

units.la: Pevs dicitur, quando ex prima tabula praestat & facit quae respiciunt Deum eiusque cultum; vt scilicet habeat ecclesiam constitutam ad praescriptum verbi Dei, cuius auctoritatem contra omnes perturbationes & contemptores tueri & vindicare debet, exemplo Mosis,Dauidis.Psalm.132.1.2.3.4. Iolaphat.lofiç, & aliorum piorum magistratuum. Pietate autem Magistratus venerabilis redditur, quæ subditorum obedientiam conciliat & insidias tollit.Nam subditi minus iniustum aliquid sperant ab eo principe pati,quem religiosum Deorumq; verentem existimant;& minus ei insidiantur,vt tutores & adiutores habenti etiam Deos, vt ait Arist.Politic.c.9.
units.tr: A ruler is called pious when from the first table he performs those duties which concern God and his worship: namely, that he maintains a church constituted according to the prescription of God's Word, whose authority he ought to defend and vindicate against all disturbances and despisers, after the example of Moses and David (Ps. 132:1, 2, 3, 4), Jehoshaphat, and other pious magistrates. Moreover, the magistrate is made venerable by piety, which wins the obedience of the subjects and removes plots. For subjects hope for less injustice to suffer from a prince whom they consider religious and God-fearing, and they plot less against him, since he has the gods also as guardians and helpers, as Aristotle says in the Politics 9.

units.la: I v s t v s dicitur, quando iudicium & iustitiam obseruat & exercet. 1.Reg.c.10.9. Psalm 82. Prou.c.16.12.&seqq. Deut.cap.17. 2.Chron. cap.19, quibus regnum & magistratum stabilit & confirmat.Prou.c.29,4.14.c.20.28.c.25.f. 2.Chron.c.13. quando bonos præmio, malos pœna afficit, 1. Sam.cap.7.15.16.17.Rom.c.13.Deut.c.17. f. 6.7.& &seqq 1.Pet c.2.13.14. oppressos & miseros protegit, & neminem prægrauat. Nehem. c.5.15. Ezech.cap.45.18. Mich.c.3.3. Iof.cap. 8.26.1.Sam.cap. 15 33 34.
units.tr: A ruler is called just when he observes and exercises judgement and justice (1 Kings 10:9; Ps. 82; Prov. 16:12 and following; Deut. 17; 2 Chron. 19), by which he establishes and confirms his kingdom and magistracy (Prov. 29:4, 14; 20:28; 25; 2 Chron. 13). He rewards the good and punishes the wicked (1 Sam. 7, 15, 16, 17; Rom. 13; Deut. 17; 1 Pet. 2:13, 14); he protects the oppressed and wretched, and burdens no one (Neh. 5:15; Ezek. 45:18; Mic. 3:3; Josh. 8:26; 1 Sam. 15:33, 34).

units.la: S o B R I v S est, quando modum & tempus tenet in potu & cibo.Ecclesiastis cap.10.13. Heiubi regio cuius rex puer est,&cuius principes mane comedunt.14. O te beatam regionem,cuius Rex natus est clarissimis, & cuius principes suo tempore comedunt ad robur,non autem ad compotationem. Proverb.c. 31.4.&Absit Regibus ô Lemoel, absit regibus, bibere vinum;&dominatoribus desiderium potus inebriantis.f. Vt non cum biberit, obliuiscatur statuti, & mutet ius vllorum afflictorum.
units.tr: A ruler is called sober when he keeps measure and time in drink and food (Eccl. 10:16, 17). "Woe to you, land whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning. O happy land whose king is of noble birth, and whose princes eat at their proper time, for strength and not for drunkenness." Prov. 31:4, 5: "It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, nor for rulers to desire strong drink; lest when they drink they forget what is decreed and alter the right of any of the afflicted."

units.la: Hisce virtutibus Princeps stabilire dicitur magistratum suum, Prouer.c.19.4.14.cap.20.28. 6.25. 6.12.5.2. Chron. c. 13. per tot. & inexpugnabile munimentum sibi facere, ut aut Senec. lib. 1. Declement. cap. 19. His exi-stimationem & auctoritatem suam conseruare dicitur, quae tanti aestimatur, ut fulcrum Regni & imperii & tutela salutis dicatur. vid. Lip. lib 4. Polit. c. 9, c. 12. cum alleg. ibid. & qua dixi lib. 1. Dicaeolog. c. 32. & seqq. & cap. De abusu potestat. public. Contra, malos reddit principes, nimia licentia, deinde rerum copia, improbi amici, satellites detestandi, aulici stulti vel detestabiles, ignorantia rerum publicarum.
units.tr: By these virtues a prince is said to establish his magistracy (Prov. 19:4, 14; 20:28; 6:25; 6:12; 5:2; 2 Chron. 13, throughout), and to make for himself an impregnable fortress, as Seneca says, De clementia 1, 19. By these he is said to preserve his reputation and authority, which is so highly valued that it is called the prop of the kingdom and empire and the safeguard of its welfare. See Lipsius, Politica 4, 9 and 12, with the citations there, and what I have said in the Dicaeologica 1, 32 and following, and in the chapter on the abuse of public power. On the other hand, unlimited licence, then abundance of wealth, dishonest friends, detestable attendants, foolish or detestable courtiers, and ignorance of public affairs make princes bad.

units.la: Auctoritas autem, hoc est, impressa subditis & externis opinio reuerens de se, eiusmodi Magistratui summe necessaria & quasi anima regni dicitur. Eiusmodi auctoritas constat ex admiratione & metu coniuncto.
units.tr: Authority, that is, a reverent opinion of oneself impressed upon subjects and outsiders, is said to be most necessary to such a magistrate, and almost the soul of the kingdom. Authority of this kind consists of admiration joined with fear.

units.la: Admiratio comparatur ex forma imperii, potentia & moribus imperantis Magistratus, ut ait Lipsius lib. 4. Politic. c. 9. quae regni fulcra a rebellione & contemptu Magistratum vindicant. vid. Lipf. Polit. lib. 4. c. 12.
units.tr: Admiration is produced by the form of government, by the power and the character of the ruling magistrate, as Lipsius says in Politics book 4, chapter 9, which are the supports of a kingdom protecting it from rebellion and contempt of the magistrates. See Lipsius, Politics book 4, chapter 12.

units.la: Forma imperii sit seuera, constans & adstricta.
units.tr: The form of government should be strict, steady and tight.

units.la: Seuera, quia perpes & assidua lenitas contemptum inducit & principatus pestem, vt ait Lipsius, & maximam illecebram peccandi impunitatis spem. Seueritas vero sanat subditos, quae tamen sit tempestiua, & Reipub. seu subditorum morbo adcommodata.
units.tr: Strict, because unbroken and constant leniency breeds contempt, which is the plague of rule, as Lipsius says, and the greatest enticement to sin is the hope of impunity. Severity, however, heals subjects, provided it is timely and suited to the disease of the commonwealth or of the subjects.

units.la: Constans ideo, quia inconstantia Magistratus vilescit & crebra mutatio subditis perniciosa.
units.tr: Steady, because the authority of a magistrate who is inconsistent becomes cheap, and frequent change is harmful to subjects.

units.la: Adstricta ideo, vt praecipua vis & honos non
units.tr: Tight, so that the chief power and honour are not

units.la: solum à gubernante Magistratu sit, sed etiam apud eundem. Siquidem ea imperandi ratio, vt non aliter constet, quam si vni reddatur & à nullo alio pendeat, vt ex Tacito Lipsius refert. Ergo honores nimios, vel longos non dabit Magistratus summus.
units.tr: only from the governing magistrate but also held in his presence. For that method of ruling is such that it cannot stand unless it is rendered to one person and depends on no other, as Lipsius reports from Tacitus. Therefore the supreme magistrate will not give excessive or long-lasting honours.

units.la: Potentia est ad sua conseruanda & aliena obtinenda idonearum rerum facultas: quae Lipsio auctore, nititur & fulcitur opibus, armis, consiliis, foederibus, & fortuna.
units.tr: Power is the ability to have suitable resources for preserving one's own and acquiring what belongs to others. According to Lipsius, it rests and is propped up on wealth, arms, counsels, alliances and fortune.

units.la: Mores imperantis decentes sunt, quae conseruant & conciliant auctoritatem & grauitate homini. de quibus supra dixi c. praeced.
units.tr: The character of the ruler should be becoming; such conduct preserves and wins authority and gravity for a man. Of these things I spoke above in the preceding chapter.

units.la: Metus censura morum iusta & obseruatione, inquisitioneq; vigilanti vitae singulorum paratur, quib. subditi intelligant peccare esse perniciosum, bene facere vero fructuosum. Censurae arma sunt multa, ignominia & poena. Inquisitionis ministri sunt delatores & corycaei, quorum opera omnia ipsi superiori innotescere possunt. Vid. Eccl. c. 10. 17. & c. 8. 2. Sam. c. 18. 13. Genes. c. 44. s. 15.
units.tr: Fear is produced by a just censure of morals and by vigilant inquiry into the lives of individuals, by which subjects understand that sinning is harmful and doing well is profitable. The weapons of censure are many: disgrace and punishment. The agents of inquiry are informers and sycophants, through whose work all things can become known to the superior himself. See Eccles. 10:17 and 8:2; 2 Sam. 18:13; Gen. 44:15.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De conuersatione parium inter se inuicem.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. On the conduct of equals towards one another.

units.la: HVcusq; de imparium conuersatione inter se inuicem; sequitur de parium conuersatione nunc inter se inuicem.
units.tr: Thus far we have spoken of the conduct of unequals towards one another; now follows the conduct of equals towards one another.

units.la: Parium ergo coüersatio inter se inuicem est, qua pares erga pares vtuntur.
units.tr: The conduct of equals towards one another is therefore that in which equals behave towards equals.

units.la: Pares vocantur, qui virtute, potentia, diuitiis, officio, professione, vita, aetateve sunt pares. hoc est, inter quos nulla caussarum illatū, quas cap. 12. retuli, imparitatem & inæqualitatem statuit.
units.tr: Those are called equals who are alike in virtue, power, wealth, office, profession, way of life or age; that is, between whom none of the causes of inequality that I set out in chapter 12 establishes any difference or inequality.

units.la: Conuersatio inter pares, sermone, vel gestu, talis esse debet, qualem sibi par à pari tribui vellet. Paritas in ætate, conditione, moribus, vita, vel professione eadem non turbante, vel impediente, magnum amorem inter pares conciliare solet. Similis enim simili gaudet & eius cō-suetudine delectatur. Eccles. c. 13. 1, 18. 19. 20. 21. c. 9. 19. 20.
units.tr: Conduct between equals, in speech or gesture, ought to be such as each would wish to be shown to himself by his equal. Equality in age, condition, character, way of life or profession, where nothing disturbs or hinders it, usually wins great affection between equals, for like delights in like and takes pleasure in its company. Eccles. 13. 1, 18. 19. 20. 21; 9. 19. 20.

units.la: Conuenit igitur hîc, dona, officiaq; in paŕe collata, externâ aliquâ verborum, aut gestuum declaratione, agnoscere. Philip. c. 2. 3. Nihil gerite per contentionem, aut inanem gloriam, sed ex modestia, alius se alium præstantiorem existimet: ita vt in dando, nō vero accipiendo honore alios aliis præire conueniat. Ephef. c. 5. 21. subiecti alii aliis cum timore Dei. Rom. c. 12. 10. Honore alii aliis præeuntes. 1. Pet. c. 2. 17. Omnes honorate, fraternitatem diligite.
units.tr: It is fitting, then, here to acknowledge by some outward declaration in words or gestures the gifts and services conferred by an equal. Phil. 2. 3: Do nothing through strife or vainglory, but in humility let each count the other better than himself; so that in giving, and not in receiving, honour, it is fitting that some go before others. Eph. 5. 21: Submit yourselves one to another in the fear of God. Rom. 12. 10: In honour preferring one another. 1 Pet. 2. 17: Honour all men; love the brotherhood.

units.la: Sed tamen valde indecorum est, quando inter se plebei, aut mediocris conditionis homines, iisdem moribus & ceremoniis quibus magnates vti inter se solent, vtuntur: aut sanè iis, quibus neq; ab inferioribus aliis honorari solet, atq; ita muli mutuum scabunt.
units.tr: Yet it is most unbecoming when commoners, or men of middling condition, use among themselves the same manners and ceremonies that great men are wont to use among themselves, or indeed those by which they are not usually honoured by their inferiors; and so, like mules, they mutually scratch one another.

units.la: Neque etiam pares, magnates & magnæ virtutis & excellentiæ viri, huiusmodi ceremonias crebro inter se adhibere debent, neque adhibitis iis delectari, aut ab aliis præter modum exigere.
units.tr: Nor should equals who are magnates, and men of great virtue and excellence, frequently employ such ceremonies among themselves, nor take delight in them when employed, nor demand them from others beyond measure.

units.la: Valde peccatur hîc, quando par pari se sermone vel gestu præponit & præfert & maiorem excellentiam quaerit. Matth.c. 20. 20. Tunc venit ad eum mater filiorum Zebedaei cum filiis suis, adorans & petens aliquid ab eo, 21. Ipse vero dixit ei, quid vis? ait ei, Dic ut sedeant isti duo filii mei, unus ad dexteram tuam & alter ad sinistram in regno tuo, 22. Respondens autem Iesus, dixit: Nescitis quid petatis. Poteritis bibere poculum, quod ego bibiturus sum, & baptismate quo ego baptizor baptizari? & verf. 24. Et cum haec audissent alii deciem, indignati sunt de duobus fratribus. Parit ergo haec praerogativae affectatio, odium & simultatem inter pares & discordiam, 1. Corinth.c.4.6. Ut in nobis discatis, non supra id quod scriptum est, sapere, ut ne alius pro alio infleminiaduersus alium, 7. Quis enim te discernit ab aliis? Galat.c.5.26. Nesimus inanis gloriae cupidi, alii aliis invidentes, neque elati, & superbe de nobis sentiamus & apud nosmetipsos sapientes simus. Romanorum c.12.
units.tr: Here one sins grievously when one equal, by word or gesture, puts himself before and above another, and seeks greater excellence. Matt. 20. 20: Then came to him the mother of the sons of Zebedee with her sons, worshipping and asking something of him. 21: And he said to her, What wilt thou? She saith unto him, Grant that these my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left, in thy kingdom. 22: But Jesus answered and said, Ye know not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with? And verse 24: And when the ten heard it, they were moved with indignation against the two brethren. Such an eagerness for precedence therefore produces hatred, rivalry and discord between equals. 1 Cor. 4. 6: That in us ye might learn not to think of men above that which is written, that no one be puffed up for one against another. 7: For who maketh thee to differ from another? Gal. 5. 26: Let us not be desirous of vainglory, provoking one another, envying one another. Let us not be proud or think highly of ourselves, nor be wise in our own conceits. Rom. 12.

units.la: INDICIA & coniecturae hominis sermone vel gestu praerogativam affectantis sunt, quando in omnibus factis, actionibus & exercitiis & negotiis semper potiorem sui rationem haberi cupit: non curans sive molestia alius, sive non afficiatur. Et quando, aequalium nos pudet; neq; quid ab aequalibus dicatur attendimus; in locis publicis pudore alium afficimus trudendo, de loco movendo, pileum abiiciendo, debitove honoris titulo fraudando. Quando quis auersatur, fastidit & improbat omnia, quae ab aliis fiunt, ut nihil quod satis placeat, ab alio quoquam fieri possit, & quidquid tandem illi dicatur, torvo vultu, vel imperiose respondet, vel agit; vel charitatis officia quae benevolentiae causa praestantur, stantur,rigidè, acerbè, aut inhumaniter exigit. Contrà, quam fecit Apostol. ad Philemonem.
units.tr: Signs and conjectures that a man is seeking precedence by word or gesture are these: when in all his deeds, actions, exercises and business he always wants his own reckoning to be given the first place, not caring whether it troubles another or not; and when he is ashamed of his equals and pays no attention to what is said by his equals; when in public places he shames another by pushing him, moving him from his place, throwing off his cap, or cheating him of the title of honour owed to him. When someone is averse to, disdainful of and disapproves of everything done by others, so that nothing done by anyone else can please him well enough; and whatever is said to him he answers or acts upon with a grim face and in an imperious manner; or he demands the services of charity, which are rendered out of goodwill, stiffly, harshly or inhumanly. The opposite of what the Apostle did in his letter to Philemon.

units.la: In conuictu igitur quotidiano parium conuersantium, adsit adfabilitas, absit seueritas. Nam ille superborum tumor vix seruis tolerabilis;hic autem affabilis mos gratus est vniuersis.Ifocrat.ad Demon.parænef. Affabilitatis est non rixari,non odiosum esse, fugere contentiones, non inuehi acerbè etiam in iratos sine caussa, sed feruente adhuc ira,illis cedere; obiurgare autem, placata, vid. Rom. cap. 12. 17. 18. 19. & seqq.
units.tr: In the daily life of equals living together, therefore, let there be affability, and let severity be absent. For that swelling of pride is scarcely tolerable even to slaves, whereas a courteous manner is pleasing to everyone. Isocrates, To Demonicus, Parenesis. Affability means not quarrelling, not being disagreeable, avoiding contentions, not railing bitterly even against the angry without cause, but yielding to them while their anger is still hot; and reproving them once they are calmed. See Rom. 12. 17, 18, 19 and following.

units.la: Adsit etiam beneuolentia & studium gratificandi cuique, Galat. c. 5. 13. Sed ex charitate ser-uite alii aliis. 14. Nam tota lex vno verbo completur, silo videlicet, Diliges proximum tuum vt teipsum. 15. Quod si alii alios mordetis & devoratis, videte ne vi-cissim alii ab aliis consumamini. Curandum itaque est & laborandum, vt si fieri potest, & quantum in nobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace viuamus. & eodem animo inter nos mutuo affecti, non elate de nobis sentientes, sed humilibus obsecundates cum proximo pari versemur. vt monet Apostolus ad Rom. cap. 12.
units.tr: Let there also be goodwill and eagerness to oblige everyone. Gal. 5. 13: But by love serve one another. 14: For all the law is fulfilled in one word, namely this: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. 15: But if you bite and devour one another, take heed lest you be consumed one by another. Care and effort must therefore be taken that, if it can be done, and as far as it lies in us, we live in peace with all men; and that, being mutually affected with the same mind, not thinking highly of ourselves but yielding to the humble, we associate with our neighbour who is our equal, as the Apostle advises in Rom. chapter 12.

units.la: Ad salutem & incolumitatem inter æquales & pares tuendam, opus amicis, aut inimicis acribus. Illi monendo, hi maledicendo à vitiis reuocant. Huc etiam refertur spes honoris & metus pœnæ, quæ sunt virtutis elementa. Illa calcar ad virtutes; hic à vitiis dehortatio & frenum reuocans seu retrahens.
units.tr: To preserve safety and wholeness among equals and peers, there is need of friends, or of sharp enemies: the former call us back from vices by admonishing, the latter by reproaching. To this also belongs the hope of honour and the fear of punishment, which are the elements of virtue. The former is a spur to the virtues; the latter, by dissuasion from vices, is a bridle recalling or restraining.

units.la: Inter amicos pares, quilibet anteuertere debet petitionem amici. Inciuile enim est & iram mouet, quando amicus non sentit quibus rebus amicus magno opere indigeat & quid magnope- rè experat.
units.tr: Among equal friends, each should anticipate the request of his friend. For it is discourteous and provokes anger when a friend does not perceive what things his friend greatly needs and what he earnestly desires.

units.la: Decet etiam de amicis rebusq; eorum honorificè loqui: eorumq; infortunio lugere & commoueri, & rebus secundis lætari, & suum illis tribuere.
units.tr: It is also fitting to speak honourably of friends and their affairs; to grieve and be moved at their misfortune, to rejoice at their prosperity, and to give them their due.

units.la: Honor igitur & fraternitas quæ inter pares est, consistit in quatuor: Primo, in φιλοτιμία, tam in rebus secundis, quam aduersis. In illis, vt cùm proximo nostro lætemur: in hisce verò vt cum eodem lugente contristemur. Nam gaudere in alterius infortunio, aut bono animo esse in rebus eius aduersis, vel patienter mala illius audire, est indicium oligoriæ & inimicitiæ.
units.tr: The honour and brotherhood that exist between equals therefore consist in four things. First, in a love of honour [φιλοτιμία], both in prosperity and in adversity: in the former, that we rejoice with our neighbour; in the latter, that we grieve with him when he grieves. For to rejoice in another's misfortune, or to be ill-disposed towards his adversities, or to hear his troubles with patience, is a sign of hatred and enmity.

units.la: Deinde, vt suus etiam honor pari tribuatur & conseruetur, videndum, ne eundem parui faciamus, vel contemnamus apud æmulos, riuales, honoratiores & venerandos, & apud eos qui nos honorant & venerantur.
units.tr: Next, that his own honour be also given to an equal and preserved, we must take care not to make light of or despise it before his rivals, competitors, more honourable men and those held in reverence, and before those who honour and reverence us.

units.la: Tertiò, vt non sint subsannatores, aut contemptores vllius hominis, inprimis sui ordinis & conditionis.
units.tr: Thirdly, let there be no mockers or scorners of any man, especially of one's own rank and condition.

units.la: Quartò observent illa Catonis:
units.tr: Fourthly, let them observe the sayings of Cato:

units.la: Vincere cum possis, interdum cede sodali:
units.tr: When you can conquer, sometimes yield to your companion:

units.la: Obsequio quoniam dulces retinentur amici.
units.tr: For by compliance sweet friends are kept.

units.la: Quæ superare potes, interdum vince ferendo:
units.tr: What you can overcome, sometimes conquer by bearing:

units.la: Maxima enim morum semper patientia virtus.
units.tr: For patience is always the greatest virtue of character.

units.la: Quod pudeat socios, prudens celare memento:
units.tr: What shames your companions, remember to conceal prudently:

units.la: Ne plures culpent id quod tibi displicet uni.
units.tr: Lest many blame what displeases you alone.

units.la: Insipiens esto cum tempus postulat aut res:
units.tr: Be foolish when the time or the matter demands it:

units.la: Stultitiam simulare loco prudentia summa est.
units.tr: To feign foolishness in its place is the highest prudence.

units.la: Noli tu quadam referenti credere semper:
units.tr: Do not always believe everything a man tells you:

units.la: Exigua est tributenda fides qui multa loquuntur. Ergo sit frons aperta, lingua parca, mens clausa. & illud Martialis. Si vitare velis acerba quaedam Et tristes animi caucre morsus; Nulli te facias nimis sodalem, Gaudebis minus, minus dolebis. & illud Ouidii: Crede mihi bene qui latuit, bene vixit, & intra Fortunam debet quisq; manere suam.
units.tr: Little trust is to be given to those who talk much. Therefore let the brow be open, the tongue sparing, the mind closed. And that saying of Martial: If you wish to avoid certain bitter things and to guard against the sad bites of the mind, make yourself no one's over-close companion; you will rejoice less, and grieve less. And that of Ovid: Believe me, he who has kept hidden has lived well, and each person ought to remain within his own fortune.

units.la: Adde monitionem Virgilii: Et bene apud memores veteris stat gratia facti.
units.tr: Add the admonition of Virgil: And a favour stands well with those who remember a past deed.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De modi peratoris sermone & gestu in conuiuii praeparatione.
units.tr: On the speech and bearing of the host in preparing a banquet.

units.la: HActenus de prima Ethicae propriae specie, conuersatione scilicet quae statui & conditioni cuiusque conuenit; seu quae statum & conditionem cuiusq; propriam respicit. Sequitur de altera, quae actionem conuiuialem concernit: seu, quae est conuiuialis.
units.tr: So far I have dealt with the first kind of ethics proper, namely the conduct that suits each person's station and condition, or that concerns each person's own status and condition. Next comes the second kind, which concerns the action of the banquet, or what is convivial.

units.la: Actio seu conuersatio conuiuialis est, quae in conuiuio vsurpatur.
units.tr: The action or conduct of a banquet is what is practised at a banquet.

units.la: Conuiuium est ciuilis, honesta, suauis & iucunda hominum conuersatio, eiusdemque cibi & potus sermonisq; communicatio, mutui amoris & amicitiae contrahendae, vel confirmandae, vel beneuolentiae, charitatis, concordiaeve testificandae, aut conseruandae causa instituta. Nam quos natura voluit simul viuere, eosdem vna frui mensa docuit, ut simul & ederent & biberent. Vnde conuiuium dicitur a conuiuendo. Luc. c. 5. 29. Et fecit ei Leui epulum magnum domus, eratq; turba multa publicanorum & aliorum qui cum ipsis accumbebant. Iohan. c.12. 2.3. Fecerunt igitur ei cœnam illic, & Martha ministrabat, Lazarus verò erat unus ex iis qui simul accumbebant. vid. exempla, 2. Sam. c. 9. 15. 16. 17. 2. Reg. cap. 25. 31. 32. 33. 2. Sam. c. 19. 34. & seqq. Psam. 104. 15. Matth. c. 26. Conuiuium eiusmodi, alias accubitus epularis, sympofium, syssitia, συνάξεις, χορωνία, συναγωγή, Agapa, epulum vocatur. vide Aret. problem. 171.
units.tr: A banquet is a civil, honourable, pleasant and agreeable gathering of people, a sharing of food, drink and conversation, established for the sake of forming, confirming or displaying mutual love and friendship, goodwill, charity or harmony, or of keeping them. For nature willed that those who were to live together should also share one table, so that they might eat and drink together. Hence the word convivium is derived from convivere, to live together. Luke 5:29: And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a great company of publicans and of others that sat down with them. John 12:2-3: There they made him a supper; and Martha served; but Lazarus was one of them that sat at the table with him. See examples in 2 Sam. 9, 15, 16, 17; 2 Kings 25, 31, 32, 33; 2 Sam. 19, 34 and following; Ps. 104:15; Matt. 26. Such a gathering, otherwise called a dinner party, a symposium, syssitia, gatherings [συνάξεις], feasts [χορωνία], assemblies [συναγωγή], agape, or epulum, is called a banquet. See Aretius, problem 171.

units.la: Cœuiuii duplex est distributio. Vna partitio integri in membra. Altera, generis in species diuisio.
units.tr: The division of a banquet is twofold: one is the partition of a whole into its parts, the other the division of a genus into its species.

units.la: Membra conuiuii videntur esse duo, Persona & communicatio commensalis.
units.tr: The parts of a banquet appear to be two: the persons, and the communication at table.

units.la: Personæ conuiuii sunt, quarum ministerio peragitur communicatio sermone & gestu. Hæ rursus sunt principales, vel administrandæ.
units.tr: The persons of a banquet are those through whose ministry the communication by speech and gesture is carried on. These in turn are either principal or subordinate.

units.la: Principales sunt, sine quibus conuiuium cõstitere & celebrari non potest. Eiusmodi sunt conuiuator & conuiuæ.
units.tr: The principal persons are those without whom a banquet cannot be set up or celebrated. Such are the host and the guests.

units.la: Conuiuator, est procurator & administrator & gubernator conuiuii. Vocatur alias magister paterfamilias, dispensator, præpositus domus. Esser c.1. Daniel. c.1. οἰκονόμος, ἀρχιτρίκλινος, Ioh. c.2. συμπόσιαρχος, ὁ τῆς συμποσίας ἡγεμών, ἐπιστάτης, οἰκοδεσπότης, οἰκονόμος, ἐπιστάτης, διάκονος modiperator, arbiter, ductor, magister, rex conuiuii, Eccles. cap. 32. 1.2. qui apud veteres forte eligebatur à conuiuis, Eccles. cap. 32. 1. Erasm. in Chiliad. adag. 47, cent. 10.
units.tr: The host is the manager, administrator and governor of the banquet. He is also called the master of the house, the steward, the head of the household, the chief of the table, the director, the arbiter, the leader, the master or king of the banquet. Esther 1; Dan. 1; steward [οἰκονόμος], head of the table [ἀρχιτρίκλινος]; John 2, master of the feast [συμπόσιαρχος], the leader of the banquet [ὁ τῆς συμποσίας ἡγεμών], overseer [ἐπιστάτης], householder [οἰκοδεσπότης], steward [οἰκονόμος], overseer [ἐπιστάτης], servant [διάκονος]. Among the ancients he was perhaps chosen by the guests. Eccles. 32:1-2. Erasmus, Adages, 47, cent. 10.

units.la: Officium conuiuatoris consistit in procuratione & gubernatione conuiuii.
units.tr: The office of the host consists in the management and governing of the banquet.

units.la: Procuratio conuiuii, consistit in inuitatione, apparatu, exceptione conuiuarū & locatione.
units.tr: The management of a banquet consists in inviting the guests, preparing the meal, receiving the guests and seating them.

units.la: Inuitatio conuiuarum, est humana & benevola ad conuiuium eorundem vocatio, facta ἀμέσως per nosmetipsos, vel ἐμμέσως, per literas nuntiosve. Inuitationis ἀμέσως factae exemplum extat Esther c. 5. 3. 4. 5. 8. vbi Esther inuitauit Regem & Haman. & 2. Sam. c. 13. 24. vbi Absalon patrem & fratres inuitauit. ἐμμέσως factae exemplum extat Luc. c. 14. 17. 23. Matth. c. 22. 1. 2. & seqq. Num. c. 25. 2. Tob. c. 2. 2. 3.
units.tr: The invitation of guests is the courteous and kindly summons of them to the banquet, made either directly, by oneself [ἀμέσως], or indirectly, through letters or messengers [ἐμμέσως]. An example of a direct invitation is found in Esther 5:3-5, 8, where Esther invited the king and Haman, and in 2 Sam. 13:24, where Absalom invited his father and brothers. An example of an indirect invitation is found in Luke 14:17, 23; Matt. 22:1-2 and following; Num. 25:2; Tobit 2:2-3.

units.la: Inuitationem decoram & ciuilem reddunt, delectus & forma inuitandorum, Luc. c. 14. 12, 13. 14. 15. Delectus habetur, quoad qualitates inuitatorum & numerum & tempus, qui nimirum, quot & quando vocentur.
units.tr: The invitation is made proper and civil by the choice and the form of those invited. Luke 14:12-15. The choice concerns the qualities of the guests, their number and the time, that is, whom one invites, how many, and when.

units.la: Delectus vocandorum est in eo, quod habetur ratio dignitatis & morum eorumdem, ne ad conuiuium vocati indigni, infamiam conuiuatori irrogent. Arguitur enim similitudo morum & vitiorum studium ex conuiuis. Et beneficium in tales collocatum est χάρις ἀχάρις, ἀντιχάρις. Inuitentur itaque probi, honesti, temperantes & virtute praediti homines. Eccles. c. 9. 15. 16. & seqq. Tob. c. 2. 1. 2. 3. Deinde tales, quibus debeamus plurimum & qui plurimum a nobis diliguntur. Nullum enim officium referendā gratiā magis necessarium. Cicer. lib. 1. Offic. Tertio, vt quisquis maxime opis indiget, ita ei potissimum opitulemur, etiam inuitando ad conuiuium. Luc. c. 14. 13. Sed cum facis epulum, voca medicos, mancos, claudos, caecos. 14. Et beatus eris, quia non possunt gratiam retribuere tibi: retribuetur enim tibi in resurrectione iustorum. vid. Cicer. libr. 1. Off. Quarto decorum est, vt etiam societatis & coniunctionis habeatur ratio: Et vt quisq; est coniunctissimus, in eum quoq; benignitatis plurimum conferatur. Cicer.lib.1.Offic.Plutarch.libr.1. Sympos.problem.5. Luca cap.14.11. vbi amici & vicini poltponuntur egenis. Quinto conuenit, vt eras illos simus liberales, qui nobis amicitia & morum similitudine sunt adfines. Sexto & ratio temporis habenda in inuitatione. Nam, vt Cicer. d.lib.1.ait, Sunt quaedam officia quae alii magis, quam alii debentur, vt, vicinum citius adiuueris, quam fratrem, aut familiam, in frugibus percipiendis. Cicer. d. loc. Proverb. cap.27. Melior est vicinus iuxta, quam frater procul. Luc. cap.15. vbi vicini amicis comparantur. Traquell. de poen.temp.cauf 23. Septimo, vt illos inuitemus qui natura & moribus, maxime inter se congruunt. Plutarch.7.problem. Vocentur ergo pares conuiuae, non admodum dispares, sicut Christus non exclusit ludam à mensa sua. Matt. cap.26. Vid. Ioh. Guil. Stuckium libr 2. cap. 1. communi. antiquit. qua in re etiam ratio habenda caussae conuiuii, ad quam conuiuae sint apti atque idonei, ne omnis generis conuiuae temere ad quamuis caussam tractandam vocentur. Ad consultationem prudetes, ad dicendum & persuadendum diserti, vocandi. Stuckius d. loc. lib.2. cap.2. Plutarch.lib.5. Symp. problem.5. Ad conuiuium virorum mulieres olim non admittebantur, apud Graecos: secus apud Romanos, Iudaeos & nos. Valer. Max.lib.2.cap.1. Cal. Rhodigin. libr. 28.cap.5. Est.cap.5. Ruth.cap.2. Iob. c.1. Daniel.c.5. Ioh.cap.2. Apud Romanos pueri ad fulcra lectorum sedentes cibum capiebant. Sueton. in Claudio. dio. Stuck. d. cap. 1. libr. 2. conuiuial. antiquit. Oc-tauo, videat conuiuator, ne vltra numerum decentem inuiter. Est enim communis senten-tia, numerum conuiuarum incipere à tribus & desinere in nouem. vt pauciores non sint tribus, neque plures nouem. Gell. lib. 13. cap. 11. Cel. Rho-digin. lib. 12. c. 9. & lib. 28. cap. 8. Macrob. lib. 3. cap. 17. Saturnaliorum. Sed D. Stuckius, lib. 2. cap. 2. conui-uium antiqui. recte existimat, numerum conuiua-rum ad conuiuii, temporis, loci, alimentorum, facultatum, aliarumque circumstantiarum ra-tionem esse adcommodandum. Ideoq; hodie numerus conuiuarum est arbitrarius vt dicit A-retius problem. 171. Sic enim Esterae conuiuium fuit duorum conuiuarum. Est. c. 5. 4 8. Abraha-mi, trium. Genes. cap. 18. Samuelis, triginta. 1. Sam. cap. 9. 22. Et Christi hominum multorum, Marc. cap. 6. 44. 40. Dauidis vero conuiuium, plurimorum. 2. Sam. cap. 6. 18. 19. & seqq. 1. Chronic. c. 16. 2. 3. & Solomonis, 1. Reg. c. 8. Assueri, Esther cap. 1. Videndum tamen conuiuatori, ne πολυ-ϑρωπα conuiuia sint, & ἀμίκτα, ἀφιλα & ἀασϑυήρια, communionis, amicitiae & collocutionis mu-tuae expertia reddantur. Vid. Stuckium d. loc. cap. 2. Plutarch. lib. 4. Symposiac. problem. 3. & Calium lib. 28. c. 8.
units.tr: The choice of those to be invited lies in this: regard must be had to their dignity and character, so that guests who are unworthy do not bring disgrace on the host. For likeness of character and the pursuit of vices are inferred from the company one keeps at table. A favour bestowed on such people becomes a thankless favour [χάρις ἀχάρις] and an ungrateful return [ἀντιχάρις]. So good, upright, temperate and virtuous men should be invited. Eccles. 9:15-16 and following; Tobit 2:1-3. Next, those to whom we owe the most, and who most value us. For no duty is more necessary for repaying a favour. Cicero, On Duties, book 1. Third, whoever most needs help, to him we should give help above all, even by inviting him to a banquet. Luke 14:13: But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind. 14: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just. See Cicero, On Duties, book 1. Fourth, it is fitting that regard be had also to fellowship and kinship, and that the one who is most closely joined to us should receive the greatest kindness. Cicero, On Duties, book 1; Plutarch, Symposiacs, book 1, problem 5; Luke 14:11, where friends and neighbours are put after the poor. Fifth, it is proper that we be generous especially to those who are related to us by friendship and likeness of character. Sixth, the time must also be considered in inviting. For, as Cicero says in the same book, some duties are owed to some people more than to others; you will sooner help a neighbour than a brother or household in gathering the harvest. Cicero, loc. cit.; Prov. 27:10: Better is a neighbour near than a brother far off. Luke 15, where neighbours are compared with friends. Traquell., On Penalties and Time, cause 23. Seventh, we should invite those who agree most with one another in nature and manners. Plutarch, book 7, problem. Let the guests be equals, not too unequal, just as Christ did not exclude Judas from his table. Matt. 26. See John Wilhelm Stuckius, book 2, ch. 1, Common Antiquities. In this matter too, regard must be had to the purpose of the banquet, for which the guests should be suited and fit, so that guests of every kind are not carelessly invited to any business whatever. Prudent men should be invited for deliberation, and eloquent men for speaking and persuading. Stuckius, loc. cit., book 2, ch. 2; Plutarch, book 5, Symposiacs, problem 5. Among the Greeks women were formerly not admitted to men's banquets; among the Romans, Jews and ourselves they were. Val. Max. book 2, ch. 1; Caelius Rhodiginus, book 28, ch. 5; Esther 5; Ruth 2; Job 1; Dan. 5; John 2. Among the Romans boys sitting at the couches took food. Suetonius, Claudius. Stuckius, loc. cit., ch. 1, book 2, Antiquities of Banquets. Eighth, the host should see to it that he does not invite more than a fitting number. For it is the common opinion that the number of guests should begin at three and end at nine, so that there are not fewer than three nor more than nine. Gellius, book 13, ch. 11; Caelius Rhodiginus, book 12, ch. 9, and book 28, ch. 8; Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 3, ch. 17. But Stuckius, book 2, ch. 2, on ancient banquets, rightly judges that the number of guests should be adapted to the reckoning of the banquet's time, place, food, resources and other circumstances. Hence today the number of guests is arbitrary, as Aretius says, problem 171. Thus Esther's banquet had two guests, Esther 5:4, 8; Abraham's had three, Gen. 18; Samuel's had thirty, 1 Sam. 9:22; Christ's had many men, Mark 6:44, 40; David's banquet had very many, 2 Sam. 6:18-19 and following; 1 Chron. 16:2-3; and Solomon's, 1 Kings 8; Ahasuerus's, Esther 1. Yet the host must take care that banquets are not overcrowded, unsociable, unfriendly and disorderly, deprived of mutual fellowship, friendship and conversation. See Stuckius, loc. cit., ch. 2; Plutarch, book 4, Symposiacs, problem 3; and Caelius, book 28, ch. 8.

units.la: Forma inuitandi talis esse debet, quae appa-reat beneuola, certa, secundum cuiusque loci consuetudinem. Beneuola est, quae amica, feria & humana. Valer. Max. lib. 2. c. 3. Non languida, remissa, simulata, vel nimis importuna, vio-lenta, odiosa, molesta. Certa est, quae tempus, locum, personam, inuitante & inuitatas complectitur.quæ varia à variis obseruari solet. Formula inuitandi quædam extat Esther c.5. 4. Dixit Esther, Si apud Regem bonum videtur, veniat rex cum Hamane hodie ad conuiuium, quod parauì ei. & verf.8. Si inueni gratiam in oculis regis, & si apud Regem bonum videtur concedere postulatum meum, & facere petitionem meam, veniat Rex & Haman ad conuiuium, quod parauero eis. Genef.c.18.3. Et dixit Abraham, Domini mei si nunc inueni gratiam in oculis tuis, ne quaso praetereas a seruo tuo. & seqq. & cap.19.2. dixit Loth: Ecce nunc domini mei, diuertite quaso, in domum serui vestri, atque pernoctate & lauate pedes, &c. & v.3. Fecit eis conuiuium. &c. Genef.c.24.31. Et dixit Laban, Ingredere benedicte a Iehona, quare maneres foris, nam ego expedui domum & locus est pro camelis tuis. Prou.c.9.5. Venite vesciminicibo meo, & bibite de vino meo, quod miscui. Matth.c.22.4. Dicite vocatis: Ecce prandium meum paraui, tauri mei, & altilia mactata sunt, & omnia parata: Adeste ad nuptias. Iohan.cap.21.12. Dicit eis Iesus, venite prandete. Hodie apud nos variæ formulæ sunt vsitatæ, quæ sunt arbitrariæ.
units.tr: The form of the invitation must be such that it appears kindly, certain, and according to the custom of each place. It is kindly if it is friendly, cordial and humane; not languid, half-hearted, feigned, or excessively importunate, violent, hateful or troublesome. Val. Max. book 2, ch. 3. It is certain if it specifies the time, place, person of the inviter and of those invited, which is observed in various ways by various people. A formula of invitation is found in Esther 5:4: Esther said, If it seem good unto the king, let the king and Haman come today to the banquet that I have prepared. and v. 8: If I have found favour in the king's sight, and if it please the king to grant my petition and perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them. Gen. 18:3: And he said, My lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant, and following; Gen. 19:2: Lot said, Behold now, my lords, turn in, I pray you, into your servant's house, and tarry all night, and wash your feet, etc. and v. 3: He made them a feast, etc. Gen. 24:31: And Laban said, Come in, thou blessed of the LORD; wherefore standest thou without? for I have prepared the house, and room for the camels. Prov. 9:5: Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled. Matt. 22:4: Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage. John 21:12: Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine. Today among us various formulas are in use, and these are arbitrary.

units.la: Apparatus conuiuatoris consistit, 1. in procurandis conuiuio necessariis; vti in alimentis & supellectili necessaria, 2. in delectu temporis & loci conuiuii.
units.tr: The host's preparation consists of (1) procuring what the feast requires, such as food and the necessary furnishings, and (2) choosing the time and place of the feast.

units.la: Alimenta eiusmodi temperari & comparari debent secundum conuiuarum ætatem, sexum, nationem, conditionem, valetudinem, palatum, religionem. Deinde, secundum tempus, æstate, hyemem; vel matutinum, vel vespertinum tempus, Stuck. lib.2.conuiu.antiqu.c.12.
units.tr: Food of this kind should be seasoned and prepared according to the guests' age, sex, nation, rank, health, taste and religion. Further, it should suit the season, summer or winter, and the time of day, whether morning or evening. Stuck. lib.2.conuiu.antiqu.c.12.

units.la: Alimenta eiusmodi sunt esculenta, vel poculenta.de quibus vide 2.Reg.c.6.22. Iudic. cap.19. Psalm.104.Luc.c.12.29.c.14.Matth.c.6.31. Prouerb.c.1.5.c.31.&l.43 l.44. l.134. §.2. de verb.sign. tit.de alim. & cibar.legat.l.3.de pen.legat.
units.tr: Such food is either solid or liquid. On these see 2 Kings 6:22; Judges 19; Psalm 104; Luke 12:29; Luke 14; Matthew 6:31; Proverbs 1:5; Proverbs 31; and the laws at D. 43, D. 44 and D. 134 §2, de verb. sign.; tit. de alim. et cibar. legat.; l.3 de pen. legat.

units.la: Esculenta sunt edulia ex nascentibus terrae, aut ex animalibus, aut animalium partibus, vel fructibus; eaque vel humectantia, vel refrigerantia, vel exsiccantia, item nutrientia, alterantia, calefacientia de quibus Stuckius d. lib.2. cap.8. Obsonia sunt omnia ea, quae praeter panem vnâ cum pane edimus. Ioh.c.21.5. Hinc, obsonatores, eduliorum coemptores; quae à coquis assantur, elixantur, vel torrentur 2.Sam.c.6.19. 1.Chron. c.16.2.3. De delectu ciborum in veteri Testamento, vid.Levit.c.3.c.7.c.11.c.17.c.19. qui postea sublatus. (Coloss.c.2.16.17. 1.Timoth.cap.4.3. Apud veteres panis & sal symbola foederis & amicitiae erant, Stuckius lib.1.c.30. & panis φιλαδέλφιας symbolum ab Apostolo dicitur, 1.Corinth.cap.10. Sal verò in omnibus sacrificiis adhibebatur, Levit.c.2.Num.c.18.Vid.1.Esd.c.4.
units.tr: Solid food consists of dishes made from the produce of the earth, or from animals, parts of animals, or fruits. Some of these are moistening, some cooling, some drying, and likewise some are nourishing, some alter the body, some warm it. On these see Stuckius, loc. cit., lib.2, c.8. Relishes are all those things we eat with bread, apart from the bread itself. John 21:5. Hence the word for a buyer of delicacies (obsonatores), and for the dishes that cooks roast, boil or fry. 2 Sam. 6:19; 1 Chron. 16:2-3. On the distinction of foods in the Old Testament see Lev. 3, 7, 11, 17, 19, which was later abolished. (Col. 2:16-17; 1 Tim. 4:3.) Among the ancients bread and salt were signs of covenant and friendship. Stuckius lib.1 c.30. The Apostle calls bread a sign of brotherly love [φιλαδελφίας]. 1 Cor. 10. Salt was used in all sacrifices. Lev. 2; Num. 18. See 1 Esdras 4.

units.la: Supellex ad conuiuium necessaria, sunt vasa escaria, vel potoria. Escaria, quibus in cibi & alimenti; Potoria, quibus in potus sumptione vtimur. de quibus late Stuckius lib.2.c.15.& seqq.
units.tr: The furniture necessary for a feast consists of eating vessels and drinking vessels. Eating vessels are those we use for taking food; drinking vessels are those we use for drinking. On these see Stuckius at length, lib.2, c.15 and following.

units.la: Tempus conuiuii eligi debet conuiuatori & conuiuis adcommodatum. Prouerb.c.31.15. Et surgens dum adhuc nox est, dat escam domui suae, & pensum puellis suis. Luc.c.12.42. Dixit autem Dominus, quisnam est fidus dispensator ac prudens, quem dominus praeficiet famulitio suo, vt in tempore det demensum? Ecclesiastic.c.10.17. Beata terra cutus rex nobilis est; & cuius principes vescantur in tem-pore suo ad reficiendum, non ad luxuriam. Esa.c.5.11, & Psal.145.15. Oculi omnium ad te spectant, quibus tu das escam suam, tempore suo.
units.tr: The time of the feast should be chosen to suit both host and guests. Prov. 31:15: "She rises while it is still night, and gives food to her household and portions to her maidens." Luke 12:42: "And the Lord said, Who then is the faithful and wise steward, whom the lord will set over his household, to give them their portion of food in due season?" Ecclesiasticus 10:17: "Blessed is the land whose king is noble, and whose princes eat at the proper time, to refresh themselves and not for drunkenness." Isa. 5:11; Psalm 145:15: "The eyes of all wait upon you, and you give them their food in due season."

units.la: A tempore vero dicebantur convivia alia diurna, alia nocturna, alia matutina, alia meridiana, alia vespertina. Matutina, vti ientaculum, 2. Reg.c.1. Act.cap.10.2. Reg.c.3.35. Iohan.cap.21 Meridiana sunt, merenda & prandium. Stuck. d. lib. 1.c.8. & seqq. Nocturna sunt comessationes, ἀπὸ τοῦ κῶμος, quod est per vicos vagari. Erant & menstrua convivia. I.cum societas, pro socio. & 1. Reg. cap. 20.5.15. Prov.c.7. Psal.81.3.
units.tr: Feasts were named by their time: some were by day, some by night, some in the morning, some at midday, some in the evening. Morning meals, such as breakfast, 2 Kings 1; Acts 10:2; 2 Kings 3:35; John 21. Midday meals are the snack and the dinner. Stuckius, loc. cit., lib.1 c.8 and following. Night feasts are revels, from κῶμος [kōmos], which means wandering through the streets. There were also monthly feasts. 1 Sam. 20:5, 15; Prov. 7; Ps. 81:3.

units.la: Locus convivii dicitur εὐπορητήριον, ad convivandum aptum; Locus ille sit amoenus, salubris, clarus, purus, mundus, temperatus sive ille sit publicus, sive privatus in aedibus convivatoris, Luc.cap.14.c.12. Marc.c.14.1. Sam.c.9.21. & seqq.
units.tr: The place of the feast is called εὐπορητήριον [euporētērion], a place suited to entertaining. That place should be pleasant, healthy, bright, clean, pure and temperate, whether it is public or private in the host's house. Luke 14:12; Mark 14:1; 1 Sam. 9:21 and following.

units.la: Olim cespes pro mensa fuit: postea vero mensa est reperta & sensim crescente gula, accessit pretium ex assere, fraxino, robore. Quadratas & rotundas confecere olim & hodie solent.
units.tr: Once the turf served as the table; later a table was devised, and as gluttony gradually grew, value was added through boards of plane wood, ash and oak. The ancients made tables square and round, and so do people today.

units.la: Exceptio convivarum est, qua convivator convivas invitatos venientes, decore excipit. cuius requisita sunt; primum, ut curet quo domus convivis advenientibus pateat, vel certe quam celerrime aperiatur, ne illi diu exspectare cogantur, arg. Luc.12.36. Et similes estote vos tis, qui exspectant quando dominus suus egressurus sit a nuptiis, ut quum venerit & pulsaverit, statim aperiant ei, 37.45.46. Apocalypsis c.3. 8.20. Quod si nocturnum tempus est, constituet lumina, ne quis impinimpingat, & deinde ipse conuiuator hospitem inuitatum in domum ipse introducat, vel per suos curet introduci, exemplo Iosephi, Genes. c. 43. 24. Introduxit igitur vir ille homines illos in domum Iosephi, &c. 1. Sam. c. 9. 22. Adsumpsit tamen Samuel Saulem & puerum eius, quos introduxit in canaculum, & verf. 14. Veteres Ethnici superstitiosi quo sitlux esset ingressus & egressus hospitum, lares & penates suos & aliorum numinum simulachra ponebant in aditu & porticu domus, Alex. ab Alex. lib. 5. Genial. dier. c. 24. vid. Esa. c. 57. 12. ubi ludai imbebantur verba legis Dei scribere, Deut. cap. 6. 9. cap. 11. 20.
units.tr: Receiving the guests is the part where the host welcomes the invited guests as they arrive with proper courtesy. Its requirements are: first, that he arranges for the house to be open to the arriving guests, or at least opened as quickly as possible, so they are not made to wait long. By inference from Luke 12:36-37, 45-46: "Be like men who are waiting for their lord to return from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once." Revelation 3:20. If it is night, he shall set out lights so no one stumbles, and then the host himself shall lead the invited guest into the house, or see that he is led in by his people, after the example of Joseph. Gen. 43:24: "The man brought those men into Joseph's house," etc. 1 Sam. 9:22: "Yet Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the chamber," and verse 14. The superstitious ancient heathens, so that there would be light when guests came in and went out, set their household gods and the images of other deities at the entrance and porch of the house. Alexander ab Alexandro, lib. 5, Genial. dier., c.24. See Isa. 57:12, where the Jews were commanded to write the words of God's law, Deut. 6:9; 11:20.

units.la: Secundum requisitum est in salutatione civili & humana, qua conuiuator vna cum vxore, liberis & tota familia, placido vultu & sereno, verbis humanis, manus datione, complexu, vel osculo, prout patriae vel loci istius mos fert, conuiuam inuitatum excipit.
units.tr: The second requirement is civil and friendly greeting, by which the host, together with his wife, children and whole household, receives the invited guest with a calm and cheerful countenance, with courteous words, and with a handshake, an embrace or a kiss, as the custom of the country or place requires.

units.la: Tertium est, in manuum ante epulas lotione; cuius facultatem conuiuis conuiuator facere debet, quae & hodie & olim vsitata. Matt. c. 15. 2. Quare discipuli tui transgrediuntur traditionem seniorum: non enim lauant manus suas, cum edunt panem (Marc. c. 7. 2. 3. 4. Luc. c. 11.)
units.tr: The third is washing the hands before the meal. The host ought to offer his guests the means of doing this, as is customary both today and in former times. Matt. 15:2: "Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread." (Mark 7:2-4; Luke 11.)

units.la: Quartum est, quod honoris causa conuiua pallio exuitur, quod deponitur a conuiuatore & arma, antequam ad mensam accumbitur. vid. Stuck. d. libr. 2. cap. 34. conuiu. quamquis in aulis, magnae dignitatis & authoritatis hospitis, vel conuiuarum honoratissimorum, conuiuae palliis suis amicti accumbant, ac non deponant, nisi iusserit superior. Iudaei cum palliis suis accumbebant, Iohan.c.13.4. Surgit à cœna & deponit pallium, acceptoq; linteo præcinxit se. 12. Postquam ergo lauisset pedes eorum & pallium suum recepisset, rursum discubuit.
units.tr: The fourth is that, as a mark of honour, the guest is relieved of his cloak, which the host takes, and of his weapons, before they recline at table. See Stuckius, loc. cit., lib.2, c.34 on feasts. Yet at the courts of princes, when the guest or the most honoured of the guests is of great dignity and authority, the guests recline with their cloaks on and do not take them off unless the superior bids them. The Jews reclined in their cloaks. John 13:4: "He rose from supper and laid aside his garments, and taking a towel girded himself." 13:12: "So when he had washed their feet and taken his garments, he sat down again."

units.la: Locatio conuiuarum est, qua conuiuato locum conuiuæ tribuit, pro dignitate & merito eiusdem. Genef.c.43.33. Sederunt autem coram eo primogenitus secundum primogenitasua, & qui minor erat secundum minorem ætatem suam. 1.Sam.c.9.22. Adsumpsit tamen Samuel Saulem & puerum eius: quos introduxit in cænaculum, deducq; ius locum in summo inuitatorum, &c. Luc.c.14.9. Et veniens qui te vocauit, dicat tibi, Da huic locum, &c. 10. Sed cum vocatus fueris, vade discubitum in vltimum locum, vt cum venerit qui te vocauit, dicat tibi, Amice, ascende superius, &c. Marc.c.6.39. Tunc imperauit eis vt facerent discumbere omnes per conuiuia super viridi gramine. Iacob.c.2.3. Et respexeritis ad eum qui vestem gestat splendidam & dixeritis ei, Tu sede hic pulchre. Pauperi vero dicatis, Tu sta illic, aut sede hic subter scabellum meum. quem locum de conuentibus Ecclesiasticis accipiunt alii, Matth.c.23.6. Prou.c.25.6,7. vid. Alex. ab Alex.lib.5.c.21. Srne. lib.3. Deira.
units.tr: The seating of guests is when the host assigns each guest a place at table according to his rank and merit. Gen. 43:33: "They sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his age." 1 Sam. 9:22: "Yet Samuel took Saul and his servant, whom he brought into the chamber and gave them a place at the head of the guests," etc. Luke 14:9: "And he who invited you will come and say to you, Give this man a place." 14:10: "But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you, Friend, go up higher," etc. Mark 6:39: "Then he commanded them to make all sit down by companies upon the green grass." James 2:3: "If you look upon the one who wears fine clothes and say, Sit here in a good place, but say to the poor man, Stand there, or sit here under my footstool." Some take this place as referring to ecclesiastical assemblies: Matt. 23:6; Prov. 25:6-7. See Alexander ab Alexandro lib.5 c.21; Srnec. lib.3 Deira.

units.la: Collocabit autem conuiuas pro ratione sexus, ætatis, dignitatis, conditionis, aliarumque circumstantiarum, ne collocator in odium offensionemq; conuiuarum incidat, vel inter conuiuas æmulationem, odia & simultates excitet. Primum itaque in locatione obseruabit patrium morem & consuetudinem. Deinde vrperegrinis, senioribus, atque magistratibus magis honorifica quam ciuibus, iunioribus & priuatis loca adsignet. Quod si multi sint pares dignitate conuiuæ, honorabit & collocabit vnum ex illis loco primo, alium medio, alium iuxta se collocabit, aut alium familiarem suum, aut magistrum aliquem. Reliquis deinde, vel munusculis, vel assiduis, humanis & honorificis salutationibus, compellationibus, colloquiis satisfacere conabitur, vt vult Plutarchus. Potest etiam patri, si adest, aut auo, socero; aut alicui cognatorum, ei denique, cui apud conuiuatorem peculiaris quædam honoris prærogatiua est, honestissimum locum tribuere, vt neuter ex illis qui honore & dignitate æquales sunt, locum illum accipiat. Sed tamen in collocatione, non semper ad gloriam, sed ad iucunditatem respiciendum, quomodo ipsis inter se conueniat, vt ex diuersorum mixtione opus pulchrum existat, & cuique quod deest, adcommodetur; vti moroso, mansuetum; loquaci seni, adolescentem audiendi cupidum; iracundo, tacitum; diuiti, pauperem; glorioso, sublannatorem opponamus.
units.tr: The host shall seat the guests according to sex, age, rank, condition and other circumstances, so that he does not incur the hatred and offence of the guests, or stir up rivalry, hatred and quarrels among them. First, then, in the seating he shall observe the custom and usage of his country. Next, he shall assign more honourable places to foreigners, elders and magistrates than to citizens, younger men and private persons. If several guests are equal in rank, he shall honour one of them and seat him in the first place, another in the middle, and another beside himself, or another of his familiars, or some teacher. He shall then try to satisfy the rest with small gifts, or with constant, courteous and honourable greetings, forms of address and conversation, as Plutarch advises. He may also give the most honourable place to the father, if present, or to the grandfather, father-in-law, or to some relative, or to whoever has a special prerogative of honour with the host, so that none of those who are equal in honour and dignity takes that place. Yet in seating, one should look not so much to glory as to pleasure, and how the guests suit one another, so that from the mixing of different people a fine whole arises, and each gets what he lacks: we set a gentle man against a grumpy one, a young man eager to listen against a talkative old man, a quiet man against an angry one, a poor man against a rich one, and a scoffer against a boaster.

units.la: Conuiuator deniq; ipse conuiuis adsidere debet. Eccles. c. 31. & locum postremum sibi postremo deligere; qui ad circumspiciendum, atq; ad surgendum est adcommodatus.
units.tr: Finally, the host himself ought to sit down with his guests. Eccles. c. 31. He should choose for himself the last place, the one that suits him for looking around and for getting up.

units.la: Sequitur de gubernatione conuiuii, quod secundum est conuiuatoris officium, quo totum actum conuiuii decenter regit & moderatur, secundum scopum instituti conuiuii, quod constat requisitis tribus. Primum est, vt in toto conuiuio conuiuator se humanum, hospitum amatem, affabilem, comitatis plenum, cibi & vitæ
units.tr: Next comes the government of the banquet, which is the host's second duty: he directs and moderates the whole course of the feast becomingly, in keeping with the purpose of the banquet. This rests on three requirements. The first is that throughout the banquet the host shows himself humane, fond of his guests, affable and full of courtesy, a man of fine and clean food and way of life, well dressed, decorous, friendly, cheerful and energetic. He should not be a stranger to the guests' jokes, but should be well tempered to both serious talk and merriment.

units.la: lautæ mundæq; hominem & ornatum, decorum, familiarem, alacrem & impigrum præstet & exhibeat, à iocis conuiuarum non alienū, sed ad vtraque probè attemperatum. Secundum, vt suorum conuiuarum habeat curam, ne quid hisce defit, vel impedimentum creet, quo minus scopo conuiuii conuenienter conuiuari possint. Eccl.c.31.2. Curam eorum (conuiuarum) habe, atq; ita sede.3.Et omnem tui copiam facuo, cuq; probaueris te, requiescuto vt per illos afficiaris lætitia. Tertium est, vt leges conuiuiales, ῥόμως συμπόσιαλ præscribat, quæ magisteria à Cicerone vocantur, quæ de modo & demensò bibendi præscripto, secundum cuiusque naturam, vires, ætatem, & propensionem quam exploratam habere debet, arg.Psalm.25. Deinde, de sermonibus, spectaculis, aliisque oblectationibus, vtilibus ac honestis in conuiuio procurandis iis quæ ad finem conuiuii accedunt, vt seria iocis temperet, vel iocosa seriis, quibus à nausea conuiuæ reficiantur & recreentur voluptatibus nō omnino prohibeat, quæ iubet, factu sint facilia illis, quibus imponit, sicuti Christus Architriclino sobrio vini gustationem mandat, Ioh. c.2. Contrà lusus & iocos futiles & inanes prohibebit, neq; turpiter agere conuiuis permitteret, non sit vinosus, contumeliosus, iniucundus & alienus, sordidus, μισογελωτος, neq; luxuriosus aut iactabundus.
units.tr: The second is that he takes care of his guests, so that nothing is lacking to them and he creates no obstacle that would keep them from feasting fittingly for the purpose of the banquet. Eccl. c. 31.2. Take care of them, and so sit down. And when you have supplied all your abundance, and have shown yourself, then rest, that you may be gladdened by them. The third is that he lays down symposiac laws [νόμους συμποσιακούς], which Cicero calls magisteria, concerning the measure and set manner of drinking, adjusted to each person's nature, strength, age and inclination, which he ought to have examined. arg. Psalm. 25. Then, concerning talk, shows and other amusements that are useful and honourable and suited to the purpose of the banquet, he should arrange them so that he tempers serious matters with jests, or jests with serious matters, so that the guests are refreshed and restored from weariness. He does not altogether forbid pleasures, but commands what he imposes, making it easy for those he imposes it on to do, just as Christ commanded the sober master of the feast to taste the wine. Joh. c. 2. On the other hand, he forbids frivolous and empty jokes and games, and does not allow his guests to behave disgracefully. He himself should not be drunken, abusive, disagreeable and unpleasant, filthy, a hater of laughter [μισογέλωτος], nor luxurious or boastful.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: De conuiuis & ministris conuiuii, eorumq; moribus conuiualibus ante alimentorum sumptionem.
units.tr: On the guests and the servants of a banquet, and their table manners before the food is eaten.

units.la: TAntum de conuiuatore. Sequitur de conuiua, qui à modiperatore ad conuiuium vocatur, & dicitur <bl>ἐμφάγ</bl>, <bl>ὀμέτρ</bl>, <bl>σωτρ</bl>, <bl>ἐμφτρ</bl>.
units.tr: That is enough about the host. Next comes the guest, who is invited to the banquet by the master of the feast, and who is called <bl>ἐμφάγ</bl>, <bl>ὀμέτρ</bl>, <bl>σωτρ</bl>, <bl>ἐμφτρ</bl>.

units.la: Conuiuæ conuersatio alia est in inuitationis actu, alia in sequentibus occupationibus.
units.tr: The guest's conduct is different at the time of the invitation and in the duties that follow.

units.la: In actu inuitationis, verbis gestibusque magnam humanitatem præ se ferre debet, & ob tam humanam inuitationem gratias agere: sed non temere promittet vel recusabit venire. In recusatione videndum illi, ne inhumanitate, morositate, auaritia, superbia aut aliis prauis affectibus, quæuis etiam amicorum atq; familiarium hominum honesta conuiuia refugiat. Nam inuitantium humanitatem, charitatem & beneuolentiam negligere & aspernari, indecorum & odiosum est. Cauendum quoque, ne, si à quoquam primo es inuitatus & recusaueris, postea alteri promittas; ne prior ille se à te contemptum existimet, atq; ita in ipsius offensionem & odium incurras.
units.tr: When he is invited, he should show great courtesy in his words and gestures, and give thanks for so kind an invitation. He should not promise or refuse to come rashly.
