If he refuses, he must take care that he does not, out of inhumanity, moroseness, greed, pride or other bad feelings, shun any respectable banquet, even one given by friends and familiars. For it is unseemly and offensive to neglect and spurn the kindness, love and goodwill of those who invite us. He must also take care that, if he has been invited first by someone and refuses, he does not afterwards promise himself to another, lest the first man think he has been slighted, and so you incur his offence and hatred.

units.la: In recusatione vtendum probabili causa, qua te excuses, Luc.c.14.18. &seqq. ne inuitator vel contemptu, vel maleuolentia aliqua te suæ petitioni deesse suspicetur.
units.tr: When he refuses, he should use a reasonable excuse, Luke 14:18 and following, lest the host suspect that you despise his request or bear him some ill will.

units.la: De aduentu suo promittere & spem facere temerè non debet, prius quam inuitatorum reliquorum conuiuarum mores exploratos ha-
units.tr: He should not rashly promise or raise hopes of coming before he has examined the manners of the other guests who have been invited,

units.la: liquorum conuiuarum mores exploratos habear,aut cum his conuersari possit, vel consul-tum illi sit. Neque etiam facile crebro ad quas-uis hominum improborum conuiuia accedendum. Vide Prou. c. 23. per tot. Quod si promisisti te venturum, standum promissis, nisi ex iustissima & grauissima causa te excuses. Vid. Luc. c. 14. 18. & seqq. Matth. c. 22.
units.tr: and whether he can get along with them, or whether it is advisable for him. Nor should he readily go often to the banquets of any wicked men. See Prov. 23 throughout. But if you have promised to come, you must keep your promise, unless you excuse yourself for a most just and weighty reason. See Luke 14:18 and following; Matt. 22.

units.la: Porro conuiuia qui spem sui aduentus fecit, occupatur in praeparatione sui ad conuiuium & in accessu.
units.tr: Next, the guest who has given hope of his coming occupies himself in preparing for the banquet and in setting out.

units.la: Praeparatio eiusmodi est animi, vel corporis.
units.tr: Such preparation concerns either the mind or the body.

units.la: Animi praeparatio est examinatio in vera fide & charitate. 1. Corinth. c. 10. Siue igitur edatis, sive bibitis, omnia ad gloriam Dei facite. Corporis praeparatio est exercitatio eiusdem, vel mundatio, vel vestitus, vel ornatus. Corporis exercitatio vtilis dicitur, quae consistit in luctatione, cursu, saltu, disci iactu, follis, pilae palmariae & similiu: quandoque etiam in venatione, equitatione, iaculatione, ambulatione, chorea, modulatione vocis, cantu, frictione, clara lectione, vid. Stuck. lib. 2. cap. 24. conuiu. Balnea quoque & vnctiones ante epulas apud veteres vsitatae fuerunt. vid. 2. Sam. c. 11. Exod. c. 2. & Daniel. cap. 13. & lotiones. Matth. c. 15. 2. 3. Marc. c. 7. 2. 3. 4. 2. Reg. cap. 3. 11. Iohan. c. 13. 3. 4. & seqq. 1. Timoth. c. 5. Iudic. c. 9. 21. Genef. c. 43. c. 18. & c. 19. vide Stuck. d. lib. 2. c. 33. Hodie non sunt in vsu, quamuis minime decorum est, vt conuiua sordidatis capillis & vnguibus & omnino capite capillis, manibus, facie vultuque immundo, sordido aut squalido, ad conuiuia accedat, ne ludibrio conuiuatori & conuiuis & nauseae & fastidio sit. Ideoque cauencauendæ omnes sordes & illuuies in corpore.
units.tr: Preparation of the mind is an examination of true faith and love. 1 Cor. 10: Whether therefore you eat or drink, do all to the glory of God. Preparation of the body is exercise of it, or cleansing, or dress, or adornment. Bodily exercise that is called useful consists in wrestling, running, leaping, throwing the discus, the ball-game, the palm-ball and the like; sometimes also in hunting, riding, javelin-throwing, walking, dancing, modulating the voice, singing, rubbing, and reading aloud. See Stuckius, lib. 2, cap. 24, on banquets. Baths and anointings before feasts were also customary among the ancients. See 2 Sam. 11; Exod. 2; Dan. 13; and washings: Matt. 15:2-3; Mark 7:2-4; 2 Kings 3:11; John 13:3-4 and following; 1 Tim. 5; Judg. 9:21; Gen. 43, 18 and 19. See Stuckius, lib. 2, cap. 33. Today these are not in use, though it is by no means seemly for a guest to come to a banquet with dirty hair and nails, indeed with a head, hands, face or expression unclean, filthy or squalid, lest he become a laughing-stock to the host and the guests, and a cause of nausea and disgust. Therefore all filth and grime on the body must be avoided.

units.la: Vestitus conuiuarum decorus, est honestus, mundus, & splendidior quotidiano vestitu. Vnde vestes nuptiales.Matth.c.22.11.Intrauit autem rex vt videret discumbentes: & vidit ibi hominem non vestitum veste nuptiali. 12. Et ait illi, Quomodo huc intrasti amice, non habens vestem nuptialem Iudith. c.12. 15. qui plerunque tam apud Iudæos, quam Græcos & Romanos erat albus.vid. Stuck.d.lib.2.c.26.&27.&seqq.&sup.c.10.
units.tr: The guests' dress should be decent: respectable, clean, and rather finer than everyday clothes. Hence the wedding garments. Matt. 22:11-12: But when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. And he said to him, Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment? Judith 12:15, which was generally white both among the Jews and among the Greeks and Romans. See Stuckius, lib. 2, cap. 26, 27 and following, and above, cap. 10.

units.la: Accessus conuiuæ ad conuiuium non fit nimis maturus vel tardus, in quo se consuetudini loci adcommodabit, vterque enim molestus, Ex maturo nimis accessu τρεχίδωτος, ex tardo ζοφιεγδίμφες dicuntur. Plutarch. probl. 7. Sympos. vtrique sibi met ipsis, conuiuis, conuiuatori vt in loco, cibo, variis, ita sedium mutatione, noua vocatione facienda, incommoda conciliant. Nam moratores denuo vocare necesse habet paterfamilias.Luc.c.14,22.23.24.
units.tr: The guest's arrival at the banquet should be neither too early nor too late; he should adapt himself to the custom of the place. For both are troublesome: those who arrive too early are called τρεχίδωτος, those who come too late ζοφιεγδίμφες. Plutarch, Problems 7, Symposiaca. Each, by his lateness or earliness, brings inconvenience upon himself, the other guests and the host, since the place, the food, the seating and so on must be changed, and a fresh summons made. For the householder must send out again to call those who linger. Luke 14:22-24.

units.la: Conuiuam, vicinum, vel amicum, accedere quem inuitatum esse scit, vocare & illo comitatum ad conuiuium venire, decorum & ciuile, atque amicitiæ & beneuolentiæ significatio est.
units.tr: For a guest to go to a neighbour or friend whom he knows to have been invited, to summon him, and to come with him to the banquet, is seemly and civil, and a sign of friendship and goodwill.

units.la: Quando ad conuiuatoris domum peruentum est, cauebit ne in illam temere irrumpat, aut ianuam nimis crebro, proterve, vel violenter pulsando, conuiuatori eiusque familiæ molestiam aliquam exhibeat, sed patienter, donec ei domus aperiatur, exspectet. arg.Luc.c.12.36.37. De ianuæ pulsatione Apocal.c.3. Matth.c.7. Act.c.12.1. Chron.c.26.
units.tr: When you have reached the host's house, take care not to rush in rashly, nor to cause the host or his household any annoyance by knocking at the door too often, impudently or violently. Rather, wait patiently until the house is opened to you. Argument from Luke 12:36-37. On knocking at the door: Rev. 3; Matt. 7; Acts 12:13; 1 Chron. 26.

units.la: Ingressus, vel introductus in domum conui-uatoris, patrem fam. & familiam eius humaniter & officiose salutabit. argum. Matth. c.10.12. Intrantes autem in domum salutate eam, dicentes, Pax huic domui. 13. Et si quidem domus illa digna, veniet pax vestra super eam. Sin autem non fuerit digna, pax vestra revertetur ad vos. alias in domo aliena tamquam mut°, vel surdus esto. Vid. Stuck. d. loc. c. 31.
units.tr: On entering, or being brought into the host's house, he shall greet the householder and his household courteously and dutifully. Argument from Matt. 10:12-13: And when you enter the house, greet it, saying, Peace be to this house. And if the house is worthy, your peace shall come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace shall return to you. Otherwise, in another's house, be like a mute or a deaf man. See Stuckius, loc. cit., cap. 31.

units.la: Porrò conuiuiis similes sunt ἰσιχλητοι, vel ἀχλητοι, hoc est, umbrae, vel parasiti. ἰσιχλητοι & σκιαι, umbrae, & conuiuarum comites vocantur, qui non a conuiuatore, sed conuiuarum aliquo invitati accedunt. Sed adducenti umbram cauendum, ne multos adducat. Deinde adducendorum delectum habeat, quo adducat qui conuiuatori noti, familiares & amici, vel certe moribus cum ipso congruentes, ne illi molestiam, aut fastidium pariant. Tertio considerandum quoque umbrae, ad quem adducatur, an honestum sit quoque comitari deducentem. Vid. Stuck. d. lib. 2. c. 6.
units.tr: Similar to the guests are the ἀκλητοι or ἰσιχλητοι, that is, the shadows or parasites. The σκιαι, shadows, are also called the companions of the guests: those who come not at the invitation of the host but at that of some guest. But the man who brings a shadow must take care not to bring many. Next, he should make a choice of whom he brings: persons known to the host, familiars and friends, or at least men whose manners agree with his, lest they cause him trouble or disgust. Thirdly, one must consider to whom the shadow is brought, and whether it is respectable for the one escorting him to accompany him. See Stuckius, lib. 2, cap. 6.

units.la: Parasiti sunt mensarum affectae, gnathones, seipsos ingerentes. Eccles. c. 40.30. Vir respiciens ad alienam mensam, non habet vitam, quae reputanda sit vita; inquinat animam suam scienter alienis. 31. Vir autem sciens & eruditus, cauet. 32. In ore imprudentis suauis est mendicitas, sed ignis ardet in ventre eius. Eiusmodi recte muscis comparantur, quae bestia impudens, audax, vorax, importuna & molesta est. Graecis eleganter hi vocantur, κλητοι, αὐτόκλητοι, αὐτόματοι, δειπνομανεῖς, ἐπιθυμοδείπνοι, φιλοδείπνοι, δειπνοδιώκτης, ὠψοφάγοι, ἀλογεσοφάγοι, ῥιγ- λακες,
units.tr: Parasites are those greedy for tables, buffoons who thrust themselves in. Ecclus 40:29-31: The man who looks to another's table does not have a life that can be counted as life; he defiles his soul knowingly with other men's goods. But a wise and learned man takes care. In the mouth of the foolish, begging is sweet, but a fire burns in his belly. Such people are fitly compared to flies, an impudent, bold, greedy, troublesome and annoying creature. The Greeks elegantly call these men κλητοι, αὐτόκλητοι, αὐτόματοι, δειπνομανεῖς, ἐπιθυμοδείπνοι, φιλοδείπνοι, δειπνοδιώκτης, ὠψοφάγοι, ἀλογεσοφάγοι, ῥιγ-

units.la: λάκες, δωτιόλογοι, κλεπτόφογαι, τεραπεζόλοιχοι, ψυμόδυλοι, γαστέμαργοι. de quibus vocibus & appellationibus latius Stuckius d.lib.2.c.4. Cæl.Rhodigin.lib.20. c.33. Stob.serm.64. & 65. Plutarch. de discrim. adul. & amic.
units.tr: λακες, δωτιόλογοι, κλεπτόφογαι, τεραπεζόλοιχοι, ψυμόδυλοι, γαστέμαργοι: the invited, the self-invited, the self-moved, the dinner-mad, the lovers of dinner, the dinner-hunters, the relish-eaters, the glutton-eaters, the ... , the gift-talkers, the thieves of food, the table-lickers, the mouth-hunters, the belly-gluttons. On these words and names, see more fully Stuckius, lib. 2, cap. 4; Caelius Rhodiginus, lib. 20, cap. 33; Stobaeus, sermons 64 and 65; Plutarch, On the Difference between a Flatterer and a Friend.

units.la: Qui necessitatis, paupertatis, vel honestatis causa ad conuiuia accedunt, vt mendici; Luc. c. 16. & canes. Matth. c.15. huc non refero. Canis ad conuiuium non adducendus.
units.tr: Those who come to banquets out of necessity, poverty or self-respect, like beggars, I do not count here. Luke 16; and dogs: Matt. 15. A dog should not be brought to a banquet.

units.la: Obseruandum etiam hic, à conuiuis quandoque symbolum conferri. vnde conuiuia collatitia, symbolica, in quibus quilibet conuiuarum confert portionem ad conuiuium. qualia vsitata inter vicinos in quibusdam locis videmus.
units.tr: It must also be observed here that sometimes a contribution is made by the guests to the meal. Hence the banquets called collatitia and symbolica, in which each guest contributes a share to the feast. We see such customs in use among neighbours in some places.

units.la: Sequitur de administris, qui conuiuiali conuersationi inseruiunt opera, industria & ministerio suo. Luc. c.17.7. Quis vestrum habet seruum arantem aut pascentem qui regresso ab agro dicat statim, accede & discumbe. 8. Immo nonne dicit ei, para quod canem & pracinctus ministra mihi, vsquedum edero ac bibero & postea edito tu & bibito.9. Num gratiam seruo illi habet, quia fecit quae ipsi praecepta fuerant? non puto. Appellantur eiusmodi ad ministrantes & serui Efter c.1.7. & seqq.1. Reg. cap. 1.4. Luc. c.17.8. c.10.40. Matth. c. 22.13.3.4.5. 8. & cap.22.13.3.4.5.8. Ioh.c.12 3.c.2.5.9. Luc.c.12. 27. Nam vter maior est, qui discumbit an qui ministrat? nonne qui discumbit? at ego sum inter vos vt qui ministrat.
units.tr: Next we come to the attendants, who serve the convivial gathering by their labour, diligence and ministry. Luke 17:7-9: Which of you, having a servant ploughing or keeping sheep, will say to him when he comes in from the field, Come at once and sit down to eat? Will he not rather say to him, Prepare my supper, and dress yourself and serve me until I have eaten and drunk; and afterward you shall eat and drink? Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? I think not. Such ministers and servants are called Esther 1:7 and following; 1 Kings 1:4; Luke 17:8; 10:40; Matt. 22:13; 3-5, 8; John 12:3; 2:5, 9; Luke 12:27. For who is greater, he who sits at table or he who serves? Is it not he who sits at table? But I am among you as one who serves. Luke 22:27.

units.la: Eiusmodi ministrorum & famulorum conuiuialium, tam iuuenum masculorum quam feminarum. Luc.cap.12.37.38. Cæl, Rhodig. libr. 25.
units.tr: Of such ministers and servants at table, both young men and women. Luke 12:37-38. Caelius Rhodiginus, book 25.

units.la: cap.18. Varia sunt genera & officia, quorum quædam consistunt in præparatione, quædam in ipso actu conuiuii. arg. Luc. cap. 17. Para quod cenem, & ibid. præcinctus mihi ministra mihi, donec edero & bibero. In præparatione & apparatu consistunt hæc seruorum officia & ministeria. Quidam enim ex his, scopis purgant triclinia, mensas spogiis abstergunt, quidam pocula emundant, mensas extendunt, iisque circulum, salinum, orbiculos, quadras, panes, cochlearia imponunt, vel pocula; quidam vinum in crateræ miscent, pocula porrigunt; quidam adferunt aquam & ignem accedunt, manibus aquam infundunt ex gutturnio in polubrum, trullum. de quibus 2. Reg. c. 3. 11. Luc. c. 7. 37. 38. Marc. c. 7. Johan. c. 13. 4. & seqq. Cal. Rhodig. lib. 28. c. 1. Sunt alii qui cibos mensis apponunt, alii αλιτροπ vocatores. Luc. cap. 14. alii obsonatores, scoparii, lecti-sternatores, atriarii, siue atriensis, dapiferi & διαγωγεύς, quales sæpè sunt ipsimet conuiuatores. Genes. c. 18. Judic. c. 6. vel ministri, Marc. 8. 6. c. 6. 39. 1. Sam. c. 9. 21. & seqq. Matth. c. 14.
units.tr: Chapter 18. There are various kinds of servants and duties: some consist in preparation, others in the very act of the banquet. Compare Luke 17: "Prepare what I may sup on, and gird yourself and serve me, until I have eaten and drunk." These duties and ministries of servants consist in preparation and setting out. For some of them sweep the dining-rooms with brooms, wipe the tables with sponges, some clean the cups, spread the tables, and place upon them the salt-cellar, small plates, dishes, bread, spoons, or cups; some mix wine in the mixing-bowl and hand round the cups; some bring water and light the fire, pour water over the hands from the ewer into the basin and the bowl. Concerning these see 2 Kings 3:11; Luke 7:37-38; Mark 7; John 13:4ff. Caelius Rhodiginus, book 28, chapter 1. There are others who set the food on the tables, others are called αλιτροπ (summoners) Luke 14; others are purveyors, sweepers, couch-makers, attendants of the hall, or the steward, carvers and διαγωγεύς (guide), such as the guests themselves often were. Genesis 18; Judges 6; or servants, Mark 8; Mark 6:39; 1 Samuel 9:21ff.; Matthew 14.

units.la: In ipso actu conuiuii famulantur & inseruiunt præguSTatores & exploratores, ne venenum misceatur, quo dominus & conuiuæ securè vescantur cibo, quidam pocillatores, vel à poculis. Genes. c. 40. Nehem. cap. 2. Psalm. 102. qui Græcis dicuntur οἰνοχόοι, siue οἰνοχοῦμενοι, at οἰνόστης observatores bibentium. Quidam præterea ciborum diuisores, cibos apte & artificiose secantes & distribuentes, qui Latinis dicuntur structores. Habebant etiam veteres ministros reliquias colligentes cadentes è mensa, analectas, item murmur compescentes, lordesque pauimenti eiicientes. Vid. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 5. Genial. dier. c. 21. Turneb. lib. 24. aduers. c. 33.
units.tr: In the very act of the banquet there serve and attend the taste-testers and tasters, lest poison be mixed in, so that the master and guests may eat their food safely; some are cupbearers, or pourers of drink, who among the Greeks are called οἰνοχόοι or οἰνοχοῦμενοι, while οἰνόστης denotes those who watch over drinkers. Besides these there are carvers of food, who cut and distribute the dishes skilfully and artfully, who in Latin are called structores. The ancients also had servants who gathered up the scraps falling from the table, analectae, and likewise those who quieted the murmuring and cast out the filth from the floor. See Alexander ab Alexandro, book 5, Genialium dierum, chapter 21; Turnebus, book 24, Adversaria, chapter 33.

units.la: Pincernæ officium consistit in poculis eluendis, abluendis & purgandis. Deinde in vino aqua miscendo & temperando in cratere, quem ad summum implebant boni ominis causa. Prou. c. 9. 5. Venite vescimini cibo meo, & bibite de vino meo quod miscui. Esa. c. 5. v. 22. Et strenuus ad miscendum potum inebriantem. Erant & apud veteres ministri voluptatum, qui dictis, factis & gestib. ridiculis conuiuas exhilarare studebant, qui Graecis dicuntur φλυαρος, Clem. Alex. lib. 3. c. 4. Paedag. Sunt & promi, qui alimentis depromendis, vel recondendis seruandisque praesunt, qui & procuratores peni cellarii, promicondi, & Graecis ταμιεῖα & ταμίαι vocantur. Sunt etiam famuli, qui conuiuas domum deducunt, comitantur, iis praelucent, qui λυχνοῦχοι, λυχνοφόροι & διαδέχοι vocantur. Matth. c. 25. 1. 2. & seqq. de quibus ministris mensarum & conuiuiorum. late Ludou. (Vid. Rhodigin. & Clem. Alex.
units.tr: The office of the cupbearer consists in rinsing, washing and cleaning the cups; then in mixing and tempering water with the wine in the mixing-bowl, which they used to fill to the brim for the sake of good omen. Proverbs 9:5: "Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine which I have mixed." Isaiah 5:22: "and the valiant men to mix strong drink." Among the ancients there were also jesters, who strove to cheer the guests with words, deeds and ridiculous gestures; the Greeks call them φλυαρος. Clement of Alexandria, book 3, chapter 4, Paedagogus. There are also stewards who preside over the bringing out and storing away and keeping of provisions; they are called procurators of the pantry, store-keepers, and in Greek ταμιεῖα and ταμίαι. There are also servants who escort the guests home, accompany them, and light the way before them; they are called λυχνοῦχοι, λυχνοφόροι and διαδέχοι. Matthew 25:1ff. Concerning these ministers of tables and banquets, see at length Ludovicus... (See Rhodiginus and Clement of Alexandria.)

units.la: Sed tamen saepe vnus & idem famulus plura horum munera in conuiuio obire potest & solet. Sane multitudo seruorum & ministrorum mensae, confusionis & perturbationis causa esse solet, & plerunque negligenter fieri solent, quae pluribus committuntur, vel a pluribus fiunt.
units.tr: Yet often one and the same servant can and usually does discharge several of these functions at a banquet. Indeed a multitude of servants and ministers at table is usually a cause of confusion and disorder, and things committed to many, or done by many, are generally done carelessly.

units.la: Praefecti hisce ministris vocantur dispensatores. Luc. c. 12. 42. Architriclini. Ioh. c. 2. seu triclniarchae. Dan. c. 1. Genes. c. 51. Apud Iudaeos Leuitae inseruiebant sacris epulis & conuiuiis.
units.tr: The overseers of these servants are called stewards. Luke 12:42. Architriclinus, John 2, or triclinarchs. Daniel 1; Genesis 51. Among the Jews the Levites served at the sacred feasts and banquets.

units.la: Habitus & gestus horum ministrorum est, vt sint præcincti. Luc. c. 17. 8. Stentque ad ministrand im omnino prompti & expediti, alacres, industrii, laboriosi, obsequentes monitis dominorum & ad illius nutum inseruientes. Genes. c. 18. Luc. 17. 8. 9. Daniel. cap. 1. 1. Reg. cap. 1. Genes. cap. 41. Apud Romanos ferui ad mensam stabant. Seneca lib. 3 De benefic. & lib. 6. Epist. 46. & 47. & lib. 15. epist. 96. Sueton. in Galb. circa finem. 1. Sam. c. 25. 27. Vestirus horum ministrorum esse debet elegans & mundus, nitidus, a sordibus & omni deformitate vacuus. Gestus eorum liberales, compositi ad hilaritatem, comitatem, modestiam & benevolentiam erga convivas & dominum.
units.tr: The bearing and gesture of these servants is that they are girded up. Luke 17:8. They should stand wholly ready and prepared for serving, cheerful, diligent, hardworking, obedient to the admonitions of their masters, and attentive to their nod. Genesis 18; Luke 17:8-9; Daniel 1:1; 1 Kings 1; Genesis 41. Among the Romans servants stood at table. Seneca, De beneficiis, book 3, and Epistles 46, 47 and book 15, epistle 96. Suetonius, Galba, near the end. 1 Samuel 25:27. The dress of these servants ought to be neat and clean, bright, and free from dirt and every unsightliness. Their gestures should be courteous, composed to cheerfulness, affability, modesty and goodwill towards the guests and the master.

units.la: In ministeriis mensæ occupati, nullo modo, aut caput, aut quamcumque partem alteram corporis in conspectu accumbentium scabere aut fricare; neque etiam quæcunque ea sint membra, vestibus cooperta, manibus contingere, aut gestuum similitudine eius rei indicium præ se ferre debent.
units.tr: Those engaged in the duties of the table must in no way scratch or rub their head, or any other part of the body, in the sight of those reclining; nor touch with their hands any parts whatever, even if covered with clothing, nor show by gestures any sign of such things.

units.la: Cum infundendum, porrigendum, aut apponendum quid fuerit, neminem perfundant, quadras mutent ad ferculorum varietatem; vina varia non commiscceant. Pro emungendis lucernis euigilent, & emunctusimiliter è mensa tollant.
units.tr: When something is to be poured out, handed round, or set down, they should not splash anyone; they should change the dishes to suit the variety of the courses; they should not mix various wines together. They should keep watch to trim the lamps, and likewise remove the snuff from the table.

units.la: Decet quoque hosce manus habere lotas & mundas; ne, quod spurcitiei alicuius signum in iis appareat, & palàm in conspectu aliorum citra vllam suspicionem manus proferre debent.
units.tr: They ought also to have their hands washed and clean, so that no sign of any filth appears on them; and they must bring their hands forward openly in the sight of others, without any suspicion.

units.la: Iisdem, cum aut patinas mensæ imponendas
units.tr: When they bring the plates to be placed on the table, or hand out cups to one about to drink,

units.la: das afferunt, aut pocula bibituro porrigunt, eo ipso tempore ab eiectione sputi & tussiendo,& multò magis à sternutamento sibi cauebunt.
units.tr: they should guard themselves at that very moment from spitting, coughing, and much more from sneezing.

units.la: Quod si aliquando pyrum assatum foco exemeris, aut panem tostum è prunis sustuleris, non debebis in ea cineris tollendi causa inflare.Numquam enim ventus sine aqua est; sed potius ad patellam leui brachio cinerem excuties, vel cogitabis num qua ratione alia eximi commodè possit.
units.tr: If ever you take a roasted pear from the hearth, or lift toasted bread from the embers, you should not blow on it to remove the ash. For wind is never without water; rather, brush the ash off onto the plate with a light hand, or think whether there is some other way to take it off conveniently.

units.la: Linteolum tuum quasi recens lotum, alteri non porriges; is cui porrigis, an mundum sit, ignorat. Ideoque facile hoc modo offendi posset.
units.tr: Do not hand over your napkin as if freshly washed to another; the one to whom you hand it does not know whether it is clean. Thus he could easily be offended.

units.la: Cauebit omnino nequid fastidii aut immunditiæ suspicionem crect, aut sinistrè suspicandi occasionem præbeat.
units.tr: Let him take care above all not to raise any suspicion of distaste or uncleanness, or to give occasion for an unfavourable suspicion.

units.la: CAP. XI. De conuersatione & moribus apud sumptionem alimentorum.
units.tr: CAP. XI. On conversation and manners at the taking of food.

units.la: HVc vsq; de primo membro conuiuii, personis nimirum: sequitur nunc de communicatione mensali seu symbolarum mensalium.
units.tr: So far, concerning the first part of the banquet, namely the persons. Now follows the sharing of the table, or the table-shares (symbola mensalia).

units.la: Symbola mensalis dicitur, quæ vel à conuiuatore, vel à conuiuis decenter & ciuiliter in commune conferrur & comunicatur conuiuis.
units.tr: A table-share is that which is contributed and communicated to the guests, decently and courteously, either by the host or by the guests themselves.

units.la: In hac primò species communicationis considerandæ. Deinde, habitus & gestus communicationis. Species eius sunt duæ communicatio alimentorum, vel sermonis. Alimentorum communicatio est eorundem sumptio & participatio,& vlus ad corporis & genii refectione & voluptatem à conuiuis facta. Eccles.cap.10.14. quæ Græcis χοινωνία dicitur.1. Corinth. c.10.18. Act. c.27.35. &feqq. Alimenta sunt esculenta & poculenta, quæ conuiuator pro conuiuis præparauit.
units.tr: Here the kind of sharing must be considered first, and then the habit and gesture of sharing. There are two kinds: sharing of food, or sharing of speech. Sharing of food is the partaking and participation in the same foods by the guests, and their use for the refreshment and pleasure of body and spirit. Eccles. 10.14. The Greeks call this koinonia [κοινωνία]. 1 Cor. 10.18; Acts 27.35 and following. Foods are solid and liquid things that the host has prepared for the guests.

units.la: Alimentorum communicationem quædam præcedunt,quædam sequuntur.
units.tr: Some things come before the sharing of food, and some after.

units.la: Præcedunt sumptionem alimentorum 1.apositio eorundem.2.consecratio.3.prægustatio. 4.distributio.
units.tr: Before the eating of food come: (1) the setting of it out, (2) consecration, (3) tasting beforehand, and (4) distribution.

units.la: Appositio alimentorum, est eorundem in mensam ad quam conuiuæ sunt locati, impositio,illatio & propositio ad sumendum & vtendum.1. Corinth.cap.10.27. Quod siquis infidelium vos vocat, & vultis ire; quidquid apponitur vobis, edite,nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam. &feqq. Act.c.27.33. &feqq.1.Timoth.c.4.3.4. Ester cap.1. 7.8. Genes.c.24.33.54. Videsolemnitatem ablationis apud Alex.ab Alex.lib.5.cap.21. Ciborum appositio fieri solet à dapifero; poculentorum vero à pincerna: vtroque tamen munere sæpè ipse conuiuator vel materfam.aut eorundem famuli,vel ancillæ funguntur,vti constat ex exemplis Abrahami,Genes.c.18. Gedeonis,Iud.c.6. Christi discipulorum,Marc.cap.8.6.cap.6.39. Matth. cap.14.
units.tr: The setting out of food is the putting, bringing in and presenting of the same on the table at which the guests have been placed, to be taken and used. 1 Cor. 10.27: "If any of the unbelievers invites you, and you are willing to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no question for conscience' sake," and following. Acts 27.33 and following. 1 Tim. 4.3-4. Esther 1.7-8. Gen. 24.33, 54. For the solemnity of the removal of the dishes, see Alexander ab Alexandro, bk. 5, ch. 21. The setting out of solid food is usually done by the steward (dapifer), and of drinks by the cupbearer (pincerna). Yet in both duties the host himself, or the hostess, or their male or female servants, often serve, as is plain from the examples of Abraham (Gen. 18), Gideon (Judg. 6), and the disciples of Christ (Mark 8.6; 6.39; Matt. 14).

units.la: Esculentorum appositio priori loco & tempore fit & apud quosdam quandoque ex scheda, quæ describitur ordine habet obsonia, quid primum,secundum,postremum coquus sit missurus.Poculentorum posteriori tempore & loco fit appositio.1.Sam.c.9.23.24. Esl.c.1,8. Prout autem alimenta conuiuii & apparatus exiguus vel magnus est,conuiuia dicuntur & appellantur.ibi moderata,frugalia,ccenaSaturnia, Hecatæ,philosophica, Platonica, rustica, Laconica,sordida,Cynica, Timonica: Stuck lib.1.c.5. vel contra, splendida,magnifica, luxuriosa,ccena dubia,popularis, ebria, regalis, mensa Persica,conuiuium Sybariticum. de quibus vide Esa. c.25. Amos c.6. Ofea c.4. Nahum.c.1.3. Efd.c.3. Est. c.1. Iudic.c.14.1. Sam.c.25. Daniel.c.5. quæ conuiuia decent magnos & locupletes. Et fumptuofiffima celebrauit Cæsar, Nero, Heliogabalus, Caligula, Vitellius, Titus, Geta. Vid. Alex. ab Alex. Gen. dier.lib.5.c.21.
units.tr: The setting out of solid food comes first in place and time, and among some peoples sometimes from a written list, which gives the order of the dishes: what the cook is to send in first, second, and last. The setting out of drinks comes later in time and place. 1 Sam. 9.23-24; Esth. 1.8. Feasts are called and named according to how plain or lavish the food and preparation are. Moderate, frugal, Saturnian, Hecatean, philosophical, Platonic, rustic, Laconian, squalid, Cynic, Timonian suppers; or, on the other hand, splendid, magnificent, luxurious, doubtful, popular, drunken, royal feasts, a Persian table, a Sybaritic banquet. On these see Isa. 25; Amos 6; Hos. 4; Nahum 1.3; Ezra 3; Esth. 1; Judg. 14.10; 1 Sam. 25; Dan. 5. Such feasts suit the great and the wealthy. The most lavish were given by Caesar, Nero, Heliogabalus, Caligula, Vitellius, Titus and Geta. See Alexander ab Alexandro, Dies geniales, bk. 5, ch. 21.

units.la: Consecratio mensæ & alimentorum, est nominis Diuini inuocatio, pro benedictione illorum. 1.Sam.c.9.13. Nam non comedet populus vsque dum aduenerit, quum ipse benedixerit conuiuio, postmodum comedent conuiuæ inuitati. 1.Timoth. c.4.3. Cibos, quos Deus creauit ad participandum cum gratiarum actione fidelibus, &c. 4. Nam quidquid creauit Deus, bonum est; nec quicquam reiiciendum est, si cum gratiarum actione sumatur. 5. Sanctificatur enim per verbum Dei & preces. 1. Corinth.c.10.30. Et, si ego per gratiam cibum participo, cur ob id amplius iudicor, pro quo ego gratias ago? 31. Siue igitur bibitis, siue editis, siue quid agitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Psalm.145.1.2.15. Oculi omnium in te spectant, & tu das illis escam suam in tempore suo, &c. Psalm.104.11.12.13.14.15. Mat. c.14.19. Acceptis quinque illis panibus ac duobus piscibus, suspiciens in cælum, benedixit, & cum fregisset, dedit discipulis panes, discipuli vero turbæ. Marc.c.6. 41. Cum suspexisset in calum, benedixit ac fregit panes, &c. Actor.cap.27.35. Et cum hæc dixisset & accepisset panem gratias egit Deo in conspectu omnium; & cum fregisset, coepit edere. Apud Ethnicos libationes ante epulas adhibebantur, de quibus Macrob. Saturn. lib.3. c.11. Stuck. lib.2. cap.37. convivii, quibus adde Num. c.18.c.19. Exod.c.25.2. 2. Reg. c.23.
units.tr: The consecration of the table and of the food is the invocation of the divine name for their blessing. 1 Sam. 9.13: "The people will not eat until he has come, since he must bless the sacrifice; afterwards the invited guests will eat." 1 Tim. 4.3: foods which God created to be shared with thanksgiving by believers, etc. (4) For whatever God has created is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is taken with thanksgiving. (5) For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. 1 Cor. 10.30: "If I partake of food with grace, why am I judged for that for which I give thanks?" (31) "Whether therefore you drink or eat, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." Psalm 145.1-2, 15: "The eyes of all wait upon you, and you give them their food in due season," etc. Psalm 104.11-15. Matt. 14.19: "Taking the five loaves and the two fish, looking up to heaven, he blessed them, and breaking them he gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowd." Mark 6.41: "When he had looked up to heaven, he blessed and broke the loaves," etc. Acts 27.35: "And when he had said this and taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the sight of all; and when he had broken it, he began to eat." Among the heathen, libations were used before feasts, of which Macrobius, Saturnalia, bk. 3, ch. 11, and Stuckius, bk. 2, ch. 37, of banquets; to which add Num. 18.19; Exod. 25.2; 2 Kings 23.

units.la: Prægustatio, est qua alimenta mensæ impositæ explorantur, ne quid veneni sit mistum, quod sumptum, convivis nocere possit, quæ sit ideo, quo convivæ secure alimentis vesci possint.
units.tr: Tasting beforehand is the testing of the food set on the table, so that no poison mixed in it may be taken and harm the guests. It is done so that the guests may eat the food safely.

units.la: Hæc est duplex. Vna ciborum; altera, potus; illa, cibi à dapifero; hac, potus à pincerna exploraтur.
units.tr: This is twofold: one of solid food and the other of drink. The solid food is tested by the steward (dapifer), and the drink by the cupbearer (pincerna).

units.la: Prægustator, pincerna ex cyatho hauriebat & in sinistram manum effundebat & exforbebat. Hodie in scyphum argenteum aliumve vel operculum poculi infundit & infusum prægustare & delibare solet, & postea phialam extremis manibus tenet, & convivis tradit & porrigit. Genes. cap.40.13.14.21. Nehem. cap.2.1.2. & Cyrip. ad. lib.1. Stuck. lib.2. antiquit. convivial. cap.21.
units.tr: The cupbearer, as taster, used to draw from the cup with a ladle, pour it into his left hand and sip it. Today he is accustomed to pour it into a silver bowl or some other vessel or the lid of the cup, and having poured it, to taste and sip it. Afterwards he holds the flask with his fingertips and hands it to the guests. Gen. 40.13-14, 21; Neh. 2.1-2; Cyprianus, bk. 1; Stuckius, bk. 2, Antiquitates convivales, ch. 21.

units.la: Distributio alimentorum est, qua illa inter convivas in mensa distribuuntur & diuiduntur & porriguntur. Estque vel esculentorum, vel poculentorum.
units.tr: Distribution of food is that by which the foods are divided and portioned out among the guests at table and handed round. It is either of solid food or of drinks.

units.la: Distributio ciborum est, qua cibi & esculenta mensæ impositæ in partes secantur & singulis differta ad edendum porriguntur.
units.tr: Distribution of solid food is that by which the food and dishes set on the table are cut into pieces, and the pieces, each set apart, are offered to each person to eat.

units.la: Ergo huius distributionis sunt duæ partes: una, dissectio; altera, porrectio. Dif-
units.tr: So this distribution has two parts: one, carving; the other, serving.

units.la: Dissectio est esculentorum appositorum decora incisio. Itaque scire oportet distribu- torem aptam & commodam incidendi obfo- nia rationem, quæ partes internæ, quæ externæ cuiufq; cibi,quæq; partes magis, vel minus lau- tæ & delicatæ,quo honorarioribus & digniori- bus semper partes meliores & præstantiores proponat. de qua re Sen. lib. 6. epift. 45. Alius pre- riofas aues scindit per pectus & clunes,certis du- ctibus circumferens eruditam manum, frusta excutit. Infelix qui huic vni rei viuit,vt altilia de- center secet, nisi quod miserior est, nisi qui vo- luptatis causa docet, qua qui necessitatis discit. Senec. De vit. breuit. adde Iuuenal. Satyr. 5.
units.tr: Carving is the graceful cutting of the food set out. So the carver must know the suitable and convenient way of cutting the dishes: which parts of each food are inside and which outside, and which parts are more or less choice and delicate, so that he always offers the better and more excellent parts to the more honourable and worthy. On this matter see Seneca, Epistles, bk. 6, ep. 45. Another carves costly birds through the breast and rump, moving his skilled hand along fixed lines, and shakes out the pieces. Unhappy is the one who lives for this single skill, to carve fowl decorously; yet more wretched is one who teaches it for pleasure than one who learns it out of necessity. Seneca, De brevitate vitae. Add Juvenal, Satire 5.

units.la: Instructorem interea, ne qua indignatio defit, Spectantem spectas, & cheironomonta volanti Cultello, donec peragat dictata magistri, Omnia; nec minimo sane discrimine refert Quo gestu lepores, & quo gallina secetur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, that no indignation be lacking, you watch the carver as he watches the bird, and the man who gestures with the flying knife, until he has carried out all his master's instructions. Nor, certainly, does it make much difference with what gesture hares or hen are carved.

units.la: Ne igitur in sectione hac à structore & diuisore solœcismus & indecorum committatur,solet in culina & abaco præparatio fieri.
units.tr: So that no solecism or impropriety is committed in this carving by the server or the carver, the preparation is usually made in the kitchen and at the sideboard.

units.la: Apud Iudæos hæc esculentorum & epulorū diuisio fractio dicebatur. Esa. c. 58.7. Matth. c. 14. 19. Marc. c. 6. 41. Act. cap. 27. 35. 36. Luc. cap. 9. 16. Et fiebat per conuiuatorem, vt patet ex d. locis & exemplo Dauidis 2. Sam. c. 6. 19. & partitus est vniuersa multitudini Israel tam viro quam mulieri, singulis collyridam panis vnam, & affaturam bubula carnis vnam & similam frixam oleo, &c. 1. Chron. c. 16. 3. 1. Sam. c. 1. 45. c. 9. 23. 24. Nehem. cap. 8. 12. 3 Est c. 9. 15. Genes. c. 43. 34. vid. Plutarch. lib. 1 problem. Cal. Rhodigin. lib. 28. c. 1. Hodie eiufmodi dissectio committi solet à conuiuatore, vel ab aliquo conuiuarum honoratiori in mensa, & digniori, vel peritiori in ea arte, & quandoq; iuuenibus, quandoq; etiam puellis.
units.tr: Among the Jews this division of food and of feasts was called "breaking." Isa. 58.7; Matt. 14.19; Mark 6.41; Acts 27.35-36; Luke 9.16. It was done by the host, as is clear from these passages and from the example of David: "and he distributed to all the multitude of Israel, both man and woman, to each one a cake of bread, and a piece of roast beef, and a flagon of raisins," 2 Sam. 6.19; 1 Chron. 16.3; 1 Sam. 1.4-5; 9.23-24; Neh. 8.12; Esth. 9.15; Gen. 43.34. See Plutarch, Problems, bk. 1; Caelius Rhodiginus, bk. 28, ch. 1. Today such carving is usually done by the host, or by one of the more honoured guests at table, or by one more skilled in that art, and sometimes by young men, and sometimes even by girls.

units.la: Porrectio est, qua instructor id quod dissectum est conuiuis porrigit cultro, vel quadra. Atque hic praestantioribus, dignioribus & honoratioribus, qui primo loco sunt locati primò proponit & porrigit meliores & praestantiores partes.vid. Plutarch.lib.7.problem. 4.1. Sam.c.9.23. Tum dixit Samuel coquo, cedo partem illam, quam dederam tibi, de qua dixeram tibi, repone eam apud te.24. Cumq; deprompsisset coquus armum quendam & quae harebant ei, apposuit Samuel ante Saulem, dicens, Ecce quod reliquum fuerat, ponens ante te, comede. nam in hoc tempus reseruatum tibi fuit, &c. Quandoque tamen pars praestantior, chariotibus proponitur.1.Samuel.c.1.5. Channa vero dabat partem vnam duplam, eo quod Channam diligeret, & Iehoua occlusisset vuluam eius. Genes.cap. 43.34.
units.tr: Serving is when the server offers to the guests what has been carved, on the knife or on the dish. Here he first offers the better and more excellent portions to those of the first rank, who are the more eminent, worthy and honoured. Plutarch, Problems, bk. 7, ch. 4. 1 Sam. 9.23-24: "Then Samuel said to the cook, 'Bring the portion I gave you, of which I told you, "Put it aside."' And when the cook had brought up the thigh and what was on it, he set it before Saul, saying, 'Behold what was left; set it before you and eat, for it has been kept for you until this time,' etc." Sometimes, however, the more excellent portion is offered to the dear ones: 1 Sam. 1.5, "Hannah gave a double portion, because she loved Hannah, and the LORD had closed her womb." Gen. 43.34.

units.la: Deinde ordine sequentibus particulas sedas praebet & porrigit. Est etiam in quibusdam locis consuetudo, vt abscentibus ex conuiuio partes mittantur, vt testatur Sueton. in Caligula, quod valde probat Johan. Wilhel. Stuckius lib.3. cap.3.conuiu.antiq. & cuius exemplum extat Genes. c.43.34. Et accipiens fercula de eo quod erat appositum in conspectu suo Iosephi, mittebat ad eos, maiusq; fuit ferculum Beniaminis, quam fercula singulorum illorum quintuplo. vbi Iun. & ad hoc ipsum allegat Athen.lib.1. Dipnosoph. quib. adde Nehem. cap.8.12.13. Stuck.lib.3.c.3. conuiu.antiq.
units.tr: Next, in order, he serves and passes round the smaller portions. In some places it is also the custom to send portions to those absent from the feast, as Suetonius attests in his Life of Caligula, which Johann Wilhelm Stuckius strongly approves (Stuckius, Convivia antiqua, bk. 3, ch. 3). An example is in Genesis 43:34: "And he took portions from what was set before him, and Benjamin's portion was five times greater than theirs." Junius, on this same point, also cites Athenaeus, Deipnosophists, bk. 1. To these add Nehemiah 8:12–13 and Stuckius, bk. 3, ch. 3.

units.la: Poculentorum distributio est, qua singulis conconuiuis poft cibi appofitionem & diftribuſio-nem pocula porriguntur á primo & honora-tiore faͤto initio vſq;ad vltimũ,ipfum conuiua-torem.Pocula maiora,& praeſtantiora praeſtan-tioribus& dignioribus offeruntur & porrigun-tur.Vid. •Alex.ab Alex.lib.ſ.c.21.Gen.dier.
units.tr: The distribution of cups is when, after the food has been set out and shared, drinks are handed to each of the guests, beginning with the first and most honoured and going on down to the host himself. Larger and finer cups are offered and passed to the more eminent and worthy guests. See Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, bk. 5, ch. 21.

units.la: Sequitur de alimentorum participatione & fumptione:quae duplex.Prior vel vlterior. Illa, prior:haec,posterior menfa vocatur. Vid. Alex. ab Alex.lib.5.Gen.dier.c.21.Stuck. d.lib.3. c.1. conuiui. antiq.
units.tr: The sequence concerns the sharing and taking of food, which is twofold: the first course and the later course. The first is called the prior mensa, the second the posterior mensa. See Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, bk. 5, ch. 21; Stuckius, bk. 3, ch. 1.

units.la: Prior eft,qua prima fercula menfae impofita, comeduntur & fumuntur. Haec rurfum diuidi-tur in antecoenam,feu anteprandium; vel ipfam coenam & prandium.Stuc.d.lib.3.c.1.
units.tr: The first course is that in which the first dishes placed on the table are eaten and taken. This is again divided into the fore-supper, or pre-dinner, and the supper or dinner proper. Stuckius, loc. cit., bk. 3, ch. 1.

units.la: Anticoena eiufmodi dicitur principium & proœmium conuiuii,feu prandium. Germanis ein vor effen/ conuiuium primum, quo ftoma-chus, vel ventriculus latrans, primo liquidio-ribus & concoctu facilioribus cibis, potuq; placatur, & ad alios cibos & alimenta capienda, quasi praeparatur.
units.tr: A fore-supper of this kind is the beginning and prelude of the meal, or pre-dinner. The Germans call it ein vor Essen, the first course, by which the stomach, or the barking belly, is calmed first with liquid and easily digested foods and drink, and is in a manner prepared to take other foods and nourishment.

units.la: Coena, vel ipfum prandium eft, quo cibi & potus folidiores capiuntur. Germanis dicitur, ein mittell effen/conuiuium intermedium.
units.tr: The supper, or the dinner itself, is that in which the more solid foods and drinks are taken. The Germans call it ein mittel Essen, the middle meal.

units.la: Secunda menfa eft,qua cibi fuaues & delicati ftatim poft priorem menfam remotam appofiti,vti bellaria mellita, ταγυ... ad famem fitimq; extinctam quasi rurfus accenden-dam & irritandam,fumuntur. Germani vocant ein nachf/ober Nachessen: Clem.•Alex.lib.2.cap.1. Pedag. Quocirca, ait,ii cibi cauendi funt qui no efurientes nos cogunt comedere, appetitiones nostras veluti quibusdā præstigiis fallere. Qua-les fuerint mensæ primæ & secundæ apud Ro-manos, tradit Alex.ab Alex.lib.5.Genial.diar.c.21, & de veterum vgaliitate Seneca lib.1.de tranq.& lib.de paupert lib. epist.20 & 25. & lib.22 epist.113. & 124. & lib.13 epist 87. & Stuck d.loco. Sumptuo-sissima fuerunt convivia Iulii Cæsaris, Neronis, Heliogabali, Caligulæ, Vitellii, Titi, Getæ. Vide Clem. Alex lib. 2.Padag.c.1.
units.tr: The second course is that in which sweet and delicate foods are served immediately after the first course has been removed, such as honey sweetmeats [ταγυ...], and are taken to rekindle and stir up the hunger and thirst that have been quenched. The Germans call it ein Nachessen or Nachessen. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, bk. 2, ch. 1. Hence he says: "Foods are to be avoided which force us to eat when we are not hungry, and which deceive our appetites with a kind of trickery." What the first and second courses were like among the Romans is recorded by Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, bk. 5, ch. 21, and on the luxury of the ancients Seneca, On Tranquillity, bk. 1; On Poverty; Letters 20, 25, 113, 124 and 87, and Stuckius, loc. cit. The most sumptuous banquets were those of Julius Caesar, Nero, Heliogabalus, Caligula, Vitellius, Titus and Geta. See Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, bk. 2, ch. 1.

units.la: Statim apponi debent post priorem men-sam remotam: quia interuallum ferculorum si est longum, odiosum & damnosum est ventri-culo, inquo cocta crudis miscentur, unde χύμια. Has mensas sublatas omnino cupit Stuckius d.lib.3.c.2.& Clem. Alex.d.c.1. quamuis nu-merus ordinariorum ferculorum, hodie apud nobiles & diuites ex praua consuetudine excre-uerit. De ordine vero ferculorum apponendorum, & olim & hodie variæ variorum extant consue-tudines. Vid.Turneb.in Aduers.suis, Lips.lib.3. Antiqu.lection. Sed medici in hac re consulendi. Ve-teres solebant tibicine præcedente noua fercula apponere, & conuiuæ manus lauare per singula fercula. Germanis mos est, vt singulis ferculis benedictio addatur, Das Gefegnet Gott. Cibus vero & alimenta sumuntur in die sæpius; vt ientaculum, merenda, antecœnium, cœna, postcœnium. vid. Aret.problem. 171.
units.tr: Dishes should be set out immediately after the first course has been removed, because if the interval between courses is long, it is burdensome and harmful to the stomach, in which cooked and raw food get mixed, whence come the chymia [χύμια]. Stuckius, loc. cit., bk. 3, ch. 2, and Clement of Alexandria, loc. cit., ch. 1, would have these removed altogether, although the number of ordinary courses has grown today among the nobility and the rich through bad custom. As to the order in which dishes are to be served, both in former times and today there are various customs among different peoples. See Turnebus, in his Adversaria, and Lipsius, Antiquae lectiones, bk. 3. But physicians should be consulted in this matter. The ancients used to serve new dishes with a flute-player going before, and the guests washed their hands between each course. Among the Germans it is the custom that a blessing is added to each course: Das Gesegnet Gott. Food and nourishment are taken several times a day, such as breakfast, afternoon snack, fore-supper, supper and after-supper. See Aretaeus, Problems, 171.

units.la: De alimentorum communicatione hucus-que: sequitur de sermonis communione in co-uiuio: qui sermo est colloquium, vel Musica. De colloquio Ecclesiasticus c.31. in sin. & c.32. quod Græcis dicitur ἐπιγραφὴ, ἐπιγραφὰς, συμπόσιον, συμ-
units.tr: So far on the sharing of food. Next comes the sharing of conversation at table, which is talk or music. On conversation at table see Ecclesiasticus 31 near the end and 32, which in Greek is called [ἐπιγραφὴ, ἐπιγραφὰς, συμπόσιον, συμ-]

units.la: πόσιαποσιαστικὸς, ἑσπερολόγιαι, ynde ἑσπερολόγοι, seu λογόδαι- ποι, κυλικηγόγοι.
units.tr: [πόσια, ποσιαστικὸς, ἑσπερολόγιαι], whence [ἑσπερολόγοι, or λογόδαιποι, κυλικηγόγοι]: table-talkers, evening-chatterers, cup-talkers.

units.la: Eiusmodi colloquium conuiuale, condimé-tum & anima conuiuii dicitur, sine quo illud κωφὸν κοἰ ἀφωνον dicitur. Nam non tam cibi & potus,quam sermonis communione amicitia beneuolentiaque conciliatur & conseruatur. Plutarch.lib. 4. συμπο. alimentis corpus, colloquii animus pascitur.illa, corporis; haec, animi pabulum.
units.tr: Conversation of this kind at table is called the seasoning and soul of the feast, and without it the feast is called [κωφὸν καὶ ἄφωνον], dumb and speechless. For friendship and goodwill are won and kept not so much by the sharing of food and drink as by the sharing of talk. Plutarch, Table Talk, bk. 4. The body is fed with food, the mind with conversation: the one is the nourishment of the body, the other of the mind.

units.la: In colloquio conuiuiali duo inprimis conuiuae consideranda: Materia sermonis, & eiusdem moderatio.
units.tr: At table conversation two things above all must be considered: the matter of the talk, and its moderation.

units.la: Materia colloquii talis esse debet, quae beneuolentiae & charitati non refragatur. Solet vero praecipuè esse talis, quales sunt couiuae. Vid. Gell. lib.13.c.11, qui inter epulandum sermones iucundos, inuitabiles, suaues & cum quadam illecebra & voluptate vtiles, ex quib. ingenium nostrum venustius fiat & amoenius. Quod euenient si de illis loquamur, de quibus in foro atq; in negotiis agendis loqui non est otium. Vid. Macrob. lib.7. Satur.c.1.& Stuck. lib 3 c.17. Extat etiam sympos. Platonis, Xenophontis, Luciani, Plutarchi, Athenei, Georgii Pictoris, Francisci Philelphi, Manlii & aliorum.
units.tr: The subject of conversation should be such that it does not oppose goodwill and charity. It is usually such as the guests themselves are. See Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, bk. 13, ch. 11, who speaks of pleasant, agreeable, sweet talk at dinner, which is also useful with a certain charm and delight, from which our wit becomes more graceful and pleasant. This will happen if we speak of those things about which it is not leisure to speak in the forum or while doing business. See Macrobius, Saturnalia, bk. 7, ch. 1, and Stuckius, bk. 3, ch. 17. There also exist the Symposium of Plato, the works of Xenophon, Lucian, Plutarch, Athenaeus, George Pictor, Francesco Filelfo, Manlius and others.

units.la: Solet autem materia eiusmodi esse duplex: vna, iocosa; altera, seria.
units.tr: Such subject matter is usually twofold: one is playful, the other serious.

units.la: Iocosa materia sermonis & colloquii conuiualis imprimis conuenit; quales sunt quaestiones iocosae, ioculares, ludicrae, sed argutae & scrupulosae gryphi & aenigmata: de quib. extat exemplum Iudic.c.14. facetiae, sales, cauillationes, disteria, parabolæ. Vid. Stuc. lib. 3. c. 17. convív. antiq. Joh. Heidfeldii Sphingem.
units.tr: Playful matter is especially suited to conversation at table; such are jesting questions, witticisms and playful puzzles, but clever and intricate riddles and enigmas, of which there is an example in Judges 14; jokes, witticisms, quibbles, double meanings, parables. See Stuckius, Convivia antiqua, bk. 3, ch. 17; Johann Heidfeld, Sphinx.

units.la: Seria materia sermonis potest esse sacra, vel profana. Sacra, est Theologica, de qua exempla vid. Luc. c. 14. c. 11. c. 7. c. 22. Matth. c. 26. & passim alibi. Profana est philosophica, politica, ethica, œconomica, physica, iuridica, historica, Theologica, eaq; lecta, vel enarrata. Sit ne interpocula philosophandum, disserit Plutarchus libr. 1. sympos. problem. 1. Macrob. lib. 7. c. 1. Gell. lib. 6. c. 13. Stuckius late lib. 3. c. 18. & 19.
units.tr: Serious matter may be either sacred or profane. Sacred matter is theological, examples of which are in Luke 14, 11, 7 and 22, Matthew 26, and elsewhere passim. Profane matter is philosophical, political, ethical, economic, physical, legal, historical or theological, whether read or recounted. Whether one ought to philosophise between cups is discussed by Plutarch, Table Talk, bk. 1, problem 1; Macrobius, bk. 7, ch. 1; Gellius, bk. 6, ch. 13. Stuckius treats it at length in bk. 3, chs. 18 and 19.

units.la: In materia hac conuiuialis sermonis conuiua sit φιλόφρων non ὑπερφρων, humanus, non nimis alte sapiens, σπουδαῖος, non tamen ἀστεῖος & ἀσπουδαστὸς, honestus & probus, non nimium rebus seriis gaudens. Sit quoq; εὐτράπελος, aptus & ingenuus in dicendo, non παλαμήδης, σχημα-τισμός, fictus, personatus, simulator, dissimulator, εἴρων non ἀπονευστής, non ἐπισκωπτης, φιλόγελως, nec tamen γελωτοποιὸς & κολακικὸς ad risum pronus, nec tamen futili immoderataque lætitia gestiens. φιλοπαίγμων & πιθανὸς, hoc est, cauillator facetus, nec tamen scurrili dicacitate laborans, vt refert Stuck. d. loco.
units.tr: A man in conversation at table on such matters should be [φιλόφρων], kindly, not [ὑπερφρων], haughty; humane, not too profoundly wise; [σπουδαῖος], earnest, yet not [ἀστεῖος] and [ἀσπουδαστὸς], and not frivolous; honest and upright, not overly fond of serious things. He should also be [εὐτράπελος], ready and gentle in speech, not [παλαμήδης], crafty, nor [σχηματισμός], feigned, masked, a pretender, a dissembler, an [εἴρων], ironist, not [ἀπονευστής] nor [ἐπισκωπτης], a mocker; [φιλόγελως], fond of laughter, yet not [γελωτοποιὸς] or [κολακικὸς], a buffoon or flatterer, prone to laughter; nor should he rejoice in silly and immoderate mirth. He should be [φιλοπαίγμων] and [πιθανὸς], that is, a witty joker, yet not troubled with buffoonish gibing. So Stuckius reports, loc. cit.

units.la: Moderatio sermonis inter duo extrema versatur. vnum est excessus, garrulitas, & loquacitas effusa & effrænis; quæ Græcis est ἀδολεσχία, φλυαρία, de qua sup. lib. 1. dixi: futilis, inanis & importuna, quod in buccam venerit, effutiendi licentia; quæ ebrietatis index, sicuti & λογομαχία, μισχεφλοχία, μωρολογία, λήρησις, παίγνιον. & Cato:
units.tr: Moderation in talk lies between two extremes. One is excess: garrulousness and loose, unbridled chatter, which the Greeks call [ἀδολεσχία], [φλυαρία], trifling, empty and tiresome talk, the licence of blurting out whatever comes into the mouth. I spoke of this above in bk. 1. Such talk is a sign of drunkenness, as are [λογομαχία], wrangling; [μισχεφλοχία], [μωρολογία], foolish talk; [λήρησις], nonsense; [παίγνιον], trifling. And Cato says:

units.la: Inter conuiuas fac sis sermone modestus:
units.tr: "Among your fellow-diners, see that you are modest in speech;

units.la: Ne dicare loquax, dum vis vrbanus haberi.
units.tr: do not be talkative, while you wish to be thought witty."

units.la: Alterum est defectus, taciturnitas, silentium pertinax & perpetuum. Gell.lib.13. c.11. Vid sup. cap.5. Ob hanc causam conuiuium Plutarchus dixit simile Alphabeto, & in quo sunt vocales, semiuocales, mutæ & consonantes. Vocales sunt senes, prudentes & vsuperiti. Semiuocales, sunt iuuenes & fœminæ; Eccles. cap.26.11.17.32. 1. Timoth. c.2.11. Mulier cum silentio discito cum omni submissione. 12. Mulieri enim docere non permitto, neque authoritatem vsurpare in maritum; sed mando vt sit in silentio. Mutæ, sunt ministri & famuli mensæ. Vid.Eccl.c.32.9.10. & seqq Vid.Clem.Alexan. libr.2. Pad cap.7. Eccles.c.32.c.7. Stuck. libr 3. c.17. conuiu.antiq.
units.tr: The other extreme is deficiency: taciturnity, stubborn and perpetual silence. Gellius, Attic Nights, bk. 13, ch. 11; see above, ch. 5. For this reason Plutarch likened a banquet to the alphabet, in which there are vowels, semivowels, mutes and consonants. The vowels are the old men, the prudent and experienced. The semivowels are the young men and the women: Ecclesiasticus 26:11, 17; 32; 1 Timothy 2:11–12: "Let a woman learn in silence with all submissiveness. For I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over her husband, but to be in silence." The mutes are the servants and attendants of the table. See Ecclesiasticus 32:9–10 and following; Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, bk. 2, ch. 7; Ecclesiasticus 32, ch. 7; Stuckius, Convivia antiqua, bk. 3, ch. 17.

units.la: In sermone hoc & colloquio omnino scommata vitari debent. Tectam enim continet iniuriam, inprimis quando risus præsentium sequitur. Eccles.c.31.35. In conuiuio vinoso, ne redarguas propinquum, neque facias eum nihil in lætitia eius.39. Sermonem probrosum ne dixeris ei neque angas eum obseruantem tibi. Prouerb. cap.14.3. & dixi sup. Hæc enim contraria sunt fini conuiuii, qui est beneuolentia.
units.tr: In such talk and conversation, jests must altogether be avoided. For a jest conceals an insult, especially when the laughter of those present follows it. Ecclesiasticus 31:35: "At a drinking feast, do not rebuke your neighbour, nor make light of his joy. 39: Do not speak an insulting word to him, nor press him when he is in your debt." Proverbs 14:3; and I have said so above. For these things are contrary to the purpose of a feast, which is goodwill.

units.la: Indecorum quoq; valde est indicare, quod magnam voluptatem ex edulio vel vino capias. Eccles.c.31.12. Admensam magnificam assidens, ne aperias fauces tuas in ea.13. Neque dicas, multa certe sunt impositia ei.14. Memento, malam rem esse oculum nequam. Prou. c.23.3. Ne afficiaris desiderio cupediarum eius: est enim cibus mendax.6. Ne vescitor cibo maligni oculo, neq; afficitor desiderio cupediarum eius.& seqq.
units.tr: It is also very unseemly to show that you take great pleasure in the food or the wine. Ecclesiasticus 31.12: "When you sit at a lavish table, do not open your mouth over it. 13: Do not say, 'Surely there is much set before him.' 14: Remember that a covetous eye is an evil thing." Proverbs 23.3: "Do not long for his delicacies, for it is deceptive food." 6: "Do not eat the bread of a man with an evil eye, nor long for his delicacies," and what follows.

units.la: Inciuile quoq; est eos qui mensæ adsidunt, ad bibendum comedendumve inuitare & vrgere instanter. Efficitur enim his inuitationibus vt inuitatus postea in conuiuio minus sit liber & pudore suffundatur,cum se quodam modo observari arbitretur. Leuiter&humaniter inuitare; Stuckius putat esse decorum. lib.3. c.4. Inciuile quoq; est inter comedendum loqui. Clem.Alex. lib.2.c.1.Pædag. vbi ait, quod inde fiat vox indecora,non satis expressa & significans,vt quæ plenis maxillis in angustum coerceatur; & lingua quæ nutrimento premitur,à naturali operatione præpedita expressam non edit prolationem. Maximè vero indecorum, suum cuiq; dolorem refricare in conuiuio.
units.tr: It is also uncivil for those who sit at the table to urge and press the others insistently to drink or to eat. Such invitations have the effect that the one invited is afterwards less free at the feast and is overcome with shame, since he thinks that he is being watched in a certain way. To invite gently and courteously, Stuckius thinks, is proper. Book 3, ch. 4. It is also uncivil to talk while eating. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, book 2, ch. 1, where he says that this produces an unseemly sound, not clearly expressed and not meaningful, as happens when the mouth is full and crammed, and when the tongue, pressed down by food, is hindered in its natural action and does not produce clear speech. Most unseemly of all, however, is to stir up one's own grief at a feast.

units.la: Musica, vel vocalis, vel instrumentalis in conuiuio adhiberi poterit, nisi impediat tempus, locus, vel finis conuiuii. Eccles.c.32.s.Sed cum accurata scientia agitur,musicos etiam modulos impedi. 6. Vbi est concentus,ne effundas eloquium; neq; intempestiue agas sapientem. 7. Sigillum carbunculi impositum ornamento aureo, est concentus musicorum in vinoso conuiuio. 8. Sigillum smaragdi in aureo instrumento est musicorum melos ad vinum suaue. & probat Stuckius ex Marc.c.14. Ephes c.5.18.19. Esa.c. 24.8. Amos c.6. Luc.c.15.16. Deus enim in conuiuiis hilaritatem præcipit. Deut.c.16. Nehem.c.18. ad quã efficiendam Musica conducit. Vid. Clem. Alex. lib.2.Pæd.c.4.
units.tr: Music, whether vocal or instrumental, may be used at a feast, unless the time, the place or the purpose of the feast stands in the way. Ecclesiasticus 32.5: "But when it is carried on with exact skill, do not hinder even the musical tunes." 6: "Where there is a concert, do not pour out speech; nor act wisely at an untimely moment." 7: "A seal of carbuncle set in a golden ornament is a concert of musicians at a wine feast." 8: "A seal of emerald in a golden instrument is the music of musicians with pleasant wine." Stuckius also proves this from Mark 14, Ephesians 5.18–19, Isaiah 24.8, Amos 6, Luke 15.16, for God commands cheerfulness at feasts. Deuteronomy 16; Nehemiah 18, to bring about which music is useful. See Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, book 2, ch. 4.

units.la: CAP. XII. De habitu & gestu sumendi alimenti decoro, vel contrà.
units.tr: CAP. XII. On the decorous or indecorous bearing and manner of taking food.

units.la: TAntum de communicationis speciebus. Sequitur de utriusq; habitu & gestu.
units.tr: That is all on the kinds of communication. Next comes the bearing and demeanour of each of these.

units.la: Habitus itaq; & gestus communicationis cōsistit & spectatur in modo & forma vescendi, bibendi & sermonis habendi.
units.tr: The bearing and demeanour of communication therefore lie in, and are judged by, the manner of eating, drinking and speaking.

units.la: Modus edendi & bibendi positus est in temperantia, qua neq; in excessu, neq; in defectu peccamus, sed tantum edimus & bibimus, quantum natura postulat, non quantum cupiditas expedit. Vid. Alex. ab Alex. lib. 5. c. 21. Gen. diser. Huc observans modum, vocatur σύμπρκης, ὀλιγοδίης, ὀλιγοέιτ, νηφων, μετεχωτ, μετεχοιτ, hoc est, tenui atque frugali victu potuq; contentus, non ἀπλήστος, πολύφαγος, ἔδων, μεθύων, χαμαιπαλών, id est, insatiabilis, vinosus, ebriosus, crapulæ deditus, cum ὀψοφαγία, λιμαργία, γαστριμαργία. Vid. Luc. Cal. Rho. lib. 30. c. 36. Gell. lib. 13. c. 11. Plutarch. de tuend val. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Paed. c. 1, c. 2, c. 3, c. 4. lib. 3. c. 7. Stuck. lib. 1. c. 1. convivi. antiq.
units.tr: The manner of eating and drinking consists in temperance, by which we sin neither by excess nor by deficiency, but eat and drink only as much as nature requires, not as much as appetite desires. See Alexander ab Alexandro, bk 5, ch. 21; Gen. diser. Observing this measure, a man is called σώφρων, ὀλιγοδιαιτος, ὀλιγοεδής, νηφάλιος, μετριοπαθής [sophron, oligodiaitos, oligoedes, nephalios, metriopathes], that is, content with a thin and frugal diet and drink, not ἀπλήστος, πολύφαγος, ἔδων, μεθύων, χαμαιπαλών [aplestos, polyphagos, edon, methyon, chamaipalon], that is, insatiable, a glutton, a drunkard, given over to drunken revelry, along with ὀψοφαγία, λιμαργία, γαστριμαργία [opsophagia, limargia, gastrimargia]. See Lucius Caelius Rhodiginus, bk 30, ch. 36; Gellius, bk 13, ch. 11; Plutarch, On the Preservation of Health; Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus bk 2, chs 1–4, bk 3, ch. 7; Stuckius, bk 1, ch. 1, On Ancient Banquets.

units.la: Parce igitur & sobrie edendum & bibendum est eo modo, quo robur corporis & pietas animæ vegetior atq; alacrior fiat, non autem obtorpescat & obruatur. Rom. c. 13. in sin. 1. Thess. c. 5. 6. 7. 8. 1. Timoth. c. 5. Vino modico utere, &c. Luc. c. 21. 3. 4.
units.tr: Therefore one must eat and drink sparingly and soberly, in such a way that the strength of the body and the piety of the soul become more lively and alert, and not dulled and overwhelmed. Rom. 13 at the end; 1 Thess. 5:6–8; 1 Tim. 5 ("Use a little wine," etc.); Luke 21:3–4.

units.la: Cauete autem vobis, ne quando grauentur corda vestra crapula & ebrietate & curis huius vitæ & repente superueniat vobis dies ille. Prov. cap. 23. 29. Cui væ? cui eheu? cui contentiones? cui loquacitas? cui vulnera impune? cui robur oculorum est? 30. Immorantes tibus apud vinum, euntibus ad inuestigandum vi-num mistum. 31. Ne respicito vinum quum rubescit, quum exhibet in poculo colorem suum, indesinenter monetur recte issimè. 32. Tandem velut serpens mordebit, & vt hamorrhous punget, & seqq. Ecclesiastis capite 10.13. Hei tibi regio, cuius rex est puer, & cuius Principes mane comedunt. 14. O te beatam regionem, cuius rex natus est clarissimus, & cuius principes suo tempore comedunt, ad robur, non autem ad compotationem. Philip.cap 3.19. quorum Deus est venter. Esa. c.5.11. Væ surgentibus summo mane, vt potum inebriantem sectentur, prorogantibus ad crepusculum vsq; vt vinum incendat ipsos. & v. 22. Væ valentibus potare vinum, & strenuis ad miscendum potum inebriantem, cap.28.1.2 Eccl.c.37.32. Ne esto insaturabilis omnibus deliciis, neque proiectus esto ad escas. 33. Nā multis cibis adhæret morbus, & insatiabilis voracitas proximè accedit choleram. 34. Voracitate insatiabili multi sunt mortui; sed qui attendit sibi, vitam propagaturus est. & c.31.19. neq; esto insatiabilis, ne forte offendas. & v.seqq.21. Quam sufficit homini erudito res modica? nam in cubili suo non anhelat. Somnus sanus est, cum intestino mediocri: surgit mane compos animæ suæ. 22. Laboriosæ vigilia & cholera tormina- que adsunt viro insatiabili. 28. In vino ne agas virum, nam vinum multos perdidit. & c.30. Tanquam vita est vinum hominibus, si moderate illud biberis. 31. Quænam vita est homini qui destituitur vino? hoc n. creatum est ad lætitiam hominibus. 32. Exsultatione cordis lætitiamque animi efficit vinum potum tempestiue, quod satis est. & vers seqq. Ephe.c.5. Neinebriamini vino, in quo est luxuria. Amos.c.6. Qui biibunt vinum percolatum & super lectum sedeni eburneum. neum. Prou. c. 25. 16. Mel inueniens, comedis quod satis est tibi. ne saturatus illo euomas illud, & c. 31. 4. 5. 6. 7. Prou c. 23. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. c. 20. Rom. c. 13. 14. Carnis curam ne habete ad explendas cupiditates. 1. Cor. c. 9. 27. Contundo corpus meum & in seruitutem redigo. Senec. lib. 22. epist. 124. Ad mensam adferat bene moratum ventrem & contumelia patientem. & lib. 1. De tranquil. vit. Cibus, inquit, famem domet & potio sitim. & lib. 3. Epist. 21. in sin. Venter praecepta non audit, poscit, appellat. Non est tamen molestus creditor: parvo dimittitur, si modo das illi quod debes, non quod potes. Itaque ut idem Senec. lib. De pauper. loquitur, parvo fames & sitis constat, magno vero fastidium.
units.tr: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly" (Luke 21:34). Prov. 23:29–35: "Who has woe? who has alas? who has contentions? who has babbling? who has wounds without cause? who has redness of eyes? They who tarry long at the wine, they who go to seek mixed wine. Do not look upon the wine when it is red, when it shows its colour in the cup; it is recommended without ceasing, most rightly. In the end it will bite like a serpent and sting like a viper." Eccl. 10:16–17: "Woe to you, land whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning. O blessed land, whose king is noble, and whose princes eat in their time, for strength and not for drunkenness." Phil. 3:19: "whose god is the belly." Isa. 5:11: "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to follow strong drink, who linger until evening until wine inflames them." And v. 22: "Woe to those who are mighty to drink wine, and valiant to mix strong drink;" Isa. 28:1–2. Ecclus 37:32–34: "Do not be insatiable in any delicacy, nor be given over to food. For many dishes bring sickness, and insatiable greed brings on bile. Many have died of insatiable greed; but whoever takes care of himself will prolong his life." And Ecclus 31:19: "Do not be insatiable, lest you give offence." And vv. 21ff.: "What is a modest portion enough for a learned man? For he does not gasp in his bed. Sleep is sound with a moderate stomach; he rises in the morning in command of his soul. Labour, watching, bile and gripes come upon the insatiable man. Do not make yourself a man of wine, for wine has destroyed many. Wine is like life to men, if you drink it in moderation. What life is it for a man who is deprived of wine? For it was made to bring joy to men. Wine drunk in its time and in due measure produces exultation of heart and gladness of mind." And the following verses. Eph. 5:18: "Do not be drunk with wine, in which is excess." Amos 6:4–6: "Who drink wine by the bowlful, and lie on beds of ivory." Prov. 25:16: "If you find honey, eat what is enough for you, lest, being filled with it, you vomit it up." And 31:4–7; Prov. 23:1–3ff.; Prov. 20. Rom. 13:13–14: "Make no provision for the flesh to satisfy its lusts." 1 Cor. 9:27: "I beat my body and bring it into subjection." Seneca, Letter 124 (bk 22): "Let him bring to the table a well-behaved belly that can bear rebuke." And bk 1, On Tranquillity of Mind: "Food, he says, should tame hunger, and drink thirst." And bk 3, Letter 21, near the end: "The belly does not heed precepts; it demands, it calls. Yet it is not a troublesome creditor: it is put off cheaply, if only you give it what you owe, not what you could." So, as the same Seneca says in his book On Poverty, hunger and thirst are satisfied cheaply, but surfeit at great cost.

units.la: Modus bibendi honestus, est vel medicus vel liberalis; necessitatis, inquam, & sanitatis; vel voluptatis & liberalitatis. Lud. Cel. Rhod libr. 15. c. 16. tres crateras miscedos ait; quorum primus, est sanitatis; secundus, voluptatis; tertius, somni; quartus & reliqui inciuiles. Esl. c. 1. 7. Et potum praebebant ministri in vasis aureis & vasis inter se variis, vinumque regium plurimum pro facultate regis. 8. Potum autem ex iure nemo exigebat. sic enim constituerat Rex unicuique magistro domus sue, ut facerent pro voluntate cuiusque. Prou. c. 13. 25. Iustus comedit ad satietatem animae sue, venter autem improborum eget. Modesti & verecundi hominis est in cibo & potu quod minus est, eligere, idque tardius, & non procliuius. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Paed. c. 7. per Eccl. c. 31. Isocrates ad Demonic. Fuge quantum potes compotationes; sed si quando in has per tempus incideris, fac discedas ante ebrietatem. Vbi enim vinum corrumperit mentem, euenit quod curribus spoliatis magistro. Et quod est in corde jobru, id est in lingua ebru.
units.tr: The honourable manner of drinking is either medicinal or liberal: that is, of necessity and health, or of pleasure and generosity. Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, bk 15, ch. 16, says that three mixing bowls should be used: the first is for health, the second for pleasure, the third for sleep; the fourth and the rest are uncivil. Esther 1:7–8: "And the servants gave drink in golden vessels, and vessels differing among themselves, and the royal wine in great plenty, according to the king's means. Now no one was compelled to drink; for the king had so ordered each steward of his house, that they should do according to each man's will." Prov. 13:25: "The righteous eats to the satisfying of his soul, but the belly of the wicked is in need." It is the mark of a modest and bashful man, in food and drink, to choose what is less, and to do so slowly and not eagerly. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus bk 2, ch. 7, citing Ecclus 31. Isocrates, To Demonicus: "Avoid drinking parties as far as you can; but if at any time you fall into them, see that you leave before drunkenness. For when wine corrupts the mind, it happens as with a charioteer stripped of his chariot." And what is in the heart of the drunk is in the tongue of the drunk.

units.la: Y
units.tr: Y

units.la: Forma conuiuandi,seu comedendi & bibendi, consistit in gestibus & actionibus decentibus assumendis & vtendis, vel indecoris omittendis.
units.tr: The form of feasting, or of eating and drinking, consists in taking up and using decent gestures and actions, and in leaving off indecorous ones.

units.la: Gestus & habitus decori sunt, qui hilares, humani, vrbani, ciuiles & moderati sunt.
units.tr: Decorous gestures and bearing are those that are cheerful, humane, courteous, civil and moderate.

units.la: Debet ergo conuiua, nisi scopus conuiuii & tempus & locus prohibeat, esse hilaris, non tristis, tetricus gestu & habitu εὐπροσώπως. Eccles. cap. 9. 9. Agedum, comede cum laetitia cibum tuum, & bibe animo hilari vinum tuum, quando-cunque beneuole prosequitur Deus facta tua, & seqq. Actor. cap. 2. 46. Et quotidie perdurantes concorditer ac frangentes domi panem, capiebant cibum cum exultatione ac simplicitate cordis. 47. Laudantes Deum, habentes gratiam apud totum populum. Genef. c. 43. 34. sic conuiuati sunt & effatim biberunt cum eo. Deut. c. 12. 7. Vt comedatis ibi coram Iehoua Deo vestro, & laetemini, vos & familia vestra, comedentes ex omni re ad quam admoueritis manum, qua benedixerit tibi Iehoua Deus tuus.
units.tr: A guest, therefore, unless the purpose of the feast, the time or the place forbids it, ought to be cheerful, not sad, and not sullen in gesture and bearing, εὐπροσώπως [euprosopos]. Eccl. 9:7: "Go, eat your bread with gladness, and drink your wine with a merry heart, since God has already favourably accepted your works." Acts 2:46: "And continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, they took their food with exultation and simplicity of heart. Praising God, and having favour with all the people." Gen. 43:34: "So they feasted with him and drank freely." Deut. 12:7: "That you may eat there before the LORD your God, and rejoice, you and your household, eating of everything to which you put your hand, wherein the LORD your God has blessed you."

units.la: Deinde conuiua gestu & habitu suo ad societate propensus & procliuis esse debet, vt Stuck. lib. 2. cap. 1. conu. antiqui. refert ex Polluce: cuius alis conuiua dicitur συμποτικὸς, ἁμικτὸς, ἐνεπιμικτὸς, ἀξιοκρινὴς, χρηστικὸς, συνδειπνος, cui opponitur ἁμικτὸς.
units.tr: Next, by his gestures and bearing a guest ought to be inclined and prone to fellowship, as Stuckius, bk 2, ch. 1, On Ancient Banquets, reports from Pollux. From this the guest is called συμποτικός [sympotikos], ἄμικτος [amiktos], ἐνεπιμικτός [enepimiktos], ἀξιοκρινής [axiokrines], χρηστικός [chrestikos], σύνδειπνος [syndeipnos], and the opposite of this is ἄμικτος [amiktos], unsociable.

units.la: Tertio debet esse ἁπλοῦς, εὐαρμοστικός, vrbanus, apertis & decoris gestibus praeditus: cui opponitur ἀγροικος, βαρὺς, φορτικὸς, ἰταμός, id est, agrestis, grauis, durus, odiosus, importunus.
units.tr: Thirdly, he ought to be ἁπλοῦς [haplous], εὐαρμοστικός [euarmostikos], courteous, and endowed with open and becoming gestures. The opposite is ἀγροικος [agroikos], βαρὺς [barys], φορτικὸς [phortikos], ἰταμός [itamos], that is, boorish, heavy, coarse, and insolent.

units.la: Quarto debet esse ciuilis, moderatus, mansuetus, non ἀλαζὼν, ὑπερήφανος, κομπαστής, ὑβριστής, superbus, arrogans, suspiciosus, iactator.
units.tr: Fourthly, he ought to be civil, moderate and gentle, not boastful (ἀλαζὼν), haughty (ὑπερήφανος), vainglorious (κομπαστής), insolent (ὑβριστής), proud, arrogant, suspicious or a braggart.

units.la: Forma bibendi in conuiuiis vsitata est propinatio, quæ Græcis dicitur φιλοτησία, seu amica invitatio. de qua apud Habacuc. 2.15.16. Est. c.1.7.8. Iob. c.22.7.
units.tr: The customary form of drinking at banquets is the toast, which the Greeks call φιλοτησία [philotēsia], that is, a friendly invitation. Concerning this see Habakkuk 2.15, 16; Esther 1.7, 8; Job 22.7.

units.la: Propinatio apud Hebræos fiebat ita: paterf. dextera manu poculum tenens, præmissis certis quibusdā precib. propinationem auspicabatur, præbibens; quem reliqui conuiuæ ex ordine sequebantur. Græci & Romani à dextera propinando & præbibendo incipiebant, & in orbe pergebant & continuabant. Vid. Stuck. lib.3.c.11.12. &seq. d.loc. quæ methodus propinandi, hodie in quibusdam locis obseruatur. In quibusdam verò fine ordine ex arbitrio conuiuarum præbibentiū propinatio peragitur, modo in orbem, modo in transuersum. Quæ in orbem fit, dicitur circularis propinatio, circumpotatio, κυκλοπστοσία.
units.tr: Among the Hebrews the toast was made thus: the host, holding the cup in his right hand, began the drinking with certain set prayers, drinking first; the other guests followed him in order. The Greeks and Romans began drinking and passing the cup from the right, and went on and continued around the circle. See Stuckius, book 3, chapters 11 and 12 and following, in the place cited. This method of toasting is still observed today in some places. In others, the toasting is carried out without order, at the will of the guests who drink first, sometimes around the circle, sometimes across the table. The toast that goes around the circle is called the circular toast, circumpotation, κυκλοπστοσία [kyklopotosia].

units.la: Propinatio à sympofiarcha incepta, solet in quibusdam locis à minoribus. ad maiora pocula procedere. De poculorum quantitate, de more ad certam mensuram poculorum, atq; numerum propinandi, vid. Stuck. d. lib.3. c.12.
units.tr: A toast begun by the master of the feast is often, in some places, passed from smaller cups to larger ones. On the size of the cups, on the custom of a fixed measure of cups and the number of toasts, see Stuckius, book 3, chapter 12, cited above.

units.la: In edendo labra continenda cum cibus mandetur, neq; hiare sinenda. Buccellas, non nimis amplas, aut densas, hianti ore capiat: integros bolos, magno gutturis hiatu deglutire indecorum. Neq; oblonii multum est ingerendum, sed cum pane sumendum.
units.tr: When eating, one must keep the lips closed while the food is chewed, and not let the mouth gape. He should take morsels that are not too large or too thick, with the mouth closed; it is unseemly to swallow whole mouthfuls with a wide gaping of the throat. Nor should much be thrust into the mouth at once from a dish of pottage, but it should be taken with bread.

units.la: Quod ante aliquem appositum in orbiculo, retinendum, nisi plus sit, quam sine crimine vo-racitatis absumptum esse videri possit. tum enim refectâ particulâ, reliquum confixum sultello, reponendum ante illum, qui apposuit. aut proximum, aut in patinam referendum.
units.tr: What has been set before someone on a small plate should be left alone, unless there is more than could be consumed without being thought greedy. Then, when he has eaten a little, the rest, fixed on the knife, should be put back in front of the one who set it there, or next to him, or returned to the dish.

units.la: Indecori gestus conuiuiales omittendi sunt, qui sensibus interioribus, vel exterioribus hominis contrarii, &c, per consequens illiciti & indecentes conspiciuntur in ipso actu conuiuandi, vel in incidentibus in conuiuio.
units.tr: Unseemly gestures are to be avoided at banquets; these are the ones that are contrary to the inner or outer senses of a man, etc., and are consequently seen to be unlawful and indecent in the very act of dining, or in the incidents that occur at the banquet.
