units.la: In ipso edendi bibendive actu indecentes sunt gestus & habitus sequentes.
units.tr: In the very act of eating and drinking, the following gestures and manners are unbecoming.

units.la: Cum quadam vorandi ingluuie ita auide cibos ingerere, vt ex eo singultus, vel aliud quippiam visu & auditu indecorum audiatur. Sicuti faciunt ii, qui inter epulandum ita properant, vt flatu & anhelitu suo, omnibus qui adsunt, molesti sint. Prou. cap. 23. 18. Intelligere resp propinqui & de omni verbo cogita. Comede, vt homo, quae apposita sunt tibi, neque deuora, ne odio habearis. 19. Cessa primum, eruditionis gratia, neq; esto insatiabilis, ne forte offendas. & Eccles. c. 21. 18. 19. Et cap. 37. 32. Neefto insatiabilis omnibus delicijs, neq; profectus ad esca. vid. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. c. 1. Paed. c. 7.
units.tr: To gulp down food so greedily, with a certain gluttonous devouring, that hiccups or something else unseemly to sight and hearing is heard. Such are those who hurry so much at the meal that they become a nuisance to everyone present with their puffing and panting. Proverbs 23.18, 19: "Consider, if you sit to eat with a ruler, what is set before you, and put a knife to your throat; do not desire his dainties, for they are deceitful food." Ecclesiasticus 21.18, 19; and 37.32: "Be not insatiable in any delicacy, nor eat greedily of meat." See Clement of Alexandria, book 2, chapter 1, Paedagogus, chapter 7.

units.la: Inter manducandum quassatione oris & labiorum, velut poppysmate, vel inflatis buccis, sonitu quodam nouo aures offendere, indecorum. vid. Prou. d. cap. 23. 18. Lingua quasi repurgare dentes, ac palatum interius, & buccas lambere, foedum; & foedius, exterius labra; turpius, quando ex ore inter edendum, vel bibendum quid excidit vel effluit.
units.tr: While chewing, to strike the mouth and lips together, as with a smack, or to puff out the cheeks and make some strange noise, offends the ears; it is unseemly. See Proverbs 23.18, cited above. To lick the teeth and the inner palate with the tongue, as though cleaning them, and to lick the cheeks, is foul; and more foul is licking the outer lips; more shameful still is when something falls or runs out of the mouth while eating or drinking.

units.la: Instar porcorum, toto quasi rostro sine intermissione iuri immersum esse, vt ne semel quidem faciem attollas, aut oculos, atq; adeo multo minus manus a cibis appositis quoquam dimoueas, valde inciuile. Clem. Alex. d. c. 1.
units.tr: To have the face plunged into the broth with the whole snout, like pigs, without pause, so that one does not lift the face or eyes even once, much less take the hands away from the food set before one for any reason, is very uncivil. See Clement of Alexandria, cited above, chapter 1.

units.la: Brachiis in mensam procumbere non decet; aut ambas buccas ita cibo implere, vt malæ intumescant.
units.tr: It is not becoming to lean on the arms over the table, or to fill both cheeks with food so that the jaws swell.

units.la: Item, manus pene ad cubitum vsq; commaculare, & mantilia eum in modum conspurcare, vt panni illi laceri & sordibus abstergendis destinati, nonnunquam his mundiores esse deprehendantur.
units.tr: Likewise, to soil the hands almost up to the elbows and to smear the napkins in such a way that those cloths, meant for wiping off dirt, are sometimes found cleaner than the hands.

units.la: Similiter ob festinationem & studium vorandi immodico sudore in facie, vel fronte, vel collo diffluere.
units.tr: Similarly, from haste and eagerness to devour, to drip with excessive sweat on the face, forehead or neck is unseemly.

units.la: Digitos inungere, barbam polluere, vt inde mantile vel thorax contaminetur, & videnti nausea moueatur, indecorum.
units.tr: To grease the fingers, to foul the beard, so that the tablecloth or the breast is stained, and the sight provokes nausea, is unseemly.

units.la: Poculum vini, è quo alius, vel tu ipse bibiturus es, aut cibum, qui alteri apponitur comedendus, vel quem ipsemet esurus es, odorandi gratia ad nasum mouere.
units.tr: To move a cup of wine, from which another or you yourself are about to drink, or food that is set before another to be eaten, or that you yourself are about to eat, to the nose for the sake of smelling it, is unseemly.

units.la: Simul edere & bibere, vel ore pleno bibere aut loqui, valde indecorum. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. c. 1. Pædag.
units.tr: To eat and drink at the same time, or to drink or speak with a full mouth, is very unseemly. See Clement of Alexandria, book 2, chapter 1, Paedagogus.

units.la: In mandendo, labiorum deductu, more porcorum sonitum edere & instar equi, vaccæ, vel canis edere, deglutire, vel sorbere, vel bibere cum lachrimis & exclusione spiritus, indecorum, sæpius quando cum susurro potus magno impetu fertur & plurimo spiritu & hiatu attrahitur, perinde ac si in vas fictile infundatur & gutture sonet ob rapidam ingurgitationem. Vid. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Pæd. c. 2.
units.tr: While chewing, to make a noise with the lips drawn back, in the manner of pigs, or to make a sound like a horse, cow or dog, to swallow, to slurp, or to drink with tears and forcing out the breath, is unseemly; most often when the drink is carried with a loud gulp and drawn in with great force, breath and gaping, as if poured into an earthen vessel, so that the throat sounds from the rapid gulping. See Clement of Alexandria, book 2, Paedagogus, chapter 2.

units.la: Vultu instabili, huc illuc inter bibendum alios intortis oculis intueri, ceruicē in tergum reiicere, mentum conspergere, inciuile. Clem. Alex. d. li. 2. Pæd. c. 2.
units.tr: To look at others while drinking, with an unsteady face, turning the eyes here and there with a squint, to throw the neck back, or to spatter the chin, is uncivil. See Clement of Alexandria, cited above, book 2, Paedagogus, chapter 2.

units.la: Calidiufculas offulas, veliufcula, vehemen-ter & violenter afflare plenis buccis, tanquam é follibus, indecorum. Pollice, vel alio digito, vel lingua oua elixa excauare non decet.
units.tr: To blow on rather hot morsels, or on very hot ones, violently and forcefully with full cheeks, as from bellows, is unseemly. It is not proper to scoop out a boiled egg with the thumb, another finger, or the tongue.

units.la: In patinam appositam in medium manum primo inter conuiuas alios praestantiores extendere. Eccles. c. 31. 20. Quod si inter plures consideris, ne primum eorum extendas manum tuam: neque immitte manum in omnes patina plagas. Eccles. c. 31. 16. 17. neque eandem patinam circumage, vt lautiora adta perueniant.
units.tr: To stretch out one's hand first into the middle of the dish set before the guests, ahead of the other, more distinguished guests. See Ecclesiasticus 31.20: "If you sit among many, do not stretch out your hand first among them, nor put your hand into every dish." Ecclesiasticus 31.16, 17: nor should one pass the same dish around, so that the more dainty dishes come to the others.

units.la: Non decet quoque digitos ore praelingere vel salino illos intingere, vel ad tunicam exter-gere, vel gesticulari manibus, digitis, cultello pedibusve.
units.tr: It is also not fitting to lick the fingers with the mouth, or to dip them in salt, or wipe them on one's tunic, or to gesticulate with hands, fingers, knife or feet.

units.la: In patinas praemorsum inferere inciuile, vel praemorsum iterum in ius immergere: turpe vero cibum mansum e faucib' eximere, & in quadram reponere.
units.tr: To put back into the dishes a morsel already bitten is uncivil, or to dip a half-eaten bite into the broth again; but it is shameful to take out chewed food from the mouth and put it on the plate.

units.la: In incidentibus in ipso conuiuio & actu edendi & bibendi gestus & habitus indecori & inciuiles, sunt sequentes.
units.tr: Among the gestures and manners that are unseemly and uncivil in the incidents of the banquet itself and of the act of eating and drinking, are the following.

units.la: Nimirum inter accumbendum partem aliquam corporis scabere.
units.tr: Namely, to scratch some part of the body while reclining at table.

units.la: Tempore mensae seu conuiuii exspuere, vel emungere nasum, vel excreare. Clem. Alex. libr. 2. c. 7. Paedag. Non enim sicuti asinis & bobus simul est praesepium & sterquilinium. Quod si necessitas haec facere vrgeat, faciendum id cum quodam decenti modo, facie auersa ab epulis & poculis & hominibus.
units.tr: To spit, blow the nose or clear the throat at the time of the table or banquet. See Clement of Alexandria, book 2, chapter 7, Paedagogus. For there is not, as with asses and oxen, a manger and a dunghill together. But if necessity urges this, it should be done in a becoming manner, with the face turned away from the meal, the cups and the people.

units.la: Ructus edere, sternutare, oscitare, aures fricare, crepitu vetris emittere, turpe. Clem. Alex. li. 2. c. 7. Stuckius. 3. antiqu. conu. c. 19. Dentes mappâ, vel linteolo, digitis, vel cultello fricare, indecorum.
units.tr: To belch, sneeze, yawn, rub the ears, or to release wind with a noise from the belly, is shameful. See Clement of Alexandria, book 2, chapter 7; Stuckius, book 3, Antiquitates convivales, chapter 19. To rub the teeth with a napkin or a little cloth, or with the fingers or a knife, is unseemly.

units.la: In praesentia aliorum os eluere, aut vinum, quo id feceris, exspuere.
units.tr: In the presence of others, to rinse the mouth, or to spit out the wine with which you have done so, is unseemly.

units.la: Vitrum, vel poculum, quo tu biberis, alteri, vt bibat porrigere; nisi forte plusquam domestica familiaritate tibi sit ille notus, vel consuetudo illud requirat. Similiter indecorum, mensam vel quadrā, aut orbiculū subinde fodere. in poculo apparere supernatante pinguedine autsagimen.
units.tr: To hand a glass or cup from which you have drunk to another, for him to drink from, unless perhaps he is known to you with more than household familiarity, or custom requires it. Likewise it is unseemly to keep digging into the table, or the tablecloth, or the dish, now and then, or to let grease or fat float on the surface of the cup.

units.la: Ex patina alteri aliquid porrigere inciuile habetur: nisi forte is qui porrigit, prae altero multo maioris sit dignitatis, ita vt is qui accipit, eadem opera honore afficiatur, vt exemplis Iosephi. Genef. c. 43. 34. Samuelis. 1. Sam. c. 9. 23. 24. vbi Iun. & c. 1. 45. Ruth. c. 2. 14. constat. Nam si inter aequales hoc fiat, videtur is qui porrigit alteri, quodam modo se praeponere, aliquando etiam id quod porrigitur, alterius palato non conuenit, praesertim quod ille iudicet conuiuium non satis liberaliter esse instructum aut certe patellas ordine praepostero collocatas, cum alter abundet, alter egeat. Fieri quoq; posset vt conuiuator id in malam partem acciperet. Nihilominus tamen & hic, quod vulgo fieri videmus, faciendum est potius, quam id quod bene fieri existimatur. Verum quicquid in hoc deceat, vel non, tu tamen id quod tibi porrigitur, non recusabis; sed sumes quadra, vel trib. digitis vel cultro: videris alias eum qui porrigit, vel aspernari vel reprehendere.
units.tr: To hand something to another from one's own dish is regarded as uncivil, unless perhaps the one who hands it over is of much greater dignity than the other, so that the one who receives it is at the same time honoured, as is clear from the examples of Joseph (Genesis 43.34), Samuel (1 Samuel 9.23, 24, where see Junius), and Ruth (Ruth 2.14; see also 1.45). For if this is done among equals, the one who hands it to another seems in some way to set himself above him, and sometimes what is handed over does not suit the other's palate, especially since he may judge that the banquet has not been furnished generously enough, or that the plates are arranged in a wrong order, one man having plenty while another lacks. It could also happen that the host would take it in bad part. Nevertheless, here too, what we see commonly done is to be done rather than what is thought to be done well. But whatever is proper in this matter or not, you will not refuse what is handed to you; you will take it with the hand, or with three fingers, or with the knife, lest you seem to scorn or rebuke the one who hands it to you.

units.la: Foedum est extimulare cultello, si quid forte inter dentes haeserit.
units.tr: It is ugly to pick at your teeth with a knife if something has stuck between them.

units.la: Panem decorticare, vel excauare aliis, edentulo excepto, indecorum est.
units.tr: To peel bread or hollow it out for others is indecent, except for the toothless.

units.la: Similiter cogitabundum accumbere & stupere, nec nō oculis circumactis obseruare, quid quilibet comedat vel transuersim hirquis intueri, qui eodem accumbunt latere, aut retorto in tergum capite contemplari, quid rerum geratur in altera mensa. Rectè tamen & decorè potest, pater filios; dominus seruos; magistratus subditos; doctor auditores & discipulos in eadem vel altera mensa accumbentes obseruare. Præsertim, si clamores, turbas, rixas aliosve indecoros gestus ob causam suspicetur.
units.tr: Likewise, it is indecent to sit lost in thought and gape, or to glance about and watch what each person is eating, or to stare sideways at the goats who recline on the same couch, or to crane your head back over your shoulder and gaze at what is going on at the other table. It is, however, right and proper for a father to watch his sons, a master his servants, a magistrate his subjects, and a teacher his pupils and students who recline at the same table or at another; especially if he suspects shouting, disorder, quarrels, or other unseemly behaviour as the cause.

units.la: Canes inter comedendum tractare, vel pascere, inciuile.
units.tr: To handle or feed dogs during the meal is uncivil.

units.la: Panem, pyrum, aut quemuis alium fructum, dentibus suis arrosum, vel alia semesa, alteri dare, vel porrigere.
units.tr: To give or pass to another a piece of bread, a pear, or any other fruit that you have gnawed with your teeth, or any other half-eaten food, is improper.

units.la: Iisdem mantilibus, quibus in mensa vteris, sudorem abstergere, aut nasum emungere, non decet.
units.tr: It is not fitting to wipe your sweat or blow your nose with the same napkins you use at the table.

units.la: Nulli propinare in conuiuio, est illiberale & inciuile, ἀχαριστητος, ἀντλαυθεγ.
units.tr: Not to drink to anyone at a banquet is illiberal and uncivil: ἀχαριστητος, ἀντλαυθεγ.

units.la: Maioribus, vel pluribus iteratis poculis propinare, & inuitos compotando molestare & certare, & in eo suum robur ostendere, turpe est. Eccles. c. 31. 28. In vino ne agasvirum. Esa. c. 5. 22. Va valentibus potare vinum & strenuis ad miscendum potum inebriantem. Quartus cyathus non est noster, sed contumelia. Quintus, vociferationis. Sextus, lasciuia. Septimus, fuggillationum. Octauus, clamantis. Nonus, bilis. Decimus, insania, vt dicit Lud. Cœl. Rhodigin. lib. 15. c. 16.
units.tr: To pledge others with larger or repeated cups, to pester and contend with unwilling drinkers by forcing them to drink, and to show off your own strength in this, is shameful. Ecclesiasticus 31:28: "Do not be the master of the wine-jar" (In vino ne agasvirum). Isaiah 5:22: "Woe to those who are mighty to drink wine and valiant at mixing strong drink." The fourth cup is not ours but is an insult; the fifth is for shouting; the sixth for wantonness; the seventh for slander; the eighth for clamour; the ninth for bile; the tenth for madness, as Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus says, book 15, chapter 16.

units.la: Quod si ab alio inuiteris ad bibendum, non omnino repugnato, sed gratias agito, & dicito te libenter illi victoriam concedere, aut etiam sine hausti liberaliore, vel largiori, leuiter quod datum est, degustato.
units.tr: But if you are invited to drink by another, do not refuse outright; rather give thanks, say that you gladly yield the victory to him, or, even without drinking, taste lightly what has been given, whether it is a larger or a more generous draught.

units.la: Vinum vel escam effundere, vel perdere, & mensam vel cænaculum commaculare, indecorum. Eiusmodi inciuiles dicuntur κοτταβίζοντες vel, κότταβοι, à cottabis veterum, atque hinc cottabismus, vomitio, Kotzen. Vid. Lud. Cal. Rhodig. lib. 18. c. 5.
units.tr: To spill or waste wine or food, and to stain the table or dining room, is unseemly. Such ill-mannered people are called κοτταβίζοντες or κότταβοι, from the cottabus of the ancients, and hence "cottabism," the vomiting game, Kotzen. See Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, book 18, chapter 5.

units.la: Mensis sublatis, dentiscalpium ori infertum, instar auiculæ nidum construentis circumferre, aut id ipsum supra aurem tonsorum more reponere, indecorum existimatur.
units.tr: When the tables have been cleared, to carry a toothpick in the mouth and move it about like a little bird building its nest, or to put it back behind the ear in the manner of barbers, is judged indecent.

units.la: Gesticulationibus ludisque histrionicis uti in copotando & præbibendo inciuile est, videlicet ἀμυστὶ ψαλ ἀπνιστὶ πίνειν, drincken ohn schnauben vnd bart wüschen/ quæ gesticulationes ex imperio conuiuatoris vel conuiuarum arbitrio, poenis & præmiis indictis præscribi solent. Vid. Turnebus lib. 7. c. 9. aduerf. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Paedag. c. 2, Plin. lib. 14. c. 22. Plutarch. lib. 1. Sympos. problem. 4. & Stuckium d. loco.
units.tr: To use gestures and theatrical antics while drinking or pledging is uncivil, namely ἀμυστὶ ψαλ ἀπνιστὶ πίνειν, drinking without blowing or wiping the beard, "drincken ohn schnauben vnd bart wüschen". Such gestures are usually prescribed by the command of the host or by the decision of the company, with penalties and rewards appointed. See Turnebus, book 7, chapter 9, against Clement of Alexandria, book 2 of the Paedagogus, chapter 2; Pliny, book 14, chapter 22; Plutarch, book 1 of the Symposiacs, problem 4; and Stuckius in the same place.

units.la: CAP. XIII. De clausula conuiuii eiusque speciebus.
units.tr: CAP. XIII. On the closing of a feast and its kinds.

units.la: EX positis iis, quæ conuiuium antecedunt & sunt in ipso conuiuii actu: sequitur de iis, quibus conuiuium clauditur & finitur.
units.tr: Having set out what comes before a feast and what belongs to the feast itself, we now turn to the things by which a feast is closed and ended.

units.la: Eiusmodi sunt: 1, Surrectio. 2, ablutio manuum. 3, propinatio τῆς φιλοτησίας ergo. 4, precatio. 5, valedictio & gratiarum actio. 6, deductio domum.
units.tr: These are: (1) rising from the table; (2) washing the hands; (3) the toast of friendship [τῆς φιλοτησίας]; (4) prayer; (5) farewell and thanksgiving; (6) escorting the guest home.

units.la: Surrectio conuiuæ matura, decora & ciuilis est.Ecclesiastic. cap. 32. 14. Tempestiue surge, ne aciem extremam aguto; excurre domum, ac ne desideto. unde conuiuia ἀνακείμενοι & ἀνάστασις. Unde Clemens Alexand. lib. 2. Paedag. c. 7. dicit, Ante multos surgere, eque conuiuio excedere, esse hominis valde modesti.
units.tr: Rising from the table at the proper time is seemly and courteous. Ecclesiasticus 32:14: Rise early, lest you come to the last place; go out home, and do not linger. Hence the Greek words for reclining at table [ἀνακείμενοι] and for rising [ἀνάστασις]. Hence Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 2, chapter 7, says: To rise before the others and leave the feast early is the mark of a very modest man.

units.la: Consurgendi autem initium faciant ii, qui cæteris ætate, dignitate & authoritate præstant, quiq; minima conuiuatori necessitudine sunt iuncti, sed non nisi cū conuiuatoris venia. Quod si quate necessitas vrgeat, vt nondum finitis epulis surgere & discedere cogaris, caussam probabilē tui discessus afferes, veniamq; submisse conuiuatore & conuiuis petes. Putat Guil. Stuckius more esse optimum vt omnes simul consurgat, quamuis iuniorib. decorum sit vt in tempre ante seniores surgant, iisque administrent ad mensam.
units.tr: Those who excel the rest in age, rank and authority should begin to rise, as should those who are most closely bound to the host; but they should do so only with the host's permission. If some pressing need compels you to rise and leave before the meal is finished, you should give a plausible reason for leaving and humbly ask pardon of the host and the guests. William Stuckius thinks the best custom is for everyone to rise together, although it is becoming for younger guests to rise before their elders at the table and to wait on them there.

units.la: Conuiuator vltimo surget & conuiuas prius surgentes ad diutius manendum epulandumq; humanissimis verbis & precibus inuitabit, importune vero neminem inuitum detinebit, præsertim senes, mulieres grauidas vel minus bene, corpore vel animo affectos, aut quibus necessaria negotia sunt peragenda.
units.tr: The host rises last. He will invite the guests who have risen first to stay longer and to eat, with the most courteous words and entreaties; but he will not unreasonably detain anyone against their will, especially the elderly, pregnant women, those who are unwell in body or mind, or those who have necessary business to attend to.

units.la: Manuum ablutio in quibusdam locis post surrectionem à mensa, in quibusdam adhuc sedentib. ad mensam, peragitur.
units.tr: In some places the washing of hands is done after rising from the table; in others it is still done while seated at the table.

units.la: Propinatio post lotionem à conuiuatore fit, & poculum ὑγιείας & φιλοτησίας, sanitatis & benevolentiæ, conuiuis porrigitur. Pre-
units.tr: The toast is made after the washing by the host, and the cup of health [ὑγιείας] and of friendship [φιλοτησίας], that is, of health and goodwill, is handed round to the guests. Pre-

units.la: Precatio peragitur precibus conceptis & recitatis, vel cantiuncula. Deut. 8. 8. 10. Cum comederis & satiatus fueris, benedices quoq; Iehoua Deo tuo in illa terra optima quam dederit tibi. 11. Caue tibi ne obliuiscaris Iehoua Dei tui, Matth. c. 26. 26. 27. 28. 1. Tim. c. 4. 3. 4. 1. Cor. c. 10. 30. 31. Eccl. c. 32. 16, atque hus fruens benedic ei qui fecit te & qui inebriat te bonis suis.
units.tr: Prayer is said with prayers composed and recited, or with a short song. Deuteronomy 8:10–11: When you have eaten and are satisfied, you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you. Take care lest you forget the LORD your God. Matthew 26:26–28; 1 Timothy 4:3–4; 1 Corinthians 10:30–31; Ecclesiasticus 32:16: Enjoying this, bless him who made you and who fills you with his good things.

units.la: Valedictio & gratiarum actio primum fit a conuiua pro beneficiis & officiis praestitis quae verbis extollit & referendae gratiae animu & voluntatem propensam defert conuiuatori & pollicetur.
units.tr: The farewell and thanksgiving are first made by the guest, who, with words, praises the benefits and kindnesses received, and expresses to the host his readiness to repay the favour and his goodwill.

units.la: Huic conuiuator gratias agendo respondet, quod ad epulas suasvenire non sint grauati, eosque rogat ut tenuitatem aequi boniq; consulant; non voluntatem, sed facultatem illos liberalius pro illorum dignitate atq; meritis tractandi, defuisse indicat.
units.tr: The host replies with thanks, saying that they were not reluctant to come to his feast and asking them to take the meagreness of the meal in good part and kindly. He declares that it was not his willingness but his means that were lacking to entertain them more generously, as their rank and merits deserved.

units.la: Deinde antequam discedatur, variae & multiplices salutationes, valedictionesq; honorificae & amicae inter conuiuatorem & conuiuas fieri solent, idq; partim verbis, partim gestibus, manuum datione mutua, osculo, vel complexu. Atque tum apud quosdam munera conuiuis, & collectae, comessalia conuiuatori dari in quibusdam locis solent.
units.tr: Then, before the company breaks up, various and manifold greetings and honourable, friendly farewells are usually exchanged between host and guests, partly in words, partly in gestures, by clasping hands, by a kiss or by an embrace. In some places gifts and contributions are then given to the guests, and a feast-gift to the host.

units.la: Deductio domum fieri debet, vel curari, a conuiuatore per lucernae gestorem, si nox est. Eccles. c. 32. 14. 2. Sam. c. 6. 19. 20. 1. Sam. c. 9. 25. 26. 27. c. 10. 1. 2. 9. 10. Matth. c. 25.
units.tr: The guest should be escorted home, or the host should see to it that he is escorted, by a man carrying a lantern if it is night. Ecclesiasticus 32:14; 2 Samuel 6:19–20; 1 Samuel 9:25–27; 10:1–2, 9–10; Matthew 25.

units.la: Reliquiae conuiuii, quae dicuntur, colligendae ab analectis. Matth. c. 14. Marci. cap. 8. 2. Reg. cap. 4. Leuit, cap. 8. Plutarch. l. b. 7. Sympos. problem. 4. & mensa tollenda eodem modo, quo parata. Itaq; orbes colliguntur primò, deinde salsamenta, caseus & reliqua, & vltimo vnà cum pane remouetur & mappa.
units.tr: The leftovers, as they are called, should be gathered up by those who collect scraps. Matthew 14; Mark 8; 2 Kings 4; Leviticus 8; Plutarch, Symposiaca, book 7, problem 4. The table is cleared in the same order in which it was laid. So the dishes are gathered first, then the salted foods, the cheese and the rest, and last of all the bread and the cloth are removed.

units.la: Atq; tantum de membris conuiuii; sequitur de eiusdem speciebus.
units.tr: This is enough on the parts of a feast; we now turn to its kinds.

units.la: Sunt igitur, vt Stuckius lib.1. cap.16. & seqq. conuiu. antiq. refert, alia conuiuia natalitia, alia puerperalia, repotia, alia ablactationis. Gen.cap.21. 1.Sam.c.1. alia quę in numerum, vel ordinem religiosorum vel alium susceptione, siue initiatione celebrantur. de quib. Exo.c.29. Levit.c.6. cap.8. Macrob.lib.3. Saturnal.cap.13. Conuiuium inaugurale Papæ Romani describit Stuckius lib.1.c.18. & in initiatione monachorum & monialium, & regum: de quibus 1.Sam.c.9.1.Chro.c.12. 2.Sam. c.6.1.Reg.c.1.Est. c.1. Huc etiam conuiuia inauguralia Imperatorum, Doctorum, Magistrorum, Rectorum, Consulum: Item, conuiuia foederalia, Genes.c.26. 2.Sam.c.3.20. Genes.c.31.c.21. in quibus panis & sal, fœderis symbola apud veteres.
units.tr: There are therefore, as Stuckius reports in book 1, chapters 16 and following of Convivia antiqua, different feasts: birthday feasts, lying-in feasts, wedding-after feasts (repotia), and feasts for weaning. Genesis 21; 1 Samuel 1. Others are celebrated for the admission of someone to a number or order of religious persons, or for their initiation in some other way, concerning which see Exodus 29; Leviticus 6; 8; Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 3, chapter 13. Stuckius, book 1, chapter 18, describes the inaugural feast of the Pope of Rome, and feasts at the initiation of monks, nuns and kings. On these see 1 Samuel 9; 1 Chronicles 12; 2 Samuel 6; 1 Kings 1; Esther 1. To these belong also the inaugural feasts of emperors, teachers, masters, rectors and consuls; likewise covenant feasts, Genesis 26; 2 Samuel 3:20; Genesis 31:21, in which bread and salt were among the ancient symbols of a covenant.

units.la: Sunt etiam conuiuia militaria, victorialia, triumphalia, de quibus Stuckius lib.1.c.21. vbi etiam de donatiuis & congiariis. De victu militari Iudæorum, vid.1.Sam.c.17.2.Reg.c.17. Levit.c.23. Ruth.c.2. de epulis victorialibus, Iudic.c.16.1.Reg. c.18. & 2.Chronic.c.20.Iudith.c.15.
units.tr: There are also military feasts, feasts of victory and triumphal feasts, of which Stuckius speaks in book 1, chapter 21, where he also treats of gifts to soldiers and largesses. On the military fare of the Jews see 1 Samuel 17; 2 Kings 17; Leviticus 23; Ruth 2. On victory feasts see Judges 16; 1 Kings 18; 2 Chronicles 20; Judith 15.

units.la: Sunt alia artificum, opificum, rusticorum, in tonsura ouium, 1.Sam.c.25. 2.Sam.c.13. quorum varia genera apud rusticos Germanos recenset Stuckius lib.1.c.23. Et alia vsitata in muneris depositione, alia in peregrinatione, loci domiciliiue mutatione, 2. Reg. cap. 19. Stuck. d. libr. 1. cap. 29.
units.tr: There are other feasts of craftsmen, workmen and country folk, such as at the sheep-shearing, 1 Samuel 25; 2 Samuel 13, the various kinds of which Stuckius lists among the German peasants in book 1, chapter 23. Others are customary at the laying down of an office, others on a journey, or at a change of residence. 2 Kings 19. Stuckius, the same book, chapter 29.

units.la: Rursum alia conuiuia erant nuptilia, Genes. c. 24. Tob. c. 10. Iohan. c. 2. alia funeralia, feralia, exequialia, sepulchralia. 1. Sam. c. 31. 35. Eccles. cap. 30. Tob. c. 1. Baruch. c. 6. 17. Ezech. cap. 24. quae etiam Graecis & Romanis visitata fuere; Liu. lib. 9. decad. 4.
units.tr: Again, there were wedding feasts, Genesis 24; Tobit 10; John 2; and funeral, memorial, burial and sepulchral feasts. 1 Samuel 31, 35; Ecclesiasticus 30; Tobit 1; Baruch 6, 17; Ezekiel 24. These were also practised among the Greeks and Romans; Livy, book 9, decade 4.

units.la: Alia conuiuia porro sunt popularium, adue-narum, hospitum, peregrinorum, conducta em-ptave, vel gratis exhibita peregrinis, humanita-tis, benignitatis & beneuolentiae testificandae causa, quae Graecis φιλοξενία: quorum exempla ex-tant Genes. cap. 18. c. 19. c. 24. Hebr. c. 13. Iudic. cap. 6. Iosue c. 2. 2. Reg. c. 4. Exod. c. 18. 1. Sam. c. 9. 22. Luc. c. 10. Iob. c. 11. 1. Pet. c. 4. 1. Timoth. c. 4. Tit. c. 1. Eiusmodi hospites molliter collocandi, ad cibum potum-que inuitandi, defendendi ab iniuria, non inui-ti retinendi, sed dimittendi, deducendi, Gell. lib. 5. c. 13. Vid. latius Stuck. d. lib. 1. c. 27. 28. de merce-naria peregrinos excipiendi ratione, de stabulis & diuersoriis mercenariis.
units.tr: Further feasts are given to fellow citizens, to strangers, to guests and to travellers, whether hired or provided free to travellers, to show humanity, kindness and goodwill; the Greeks call this hospitality [φιλοξενία]. Examples are found in Genesis 18; 19; 24; Hebrews 13; Judges 6; Joshua 2; 2 Kings 4; Exodus 18; 1 Samuel 9; 22; Luke 10; Job 11; 1 Peter 4; 1 Timothy 4; Titus 1. Such guests should be lodged gently, invited to food and drink, defended from injury, and not kept against their will, but dismissed, and escorted on their way. Gellius, book 5, chapter 13. On the better-known way of receiving travellers for payment, and on hired inns and lodgings, see Stuckius, the same book, chapters 27 and 28.

units.la: Erant & alia sacra conuiuia apud Iudaeos, e-pulum Paschalis, Exod. c. 12. Pentecostes, Num. c. 28. Deut. c. 16. de festo tabernaculorum, Leu. c. 23. De conuiuio Calendarum, seu Nouilunii. 1. Sam. c. 20. 5. 15. Prou. c. 7. Psalm. 81. 3. Imo in plerif-que Iudaeorum sacrificiis anniuersariis conuiuia totius populi erant. Deut. c. 1. v. 23. & 26. c. 16. 11. Leuit. c. 7. v. 5. 6. Exempla extant 1. Sam. c. 1. c. 16. c. 9. 1. Reg. c. 8. 1. Chron. c. 16. Nehem. c. 8. de Christi conuiuio, Matth. c. 26. Marc. c. 14.
units.tr: There were also other sacred feasts among the Jews: the Passover feast, Exodus 12; Pentecost, Numbers 28; Deuteronomy 16; the Feast of Tabernacles, Leviticus 23; the feast of the calends, or of the new moon, 1 Samuel 20:5, 15; Proverbs 7; Psalm 81:3. Indeed, in most of the annual sacrifices of the Jews, feasts were for the whole people. Deuteronomy 1:23, 26; 16:11; Leviticus 7:5–6. Examples are found in 1 Samuel 1; 16; 9; 1 Kings 8; 1 Chronicles 16; Nehemiah 8. On the feast of Christ, see Matthew 26; Mark 14.

units.la: Apud Christianos visitatae quandoque fue-runt Agapae, quae charitatis symbolum & testera,in quibus diuites & pauperes promiscue dif-cumbebant & abstentibus mittebantur portiones:&ditiores conferebant vinum,panes,pecuniam,&c.de quibus mentio fit Act. c.2. c.4.2. Pet.c.2.Tertullian.in sua Apolog. c.39. & quorum abusus taxatur 1.Cor.c.10.add.Eccles.c.9.10. Apud Ethnicos quoque conuiuia sacra celebrata fuere Bacchanalia, Saturnalia & plura alia, de quib. late Stuckius.
units.tr: Among Christians, the love-feasts (Agapae), which were a symbol and token of charity, were at times practised. In them rich and poor reclined together, and portions were sent to those who did not attend; the wealthier brought wine, bread, money and so on. These are mentioned in Acts 2; 4; 2 Peter 2; Tertullian, Apology, chapter 39, and their abuse is condemned in 1 Corinthians 10, and cf. Ecclesiastes 9:10. Among the heathen too, sacred feasts were celebrated: the Bacchanalia, the Saturnalia and many others, of which Stuckius writes at length.

units.la: Erant & quaedam priuata conuiuia amicorum familiarium, quae per vices agitabantur, quorum exempla extant in Job c.1.& in charistia Romanorum, Val.Max.lib.2. c.1. Mutua eiusmodi conuiuia agitare est muritare, vt ait Gellius lib.2.c.24. Sunt & hodie in quibusdam locis visitata conuiuia sodalitia, & collegiatae coitiones & fyfitia.Stuck.d.lib.1.c.31. & quaedam publica conuiuia in prytaneo.
units.tr: There were also certain private feasts of friends and familiars, which were held in turn; examples are found in Job 1, and in the Roman charistia, Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 1. To hold such feasts in turn is to reciprocate, as Gellius says, book 2, chapter 24. Clubs, fellowships and associations that dine together, and what are called syssitia, are also still practised in some places today. Stuckius, the same book, chapter 31; and certain public feasts in the prytaneum.

units.la: Pro epilogo huius materiae subiungam ex Joh. Guil.Stuckio lib.1. cap.3. duo extrema vitia couiuiorum, conuiuarum & conuiuatorum. Vnum,quo in defectu peccatur,quod est, prorsus abhorrere a consuetudine conuiuiorum, dum alios ad epularum nostrarum communionem non inuitamus, neque inuitati ad alio- rum conuiuia accedimus: (quales sunt μονοφάγοι) nisi ex iusta causa illud fiat,qualis fuit monophagia Iohannis Baptiste & Ieremia c.16. Deinde, quando quis alios quidem inuitat, iisque epulas suas impertit, at aliorum epulas & conuiuia aspernatur, quod insolentiae, superbiae & morositati adscribendum. Tertio, quando quis inuitatus libenter quidem ad aliorum con-uiuia ũiuia accedit, at ille neminem inuitat; quod vitium est ingratitudinis & impudentiæ; ex quo dicitur ἀποτρωφάγῳ. Quarto, quando quis inuitatos nimis tenuiter & sordide tractat, semifamelicos, vel litientes dimittit, qui μικρολογούμενοι dicuntur.
units.tr: As an epilogue to this subject I will add, from Johann Wilhelm Stuck, book 1, chapter 3, the two extreme vices of banquets, those of hosts and those of guests. The first, which is a fault of deficiency, is to shrink entirely from the custom of feasting: a man neither invites others to share his meals nor, when invited, goes to their banquets. Such people are the solitary eaters [μονοφάγοι]. This is excusable only if it is done for a just cause, as with the solitary life of John the Baptist and Jeremiah, ch. 16. Second, when someone does invite others and shares his meals with them, but scorns the meals and banquets of others, this is to be ascribed to insolence, pride and surliness. Third, when someone gladly goes to the banquets of others when invited, but never invites anyone himself, this is the vice of ingratitude and shamelessness, and such a person is called a free-loader [ἀποτρωφάγος]. Fourth, when someone treats his guests too meanly and sordidly, dismissing them half-starved or barely fed, they are called the niggardly [μικρολογούμενοι].

units.la: Alterum vitium extremum est in excessu, comessabilitas scilicet, qua inordinata, immoderata & effrena conuiuiorum cupiditate detestamur, non ex honestatis charitatisque erga proximum studio, sed ex ambitione, superbia, insatiabili quadam & inexplebili voluptatum cupiditate. Cognoscitur id vitium ex nimia conuiuiorum cupiditate, crebritate & frequentia, item in eorum effuso sumptuosoque apparatu, ferculorum luxuriosò splendore, varietate & nimia turba, in temporis ἀκαιρίᾳ, in dictorum & factorum obscœnitate. Horum finis est, non gloria Dei, non mutui amoris, benevolentiæ, charitatisve conseruatio; sed voluptatis amor, libido, superbia, auaritia, ambitio. Hac crebro luxurioseque conuiuandi consuetudine qui flagrant, eleganter à Græcis dicuntur φιλοδείπνοι, τρισχιλιόδειπνοι, ὑπερμεγαλοδείπνοι, δειπνομανεῖς, ἀπολωφάγοι.
units.tr: The second extreme vice is the excess, namely comessation, or revelry, by which we denounce an unrestrained, immoderate and wild desire for banquets. This does not arise from zeal for honesty or from love of neighbour, but from ambition, pride and an insatiable, boundless craving for pleasures. This vice is recognised by an excessive desire for banquets, by their frequency and crowding; likewise by their lavish and costly preparation, the luxurious splendour of the dishes, their variety and excessive throng; by unseasonable timing [ἀκαιρία]; and by obscenity in words and deeds. Their end is not the glory of God, nor the preservation of mutual love, goodwill or charity, but the love of pleasure, lust, pride, greed and ambition. Those who burn with this habit of frequent and luxurious feasting are elegantly called by the Greeks dinner-lovers [φιλοδείπνοι], thrice-thousand-dinner men [τρισχιλιόδειπνοι], super-great-dinner men [ὑπερμεγαλοδείπνοι], dinner-maniacs [δειπνομανεῖς], and gobblers [ἀπολωφάγοι].

units.la: Ex his sequitur malum esse finem conuiuiorum, vanam illam & inanem magnificentiæ, potentiæ, opulentiæ, ostentationem. Vid. Ester cap. 1. Deinde, ventrem tanquam Deum sibi proponere, vt hic saginetur & distendatur immodico cibo potuque. Quidam etiam auaritiæ suæ tegendæ causa, conuiuiorum splendore vtuntur. Quidam maiorum commodorum consequendorum caufla lautis & opi-paris conuiuiis alios inescare student. Quidam, quo scelerum impunitatem consequantur, iudicum aliorumque ora offis illis obiectis obturare cogitant & mentes eorum excæcare. Quidam gratiam suis conuiuiis aucupare student, & viam atque aditum ad honores vel munera sibi muniunt. Denique conuiuiis sæpe homines ad aliorum exitium interitumque abutuntur, dum inuitatos vi aperta vel clam veneno impiė &nefariė vita priuant,quæ sunt conuiuia Thyestea, Agamemnonia atque Cyclopica. Vid. Ieremi. cap. 4. 2. 2. Reg. cap. 25. 1. Reg. cap. 13. 1. Macchab. c. 13. Efter cap. 6. Judith. cap. 12. 13.
units.tr: From this it follows that it is an evil aim of banquets when they serve that vain and empty ostentation of magnificence, power and opulence. See Esther ch. 1. Next, a man proposes his belly to himself as a god, so that it may be stuffed and distended with immoderate food and drink. Some use the splendour of their banquets to conceal their avarice. Some strive to lure others with lavish and sumptuous feasts in order to gain greater advantages. Some, to secure impunity for their crimes, plan to stop the mouths of judges and others with morsels thrown to them, and to blind their minds. Some seek to win favour through their banquets and pave for themselves a way and access to honours or gifts. Finally, men often abuse banquets for the destruction and ruin of others, when they impiously and wickedly deprive their guests of life, either by open force or secretly by poison. These are the Thyestean, Agamemnonian and Cyclopean banquets. See Jer. 4. 2 Kings 25. 1 Kings 13. 1 Maccabees 13. Esther 6. Judith 12, 13.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: END
